units.la: [?]LARISSIMO VIRO IOANNI DALLÆO.
units.tr: To the most distinguished man, John Dallaeus.

units.la: PRODIIT non ita pridem VIR CLARISSIME Scriptorum Anglorum Trias, qui etsi diuersa tractárint [?]umenta, in eo tamen conuenerunt omnes, quod [?]busdam Parentis tui τῷ μακαρίτῃ lucubrationialiquod vulnus infligere sint conati ; sed [?]ssu parùm fœlici : Primus eorum Ioannes [?]sonius Presbyter, Vir sanè doctus & in antiquitate Ecclesiasticâ exercitatissimus, S. [?]ctij Epistolarum Vindicias edidit, aduersus ea quæ scripserat Pater tuus, ut omni[?]nanifestum faceret, suppositicias esse quæ [?]ij nomine circumferuntur Epistolas, & [?]issimo Martyre prorsus indignas: Secundus [?]elmus Beveregius Presbyter ipse quoque, hoc litterarum genere non sine laude versatus, cùm ægrè ferret recentiorem quàm vellet Epocham, Canonibus qui Apostolorum nomen falsò præferunt, à præstantissimo Dallæo assignatam esse, tertium illius librum de Pseudigraphis Apostolicis impugnantium quodammodo suscepit. Tertius denique Matthæus Scriverenus Presbyteri etiam nomine & dignitate gaudens, ejusdem Dallæi Tractatum de usu Patrum adortus est; sed tantâ animi impotentiâ, ut convitijs illum certare dixeris, potiùs quàm rationum momentis: Quamobrem prætermissò isto Scriptore qui sibi temperare non potest ab obtrectationibus ac maledictis, in quibus præcipuum causæ quærit præsidium; Et observationibus quas in aliorum scripta exaravi contentus, ut auctoris maledicentissimi librum expenderem & confutarem à me impetrare non potui. Porrò has Observationes quæcunque sint, meo statim privato usui destinaveram; fecit tamen tanti Viri Parentis tui nomen, cujus amicitiam dùm vixit ambitiosè colui, & cujus memoria mihi bonisque omnibus semper erit carissima, fecit, inquam, ut eas tecum mutato consilio libenter communicarem. Unum illius crimen si nosse velis, audi, Episcoporum ὑπεροχὴν supra Presbyte-ros ab hominum institutione vel ab an-tiquâ admodùm consuetudine derivavit, nec juris esse divini uspiam confessus est: ingens piaculum si istis credis; nempe illa Episcopatus ὑπεροχὴ in delicijs est Viris hisce Eruditis, qui eam impatienter diligunt; hinc fit ut corrasis undique argumentis, & conquisitis rationibus, omnes ingenij vires explicent, ad probandum Episcopatus gradum, si non ab ipso Christo, saltem ab illius A-postolis à Presbyteratus gradu sejunctum esse, & utrumque separatim institutum, adeò ut ab initio duo fuerint ordines inter se distincti; Et quia desunt ad probandum primæ Antiquitatis vera ac genuina monumenta, ad salsa, apocrypha, & ὑποβολιμαῖα confugiunt, qualia sunt pluribus, quorum unus fuit Dallæus, Ignatianæ Epistolæ; omnibus verò Eruditis: Canones qui Apostolorum inscribuntur; Nemo enim est in scriptis Patrum vel leviter versatus, qui non ingenuè profiteatur, sanctos Domini Apostolos Canones istos minimè condidisse; Quare omnis inter litteratos de hoc argumento controversia, ad majorem vel minorem regularum istarum spectat vetustatem, aliis maturiùs sancitas, aliis verò tardiùs conflatas existimantibus. Cave tamen CLARISSIME DALLÆE ne ita meam mentem explices, velut Episcopatui qualis inter Protestantes Anglos obtinet infensius essem, ab sit à me talis animi cogitatio: Episcopatum enim ipsum juris esse divini ingenuè prositeor: Et quamvis Episcoporum eminentiam supra Presbyteros institutionis esse mere humanæ firmissimè credam, præstat tamen meo quidem judicio regimen illud Episcopale patienter ferre, eiquè ultrò ac sponte se subjicere, quàm dissidia aut Schismata illius occasione excitare & fovere in Ecclesiâ, in quâ omnia εὐσχημόνως καὶ κατὰ τάξιν fieri debent: Episcopos autem quod attinet , æquum est ut aliquid infirmitati condonent humanæ , ritus & cærimonias quæ ab Evangelij simplicitate nimis discedere pluribus videntur, in gratiam infirmorum resecent ; potestatem suam intra legitimos coërceant limites istorum D. Petri verborum memores, non ut dominantes Cleris, sed ut sitis exemplaria Gregis ; Synodos frequentiús convocent, in quibus condantur vel renoventur decreta, veritati propagandæ, imperioque Domini nostri Iesu Christi stabiliendo ac dilatando, apta atque idonea , Presbyteranorum denique quos vocant Ministros in numero fratrum habeant, eosque tanquam Symmystas & in eodem Domini opere συνεργῶς[?] amplestantur, exemplo Prædecessorum qui arctissimam cum illis semper & Christianissimam coluerunt unionem. Vtinam idem sentiamus omnes , nihilque habeamus antiquius, quàm Dei gloriam & Ecclesiæ ædificationem , ad quam referri debent omnia studia nostra, ut dum sistemur apud Christi tribunal, eum nos sic blandè singulos compellantem audire mereamur, serve bone & fidelis, ingredere in gaudium Domini tui. Cæterum VIR CLARISSIME de nomine meo noli esse sollicitus: expressum Scriptoris nomen nihil addit ejus lucubrationibus, suppressum nihil admit: Unum est quod à te sciri vehementer cupio; ab amicâ videlicet manu proficisci quæ tibi offeruntur observationes, eas ergo faventibus accipe oculis, ut certum ac sincerum amicitiæ symbolum, meæque erga Parentis tui nomen nunquam moriturum reverentiæ sempiternum pignus. Vale.
units.tr: Not long ago there appeared the Trias of English Writers, most distinguished sir, and although its three authors handled different matters, they all agreed in this: that they tried to inflict some wound on certain writings of your father of blessed memory [τῷ μακαρίτῃ], but with little success. The first of them, John [Pearson], a presbyter and a truly learned man, very well practised in ecclesiastical antiquity, published the Vindiciae of the Epistles of St. Ignatius, against what your father had written, in order to show clearly that the letters which circulate under Ignatius's name are spurious and wholly unworthy of so great a martyr. The second, Bevereg[e], also a presbyter, who had himself practised this kind of writing not without praise, took up, in some measure, the third book of Dallaeus's work on the apostolic pseudepigrapha, since he was vexed that the most excellent Dallaeus had assigned the Canons, which falsely bear the apostles' name, to a later date than he wished. The third, Matthew Scriverius, who likewise enjoys the name and rank of presbyter, attacked the treatise of the same Dallaeus on the use of the Fathers; but with such loss of temper that you would say he contended with abuse rather than with the weight of argument. For this reason I have set aside that writer, who cannot restrain himself from detraction and abuse, in which he seeks his chief defence of his cause. Content with the observations I have written on the works of others, I could not bring myself to weigh and refute the book of that most abusive author. Indeed, these Observations, whatever they are worth, I had intended from the start for my own private use. Yet the name of your father, a man of such standing, whose friendship I eagerly cultivated while he lived, and whose memory will always be most dear to me and to all good men, prompted me, I say, to change my plan and gladly share them with you. If you wish to know the one charge brought against him, hear it: he derived the pre-eminence of bishops over presbyters [ὑπεροχὴ] from human institution or from very ancient custom, and admitted that it is nowhere of divine right. That is, if you believe these men, a monstrous crime. Clearly that pre-eminence of bishops is a delight to these learned men, who love it impatiently. Hence, having gathered arguments from every quarter and sought out reasons, they exert all the powers of their wit to prove that the episcopal office, if not from Christ himself, at least from his apostles, was separated from the presbyterate, and that the two were instituted separately, so that from the beginning there were two distinct orders. And since they lack true and genuine monuments of the earliest antiquity to prove this, they take refuge in false, spurious and supposititious writings, such as, for many of them, the Epistles of Ignatius were, one of which was Dallaeus's; but for all learned men, the Canons which are inscribed with the apostles' names. For there is no one who has even lightly worked through the writings of the Fathers who does not frankly confess that the holy apostles of the Lord did not compose those Canons. So the whole controversy among scholars on this subject concerns only whether those rules are more or less ancient, some thinking they were enacted earlier, others that they were put together later. Yet, most distinguished Dallaeus, take care not to explain my mind in such a way as to suppose that I am more hostile to episcopacy, of the kind that prevails among the English Protestants. Far be such a thought from me. For I frankly profess that episcopacy itself is of divine right. And although I firmly believe that the pre-eminence of bishops over presbyters is purely of human institution, in my judgement it is better to bear patiently that episcopal government, and to submit to it willingly and of our own accord, than to stir up and foster quarrels or schisms in the Church on its account, in which all things ought to be done decently and in order [εὐσχημόνως καὶ κατὰ τάξιν]. As for the bishops, it is right that they should yield something to human weakness, and cut away, for the sake of the weak, those rites and ceremonies which many think depart too far from the simplicity of the Gospel. Let them confine their power within lawful limits, mindful of the words of St. Peter, not as lords over the clergy, but as examples to the flock. Let them convene synods more often, in which decrees are enacted or renewed, suitable and fit for spreading the truth and for establishing and extending the sway of our Lord Jesus Christ. Lastly, let them count among their brethren those whom they call presbyterian ministers, and embrace them as fellow-workers and as synergists [συνεργῶς] in the same work of the Lord, following the example of their predecessors, who always maintained the closest and most Christian unity with them. Would that we all thought alike, and had nothing more at heart than the glory of God and the building up of the Church, to which all our efforts ought to be directed, so that when we are set before the judgement seat of Christ we may deserve to hear him address each of us so kindly: Well done, good and faithful servant, enter into the joy of your lord. For the rest, most distinguished sir, do not be anxious about my name. A name written out adds nothing to a writer's works; a name suppressed takes nothing away. There is one thing I very much wish you to know: that the observations offered to you come from a friendly hand. Receive them, therefore, with a favourable eye, as a sure and sincere token of friendship, and as an everlasting pledge of my reverence for your father's name, which will never die. Farewell.

units.la: OBSERVATIONES IN PRIOREM VINDICIARUM PARTEM.
units.tr: OBSERVATIONS ON THE FIRST PART OF THE VINDICIAE.

units.la: I[?]Gnatianæ eruditissimi Pearsonij vindiciæ à quibus nostras inchoamus observationes, nihil aliud sunt proprie quàm exceptiones ad Dallæi argumenta, quibus Epistolas quarum. patrocinium suscipit vir doctus, impugnare, cásque à plano quodam S. Ignatio subditas esse demonstrare aggressus est. Verùm ex numerosissimâ Dallæanorum argumentorum turbâ, præcipua tantùm & magis necessaria selegi expendenda, non solùm quia varijs distractus occupationibus duo adversus Pearsonium & Beveregium justa conscribere volumina vix permittor:sed imprimis quoniam ex ijs quæ ab omnibus Pearsonianis exceptionibus vindicaturi fumus argumentis, liquidò constabit à scriptore S.Ignatio longè juniore consarcinatas esse quas impugnavit Dallæus epistolas. Doctissimus vindiciarum auctor in totius Operis Proëmio de ortu,progressu,& hodierno statu controversiæ fusissimè tractat : In numero tamen Epistolarum non ei convenit cum Vsserio suo Archiepiscopo Armachano,Pearsonius enim septem ab Eusebio S. Ignatio attributas censet, inter quas Epistolam ad Polycarpum numerandam esse contendit : Vsserius verò non propter nullius momenti suspiciunculas, ut ait vir quidam eruditus notis in hanc ipsam ad Polycarpum Epistolam, sed validissimis, ut putabat, ad id impulsus rationibus Vsserius, inquam, Ignatio eam abjudicat, nullámque Polycarpo privatim inscriptam extitisse Epistolam arbitratur,sed illam unicam quæ ipsi cum Smyrnæis suis communiter est dicata, plurésque laudat suæ sententiæ adstipulatores, Proleg. ad Ignat. cap.2. pag. 8.immò hanc fuisse Hieronymi mentem non dubitat:quod imprimis colligit ex Honorio Augustodunensi, qui in libro de Luminaribus Ecclesiæ( cui inquit Hieronymianum scriptorum catalogum in Epitomen à se redactum inseruit ) Epistolam ad Polycarpum in censu scriptorum Ignatij plane prætermittendam esse judicavit, ita videlicet verbis Hieronymi acceptis, ac si nulla peculiaris ad Polycarpum data, intellecta hic ab eo fuisset Epistola; sed illa ad Smyrnæos, tum eis tum ipsi præcipuè, ut eorum Episcopo conjunctim inscripta fuisset; nec desunt hodie etiam in Ecclesiâ Romanâ hujusce Vsferij opinionis suffragatores, verbi gratia, Cardinalis Bona lib. 1. Rerum Liturgicarum cap. 22. pag. 189. ibi enim respondens Baronio verbis quibusdam Epistolæ ad Polycarpum abutenti, hæc habet Addo quod hanc Epistolam non genuinum Ignatij fœtum esse, sed supposittitium viri eruditi dudum observarunt, & ad id probandum multa afferunt non parvi ponderis argumenta. Hinc argumentum non leve deducitur adversus omnes Ignatianas Syllloges Polycarpi Epistolas; nam si Epistola Polycarpo inscripta in dubium vocatur, si incertæ est fidei, si ut spuria à pluribus rejicitur, si viri eruditi observarunt non genuinum Ignatij fœtum esse, sed suppositium, idque probarunt argumentis non contemnendis, ut asserit Cardinalis Bona, quis mihi cæterarum fidem præstiturus est? Nutat istius fides; aliarum etiam fidem nutare necesse est; reperiuntur omnes in eâdem collectione, ergo vel tota approbanda sylloge vel tota reprobanda, partim reprobari, partim autem probari non potest, alioquin sequeretur unum eundemque unius ejusdémque ingenij foetum, partim genuinum partimque suppositium esse, quod fieri nequit; nisi forte aliquid alienâ manu assutum demōstretur. Nam quemadmodum in Logicis unicus sufficit ut ita dicam defectus, seu potiùs unica exceptio ad evertendam universalem propositionem affirmantem, sic ad omnem alicui scripto fidem detrahendam unica sufficit suppositionis nota; jam autem quodnam isto majus excogitari potest suppositionis τεκμήριον [?] ? in sylloge quâ de agitur septem extant Epistolæ Ignatio æqualiter attributæ, tamen quæ inter illas ad Polycarpum data est, ab Vsserio, à Cardinale Bona aliisque suæ communionis viris eruditis, tanquam supposititia & Ignatio indigna rejicitur: Nonne eâdem ratione respuenda erit universa sylloge quæ tanto laborat incommodo, & quæ suo se prodit judice? Nec me movet quod Vsserius Hieronymi verba ita explicat, ac si intactis sex istius sylloges Epistolis, solam quæ ad Polycarpum data est, è censu scriptorum Ignatij expungere sibi liceret; cùm enim Hieronymus sua de Ignatianis ab Eusebio mutuatus sit , liquet veram mentis illius interpretationem ab ipso Eusebio esse petendam,Eusebius verò non minùs diserte loquitur de Epistolâ Polycarpo inscripta , quàm de cæteris in collectione Polycarpiana comprehensis ; si igitur ficta est & suppositicia Epistola Polycarpo inscripta, ut volunt quidam viri docti Pearsonio hac in controversia minimè suspecti, periclitabitur sanè de falso tota syllogé, & deinceps à nasutis & sagacibus velut scriptum sublestæ fidei reputabitur. Hoc vidit eruditus Pearsonius, & illi seriò dolens quod Vsserius de numero Epistolarum ab illo dissentiret, nihil in proëmio intactum reliquit ; ut istius ad Polycarpum Epistolæ vacillantem fidem firmaret, eíque labanti humeros substerneret : Verùm pace tanti viri dixerim, non æquum est ut Pearsonij & ὁμοφώνων[?] sententia, Vsserij & aliorum eruditorum sententiæ præponderet, viri sunt utrínque docti, Ignatianorum fautores, eorúmque flagrantissimo amore correpti; interea ex eorum conflictu hoc emolumenti ad nos redit , quod sibi contrarij esse non possunt, quin nobiscum faciant , nimirum id agunt sua dissensione, ut syllogen illam cui praecipuè innititur tota Pearsonianæ disputationis moles, nobis magis ac magis suspectam, dubiam & ancipitem reddant; ac proinde inutilem ad probandum quæ probanda vir doctus in se receperat.
units.tr: Pearson's most learned Vindiciae of the Ignatian letters, which I am beginning my observations on, are properly nothing other than replies to the arguments of Daillé, by which that learned man attacks the letters whose defence he has taken up, and he sets out to show that they are the work of some forger later than Ignatius. But from the very large crowd of Daillé's arguments I have chosen only the chief and most necessary ones for examination. I have done this not only because I am scarcely allowed, distracted as I am by various occupations, to write two full volumes against Pearson and Beveridge, but above all because, from the arguments which I shall defend against all Pearson's objections, it will be clear beyond doubt that the letters Daillé attacked were cobbled together by a writer much later than Ignatius. The most learned author of the Vindiciae, in the Preface to the whole work, treats at great length the origin, progress and present state of the controversy. Yet on the number of the letters he does not agree with his own Archbishop of Armagh, Ussher. For Pearson thinks that seven letters are attributed to Ignatius by Eusebius, and he contends that the letter to Polycarp must be counted among them. Ussher, however, moved not by mere trifling suspicions, as a certain learned man puts it in his notes on this very letter to Polycarp, but by what he believed to be very strong reasons, rejects it from Ignatius. He holds, I say, that no letter addressed to Polycarp alone ever existed, but only that single letter which is dedicated jointly to Polycarp and to his own Smyrnaeans. He cites several supporters of his opinion (Prolegomena to Ignatius, ch. 2, p. 8). Indeed he does not doubt that this was also the mind of Jerome. He gathers this chiefly from Honorius of Autun, who, in his book On the Luminaries of the Church, into which he inserted Jerome's catalogue of writers reduced to an epitome by himself, judged that the letter to Polycarp should be passed over entirely in the list of Ignatius's writings. He understood Jerome's words as though no separate letter had been addressed to Polycarp, and as though the letter he had in view was the one to the Smyrnaeans, addressed jointly to them and especially to their Bishop. Nor are there lacking today, even in the Roman Church, supporters of this opinion of Ussher. For example, Cardinal Bona, in book 1 of his Rerum Liturgicarum, chapter 22, p. 189, replying to Baronius, who makes improper use of certain words from the letter to Polycarp, says the following: "I add that learned men have long observed that this letter is not a genuine offspring of Ignatius but a spurious one, and they bring many arguments of no small weight to prove it." From this a weighty argument follows against all the Ignatian collections of letters. For if the letter addressed to Polycarp is called in doubt, if its faith is uncertain, if many reject it as spurious, and if learned men have observed that it is not a genuine work of Ignatius but a forgery, and have proved this with arguments not to be despised, as Cardinal Bona asserts, then who will give me assurance of the rest? The credibility of that letter wavers, and the credibility of the others must waver too. They are all found in the same collection. Therefore the whole collection must either be approved or wholly rejected. It cannot be partly rejected and partly accepted; otherwise it would follow that one and the same product of one and the same mind was partly genuine and partly spurious, which cannot be, unless perhaps something is shown to have been stitched on by another hand. For just as in logic a single failure, or rather a single exception, suffices to overturn a universal affirmative proposition, so a single mark of forgery suffices to strip any writing of credit. Now what greater proof of forgery could be devised than this? In the collection under discussion seven letters stand equally attributed to Ignatius, yet the one among them addressed to Polycarp is rejected by Ussher, by Cardinal Bona and by other learned men of his own communion as spurious and unworthy of Ignatius. Must not the whole collection, which suffers from this same defect and betrays itself by its own judgement, be rejected on the same ground? Nor am I moved by Ussher's explanation of Jerome's words, as though he were free to strike out of the list of Ignatius's writings only the letter addressed to Polycarp while leaving the other six in the collection untouched. For since Jerome took what he said about the Ignatian writings from Eusebius, it is clear that the true meaning of his mind must be sought from Eusebius himself. Eusebius speaks no less plainly about the letter addressed to Polycarp than about the others included in the Polycarpian collection. So if the letter addressed to Polycarp is fictitious and spurious, as certain learned men maintain, men by no means suspect to Pearson in this controversy, then the whole collection will certainly be exposed as false, and thereafter the sharp-nosed and shrewd will regard it as a writing of doubtful faith. Learned Pearson saw this, and, grieving that Ussher dissented from him about the number of the letters, he left nothing untouched in his Preface, in order to strengthen the wavering credibility of that letter to Polycarp and to put his shoulders under it as it totters. But with all respect to so great a man, I must say that it is not fair for the opinion of Pearson and of those who agree with him to outweigh the opinion of Ussher and of other learned men. Both sides are learned men, lovers of the Ignatians, and seized with the most burning affection for them. Meanwhile, from their conflict this advantage comes to us: since they cannot be opposed to us, they must in fact side with us. By their disagreement they bring it about that that collection, on which the whole mass of Pearson's argument chiefly rests, becomes more and more suspect to us, doubtful and uncertain, and therefore useless for proving what the learned man had undertaken to prove.

units.la: Verùm ad ipsas accedamus vindicias quas in duas partes divisit Autor, in capite autem tertio prioris partis dicit argumentum de scripti viri Apostolici à testimonijs petitum fallere non posse, nimirum post enumerata in capite secundo omnia veterum testimonia quæ coacervare potuit, ad suam de Ignatianis hypothesim stabiliendam & firmandam, hæc habet initio capitis tertij, certè habemus argumentum de scripto viri Apostolici Ecclesiastico locupletissimum firmissimumque, & quale nunquam adhuc quemquam fefellit, neque si cætera respondeant, quæ in argumento interno afferemus, fallere potuisse putandum est. Hæc observatio quæ viro erudito tanti visa est, majorem mihi lucem desiderare videtur, nam*per scriptum illud viri Apostolici, vel intelligit scriptum cujusdam Apostolorum Discipuli, quales fuerunt Clemens, Ignatius, Polycarpus, vel scriptum viri cujusdam Apostolorum Discipulis æqualis vel supparis, quales iterum fuere Iustinus martyr cujus Martyrium Polycarpi martyrio prius fuit, & Irenæus qui vir audiebat Apostolicus, & plures alij qui Apostolici dici meruerunt. Quoquò se vertat vir doctus causâ cadet, si enim priùs intelligit, quid inde collecturus sit non video, colliget forsan Ignatium legitimum esse patentem Epistolarum de quibus controvertitur; sed si hanc elicit conclusionem petit [illegible, ~8 letters], & quod est in quæstione supponit, quia Dallæus has Epistolas genuinum esse Ignatij fœtum negabat, & præterea pertendebat t[?]rium primorum sæculorum testes, quos Ignatianorum fautores adducere solent intestabiles esse, vel saltem nullius ferè ponderis, cùm scripta è quibus testimonia eruuntur dubia sint, ideóque fidei faciendæ haud idonea, expendenda ergò erant celeberrimi Dallæi argumenta, antequam clarissimus Pearsonius istam quam examinamus eliceret conclusionem.
units.tr: But let us come to the Vindiciae themselves, which the author divides into two parts. In chapter 3 of the first part he says that the argument drawn from the testimonies concerning the writing of an Apostolic man cannot deceive. That is, after listing in chapter 2 all the ancient testimonies he could gather to establish and confirm his hypothesis about the Ignatian letters, he says at the beginning of chapter 3: "We certainly have an argument from the writing of an Apostolic man, a most abundant and firm one, of a kind that has never yet deceived anyone, nor can it be thought to have deceived, if the rest agrees with what we shall state in the internal argument." This observation, which seemed so important to the learned man, seems to me to need further light. For by "the writing of that Apostolic man" he means either the writing of one of the disciples of the Apostles, such as Clement, Ignatius, Polycarp, or the writing of a man who was equal or near equal to the Apostles' disciples, such as again Justin Martyr, whose martyrdom came before that of Polycarp, and Irenaeus, who had heard Apostolic men, and several others who deserved to be called Apostolic. Whichever way the learned man turns, his case falls. For if he means the former, I do not see what he will infer from it. He will perhaps infer that Ignatius is the legitimate author of the letters in dispute. But if he draws this conclusion he begs the question [illegible, about 8 letters] and assumes what is in question, since Daillé denied that these letters are a genuine product of Ignatius, and moreover maintained that the testimonies of the first three centuries, which Ignatian supporters are accustomed to bring forward, are worthless, or at least of almost no weight, since the writings from which the testimonies are drawn are doubtful and therefore unfit to establish belief. The famous arguments of Daillé therefore had to be weighed before the most distinguished Pearson could draw the conclusion we are examining. But if he means the latter, namely the writing of a man who was equal or near equal to the Apostles' disciples, then the learned man is mistaken in his opinion. And so that I may not go too far afield, I shall be content with a single example, from which it will be clear that the learned man has gone astray. The example will be taken from the books of…

units.la: Si verò posteriùs intelligit, nempè scriptum viri cujusdam Apostolorum Discipulis æqualis vel supparis, falsus est sua opinione vir eruditus, & ne longiùs abeam, unico contentus ero exemplo, ex quo liquebit hallucinatum esse virum doctum; Exemplum autem desumptum erit è libris sibyllinis qui conscripti sunt ut probavit Blondellus noster, circa annum Æræ Christianæ 142. plus minus, quicquid enim dicit Pearsonius in toto illo capite tertio supra laudato, de testimoniis in gratiam Ignatianorum adductis, dici etiam potest de iis quæ afferri possunt in gratiam sibyllinorum oraculorum, certè neque plura, neque majora, neque certiora extant pro Ignatianis suffragia in veterum Christianorum monumentis, quàm pro sibyllinis, saltem si sæcula ista percurras, secundum scilicet, tertium, quartum & quintum; cùm enim viciniora sint temporibus quæ investigamus, quin majoris momenti esse debeant remotioribus, nemo ut opinor inficias ibit, adducit quidem Pearsonius pro suis Ignatianis Polycarpum & Irenæum secundi sæculi testes, ego pro sibyllinis afferam Iustinum Martyrem, Athenagoram, Theophilum Antiochenum Episcopum, Clementem Alexandrinum, ejusdem sæculi scriptores, Origeni à Pearsonio citato pro tertio, opponam eundem Clementem qui primos illius sæculi annos attigit, Tertullianum, Lactantium qui tertio & quarto floruit, hoc tamen interest inter utráque testimonia, quod ea quæ Pearsonius adducit pro Ignatianis, petita sint è monumentis quorum fides nutat atque vacillat, scripta vero quæ argumenta in gratiam sibyllinorum subministrant & sufficiunt, certissima sunt & indubitata ; cum Pseudo - Dionysio Areopagitâ , Eusebio & Chrysostomo , quarti sæculi testibus à Pearsonio delectis, conferam Lactantium, Autorem constitutionum Apostolicarum , hoc sæculo ut quibusdâ placet consarcinatarum, Constantinum Imperatorem, Eusebium, Optatum, Milevitanum, & cum Theodoreto & Gelasio Papa primo , qui ad quintum pertinent, Hieronymum, Augustinum, Prosperum , Palladium , Sozomenum ; à cæteris sæculis examinandis libens supersedeo ; nam quæ hactenus diximus abundè sufficiunt ad convellendam Pearsonij ratiocinationem, unum tamen addere lubet, nempè hanc observationem Autoris indicis Chronologici & indicis Alphabetici Magnæ Bibliothecæ Patrum. Sibyllarum Oracula magnæ fuisse apud primos Christianos autoritatis , nemini in antiquorum Patrum scriptis vel leviter versato , potest esse dubium, quippe ad quorum lectionem ipsum S. Paulum Christianos adhortatum fuisse , testis est Clemens Alexandrinus lib. 6. Stromatum. Quæ dicit de Clemente Alexandrino verissima sunt, & summam sibyllinorum Oraculorum continent commendationem; constat tamen inter eruditos quorum præjudicata opinio non obruit judicium, sibyllina illa Oracula à plano quodam & impostore, sæculo secundo circiter medio confićta esse, fallere ergo potest argumentum à testimoniis duĉtum, neque fallere modò potest, sed etiam rei-ipsa fallit, claudicat igitur Pearsonij ratiocinatio quàm tanto viro excidisse doleo. Dicet fortèan Pearsonius, sibyllinos libros non esse scriptum Ecclesiasticum, neque scriptum viri Apostolici, sed utrúmque negari posset, primum quidem, quia suum occupat locum in Bibliothecâ SS. Patrum, quia Antiqui Ecclesiæ Doćtores plura ex his libris sumpserunt ad sua probanda dogmata, & quia denique ab homine Christiano conflatum est; secundùm itidem; nam etsi impostor qui sua somnia nobis vendidit, Apostolicus non fuerit ratione doćtrinæ, fuit tamen ratione ætatis, suppar quippè, imò aliquo modo æqualis Ignatio& Polycarpo Apostolorum Discipulis, sua enim consarcinavit figmenta triginta circiter annos post passionem Ignatii, & viginti quatuor ante Polycarpi martyrium. Verùm enimverò ut omnis cavillandi ansa viro doćto præcidatur, concedamus illi scriptum sibyllinum non esse scriptum Viri Apostolici Ecclesiasticum, quid inde deducetur, istud nimirum, argumentum de scripto non Ecclesiastico & viri non Apostolici à testimonijs petitum fallere posse, cùm idem argumentum de scripto viri Apostolici Ecclesiastico nunquam fallat, mira profecto consequentia; nempe veteres Ecclesiastici scriptores varias pro arbitrio induebant formas, variifque erant ornati dotibus, pro varijs librorum characteribus, de quibus testimonium erant laturi, adeò ut aliorum respectu effent plane ἀναμάρτητοι[?], & extra errandi periculum atque aleam constituti, cæterorum autem respectu errori obnoxij & tales ut fides illis adhiberi nequeat nec debeat; nonne hæc sunt suavia vigilantium somnia è solo causæ studio nata; præsertim cùm in Ignatianis Epistolis deprehendantur suppositionis notæ, æquè ac in libris sibyllinis.
units.tr: If, however, he means the later one, namely the writing of a certain man who was contemporary with or on a par with the Apostles' disciples, the learned man is wrong in his opinion. To avoid going on at too great length, I will rest on one example, which will show that the learned man has been mistaken. The example will be taken from the Sibylline books, which were written, as our Blondel has proved, around the year of Christ 142, more or less. For whatever Pearsonius says in the whole of that third chapter cited above, about the testimonies brought in favour of the Ignatians, can also be said of those which can be brought in favour of the Sibylline oracles. Certainly the witnesses in favour of the Ignatians in the monuments of the ancient Christians are neither more numerous, nor greater, nor more certain than those for the Sibyllines, at least if you run through the centuries, namely the second, third, fourth and fifth. Since the nearer witnesses ought to carry more weight than the remoter ones, I suppose no one will deny that Pearsonius brings forward Polycarp and Irenaeus as witnesses of the second century for his Ignatians. For the Sibyllines I will bring forward Justin Martyr, Athenagoras, Theophilus, bishop of Antioch, Clement of Alexandria, writers of the same century. Against Origen, whom Pearsonius cites for the third century, I will set the same Clement, who touched the first years of that century, Tertullian and Lactantius, who flourished in the third and fourth. There is this difference between the two sets of testimony: what Pearsonius brings forward for the Ignatians is taken from monuments whose credibility wavers and totters, whereas the writings which supply and suffice as arguments in favour of the Sibyllines are most certain and beyond doubt. I will set against Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, Eusebius and Chrysostom, witnesses of the fourth century chosen by Pearsonius, Lactantius, the author of the Apostolic Constitutions, which in this century, as some think, was patched together, the Emperor Constantine, Eusebius, Optatus of Milevis, and, with Theodoret and Gelasius, the first Pope, who belong to the fifth century, Jerome, Augustine, Prosper, Palladius, Sozomen. I willingly pass over the other centuries still to be examined. For what we have said so far is quite enough to overthrow Pearsonius's reasoning. Yet I should like to add one thing, namely this observation of the author of the Chronological Index and the Alphabetical Index of the Great Library of the Fathers: That the Oracles of the Sibyls were of great authority among the first Christians, can be doubted by no one who has even lightly looked into the writings of the ancient Fathers; for Clement of Alexandria, in book 6 of the Stromata, bears witness that St Paul exhorted the Christians to read them. What he says of Clement of Alexandria is most true, and contains the highest commendation of the Sibylline oracles. Yet it is agreed among learned men whose judgment is not overwhelmed by prejudice that those Sibylline oracles were forged about the middle of the second century by a certain plain and impostor. So the argument drawn from the testimonies can mislead, and not only can it mislead, but in fact it does. Pearsonius's reasoning therefore limps, and I grieve that so great a man should have fallen into this. Perhaps Pearsonius will say that the Sibylline books are neither an ecclesiastical writing nor the writing of an Apostolic man. But both claims could be denied. First, the Sibylline books hold their place in the library of the holy Fathers; the ancient teachers of the Church drew many of their proofs for their doctrines from these books; and finally, they were composed by a Christian man. Secondly, the same holds: for although the impostor who sold us his dreams was not Apostolic in respect of doctrine, he was so in respect of age, being indeed on a par with, or even in some sense contemporary with, Ignatius and Polycarp, the disciples of the Apostles. For he patched together his fictions about thirty years after the passion of Ignatius, and twenty-four years before the martyrdom of Polycarp. But indeed, so that every handle for cavilling may be cut off from the learned man, let us grant him that the Sibylline writing is not an ecclesiastical writing of an Apostolic man. What follows from this? Namely this: that an argument drawn from testimonies concerning a non-ecclesiastical writing and a non-Apostolic man can mislead, while the same argument concerning an ecclesiastical writing of an Apostolic man never misleads. This is indeed a remarkable consequence: that the ancient ecclesiastical writers put on various forms at their pleasure and were endowed with various gifts according to the various characters of the books about which they were to give testimony. So with respect to some they would be wholly free from error [ἀναμάρτητοι] and placed beyond the danger and hazard of erring, but with respect to others they would be liable to error and such that no faith can or ought to be placed in them. Are these not pleasant dreams of men who are awake, born from nothing but zeal for their cause? Especially since marks of spuriousness are detected in the Ignatian epistles, just as in the Sibylline books.

units.la: Sed agè transeamus ad caput vindiciarum quartum, quod capiti scripti Dallæi ni quarto respondet, protulerat Dallæus sichometriam Nicephori Patriarchæ Constantinopolitani, non ad depellendam invidiam tantùm ut ait Pearsonius, vox tantùm Dallæi non est, sed etiam ad suam de Ignatianis sententiam constituendam, en tibi ipsissima Dallæi verba pag. 243. Quanquam nos quidem stichometriam hoc loco, non tam ad constituendam nostram de Ignatianis sententiam, quàm ad de-pellendam invidiam asserimus, qui ita loquitur satis supérque innuit stichometriam in utrumque finem à se adductam fuisse, quamvis illam fateatur adduxisse se in eum præcipuè finem, ut probet Salmasium & Blondellum non fuisse primos qui Ignatianas Epistolas confictas putarent, sed attende quaeso quomodo sibi caverit vir sagacissimus istis verbis hoc loco, nempè primus Dallæi scopus hoc loco fuit, depellere invidiam summis viris Salmasio & Blondello iniquè conflatam, quasi omnium mortalium primi Ignatiana repudiassent, salvo tamen jure eâdem utendi stichometriâ, dum sese offeret occasio, ad suam hypothesim confirmandam; immeritò igitur Pearsonius Dallæum hanc stichometriam adducentem reprehendit, eúmque in adducenda affectatæ ambiguitatis seu obscuritatis insimulat, cùm tamen ita dilucidè loquutus sit, animíque sensa tam clarè tàmque perspicuè expresserit, ut ejus sermo nemini nisi sponte cæcutienti ambiguus aut obscurus videri queat; Quidquid sit quia Nicephori sti-chometria Pearsonio incommodat, sese in omnes partes versat, ut ejus autoritatem frangat, robúrque enervet ac debilitet; sed frustrà se torquet, non enim rationibus & conjecturis concuti & convelli solent, facta omnibus veri notis & characteribus insignita, & praeterea codicum omnium manuscriptorum & impressorum fide suffulta, nisi forte velit vir doctus animum reddere moriturae jamjam Arnaldi Sorbonici methodo qua Ecclesiae traditionem veterum subnixam testimoniis, levissimis quibusdam rationibus evertere frustra conatus est. Nicephoro socium dedit Dallaeus Anastasium Bibliothecarium, hominem noni saeculi, Nicephoro supparem, cujus haec verba adfert pag. 244. ex Praefatione Historiae Ecclesiasticae ad Ioannem Diaconum; Huic sane operi rarum duxi B. Nicephori Constantinopolitani Episcopi Chronographiam praeponere; ut scilicet & ex ea possis aliquantula carpere, & sicubi fortasis[?] hac utendum judicaveris, tuam non lateat omnino notitiam. Deinde observat idem Dallaeus hujus Chronographiae partem ultimam esse illam librorum à se laudatam stichometriam, Patriarcharum Christianorum indiculis subtextam; quam quidem stichometriam editio Anastasii Regia a. 1649. Lutetiae procurata, exhibet in calce historiae Anastasianae, ubi plane sic, ut in Graecis Nicephori, Ignatiana in Apocryphorum Novi Testamenti censu reponuntur, ac proinde ab utroque Nicephoro inquam qui stichometriam edidit, & Anastasio qui adoptavit, tanquam spuria & adulterina octingentis abhinc plus minus annis damnata sunt & reprobata. Sed ut aliquid amplius dicam, vehementi sollicitor suspicione ut credam istam quâ de agimus stichometriam Nicephoro ipso vetustiorem esse, neminem enim eorum, qui hæc studia vel summis labris degustarunt, latere puto, horum indiculorum usum diu ante Nicephorum obtinuisse; à verò igitur non abhorret Nicephorum istam stichometriam à scriptore se admodum vetustiore habuisse, vel potius eam in calce antiquissimi cujusdam sacrorum librorum codicis nactam sibi adoptasse, suaeque chronographiæ subtexuisse, quod si ita est ut conjicio, augustiori augebitur autoritate stichometria, longeque majoris erit ponde-ris.
units.tr: But come, let us pass on to the fourth chapter of the Vindiciae, which answers the fourth chapter of Dallaeus's writing. Dallaeus had produced the stichometry of Nicephorus, Patriarch of Constantinople, not, as Pearsonius says, merely to remove odium. The word merely is not Dallaeus's. Here are Dallaeus's very words, page 243: Although we, indeed, assert the stichometry in this place, not so much to establish our view of the Ignatians our opinion as to repel odium. Whoever speaks thus sufficiently and more than sufficiently hints that he adduced the stichometry for both purposes, although he admits that he adduced it chiefly for this end, namely to prove that Salmasius and Blondel were not the first to think the Ignatian epistles forged. But notice, I beg you, how cautiously that most shrewd man guarded himself with the words in this place. Dallaeus's primary aim in this place was to repel the odium unjustly brought upon the highest men, Salmasius and Blondel, as if they were the first of all mortals to reject the Ignatian writings. Yet he kept the right of using the same stichometry, whenever an occasion offered itself, to confirm his own hypothesis. Pearsonius therefore rightly blames Dallaeus for adducing this stichometry, and accuses him of affected ambiguity or obscurity in adducing it. Yet Dallaeus spoke so clearly, and expressed the sense of his mind so plainly and perspicuously, that his speech can seem ambiguous or obscure to no one except one who has willingly made himself blind. However that may be, since Nicephorus's stichometry is inconvenient for Pearsonius, he turns it every way to break its authority and weaken and enfeeble its strength. But he labours in vain. For facts marked with every sign and character of truth, and moreover supported by the faith of all the manuscript and printed codices, are not usually shaken and overthrown by reasonings and conjectures, unless perhaps the learned man wishes to restore the spirit of Arnauld the Sorbonist, who, with the method by which he tried in vain to overturn the tradition of the ancients supported by testimonies, used certain very light reasonings. Dallaeus gave Nicephorus a companion, Anastasius the Librarian, a man of the ninth century, a contemporary of Nicephorus, whose words he cites on page 244 from the Preface to the Ecclesiastical History addressed to John the Deacon: I have thought it a rare thing to prefix to this work the Chronography of the blessed Nicephorus, Bishop of Constantinople, so that you may from it both pick out a few things, and, if you judge it should be used somewhere, may not be wholly ignorant of it. Then the same Dallaeus observes that the last part of this Chronography is that stichometry of books which he praised, appended to the lists of the Christian patriarchs. Indeed, the royal edition of Anastasius, published at Paris in 1649, presents this stichometry at the end of the Anastasian history, where, exactly as in Nicephorus's Greek text, the Ignatian writings are placed in the list of the Apocrypha of the New Testament. Accordingly, both Nicephorus, I say, who published the stichometry, and Anastasius, who adopted it, condemned and rejected them as spurious and adulterine more or less eight hundred years ago. But to say something more: I am strongly inclined to suspect that this stichometry which we are discussing is older than Nicephorus himself. For I think no one who has tasted these studies even superficially is unaware that the use of these lists was current long before Nicephorus. It is therefore not unlikely that Nicephorus had this stichometry from a writer much older than himself, or rather that he found it at the end of some very ancient codex of the sacred books and adopted it, appending it to his own chronography. If this is so, as I conjecture, the stichometry will gain greater authority and be of much greater weight.

units.la: IV. Eruditus Pearsonius ut ictum lethalem à Nicephoro & Anastasio ante octo sæcula Ignatio suo illatum declinet, ludit in ambiguo, & dubiâ seu homonymâ vocis apocryphi significatione abutens, dicit Nicephorum, dùm Ignatiana inter apocrypha numerat, nihil aliud voluisse nisi Ignatij Epistolas esse à Canone S. scripturæ removendas,opponendo videlicet apocrypha libris divinitus inspiratis, non autem Ecclesiasticis qui utilissimi sunt, & à Pijs cum magno fructu legi possunt & debent, ingeniosa viri solutio, ut illi quidem videtur, sed quæ plus subtilitatis habet quàm soliditatis, non quæritur proprie quot modis usurpetur vox apocryphum seu apocryphus, sed quo sensu id vocabulum à Nicephoro sumatur, consulenda igitur illius stichometria, ut videamus quænam sunt ista, quæ ille Apocrypha censet. I. inquit, itinerarium Petri versuum 2750. II. itinerarium Ioannis versuum 3600. III. itinerarium Thomæ versuum 1600.IV.Evangelium secundum Thomam versuum 1300. V. Doctrina Apostolorum versuum 200. VI. Clementis libri xxxij. versuum 2600. VII. Ignatii, Polycarpi, Pastoris, & Hermæ libri. Quibus omnibus hunc titulum præfixit, quæ Novi Testamenti sunt apocrypha: jam quivis videt hæc omnia à Nicephoro in eodem apocryphorum censu reponi, ideóque vel omnia ab ea damnari, vel omnia absolvi, utraque enim uno eodémque simplicissimo apocryphorum elogio donata sunt, si igitur hoc elogio Ignatiana ad insignem in Ecclesiâ honoris gradum evecta sunt, eodem pariter frui honore, & ad eandem gloriam promoveri debent itineraria & Clementina, eodem cum Ignatianis elogio donata; itineraria autem & Clementina & cætera in indiculo comprehensa & recensita Nicephori elogio notata sunt & damnata; Ergo velit nolit vir doctus eadem quoque decretoriâ sententiâ damnata notatáque itidem fuisse Ignatiana necessariò fatendum est; omnibus enim istis libris una eademque ignominiæ nota à Constantinopolitano Patriarcha inusta fuit & impressa, eos omnes extra omnem scripturarum non modò divinarum, sed etiam ecclesiasticarum probatarum & authenticarum censum eiiciendo, & ad eas relegando, quæ cavendæ sunt, & à publica Ecclesiæ luce removendæ. Et ne diutius in istis immoremur, attendatur quæso ordo quem sequutus est Nicephorus in Veteris Novíque Testamenti libris recensendis, utriusque enim fœderis libros in classes distinxit, prima exhibet libros Veteris Testamenti canonicos ab omnibus fidelibus recipiendos, secunda canonicos Novi, tertia Veteris ἀντιλεγομένης [?] id est eos quibus contradicitur, vel ut alij loqui amant dubios seu dubiæ autoritatis, quarta Novi ἀντιλεγομένης [?], quinta verò & ultima ejusdem Novi fœderis apocryphos; nempè duas modò librorum Veteris Testamenti constituit classes, canonicorum alteram, alteram verò ἀντιλεγο-μένων, ἀφῶν[?], tres autem librorum Novi Fœderis, primam Canonicorum pariter, secundam ἀντιλεγομένων[?], tertiam apocryphorum, apocryphorum inquam, qui quò magis distant à Canonicis, eò sunt deteriores, distant autem magis à Canonicis quàm dubij seu ἀμφιλεγομένοι[?], ergo pejoris sunt notæ apocryphi quàm dubij, hæc saltem mens Nicephori qui dubios opponit tantùm Canonicis, apocryphos verò è quorum numero sunt Ignatiana utrisque Canonicis videlicet & dubijs; libri igitur apocryphi sunt Nicephoro, libri falsi, ficti & adulterini; Eadem mens Henrico Valesio viro doctissimo, qui libros apocryphos discernens ab ijs quorum ambigua est inter scriptores auctoritas, ita loquitur, magnum discri-
units.tr: IV. Learned Pearson, to escape the deadly blow that Nicephorus and Anastasius struck against his Ignatius eight centuries ago, plays on words. He abuses the ambiguous and double meaning of the word apocryphal, and says that when Nicephorus counts the Ignatian letters among the apocrypha, he meant nothing more than that the Epistles of Ignatius should be removed from the canon of Holy Scripture. In other words, he sets apocrypha against books inspired by God, not against ecclesiastical books, which are very useful and which the pious can and should read with great profit. This is a clever solution, as it seems to him, but it has more subtlety than solidity. The question is not properly how many senses the term apocryphum or apocryphus may bear, but in what sense Nicephorus used the word. We must therefore consult his stichometry and see what those works are which he counts as apocrypha. First, he says: Itinerary of Peter, 2750 verses. Second, Itinerary of John, 3600 verses. Third, Itinerary of Thomas, 1600 verses. Fourth, Gospel according to Thomas, 1300 verses. Fifth, Teaching of the Apostles, 200 verses. Sixth, Books of Clement, 32 books, 2600 verses. Seventh, Books of Ignatius, Polycarp, the Shepherd, and Hermas. He prefixed to all of these the heading: what are apocrypha of the New Testament. Now anyone can see that Nicephorus places all of these in the same list of apocrypha. Therefore either all of them are condemned by him, or all are acquitted, for both have been given one and the same simple label of apocrypha. If the Ignatian writings have been raised by this label to a distinguished rank of honour in the Church, then the Itineraries and the Clementine books, which were given the same label as the Ignatian writings, ought equally to enjoy that honour and be promoted to the same glory. But the Itineraries, the Clementine books, and the rest included and listed in the catalogue are all marked and condemned by the label of Nicephorus. Therefore, whether the learned man wills it or not, it must necessarily be admitted that the Ignatian writings were likewise condemned and marked by that decisive sentence. For one and the same mark of disgrace was branded and impressed upon all these books by the Patriarch of Constantinople, who cast them all out from the census not only of divine Scriptures, but also of approved and authentic ecclesiastical writings, and relegated them to those which must be avoided and removed from the public light of the Church. And that we may not linger longer on these matters, let us please note the order which Nicephorus followed in listing the books of the Old and New Testaments. For he divided the books of both covenants into classes. The first class contains the canonical books of the Old Testament, to be received by all the faithful; the second, the canonical books of the New; the third, the Old Testament books of the antilegomenē [ἀντιλεγομένης], that is, those which are contradicted, or, as others prefer to say, the doubtful or of doubtful authority; the fourth, the New Testament books of the antilegomenē [ἀντιλεγομένης]; and the fifth and last, the apocryphal books of the same New Testament. Thus he constituted only two classes of books of the Old Testament: one of canonical books, and the other of antilegomena [ἀντιλεγομένων], and aphōn [ἀφῶν]. Of the books of the New Testament he made three: the first of canonical books, likewise; the second of antilegomena [ἀντιλεγομένων]; the third of apocrypha, apocrypha I say, which, the further they are from the canonical books, the worse they are. Now they are further from the canonical books than the doubtful, or amphilegomenoi [ἀμφιλεγομένοι]. Therefore apocrypha bear a worse mark than doubtful books. This at least is the mind of Nicephorus, who sets the doubtful against the canonical alone, but the apocrypha, among whom are the Ignatian writings, against both the canonical and the doubtful. Therefore for Nicephorus the apocryphal books are false, fictitious and spurious books. The same is the mind of the most learned Henri de Valois, who, distinguishing apocryphal books from those whose authority is disputed among writers, speaks thus: There is a great difference between apocryphal books and those whose authority is disputed among writers.

units.la: men est inter libros apocryphos, & eos quorum ambigua est inter scriptores auctoritas. Nam apocryphi palàm falsi sunt, & ab hæreticis ut plurimùm conficti; quod probat Hegesippi antiquissimi scriptoris testimonio, seu potiùs Eusebij hæc de illo narrantis, Hege-
units.tr: For apocryphal books are manifestly false, and for the most part forged by heretics. This is proved by the testimony of the most ancient writer Hegesippus, or rather by Eusebius's account of him, Hege-

units.la: sippus agens de libris qui apocryphi dicuntur, quosdam eorum sua ætate ab nonnullis hæreti- cis compositos esse scribit; hæc præterea Hieronymi verba ex libro secundo adversus Ruffinum adducit idem Valesius, apocrypha Ecclesia non recipit. Eodem planè sensu apocrypha definit Gelasius in suo Decreto de quo sumus acturi; Ergo Nicephorus per scripta apocrypha pessimæ notæ scripta intellexit, eáque ab Ecclesiâ penitùs eliminanda censuit: quod autem objicit Pearsonius de Polycarpi epistolâ ad stichometriæ auctoritatem labefactandam, suo loco discutietur; quæ dicit de doctrinâ Apostolorum, de libro videlicet Apostolorum Διδαχὴ[?] cognominato, nihil ad rem quâ de agitur; non enim quæritur quo jure Nicephorus hunc librum damnarit, sed num damnarit, constat de facto, de jure non est quòd anxiè solliciti simus, idem esto judicium de libris Clementinis[?] XXXII. sed inquit Pearsonius non docet Dallæus quænam fuerint illa Clementina quæ in hoc Indiculo memorantur, quid tum, nescivit Dallæus, nescit ipse Pearsonius & nisi me fallit animus, ignorant hodie literati omnes, etsi vir quidam eruditus conjecturis suis id assequi nuper tentarit, sed si quæ fuerint illa Clementina nos hodie ignoramus, non ignoravit Nicephorus, & quia plura in illis suppositionis animadvertit τεκμήρια[?], plurésque reprobæ doctrinæ notas, ea censuræ suæ obelo jugulare ac confodere non dubitavit.
units.tr: sippus, speaking of the books which are called apocryphal, writes that some of them were composed in his own time by certain heretics. Valois also cites the following words of Jerome from the second book against Rufinus: the Church does not receive apocrypha. Gelasius defines apocrypha in exactly the same sense in his Decree, which we are about to discuss. Therefore Nicephorus by apocryphal writings understood writings of the worst repute, and he judged that they must be utterly removed from the Church. As to what Pearson objects concerning the Epistle of Polycarp, in order to shake the authority of the stichometry, it will be examined in its proper place. What he says about the Teaching of the Apostles, the book of the Apostles called Didachē [Διδαχή], is nothing to the point under discussion. For the question is not by what right Nicephorus condemned this book, but whether he condemned it. That he did is certain as a fact; as to right, we need not be anxiously concerned. The same judgment stands for the Clementine books XXXII. But, says Pearson, Dallaeus does not show what those Clementine books were that are mentioned in this Index. What of it? Dallaeus did not know, Pearson himself does not know, and, unless I am mistaken, all learned men today are ignorant of it, although a certain learned man has recently tried to reach it by his conjectures. But if we today do not know what those Clementine books were, Nicephorus did not fail to know. And since he noticed in them many tekmēria [τεκμήρια] of forgery and more marks of reprobate doctrine, he did not hesitate to pierce and slay them with the obelus of his censure.

units.la: Sed majorem Viro docto molestiam creat sententia adversus Hermæ librum lata, ut autem Dallæum ex libri Hermæ censurâ contra Ignatiana argumentantem inducat, hæc observat Pearsonius, Quintò, quod Hermas cum Ignatianis nomine- tur, negari non posse volunt (nempè Dallæus & ὁμόψηφοι[?]) quin Nicephorus eadem habuerit pro falsis, adeóque fictis & spuriis. Tamen Dallæus libri Hermæ respectu,refpondentis vices agebat, non opponentis, ut liquet ex istis ipsius Dallæi verbis, quod verò de Herma addunt viri doctissimi (Vsserius videlicet & Hammondus) neque id quicquam eorum causam juvat, quibus hæc virorum illorum doctorum verba subnectit, Hermam, (inquiunt) Nicephorus in eadem cum Ignatianis apocryphorum classe reposuit; huic autem objectioni in sequentibus respondet Dallæus. Verùm demus clarissimo Pearsonio Dallæum collegisse ex Hermæ censurâ Nicephorum Ignatiana habuisse pro fictis ac spurijs, quid inde illaturus est in gratiam suæ hypothesis, nempè contrarium evinci posse, si vetustissimorum ut ait doctissimorúmque in Ecclesia scriptorum de libro Hermæ sententiæ animadvertantur: cùm enim plures è veteribus de hoc libro cum laude loquuti sint, eósque, si Pearsonium audimus, sequutum fuisse Autorem stichometriæ par sit credere, infert vir doctus Nicephorum cui ista tribuitur stichometria, Ignatiana sua ad apocrypha id est pessimi commatis scripta minimè ablegasse; Et ut voti sui compos esse queat, multa veterum scriptorum congerit testimonia li-bro Hermæ favorabilia, scilicet Irenæi, Clementis Alexandrini, Origenis, Eusebij, Athanasij, Didymi, Ruffini, Hieronymi, Cassiani, & Maximi Pseudo-Dionysij Areopagitæ scholiastis; sed plura regeri possunt adversus hæc testimonia à Viro doćto allata. 1. agitur hic de Nicephoro, non de testibus à Pearsonio addućtis, de Nicephoro, inquam, qui à testibus citatis seorsum abit, eum ipsum librum quem illi laudant in apocryphorum censu reponendo; & à publicâ Ecclesiæ luce removendo; sed ait vir doćtus par est credere stichometriæ Autorem scriptores illos sequutum esse, imò par est credere non sequutum esse, scriptores enim illi de libro Hermæ sine præfatione honoris, ut ita dicam, non loquuntur; à Nicephoro autem istius stichometriæ Autore damnatus fuit & notatus, non ad honorem prosećtò, se ad labem atque ignominiam sempiternam; miror sanè virum doćtum conjećturis suis adeò indulgere, ut illis quantumvis levissimis vel stichometriæ fidem detrahere, vel illius Autorem in suas partes ducere posse putet. 2. quidam ex ipsis Pearsonij testibus satis innuunt istum librum Hermae à pluribus non recipi, imò à quibusdam penitus contemni, quidni igitur à Nicephoro despectus fuerit,& velut apocryphus notatus atque damnatus, & ne haec à nobis gratis confingi putes, attende ad ista verba Origenis summi alioquin istius libri laudatoris, si cui scripturailla recipienda videtur, si cui libellus ille recipiendus videtur, & lib. 4. de Principijs cap. 2. & in Philocalia cap. 1. ideo nos &illud in Pastore; libro qui à quibusdam contemnitur, &c. Hieronymus qui in scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum Catalogo, observavit hunc librum apud quasdam Graeciae Ecclesias publicè legi,& revera utilem esse, de illo tamen alibi dubitanter loquitur, si cui tamen, inquit, placet illiusrecipere lectionem, neque id solum , ulteriùs progreditur, eúmque rotundè apocryphum pronuntiat; Liber ille apocryphus stultitiae condemnandus est in quo scriptum est, quendam Angelum nomine Tyri praesse reptilibus; alluditantem[?] ad verba quae extant in Hermae Pastore lib. 1. visione 4. cap. 2. neque in solo apocryphi elogio consistit Hieronymus, illum praeterea librum stultitiae condemnandum esse asserit; quid vilius, quid despectius de quocunque libro dici potest; 3. hic liber adeo vilis erat pretij ut Latinis vel ignotus[?] fuerit, vel ab illis contemptus, vel denique damnatus; primùm asserit Hieronymus, apud Latinos, inquit, pene ignotus est; secundùm docet nos Prosper, disputans enim contra collatorem, Ioannem[?] videlicet Cassianum qui testimonium de libro Pastoris adduxerat, contemptim de illo libro loquitur, & nihili faciendum significat, testimoniúmque quod de libro Hermæ disputationi suæ inseruerat Cassianus, nullius authoritatis testimonium indigetat; & merito sanè, cum S. Prosper modestius loqui non potuerit de libro qui scriptori in Semipelagianorum castris ut quibusdam placet militanti, adversus Catholicos gratiæ Christi defensores & patronos, arma sufficit; tertium denique caput librum scilicet Hermæ à Latinis damnatum esse, ita exploratum est, ut de eo dubitari non liceat; Dallæus hæc responderat Vsserio & Hammondo qui ægrè ferebant Hermam à Nicephoro in eadem cum Ignatianis apocryphorum classe reposi-tum fuisse; Quidni reponeret, cujus scri-pturam adulterinam dicit Tertullianus, ab omni Concilio Ecclesiarum, inter apocrypha & falsa, jam olim suo ævo (id est circa initia tertij à Christo nato sæculi) judicatam fuisse docet ex quibus Tertulliani verbis liquidò confirmari asserebat vir clarissimus, apocrypha à Nicephoro, quæ recenset, damnari, ut ficta vel periculosa; non laudari vel ornari,ut divinis proxima, & post ea secundo in Ecclesia loco censenda, quod est, inquit, doctissimorum virorum dictatum ( Vsserium & Hammondum intelligit) sed ut ista magis ac magis elucescant, integrum Tertulliani testimonium adducendum est, cederem tibi, si scriptura Pastoris, quæ sola mœchos amat, divino instrumento meruisset incidi, si non ab omni Concilio Ecclesiarum etiam vestrarum inter apocrypha & falsa judicaretur, adultera & ipsa; Quid ad hæc clarissimus Pearsonius, primum quædam adfert ex Tertulliani libro de Oratione ab eo adhuc Catholico exarato, in illo enim libro meminit, Hermæ ejúsque scripturæ quæ Pastor inscribitur; sed hæc viri docti causam minime juvant, agitur ibi de quadam sedendi consuetudine oratione peractâ, quam sedendi consuetudinem damnat Tertullianus, etsi illius ignoret originem, suspicatur tamen hunc morem à Pastoris libro initium duxisse, nisi, inquit, si Hermas ille, cujus scriptura ferè Pastor inscribitur, transactâ oratione non super lectum assedisset. Qui de aliquo libro ita loquitur, significat librum illum sibi contemptui esse,nullóque in pretio à se haberi: sed inquit secundò vir doctus, Tertullianus non rejicit libri autoritatem, sed admittit; pace tuâ inquam ego vir clarissimè, non admittit Tertullianus libri autoritatem, eam potius rejicit, illum videlicet despiciendo, & consuetudinem quam ab eo libro manasse conjiciebat, reprehendendo & damnando; tertiò Pearsonius dicit consuetudinem sedendi finitâ oratione à Christianis quibusdam Tertullianei ævi observatam, ostendere quanto tùm in pretio liber ille Hermæ fuit, ut ex eo ritus in Ecclesiæ disciplinam transfunderetur. Miror hæc viro docto in mentem venire potuisse, quasi vero, ritum quo de agimus in Ecclesiam transfusum dicemus, quia à quibusdam Christianis,ijsque ut videtur simplicibus, observabatur; eadem plane ratione colligam ritum cereos accendendi in honorem Martyrum in Ecclesiam Hieronymi ætate transfusum suisse, quia à Christianis quibusdam pariter observabatur; sed tantum abest ut Hieronymus istam eliciat Pearsonianam conclusionem, quod potius eam damnet consuetudinem, quemadmodum aliam damnaverat Tertullianus, eòsque reprehendat, qui propter imperitiam, & simplicitatem secularium hominum, vel certè religiofarum fœminarum , hoc pro honore Martyrum faciunt. Quidquid sit , Tertullianus, inquiunt, Montanista erat dum Hermæ librum apocryphi elogio donavit , fateor, sed propterea nihil ejus testimonio decedet, nec minorem merebitur fidem; si de re Montanistas inter & Catholicos controversâ ageretur, non audiendus esset Tertullianus, sed cùm agatur de Hermæ libro non à Montanistis modò , verum etiam à Catholicis proscripto & ad apocrypha relegato, nulla potest dari legitima ratio ob quam repudiandum sit Tertulliani testimonium; notatus fuit à Veteribus Tertullianus quod à Catholicis ad Montanistas desciverit, sed à nemine quod sciam reprehensus, quod Pastoris librum in apocryphorum censu repositerit; præterea non ipse solus adversus Hermæ librum sententiam tulit, sed etiam à Catholicarum Ecclesiarum Concilio latam fuisse affirmat, ab omni concilio Ecclesiarum etiam vestrarum, Ecclesiarum videlicet, ut ego interpretor Latinarum & Græcarum, quâ fronte quæso Catholicos alloquens hæc proferre ausus esset Tertullianus, nisi de re certâ, miniméque dubiâ , & ipsis Catholicis cognitâ loquutus esset; unica viro docto superesset via quâ elabi posse putat & suo Hermæ patrocinari, nimirum dicendo in Tertulliani verbis nihil aliud fortasse contineri, quàm Pastorem Hermæ non fuisse ex judicio Ecclesiæ librum Canonicum, sed potiùs inter Apocryphos, id est, non Canonicos numeratum; bene est quod fortasse dixerit, absque una hæc dubitandi particula foret, ludibrium lectori deberet; scriptura Pastoris ab omni Concilio Ecclesiarum etiam Catholicarum, inter apocrypha & falsa judicata est, tamen juxta Vindiciarum Autorem, hæc nihil aliud sonant, quàm Pastorem Hermæ non fuisse ex judicio Ecclesiæ librum Canonicum, sed potiùs inter Apocryphos, id est, non Canonicos numeratum. Nempè scripta apocrypha, falsa, ficta, spuria, & adulterina, viro docto sunt scripta Ecclesiastica, probata, authentica, secundi in Ecclesia ordinis, à pijs omnibus semel, iterùm, tertiò, imò saepissimè legenda & relegenda, uno verbo scripta tantùm non Canonica, sed Canonicis proxima; en quò clarissimum virum abripiat causæ studium, cui nimiùm concedere illum vereor; meliùs & saniùs de isto Hermæ libro judicabat Ioannes Maria Bralichellanus Magister sacri Palatij, dubitandum, inquit, nullo pacto est libellum hunc Pastoris, ut modò scriptus habetur, ab Herma Pauli discipulo non esse conscriptum, cùm & hæresibus & fabulis sit oppletum: eum S. Gelasius in Romano Concilio inter apocrypha scripta abjicit: item & S. Prosper libro contra Cassianum cap. 30. nullius autoritatis esse pronuntiat. Ad illud Gelasij decretum attendebat Antonius Augustinus dum hæc scribebat, ut posteriores cogitationes Graeco Proverbio meliores esse dicuntur, sic etiam posterior ætas certiora de libro Pastoris statuit. Hanc Gelasij de libro Hermæ censuram repræsentat sæculo decimo Atto Vercellensis tom. 8. spicileg. p. 41. Liber qui appellatur Pastoris apocryphus.
units.tr: But the sentence passed against the book of Hermas causes a greater trouble for the learned man. To bring Dallaeus into the argument against the Ignatian letters from the censure of Hermas' book, Pearsonius makes this observation: Fifthly, they want it not to be denied that, since Hermas is named together with the Ignatian letters, (namely Dallaeus and the like-minded men [ὁμόψηφοι]) Nicephorus held the same works to be false, and therefore fictitious and spurious. Yet Dallaeus was speaking on behalf of the one answering, not the one objecting, as is clear from his own words: As for what the very learned men add about Hermas (namely Usserius and Hammond), none of it helps their cause. To these he attaches the words of those learned men: Nicephorus, they say, placed Hermas in the same class of apocryphal writings as the Ignatian letters; Dallaeus answers this objection in what follows. But grant to the most distinguished Pearsonius that Dallaeus inferred from Hermas' censure that Nicephorus held the Ignatian letters to be fictitious and spurious. What will he gain from this in support of his hypothesis? The opposite can be shown, if we attend to the opinions of the most ancient and, as he says, the most learned writers in the Church about the book of Hermas. For since many of the ancients have spoken about this book with praise, and since, if we listen to Pearsonius, it is fitting to believe that the author of the stichometry followed them, the learned man infers that Nicephorus, to whom that stichometry is attributed, did not relegate his Ignatian writings to the apocrypha, that is, to writings of the worst sort. To achieve his aim he heaps up many testimonies of the ancient writers favourable to the book of Hermas, namely those of Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Eusebius, Athanasius, Didymus, Rufinus, Jerome, Cassian, and the scholiast Maximus, the Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite. But many things can be objected against these testimonies brought forward by the learned man. 1. The matter here concerns Nicephorus, not the witnesses cited by Pearsonius. I say concerning Nicephorus, who departs from the cited witnesses by placing in the list of apocrypha that very book they praise, and removing it from the public light of the Church. But the learned man says it is fitting to believe that the author of the stichometry followed those writers. Indeed it is fitting to believe he did not follow them, for those writers do not speak of the book of Hermas without a preface of honour, so to speak, whereas Nicephorus, the author of that stichometry, condemned and marked it, not for honour at all, but for lasting disgrace and ignominy. I marvel that the learned man so indulges his conjectures that he thinks he can, by means of them however slight, either take away the credibility of the stichometry or draw its author to his own side. 2. Some of Pearsonius' own witnesses sufficiently hint that this book of Hermas was not received by many, and was even wholly despised by some. Why, then, should it not have been looked down upon by Nicephorus, and marked and condemned as apocryphal? Lest you think we invent this without grounds, attend to these words of Origen, the highest praiser of this book otherwise: if anyone thinks that writing ought to be received, if anyone thinks that little book ought to be received, and in the fourth book On First Principles, chapter 2, and in the Philocalia, chapter 1: therefore we also cite that in the Shepherd, a book which is despised by some, etc. Jerome, who in his Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers observed that this book was publicly read in some Greek churches and was indeed useful, nevertheless speaks of it doubtfully elsewhere: if anyone, however, he says, is pleased to receive its reading. Nor does he stop there, but goes further and flatly pronounces it apocryphal: That apocryphal book deserves to be condemned as foolish, in which it is written that a certain angel named Tyri presides over reptiles, alluding to the words found in the Shepherd of Hermas, Book 1, Vision 4, chapter 2. Nor does Jerome rest in the mere epithet "apocryphal"; he further asserts that the book deserves to be condemned as foolish. What could be said of any book that is cheaper or more despised? 3. This book was of such little worth that it was either unknown to the Latins, or despised by them, or finally condemned. First, Jerome asserts that among the Latins, he says, it is almost unknown. Second, Prosper teaches us this: disputing against the collator, namely John Cassian, who had cited a testimony from the book of the Shepherd, he speaks of that book with contempt, and signifies that it is to be made of no account, and he calls the testimony which Cassian had inserted from the book of Hermas into his argument a testimony of no authority. And rightly so, since St Prosper could not speak more modestly of a book which supplies arms to a writer who, as some think, fights in the camp of the Semipelagians against the Catholic defenders and champions of the grace of Christ. Third and finally, that the book of Hermas was condemned by the Latins is so well established that it may not be doubted. Dallaeus had answered this to Usserius and Hammond, who took it hard that Hermas had been placed by Nicephorus in the same class of apocryphal writings as the Ignatian letters. Why would he not reply, when Tertullian calls it a spurious writing, and teaches that it was judged, among the apocrypha and falsehoods, by every council of the Churches, already long ago in its own age (that is, around the beginning of the third century after Christ's birth)? From the words of Tertullian, the most distinguished man asserted, it is clearly confirmed that the apocrypha which Nicephorus lists are condemned as fictitious or dangerous, not praised or adorned as close to the divine books and to be counted second in the Church. This is, he says, the dictum of the most learned men (he means Usserius and Hammond). But so that these points may shine out more and more, the whole testimony of Tertullian must be cited: I would yield to you, if the writing of the Shepherd, which alone loves adulterers, had deserved to be included in the divine instrument, if it were not judged among the apocrypha and falsehoods by every council even of your Churches; it is adulterous too. What does the most distinguished Pearsonius say in reply? First he brings forward certain things from Tertullian's book On Prayer, written while he was still a Catholic. For in that book he mentions Hermas and his writing which is commonly called the Shepherd. But these things hardly help the learned man's cause. There it is a matter of a custom of sitting down after prayer is finished, which custom Tertullian condemns. Although he does not know its origin, he suspects that this custom took its beginning from the book of the Shepherd: unless, he says, perhaps that Hermas, whose writing is commonly called the Shepherd, had not sat down upon the couch after finishing his prayer. One who speaks of a book in this way signifies that the book is contemptible to him and held by him in no esteem. But secondly, the learned man says, Tertullian does not reject the authority of the book but admits it. With respect, I say, most distinguished sir, Tertullian does not admit the authority of the book; rather he rejects it, namely by looking down upon it and by reproving and condemning the custom which he conjectured had sprung from that book. Thirdly, Pearsonius says that the custom of sitting down after prayer, observed by certain Christians of Tertullian's age, shows how much that book of Hermas was valued at that time, so that the rite was passed into the discipline of the Church. I marvel that these things could come into the learned man's mind, as if we should say that the rite we are discussing had been passed into the Church because it was observed by certain Christians, and those, it seems, simple ones. By the same reasoning I would conclude that the rite of lighting candles in honour of the martyrs was passed into the Church in Jerome's age, because it was likewise observed by certain Christians. But Jerome is so far from drawing that Pearsonian conclusion that he rather condemns the custom, just as Tertullian had condemned another, and reproves those who, through the inexperience and simplicity of worldly people, or certainly of religious women, do this in honour of the martyrs. Whatever the case, they say, Tertullian was a Montanist when he gave the book of Hermas the epithet of apocryphal. I grant it, but this will not detract from his testimony, nor will it deserve less credit. If the matter at issue were a dispute between the Montanists and the Catholics, Tertullian ought not to be heard. But since the question concerns the book of Hermas, which was proscribed and relegated to the apocrypha not only by the Montanists but also by the Catholics, no legitimate reason can be given why Tertullian's testimony should be rejected. The ancients did rebuke Tertullian for having deserted from the Catholics to the Montanists, but to my knowledge no one reproved him for placing the book of the Shepherd in the list of the apocrypha. Moreover, he did not pronounce this judgement against the book of Hermas alone, but affirms that it was also passed by a council of the Catholic Churches: by every council even of your Churches, namely of the Churches, as I interpret it, of the Latins and the Greeks. With what face, I ask, would Tertullian have dared to put this forward while addressing Catholics, unless he were speaking of a matter certain and by no means doubtful, and known to the Catholics themselves? The learned man has only one way left by which he thinks he can slip away and defend Hermas with his own arguments, namely by saying that perhaps nothing more is contained in Tertullian's words than that the Shepherd of Hermas was not, by the judgement of the Church, a canonical book, but was rather numbered among the Apocryphal, that is, the non-canonical. It is well that he wrote perhaps; without this little word of doubt he would be making a mockery of the reader. The Shepherd's writing was judged among the apocrypha and falsehoods by every council of the Churches, even the Catholic ones; yet according to the author of the Vindiciae, these words sound nothing more than that the Shepherd of Hermas was not, by the judgement of the Church, a canonical book, but was rather numbered among the Apocryphal, that is, the non-canonical. Clearly, to the learned man, writings that are apocryphal, false, fictitious, spurious, and adulterous are ecclesiastical writings, approved, authentic, of the second order in the Church, to be read and re-read by all the pious once, twice, thrice, indeed very often; in a word, writings not canonical but close to the canonical. See where the zeal of his cause carries this most distinguished man, to whom I fear I concede too much. Giovanni Maria Bralicellanus, Master of the Sacred Palace, judged this book of Hermas better and more soundly: It must in no way be doubted that this little book of the Shepherd, as it is now held, was not written by Hermas, the disciple of Paul, since it is filled with heresies and fables. St Gelasius in the Roman Council rejects it among the apocryphal writings; likewise St Prosper, in his book against Cassian, chapter 30, declares it to be of no authority. Antonius Augustinus, writing this, paid attention to that decree of Gelasius; as the Greek proverb says that later thoughts are better, so a later age has also determined more certain things about the book of the Shepherd. Atto of Vercelli, in the eighth tome of the Spicilegium, page 41, reports this censure of Gelasius on the book of Hermas of the tenth century: The book which is called the Shepherd is apocryphal.

units.la: Posterior igitur illa ætas cujus meminit Antonius Augustinus, tempus illud spectat quo Gelasius Papa primus cum septuaginta Episcopis celeberrimum in Synodo Romanâ decretum edidit de libris Canonicis, Ecclesiasticis, & Apocryphis; Decretum autem illud librum Hermæ in apocryphorum censu reponit, hanc Gelasij Notitiam laudarat Dallæus, & ex eâ ostenderat Gelasium Hermam in eo apocrypharum scripturarum ordine censuisse, quæ opponuntur, non simpliciter libris Veteris ac Novi Testamenti Canonicis, sed ijs in genere omnibus libris qui apud Christianos orthodoxos probati habentur, sive Divini divinitúsque inspirati, sive Ecclesiastici, quales sunt veterum scriptorum orthodoxorum piæ ac utiles lucubrationes, & ut res melius procederet, paterétque omnibus librum Pastoris à Nicephoro & Gelasio eodem planè sensu inter apocrypha scripta numeratum esse, Nicephori Indiculum cum Gelasij Decreto contendit, & post acuratam Indiculi & Decreti collationem, hæc subjicit. Vtriúsque censoris, Romani, & Constantinopolitani, & quidem utriúsque summam in Ecclesiâ dignitatem suo seculo gerentis, concors est, ut vides, planéque ejufdem generis censura; Eruditus Pearsonius ista celeberrimi Dallæi verba ridet, suave, inquit, omnino somnium est; somnium sunt clarissimo Vindiciarum Autori, quia forte ejus palato sapiunt spuria, nobis verò qui genuina tantùm amplectimur, fictáque abominamur, nequaquàm somnium erunt, sed constans & firma veritas; Verùm aliquid viro docto condonandum, illum urget concors illa censura, ideoque magno insurgit impetu in Gelasianum Decretum, omnémque movet lapidem ut illud Gelasio abjudicet, vel saltem ejus labefactet autoritatem, sperans forè ut si Gelasij Decreto fidem detrahere posset, se eadem quoque ratione stichometriæ Nicephori prorsus adempturum esse; sed ereor ne incassum laboret, atque oleum & operam perdat; primò dicit MSS. Colices multorum sæculorum in assignando Decreti Autore plurimùm variare, quia extat vetustissimus Codex Collectionis Dionysianæ in quo Decretum hoc Damaso Papæ tribuitur; Codex Ecclesiæ Vrgellensis,& Iurensis pervetustus ascribunt Hormisdæ;Alij Gelasium Autorem agnoscunt; mira profectò varietas, sed mirabilius Viri docti Consilium, qui in rebus nihili causæ quærit præsidium, ex infinitis ut ita dicam Gelasiani Decreti MSS.
