Codicibus, tres tantùm memorantur, qui in assignando Decreti Autore variant, cæteri magno consensu Gelasium Autorem agnoscunt [illegible, ~1 letter]ùm igitur tres illi codices qui variant in assignando Decreti Autore, numero sint pauciores, nec alijs antiquitate præstare dicantur, quin potior majórque debeat esse aliorum autoritas, quàm trium dubitabit nemo cui sanum erit sinciput; Deinde si valet ista Viri docti ratiocinatio, quid fiet de plærísque [?]Veterum scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum libris? cùm varient sæpissimè codices in assignandis istorum librorum Autoribus; quid quæso certi remanebit? si ob quotundam Codicum varietatem, vera ac genuina scripta veris ac legitimis parentibus abjudicentur ; praeterea diffiteri non potest Vir eruditus extare antiquissimum cujusdam Pontificis Romani Decretum, quo liber Hermae ad apocrypha ablegatur, & hoc sufficit, quamvis de Decreti Autore non constaret.
units.tr: That later age, then, of which Antonius Augustinus speaks, looks to the time when Pope Gelasius, with seventy bishops, issued in a Roman Synod his famous decree concerning the canonical, ecclesiastical and apocryphal books. That decree places the book of Hermas among the apocrypha. Dallaeus had praised this notice of Gelasius and had shown from it that Gelasius counted Hermas in that order of apocryphal writings which are set over against not simply the canonical books of the Old and New Testament, but in general against all the books approved among orthodox Christians, whether divine and divinely inspired, or ecclesiastical, such as the pious and useful works of orthodox writers of old. And so that the matter might go forward more smoothly, and that it might be plain to everyone that the book of the Shepherd was numbered among the writings called apocryphal by Nicephorus and Gelasius in exactly the same sense, he set the list of Nicephorus beside the decree of Gelasius, and after a careful comparison of the list and the decree he adds these words: The judgment of both censors, the Roman and the Constantinopolitan, each of whom held the highest dignity in the Church in his own age, is in agreement, as you see, and is plainly of the same kind. The learned Pearson mocks these words of the most renowned Dallaeus: It is an utterly sweet dream, he says. To the most distinguished author of the Vindications they are a dream, because perhaps spurious things taste good to his palate; but to us, who embrace only what is genuine and abominate what is fabricated, they will be no dream at all, but a constant and firm truth. Yet something must be forgiven a learned man, and that agreeing judgment presses him hard; therefore he rushes with great force against the Gelasian decree, and moves every stone to deny it to Gelasius, or at least to weaken its authority, hoping perhaps that if he could take away belief from the decree of Gelasius, he would also wholly strip away in the same way the stichometry of Nicephorus. But I fear he labours in vain and wastes his oil and effort. First, he says that manuscript codices of many centuries differ very much in assigning the author of the decree, because there exists a very ancient codex of the Dionysian Collection in which this decree is ascribed to Pope Damasus; the codex of the Church of Urgel, and a very old Jurensian one, ascribe it to Hormisdas; others acknowledge Gelasius as author. A wonderful variety indeed, but more wonderful is the counsel of the learned man, who in matters of no importance seeks support, when out of the countless manuscripts of the Gelasian decree, as one might say, only three are recorded which differ in naming the author of the decree, while the rest agree in acknowledging Gelasius as author. Since those three codices which differ in naming the author of the decree are fewer in number, and are not said to surpass the others in antiquity, surely the authority of the majority and the better ones ought to outweigh that of three; no one of sound mind will doubt this. Next, if this reasoning of the learned man holds good, what will become of very many books of the ancient ecclesiastical writers? For the codices very often vary in naming the authors of those books; what, I ask, will remain certain? If genuine and true writings are to be taken away from their true and lawful parents because of the variety of certain codices, then... Moreover, the learned man cannot deny that there exists a very ancient decree of a certain Roman Pontiff, by which the book of Hermas is relegated to the apocrypha; and this is enough, even though it were not certain who the author of the decree was.

units.la: Instat secundo doctissimus vindiciarum Autor, observátque referre quidem Gratianum, Decretum hoc scriptum fuisse à Gelasio in Concilio LXX. Episcoporum, sed tamen in vetustissimis MSS. illa de Concilio desiderari, quod probat autoritate Codicis MS. qui Cantabrigiae asservatur, & qui hunc titulum praefert, Decreta Gelasij Papae de recipiendis & non recipiendis Libris, quae scripta sunt ab eo cum LXX. eruditissimis Episcopi[?] conjicit autem hunc titulum fuisse antiquissimum, tum quod apud Burchardum ita concipitur, tum quod maximè, inquit, illis convenit quae apud Lupum Ferrariensem Epist. 128. legimus. Quoniam docet Gelasius cum LXX. Episcopis viris eruditissimis, qui scriptores essent vel non essent recipiendi. Utinam Gratianus gravius nunquam peccasset, & ab hac observatione se abstinuisset Vir doctus; nam etsi daremus Gratianum de suo illa de synodo addidisse, peccatum erit meâ quidem sententiâ levissimum, quoniam quae de suo ex suppoione addidit, nihil aliud sunt quàm plicatio verborum quæ ex MS. suo codice, & ex Epistola 128. Lupi Ferrienfis adducit Vir doctus: videbat Gratianus [?] Gelasium non solum qui[?]dem, sed una cum LXX. Episcopis Decretum de recipiendis & non recipiendis libris edidisse, hinc consequentiâ haud illegitimâ inferebat Decretum illud in quadam synodo conditum fuisse, & in quadam synodo Romanâ, quia Gelasius Romanæ sedis erat Episcopus: secundò nihil nos urget dicere Gratianum aliquid de suo hujusce Decreti titulo inseruisse; vidit scilicet Gratianus Codices MSS. quos præstantissimo Pearsonio videre non contigit, & qualem in illis Codicibus titulum reperit, bona fide repræsentavit, pergit Vir doctus & ait, aliqui autem MSS. Codices addiderunt Concilio huic etiam suos consules, celebratúmque tradiderunt ASTERIO & PRÆSIDIO COSS. Inde Baronium in Annalibus referre dicit congregatum Romæ Concilium LXX. Episcoporum tertio Gelasiani Pontificatus anno, Domini verò 494. cùm tamen nullum ejus in Historiâ Ecclesiasticâ extare monumentum aut vestigium existimet Pearsonius, Baronium secutus est in editione Conciliorum Binius, & Philippus Labbæus in Historicâ omnium Conciliorum synopsi ; verba autem Labbæi adfert quæ Concilium istud Gelasianum in hunc annum conferunt, & sub illis Consulibus celebratum ostendunt ; sed contrarium evincere conatur eruditusPearsonius,pluribus probas rationibus Gelasium nullum hoc anno convocasse Concilium ; esto, neque litem movere Viro docto in præsentiarum est animus , nullum convocârit hoc anno Concilium Gelasius , erraverit Baronius, & qui eum sequuti sunt Binius & Labbæus, ideóne hoc Concilium rejiciemus tanquam fictum & suppositititum, nimis certe iniquum esset aliquod reprobare Concilium ob unius aut alterius anni prochronismum sive metachronismum, non ignorat Vir doctus quantum sæpissimè varient scriptores in assignandis veris Conciliorum epochis , cùm tamen de ipsorum Conciliorum veritate inter se optimè conveniant ; nullum , inquit Pearsonius illius Concilij Gelasiani in Historiâ Ecclesiasticâ extat monumentum aut vestigium , quid tum , nonne plura sunt ad res Ecclesiæ spectantia , quorum tamen nulla prorsus mentio in Historiâ Ecclesiasticâ ? Nonne quotidie è tenebris eruuntur antiqua monumenta quæ ipsi Historiæ Ecclesiasticæ plurimùm lucis fœnerantur? einde si nullum istius Concilij Gelasiain Historiâ Ecclesiasticâ extabat moumentum aut vestigium, unde illius notiam expiscati sunt noni saeculi scriptores qui fatente Pearsonio Decreti quo degimus mentionem fecêre: ergo ante illud tempus extabat aliquod hujusce Concilij vestigium; divinare enim non poterant illi scriptores habitum fuisse sub Gelasio Romanum Concilium quo libri sacri & authentici ab Apocryphis sunt discreti; respondebit forsan hanc Concilij notitiam MSS. Codicum subsidio consequutos esse, igitur regeram ego extabant ante illud tempus Codices MSS. qui Gelasio & Synodo Romanæ istud Decretum ascribebant; si autem Codices illi MSS. adeò venerandæ erant Antiquitatis ut Gelasianum saeculum plane redolerent, nonne invictissimum pro Decreto quod ventilamus suppeditabunt argumentum: jam vero vetustissimos esse par est credere; quia si recens scripti fuissent, aliquam noni saeculi scriptoribus falsitatis suspicionem ingessissent, nullam ingessisse liquet, non igitur dubitandum est quin scriptoribus illis antiquissimi visi sint; audiendus esset Vir doctus si veterum auctoritate fultus Decretum Gelasianum impugnare esset aggressus, sed id conjecturis præstare velle, adversus tot scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum testimonia, tótque MSS. Codicum fidem, qui Gelasio hoc Decretum tribuunt, adeò frivolum est & inauditum, ut mirer Virum doctum talibus armis instructum in acie stare & certamen inire voluisse; quid ad hæc responsurus sit vindiciarum Autor non video; fatetur ipse plures noni sæculi scriptores hujus Decreti sub Gelasij nomine mentionem fecisse; diffiteri etiam non potest Codices MSS. quibus usi sunt sæculo nono vetustiores esse, ergo fateri etiam necesse est, Decretum istud Gelasio longè ante nonum sæculum attributum fuisse; nec obstat quod in aliquibus Codicibus notæ Consularis immeritò, ut ait Pearsonius addita sit; nam 1. de quibusdam tantùm agitur Codicibus, non de omnibus, 2. quamvis de omnibus ageretur Codicibus, non propterea abjudicandum esset Gelasio Decretum, ut patet ex ijs quæ diximus; 3. fieri potest ut Antiquarius quidam conjecturam suam de tempore Concilij ad oram libri seu Codicis scripserit, quæ postea in textum irrepsit, vel Amanuensium incuriâ velut ad textum pertineret, id est ad ipsum Concilij titulum, uno tenore transcripta fuit. Ejusdem propè farinæ sunt quæ de Eusebio observat ir doctus, nempe Gelasium Eusebij Historiam in Apocryphorum censu reponere, cùm tamen verus Gelasius ipsum inter Catholicos Patres numeret, illiusque testimonia ad confirmandam Ecclesiæ de duabus naturis Christi doctrinam adhibeat; unde colligit Pearsonius, Auorem Decreti verum Gelasium esse non videri[?], sed malè hanc elicit conclusionem Vir doctus: Gelasij Decretum duobus in locis Eusebij meminit; ideóque ab ipso Gelasio conciliatio petenda, primò Eusebij Chronica & Historiæ libros, inter libros Ecclesiasticos numerat, quos Ecclesia recipit Catholica, sed cum cautione quædam, id est non tàm recipiendos declarat, quàm usquequáque non renuendos, Chronica, inquit, Eusebij Cæsariensis, atque ejusdem Historiæ Ecclesiasticæ libros, quamvis in primo narrationis suæ libro tuerit, & post in laudibus atque excusatione Origenis schismatici unum conscripserit librum: propter rerum tamen singularum notitiam quæ ad instructionem pertinent, usquequáque non dicimus renuendos. Hæc Gelasij verba, ut quivis videt, partim probant, partim verò reprobant Historiæ Eusebij Ecclesiasticæ libros, dum igitur posteà dicit, Historia Eusebij Pamphili Apocrypha: Nemo non videt hæc ultima verba non simpliciter & absolutè accipienda, sed juxta mentem praecedentium explicanda ; praecedentia autem verba non omnia plane in Historiae libris reprobant, sed quaedam tantum quorum respectu Eusebij Historia Ecclesiastica Gelasio apocrypha indefinitè dicitur : nullo profecto incommodo laborat haec conciliatio, ab ipso Gelasio petita, non verò gratis ficta ; Et inde liquet Gelasium Eusebij Autoritatem, quicquid dicat, Pearsonius, ad confirmandam Ecclesiae doctrinam adhibere potuisse, cum omnia illius Viri in suo Decreto non reprobaverit ; frustra igitur haec Gelasij verba, Hi-storia Eusebij Pamphili apocrypha, huic decreto adjecta fuisse opinatus est vir quidam eruditus, nec melius alter qui de alio Eusebio quàm de illo Caesariensi ea intelligenda esse credidit apud Baluz. in notis ad Grat. pag. 445.446. nec denique ad tollendam eam repugnantiam, non quae esset, sed quae esse videretur, ad nescio quam apocryphorum distinctionem necesse est confugere ; cùm satis commodè alia ratione fuerit sublata.
units.tr: The most learned author of the Vindiciae presses a second point. He observes that Gratian does indeed report that this decree was written by Gelasius in a council of seventy bishops, but that the mention of the council is missing from the oldest manuscripts. He proves this on the authority of a manuscript codex kept at Cambridge, which bears the title The decrees of Pope Gelasius on the books to be received and not received, which he wrote together with seventy most learned bishops. He conjectures that this title is very old, both because it is given in this form by Burchard and especially because, as he says, it agrees best with what we read in the 128th letter of Lupus of Ferrières: Since Gelasius teaches, together with seventy most learned bishops, which writers are to be received and which are not. I wish Gratian had never erred so gravely, and that the learned author had refrained from this observation. For even if we grant that Gratian added the reference to the synod on his own, in my judgment the fault would be very slight, since what he added of his own accord is nothing more than a paraphrase of the wording which the learned author draws from his manuscript codex and from the 128th letter of Lupus of Ferrières. Gratian saw that Gelasius had issued the decree on the books to be received and not received not by himself alone but together with seventy bishops. From this he drew a not unreasonable inference that the decree had been made in some synod, and in a synod at Rome, since Gelasius was bishop of the Roman see. Secondly, there is no need for us to say that Gratian inserted anything of his own into the title of this decree. Gratian saw manuscript codices, which the most distinguished Pearson did not have the chance to see, and he faithfully reproduced the title he found in those codices. The learned author goes on and says: But some manuscript codices also added to this council their consuls, and handed down that it was held in the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius. From this he says that Baronius, in the Annals, reports that a council of seventy bishops was assembled at Rome in the third year of the pontificate of Gelasius, that is, in the year of the Lord 494; yet Pearson thinks that no monument or trace of it survives in ecclesiastical history. Binius in his edition of the councils followed Baronius, and so did Philip Labbé in his historical synopsis of all the councils. The learned author cites the words of Labbé, which assign that Gelasian council to this year and show that it was celebrated under those consuls. But the learned Pearson tries to prove the contrary, and by several arguments shows that Gelasius convened no council this year. Granted; nor is it my intention at present to start a quarrel with the learned author. Suppose Gelasius convened no council this year, and Baronius erred, and Binius and Labbé who followed him: shall we therefore reject this council as fictitious and spurious? It would certainly be far too unjust to condemn a council on account of an anachronism of one year or another. The learned author is not unaware how very often writers differ in assigning the true dates of councils, while agreeing very well about the reality of the councils themselves. Pearson says: No monument or trace of that Gelasian council survives in ecclesiastical history. So what? Are there not many matters pertaining to the affairs of the Church of which no mention at all is made in ecclesiastical history? Do not ancient monuments come out of darkness every day, which bring much light to ecclesiastical history itself? Then, if no monument or trace of this Gelasian council survived in ecclesiastical history, from where did the writers of the ninth century, who, as Pearson admits, made mention of the decree we are discussing, get knowledge of it? Therefore some trace of this council survived before that time, for those writers could not have guessed that a Roman council had been held under Gelasius at which the sacred and authentic books were distinguished from the apocryphal ones. Perhaps someone will reply that they came to know of this council with the aid of manuscript codices. Then I ask in return: did manuscript codices exist before that time which ascribed this decree to Gelasius and the Roman synod? And if those manuscript codices were of such venerable antiquity that they plainly smelled of the Gelasian age, will they not supply an most invincible argument for the decree we are examining? Indeed, it is right to believe they are very ancient; for if they had been written recently, they would have aroused some suspicion of forgery in the writers of the ninth century. It is clear they aroused none. Therefore there is no reason to doubt that they seemed very ancient to those writers. The learned author would deserve a hearing if, supported by the authority of the ancients, he had set out to attack the Gelasian decree. But to attempt to achieve this by conjectures, against so many testimonies of ecclesiastical writers and the faith of so many manuscript codices, which ascribe this decree to Gelasius, is so flimsy and unheard of that I am amazed the learned author wished to take the field and enter the contest armed with such weapons. I do not see what the author of the Vindiciae will reply to these points. He himself admits that several writers of the ninth century made mention of this decree under the name of Gelasius. Nor can he deny that the manuscript codices which those writers used are older than the ninth century. Therefore he must also admit that this decree was attributed to Gelasius long before the ninth century. Nor does it count against this that a note of the consulship has been wrongly added in some codices, as Pearson says. For, first, only some codices are in question, not all. Second, even if all codices were in question, the decree would not therefore have to be denied to Gelasius, as is clear from what we have said. Third, it may happen that some antiquary wrote his own conjecture about the date of the council in the margin of a book or codex, and this later crept into the text, or, through the carelessness of copyists, was transcribed in one stroke as though it belonged to the text, that is, to the title of the council itself. Of much the same kind are the points which the learned author makes about Eusebius: namely, that Gelasius places the History of Eusebius among the apocryphal books, although the true Gelasius counts Eusebius himself among the Catholic Fathers and uses his testimonies to confirm the Church's doctrine of the two natures of Christ. From this Pearson concludes that the author of the decree does not seem to be the true Gelasius. But the learned author draws this conclusion badly: Gelasius's decree mentions Eusebius in two places, and therefore the reconciliation must be sought from Gelasius himself. First, he counts the Chronicle and the books of the History of Eusebius of Caesarea among the ecclesiastical books which the Catholic Church receives, but with a certain caution. That is, he declares them not so much to be received as to be on no account rejected. The Chronicle, he says, and the books of the Ecclesiastical History of Eusebius of Caesarea, although in the first book of his narrative he erred, and afterwards wrote one book in praise and defence of the schismatic Origen, we nevertheless say are on no account to be rejected for the sake of the knowledge of individual matters which pertain to instruction. As anyone can see, these words of Gelasius partly approve and partly reject the books of Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History. Therefore when he says afterwards, The History of Eusebius Pamphili is apocryphal, no one fails to see that these last words are not to be taken simply and absolutely, but must be explained according to the sense of the preceding words. The preceding words, however, do not reject everything in the books of the History, but only certain parts; with respect to these the Ecclesiastical History of Eusebius is called apocryphal by Gelasius in an indefinite way. This reconciliation, sought from Gelasius himself and not invented at will, suffers no inconvenience at all. From this it is clear that Gelasius could have used the authority of Eusebius to confirm the Church's doctrine, whatever Pearson says, since he did not reject all of that man's works in his decree. Therefore some learned man was mistaken in supposing that these words of Gelasius, The History of Eusebius Pamphili is apocryphal, were added to this decree in vain; and another who believed they were to be understood of a different Eusebius and not of the Caesarean one was no better, see Baluze in his notes on Gratian, pp. 445-446. Nor, finally, is it necessary to take refuge in some distinction of apocryphal books, I know not what, in order to remove the contradiction, not one that really exists but one that only seems to exist, since it has been removed quite conveniently in another way.

units.la: Sed Decretum Gelasianum majori impetu adoritur Vir doctus, ex censurâ videlicet Canonum Apostolicorum contra illud argumentando : in hoc enim Deto istam Canonum illorum censuram imus, Liber qui appellatur Canones Apoorum Apocryphus; sibi autem persuadenon potest Pearsonius hanc censuram [?]lasio tribuendam esse, imo potius ei iudicandam putat,pluribus ad hoc im[?]ipsius rationibus,praesertim Dionysij exiii[?] autoritate, qui hos Canones Apostolorum interpretatus est, & reliquis praefiit Canonibus, minimè facturus si Gelaij quem [illegible, ~2 letters]ntopere admiratus est, constiuto tra[illegible, ~2 letters]xos atque jugulatos cognoisset, & ut nodum fortius stringat addit Vir eruditus,Dionysium post tam gravem censuram nunquam in Præfatione Operis sui, his verbis usum fuisse. In principio itaque Canones, qui dicuntur Apostolorum, de Græco transtulimus: quibus quia plurimi consensum non præbuere facilem, hoc ipsum vestram noluimus ignorare sanctitatem: quamvis postea quaedam constituta Pontificum ex ipsis Canonibus adsumpta esse videantur. Ex his Dionysij verbis infert Vir doctus Gelasium Canones Apostolorum in Apocryphorum classe haudquaquam censuisse; quia si censuisset, Dionysius non tantummodo dixisset plurimos consensum non praebuisse facilem, nec de hac dubitatione Stephanum Salonitanum Episcopum monendum duxisset, ne scilicet hoc ipsum ignoraret, qui quid à Gelasio in Concilio decretum fuit ignorare non potuit, nec denique posteà constituta Pontificum ex illis[?] Canonibus adsumpta fuisse notasset sed plura reponi possunt, primò nova est & ferè inaudita Viri docti methodus, agitur de Codicum MSS. & editorum fide quae rationibus convelli non potest, & tamen id facere conatur vindiciarum Autor, opponat Codices Codicibus, contendantur alij cum alijs, & praeferantur qu[?]i caeteris Antiquitate praestabunt; sed quamdiu conjecturis quibus nimiùm indulget Vir eruditus, res facti firmissimè stabilitas sollicitare aut evertere tentabit, haerebit illi aqua, nec propositum unquam consequetur finem: Secundò quamvis aliquo laboraret incommodo Gelasianum Decretum, non propterea statim reprobandum foret, plura sunt Ecclesiastica scripta, quae etsi varijs graventur incommodis, varijsque urgeantur difficultatibus, nihilominùs tamen ijs quorum nomina praeferunt Autoribus vindicantur: Tertiò argumentatur Vir doctus ex eo quod ait Dionysius exiguus constituta Pontificum ex Canonibus A-postolicis adsumpta esse: Verùm non ita se habent Dionysij verba, nihil plané affirmat, quid ipse sentiat tantùm aperit, & quid sibi videatur declarat, non autem id reapse sit ; quamvis postea , inquit, ædam constituta Pontificum ex ipsis Canonibus adsumptae esse videantur, nec per Pontifices necesse est intelligere Pontifices Romanos, sed in genere Episcopos, quorum è numero aliqui temporis lapsu Canonum Apostolorum autoritate uti poterunt, cùm anteà plurimi, ut Dionysij verba usurpem, consensum non præbuerunt facilem ; aliter quidem Dionysij verba explicat eruditus Pearsonius, & de Pontificibus Romanis intelligenda putat, sed ni fallor contra Autoris mentem, ut ex integrâ liquet Epistolâ, ex istis præsertim verbis, sacratissima jura Pontificalibus per Dei gratiam digesta conventibus: Pontificales enim illi conventus, nihil aliud sunt Dionysio quàm Episcoporum Concilia : cur igitur per Pontificum constituta non intelligemus eorundem Episcoporum sanctiones atque decreta ? nec est quòd Pearsonius ista clarissimi Dallæi damnet, Ego verò putaverim non ex Canonum collectione suâ decreta Pontifices, sed ex Pontificum constitutis suos Canones assumpsisse primum eorum collectorem. Dallæus ait Vindiciarum Autor, seipsum Dionysio directè & ex diametro opponit, nequaquàm, Dionysius non affirmat, non negat Dallæus, nulla est igitur ex diametro oppositio ,utérque suum modò interponit judicium,existimabat Dionysius quædam Pontificum constituta ex Canonibus Apostolorum fuisse assumpta , alia mens Dallæo, nempè conjecturis agunt ambo, & quid de istis sentiant proferre contenti, nihil præcisè affirmare , nihil exertè negare, in animo habuerunt. Quidquid sit probat Vir doctus Canones Apostolorum post Dionysij translationem statim receptos fuisse , probat autem hisce Cassiodori verbis Divin. lect. cap 23. Petitus à Stephano Episcopo Salonitano ex Græcis exemplaribus Canones Ecclesiasticos moribus suis, ut erat planus & disertus, magnâ eloquentiæ luce composuit, quos hodie usu celeberrimo Ecclesia Romana completitur: Non nego Ecclesiam Romanam Dionysij collectione usam esse , eámque statim Priscæ translationi prætulisse , sed ita tamen ut Canones Apostolicos ab hoc usu segregasse valdè sit probabile, ignorare quippè non poterat Gelasij Decreto ad apocrypha relegatos esse ,& hoc innuere videtur ipse Cassiodorus dùm Canones memorat Ecclesiasticos , nullâ Canonum Apostolorum mentione factâ ; Quamvis enim quinquaginta ex illis Canonibus Dionysianæ collectioni præfixi sint , tamen quia ab omnibus non recipiebantur, ectorem moniturus erat Cassiodorus, cclesiam Romanam istos etiam cum caeteris in eadem collectione comprehensis, su[?], ut ait, celeberrimo completi. Verum ut Cassiodori verba ad Canones Apostolicos extendat Vir doctus, confugit ad quandam Ioannis 2. Pontificis Romani Epistolam, cui subjecti sunt Canones Apostolici XXV. & XXIX. Hanc Epistolam edidit Sirmondus doctissimus & diligentissimus scriptor, eámque contulit in annum 533. Et post Epistolam extant quilam Canones tanquam ab Ioanne 2. transmissi, inter quos duo numerantur Apotolici; sed ut liberè dicam quod sentio, non mihi usquequaque probatur haec Epistola, imò plura sunt quae suppositiiam suadent. 1. non est credibile Pontificem Romanum haec boni sensus prorsus acua effutisse, si qui tamen Pontificatus immemores criminibus se fortasse involve-int, & eorum personas vulgus cognoscat: facilius enim à delictis cavent, si non videant etiam hominibus secreta esse quae fecerint, quid sibi velint ista, divinare non est facie, 2. sequentia cum istis non cohaerent. Quae vero de his Canones praecipiunt subter adjecimus. 3. Titulus Canonibus praefixus suspicionem auget. Hi tituli Canonum, quos nobis suprascriptus sanctus & domnus meus Ioannes Papa sedis Apostolicæ cum præfata auctoritate direxit, certè verisimile non fit Cæsarium Arelatensem scientiâ & dignitate conspicuum, tàm serviliter támque barbarè ac insulsè loquutum esse. 4. Deest nota Consularis quàm suis Epistolis Pontifices Romani tunc temporis apponere solebant, ut ex aliis ipsius Ioannis 2. Epistolis liquet. 5. quid significet vox sacrius ignoro, non me latet sacrium in genere neutro succini & electri genus esse, sed sacrius in genere masculino quàm significationem habeat nescio, præsertim cum de homine dicitur, illam enim vocem usurpat Ioannes 2. de contumelioso Regensi Episcopo verba faciens; ita enim Cæsarium alloquitur; Caritatis tuæ literas animo libenti suscepimus, in quibus corporeas necessitates allegans, etiam quæ sacrius ille, qui lapsus est, fecerit indicasti: Contumeliosus scilicet ob admissi criminis notam ab Episcopatu dejectus est, ideóque lapsum esse dicit Pontifex. 6. Denique Pontifices Romani nihil antiquius habuêre, quàm ut appellationum jura suæ sedi assererent; tamen si genuina esset quam examinamus Epistola, Ioannes 2. contrarium planè faceret: nam inter Canones quos Epistolæ suæ subtexuisse dicitur, numeratur Concilij Antiocheni Caon XV. qui appellationes perimit ominò atque jugulat. Si quis Episcopus de ertis criminibus accusatus condemnatur ab mnibus Episcopis ejusdem Provinciae, cunctlique consonanter eandem contra eum formam decreti protulerint; hunc apud alios nullo modo judicari, sed firmam concordantium Episcoporum Provinciae manere sententiam. Itane suae sedi iniquus erat Ioannes Papa 2. Illiusque juribus infensus, ut quam tueri debebat causam prodat: Contumeliosus à Provinciae suae Episcopis condemnatus fuit, ad sedem appellavit Romanam, vel ut de illo loquitur Agapetus Ioannis successor, ad appellationis voluit auxilium convolare: Quis igitur sibi persuadere poterit Ioannem ea ad Caesarium Arelatensem contumeliosi Metropolitanum scribere voluisse, quibus transfiguntur illa omnia appellationum jura pro quibus tanquam pro aris & focis dimicarunt Episcopi Romani; Omnibus istis ductus rationibus hanc Epistolam Ioanni 2. abjudico, & abjudicabit mecum quisquis paulò attentius quae scripsimus considerare ac perpendere dignabitur; Nec propterea haec scripsi quasi nulla alia ad objectionem Viri docti nobis suppeteret solutio: quamvis enim concederemus Vindiciarum Autori, Epistolam quâ de agimus genuinum esse Ioannis Papae 2. foetum, minimè sequeretur Canones Apostolorum à Gelasio inter apocrypha non fuisse rejectos, nam si multa in ipsis haereticorum libris leguntur, quae cùm ad fidem pertineant, non refutanda sunt, sed suscipienda; quidni libris apocryphis plura in esse poterint bona à nobis pariter suscipienda & cum fructu legenda, istiùs autem apocryphorum generis sunt Canones Apostolorum, in quibus, ut ait Hincmarus, quaedam receptibilia, quaedam vero sunt non servanda: non mirum igitur si Ioannes 2. salvo Gelasiani Decreti jure, Canones istos adferre non dubitaverit, quoniam, ut ait iterùm Hincmarus, in quibusdam ad instructionem valent. Negari equidem non potest quosdam Canones seu titulos, ut vocant, antiquorum Patrum à Ioanne Papa 2. ad Cæsarium Arelatensem transmissos esse, saltem id nos expresse docet Tractatus Anonymus, quem Cæsarij ipsius esse conjicit Sirmondus, & qui post Ioannis Epistolam, eique annexos Canones editus est; sed an ipsifsimi sint quos habemus Canones, eadémque Ioannis Epistola, haud liquidò constat, imò multus superest dubitandi locus, ob rationes à nobis suprà commemoratas, quibus adjicias velim hanc Sirmon[?]li[?] annotatiunculam, nempè quæ edidit [?]d contumeliosi causam pertinentia, non [?]mnia ex uno, sed ex diversis Codicibus derompta esse: Hinc facilior fraudi ac suppositioni nascitur occasio, proniorque in errorem lapsus. Insuper conjecturas [?]neas de Ioannis Epistolâ, subjectisque [?]anonibus à quopiam non ita accipi vellim, velut ijs seu firmissimis inniterer demonstrationibus, conjecturæ sunt, sed conjecturæ quæ verisimilitudine non carent, & quæ ideò ad scriptorum istorum fidem convellendam aptissimæ sunt.
units.tr: But the learned author attacks the Decretum of Gelasius with greater force, arguing against it from the censure of the Apostolic Canons. In that book, he says, we find this censure of those Canons: The book called the Apocryphal Canons of the Apostles. Pearson, however, cannot persuade himself that this censure should be attributed to Gelasius. He thinks it should rather be judged to be the work of someone else, and he gives several reasons for this, especially the authority of Dionysius Exiguus, who translated these Canons of the Apostles and prefaced the rest of the Canons. Dionysius would hardly have done so if he had known that Gelasius, whom he greatly admired, had condemned them and cut them down. To tighten the knot further, the learned author adds that Dionysius, after so grave a censure, never used the following words in the preface to his work: At the beginning, then, we have translated the Canons that are called the Apostles' from the Greek. Since many have not given them easy assent, we did not want your holiness to be ignorant of this, although certain decrees of the Pontiffs seem later to have been taken from these Canons. From these words of Dionysius the learned author infers that Gelasius did not by any means count the Apostolic Canons among the apocrypha, for if he had, Dionysius would not merely have said that many had not given easy assent, nor would he have thought it necessary to warn Stephen, Bishop of Salona, lest he, that is, should be ignorant of this very thing, since he could not be ignorant of what had been decreed at the council by Gelasius; nor would he have noted that later decrees of the Pontiffs had been taken from those Canons. But many points can be put in reply. First, the author's method is new and almost unheard of. The question concerns the good faith of manuscripts and editions, which cannot be overturned by arguments, and yet the author of the Vindiciae tries to do this. Let him set manuscripts against manuscripts, let them be weighed against one another, and let those be preferred that excel the rest in antiquity. But as long as he tries to shake or overturn a fact firmly established by conjectures, in which the learned author indulges far too much, he will be stuck fast in the water and will never reach his goal. Second, even if the Decretum of Gelasius suffered from some difficulty, it would not therefore have to be rejected at once. There are many ecclesiastical writings which, though burdened with various difficulties and pressed by various problems, are nonetheless vindicated as the work of the authors whose names they bear. Third, the learned author argues from what Dionysius Exiguus says, that decrees of the Pontiffs were taken from the Apostolic Canons. But Dionysius's words do not stand as he presents them. He affirms nothing outright; he only reveals what he himself thinks and declares what seems so to him, and not what is actually the case. He says: although later certain decrees of the Pontiffs seem to have been taken from these very Canons. Nor must we understand by "Pontiffs" the Roman Pontiffs in particular; he means bishops in general, some of whom in the course of time could make use of the authority of the Apostolic Canons, since before this, to use Dionysius's own words, many had not given easy assent. Learned Pearson explains Dionysius's words differently and thinks they are to be understood of the Roman Pontiffs, but, unless I am mistaken, this is against the author's meaning, as is clear from the whole letter, especially from these words: the most sacred laws, arranged by the grace of God in Pontifical assemblies. For those Pontifical assemblies are, for Dionysius, nothing other than councils of bishops. Why then should we not understand by "decrees of the Pontiffs" the sanctions and decrees of those same bishops? Nor is there reason for Pearson to condemn what the most distinguished Dallaeus says: I should think that the first collector of them took his Canons not from the Pontiffs' decrees, as from his own collection, but from the decrees of the Pontiffs. The author of the Vindiciae says that Dallaeus directly and diametrically opposes himself to Dionysius. By no means: Dionysius does not affirm, and Dallaeus does not deny. There is therefore no diametrical opposition; each simply offers his own judgment. Dionysius thought that certain decrees of the Pontiffs had been taken from the Apostolic Canons; Dallaeus had a different opinion. Both proceed by conjecture, and both, content to state what they think of these matters, intended neither to assert anything precisely nor to deny anything plainly. Whatever the case, the learned author proves that the Canons of the Apostles were received at once after Dionysius's translation, and he proves it by these words of Cassiodorus, Divine Readings, chapter 23: Asked by Stephen, Bishop of Salona, he composed the ecclesiastical Canons from Greek copies in his own manner, with great light of eloquence, as he was clear and skilled; these the Roman Church now completes with most famous use. I do not deny that the Roman Church used Dionysius's collection and at once preferred it to the old translation. But it is quite probable that the Roman Church kept the Apostolic Canons apart from this use, since it could not be ignorant that they had been relegated among the apocrypha by the Decretum of Gelasius. Cassiodorus himself seems to hint at this when he mentions the ecclesiastical Canons without any mention of the Canons of the Apostles. For although fifty of those Canons were prefixed to Dionysius's collection, nevertheless, since they were not received by all, Cassiodorus would have had to warn the reader; the Roman Church, as he says, completed them with most famous use together with the others included in the same collection. But in order to extend Cassiodorus's words to the Apostolic Canons, the learned author takes refuge in a certain letter of John II, Bishop of Rome, to which are appended Apostolic Canons XXV and XXIX. This letter was published by Sirmond, a most learned and diligent writer, who dated it to the year 533. After the letter there follow some Canons as if sent by John II, among which two are numbered as Apostolic. But, to speak freely as I think, this letter does not win my approval in every respect; indeed, there are many things that suggest it is spurious. (1) It is not credible that a Roman Pontiff would have uttered such ill-considered sentiments: if some who, forgetful of the pontificate, perhaps become involved in crimes, and their persons are known to the common people; for they more easily guard against misdeeds if they see that what they have done is not hidden even from men. What these words mean, it is not easy to guess. (2) The following sentences do not cohere with these: What the Canons prescribe about these we have added below. (3) The title prefixed to the Canons increases suspicion: These titles of the Canons, which the aforesaid holy and lord, my John, Pope of the Apostolic See, sent to us with the said authority. It is certainly not likely that Caesarius of Arles, distinguished for learning and rank, spoke so servilely, so barbarously and so insipidly. (4) The consular date, which the Roman Pontiffs of that time customarily added to their letters, as is clear from other letters of John II, is lacking. (5) I do not know what the word sacrius means. I am not unaware that sacrium in the neuter gender is the name of a kind of amber and electrum, but what sacrius in the masculine gender means I do not know, especially when it is said of a man. John II uses this word of the insolent Bishop of Riez, speaking as follows to Caesarius: We have received your charity's letters with a willing mind, in which, pleading bodily needs, you have also indicated what that sacrius man who has fallen has done. Evidently the insolent man was deposed from the episcopate on account of the stain of an admitted crime, and therefore the Pontiff says that he has fallen. (6) Finally, the Roman Pontiffs held nothing more important than to assert the rights of appeal for their see. Yet if the letter we are examining were genuine, John II would be doing the plain opposite. For among the Canons which he is said to have appended to his letter is Canon XV of the Council of Antioch, which utterly destroys and cuts down appeals: If any bishop accused of certain crimes is condemned by all the bishops of the same province, and they all agree in pronouncing the same form of decree against him, he may in no way be judged by others, but the sentence of the agreeing bishops of the province shall stand firm. Was John II, then, so unfair to his own see, and so hostile to its rights, that he betrays the cause he ought to defend? The insolent man was condemned by the bishops of his own province; he appealed to the Roman see, or, as Agapetus, John's successor, says of him, he wished to fly for the aid of appeal. Who then can persuade himself that John wrote to Caesarius, metropolitan of the insolent man, things by which all those rights of appeal are overthrown, for which the Roman bishops fought as for their altars and hearths? Moved by all these reasons, I reject this letter as the work of John II, and whoever deigns to consider and weigh what we have written a little more carefully will reject it with me. Nor have I written these things as if no other answer to the learned author's objection were available to us. For even if we granted to the author of the Vindiciae that the letter in question is a genuine product of John II, it would by no means follow that the Apostolic Canons were not rejected by Gelasius among the apocrypha. For if many things are read in the books of heretics which, since they pertain to faith, are not to be refuted but to be accepted, why should not apocryphal books also contain many good things that we likewise ought to accept and read with profit? Of this kind of apocrypha are the Apostolic Canons, in which, as Hincmar says, some things are to be received, but some are not to be observed. It is therefore no wonder if John II, without prejudice to the law of the Decretum of Gelasius, did not hesitate to bring forward these Canons, since, as Hincmar says again, in some matters they are useful for instruction. Certainly it cannot be denied that John II sent certain Canons, or titles as they are called, of the ancient Fathers to Caesarius of Arles. At least the anonymous treatise, which Sirmond conjectures to be Caesarius's own and which was published after John's letter and the Canons annexed to it, expressly teaches us this. But whether the Canons we have are truly those very ones, and whether that same letter of John's is genuine, is not clearly established. Indeed, much room for doubt remains, for the reasons I mentioned above. To these I should like to add this small note of Sirmond's, namely that what he published concerning the affair of the insolent man was not all taken from one manuscript but from different manuscripts. Hence an easier occasion for fraud and forgery arises, and a more ready slip into error. Moreover, I would not have anyone take my conjectures about John's letter and the Canons appended to it as if they rested on the most certain demonstrations. They are conjectures, but conjectures that lack no verisimilitude, and which are for that reason very well suited to shaking the credibility of those writings.

units.la: Unum adhuc superesset Viro docto ad-versus Gelasij Decretum ex Dionysio exiguo petitum argumentum; scribit siquidem Dionysium Apostolorum Canones tam leni censurâ minimè perstricturum esse, nec tantummodo plurimos consensum non præbuisse facilem, id est, aliquo modo de eorum autoritate dubitâsse dicturum, si ante paucos annos Pontificem Romanum in Concilio eos numerâsse inter illa scripta, quæ Catholicis vitanda sunt, & quæ nullatenus recipit Catholica & Apostolica Romana Ecclesia novissęt. Sed fallitur eruditus Pearsonius nec modum agendi Dionysij animadvertit, non potuit ignorare Dionysius qui Gelasij ævo erat proximus, ac penè ejus par, Canones Apostolicos à Pontifice illo damnatos esse, & inter scripta apocrypha recensitos; sed quia propensissimo erga eos erat animo, ut potè homo ortu ac natu, cultúque ac eruditione exterus, à se obstinere non potuit, quin Græcos suæ gentis Canones in Latinam linguam à se translatos, Romanis, apud quos vivebat, communicaret, ac ne eorum animos rei novitate offenderet, invidiam, quâ eos flagrare noverat, lenire imprimis modestâ præfatione studuit, non dissimulans quidem rejectos à plurimis, sed tamen eos tacitè purgans, aut certè excusans, dùm ait quædam constituta Pontificum ex ipsis assumpta esse videri; Hinc patet Vindiciarum Autorem laborasse incassum cum Gelasij Decretum Dionysij exigui autoritate evertere est aggressus, certè nisi Dionysius ex præiudicatâ quadam opinione egisset, nimióque erga Canones istos studio, non dubitandum est quin eos ex Gelasij disciplina in sua collectione prætermisset, perinde ac Ferrandus Diaconus, qui nullum ijs dedit locum in suo Ecclesiasticorum Canonum Breviario, quod ijsdem propemodùm temporibus confecit. Sed si Ferrandus Canones Apostolorum silentio suo notat paulò post sexti sæculi initia; Isidorus Hispalensis Archiepiscopus anno septimi sæculi sexto tricesimo denatus, eosdem Canones iserte[?] damnavit, & tristius atque atrociùs quàm alij de his decrevit.Ejus autem a de re verba, & à Gratiano in Decretum relata, & teste Antonio Augustino longè doctissimo Viro, in omnibus veteribus libris Hispaniae Conciliorum inventa, ita habent, Canones qui dicuntur Apostolorum, sed quia eosdem nec sedes Apostolica recepit, nec sancti Patres illis assensum praebuerunt, ro eo quòd ab haereticis sub nomine Apostolorum compositi dignoscuntur; quamvis in eis utilia inveniantur, tamen ab auctoritate Canonum, atque Apostolica, eorum gesta constat esse remota, atque inter apocrypha deputata. Hactenùs Hispalensis Isidorus; planè contra sentiens, quàm ille alter Isidorus vulgò Mercator dictus, noni saeculi tenebrio, planus & impostor, cujus verba Gratianus quoque recitat; Gratianus verò ut observat Antonius Augustinus, non distinxit varietatem horum scriptorum, ut debuit, cùm contraria dicerent. Hic enim Mercator hos Canones probat, quos ille (Hispalensis scilicet Isidorus) rejecerat. Nec Isidorum deterruit audax Dionysij Exigui facinus hos Canones suae Collectioni inserentis, quin potiùs illum tacitè notat, cùm asserit sanctos Patres illis assensum non praebuisse: Dionysius enim non de sanctis Patribus, sed de plurimis, non de assensu simpliciter, sed de assensu facili loquitur, quibus plurimi, inquit, consensum non præbuêre facilem; De inde Isidorus hos Canones ab hæreticis sub nomine Apostolorum compositos, à sede Apostolicâ non receptos, nec à Patribus probatos, sed inter apocrypha deputatos, & ab autoritate Canonicâ, atque Apostolicâ remotos fuisse, liquidò & rotundè pronuntiat: Dionysius de his omnibus ne γῷ[?] quidem, nempe Dionysij intererat ista silentio præterire, ne Latinorum animos quibus Græcanicos suos Canones sensim commendatos volebat, ab iis averteret. Præterea dum hæc scribebat Isidorus ejus animo obversabatur Gelasij decretum quo Canones Apostolici jugulati sunt atque transfixi; Dionysius qui celeberrimi illius Decreti memoriam sepultam & extinctam cupiebat, illud ab hominum mentibus procul arcere studebat, nullâ prorsus ejus mentione factâ. Denique Isidorus rem ut est candidè narrat, sincerè agit, uníque veritati litat; Dionysius verò omnia suo proposito accommodat, Canones purgat, excusat, invidiam quâ eos gravari intelligebat lenit, illis patrocinatur, nihilque non agit ut lectorem experiantur favorabilem. Iam utriùs potior sit ac major autoritas, si ro-gas, gas, hoc habeto responsum: potiorem ac majorem esse Isidori autoritatem quàm Dionysij, Isidorus quippè Archiepiscopus fuit, scientiâ, eruditione ac merito clarissimus; Dionysius verò erat professione Monachus & posteà Romani Monasterij Abbas, eximijs quidem ornatus fuit dotibus, Isidoro tamen merito ac dignitate longè inferior; ex his omnibus liquet viguisse adhuc septimo sæculo inchoato & ferè medio Gelasiani Decreti famam atque robur, liquet præterea Dionysium Exiguum Decretum illud dissimulasse, quia proposito suo adversabatur; frustrà igitur ex leni Dionysij quâ Canones Apostolicos notatos volunt censurâ, argumentatur contra Gelasij Decretum clarissimus vindiciarum Autor.
units.tr: One argument against Gelasius's Decree drawn from Dionysius Exiguus would still remain for the learned man. He writes that Dionysius would not have criticised the Apostolic Canons so mildly, and would not merely have said that many did not give them ready assent, that is, that he doubted their authority in some way, if only a few years earlier the Roman Pontiff had counted them among those writings that are to be avoided by Catholics and that the Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church has by no means received. But the learned Pearson is mistaken and does not notice Dionysius's way of proceeding. Dionysius, who lived close in time to Gelasius and was nearly his equal, could not have been unaware that the Apostolic Canons had been condemned by that Pontiff and listed among the apocryphal writings. But because he was strongly disposed towards them, being by birth, upbringing, culture and learning a foreigner, he could not refrain from passing on to the Romans among whom he lived the Greek Canons of his own nation, translated by himself into Latin. So that he would not offend their minds by the novelty of the matter, he took care above all, by a modest preface, to soften the odium which he knew they blazed with. He did not indeed deny that they were rejected by many, but he quietly excused or at least defended them, saying that certain decrees of the Pontiffs appear to have been taken from them. From this it is clear that the author of the Vindiciae laboured in vain when he set out to overthrow Gelasius's Decree on the authority of Dionysius Exiguus. Indeed, unless Dionysius had acted from some prejudged opinion and from excessive zeal for those Canons, there is no doubt that he would have left them out of his collection in line with Gelasius's discipline, just as Ferrandus the deacon, who gave them no place in his Breviarium of Ecclesiastical Canons, compiled at almost the same time, did. But if Ferrandus passed over the Apostolic Canons in silence shortly after the beginning of the sixth century, Isidore of Seville, archbishop, who died in the sixth year of the seventh century, expressly condemned the same Canons, and decided about them more sternly and savagely than others did. His own words, which Gratian reports in the Decretum, and which, according to Antonio Augustino, a most learned man, are found in all the old books of the Councils of Spain, read thus: The Canons which are called the Apostles', but because neither the Apostolic See received them, nor the holy Fathers gave them assent, for the reason that they are known to have been composed by heretics under the name of the Apostles; although useful things are found in them, nevertheless it is established that their acts are removed from the authority of the canons and of the Apostles, and are reckoned among the apocrypha. So far Isidore of Seville. He thinks quite the opposite of that other Isidore, commonly called Mercator, a darkness of the ninth century, a plain impostor, whose words Gratian also cites; and Gratian, as Antonius Augustinus observes, did not distinguish the variety of these writers, as he ought to have done, since they said contrary things. For this Mercator approves those Canons which the other (namely Isidore of Seville) had rejected. Nor did the bold deed of Dionysius Exiguus, who inserted these Canons into his collection, deter Isidore from quietly censuring him, when he asserts that the holy Fathers did not give them assent. For Dionysius does not speak of the holy Fathers but of many, and not of assent simply but of ready assent: to which many, he says, have not given ready assent. Then Isidore plainly and roundly pronounces that these Canons were composed by heretics under the name of the Apostles, not received by the Apostolic See, nor approved by the Fathers, but reckoned among the apocrypha, and removed from canonical and apostolic authority. Dionysius said not a word about any of these matters. It was in his interest to pass them over in silence, lest he turn away the minds of the Latins, to whom he was gradually wanting to recommend his Greek Canons. Moreover, while Isidore was writing these things, Gelasius's decree, by which the Apostolic Canons were slain and pierced through, was before his mind. Dionysius, who wished the memory of that very famous Decree buried and extinguished, strove to keep it far from men's minds, making no mention of it at all. Finally, Isidore relates the matter as it is, frankly, sincerely, and sacrifices only to truth. Dionysius, on the other hand, fits everything to his purpose: he cleanses the Canons, excuses them, softens the odium which he understood weighed upon them, defends them, and does everything so that the reader may find them favourable. Now, if you ask which of the two has the greater and weightier authority, take this as the answer: the authority of Isidore is greater and weightier than that of Dionysius. Isidore was indeed an archbishop, most distinguished for learning, erudition and merit; Dionysius was by profession a monk and afterwards abbot of a Roman monastery, endowed with excellent gifts, but far inferior to Isidore in merit and dignity. From all this it is clear that the fame and strength of Gelasius's Decree still flourished at the beginning and nearly the middle of the seventh century; it is clear too that Dionysius Exiguus passed over that Decree because it stood against his purpose. Therefore the most distinguished author of the Vindiciae argues in vain against Gelasius's Decree from the mild censure with which they would have Dionysius mark the Apostolic Canons.

units.la: Verùm eniimverò animum non despondet Vir doctus, qui molestè ferens ignominiæ notam Gelasij constituto Apostolorum Canonibus ceu ferro candére inustam esse, aliâ viâ probare nititur eos ab illo Pontifice minimè notatos esse, non pauca sunt, inquit, quæ me movent, ut cre-dam ipsum Gelasium Canones, qui dicuntur Apostolorum, & admisisse, & in suis Epistolis Decretalibus usum ipsis fuisse. Mira prosectò Gelasij lenitas & inconstantia, si, ut ait Pearsonius hos Canones probat inEpistolis, quos alibi damnasse demonstravimus; sed ne tanta Pontifici fiat injuria, examinemus quae dicit eruditus Ignatianorum Vindex, primo tricesimum citat Apostolorum Canonem, qui aliis est vigesimus-nonus, si quis Episcopus, aut Presbyter, aut Diaconus, per pecunias hanc obtinuerit dignitatem; deiiciatur & ipse, & Ordinator eius, & a communione modis omnibus abscindatur, sicut Simon Magus a Petro: hoc Canone usum esse Gelasium in sua Epistola Decretali ad Episcopos Lucaniae, existimat Vir doctus istis Epistolae verbis fretus. Quos vero constiterit indignos meritis, sacram mercatos esse pretio dignitatem, convictos oportet arceri, non sine periculo facinus tale perpetrantes (vel ut legit Pearsonius ex Codice MS. perpetrantis) quia dantem pariter & accipientem damnatio Simonis, quam sacra lectio testatur, involvit. Respondet Dallaeus, inquit, de Pseud. Apost. lib. 3. c. 4. Gelasij locus nullum omnino Canonem laudat, neque Apostolicum, neque Ecclesiasticum. Tantum SIMONIS DAMNATIONEM memorat, quam SACRA LECTIO, Actuum scilicet Apostolicorum, ut notum est, testatur. Verum est haec scripsisse praestantissimum Dallaeum, & appositè certè, cùm nullum planè Canonem laudet Gelasius, nec hoc diffitetur Pearsonius, ait modò, hoc Gelasij constitutum ex illo Canone adsumptum esse, nec ullâ aliâ ratione probat suam hanc assertionem, quàm istâ, agi scilicet in hoc Gelasij constituto, perinde ac in Canone Apostolico, de simoniacè promoto ac promovente, arceatur dans pariter accipiensque. Sed nullâ inde necessariâ consequentiâ deduci potest Gelasij sanctionem ex Canone Apostolico adsumptam esse, si nullum hac de re indubitatum extaret Gelasio vetustius Decretum, aliquam forte veri speciem haberet Viri docti ratiocinatio: sed cùm plura reperiantur ejusmodi Decreta in veris ac genuinis Antiquitatis Ecclesiasticæ monumentis, quin ad ea respexerit Gelasius nullus dubito; primò habemus S. Basilij Epistolam ad Episcopos sibi subjectos, quæ in novissimâ Canonicarum SS. Patrum Epistolarum editione, ut illius Canon XCI. repræsentatur, in hac autem Epistolâ agit cótra simoniacos, vetátque ne in posterum propter pecunias fiant ordinationes,historiam tangit Simonis Magi, qui pecuniâ spiritus sancti gratiam emere volebat, & depositioni subjicit juxta Balsamonis explicationem tam eos qui ordinant, quàm qui ordinantur, sive ante ordinationem pecunias acceperint vel dederint; sive post ordinationem : obijt verò Basilius centum plus minus annos antequàm Gelasius ad Pontificatum promoveretur. Secundò Canon 2. Concilij Calchedonensis contra simoniacas promotiones 4o. ante Gelasium annos conditus est hoc pacto.
units.tr: But the learned man does not lose heart. Taking it hard that the mark of ignominy is burned into the Apostolic Canons as with a red-hot iron by Gelasius's decree, he seeks to prove by another route that they were by no means marked by that Pontiff. There are not a few things, he says, which move me to believe that Gelasius himself both admitted the Canons which are called the Apostles' and used them in his Decretal Epistles. Truly a strange gentleness and inconsistency on Gelasius's part, if, as Pearson says, he approves in his letters those Canons which we have shown he condemned elsewhere! But so that such a great injury is not done to the Pontiff, let us examine what the learned champion of the Ignatians says. First he cites the thirtieth Apostolic Canon, which by others is the twenty-ninth: If any bishop, or presbyter, or deacon, has obtained this dignity through money, let him be deposed, both he and his ordainer, and be cut off from communion in every way, just as Simon Magus was by Peter. The learned man thinks that Gelasius used this Canon in his Decretal Epistle to the bishops of Lucania, relying on these words of the letter: Those who are known to be unworthy of merit and to have bought holy dignity for a price, must be convicted and kept away, since those who commit such a crime do so not without danger (or, as Pearson reads from a manuscript copy, committing), because the condemnation of Simon, which holy Scripture attests, involves alike the giver and the receiver. Dallaeus, he says, answers in On Pseudo-Apostles, book 3, chapter 4: Gelasius's passage cites no Canon at all, neither Apostolic nor ecclesiastical. It mentions only the CONDEMNATION OF SIMON, which the HOLY READING, that is, of the Acts of the Apostles, as is well known, attests. It is true that the most excellent Dallaeus wrote these things, and certainly to the point, since Gelasius cites no Canon whatever, and Pearson does not deny this. He merely says that this decree of Gelasius was taken from that Canon, and he proves this assertion by no other reasoning than this: that in this decree of Gelasius, as in the Apostolic Canon, the matter concerns one who has been promoted by simony and the one who promotes, and that the giver and receiver alike must be kept away. But no necessary consequence can be drawn from this that Gelasius's sanction was taken from the Apostolic Canon. If no certain older decree than Gelasius's existed on this matter, the learned man's reasoning might have some appearance of truth. But since many decrees of this kind are found in the genuine and authentic monuments of ancient Church history, and I have no doubt that Gelasius looked to them, first we have the Epistle of St Basil to the bishops subject to him, which in the most recent edition of the Canonical Epistles of the holy Fathers is presented as Canon 91. In this Epistle he acts against simoniacs and forbids ordinations to be made in future on account of money. He touches on the history of Simon Magus, who wished to buy the grace of the Holy Spirit with money, and he subjects to deposition, according to Balsamon's explanation, both those who ordain and those who are ordained, whether they gave or received money before the ordination or after it. Basil died about a hundred years, more or less, before Gelasius was promoted to the pontificate. Secondly, Canon 2 of the Council of Chalcedon, enacted against simoniacal promotions about forty years before Gelasius, runs as follows.

units.la: Si quis Episcopus propter pecunias ordinationem fecerit, & gratiam quae vendi non poterit sub pretio redegerit, & propter pecunias ordinaverit Episcopum, vel Cherepiscopum, vel Presbyteros, vel Diaconos &c. qui hoc tentasse convictus fuerit, sui gradus periculum subeat, & qui est ordinatus, nihil ex ordinatione vel promotione per quaestum vel mercaturam facta juvetur; sed sit alienus a dignitate & sollicitudine, quam pecuniis adeptus est. Si quis autem mediator tam turpibus & nefariis lucris apparuerit, hic quoque si sit quidem clericus proprio gradu excidat. Sin autem laicus vel monachus, anathematizetur. Nemo igitur non videt Gelasium ad haec Decreta vel saltem ad utrumlibet eorum respexisse, potiùs quàm ad fictum Apostolorum Canonem; certè Guillelmus Beveregius Vir Doctissimus & Joannis Pearsonij Popularis, hunc ipsum Canonem notis suis illustravit, pluráque Veterum loca ad eandem rem pertinentia indicavit, de Gelasio verò penitus tacuit, nec cum Vindiciarum Autore ausus est affirmare illius quò de agimus Decretum ex isto Canone assumptum esse: Existimat quidem Beveregius hæc Dionisij Exigui verba, quædam constituta Pontificum ex ipsis Canonibus adsumpta esse, ad Romanos Pontifices, inter quos Gelasium numerat, referri debere, sed hunc nodum superius solvimus, ideóque superfluum esset repetere ea quæ ibi diximus. Aliud Gelasij constitutum ex eadem ad Episcopos Lucaniæ Epistolâ memorat eruditus Pearsonius, contra eos qui se ipsos abscindunt, verùm non diffitetur Gelasium per paternos Canones, de quibus mentionem facit, Nicænos intelligere, sed ita tamen, inquit, ut iidem Nicæni Canones agnoscant eadem in Prioribus Canonibus (scilicet Apostolicis) præcepta fuisse; num res ita se habeat ut ait Vir doctus alibi examinaturi sumus, dùm scilicet Beveregij in Canones Apostolorum annotationes expendemus, quare dilatâ eò usque responsione nostrâ, ad alia Vindiciarum autoris argumenta properamus.
units.tr: If any bishop, for the sake of money, has performed an ordination and has put up for sale grace, which cannot be sold, and for money has ordained a bishop, or a chorepiscopus, or presbyters, or deacons, etc., let him, if he is convicted of having attempted this, undergo the danger of losing his rank; and let the one who was ordained receive no help from the ordination or promotion obtained by gain or trade, but let him be a stranger to the dignity and the charge which he obtained with money. If, however, any go-between has appeared in such shameful and wicked gains, let him also, if he is a cleric, fall from his own rank. But if he is a layman or a monk, let him be anathematized. No one therefore fails to see that Gelasius had regard to these decrees, or at least to one of them, rather than to the spurious Canon of the Apostles. Certainly William Beveridge, a most learned man and a countryman of John Pearson, illustrated this very Canon with his notes and pointed out several passages of the Fathers bearing on the same matter, but he said nothing at all about Gelasius, and he did not dare, with the author of the Vindiciae, to assert that the decree of Gelasius which we are discussing was taken from this Canon. Beveridge indeed thinks that these words of Dionysius Exiguus, certain constitutions of the Pontiffs were taken from the Canons themselves, ought to be referred to the Roman Pontiffs, among whom he counts Gelasius; but we solved this knot above, and so it would be superfluous to repeat what we said there. The learned Pearson cites another constitution of Gelasius from the same letter to the bishops of Lucania, against those who castrate themselves; yet he does not deny that by the paternal Canons, which Gelasius mentions, he understands the Nicene Canons, but in such a way, he says, that the same Nicene Canons acknowledge that the same things were prescribed in the earlier Canons (namely the Apostolic ones). Whether the matter stands as the learned man says, we shall examine elsewhere, when we weigh Beveridge's notes on the Canons of the Apostles. So, having deferred our reply to that point, we hasten on to the other arguments of the author of the Vindiciae.

units.la: Novum quærit subsidium, in suo MS. Codice ante sexcentos ferè annos exarato, in quo non comparent Gelasiani Decreti verba quæ Canones Apostolicos in Apocryphorum censu reponunt; quid contineat Codex ille MS. cujúsve sit ætatis penitus ignoro, fidem tamen Viri docti quam puto optimam in dubium vocare nolo. forte eum fefellit conjectura sua in designandâ sui Codicis ætate: Ut ut sit nihil ad rem facit Censurae Canonum omissio: rari sunt MSS. Codices in quibus non reperias omissiones ejusmodi quae à Librariorum negligentiâ ac supinitate proficiscuntur; sed istis Hincmari verbis se tuetur Vir doctus. Sed & Beatus Gelasius in Catalogo qui libri ab Ecclesiâ Catholicâ recipiantur, de his Apostolorum Canonibus penitus tacuit, sed nec inter Apocrypha eos misit. Haec ex Hincmaro Opusc. c. 24. unde colligit ista verba, Liber qui appellatur Canones Apostolorum apochryphus, non exhibere in Decreto Gelasij Hincmari Codicem ducentis annis suo vetustiorem, dixerat Ballaeus ultima illa verba, sed nec inter apocrypha eos misit, vel memoriae lapsu imprudenti excidisse vel certè mendosa esse, & restituto verbo omisit pro eo, quod in codicibus vulgatis legit misit, corrigenda, ut ita scripserit Hincmarus, sed nec inter apocrypha eos misit; hàc clarissimi Dallaei criticeim [?] non probat doctissimus Vindiciarum Autor, liquet tamen ex omnibus quae hactenus diximus, Gelasium Canones Apostolorum inter apocrypha relegasse ac rejecisse, cum igitur Hincmarus de Canonibus istis juxta mentem Gelasij loquutus sit, ut patet ex ijs quae nuper ex illo adduximus {†} ò[?] ex toto capite unde illa deprompsiis, in mendo cubare verba controversa rito conjecit Dallæus: verùm mendoesse illa verba, vel saltem aliquam in s esse transpositionem aliâ viâ demonstre aggrediar, ut res melius procedat edam imprimis consideranda veniunt. Canones istos ab Apostolis conditos at, ab Authenticis Ecclesiæ regulis excludit, non per omnia recipiendos et, & in Canonum libris seorsim ante ncilia[?] ad instructionem,& propter vulam eorum famam poni affirmat ; 2. bat hos Canones ab Apostolis minimè ditos esse, ex eo quod præter quinque, s enumerat Synodos[?], nullam aliam ostoli habuisse legantur, in qua istos nones condiderint : 3. ab authenticis robatis Ecclesiæ regulis excludi oftenGelasiani Decreti auctoritate, in quo memorantur regulæ omnes probatæ uthenticæ, nullâ prorsus Canonum ostolicorum mentione factâ ; tamen t constabat hos Canones Gelasij conito fuisse notatos, hoc quoque obser-: non neglexit Hincmarus in verbis mox citavimus, de his Apostolorum nibus penitùs tacuit, sed nec inter apoba eos misit. Vnius vocula nec translio verborum istorum sensum turbavit, quem facilimè restitues, si vocula illam suo reponas loco, & totam Hincmari observationem uno tenore legas hoc pacto : sed & beatus Gelasius in Catalogo qui libri ab Ecclesia Catholica recipiantur descripto, authenticis scripturis, & Nicaenae, Constantinopolitanae, ac Ephesinae, Chalcedonensis quoque Synodi, & aliis Concilijs a sanctis Patribus institutis, & Orthodoxorum opusculis, atque Decretalibus Epistolis Apostolicae sedis Pontificum, aliisque scripturis discrete commemoratis, NEC DE HIS APOSTOLORUM CANONIBUS PENITUS TA-CUIT, SED INTER APOCRYPHA EOS MISIT. Id est reiecit & relegavit, & quoniam Hincmarus di[?]erat quaedam in illis esse receptabilia, & quaedam non servanda, & seorsim ante Concilia ad instructionem poni solitos, hanc Gelasij cautelam, dum leguntur, adhiberi praecipit, omnia probate, quod bonum est tenete. Jam, ut quivis videt, verborum Hincmari sensus planus est, facilis, ac expeditus, omnia sponte fluunt, illiusque menti & scopo omnino congruunt; nihil additum est, nihil detractum, sola particula nec sedem mutavit, mutandóque Hincmari sermonem intellectu facilem reddidit; spes igitur est Virum doctum tandem aliquando manus daturum, & Gelasij Decretum quo Canones Apostolici damnati sunt, ab Hincmaro agnitum atque probatum fuisse, deinceps ingenuè esse professurum; præsertim si animo perpendere velit Attonem Vercellensem Episcopum, qui centum circiter annos post Hincmarum florebat, hanc eandem Canonum Apostolorum censuram repræsentare in calce Capitularis sui, ubi Gelasianum exhibet Decretum, solis Veteris & Novi Testamenti libris exceptis; exhibet quidem suppresso Gelasij nomine, sed ita tamen ut ad illum respexisse hisce verbis sufficienter innuat, post illas Veteris & Novi Testamenti, quas regulariter suscipimus, etiam has suscipi non prohibet scripturas; enumeratis autem scripturis Ecclesiasticis probatis & authenticis, ad cætera transit, quæ ab Hæreticis sive Schismaticis conscripta vel prædicata sunt, & quæ nullatenus recipit Catholica & Apostolica Ecclesia, & inter scripta illa reprobata & apocrypha Canones numerat Apostolicos. Liber qui appellatur Cu[?]ones Apostolorum, apocryphus.
units.tr: He seeks a new support in his manuscript codex, written almost six hundred years ago, in which the words of the Gelasian decree that place the Apostolic Canons among the Apocrypha do not appear. I am entirely ignorant of what that manuscript contains and of its age, yet I do not wish to call into doubt the opinion of so learned a man, which I think is excellent. Perhaps his conjecture about the age of his codex misled him. However that may be, the omission of the censure of the Canons makes no difference to the matter: manuscripts are rare in which you will not find omissions of this kind, arising from the carelessness and sloth of copyists. But the learned man defends himself with these words of Hincmar: But also the blessed Gelasius, in his catalogue of the books which are received by the Catholic Church, said nothing at all about these Canons of the Apostles, but he did not place them among the Apocrypha either. From these words of Hincmar, in Opusc. c. 24, he gathers that the codex of Hincmar, two hundred years older than his own, did not contain in the decree of Gelasius the words the book which is called the Canons of the Apostles is apocryphal. Ballaeus had said that those last words, but he did not place them among the Apocrypha either, had either slipped out through an unwary lapse of memory or were certainly corrupt, and should be corrected by restoring omisit (he left out) in place of misit (he sent), which is what the printed codices read, so that Hincmar wrote: but he did not leave them out among the Apocrypha. The most learned author of the Vindiciae does not approve this criticism of the most distinguished Dallaeus. Yet it is clear from everything we have said so far that Gelasius consigned the Canons of the Apostles among the Apocrypha and rejected them. Since, therefore, Hincmar spoke of these Canons in keeping with the mind of Gelasius, as is evident from what we have just quoted from him and from the whole chapter from which he drew those words, Dallaeus conjectured that the disputed words lie in error. But I shall proceed to show by another way that those words are corrupt, or at least that there is some transposition in them, so that the matter may proceed better; and first of all the following points must be considered. Hincmar affirms that these Canons were made by the Apostles, but that they are excluded from the authentic rules of the Church, that they are not to be received in every respect, and that they were placed apart in the books of Canons before the Councils for instruction, and for the sake of their ancient fame. Second, he says that these Canons were by no means made by the Apostles, because, apart from the five synods which he enumerates, no other synod is read of in which the Apostles are said to have made these Canons. Third, he shows that they are excluded from the authentic rules of the Church by the authority of the Gelasian decree, in which all the approved and authentic rules are mentioned, with no mention at all of the Apostolic Canons. Yet it was established that these Canons had been noted by Gelasius. Hincmar did not neglect this point either, in the words we quoted a little while ago: he said nothing at all about these Canons of the Apostles, but he did not place them among the Apocrypha either. The single little word nec (neither) in the translation has disturbed the sense of these words, but it can be very easily restored if you put that little word back in its place and read the whole observation of Hincmar in one continuous sentence, thus: But also the blessed Gelasius, in the catalogue of the books received by the Catholic Church, described the authentic Scriptures, and the Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople and Ephesus, and also the Council of Chalcedon, and other councils instituted by the holy Fathers, and the writings of the orthodox, and the decretal letters of the Popes of the Apostolic See, and other writings, distinctly listed; he NEITHER said anything at all about these Canons of the Apostles, NOR DID HE SEND THEM AMONG THE APOCRYPHA. That is, he rejected and consigned them to the apocrypha. And since Hincmar said that some things in them were acceptable and some were not to be observed, and that they were customarily placed apart before the Councils for instruction, he directs that this caution of Gelasius be applied while they are read: Test all things; hold fast what is good. Now, as anyone can see, the sense of Hincmar's words is plain, easy and straightforward; everything flows naturally and fits entirely with his meaning and purpose. Nothing has been added, nothing taken away; only the particle nec has changed its place, and by moving it the sense of Hincmar's language has been made easy to grasp. There is therefore hope that the learned man will at last yield, and will henceforth openly confess that the Gelasian decree by which the Canons of the Apostles were condemned was recognized and approved by Hincmar. This is especially so if he is willing to consider Atto, bishop of Vercelli, who flourished about a hundred years after Hincmar, and who sets forth this same censure of the Apostolic Canons at the end of his Capitulary, where he gives the Gelasian decree, except that the books of the Old and New Testament are excluded. He gives it, indeed, with the name of Gelasius suppressed, but in such a way that he sufficiently hints by these words that he had regard to Gelasius: after those books of the Old and New Testament which we ordinarily receive, he does not forbid these writings also to be received; and after listing the approved and authentic ecclesiastical writings, he passes on to the rest, which were written or preached by heretics or schismatics, and which the Catholic and Apostolic Church does not receive at all; and among those writings rejected and apocryphal he numbers the Apostolic Canons. The book which is called the Canons of the Apostles is apocryphal.

units.la: Cætera Viri docti argumenta non mobuntur nos diutius; 1. hæc Decreti verba adfert, sed & si qua sunt Concilia à SS. [illegible, ~2 letters]tribus hactenus instituta, post horum auitatem[?] & custodienda & recipienda & decernimus[?] & mandamus; non de Concihis[?] Generalibus de quibus ante locutus est, hoc dixit Gelasius, ut putat eruditus Pearsonius sed de Concilijs particularibus Orthodoxis & probatis, quibus propterea secundam post Concilia Generalia tribuit autoritatem; Hincmarus hæc Concilia particularia à Generalibus ita distinxit, & alijs Concilijs à SS. Patribus institu-tis. 2. argumentatur ex eo quod in Gelasij Decreto fit mentio scripturæ de inventione Dominicæ Crucis, & scripturæ de inventione capitis B. Ioannes Baptistæ, quia tales scripturas, sive libros, Gelasij ævo, inquit, extitisse non apparet; sed cum Vir doctus conjecturam suam nullis confirmet rationibus, nullius plane ponderis est illius argumentum adversus Decreti Autorem, qui de libris istis tanquam de novellis relationibus expresse loquitur. 3. ejusdem sunt commatis ista alia ejusdem Decreti verba, in quibus agitur de Russi-no quem Hieronymus, ut ait, in aliquibus de arbitrij libertate notavit, illa sentimus quæ Beatum Hieronymum sentire cognoscimus, & non solùm de Ruffino, sed etiam de universis, quos vir sæpius memoratus, ze-lo Dei & fidei religione reprehendit. Hæc ver-ba quicquid dicat Pearsonius,& Concilio & Pontifici Romano satis conveniunt agitur enim tantum de ijs omnibus qui à sede Romanâ æquè ac ab Hieronymo reprobabantur, verbi gratia de Luciferianis, de Vigilantio, de Ioviniano, de Ioanne Hierosolymitano, & cæteris Origenis fautoribus, quibus accenseri possunt Pelagiani. 4. novum Viro docto argumentum subministrat Gelasij Decretum, dum docet Marcum Evangelistam gloriosum consummasse Martyrium; at hoc, inquit, neque Eusebius, neque Hieronymus ante Gelasium tradidit, neque post eum Isidorus Hispalensis, ut vita S. Marci, in quâ eius martyrium describitur, post Isidori, ante Bedæ, & Autoris Decreti tempora scripta esse videatur. Doleo hæc Viro docto imprudenter excidisse; nam etsi Eusebius & Hieronymus ante Gelasium de S. Marci Martyrio nihil planè tradiderint, neque post eum Isidorus Hispalensis, non propterea sequitur ante illa tempora ignotum fuisse; non propriè quæritur utrum vita S. Marci Evangelistæ post Isidori, ante Bedæ tempora scripta fuerit, sed utrum illius Martyrij ante Gelasium, & post eum ante Isidorum meminerint quidam Ecclesiastici scriptores; quoniam si utrumque compertum est, causâ cadet Vindiciarum Autor, & vitam S. Marci ante tempus à Viro docto præsti-tutum scriptam esse par erit credere; hæc duo igitur probanda nobis incumbunt; Martyrij scilicet S. Marci ante Gelasium, & post eum ante Isidorum extare mentionem, primùm caput quod attinet probatur testimonio Palladij qui 8o. plus minùs ante Gelasium annos de Philoromo Presbytero in Historiâ Laufiacâ ita scribebat; Is pedestri itinere venit Romam usque ad orandum in sanctissimo beatorum & sanctorum Christi Apostolorum Petri & Pauli martyrio: pervenit autem etiam usque ad Alexandriam, ad orandum in martyrio venerandi Athletæ Marci; Vides martyrium Marco æquè ac Petro & Paulo sæculo quarto dicatum fuisse, quia glorioso martyrio vitam finijsse vulgò credebatur. Secundum caput vindicat Gregorius Turonensis quadraginta circiter annos ante Isidorum Hispalensem denatus; Is enim de persecutione à Nerone excitatâ agens, hæc habet, tunc & Iacobus frater Domini, & Marcus Evangelista, pro Christi nomine glorioso martyrio coronati sunt. Frustrà igitur ex martyrio S. Marci cujus meminit Gelasianum Decretum, illius sugillandi ansam arripuit Vir doctus, cùm certo certiùs sit longè ante Gelasium Christianis innotuisse illud martyrium. Ex omnibus quæ hactenus dicta sunt patet omnes Viri docti in Nicephori stichometriam & Gelasij Decretum conatus plane irritos suisse; stat enim utrinque sarta, tecta & firma autoritas, quam praestantissimus Vindiciarum Autor nequaquam covellere potuit, quamvis eam maxima cum impetu adortus sit, illamque undique sollicitare tentaverit: nec Viri docti causam juvat quod postremo dicit, Ignatij Epistolas in Nicephori Indiculo, nec nominari, nec innui, nec quovis modo contineri, sed Ignatij [illegible, ~5 letters] seu [illegible, ~9 letters], id est do-ctrinam quam omnes apocrypham & spuriam fatentur, ut hoc probet, ad Indiculum confugit MS. qui extat inter libros Baroccianos in Bibliotheca publica Oxonij, in quo liber ille qui Ignatij doctrina inscribitur inter apocrypha relegatur; similem Indiculum, ex Bibliotheca Christianissimi Regis edidit Ioannes Baptista Cotelerius, ex quo quemadmodum ex suo MS.
