Vindiciarum Autor, colligit Laterculum Nicephorianum non amandare ad apocrypha Epistolas Ignatij, sed librum illum qui Ignatij doctrina cognominatur; quid audio, Nicephorus Ignatiana absque ulla distinctione in apocryphorum ordine ac classe censet, Viri autem isti eruditi ad Ignatij [illegible, ~6 letters] referunt, quae Patriarcha Constatinopolitanus de Ignatianis in genere pronuntiavit; De Herma eodem planè modo loquitur ac de Ignatio, negare non possunt Viri docti omnia Hermæ ab Indiculi autore inter apocrypha fuisse rejecta, fateantur ergo necesse est Ignatiana omnia eadem sententiâ fuisse pariter notata atque damnata, nullum enim inter utrorumque damnationem cernitur ne minimum quidem discrimen; tantine constitissent Nicephoro tria aut quatuor verba, ut distinguerentur quæ distinguenda erant? & si eum non piguit cætera apocrypha sigillatim recensere, cur quæso piguisset Ignatii spuria & ficta, à veris ac genuinis secernere: sed quia quotquot Ignatii nomine circumferebantur Nicephoro adulterina & suppositicia videbantur, ea omnia eadem damnationis sententiâ involvere non dubitavit.
units.tr: The other arguments of these learned men do not detain us any longer. (1) They cite the words of the Decree itself: "But if there are any councils established hitherto by the holy fathers, after their authority, we decree that they are both to be kept and to be received and mandated." The learned Pearson holds that Gelasius did not mean the general councils, of which he had spoken before, but the orthodox and approved particular councils, to which he therefore gave a second authority after the general councils. Hincmar distinguished these particular councils from the general ones in this way: and other councils established by the holy fathers. (2) He argues from the fact that the Gelasian Decree mentions writings on the finding of the Lord's Cross, and writings on the finding of the head of the blessed John the Baptist, because, he says, such writings, or books, do not appear to have existed in the age of Gelasius. But since the learned man supports his conjecture with no reasons at all, his argument against the author of the Decree has no weight whatever, for the Decree speaks expressly of these books as new reports. (3) The following words of the same Decree belong to the same passage, where it treats of Rufinus, whom Jerome, as it says, criticised on some points concerning freedom of the will: We hold those things which we know the blessed Jerome held, and not only concerning Rufinus, but also concerning all those whom that oft-mentioned man rebuked with zeal for God and devotion to the faith. Whatever Pearson may say, these words agree well enough both with the Council and with the Roman Pontiff. For they refer only to all those who were rejected by the Roman see just as much as by Jerome: for example, the Luciferians, Vigilantius, Jovinian, John of Jerusalem, and the other followers of Origen, among whom the Pelagians may also be counted. (4) The Gelasian Decree supplies the learned man with a new argument, in that it teaches that Mark the Evangelist consummated a glorious martyrdom. But this, he says, was not handed down by Eusebius or Jerome before Gelasius, nor by Isidore of Seville after him; and the Life of St. Mark, in which his martyrdom is described, seems to have been written between Isidore and Bede, and at the time of the author of the Decree. I regret that these things slipped from the learned man carelessly. For although Eusebius and Jerome before Gelasius said nothing at all about the martyrdom of St. Mark, and neither did Isidore of Seville after him, it does not follow that it was unknown before those times. The question is not properly whether the Life of the Evangelist St. Mark was written between the times of Isidore and Bede, but whether certain ecclesiastical writers mentioned his martyrdom before Gelasius, and after him and before Isidore. For if both of these are established, the author of the Vindiciae is undone, and we must believe that the Life of St. Mark was written before the time fixed by the learned man. Two things therefore fall to us to prove: that mention of the martyrdom of St. Mark existed before Gelasius, and after him and before Isidore. As for the first point, it is proved by the testimony of Palladius, who, some eighty years or so before Gelasius, wrote thus about Philoromus the presbyter in his Lausiac History: He came on foot to Rome, to pray at the most holy martyrdom of the blessed and holy apostles of Christ, Peter and Paul; and he also came to Alexandria, to pray at the martyrdom of the venerable athlete Mark. You see that the martyrdom of Mark, just like that of Peter and Paul, was ascribed to the fourth century, because it was commonly believed that he had ended his life in glorious martyrdom. The second point is vindicated by Gregory of Tours, who died about forty years before Isidore of Seville. For when he speaks of the persecution stirred up by Nero, he has this: Then James the brother of the Lord and Mark the Evangelist were crowned with glorious martyrdom for the name of Christ. It is therefore in vain that the learned man has seized on the martyrdom of St. Mark, which the Gelasian Decree mentions, as an occasion to disparage it, since it is quite certain that this martyrdom was known to Christians long before Gelasius. From all that has been said so far it is clear that all the efforts of the learned men against the Stichometry of Nicephorus and the Gelasian Decree have been wholly futile. For on both sides there stands a whole, sound and firm authority, which the most distinguished author of the Vindiciae could by no means shake, although he attacked it with the greatest force and tried to unsettle it on every side. Nor does it help the cause of the learned man that he says at the end that the Epistles of Ignatius are neither named, nor hinted at, nor in any way contained in the Indiculus of Nicephorus, but rather the doctrine of Ignatius, or something of the kind, that is, a doctrine which everyone admits to be apocryphal and spurious. To prove this, he has recourse to a manuscript Indiculus, which exists among the Barocci books in the public library at Oxford, in which that book which is entitled the Doctrine of Ignatius is listed among the apocrypha. John Baptist Cotelier published a similar Indiculus from the library of the Most Christian King, from which the author of the Vindiciae, just as from his own manuscript, concludes that the Nicephorian catalogue does not assign the spurious Epistles of Ignatius to the apocrypha, but that book which is nicknamed the Doctrine of Ignatius. What do I hear? Nicephorus reckons the Ignatian writings among the apocrypha in their order and class without any distinction, and yet these learned men refer to Ignatius what the Patriarch of Constantinople pronounced about the Ignatian writings in general. He speaks of Hermas in exactly the same way as of Ignatius. The learned men cannot deny that all the works of Hermas were rejected among the apocrypha by the author of the Indiculus. They must therefore confess that all the Ignatian writings were likewise noted and condemned by the same sentence, for no slightest difference can be seen between the condemnation of the one and of the other. Would three or four words have cost Nicephorus so much, that he should distinguish what needed to be distinguished? And if he did not mind listing the other apocrypha one by one, why, I ask, would he have minded separating the spurious and fabricated writings of Ignatius from the true and genuine ones? But because all the writings circulated under the name of Ignatius seemed to Nicephorus adulterated and forged, he did not hesitate to include them all under the same sentence of condemnation.

units.la: Postquam Nicephori stichometriam & Gelasii Decretum ab omnibus Viri docti objectionibus vindicavimus, & testes à Dallæo adductos, tales apparere quales ille voluit, & id omninò testari quod autoris Vindiciarum sententiæ contrarium est fusè demonstravimus. Examinandi veniunt Viri eruditi testes, an scilicet ij sint quos esse ille dicit, aut reverâ id testentur quod ipse vult: Et cum de testibus ab eo allatis verba facio, eos solos intelligo qui Eusebio vetustiores fuerunt, testes videlicet trium primorum Æræ Christianæ sæculorum; quia plerique scriptores Ecclesiastici Eusebio æquales vel suppares, vel eo etiam admodum juniores, illius de Ignatianis Epistolis sententiam, absque ullo ut fere solent prævio examine certatim amplexi sunt: quamvis in Historiâ Ecclesiasticâ in qua luculentum Ignatij Epistolis perhibet testimonium, non semel aut iterum, sed sæpius hallucinatus sit, suóque exemplo alios in errorem induxerit, quod ita tamen accipi nolim quasi antiquissimo & doctissimo scriptori, cui certè plurimum debemus obtrectandi aut subsannandi esset animus; Quicquid sit tres tantùm ætatis quam designamus testes adfert clarissimus Vindiciarum Autor, Polycarpum, Irenæum, & Origenem, quorum testimonia cap. 5. 6. 7. ab exceptionibus vindicare conatur. Equidem Virum doctum κατὰ πόλιν [?] sequi, vel omnia illius dicta ad vivum resecare aut minutatim expendere non decrevi, sed ostendere modò testes ab eo adductos non esse omni exceptione majores; cùm plura sint quæ eis fidem deesse ac vim arguant, & si intestabiles eos prorsus non reddunt, illorum saltem autoritatem ita labefactant ac infringunt, ut tantæ liti dirimendæ haud idonei videantur; agmen ducit Polycarpus in illâ quæ ejus nomine circumfertur Epistolâ, ex quâ primum pro Ignatianis petit testimonium Vindiciarum Autor, utque majoris fit ponderis pluribus probat hanc Philippensibus inscriptam Epistolam, genuinum esse Polycarpi Ioannis Apostoli Discipuli fœtum: non diffitebatur Dallæus neque ego post illum diffiteor extitisse Polycarpi nomine ad Phillipenses Epistolam, quæ magnæ erat apud nostrorum vetustissimos famæ; quæritur tantùm num aliquid prohibeat, quominus certa & indubitata sit testimonij fides; duo quædam nequaquam contemnenda hoc prohibere dixerat præstantissimus Dallæus; priùs quidem, quod ejus epistolæ, ex quâ descriptum est testimonium non sit apud omnes recepta autoritas; sunt enim, inquit scriptores, & iì quidem gravissimi, qui eam apocryphàm esse ju-dicant, & in apocryphorum censu reponunt. Scriptores illi sunt Nicephorus Patriarcha Constantinopolitanus, & Anastasius Ecclesiæ Romanæ Bibliothecarius, in Indiculo enim quem ille edidit, & quem iste adoptavit, Ignatij, Polycarpi, Pastoris & Hermæ libri vel scripta ad apocrypha amandantur: Ut telum istud declinaret[?] Vir doctus, grandem Nicephori stichometriae dicam scripsit, illius minimè esse, ac proinde nullam mereri fidem contendit: Verùm tot tantísque rationum momentis illum Indiculum Patriarchæ Constantinopolitano vindicavimus, illiúsque esse sive compositionis sive adoptionis saltem juré evicimus, ut nullus superesse queat hac de re dubitandi locus; nec Vindiciarum Autorem juvaret dicere Ni[?]cephorum in Laterculo suo non Epistolam Polycarpi sed [illegible, ~6 letters] inter apocrypha rejecisse; memoratur quidem in Indiculo à Cotelerio edito [illegible, ~6 letters] Polycarpi, quemadmodum [illegible, ~6 letters] Ignatii; sed inde non sequitur solam Ignatij & Polycarpi [illegible, ~6 letters] à Nicephoro damnari, ut nuper dicebamus ad eandem Viri docti exceptionem, omnia enim Ignatij & Polycarpi scripta ad apocrypha retulit, & apocrypha deterrimi generis, ut à nobis supra argumentis haud contemnendis probatum est. Secundò observaverat idem Dallæus, etiamsi Epistolæ de quâ lis est fides adhiberetur, non ideò rem omnem consectam esse, quia postremam Epistolæ particulam ex quâ argumentatur eruditus Pearsonius, alienâ manu assutam existimabat; quod duobus astruebat argumentis, I. quoniam videtur post conclusam ab auctore verbis proximè præcedentibus epistolam addita, quæ votum pro Philippensibus hoc continent ; Deus autem & Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, & ipse sempiternus Pontifex, Dei filius, Iesus Christus ædificet vos in fide & in veritate, & in omni mansuetudine, & sine iracundiâ, & in patientiâ, & longanimitate, & tolerantiâ & castitate, & det vobis sortem & partem inter sanctos suos, & nobis vobiscum, & omnibus qui sunt sub cœlo, qui crediturî sunt in Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, & in ipsius Patrem, qui resuscitavit eum à mortuis. Pro omnibus sanctis Orate. Orate etiam pro Regibus, & Potestatibus & Principibus, atque pro persequentibus & odientibus vos, & pro inimicis Crucis; ut fructus vester manifestus sit in omnibus, ut sitis in illo perfecti. Hisce verbis ex Epistolâ descriptis ita pergit Dallæus, in hanc decentissimam, ut omnes vident, clausulam desinebat Epistola. Quæ sequuntur, SCRIPSISTIS MIHI ET VOS ET IGNATIVS, & cætera paulò ante à nobis descripta, istis minimè cohærent, omninóque videntur temerè & præter Autoris mentem alienâ manu assuta. 2. Ostendebat aliter de Ignatio loqui particulæ scriptorem, aliter epistolæ Auctorem, imò inter se pugnantia scribere, quod validissimo illi erat argumento adversus postremam epistolæ particulam; Ut omnia clariora evadant adferenda sunt ipsissima illius particulæ verba, in quibus continetur Polycarpi de Ignatianis testimonium; Scripsistis mihi & vos & Ignatius, ut si quis vadit ad Syriam, deferat litteras meas quas fecero ad vos: si habuerimus tempus opportunum sive ego, seu legatus quem misero pro vobis. Epistolas sane Ignatii quæ transmissæ sunt vobis ab eo, & alias quantascunque apud nos habuimus, transmisimus vobis (secundum quod mandastis) quæ sunt subjectæ huic Epistolæ: ex quibus magnus vobis erit prosectus. Continent enim fidem, patientiam, & omnem ædificationem ad Dominum nostrum pertinentem. Et de ipso Ignatio, & de his qui cum eo sunt, quod certius agnoveritis, significate. Ita enim Græca reddidit Vetus Interpres Latinus, cujus versionem edidit Vsserius, si postrema verba excipias quæ tantum Latinè extant & quæ à solo habemus Interprete, Eusebius quidem Hist. Eccl. lib. 3. c. 36. totam hanc repræsentat laciniam præter ista quæ difficultatem pariunt, movéntque litem, & de ipso Ignatio & de his qui cum eo sunt, quod certius agnoveritis, significate, hæc videlicet verba apud unum Veterem Interpretem leguntur, sive ex Græco transtulerit, sive ex suo addiderit, sive potius alienâ manu subjuncta sint, quod à vero non est alienum, saltem si perpendatur in his postremis verbis agi de Ignatio ac si adhuc in vivis esset, nondúmque vitam cum morte commutasset; Epistolæ verò auctor planè alia loquitur; apertissimè affirmans Ignatium, quo tempore ipse ad Philippenses scribebat, jam fuisse Martyrij coronâ redimitum, ultimóque certaminis actu gloriosè perfunctum. Res clara est. Hortatur enim Philippenses ad illam justitiam & patientiam, quam oculatâ fide, vel ipsis oculis viderant, non solùm in beatis Ignatio, & Zosimo, & Russo, sed in quibusdam de suo grege aliis & in ipso Paulo, cæterisque Apostolis, hæc inquam ita præfatus, ista deinceps continenter de ijsdem subjicit, confidentes, quia HI OMNES non in vacuo cucurrerunt, sed in fide & justitiâ, & ad debitum sibi locum à ( vel cum ) Domino, cui & compassi sunt, abierunt, vel ut Græca sonant, persuasi quod hi omnes in vacuum non cucurrerunt, sed in fide ac justitia, & quod in debito sibi loco sint apud Dominum cum quo & passi sunt. Utráque inter se contenderat Dallæus, & cum manifestam vir emunctissimæ naris animadvertisset contradictionem, inter epistolæ Autorem & particulæ scriptorem, merito colligebat illam omnem particulam in qua cum superioribus epistolae verbis tantopere pugnantia leguntur, alterius quam Autoris epistolae manu scriptam esse, eamque falso ac vafre epistolae esse assutam ab aliquo impostore. Et sane nulla unquam excogitari potuit major contradictio: Epistolae Autor affirmat Ignatium passum esse, certaminis sui omnes actus consummavisse, denique jam coronatum suo apud Dominum loco quiescere, ac exultare, neque amplius in his terris morari: particulae vero scripto putat Ignatium adhuc superesse, vivere, valere, & ad ultimum certaminis actum festinare: Et de ipso Ignatio & de his qui cum eo sunt, quod certius agnoveritis, significate. Estne credibile Polycarpum virum sapientissimum ac veracissimum, eadem de re tam dissentanea, tamque inter se contraria ac repugnantia loquutum esse? Scripserat Philippenses persuasos esse ac confidere quod Ignatius cursu rite consummato ad locum suum apud Dominum abijt, & statim eosdem rogat, si quid de Ignatio & his qui cum eo sunt, inaudierint, ut se de his faciant certiorem, quis hoc ferat in aliquo sanae mentis homine, nedum in Polycarpo sanctissimo Martyre, totque excellentissimis ingenij dotibus praedito ac cumulato? certe erudito Vindiciarum Autori me injuriam facere putarem; ac de illo nimis abjectè sentire, si in animum induçerem, eum in tantulo spatio & eadem de re adeò contraria scribere posse; non igitur molestè ferat si, ut Polycarpum ab hoc liberemus incommodo, illúmque tam apertæ contradictionis præstemus immunem, si inquam alium fuisse epistolæ Autorem, alium verò particulæ seu laciniæ scriptorem asserimus; respondet Pearsonius hanc quâ de agimus particulam, nihil causam suam juvare si admittatur, nihil illi officere si rejiciatur; imò tibi multùm officit Vir docte, si eam tanquam additiitiam[?] rejicis: ita enim argumentari licebit, ultima particulæ de quâ lis est verba alienâ manu assuta esse constat, quis igitur cæterorum ejusdem particulæ verborum fidem mihi præstare poterit; Eusebius præstabit inquiet eruditus Pearsonius, fateor apud Eusebium legi cætera laciniæ verba, sed hoc non impedit quominus omnis illa particula ab impostore quodam dolo malo assuta fuerit, cum de postremis illius verbis diserte non negetur; nam priora particulæ verba non magis cohærent cum superioribus quàm postrema, nec majorem ea propter merentur fidem, sive maturius, sive tardius, sive eodem temporis momento cum postremis subjecta fuerint. Pergit Vir doctus & admissâ postremâ laciniæ particulâ, dicit particulæ illius Autorem non significare aut ullo modo innuere Ignatium tunc in vivis fuisse; sed quia audire poterant Philippenses aliquid de Ignatio vivo, Polycarpum id ab illis scire cupere illo defuncto: frigida profectò solutio, nam si illud negem, non video quâ ratione hanc assertionem probaturus sit Vindiciarum Autor, quia inquit Ignatius per Philippenses pertransivit Macedoniam pedes, ut referunt illius Acta, à Philippensibus autem missi sunt aliqui qui eum honoris & refrigerationis causa itinere deducerent; esto per Philippenses transierit Ignatius, ab illis deductus fuerit, & ab eo aliquid audierint qui illum deducebant, non propterea sequitur Polycarpum à Philippensibus scire cupere quod de Ignatio vivo audire poterant; si hæc Polycarpo mens fuisset, non obscurè & involutè, ut facit, rem de quâ certior fieri cupit, percontatus esset; verbis perspicuis ac expeditis rogasset Philippenses, ut quæ de Ignatio vivo audierant significare dignarentur, quod ex istis particulæ Autoris verbis ne uncis quidem ac fidiculis exsculpi potest, & de ipso Ignatio & de his qui cum eo sunt, quod certius agnoveritis[?], significate; ita videlicet loqui solemus, dum amicorum vivorum res & statum cognoscere cupimus, illis vero defunctis aliis utimur verbis si aliquid ab ijs, dum adhuc in viuis essent, prolatum scire desideramus; unde sequitur particulas scriptorem putasse Ignatium, dum haec scriberet, superesse, vivere, & ad ultimum certaminis actum festinare, ut fatetur apud Dallæum doctissimus Hammondus acerrimus Ignatianorum vindex. Hinc liquet quam temere Vir alius eruditus hanc quam urgemus ἀντιλογίαν[?] seu contradictionem rideat, quasi veritate plane esset destituta, ponatur, inquit, quemadmodum sentimus, scripsisse Polycarpum tunc temporis, cum Ignatius martyrium subiisse credebatur, incerti tamen (ut fere fit) rumores ferebantur de ijs quae in morte illius contigerant. Hoc posito, nonne conveniebat ut Polycarpus diceret, Ignatium apud Deum locum suum obtinere, simulque peteret edoceri de Ignatio & de his qui cum eo sunt, si quid Philippenses explorati accepissent. Mira ratiocinatio si solido niteretur fundamento, at eo planè destituitur: siccine Vir ille eruditus percontari solet de ijs quae in amicorum morte contigerunt? Quis unquam vel fando audivit haec verba, & de ipso amico, & de his qui cum eo sunt, quod certius agnoagnoveritis, significate, ita explicanda esse, eorum quæ in amici morte contigerunt, si quid explorati habetis, certiorem facite; obsecro tuam fidem Vir erudite, num ita ad familiares scribere, si amici cujusdam omnes mortis circunstantias scire cuperes? Non puto; cur igitur Polycarpum sic scribentem repræsentare non dubitas? Sed ad Vindiciarum Autorem redeo, ut tandem aliquando concludam Polycarpianam Epistolarum Ignatianarum collectionem adeò suspectæ esse fidei, ob fragile ac falsum cui innititur fundamentum, nempè postremam Epistolæ particulam quam alienâ manu assutam demonstravimus, ut testimonium inde descriptum nullius planè momenti esse queat, præsertim si spectentur quæ de vacillante totius sylloges fide initio observationum istarum scripsimus, quibus omnibus adjicere lubet Ignatianorum Vindicem nihil omninò reposuisse ad solutiones quibus Hammondi argumenta ex istâ Epistolæ laciniâ desumpta refellit clarissimus Dallæus.
units.tr: Having defended Nicephorus's Stichometry and the Decretum of Gelasius against all the objections of the learned author, and having shown at length that the witnesses cited by Dallaeus appear as he wished them to appear, and that they bear entirely witness to what is contrary to the opinion of the author of the Vindiciae, we now come to examine the learned witnesses: whether they are the men he says they are, and whether they really attest what he wants. When I speak of the witnesses he has cited, I mean only those who were older than Eusebius, that is, the witnesses of the first three centuries of the Christian era. Most ecclesiastical writers who were Eusebius's contemporaries or equals, or even much younger than he, eagerly embraced his opinion about the Ignatian Epistles, usually without any prior examination. Yet in his Ecclesiastical History, where he gives a clear testimony to the Ignatian Epistles, he has been mistaken not once or twice but often, and by his example he has led others into error. I would not have this taken as if I wished to show disrespect or ridicule toward so ancient and learned a writer, to whom we certainly owe very much. However that may be, the most distinguished author of the Vindiciae brings forward only three witnesses of the period we are marking out: Polycarp, Irenaeus and Origen, whose testimonies he tries to defend against objections in chapters 5, 6 and 7. I have not decided to follow the learned man step by step, nor to cut away or weigh each of his statements in detail. I mean only to show that the witnesses he has cited are not beyond all objection, since there are many points which deny them credibility and weaken their force. Even if these points do not make them wholly worthless, they so undermine and shake their authority that they seem unfit to settle so great a dispute. Polycarp leads the line. The author of the Vindiciae first seeks testimony for the Ignatian Epistles from that letter which bears his name, and to make it weightier he proves at length that the letter addressed to the Philippians is a genuine work of Polycarp, the disciple of the Apostle John. Dallaeus did not deny, and I, following him, do not deny, that a letter of Polycarp to the Philippians existed, one which was in great repute among the most ancient of our people. The question is only whether anything prevents the testimony from being certain and beyond doubt. The most excellent Dallaeus had said that two points, by no means to be despised, stand in the way. First, the epistle from which the testimony is drawn does not have universal acceptance. For there are, he says, writers, and very weighty ones too, who judge it apocryphal, and place it among the apocrypha. Those writers are Nicephorus, Patriarch of Constantinople, and Anastasius, librarian of the Roman Church. In the Indiculus which the former published and the latter adopted, the books of Ignatius, Polycarp, the Shepherd and Hermas are consigned to the apocrypha. To avoid this missile, the learned man wrote that the great Stichometry, as I shall call it, is not Nicephorus's, and therefore deserves no credence. But by so many and so weighty arguments we have defended that Indiculus for the Patriarch of Constantinople, and have shown by the right either of its composition or at least of its adoption that there can be no room left for doubt on this matter. Nor would it help the author of the Vindiciae to say that Nicephorus in his Laterculus did not reject the Epistle of Polycarp among the apocrypha. It is indeed mentioned in the Indiculus published by Cotelerius, as are the Epistles of Ignatius; but it does not follow that Nicephorus condemned only the writings of Ignatius and Polycarp, as we were just saying in reply to the same objection of the learned man. For he assigned all the writings of Ignatius and Polycarp to the apocrypha, and to the worst kind of apocrypha, as we have proved above by no contemptible arguments. Secondly, the same Dallaeus had observed that even if the Epistle from which the testimony comes were accepted, the whole matter would not be settled, because he thought the last paragraph of the Epistle, from which the learned Pearson argues, was stitched in by another hand. He supported this with two arguments. First, because the passage with the prayer for the Philippians seems to have been added after the author had concluded the letter with the words immediately preceding it. That prayer reads: And may God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the eternal High Priest himself, the Son of God, Jesus Christ, build you up in faith and in truth, and in all meekness, and without wrath, and in patience, and long-suffering, and forbearance, and chastity, and give you a lot and a portion among his saints, and us with you, and all who are under heaven, who are about to believe in our Lord Jesus Christ and in his Father, who raised him from the dead. Pray for all the saints. Pray also for kings, and powers, and princes, and for those who persecute and hate you, and for the enemies of the Cross; that your fruit may be manifest in all things, that you may be perfect in him. After quoting these words from the Epistle, Dallaeus goes on: The Epistle ended with this most becoming conclusion, as everyone can see. What follows, YOU WROTE TO ME BOTH YOU AND IGNATIUS, and the other things we have quoted a little earlier, do not agree with it at all, and they seem to have been stitched in carelessly, and against the author's intention, by another hand. Second, he showed that the writer of the paragraph speaks of Ignatius in one way and the author of the Epistle in another, and even writes things that contradict each other. This was a very strong argument against the last paragraph of the Epistle. To make everything clearer, the very words of that paragraph, which contain Polycarp's testimony about the Ignatian letters, must be cited: You wrote to me both you and Ignatius, that if anyone goes to Syria, he should carry the letters I have written to you, if we have an opportune time, either I or a messenger whom I shall send on your behalf. Indeed we have sent you the Epistles of Ignatius which were sent to us by him, and any others we have had by us, as you ordered; they are subjoined to this Epistle, and from them you will gain great benefit. For they contain faith, patience, and all edification pertaining to our Lord. And as to Ignatius himself and those who are with him, let us know what you have learned more certainly. So the old Latin translator rendered the Greek, whose version Ussher published, leaving aside the last words, which exist only in Latin and which we have from the translator alone. Eusebius, in Ecclesiastical History book 3, chapter 36, presents this whole fragment except for those phrases which cause difficulty and stir up the dispute: and concerning Ignatius himself and those who are with him, let us know what you have learned more certainly. These words are found only in one old translator, whether he translated them from the Greek, or added them from his own invention, or rather they were inserted by another hand, which is not improbable. At least, if one weighs these final words, they speak of Ignatius as if he were still alive and had not yet exchanged life for death. But the author of the Epistle speaks quite differently, plainly asserting that Ignatius, at the time when he himself was writing to the Philippians, was already crowned with the martyr's wreath and had gloriously completed the last act of the contest. The matter is clear. He exhorts the Philippians to that righteousness and patience which they had seen with the eye of faith, or with their own eyes, not only in the blessed Ignatius, and Zosimus, and Rufus, but in certain others of their own flock, and in Paul himself, and the other Apostles. Having said this, he continues about the same men: being confident, because ALL THESE did not run in vain, but in faith and righteousness, and have departed to the place due to them from (or with) the Lord, with whom they also suffered. Or, as the Greek sounds: persuaded that all these did not run in vain, but in faith and righteousness, and that they are in their due place with the Lord with whom they also suffered. Dallaeus set these two passages against each other, and when this keen-nosed man noticed the manifest contradiction between the author of the Epistle and the writer of the paragraph, he rightly concluded that the whole paragraph in which such flatly contrary statements to the preceding words of the Epistle are found was written by a hand other than the author's, and was cunningly and falsely stitched onto the Epistle by some impostor. Indeed no greater contradiction could ever be devised. The author of the Epistle affirms that Ignatius suffered, had completed all the acts of his contest, and now, crowned, rests and exults in his place with the Lord, and no longer dwells on this earth. But the writer of the paragraph thinks that Ignatius is still alive, living, well, and hastening toward the last act of the contest: And concerning Ignatius himself and those who are with him, let us know what you have learned more certainly. Is it credible that Polycarp, a most wise and most truthful man, spoke about the same matter in such discordant, mutually contrary and conflicting ways? He had written that the Philippians were persuaded and confident that Ignatius, having duly completed his course, had departed to his place with the Lord; and immediately he asks them, if they have heard anything about Ignatius and those who are with him, to inform him of it. Who would bear this in any man of sound mind, much less in Polycarp, the most holy martyr, endowed and enriched with so many excellent gifts of intellect? Certainly I would think I was doing the learned author of the Vindiciae an injustice, and thinking far too meanly of him, if I supposed he could write in so small a space, and about the same matter, things so contrary. Let him not therefore take it amiss if, in order to free Polycarp from this charge and to shield him from so plain a contradiction, we assert that the author of the Epistle was one person and the writer of the paragraph or fragment another. Pearson replies that the paragraph under discussion does nothing to help his cause if it is admitted, and does him no harm if it is rejected. Indeed, learned sir, it does you a great deal of harm if you reject it as an addition. For on that ground one may argue thus: it is established that the last words of the paragraph in question were stitched in by another hand; who then will guarantee to me the trustworthiness of the other words of the same paragraph? Eusebius will, the learned Pearson will say. I grant that the other words of the fragment are read in Eusebius, but this does not prevent the whole paragraph from having been stitched in by some impostor with evil intent, since it is not denied that the final words of it were so inserted. For the earlier words of the paragraph cohere no better with what precedes than the last ones do, and they deserve no greater credit on that account, whether they were added earlier, later, or at the same moment as the final words. The learned man goes on and, granting the last part of the fragment, says that the author of the fragment does not signify or in any way imply that Ignatius was then alive, but that because the Philippians could hear something about Ignatius while he was living, Polycarp wished to know from them about him after his death. This is truly a cold solution. For if I deny that, I do not see by what reasoning the author of the Vindiciae will prove his assertion, since he says that Ignatius passed through Macedonia on foot through the Philippians, as his Acts report, and that some were sent by the Philippians to escort him on his journey for the sake of honour and refreshment. Grant that Ignatius passed through Philippi, was escorted by them, and that they heard something from him while he was being escorted: it still does not follow that Polycarp wished to learn from the Philippians what they could hear about Ignatius while he was living. If this had been Polycarp's intention, he would not have asked obscurely and in a roundabout way about a matter on which he wished to be informed, as he does. In plain and direct words he would have asked the Philippians to deign to tell him what they had heard about Ignatius while he lived. This cannot be extracted from the words of the paragraph's author, not even with hooks and pincers: and concerning Ignatius himself and those who are with him, let us know what you have learned more certainly. We speak in that way, of course, when we wish to know the affairs and condition of friends who are alive; but when they are dead we use other words if we wish to know something they said while still alive. Hence it follows that the writer of the paragraph thought Ignatius was still alive while he was writing, and was hastening toward the last act of the contest, as the most learned Hammond, the keenest defender of the Ignatians, admits in the work of Dallaeus. From this it is clear how rashly another learned man laughs at the contradiction we press, the antilogy, as if it were wholly without truth. Suppose, he says, as we think, that Polycarp wrote at a time when Ignatius was believed to have undergone martyrdom, though uncertain rumours (as usually happens) were circulating about what had happened at his death. Granting that, would it not have been fitting for Polycarp to say that Ignatius holds his place with God, and at the same time to ask to be informed about Ignatius and those with him, if the Philippians had learned anything certain? A strange line of reasoning, if it rested on a solid foundation; but it is wholly without one. Does that learned man usually ask about what happened at the death of friends in this way? Who has ever heard, even by report, that these words, and concerning the friend himself, and those who are with him, let us know what you have learned more certainly, are to be explained as meaning: inform me if you have anything certain about what happened at the death of a friend? I beg you, learned sir, by your good faith: would you write to your intimates in this way if you wished to know all the circumstances of a friend's death? I think not. Why then do you not hesitate to represent Polycarp as writing like that? But I return to the author of the Vindiciae. To conclude at last, the Polycarpian collection of the Ignatian Epistles is of such doubtful credibility, because of the fragile and false foundation on which it rests, namely the last paragraph of the Epistle, which we have shown to have been stitched in by another hand, that the testimony drawn from it can be of no real weight at all. This is especially so if one considers what we wrote at the beginning of these observations about the wavering credibility of the whole collection. To all this I am glad to add that the defender of the Ignatians has made no reply whatever to those solutions by which the most distinguished Dallaeus refutes Hammond's arguments drawn from this fragment of the Epistle.

units.la: Polycarpum excipit Irenæus secundus à Vindiciarum Autore excitatus testis, sed an validè ac fœliciter ex illius testimonio argumentetur Vir doctus disquirendum est; fuit quidem Irenæus jam à puero Polycarpi discipulus, ideóque ignorare non potuit Ignatianarum Epistolarum syllogen à Polycarpo procuratam, si illius igitur alicubi meminit Irenæus, vel Epistolas in eâ comprehensas, si non omnes, saltem quasdam nominatim memorat, illáisque tanquam genuinum Ignatij fœtum Polycarpo cognitas esse asserit, Viri docti causæ aliquo modo patrocinabitur, quamvis nondum liquidò constaret quas hodie habemus sub Ignatij nomine Epistolas, easdem prorsus esse cum iis quæ in collectione Polycarpianâ extabant; si ulterius progrederetur Irenæus, & aliquot ex hodiernis Epistolis citaret ῥήσεις seu sententias, indicatis nominatim locis unde descriptæ fuissent, illius pro Ignatianis testimonium libenter ampleciteremur, & Ignatium Epistolas controversas scripsisse ingenuè agnosceremus: sed quoniam nihil tale ex Irenæo adducunt Ignatianorum patroni, non est quod sententiam mutemus, nec ab opinione quâ justis de causis fuimus imbuti dimoveamur. Quid igitur, inquies, ex Irenæo afferunt Viri docti in gratiam Ignatianorum? afferunt, inquiam, hæc verba quæ leguntur cap.28. extremo libri quinti adversus hæreses: Quemadmodum quidam de nostris dixit, propter martyrium in Deum. adjudicatus ad bestias : Quoniam frumentum sum Christi, & per dentes bestiarum molor, ut mundus panis Dei inveniar. Fatentur omnes Ignatium ab Irenæo hîc designari, & præterea de verbis ipsis nulla prorsus lis est, cum ab Ignatio prolata dubitet nemo; verùm quia eadem verba extant in Epistolâ ad Romanos Ignatij nomine inscriptâ, pertendit Vindiciarum Autor illa ab Irenæo ex hac Epistolâ descripta fuisse, quod negabat Dallæus, & certè merito, cum Irenæus de Epistolâ Ignatij ad Romanos nullum verbum faciat, neque hæc quæ laudat verba vel in eâ vel ex eâ Epistolâ legisse affirmet, nihil aliud scribit Irenæus, nisi hoc istum cujus meminit dixisse; si saltem, ait Dallæus, hæc eum scripsisse diceret, colorem licet salsum & evanidum, aliquem tamen haberet argumentatio : sic enim ex aliquo Ignatij scripto, inquit, hæc ejus verba Irenæum habuisse legitimè concluderes; tametsi illud unde ea sumpsisset, Ignatij scriptum, ne sic quidem con-ficeres[?] eandem illam esse quam nos hodie habemus, ad Romanos ejus nomine inscriptam Epistolam; pergit celeberrimus Dallæus, & eo futiliorem esse hanc pro Ignatianis argumentationem putat, quod Irenæus hæc quæ refert verba, Ignatium non scripsisse, sed dixisse memorat: Quid ad hæc eruditus Pearsonius ? observat primùm distinctionem illam inter ista duo dixit & scripsit, cùm verba ipsa scripta esse sciamus, nullam prorsùs vim habere cùm notum sit sententias & loca à Veteribus citata esse per verbum hoc dixit non minus, imò sæpiùs quàm per verbum alterum scripsit; Deinde plura congerit exempla ut suam hanc tueatur assertionem; sed benè est quod Vir doctus istam dictis apposuerit conditionem, cùm verba ipsa scripta esse sciamus: persuasi enim sumus Irenæum ista quæ de Ignatio narrat scripta esse haudquaquam scivisse, imò ne scire potuisse, cùm nullibi scripta legerentur; extant equidem in Epistolâ ad Romanos quæ Ignatij nomen præfert; sed Epistolam illam post Irenæi ætatem consarcinatam & conflatam esse contendimus: cùm igitur Irenæus ista quibus de agitur verba scripta esse scire non potuerit, fateatur necesse est Vir doctus distinctionem illam inter ista duo dixit & scripsit, plurimùm valere: nam affirmat modò nullam prorsùs vim habere, cùm verba ipsa scripta esse sciamus: nec sibi pro concesso sumere vellet Vindiciarum Autor, quod in quæstione est, scilicet germanam esse quæ Ignatij nomine circumfertur ad Romanos Epistolam, alioquin vitiosa efset, ut optimè novit, argumentatio: sed seponamus tantisper quam verbis suis apposuit conditionem, & distinctionem illam inter ista duo dixit & scripsit consideremus: non diffiteor, nec meâ quidem sententiâ diffiteretur Dallæus, sententias & loca à Veteribus citata esse, non solùm per verbum scripsit, sed etiam per verbum alterum dixit; Verùm concedet etiam Ignatianorum vindex verbum istud dicere proprie ad ea quæ ore proferuntur spectare, minúsque proprie ad ea quæ scripta sunt pertinere; Iam nemo nescit à nativâ & magis proprià verborum significatione temerè & absque necessitate discedendum non esse, sed ut Viro docto morem geramus, demus verbum dixit quo utitur Irenæus, & quæ voce, & quæ scripto edita sunt, indifferenter denotare, non magis illius causam juvabit Irenæi narratio quàm nostram, ac proinde omittendum erit testimonium pro Epistolis Ignatianis ex illa narratione desumptum: quod aliquo modo fecit reverendissimus Vsserius hunc Irenæi locum minimè urgendum censens, cùm verbum illud εἶπε [?] (inquit) & quæ voce, & quæ scripto edita sunt, indifferenter denotet: & hoc ipsum à sanctifsimo illo viro non solùm in Epistolâ ad Romanos exaratum, sed etiam in ipso agone fuisse repetitum, & Acta martyrij ipsius, & Hieronymus in Scriptorum Catalogo confirmant: verò similiùs esse existimant alij, ut de damnatione. Martyris ad bestias loquutus Irenæus, vocem ab eodem, audito bestiarum rugitu, prolatam potiùs quàm scripto anteà mandatam, memoriæ commendare. hic voluerit. Hæc doctissimus Vsserius non ultra premens hunc Irenæi pro Epistolis Ignatianis locum; quod autem dicit de Actis Martyrij Ignatij & de Hieronymo, verissimum est, nempe testantur ambo verba quæ examinamus ab Ignatio, audito bestiarum rugitu fuisse prolata; cùm jam dãmnatus, inquit Hieronymus, esset ad bestias, & ardore patiendi rugientes audiret leones, ait: frumentum Christi sum, dentibus bestiarum molar, ut panis mundus inveniar. Cum eo faciunt & Actorum Ignatij descriptores, qui eum ad circumstantes supremum hunc sermonem habuisse ferunt. Viri Romani, qui hoc certamen spectatis, non sine causâ laboravi, non propter pravitatem hæc patior, sed propter pietatem: frumentum Christi sum, dentibus bestiarum molar, ut panis mundus inveniar; Ita Latini apud Adonem Viennensem de festivitatibus Apostolorum D. 1. Febr. ubi observatur ista dixisse Ignatium, cum jam projectus bestias audiret rugientes: Latini vero haec a Graecis mutuati sunt, & in Ignatij Acta quibus ipsi utebantur, transtulerunt, extant enim Graece totidem verbis apud Visserium notis in Epistolam ad Romanos Ignatij nomine inscriptam; Metaphrastes ipse quoque Graecus uberius pro more sic expressit, Viri Romani & praesentes huius certaminis spectatores, non haec mihi fiunt ob aliquod maleficium, neque ut luam poenas pravorum facinorum, sed ut Deum assequar, cujus quidem teneor desiderio, & quem cupio insatiabiliter; sum enim ejus frumentum, & molor per dentes bestiarum, ut fiam ei purus panis. Breviarum Romanum ad D. 1. Febr. lect. 6. eadem plane habet cum Hieronymo, cujus ipsissima verba sibi adoptavit. Jam quivis videt & Hieronymum, & Acta Martyrij sive Graeca sive Latina, & Metaphrastem, & Breviarium Romanum testari Ignatium vocem de qua lis est, audito bestiarum rugitu protulisse, non potest igitur doctissimus Vindiciarum Autor ex Irenaei narratione pro sua causa legitime argumentari; tamen quia sibi adimi Irenaeum aegre fert Vir eruditus, omnem movet lapidem ut Hieronymo & Actis Martyrij denegetur fides, Hieronymi varias adfert ut sibi videtur hallucinationes, sed hallucinatus sit centies Hieronymus, incogitantiâ aliquando laborârit, imò plura de suo Eusebio addiderit ; num propterea rejicienda erunt tanquam falsa & absurda, quæ scribit de tempore quo Ignatius sententiam illam quam agitamus protulit ? Quid fiet de ipso Eusebio si tam rigidè cum eo agatur ? quoties ab eo peccatum est ? Et quot sunt in Historiâ illius Ecclesiasticâ hallucinationes & infirmitatis humanæ monumenta? certè si valet Viri docti adversus Hieronymum argumentatio, ruet tota ferè Pearsonianæ disputationis moles, quæ Eusebij autoritate præcipuè nititur ; Acta verò Martyrij quod attinet, dicit non illa esse quæ ætate S. Irenæi extabant, sed alia plane sexto vel septimo sæculo ficta, & fabulosis narrationibus aucta, quibus Ignatium quasi in Amphitheatro loquentem introducunt, quem ne unum tunc verbum dixisse antiquissima Acta narrant. Miror hæc à Viro docto tam confidenter dicta, nonne probabilius est Hieronymum quæ de Ignatio narrat, ex antiquis Martyrij Actis descripsisse ? Putátne eruditus Pearsonius celeberrimum illum Ecclesiæ Doctorem hæc gratis finxisse, & quæ de sanctissimo scribit Martyre ex suo cerebro hausisse ? Profectò injuriam faceret[?] antiquissimo scriptori, & de Ecclesiâ optimè merito, qui ita existimaret; satius est dicere Hieronymum in antiquissimis Martyrij Actis legisse, quæ de Ignatio habet, & si forte aliquam jam suâ ætate mutationem experta essent illa Acta, nullam tamen sensisse istius quâ de agitur circunstantiæ respectu par est credere; nam ex istis Actis vel alio quodam scripto æque vetusto quæ de Ignatio narrat, deprompsisse Hieronymum est plusquàm verisimile; Eusebius dices, istius circunstantiæ non meminit, quid tum ! illius non intererat meminisse, vel saltem eam commemorare necessarium non putavit; non ignorat Vir doctus scriptores qui ex aliis sua describunt, id pro arbitrio facere, & quæ sibi tantum conducere videntur excerpere solitos esse : Hieronymus hanc Ignatij sententiam suæ de illius Martyrio narrationi inserere haud inutile duxit, ideóque ex antiquis quæ tunc extabant Martyrij Actis eam hîc transcribere non dubitavit; eadem quæ Eusebius monumenta versare potuit Hieronymus qui Catalogum suum de Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis annos post Eusebij mortem circirciter quinquaginta exaravit; frustra igitur eum intimulat Vir doctus quasi ex suo addidisset quæ ex scriptis se admodum vetustioribus desumpserat; Dallæus prætereà argumentatus erat adversus Ignatiana ex Irenæi silentio qui in refutandis ac refellendis suæ ætatis Hæreticorum erroribus & deliramentis, Ignatij autoritate nusquam usus est, etsi quas hodie habemus Epistolæ plura contra ejusmodi Hæreticos submininistrent argumenta; secundò à solito Irenæi agendi modo, qui præstantiorum virorum se vetustiorum sententias afferre solet, in nominatis Autoribus, cùm tamen nullas ex Ignatij Epistolis suo operi insperserit: tertiò ex eo quod Clementis & Polycarpi memorat Epistolas, Ignatianas nequaquam; quartò denique quod easdem adversus Florinum agens silentio præterit, quamvis Presbyterorum qui Apostolorum discipuli fuerunt, Polycarpi in primis Autoritatem afferat. Plura hisce objectionibus reponit eruditus Pearsonius, & sese in omnes partes versat, ut tela ista declinet, sed frustrà se torquet, nec Ignatium suum ab istis ictibus tutum præstare potest, quod probatu effet facilè, nisi nobis propositum fuisset ostendere tantum testes trium primorum sæculorum à Viro docto adductos,non eos esse quos esse ille dicit, neque eorum testimonia ea pariter esse quibus omnimoda adhibeatur fides, quod cum de Polycarpi & Irenæi testimonijs fusè & clarè demonstraverimus, superest ut de Origene agamus.
units.tr: Irenaeus, the second witness, whom the author of the Vindiciae brings forward after Polycarp, follows him. But it must be examined whether the learned man argues validly and successfully from his testimony. Irenaeus was indeed a disciple of Polycarp from boyhood, so he could not have been unaware of the collection of Ignatian Letters that Polycarp had procured. Therefore, if Irenaeus mentions Polycarp anywhere and names the Letters included in that collection, or at least some of them, and says they were known to Polycarp as a genuine offspring of Ignatius, the learned man's cause would be supported to some degree, although it would not yet be clear that the letters we now have under Ignatius's name are exactly the ones that were in the Polycarpian collection. And if Irenaeus went further and cited some of today's letters as sayings [ῥήσεις] or sentences, with the places from which they were taken named, we would gladly accept his testimony in favour of the Ignatian letters and admit that Ignatius wrote the disputed letters. But since the Ignatian defenders bring forward nothing of this kind from Irenaeus, there is no reason for us to change our opinion or to be moved from the view with which, for good reasons, we have been imbued. What then, you will ask, do the learned men bring from Irenaeus in favour of the Ignatians? I answer that they bring these words, which are read at the end of chapter 28 of the fifth book Against Heresies: As one of our people said, condemned to the beasts for the sake of martyrdom to God: "I am the wheat of Christ, and I am ground by the teeth of the beasts, that I may be found pure bread of God." All agree that Ignatius is designated here by Irenaeus, and there is no real dispute about the words themselves, since no one doubts that they were uttered by Ignatius. But because the same words are found in the Epistle to the Romans inscribed with Ignatius's name, the author of the Vindiciae contends that Irenaeus took them from this Epistle. Dallaeus denied this, and rightly so, since Irenaeus makes no mention of the Epistle of Ignatius to the Romans, and does not state that he read these words in it or from it. Irenaeus writes nothing except that this man of whom he speaks said [dixisse] them. Dallaeus says that if Irenaeus said that Ignatius wrote [scripsisse] them, the argument would have some colour, though a false and faint one: for you would rightly conclude that Irenaeus had these words from some writing [scripto] of Ignatius. Yet even so, you would not prove that the writing [scriptum] from which he took them is the same as the one we have today, the Epistle to the Romans inscribed with his name. The most celebrated Dallaeus goes on, and thinks this argument for the Ignatians is all the more trifling because Irenaeus relates these words as spoken by Ignatius and not as written by him. What does the learned Pearson reply to this? First he observes that the distinction between these two, said and wrote [dixit / scripsit], since we know the words themselves were written, has no force at all, because it is well known that sentences and passages cited by the ancients are introduced by the verb said [dixit] no less, indeed more often, than by the other verb, wrote [scripsit]. He then gathers several examples to support this assertion. But it is good that the learned man added the condition since we know the words themselves were written. For we are persuaded that Irenaeus did not know, and indeed could not have known, that the things he relates about Ignatius were written, since they were nowhere read in writing. Certainly there is an Epistle to the Romans that bears Ignatius's name, but we contend that this Epistle was patched together and compiled after Irenaeus's time. Since, then, Irenaeus could not have known that these words were written, the learned man must admit that the distinction between the two verbs said and wrote [dixit / scripsit] carries great weight. For he asserts that it has no force at all since we know the words themselves were written. Nor would the author of the Vindiciae wish to assume as granted what is in question, namely that the Epistle to the Romans circulating under Ignatius's name is genuine; otherwise, as he very well knows, the argument would be faulty. But let us set aside for the moment the condition he added to his words, and consider that distinction between the two verbs said and wrote [dixit / scripsit]. I do not deny, nor would Dallaeus deny in my judgment, that sentences and passages cited by the ancients are introduced not only by the verb wrote [scripsit] but also by the other verb, said [dixit]. Yet the defender of the Ignatians will also concede that the verb to say [dicere] properly refers to things uttered by the mouth, and less properly to things that have been written. Now no one fails to know that one should not depart rashly and without necessity from the native and more proper meaning of words. But to humour the learned man, let us grant that the verb said [dixit], which Irenaeus uses, denotes indifferently things published by voice and things published in writing. Even so, Irenaeus's account will no more help his cause than ours, and therefore the testimony for the Ignatian Letters drawn from that account must be set aside. Most reverend Ussher has done this in some measure, judging that this passage of Irenaeus should not be pressed, since the verb [εἶπε] (he says) indifferently denotes things published by voice and things published in writing; and this very thing, that the most holy man not only wrote it in the Epistle to the Romans but also repeated it in the very contest, is confirmed by the Acts of his martyrdom and by Jerome in his Catalogue of Writers. Others, however, think it more likely, as in the condemnation of the martyr, that Irenaeus, having spoken of a martyr condemned to the beasts, meant to commemorate a word uttered by him when he heard the roaring of the beasts, rather than one previously committed to writing. So far the most learned Ussher, who does not press this passage of Irenaeus further in favour of the Ignatian Letters. What he says about the Acts of Ignatius's martyrdom and about Jerome is quite true: both attest that the words we are examining were uttered by Ignatius when he heard the roaring of the beasts. When he had already been condemned, says Jerome, to the beasts, and hearing the lions roaring with eagerness to suffer, he said: "I am the wheat of Christ; I am ground by the teeth of the beasts, that I may be found pure bread." The writers of Ignatius's Acts agree with him, and they report that he spoke this last address to the bystanders: Men of Rome, who are watching this contest, I have not laboured without cause; I suffer these things not because of wickedness but because of piety. I am the wheat of Christ; I am ground by the teeth of the beasts, that I may be found pure bread. So the Latins also say in Ado of Vienne, On the Festivals of the Apostles, on 1 February, where it is observed that Ignatius spoke these words when, already thrown to the beasts, he heard them roaring. The Latins, however, borrowed these things from the Greeks, and translated them into the Acts of Ignatius which they used. For the Greek text stands in the same words, as Ussher notes, in the Epistle to the Romans inscribed with Ignatius's name. The Greek Metaphrastes too, in his usual fuller manner, expresses it thus: Men of Rome and present spectators of this contest, these things are not done to me for some wrongdoing, nor that I may pay the penalty of wicked deeds, but that I may attain to God, whose desire I am bound by and whom I desire insatiably; for I am his wheat, and I am ground by the teeth of the beasts, that I may become to him pure bread. The Roman Breviary, on 1 February, lesson 6, has exactly the same as Jerome, and has adopted his very words. Now anyone can see that Jerome, the Acts of the martyrdom, whether Greek or Latin, Metaphrastes and the Roman Breviary all bear witness that Ignatius uttered the words in question when he heard the roaring of the beasts. The most learned author of the Vindiciae therefore cannot argue legitimately for his cause from Irenaeus's account. Yet because the learned man takes it hard that Irenaeus is taken from him, he moves every stone to deny credit to Jerome and to the Acts of the martyrdom. He brings forward various supposed hallucinations of Jerome. But Jerome may have been deluded a hundred times, may at times have laboured under carelessness, and may even have added much of his own to Eusebius. Will those things he writes about the time when Ignatius uttered that sentence we are discussing therefore be rejected as false and absurd? What would become of Eusebius himself if he were treated so rigorously? How often has he erred? And how many hallucinations and monuments of human weakness are there in his Ecclesiastical History? Certainly, if the learned man's argument against Jerome holds, almost the whole mass of Pearson's disputation will collapse, since it rests chiefly on the authority of Eusebius. As for the Acts of the martyrdom, he says they are not the ones that existed in the time of St Irenaeus, but other ones, invented in the sixth or seventh century and enlarged with fabulous narratives, in which they introduce Ignatius speaking as if in the amphitheatre, though the most ancient Acts relate that he spoke not a single word at that time. I wonder that the learned man says this so confidently. Is it not more probable that Jerome took from the ancient Acts of the martyrdom what he relates about Ignatius? Does the learned Pearson think that that most celebrated teacher of the Church invented these things for nothing, and drew from his own brain what he writes about that most holy martyr? Surely anyone who thought so would do an injustice to a most ancient writer who has deserved well of the Church. It is better to say that Jerome read in the most ancient Acts of the martyrdom what he has about Ignatius. And even if those Acts had already undergone some alteration in his time, it is right to believe that they did not contain any change in the circumstance we are discussing. For it is more than probable that Jerome drew what he relates about Ignatius from those Acts, or from some other equally ancient writing. Eusebius, you will say, does not mention this circumstance. So what? It was not his concern to mention it, or at least he did not think it necessary to record it. The learned man is not unaware that writers who describe the works of others do so at their own discretion, and are accustomed to excerpt whatever seems to serve their purpose. Jerome thought it not useless to insert this sentence of Ignatius into his account of his martyrdom, and therefore did not hesitate to transcribe it from the ancient Acts of the martyrdom then extant. Jerome, who wrote his Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers about fifty years after Eusebius's death, could consult the same records that Eusebius could have consulted. It is therefore in vain that the learned man accuses him, as if he had added from his own resources what he had drawn from writings much older than himself. Moreover, Dallaeus had argued against the Ignatian letters from Irenaeus's silence. In refuting and confuting the errors and ravings of the heretics of his own age, Irenaeus nowhere used the authority of Ignatius, although the letters we have today supply many arguments against such heretics. Secondly, from Irenaeus's usual manner of proceeding, since he is accustomed to cite the opinions of the more distinguished men of earlier times, naming the authors, yet has inserted nothing from the Ignatian letters into his work. Thirdly, from the fact that he mentions the Epistles of Clement and of Polycarp, but not those of Ignatius. Fourthly, and finally, because in arguing against Florinus he passes over the letters in silence, although he cites the authority of the elders who were disciples of the Apostles, and above all of Polycarp. The learned Pearson replies to these objections at length, and turns himself in every direction to avoid these missiles. But he labours in vain, nor can he keep his Ignatius safe from these blows. This could easily be proved, were it not our purpose only to show that the witnesses of the first three centuries adduced by the learned man are not those he says they are, nor are their testimonies such as deserve full credit. Since we have demonstrated this fully and clearly in the cases of the testimonies of Polycarp and Irenaeus, it remains for us to deal with Origen.

units.la: Ex Origene siquidem duo afferri solent loca ab Ignatianorum fautoribus, alter ex Prologo in Canticum Canticorum, alter verò ex Homiliâ sexta in Lucam, in priori loco hæc leguntur memini aliquem Sanctorum dixisse, Ignatium nomine, de Christo, Meus autem amor crucifixus est; posterior istis concipitur verbis, Eleganter in cujusdam Martyris Epistolâ scriptum reperi (Ignatium dico Episcopum Antiochiæ post Petrum secundum, qui in persecutione Romæ pugnavit ad bestias) Principem sæculi hujus latuit Virginitas Mariæ. En tibi duo quæ vulgò describuntur pro Ignatianis Epistolis ex Origene testimonia, quorum illud extat in eâ Epistolâ quæ nunc ad Romanos sub Ignatij nomine circumfertur Meus amor, vel ut Vsserianus liber habet, Meum desiderium crucifixum est, istud verò in ea quæ ad Ephesios inscripta est, reperitur, Latuit principem sæculi hujus virginitas Mariæ. Ad utrúmque locum simul semélque respondet Dallæus, levis esse ad rem, quæ agitur momenti, quod opusculorum ex quibus allati sunt, dubia sit & incerta auctoritas, deinde utrúmque separatim expendit, & initium faciens à loco qui ex Prologo in Canticum Canticorum desumitur, scribit gravem esse ac veram, ut videtur, magni Viri & à partium studijs alieni Erasmi censuram, quæ sic se habet: Inter opera Hieronymi ferebatur & hic commentarius (in Canticum Canticorum) cùm nec Origenis sit, nec Hieronymi, sed hominis Latini, pulcrè doctì ac bene diserti. Græcum non fuisse vel hinc colligas licebit, quod in prologo citat Græcos, velut alienos: cùm apud Græcos, inquit, qui eruditi ac sapientes videntur. Idem liquet ex interpretatione amoris, caritatis, dilectionis, & cupidinis. Addit Dallæus idem esse de hoc commentario Brunonis A-merbachij judicium, & Sixtum Senensem fateri id opus in vetustis quibusdam codicibus nomine Hieronymi prænotatum fuisse; & hinc petita testimonia Ambrosio à Thoma & Lombardo tribui, ut est, inquit, à Coco nostro iampridem observatum, quod certè verissimum est; His omnibus à Dallæo citatis scriptoribus qui opus istud in Canticum Canticorum Origeni abjudicant, duos celeberrimos Iesuitas subjungere non pigebit, Philippum videlicet Labbæum & Theophilum Raynaudum quorum utérque idem de hoc scripto sentire videtur; Labbæus enim postquam observavit quæ fuerit de hoc opere Sixti Senensis sententia,nempe pium, disertum atque eruditum opus efse, hæc continenter subnectit; sed non esse Auctoris Græci plures suadent, quorum ra-tiones non sunt hîc, ne in immensum crefcant Observationes, pluribus excutiendæ, quamvis enim in sequentibus duas confutet rationes eorum, qui hoc opus Origeni suppositum existimant, quia invalidas putat,ita tamen observationem suam sinit, ut lucubrationem istam Origeni abjudicare potiùs quàm adjudicare illum ferè non dubites. Quicquid sit mentem suam clariùs aperit Theophilus Raynaudus qui librum istum Origenis non esse disertè affirmare non veretur, Commentari in Cantica, inquit, quorum initium est, EPITHALAMIVM LIBELLVS, non possunt esse Origenis, sed sunt Latini Autoris, qualem se Autor ipse bis profitetur, agens de Logicâ in Philosophiæ divisione. Autoribus quos sequitur Dallæus opponit Vindiciarum Autor Iacobum Merlinum, Genebrardum, & doctissimum clarissimúmque virum Petrum Danielem Huetium ultimum operum Græcorum Origenis Editorem, ad quem etiam nos amandat Vir alius eruditus; tribus his Origenis editoribus addit eruditus Pearsonius, Blondellum, Albertinum, imò quod mireris Dallæum ipsum, quasi à se ipso dissentiret ; sed pace tanti viri dixerim, haud sincerè agere videtur Dallæi respectu, Dallæus enim ex hypothesi non suâ, sed Halloixij adversarij loquitur,sese illius de hoc opusculo opinioni accommodans, sicque eum alloquens lib. 1. cap. 17. de libris suppositis Dionysio Areopagitæ, merito Albertininus noster judicavit Dionysium tuum totum hunc locum à tuo Origene vel esse furatum, vel certè mutuo sumpsisse : Quivis videt hanc de quâ lis est lucubrationem Dallæo non magis probari quàm PseudoDionysij scripta, tuus, ait Dionysius, tuus Origenes, non meus, neque semel aut iterùm ita loquitur, sed sæpissimè pag. 108. 109. neque feré aliter, tamen si virum doctum audimus, Author expositionum in Canticum Canticorum,cum contra Dionysium scribit Dallæus, Origenes est; & locum quem adduximus, in eodem Origene totus hactenus orbis æquo animo tulit: quare idem non est, quare contra totum orbem militat Dallæus, cùm adversus Ignatium arma sumit ? tota autem hæc Vindiciarum Autoris argumentatio, nullo alio nititur fundamento quàm istis Dallæi ex adversarij hypotesi loquentis verbis, quod in Origene ( quem pace tuâ Dionysio tuo: multò doctiorem fuisse virum puto ) totus hactenus orbis æquo ani-mo tulit, id in Dionysio legi, noli ferre iniquius: eadem plane ratione probare posset eruditus Pearsonius Dionysij scripta quæ exagitat Dallæus & tanquam spuria confodit, genuina illi esse ac legitima, quia hoc in loco in Dionysio simpliciter dixit, æquè ac in Origene: Verum ut nullus superstit tergiversandi locus, lucéque meridianâ clarius appareat aliquid humani hîc passum esse doctissimum Vindiciarum Autorem, forte præ nimio causæ studio, describenda nobis sunt quædam Dallæi verba ex pag. 108. Extant, inquit, quatuor quædam in Canticum Canticorum Homiliæ inter Origenis opera, quas pro vero Origenis fœtu tu tuique Halloixij vulgò habetis. Tui certè ex iis adversus nos testimonia Origenis nomine laudant, ut Copus, & Coccius; Ac ut cæteros mittam, tu quidem hoc opus Origeni non semel asseris. Nam & ex Homilia tertia locum describis, ut demonstres Origenem subita Ecclesiæ incrementa celebrasse; Et paulò post tria ex eodem opere loca recitas, veluti veras Origenis sententias; & apud multos controversam Origenis de sanctissimâ Trinitate Orthodoxiam tribus itidem ex ejus operis Prologo, & Homilia tertia petitis testimonijs confirmas, om-nia absurdè & ridiculè, nisi tu hunc scriptorem pro vero Origene Adamantio, de quo quaeritur, habeas. Non potuit disertius testari praestantissimus Dallaeus, se commentarios in Cantica Origenis nomine praenotatos, pro vero illius foetu minime agnoscere: De Albertino aliter se res habet, is quidem utitur horum Commentariorum Autoritate, ac si vere Origenis essent; sed ita tamen ut eos interpolatos esse alibi non diffiteatur; Blondellus vero quaedam ex hoc opere laudat in Apologia pro sententia Hieronymi sect. 2. §. 13. sed Origenis esse neque affirmat neque negat, ideoque inter approbatores non est numerandus, quoties enim contingit varia a scriptoribus laudari opuscula sub eorum nomine quibus vulgo ascribi solent; quamvis illorum non esse probe norint.
units.tr: Two passages from Origen are usually cited by the defenders of the Ignatian letters. The first, from the Prologue to the Commentary on the Song of Songs, reads: I remember that one of the Saints said, in the name of Ignatius, concerning Christ, My love has been crucified. The second, from the sixth Homily on Luke, reads: I have found it elegantly written in the letter of a certain Martyr (I mean Ignatius, bishop of Antioch after Peter the second, who fought with the beasts at Rome): The virginity of Mary was hidden from the prince of this world. Here, then, are the two testimonies from Origen that are commonly put forward on behalf of the Ignatian letters. The first is found in the letter that now circulates under Ignatius's name to the Romans, My love, or, as Ussher's book has it, My desire has been crucified. The second is found in the letter addressed to the Ephesians: The virginity of Mary was hidden from the prince of this world. Dallaeus answers both passages together and at once, saying that it matters little for the question at hand that the short works from which they are taken have a doubtful and uncertain authority. Then he examines each separately. Beginning with the passage taken from the Prologue to the Commentary on the Song of Songs, he writes that the judgment of the great man Erasmus, who was free of party spirit, is weighty and, as it seems, true. It runs as follows: this commentary too was attributed among the works of Jerome, although it is neither Origen's nor Jerome's, but the work of a Latin man, learned and eloquent. You may gather that it was not written in Greek from this alone, that in the prologue he cites the Greeks as strangers: since among the Greeks, he says, who seem learned and wise. The same is clear from the translation of amor, caritas, dilectio and cupido. Dallaeus adds that Bruno Amerbach holds the same opinion of this commentary, and that Sixtus of Siena admits that this work was labelled with Jerome's name in certain old manuscripts; and that the testimonies drawn from it were therefore attributed to Ambrose by Thomas and Lombard, as, he says, our Coccius observed long ago, which is certainly most true. To all these writers cited by Dallaeus, who deny this work on the Song of Songs to Origen, I will not hesitate to add two very famous Jesuits, namely Philippe Labbe and Théophile Raynaud, both of whom seem to think the same about this writing. For Labbe, after noting what Sixtus of Siena thought of this work, namely that it is a pious, eloquent and learned work, continues directly: but several reasons suggest that it is not by a Greek author, whose arguments cannot be examined here, lest the Observations grow beyond measure. For although in what follows he refutes two arguments of those who think this work was falsely ascribed to Origen, because he judges them weak, he so frames his remark that he scarcely hesitates to deny the work to Origen rather than to assign it to him. Whatever the case, Théophile Raynaud makes his view clearer, not hesitating to state plainly that this book is not Origen's: The Commentaries on the Song of Songs, which begin, LIBELLUS EPITHALAMIVM, cannot be Origen's, but are by a Latin author, such as the author himself twice professes to be, when he treats of logic in the division of philosophy. Against the authors whom Dallaeus follows, the author of the Vindiciae sets James Merlin, Genebrardus, and the most learned and illustrious man Pierre-Daniel Huet, the last editor of Origen's Greek works, to whom another learned man also refers us. To these three editors of Origen the learned Pearson adds Blondel, Albertinus, and indeed, what is surprising, Dallaeus himself, as if he disagreed with himself. But with all respect to so great a man, I must say that he does not seem to deal honestly with Dallaeus. For Dallaeus speaks from a hypothesis not his own, but that of Halloix's opponent, adapting himself to that man's opinion about this little work. Addressing him thus in book 1, chapter 17, on the books falsely ascribed to Dionysius the Areopagite, our Albertinus rightly judged that your Dionysius has either stolen this whole passage from your Origen or certainly borrowed it. Anyone can see that this argument of Dallaeus, about the commentary in question, is no more convincing than his case against the writings of pseudo-Dionysius. Your, he says, Dionysius, your Origen, not mine: he speaks thus not once or twice but very often, and on pages 108 and 109 almost in the same way. Yet, if we listen to the learned man, the author of the expositions on the Song of Songs, when Dallaeus writes against Dionysius, is Origen; and the whole world has so far accepted with equanimity the passage we have quoted in that same Origen. Why, then, is it not the same, why does Dallaeus fight against the whole world when he takes up arms against Ignatius? But this whole argument of the author of the Vindiciae rests on no other foundation than Dallaeus's words, spoken from his opponent's hypothesis: what the whole world has so far accepted with equanimity in Origen (whom, with respect to your Dionysius, I think was much more learned), you must not take more unfairly when it is read in Dionysius. By the same reasoning the learned Pearson could prove that the writings of Dionysius which Dallaeus attacks and stabs as spurious are genuine and legitimate, because in this place he simply said in Dionysius just as he said in Origen. But so that no room is left for evasion, and so that it may appear more clearly than noonday light that the most learned author of the Vindiciae has suffered something human here, perhaps from too much zeal for his cause, I must quote certain words of Dallaeus from page 108. There exist, he says, four homilies on the Song of Songs among the works of Origen, which you and your Halloix commonly hold to be the true offspring of Origen. Certainly your side cites them under Origen's name against us, as Cop and Coccius do; and, to pass over the rest, you indeed assert this work to be Origen's more than once. For you both cite a passage from the third Homily to show that Origen praised the sudden growth of the Church, and shortly after you recite three passages from the same work as true opinions of Origen; and before many people you confirm Origen's orthodoxy on the most holy Trinity, which is disputed, by three testimonies taken from the Prologue of that work and the third Homily. All this is absurd and ridiculous, unless you hold this writer to be the true Origen Adamantius, whom we are asking about. The most excellent Dallaeus could not have declared more plainly that he by no means recognises the commentaries on the Song of Songs that bear Origen's name as his true offspring. It is otherwise with Albertinus: he uses the authority of these commentaries as if they were truly Origen's, yet he does not deny that elsewhere he found them interpolated. Blondel, indeed, praises certain passages from this work in his Apology for the opinion of Jerome, section 2, paragraph 13; but he neither affirms nor denies that they are Origen's, and so he is not to be counted among the approvers. For whenever various writers cite a little work under the name of those to whom such works are commonly ascribed, they do not thereby show that it is theirs, even though they well know it is not.

units.la: Supersunt igitur Vindiciarum Autori tres operum Origenis Editores, Merlinus, Genebrardus, & Huetius; sed nescio cur Genebrardum in suffragatorum classe reponat Vir doctus, cùm satis superque insuat[?] Genebrardus ipse in Collectaneis de Origenis vita & operibus, sibi non persuasum esse opusculum istud ab Origene exaratum fuisse, illiusque germanum esse foetum: postquam enim duas in Canticum Canticorum Homilias quas vertit Hieronymus, commemoravit, & integram ad
units.tr: There remain therefore for the author of the Vindiciae three editors of Origen's works: Merlin, Genebrardus and Huet. But I do not know why the learned man places Genebrardus among his supporters, since Genebrardus himself, in his Collectanea on the life and works of Origen, more than sufficiently insinuates that he was not persuaded this little work was written by Origen and is his genuine offspring. For after he mentions the two Homilies on the Song of Songs which Jerome translated, and copies out in full the short preface prefixed to them addressed to Pope Damasus, he has these words: there is also another pious, learned and eloquent work, or rather a fragment of a work, circulating under Origen's name, in which the first two chapters of the Song of Songs are explained with great eloquence and learning. This is found in certain old…

units.la: Damasum Papam præfatiunculam quæ in fronte earum præfixa est, transcripsit, hæc habet, fertur & aliud sub nomine Origenis pium, eruditum, ac disertum opus, vel potius operis fragmentum: in quo duo prima Canticorum capita eloquentissimè ac doctissimè explicantur. Hoc in vetustis quibusdam codicibus erat nomine Hieronymi præNOTATUM. Divisit nescio quis illud in quatuor Homilias, cum Homiliæ non sint, sed continens ac perpetua explanatio. Non ita loqui solemus de veris ac germanis Scriptorum operibus, sed de iis solùm quæ illorum nomine circumferuntur; Cùm igitur plures sint qui hoc opus improbent, quàm qui probent, nec illi autoritate sint iis inferiores, si forte non superiores, quin improbantium sit præferenda sententia nemo ambigere potest, præsertim si sequentes perpendantur observationes, 1. in vetustis quibusdam codicibus isti Commentarii erant nomine Hieronymi præNOTATI; quia pro germano ac genuino Origenis fœtu dubio procul non habebantur: 2. scribit Hieronymus in Prologo interpretationis Homiliarum duarum in Canticum, Origenem in decem quos in Canticum Canticorum elaboravit Tomis septuaginta Interpretes, Aquilam, Symmachum, Theodotionem, & Quintam Editionem magnificè aperteque disseruisse, quod cùm in istis quos tractamus Commentarijs non appareat, hinc consequitur Opus esse à decem illis Tomis diversum; Huic objectioni se satis fecisse putat clarissimus Huetius, si omnem culpam rejiciat in Rufinum Interpretem, cui, inquit, cùm solenne sit pervertere omnia, & ad libitum recoquere, adeò ut Tomos Origenis in Epistolam ad Romanos ad mediam partem coarctaverit, quis ullam ab eo fidem expectet? Fateor Rufinum pleráque quæ vertebat opuscula immutare ac interpolare solitum esse, sed propterea verisimile non est Rufinum, istum ut ita dicam peculiarem Origenis characterem, afferre videlicet & differere varias Interpretum Græcorum Editiones, à legitimo Origeniano opusculo auferre voluisse, imprimis post Hieronymi admonitionem; præterea non liquidò constat Rufinum hujus Operis Interpretem esse, nec tanti mihi videntur doctissimi ad id probandum Huetij rationes, ut nos in assensum trahant; Hieronymus, ait, non fuit Commentariorum istorum Interpres, esto, ergo Rufino adscribenda est hæc interpretatio, negatur consequentia; sed Gennadius, inquit, in Catalogo Virorum illustrium significare videtur, quæcunque Origenis opera Hieronymum interpretem non habent, ad Rufinum esse referenda; pace tua Vir clarissime non hoc significare videtur Gennadius, hoc tantum dicit Rufinum videlicet non omnia Origenis opuscula interpretatum esse, sed Hieronymum aliquanta etiam transtulisse, quae suis discerni amant Prologis: Origenis autem (inquit) non omnia: quia & Hieronymus transtulit aliquanta, quae suo Prologo discernuntur: Et ut Rufini translationes ab aliorum interpretationibus certissime & facilime discernere valeamus, asserit interpretationibus suis Prologos Rufinum praefigere solere, cum autem Prologus huic libro ab Interprete appositus non fuerit hinc consequitur interpretationem istam Rufino non esse adscribendam, ecce Gennadij verba de Rufini translationibus in genere agentis. Horum omnium quaecumque praemissis Prologis a Latinis leguntur, a Rufino interpretata sunt: quae autem sine Prologo; ab alio translata sunt, qui Prologum facere noluit. Multi inquit clarissimus Huetius e Rufini Prologis interciderunt, verum donec probaverit Prologum decem Tomis in Cantica praefixum intercidisse, non satisfaciet Viri doctissimi responsio: rationes ex stylo ductae, necnon ex quibusdam vocibus barbaris Rufino usitatissimis, nimium leves sunt,nec satis habent ponderis ut id evincant; de stylo enim recte judicari non potest,nisi post longam disquisitionē, & acuratam cum Rufini scriptis contentionem; voces autem illæ barbaræ ei usitatæ, alijs ejusdem ætatis scriptoribus æquè familiares esse poterant. 3. docet nos Eusebius & post eum Hieronymus Origenem decem libros ceu Tomos in Canticum Canticorum elaborasse, & hi Commentarij integrum Cantici Canticorum librum complectebantur, ut liquet ex Eusebij verbis Hist. lib. 6. c. 32. Cùm Athenis, inquit, moraretur, inchoavit expositionem in Canticum Canticorum, quam ad quintum usque librum ibidem agens produxit. Deinde Cæsaream reversus, opus illud decem omninò libris comprehensum ad exitum perduxit.
