Homiliæ autem seu potiùs Commentarij quos nunc habemus opus illud ab Hieronymo tantopere laudatum esse non possunt; illius præclari operis partem esse asserunt Viri illi eruditi quibuscum nobis res est, cætera perijsse affirmant, sed vereor ne ex præjudicata opinione id dicant, cùm nullam jacturæ istiùs certissimam habeant cognitionem; non me latet plura intercidisse Adamantij opera, è quorum numero fuit expositio in Canticum Canticorum decem libris comprehensa; imò inquiunt pars illius explanationis temporum injuriae subducta est, reliqua ab interitu vindicari nondum potuerunt; Ejus autem quae superest scriptorem esse Origenem deprehendi volunt ex stylo, ex allegoricis & tropologicis expositionibus, in quas ab historicis excurrit, & ex sententijs earum consimilibus & germanis, quae in duabus Homilijs ab Hieronymo conversis occurrunt. Alterius stylum imitari difficilimum esse non diffiteor, praesertim in longo ac prolixo opere, sed an sit minus difficile de stylo Auctoris Graeci, ex Latini interpretis versione pronuntiare, penes alios esto judicium, ego certe aeque difficilimum puto, & forte aliquanto plus; Expositiones vero allegoricas & tropologicas non unus sectatus est Origenes, & praeterea qui Origenis nomen in istis Commentarijs mentitus est, tropologicis usus est expositionibus, sive proprij ingenij viribus, sive ex germanis Adamantij operibus depromptis, ut audax occuleret facinus, & merces suas sub Origenis nomine carius venderet; in eundem finem sententias earum consimiles & germanas, quae in duabus Homilijs ab Hieronymo conversis occurrunt, sibi adoptavit, seu verius illinc descriptas huic inseruit operi, ut lectori fucum faceret, eadem permotus ratione segmentum ex secundo Tomo Commentariorum in Canticum Canticorum decerptum, quod Græcè etiamnum ad finem Philocaliæ extat, in secundâ hujus Operis Homiliâ assutum habemus; quamvis Græcis non plané respondeant Latina, quicquid dicat eruditus Pearsonius pag. iii. & hinc augetur fraudis suspicio: Ex verbis autem Cassiodori quæ ibidem adferr nihil certi colligi potest, obscura enim sunt ut fatetur Vir doctus, ac proinde ad ejus hypothesin stabiliendam nequaquam idonea. Denique tandē confitentur Viri docti qui hoc opus Origenis esse contendunt, variè ab interpretē interpolatum & immutatum fuisse, quomodo igitur ex eo certò intelligi potest, quid verè sit Origenicum; nam Origenica ab ijs quæ Interpretis sunt discernere ac separare non est facile.
units.tr: Pope Damasus transcribed the short preface prefixed to them, which reads: "There is also circulated under the name of Origen another pious, learned and eloquent work, or rather a fragment of a work, in which the first two chapters of the Song of Songs are explained most eloquently and learnedly. In some old manuscripts this was marked with the name of Jerome. Someone divided it into four Homilies, though they are not homilies but a continuous and unbroken explanation." We do not usually speak in this way of the true and genuine works of writers, but only of those that circulate under their names. Since there are more who reject this work than who approve it, and since these are not inferior in authority, if not superior, there can be no doubt that the opinion of those who reject it should be preferred, especially if the following observations are weighed. (1) In some old manuscripts these Commentaries were marked with the name of Jerome, because they were undoubtedly not regarded as a genuine and authentic offspring of Origen. (2) Jerome writes in the preface to his translation of the two Homilies on the Song that Origen, in the ten volumes he worked out on the Song of Songs, discussed magnificently and openly the Seventy translators, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion and the Fifth Edition. Since this does not appear in the Commentaries we are dealing with, it follows that the work is different from those ten volumes. The very distinguished Huetius thinks he has answered this objection sufficiently if he puts the whole blame on Rufinus the translator: "to whom," he says, "since it is customary for him to upend everything and rework it at will, so that he cut down Origen's volumes on the Epistle to the Romans to half their length, what faith can anyone expect from him?" I grant that Rufinus was accustomed to alter and interpolate most of the little works he translated. But it is not likely for that reason that Rufinus, so to speak, wished to add to Origen's distinctive character, namely by bringing in and setting out the various editions of the Greek translators, and to remove them from the genuine Origenian work, especially after Jerome's warning. Moreover, it is not clearly established that Rufinus was the translator of this work, and the reasons of the most learned Huetius for proving it do not seem so weighty as to draw us to agree. "Jerome," he says, "was not the translator of these Commentaries, granted; therefore this translation must be ascribed to Rufinus." The inference is denied. "But Gennadius," he says, "in his Catalogue of Illustrious Men, seems to indicate that whatever works of Origen Jerome does not have as translator must be referred to Rufinus." With all respect to you, most distinguished sir, Gennadius does not seem to indicate this. He says only that Rufinus did not translate all of Origen's little works, but that Jerome also translated some, which are distinguished by their own prefaces: "Not all of Origen's works," he says, "because Jerome also translated some, which are distinguished by his own preface." And so that we may very certainly and easily distinguish Rufinus's translations from those of others, he asserts that Rufinus was accustomed to place a preface before his translations. Since, however, this book has no preface by the translator, it follows that this translation is not to be ascribed to Rufinus. Here are Gennadius's words, speaking in general of Rufinus's translations: "Of all these works, whatever is read in Latin with a preface has been translated by Rufinus; but those without a preface were translated by another, who did not wish to write a preface." Many prefaces of Rufinus, says the most distinguished Huetius, have perished. But until he proves that the preface prefixed to the ten volumes on the Song has perished, the reply of this most learned man will not satisfy. The arguments drawn from style, and also from certain barbarous words very common in Rufinus, are far too slight and do not carry enough weight to prove the point. For style cannot be rightly judged without a long investigation and a careful comparison with Rufinus's writings; and those barbarous words, being common to him, could equally have been familiar to other writers of the same age. (3) Eusebius, and after him Jerome, teach us that Origen worked out ten books, or volumes, on the Song of Songs, and that these Commentaries embraced the whole book of the Song of Songs, as is clear from the words of Eusebius, Hist. book 6, ch. 32: "While he was staying at Athens," he says, "he began an exposition of the Song of Songs, which he carried on there as far as the fifth book. Then, returning to Caesarea, he brought that work, comprising ten books in all, to completion." But the Homilies, or rather Commentaries, which we now have cannot be that work so greatly praised by Jerome. The learned men with whom we are dealing assert that they are a part of that excellent work and that the rest has perished. But I fear they say this out of prejudice, since they have no very certain knowledge of that loss. I am not unaware that many of Adamantius's works have been lost, and the exposition of the Song of Songs comprised in ten books was among them. Indeed, they say, a part of that exposition has been snatched away by the injuries of time, and the rest could not yet be saved from destruction. They want to show that the surviving part is by Origen, from its style, from its allegorical and tropological expositions, into which it runs out from the historical sense, and from its similar and genuine opinions, which occur in the two Homilies translated by Jerome. I do not deny that it is not very difficult to imitate another's style, especially in a long and prolix work. But whether it is less difficult to pronounce on the style of a Greek author from the version of a Latin translator, let others judge; I myself think it equally difficult, and perhaps somewhat more so. Moreover, Origen was not the only one to pursue allegorical and tropological expositions. And whoever falsely used Origen's name in these Commentaries made use of tropological expositions, whether drawn from his own powers of mind or taken from Adamantius's genuine works, so that he might boldly hide his crime and sell his wares more dearly under Origen's name. To the same end, he adopted for himself opinions similar and genuine to those which occur in the two Homilies translated by Jerome, or rather copied them from there and inserted them into this work, so as to deceive the reader. Moved by the same reasoning, we have in the second Homily of this work a passage excerpted from the second volume of the Commentaries on the Song of Songs, which still exists in Greek at the end of the Philocalia. Yet the Latin does not wholly correspond to the Greek, whatever the learned Pearson says on page iii, and so the suspicion of fraud is increased. From the words of Cassiodorus, which he cites there, nothing certain can be gathered, for they are obscure, as the learned man himself admits, and therefore by no means suitable for establishing his hypothesis. Finally, the learned men who contend that this work is Origen's themselves confess that it was variously interpolated and altered by the translator. How, then, can it be known with certainty from it what is truly Origenian? For it is not easy to distinguish and separate what is Origen's from what belongs to the translator.

units.la: Secundum Origenis testimonium desumptum est ex Homiliâ sextâ in Lucam: Vindiciarum Autor statim observat Dallæum ad primum Origenis testimonium refellendum usum esse autoritate Erasmi; non solius Erasmi autoritate usus est doctissimus Dallæus, sed etiam aliorum: quamvis Erasmus instar multorum esset[?] posset, tantùm abest ut mirari debeat Lector effrænem illius in Veterum expendendis scriptis, & projectam temeritatem, ut ait Vir quidam clarissimus, qui forte sibi consuluisset, si cum Erasmo de litteris & litteratis omnibus optimè merito parciùs ac modestius egisset; pergit eruditus Pearsonius scribitque eundem Dallæum ad secundum Origenis testimonium elevandum suo Marte non minùs infœliciter progredi: non malè se habebunt res Dallæanæ, si secundum istud refellat argumentum æquè fœliciter ac primum; Vt hoc aggrediatur Dallæus observat primùm totum illud Homiliarum in Lucam opus Latinorum natalium indicijs scatere, quod probat variis in medium prolatis quæ ex istis Homiliis descripsit locis; quibus omnibus respondet Pearsonius hæc esse Interpretis additamenta, ut quoties opus erat, Versionis suæ rationem redderet; facilis responsio, si solida esset: nam quomodo quæso vera ac genuina à falsis & spuriis secernere poterimus, in scriptorum Græcorum operibus, quorum Versiones Latinas tantùm habemus; Nonne Adversarius ad distinctionem illam Viri docti confugiet, tanquam ad sacram Anchoram? quoties exceptionibus earum consimilibus urgebitur, quibus utitur celeberrimus Dallæus; hæc sunt inquiet Interpretis, non autem Auctoris : quid est nodos secare quos solvere non potes , si hoc non est ? Si tanto pollet acumine Vir doctus ut Interpretis verba à verbis scriptoris certò separare queat , gaudeant bene nati , nobis non licet esse tam beatis. Secundò Dallæus scribit ab ipso Origenis genio , more , ac sensu quædam esse in eodem opere aliena , quorum aliquot profert exempla , è quibus unicum expendemus ut planè innotescat Homilias in Lucam non esse germanum Origenis fœtum ; Homiliâ 39. Scriptor quisquis sit Efaiam & Psalmos litteraliter à Sadducæis intellectos esse ait. Nam cùm quædam ex utróque libro attulisset , quæ spiritaliter esse accipienda definit ; Quæ omnia ( inquit ) corporaliter intelligentibus Sadducæis , qui erant portio Iudæorum , dicit Salvator ; Nescitis Scripturas, neque virtutem Dei. Id verò à genuinis Origenis opusculis alienum esse patet , cùm à Sadducæis non alios quàm Mosis libros ex toto veteri instrumento admissos constanter scribat ; solos Mosis libros ( ait ) recipiunt Samaritæ & Sadducæi , lib. 1. contr. Cels. p. 38. ultimæ editionis ; & Tract. 22. in Matth. Sadducæi scripturas alias extra libros Mosaïcos non legebant, nec ipsos libros Mosaïcos legentes intelligebant ; Ita vetus Interpres Latinus ; Græca aliter se habent , Sadducaei aliam Scripturam à Legali non admittunt, & paucis interjectis, Sadducaei Scripturas quae Legem sequuntur non admittunt ; Hinc patet ut id obiter observem quanti sit laboris, & quantae industriae Interpretum additamenta & interpolationes ab ipsorum Scriptorum verbis separare. Vt ut est si vere Origenes esset qui in Lucam scripsit, de Sadducaeis non aliter loquutum par est credere ; sed si Vindiciarum Auctorem audimus, Scriptor Homiliae 39. in Lucam non affirmat Sadducaeos Prophetas in Canonem Scripturarum recepisse. Hoc tantum dicit, Sadducaeos male intellexisse Prophetas ; potuerunt autem (ait) & intelligere, & etiam male, ea quae pro sacris Scripturis non habuêre. Miserum profecto Viri docti effugium ; Homiliarum Auctor Sadducaeos reprehendit quòd litteraliter & corporaliter Esaiam & Psalmos intelligerent : cur quaeso reprehendebat si Prophetas pro sacris Scripturis non habuissent ? Vel saltem cur de eo lectores non monebat ? Est-ne verisimile hanc Iudaeorum portionem ab eo notatam ac perstrictam fuisse ? Nisi illi persuasum fuisset Sadducaeos , Prophetas in Canonem Scripturarum recepisse , nullaque alia idonea ratio excogitari potest istius in Sadducæos censuræ. Pergit eruditus Pearsonius & dicit Sadducæos non admittere quidem sacras Scripturas extra libros Mosaïcos, scilicet, inquit, in controversiis fidei determinandis: Mirum glossema, si ex præconceptâ opinione non proficisceretur, tuetur hoc suum glossema Vir doctus Rabbinorum & Talmudistarum Autoritate, quorum illi multas afferunt Sadducæorum in alias extra libros Mosaicos Scripturas interpretationes, isti verò disputationes sæpè referunt, in quibus Sadducæi & Samaritæ respondent ad loca ex Prophetis & Hagiographis adducta: Quasi vanissimorum illorum hominum somnia ἀντιλογίων[?] quæ est inter verum Origenem, & Homiliarum in Lucam Auctorem tollere possent, tantámque dirimere litem. Tertiò respondet Pearsonius Origenem hæc ad populum scripsisse, dum adhuc juvenis erat, & tunc fortasse, ait, non notaverat, aut certè non necesse habuit sententiam Sadducæorum peculiarem notare; At ego contra assero Origenem ea scribere debuisse quæ illum à contradictione possent præstare immunem, quod cùm non fecerit, concludendum est Homiliarum Auctorem à vero Origene esse diversum: Nec est quod Vir doctus Origenis juventutem memoret : Nam Deo dante ostendemus inferiùs nullas Origenis Homilias ante provectam illius ætatem conscriptas fuisse. Ridet eruditus Vindiciarum Auctor hanc ultimam Dallæi observationem, Origenis quæ Latinè tantùm extant à Ruffino & aliis interpretibus ita fuisse interpolata, ut ex iis vix possit certò intelligi, quid verè sit Origenicum : Pearsonius videlicet ferre non potest hæc dici de Hieronymi interpretatione, queritur tamen Ruffinus ejus Æmulus in Invectivâ suâ adversus Hieronymum lib. 2. p. 153. plura in his ipsis Homilijs ab Hieronymo fuisse subtracta, quædam mutata, quædam addita. Nec mirari debet Ignatianorum vindex Dallæum istarum Homiliarum auctoritatem in dubium vocasse & hoc opus Origeni abjudicasse : Erasmus scripserat ad Franciscum Cigalinum has Homilias alterius cujusdam esse videri quàm Origenis, nec postea ita sententiam mutavit, quin hîc multa vel suspecta vel damnata agnoscat, quod Huetio displicet, Merlinus verò Operum Origenis editor errores his Homilijs ab Origeniani nominis Æmulis aspersos asseverat, quanquam & id valdè incertum putet idem Huetius : Merlino Editori alium Editorem jungam, Genebrardum videlicet qui in Collect. de vitâ Origenis scribit Hieronymum has Homilias excusare tanquam ab Origene admodùm juvene enatas, quoniam parùm elaboratæ sunt, & nonnullis etiam damnatis erroribus inspersæ. Labbeus Iesuita Origenis opera recensens de Script. Eccl. hæc habet de Homiliis istis p.144. Tom.2. Homiliæ 39. in Evangelium S. Lucæ, cum Prologo S. Hieronymi interpretis, qui ab admodùm juvene scriptas asserit. NON DESUNT QVI AMBIGANT,
units.tr: The second testimony of Origen is taken from the sixth Homily on Luke. The author of the Vindiciae observes first that Daillé, in refuting the first testimony of Origen, relied on the authority of Erasmus. The learned Daillé did not rely on Erasmus's authority alone but on that of others too; and although Erasmus would have counted for many, the reader should not be surprised at the unbridled and reckless rashness with which he weighed the ancient writings, as a certain very distinguished man says. Perhaps this man would have done better for himself had he dealt more sparingly and modestly with Erasmus, who has deserved very well of letters and of all men of letters. Learned Pearson goes on, and writes that Daillé proceeds no less unhappily on his own to overturn the second testimony of Origen. The Daillé cause would fare well if he refuted this argument as successfully as the first. To take this up, Daillé observes first that the whole of this work on the Homilies on Luke abounds with signs of a Latin origin, and he proves this by the various passages from these Homilies that he has brought forward. To all of these Pearson replies that they are additions of the translator, made wherever he needed to explain his method of translating. It is an easy reply, if it were sound. For how, I ask, shall we be able to separate the true and genuine from the false and spurious in the works of Greek writers, of which we have only Latin versions? Will not the Opponent take refuge in that distinction of the learned man, as in a sacred anchor, whenever he is pressed by such objections as the famous Daillé uses? "These are the translator's words," he will say, "not the author's." What is this but cutting knots you cannot untie? If the learned man is so sharp that he can surely separate the translator's words from the writer's, let well-born men rejoice; we are not allowed to be so fortunate. Secondly, Daillé writes that some things in the same work are alien to Origen's own genius, manner and sense, and he gives several examples of these. We shall examine one of them, so that it may be clear that the Homilies on Luke are not a genuine offspring of Origen. In Homily 39, the writer, whoever he is, says that Isaiah and the Psalms were understood literally by the Sadducees. For when he had cited some passages from both books, which he states must be taken spiritually, he says: "The Saviour says all these things to those who understand them corporeally, the Sadducees, who were a part of the Jews: 'You know not the Scriptures, nor the power of God.'" That this is foreign to Origen's genuine little works is clear, since he consistently writes that the Sadducees admitted only the books of Moses from the whole of the Old Testament. "The Samaritans and Sadducees receive only the books of Moses," he says in Book 1 against Celsus, p. 38 of the latest edition; and in Tractate 22 on Matthew: "The Sadducees did not read Scriptures other than the Mosaic books, nor did they understand the Mosaic books even when they read them." So the old Latin translator; the Greek reads differently: "The Sadducees do not admit any Scripture other than the Law," and a few lines later, "The Sadducees do not admit the Scriptures which follow the Law." From this it is plain, as I may observe in passing, how great is the labour and industry required to separate the translators' additions and interpolations from the words of the writers themselves. However that may be, if Origen truly were the one who wrote on Luke, we ought to believe he spoke of the Sadducees in no other way. But if we listen to the author of the Vindiciae, the writer of Homily 39 on Luke does not affirm that the Sadducees received the Prophets into the canon of Scripture. He says only that the Sadducees misunderstood the Prophets; but they could (he says) both understand, and even misunderstand, things they did not hold to be sacred Scripture. A wretched refuge indeed for the learned man! The author of the Homilies rebukes the Sadducees because they understood Isaiah and the Psalms literally and corporeally. Why, I ask, did he rebuke them, if they did not hold the Prophets to be sacred Scripture? Or at least, why did he not warn his readers about this? Is it likely that this portion of the Jews was noted and censured by him unless he was persuaded that the Sadducees had received the Prophets into the canon of Scripture? No other suitable reason can be devised for this censure of the Sadducees. Learned Pearson goes on and says that the Sadducees did not indeed admit the sacred Scriptures beyond the books of Moses, "namely," he says, "in determining controversies of faith." It is a strange gloss, unless it proceeded from a preconceived opinion. The learned man defends this gloss of his by the authority of the rabbis and Talmudists, of whom the former report many interpretations of the Sadducees on Scriptures other than the books of Moses, and the latter often recount disputes in which the Sadducees and Samaritans reply to passages cited from the Prophets and Hagiographa. As if the dreams of those most vain men could remove the contradictions [ἀντιλογιῶν] between the true Origen and the author of the Homilies on Luke, and settle so great a dispute! Thirdly, Pearson replies that Origen wrote these things for the people while he was still a young man, and that then perhaps, he says, he had not noticed, or at least had no need to note the peculiar opinion of the Sadducees. But I maintain on the contrary that Origen ought to have written those things which could keep him free from contradiction, and since he did not do so, it must be concluded that the author of the Homilies is different from the true Origen. Nor is there any reason for the learned man to mention Origen's youth. For, God willing, we shall show below that no Homilies of Origen were written before his advanced age. The learned author of the Vindiciae mocks this last observation of Daillé, that the works of Origen which survive only in Latin, from Rufinus and other translators, were so interpolated that it can scarcely be known with certainty "what is truly Origenian." Pearson, of course, cannot bear for this to be said of Jerome's translation; yet Rufinus, his rival, complains in his invective against Jerome, book 2, p. 153, that many things were removed from these very Homilies by Jerome, some changed, and some added. Nor should the champion of the Ignatians wonder that Daillé called the authority of these Homilies into doubt and denied this work to Origen. Erasmus had written to Francis Cigalini that these Homilies seemed to be by someone other than Origen; and afterwards he did not change his opinion so far that he does not recognise here much that is either suspect or condemned. This displeases Huet. Merlin, the editor of Origen's works, asserts that errors which were cast upon these Homilies by rivals of Origen's name are present in them, although Huet himself thinks even this very uncertain. To Merlin the editor I will add another editor, namely Genebrard, who in his Collectanea on the life of Origen writes that Jerome excuses these Homilies as having been produced by Origen while still quite young, since they are little elaborated and sprinkled with some condemned errors. The Jesuit Labbe, in reviewing Origen's works in his book on ecclesiastical writers, has this about these Homilies, p. 144, vol. 2: "Homilies 39 on the Gospel of St Luke, with the Prologue of St Jerome the translator, who asserts that they were written by a very young man." THERE ARE NOT LACKING THOSE WHO DOUBT.

units.la: Firmiora tamen pro Origene Argumenta & pro Interprete Hieronymo adversus Latinum Authorem sibi suppetere asserit Vindiciarum Auctor, & ne vanum putes promissorem, en tibi quæ ei suppetunt argumenta; S. Hieronymus in Catalogo inter Opera à se edita, in Lucam Homilia triginta novem recitat; Homilias autem ipse nunquam scripsit. In Prologo ad Paulam & Eustochium ostendit se eas ex Origene transtulisse; Hunc Hieronymi Prologum totum in suam Invectivam transcripsit Ruffinus, satis severè exagitavit, & quid in hoc Opere infidè transtulerit ostendit aut innuit: Hæc sunt firmiora Viri docti argumenta, sed fortè minùs firma apparebunt, cùm ea singillatim expenderimus; age igitur incipiamus ab eo quod Hieronymus in Catalogo inter Opeta à se edita, in Lucam Homilias triginta novem recitat; In duabus Hieronymi editionibus quas consului, altera anni M. D. XXV. ab Erasmo procurata, altera vero à Mariano Victorio ann. M. DC. XXIV. Græcus numerus dissidet à Latino, in Latino quippè sunt triginta novem Homiliæ, in Græco viginti novem, Sophronius autem Græcus Catalogi Interpres, Hieronymi familiaris, ignorare non potuit Opera ab Hieronymo sive edita sive in Latinum conversa, tamen cùm in Græco Sophronij dissideat numerus à Latino, nec aliunde quàm ex Catalogo sciri possit Homiliarum numerus (omissus est siquidem in Prologo Homilijs prætexto) nihil certi de Homiliarum in Lucam numero affirmari potest; Iam verò si viginti novem tantum juxta Sophronij supputationem numerantur, fieri potest ut sexta ex quâ argumentantur Ignatianorum patroni in ijs non comprehendatur, hoc primum. Secundò Hieronymus ita loquitur in Catalogo ut vix capias num ipse Homilias ediderit aut scripserit, vel transstulerit modò; Homilias, inquit Pearsonius, ipse nunquam scripsit, unde hæc habes, probatione egent quæ dicis; In Prologo ad Paulam & Eustochium ostendit se eas ex Origene transtulisse. Hinc non consequitur nullas scripsisse Homilias Hieronvmum, hoc solum colligitur Hieronymum quasdã Origenis in Lucam Homilias à s[?] in Latinum conversas asserere, quod nor[?] diffiteor, neque quæ de Ruffino observat Vir doctus ut Prologum & Homiliarum translatione Hieronymo adscribat. Vnum illum rogo; nùm videlicet Hieronymus tractatus illos septem in Psalmos quorum meminit in eodem Catalogo post Homilias in Lucam, nùm, inquam, tractatus illos transtulerit modò, aut scripserit; Ex hypothesi Viri docti scribere non potuit, quia Homilias nunquam scripsit, Tractatus autem Latinis, ut optimè novit, idem sunt quod Græcis Homiliæ, ideóque Sophronius vertit Homilias septem; Ergo Tractatus septem in Psalmos à decimo usque ad decimum sextum transtulisse Hieronymum dicendum est; quæ cùm ita sint frustrà scribit eruditus Pearsonius pag. 118. ad majorem argumenti sui confirmationem addi posse ex Ruffini Præfatione ad libros de Principijs, Hieronvmum ultrà 70. libellos Origenis quos Homileticos appellavit transtulisse in Latinum, quod de 70. fatetur Hieronymus Apologiâ primâ p. 492. G. cum 491. F; Vtrúmque verùm esse agnosco, sed Vindiciarum Auctori nocere magis quàm favere pertendo ; quod sic probo, Hieronymus fatetur se septuaginta libellos Origenis Homileticos in Latinum vertisse, Ruffinus ultrà 70. illum progressum esse scribit; Atqui juxta Viri docti supputationem ultrà libellos 70. ab Hieronymo versos invenies, si triginta novem Homilias in Lucam annumeres, sepositis septem in Psalmos Tractatibus seu Homilijs [?] quarum meminit in Catalogo ; Ergo si triginta novem sunt in Lucam Homiliæ ut con[?]tendit eruditus Pearsonius, non ultrà libellos 70. Origenis Homileticos transtulerit tantùm Hieronymus, sed ultrà 80. quod Ruffini & ipsius Hieronymi verbis contrarium est; Hieronymus enim septuaginta à se conversos fatetur, Ruffinus ultrà septuaginta illum transtulisse affirmat; ut hunc reperiat numerum Vir doctus, 14. Homilias in Ieremiam numerat, totidem in Ezechielem,novem in Esaïam, duas in Canticum Canticorum, triginta novem in Lucam, quas omnes si putas & in unum colligis, habebis numerum 78. & si addis septem in Psalmos Homilias, consurget numerus 85. qui cum numero Ruffiniano consistere nequit: Tamen quoniam ambigi non potest quin Ruffino notiores fuerint Hieronymi translationes quàm nobis , ita numerandi sunt libelli Origenis Homileticì quos vertit Hieronymus, ut numero à Ruffino designato plane respondeant, responderi autem non possunt, nisi Catalogum Latinum Hieronymi, ex Græcis Sophronij corrigas, numerando scilicet viginti novem Homilias in Lucam, non triginta novem, sic enim erunt 75. libelli Homiletici ab Hieronymo conversi, ut desiderant Ruffini verba; rejiciet forsan hanc correctionem Vir doctus quia illius causæ non patrocinatur; Interea dum meliorem adferat, huic hære-bimus, & argumentum pro Ignatianis ex sextâ Homiliâ depromptum à nobis magis ac magis incertum habebitur. Aliquid amplius addam, nempè Eusebij auctoritate me admodùm moveri ut credam Hieronymum deceptum fuisse, & pro genuino Origenis fœtu Homilias in Lucam habuisse; cùm à vero non abhorreat Homilias illas juvenis cujusdam suisse tyrocinium: Et sanè Hieronymus in Præfatione Homilijs præfixa docet Origenem in his tractatibus quasi talis ludere, cùm alia sint virilia ejus, & senectutis feriâ, quæ Hieronymi verba ita explicant Genebrardus, Labbeus, Pearsonius ipse, & alij, ut Origenem hoc opus admodùm juvenem elaborasse affirmare non dubitent, quod verò Origeni competere non potest ; Vindiciarum tamen Auctor Dallæum reprehendit, quod Homilias istas annis circiter centum & quadraginta post ultimum Ignatij certamen scriptas esse conjiciebat, contendítque Homilias illas scripsisse Origenem juvenem adhuc , & ante ætatem virilem , seséque tuetur Hieronymi verbis nunc allatis , ex quibus concludit sub initio Caracallæ Origenem adhuc puerum seu adolescentem,scripsisse Homilias in S. Lucam ; sed profecto fallitur Vir doctus ; initio Imperij Antonini Caracallæ qui regnare coepit anno Domini 212. post Ignatij Martyrium 105. Origenes annum ætatis circiter vigesimum sextum attigerat,Alexandriam non penitus dereliquit ante decimum Alexandri severi annum ; hoc est ante annum Christi 234. ætatis suæ 46. vel 47. nullas autem Homilias adhuc scripsisse constat ex lib. 6. Hist. Eusebij cap. 24. ibi enim enumerat opera omnia quæ Alexandriæ elaboraverat, nullâ prorsùs istarum Homiliarum mentione factâ ; Et cap. 32. ejusdem libri idem Eusebius memorat Origenis lucubrationes Cæsareæ in Palæstinâ scriptas, & quas Athenis composuerat ; Homiliarum autem non meminit: Hæc omnia si conferas cum capitibus 3. 15.16.23. in eâ magis confirmaberis opinione, ante ætatem virilem Homilias non scripsisse Origenem, & si hæret adhuc tibi aliquis hac de re scrupulus, animo facilè eximetur, postquam audieris sexagenario majorem esse Origenem, dum suas Homilias scribi passus est, quod à Viris doctis animadversum quidem non autem accuratè perpensum, nec exactè ponderatum, mirari satis nequeo, cùm tamen id diserte testetur Eusebius ; cui uni in rebus Origenis plus credendum existimo, quàm pluribus Hieronymis vel Ruffinis. Et eò magis quod rem ita narrat, ut Ignatianorum fautoribus non parùm noceat, Cùm fides nostra, inquit, ut par erat, augeretur in dies, & doctrina Christianorum summâ ubique libertate frueretur, Origenes jam sexagenario major : ut potè qui ex diuturnâ exercitatione maximum dicendi usum sibi comparasset, CONCIONES QVAS HABEBAT AD POPVLVM, à Notariis excipi permisit, cùm id antea fieri nunquam concessisset. Τὰς [?]ἐπὶ τῇ κοινῇ λεγομένας αὐτῷ [?]Διαλέξεις, ita Latinè reddidit. Vir Clarissimus Henricus Valesius linguæ Græcæ callentissimus, conciones quas habebat ad populum, conciones id est Homilias : Hesychius, Διάλεξις ὁμιλία [?]. Ad hæc tempora respiciebat Pamphilus martyr in lib. 1. Apologiæ pro Origene, his verbis. Quodque puræ religionis observaverit disciplinam, & prae caeteris ver-bo Dei, & doctrinae operam dederit, dubium non est ex his quae ad nos laboris & studii ejus certissima designantur indicia: praecipue vero per eos tractatus quos paene quotidie in Ecclesia habebat ex tempore: quos & describentes notarii ad monimentum posteritatis tradebant. Pro Homiliis tractatus dicit Ruffinus interpres, quod idem est: Nam Latini vocare solent tractatus, quas Graeci dicunt Homilias; nec mirum si Origenes jam ætate provectus populum paene quotidie ex suggestu alloquebatur, cùm ex diuturnā exercitatione, ut nos docuit Eusebius, maximum dicendi usum sibi comparasset.
units.tr: The author of the Vindiciae claims that he has stronger arguments for Origen, and for Jerome as translator, against the Latin author. Lest you think him an empty promiser, here are the arguments available to him. St Jerome, in his Catalogue, lists among the works he published thirty-nine homilies on Luke, yet Jerome himself never wrote homilies. In the Prologue to Paula and Eustochium he shows that he translated them from Origen. Rufinus copied this whole Prologue of Jerome into his own Invective, censured it quite severely, and shows or hints that Jerome translated unfaithfully in this work. These are the firmer arguments of the learned man, but they will perhaps appear less firm when we weigh them one by one. Come, then, let us begin with what Jerome, in the Catalogue, lists among the works he published: thirty-nine homilies on Luke. In the two editions of Jerome that I consulted, one published by Erasmus in 1525 and the other by Marianus Victorius in 1624, the Greek number differs from the Latin. The Latin has thirty-nine homilies, the Greek twenty-nine. Sophronius, the Greek translator of the Catalogue and a familiar of Jerome, could not have been ignorant of the works Jerome either published or translated into Latin. Yet since the number in Sophronius' Greek differs from the Latin, and the number of homilies can be known from nowhere but the Catalogue (for the Prologue, which is prefixed to the homilies, omits it), nothing certain can be affirmed about the number of homilies on Luke. Now, if only twenty-nine are counted according to Sophronius' reckoning, it may happen that the sixth homily, on which the defenders of the Ignatians argue, is not included among them. That is the first point. Second, Jerome speaks in the Catalogue in such a way that you can hardly tell whether he himself published or wrote the homilies, or merely translated them. Homilias, says Pearson, he never wrote himself. From this you draw conclusions that need proof: In the Prologue to Paula and Eustochium he shows that he translated them from Origen. It does not follow from this that Jerome wrote no homilies at all; it is only gathered that Jerome asserts that he translated into Latin some homilies of Origen on Luke, which I do not deny, nor do I deny what the learned man observes about Rufinus, namely that he attributes the Prologue and the translation of the homilies to Jerome. I ask him one thing: did Jerome translate or write those seven treatises on the Psalms which he mentions in the same Catalogue after the homilies on Luke? On the author's own hypothesis, Jerome could not have written them, because he never wrote homilies; and treatises, as he knows very well, are for the Latins what homilies are for the Greeks, which is why Sophronius rendered them seven homilies. Therefore it must be said that Jerome translated seven treatises on the Psalms, from the tenth to the sixteenth. Since this is so, the learned Pearson writes in vain, on page 118, to strengthen his argument further, that it can be added from Rufinus' Preface to the books On First Principles that Jerome translated into Latin more than seventy little books of Origen which he called Homiletic. Jerome himself admits to seventy in his First Apology, page 492 G, with 491 F. I acknowledge that both are true, but I contend that this harms the author of the Vindiciae more than it helps him. I prove it thus. Jerome admits that he translated seventy Homiletic books of Origen into Latin; Rufinus writes that he went beyond seventy. But by the learned man's own reckoning, you will find more than seventy books translated by Jerome if you count the thirty-nine homilies on Luke, leaving aside the seven treatises or homilies on the Psalms which he mentions in the Catalogue. So if there are thirty-nine homilies on Luke, as the learned Pearson contends, Jerome translated not merely more than seventy Homiletic books of Origen but more than eighty, which is contrary to the words of Rufinus and of Jerome himself. For Jerome admits to seventy translated by himself, and Rufinus affirms that he translated more than seventy. To reach this number, the learned man counts fourteen homilies on Jeremiah, as many on Ezekiel, nine on Isaiah, two on the Song of Songs, and thirty-nine on Luke. If you add all of these together, you will have seventy-eight; and if you add the seven homilies on the Psalms, the sum will rise to eighty-five, which cannot agree with Rufinus' number. Yet since there can be no doubt that Rufinus knew Jerome's translations better than we do, the Homiletic books that Jerome translated must be counted so as to correspond exactly to the number designated by Rufinus. This can be done only if you correct the Latin Catalogue of Jerome by the Greek of Sophronius, namely by counting twenty-nine homilies on Luke, not thirty-nine. For then there will be seventy-five Homiletic books translated by Jerome, as the words of Rufinus require. Perhaps the learned man will reject this correction, because it does not support his cause. Meanwhile, until he offers a better one, we shall cling to this, and the argument for the Ignatians drawn from the sixth homily will be held to be more and more uncertain. I will add something more. I am greatly moved by the authority of Eusebius to believe that Jerome was deceived and had the homilies on Luke as a genuine offspring of Origen, whereas it is not far from the truth that those homilies were the apprenticeship of some young man. Indeed, Jerome in his Preface prefixed to the homilies teaches that Origen, in these treatises, played as it were like one of that kind, since his other works are manly, and belong to the leisure of old age. Genebrard, Labbe, Pearson himself and others explain these words of Jerome in such a way that they do not hesitate to affirm that Origen worked on this work while very young, which cannot indeed fit Origen. Yet the author of the Vindiciae reprehends Dallaeus, because he conjectured that these homilies were written about one hundred and forty years after the last struggle of Ignatius, and he contends that Origen wrote those homilies while still young and before manhood, and he defends himself by the words of Jerome just cited, from which he concludes that at the beginning of Caracalla's reign, Origen, still a boy or young man, wrote homilies on St Luke. But the learned man is certainly mistaken. At the beginning of the reign of Antoninus Caracalla, who began to reign in the year of the Lord 212, one hundred and five years after the martyrdom of Ignatius, Origen had reached about the twenty-sixth year of his age. He did not wholly leave Alexandria before the tenth year of Alexander Severus, that is, before the year of Christ 234, in his forty-sixth or forty-seventh year of life. It is certain that he had not yet written any homilies, from book 6 of Eusebius' History, chapter 24, for there Eusebius lists all the works that Origen had composed at Alexandria, with no mention at all of these homilies. And in chapter 32 of the same book, the same Eusebius records Origen's writings composed at Caesarea in Palestine, and those he had composed at Athens; but he makes no mention of homilies. If you compare all these with chapters 3, 15, 16 and 23, you will be confirmed further in the opinion that Origen did not write homilies before manhood. And if some scruple still clings to you about this matter, it will be easily removed in your mind once you have heard that Origen was older than sixty when he allowed his homilies to be written down. This has indeed been noticed by learned men, but not carefully weighed or exactly considered, and I cannot sufficiently wonder at it, since Eusebius clearly testifies to it. I think that Eusebius alone is to be believed about Origen's affairs more than many Jeromes or Rufinuses. And the more so because he tells the matter in such a way that it does no little harm to the partisans of the Ignatians: When our faith, he says, as was fitting, was growing daily, and the teaching of the Christians enjoyed the greatest freedom everywhere, Origen, being already older than sixty, since he had acquired for himself the greatest skill in speaking through long practice, was permitted to have his public addresses taken down by shorthand writers, which had never been allowed before. The Greek phrase tas epi tē koinē legomenas autō dialexeis [τὰς ἐπὶ τῇ κοινῇ λεγομένας αὐτῷ διαλέξεις], which Henri de Valois, a most distinguished man and most skilled in Greek, rendered into Latin as conciones quas habebat ad populum, that is, sermons, or homilies. Hesychius glosses dialexis as homilia [Διάλεξις ὁμιλία]. Pamphilus the martyr, in the first book of his Apology for Origen, looked back to this period in these words: "That he observed the discipline of pure religion, and above all devoted himself to the Word of God and to learning, is not in doubt, from the most certain signs of his labour and zeal which are indicated to us; above all through those treatises which he gave almost daily in the Church extempore, and which the notaries who wrote them down handed down as a memorial to posterity." Rufinus the translator renders the word tractatus for homilies, which is the same thing: for Latins are accustomed to call treatises what Greeks call homilies. Nor is it surprising that Origen, now advanced in years, addressed the people almost daily from the pulpit, since through long practice, as Eusebius taught us, he had acquired for himself the greatest skill in speaking.

units.la: Ex his omnibus consequitur Dallæum immeritò à Viro docto fuisse notatum, cùm nullas scripserit Origenes Homilias ante sexagesimum primum ætatis suæ annum, nempe 140.annos post Ignatij Martyrium ut conjecerat celeberrimus Dallæus.
units.tr: It follows from all this that Dallaeus was rightly criticised by that learned man, since Origen wrote no homilies before his sixtieth-first year, that is, 140 years after the martyrdom of Ignatius, as the very famous Dallaeus had conjectured.

units.la: Consequitur secundò Hieronymo imposuisse Homiliarum in Lucam codicem Origenis nomine prænotatum, & certè verisimile est falso codicis titulo delusum fuisse Hietonymum, tamen quoniam in illis Homiliis eximias illas ingenij Origeniani dotes non animadvertebat, quæ in germanis Origenis scriptis micare solent, ab eo admodùm juvene scriptas falsò putavit; Nam sexagenario major erat Origenes cùm Homilias suas seu conciones quas habebat ad populum à Notarijs excipi permisit, quod antea fieri nunquàm concesserat. Errantem Hieronymum secutus est Ruffinus; eò magis quòd illum sugillandi occasionem tantùm quaerebat; cùm autem eam in Homiliarum istarum Latinâ Translatione nactus esset, soli codicis titulo adhaesit, nec ampliùs scire laboravit num verè Origenis essent, quod ex illarum comparatione cum genuinis illius Operibus dignoscì poterat, & praeterea ex verbis Eusebij suprà allatis. Unum addam notatu ut mihi quidem videtur dignissimum, Eusebium videlicet non omissurum fuisse Origenis pro Ignatianis testimonium, si eorum alicubi mentionem fecisset; si enim laciniae Polycarpi Epistolae alienâ manu assutae non oblitus est, nec Ignatij sententiae ab Irenaeo memoratae; cur quaeso praetermisisset duo Origenis loca à Vindiciarum Auctore in gratiam Epistolarum Ignatianarum adducta? Origenem magni faciebat Eusebius, ejúsque nomini ita addictus & nuncupatus erat, ut Gelasij Synodique Romanae censurâ ea propter perstringi meruerit: Estne igitur credibile tantum Origenis admiratorem summúmque laudatorem, illius obliturum esse testimonia, si aliquot in germanis Adamantij scriptis Ignatij Epistolis patrocinantia extitissent ? Nequaquam; imò potiùs ea accuratè descripsisset vel saltem indicasset, ut Ignatianis suis Epistolis omnimodam conciliaret autoritatem; Nihil tale fecit, quod mihi valido est argumento nulla suâ ætate[?] extitisse in genuinis Origenis lucubrationibus quæ Eusebio notissimæ erant. Vana fuit ergo eruditi Pearsonij spes,dum sperávit forè ut Lectori persuaderet[?] Ignatium ab Origene citatum fuisse, & Origenem has illius Epistolas agnovisse: nec minus vana sunt quæ toties tam confidenter de totius secum ab omni ævo antiquitatis in suspiciendis ac reverendis Ignatianis suis consensu passim jactat atque gloriatur: Ex primâ siquidem, & Ignatij proximâ, adeóque solâ de eo testari idoneâ antiquitate, quæ à Martyris certamine per ducentos annos ad quarti sæculi annum circiter tricesimum decurrit,ne unum quidem certum ac indubitatum, & omni exceptione majorem habet testem, qui has Epistolas sibi notas fuisse, vel se de illis, fando aliquid audivisse perhibeat: Ex omni enim antiquitate primus occurrit Eusebius quarti sæculi scriptor, qui in Historia suâ Ecclesiasticâ, quàm postremis vitæ temporibus scripsit, luculentum de Ignatianis Epistolis perhibet testimonium; cùm ante illum nemo aliqua Ignatiana, certò ac indubitatò norit, sed in scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum Eusebio vetustiorum opusculis germanis ac genuinis de illis altissimum sit silentium: Leo Allatius Gente Græcus, sed mente & religione Latinus Ignatianas Epistolas supposititias suspicabatur, antequam eas vidisset quas ex antiquissimo Bibliothecæ Florentinæ Codice descripsit clarissimus Vossius, ut ingenuè fatear, inquit, Auctor Epistolarum quæ sub Ignatij nomine sæpius typis editæ vulgò prostant, semper aliàs dubius, nunc demum suspicionem adauget. Est enim, pro ea ætate; prolixior & rebus enodandis exactior verbosiorque, quamvis simplex, pius, & ut illa ferebant tempora, æquè ac alij Apostoli, Christum spiret. At ubi eruditissimus Vossius Florentinarum Epistolarum Allatio copiam fecit, sententiam aliquo modo mutavit, sed ita tamen ut sibi hærere adhuc aliquem scrupulum innuat; Vidi (inquit) apud Isaacum Vossium juvenem eruditum, & rerum antiquarum studiosissimum, cùm Romæ commoraretur, Ignatij Epistolas ex antiquissimo Bibliothecæ Florentinæ Codice descriptas, quas etiam mihi humanissimè communicavit, verbis ab editis longè diversas, sententiis ut plurimum similes, breviores tamen, succinctiores, efficaciores : ut plane Ignatii ævum referant; adeò ut eas genuinas esse Ignatii diceres : quæ præ omnium manibus sunt, earum paraphrasin. Quis unquam sic loquutus est de veris ac indubitatis Ecclesiasticæ antiquitatis scriptis ? Si Allatio erat omninò persuasum, has Epistolas germanum esse Ignatii fœtum, cur id rotundè non pronuntiat ? cur ambiguè loquitur ? certè animi pendere illum, & in dubio esse ejus animum non diffitebitur, qui hæc illius verba attentè perpenderit: eas genuinas esse Ignatii diceres. Ut ut est cùm eruditus Vindiciarum Auctor nullum ante Eusebium qui de his Epistolis testatus sit, certum ac indubitatum adducat testem, nemo non videt Virum doctum suâ falsum esse opinione, dum scripsit cap. 2. pag. 3. nullum sæculum pro S. Ignatii Epistolis suis testimonijs carere, à secundo quo primum natæ, ad Decimum quintum, quo primum impressæ sunt: Vanâ spe se lactavit Pearsonius nec votis suis responderunt industriæ suæ conatus,attulit quidem è tribus primis Centurijs testes, sed non exceptione majores ; Eorum enim testimonia vel ex ijs deprompta sunt opusculis, quæ dubia sunt, incerta & nullius plane fidei, ut Polycarpi & Origenis testimonia, vel ad Ignatianas Epistolas minimè spectant velut testimonium Irenæi; Deficientibus ergo Viro docto argumentis pro S. Ignatio è Veterum testimonijs petitis, ad interna ex ipsis Epistolis desumpta confugiat necesse est; præcipua ex internis perinde ac ex externis seligemus & expendemus; sed antequam ad illud examen accedamus, quædam animadversione digna mihi videntur in argumenti negativi refutatione quam per totum decimum caput primæ partis, quod est prolixissimum fusè exsequitur; non argumentia negantis vim usquequaque rejiciendo, sed illud in Ignatianis locum habere non posse pertendendo.
units.tr: Second, it follows that Jerome was deceived by a Latin codex of homilies on Luke, marked with Origen's name. It is quite likely that Jerome was misled by the false title of the codex. Yet because he did not notice in those homilies the outstanding gifts of Origen's genius that usually shine in Origen's genuine writings, he wrongly thought they had been written by Origen while still very young. In fact Origen was over sixty when he allowed the homilies, or sermons, which he delivered to the people, to be taken down by shorthand writers, something he had never before permitted. Ruffinus followed Jerome in his error, all the more because he was looking only for an opportunity to attack Origen. When he found one in the Latin translation of these homilies, he clung to the title of the codex alone and did not trouble himself further about whether they were truly Origen's. This could have been judged by comparing them with Origen's genuine works, and also from the words of Eusebius quoted above. I will add one point which seems to me very worthy of notice: Eusebius would surely not have omitted an Origenian testimony for the Ignatian letters, had Origen made any mention of them anywhere. For Eusebius did not forget the fragments of Polycarp's Epistle that had been stitched in by another hand, nor the sayings of Ignatius recorded by Irenaeus. Why, I ask, would he have passed over the two passages of Origen that the author of the Vindiciae cites in favour of the Ignatian letters? Eusebius held Origen in high esteem, and was so devoted to and known for his name that for this reason he earned censure from the Gelasian decree and the Roman Synod. Is it then credible that so great an admirer and praiser of Origen would have forgotten the testimonies of Origen, if some passages in the genuine writings of Adamantius had supported the letters of Ignatius? By no means. Rather, he would have copied them out accurately, or at least pointed them out, in order to win full authority for his Ignatian letters. He did nothing of the kind, which is strong evidence to me that no such passages existed in the genuine works of Origen, which were very well known to Eusebius, in his own time. So the learned Pearson's hope was vain, when he hoped perhaps to persuade the reader that Ignatius had been cited by Origen, and that Origen had acknowledged these letters of his. Equally vain are the things he so confidently and so often boasts of, namely the agreement of all antiquity from every age in esteeming and revering his Ignatian letters. For from the first antiquity, and that nearest to Ignatius, the only antiquity able to bear witness to him, which runs from the martyr's contest for about two hundred years down to about the thirtieth year of the fourth century, he does not have even one certain and undoubted witness, beyond all exception, who says that these letters were known to him, or that he had heard something of them by report. Indeed, of all antiquity the first to appear is Eusebius, a writer of the fourth century, who in his Ecclesiastical History, which he wrote in the last years of his life, gives a clear testimony concerning the Ignatian letters. Before him no one knew any Ignatian writing for certain and without doubt, and in the genuine and authentic little works of the ecclesiastical writers older than Eusebius there is the deepest silence about them. Leo Allatius, a Greek by birth but a Latin in mind and religion, suspected the Ignatian letters to be spurious even before he had seen those which the most distinguished Vossius copied from a very ancient codex of the Florentine Library. "To be frank," he says, "the author of the letters that are commonly published and circulated under the name of Ignatius, always doubtful in other respects, now increases my suspicion. For, for his age, he is more prolix, more precise in explaining things, and more wordy, though simple, pious, and, as those times allowed, breathing Christ just as the other Apostles did." But when the most learned Vossius gave Allatius a copy of the Florentine letters, he changed his opinion to some extent, yet in such a way as to hint that some doubt still clung to him. "I saw" (he says) "at Rome, in the hands of Isaac Vossius, a learned young man with great interest in antiquities, the letters of Ignatius copied from the very ancient codex of the Florentine Library, which he also most kindly communicated to me. They are far different in words from the printed editions, mostly similar in sense, but shorter, more concise and more effective, so that they plainly reflect the age of Ignatius; so much so that you would say they are the genuine letters of Ignatius: what is in everyone's hands is a paraphrase of them." Who has ever spoken like this about the true and undoubted writings of ecclesiastical antiquity? If Allatius had been fully persuaded that these letters were the genuine offspring of Ignatius, why does he not state it plainly? Why does he speak ambiguously? Surely whoever weighs his words carefully will not deny that his mind was hanging in the balance and that he was in doubt: you would say they are the genuine letters of Ignatius. However that may be, since the learned author of the Vindiciae cannot produce a certain and undoubted witness before Eusebius who bore witness to these letters, everyone can see that the learned man is mistaken in his opinion, when he wrote in chapter 2, page 3, that no century lacks testimonies for the letters of S. Ignatius, from the second, in which they were first written, to the fifteenth, in which they were first printed. Pearson flattered himself with an empty hope, and his efforts did not answer his wishes. He did indeed bring forward witnesses from the first three centuries, but they are not beyond exception. For their testimonies are taken either from those little works which are doubtful, uncertain and of no real credit, such as the testimonies of Polycarp and Origen, or they do not concern the Ignatian letters at all, like the testimony of Irenaeus. Since therefore the learned man lacks arguments for S. Ignatius drawn from the testimonies of the ancients, he must take refuge in internal arguments drawn from the letters themselves. We shall select and weigh the chief internal arguments as well as the external ones. But before we come to that examination, some points seem to me worthy of comment in the refutation of the negative argument, which he pursues at length through the whole tenth chapter of the first part. He does not reject the force of an argument from silence in every case, but contends that it cannot hold good in the case of the Ignatian letters.

units.la: XX. Dallæus adversus Ignatiana ex Veterum silentio Argumentatus erat cap.5. 6. 7. 8. 9. Eruditus Pearsonius de vi argumenti à testimonio Negativi, sive à silentio Scriptorum petiti non disputat, ingenuè fatetur aliquod hujusmodi aliquando etiam de suppositione alicujus scripti valere, ultrà progreditur, & libenter non tantùm concedit, sed & contendit tali Argumento nixum nonnunquam Eusebium ipsum, aliquorum librorum Autoritatem respuisse; Verùm affirmare non dubitat causam quam tuetur ejusmodi esse, ut in ea rite adhiberi minime possit, quia nimirum datur argumentum a testimonio affirmativum, quod negativo plane contrarium asserit & evincit. Si res ita se haberet, ut ait Vir doctus, ei libenter concederem Argumentum affirmativum, negativo esse praeferendum; sed cum nullum ex tribus primis saeculis verum ac firmum adduxerit testimonium, ut liquido constat ex iis quae huc usque scripsimus, optime procedit Clarissimi Dallaei a veterum Scriptorum qui per illa tempora floruerunt silentio, petita Argumentatio: Duo tantum Dallaei Argumenta a silentio ducta in medium proferam, & a Viri docti exceptionibus vindicabo; primum quod examinandum suscipio, petitum est a silentio vetustissimi cujusdam Scriptoris cujus meminit Eusebius, & quem Caium Victoris Episcopi Romani aequalem, vel certe supparem, Eruditi ex Photio suspicantur. Is enim adversus Artemonis Christum merum nudumque hominem delirantis haeresim disputans, ejusque novitatem demonstrare studens, haereticis illis qui suam impiam de Christo sententiam vetustissimam esse gloriabantur, eamque Zephirini Victoris successoris tempore inverti apud nostros, & mutari coepisse dicebant, is inquam antiquus Auctor Artemonicæ hæreseos sectatoribus hoc pacto occurrit, fortasse id quod dicunt, credibile videretur, nisi eis refragarentur primùm quidem divinæ scripturæ, deinde fratrum quorundam scripta, Victoris ætate antiquiora, quæ illi adversus Gentes, & contra sui temporis hæreticos pro veritatis defensione scripserunt Iustinum intelligo & Miltiadem, & Tatianum, & Clementem, aliósque quam[?] plurimos: in quorum omnium libris Christi[?] divinitas adstruitur. Nam Irenæi quidem & Melitonis & reliquorum scripta quis est qui ignoret, in quibus Christum Deum simul atque hominem prædicarunt? Psalmi quoque & cantica fratrum jam pridem à fidelibus conscripta, Christum Verbum Dei concelebrant, divinitatem ei tribuendo. Hinc colligebat Dallæus incognitas fuisse veteri illi Scriptori Ignatij Epistolas in quibus extant diserta pro divinitate Domini nostri Iesu Christi testimonia; verbi gratiâ in Vsserianis ac Vossianis ad Ephesios & ad Magnesianos Epistolis hæc leguntur, Christum Deum in carne factum esse, Deum humanitus manifestatum, eúmque ante secula apud Patrem fuisse, & in fine apparuisse, eundem esse Dei Verbum æternum. Profectò non est verisimile Caium Ignatium prætermissurum fuisse, si suâ ætate extitissent quæ Ignatij nomine circumferuntur[?].
units.tr: XX. Dallaeus argued against the Ignatian letters from the silence of the ancients in chapters 5 to 9. Pearson does not dispute the force of an argument drawn from the silence of writers, or from the lack of testimony. He frankly admits that an argument of this kind sometimes holds good even when a writing is supposed, and he goes further: he readily concedes, and even maintains, that Eusebius himself sometimes rejected the authority of certain books on the strength of such an argument. But he does not hesitate to affirm that the cause he defends is of such a kind that this argument cannot properly be applied to it, because, of course, there is an affirmative argument from testimony which plainly asserts and proves the opposite of the negative one. If the matter stood as the learned man says, I would gladly grant that the affirmative argument should be preferred to the negative. But since he has produced no true and firm testimony from the first three centuries, as is clear from what we have written so far, the argument of the most distinguished Dallaeus, drawn from the silence of the ancient writers who flourished in those times, proceeds quite correctly. I will bring forward only two arguments from silence drawn by Dallaeus, and I will defend them against the learned man's objections. The first, which I take up for examination, is drawn from the silence of a very ancient writer, whom Eusebius mentions, and whom the learned men, following Photius, suspect to have been a contemporary, or at least an equal, of Caius, the Roman bishop Victor. This writer, disputing against the heresy of Artemon, who raved that Christ was a mere and bare man, and striving to show its novelty, met those heretics who boasted that their impious opinion about Christ was very ancient, and who said that it had been overturned and begun to be changed among our people in the time of Zephyrinus, successor of Victor. This ancient author met the followers of the Artemonite heresy in the following way: "What they say might perhaps seem credible, were it not that the divine Scriptures first contradict them, and then the writings of certain brethren, older than the time of Victor, which they wrote in defence of the truth against the Gentiles and against the heretics of their own time. I mean Justin, Miltiades, Tatian, Clement, and very many others, in whose books the divinity of Christ is affirmed. For who does not know the writings of Irenaeus and Meliton and the rest, in which they proclaimed Christ to be God as well as man? The psalms and hymns too, written long ago by the faithful brethren, celebrate Christ as the Word of God, ascribing divinity to him." From this Dallaeus concluded that the ancient writer did not know the Ignatian letters, in which there are clear testimonies to the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ. For example, in the Ussherian and Vossian letters to the Ephesians and to the Magnesians these things are read: that Christ was God made flesh, God manifested in human form, that he was with the Father before the ages and appeared at the end, and that he is the same eternal Word of God. Surely it is not likely that Caius would have passed these over, if the letters now circulated under the name of Ignatius had existed in his time. Ignatius the letter-writer splendidly refutes the blasphemy of Artemon; he ought therefore to have been the first thing objected, yet he is not even mentioned. That ancient writer, then, did not know him. The author of the Vindiciae denies that this follows from it: for, he says, even if it is established that Caius was ignorant of Ignatius...

units.la: Epistolae : Ignatius Epistolicus Artemonis blasphemiam splendidè confutat, primus ergo objici debuerat, tamen ne commemoratus quidem est ; Eum nempè vetus ille Scriptor cognitum non habuit. Vindiciarum Auctor id inde sequi negat: Nam ut Caium, inquit, ideò ignorasse Ignatium constet, quia eum non nominavit, necesse est ut etiam constet eum omnes, quos idem scripsisse nôrit nominasse. Id verò constare non posse assi mat ; sed pace Viri docti dixerim, ut validissimum sit celeberrimi Dallaei argumentum, sufficit Caium praecipuos ac celeberrimos commemorasse qui ante Zephyrinum scripserunt, & Christum Deum & hominem dixerunt ; jam autem nullus Ignatio aut antiquior aut celebrior fuit, si igitur Caio cognitae fuissent Ignatianae Epistolae, quin eum cum caeteris nominasset, immò omnibus praetulisset, non dubitabit aequus rerum istarum aestimator; praeterea Caius in suis testibus recensendis consistit in Iustino[?], nec[?] ascendit altius: quia videlicet neminem Iustino antiquiorem noverat, qui Christum Deum simul atque hominem diserte praedicasset ; noverat quidem si Virum doctum audimus, sed ideò praeterijt, quod ejus scripta omnibus nota putaret; quasi verò ? nulla sanè scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum opera ante Ze-phyrinum elaborata, notiora fuerunt quàm Iustini, Miltiadis, Tatiani, Clementis, Irenæi, Melitonis, ea tamen memorat vetus ille Scriptor, Ignatij Epistolas memoraturus si tunc temporis notæ fuissent; Pearsonius de primis diffidens solutionibus, ad hanc tertiam confugit; Caium videlicet eos solos scriptores producere statuisse, qui adversus Gentes scri-pserunt, & ex professo adversus Hæreticos, quod de Ignatio dici nequit: Miserum Viri docti effugium; vetus ille Scriptor Artemonis hærelim confutans, & novam esse demonstrare contendens, præcipuos scriptores recenset qui ante Zephyrinum floruerunt, & Christi divinitatem sive ex professo sive aliter asseruerunt; nemo autem id clarius asseruit quàm Ignatius Epistolicus, illum igitur non omissurus erat Caius, si illi cognitus fuisset, sed agmini ducendo eum præfecisset.
units.tr: Epistle: Ignatius's Epistle refutes the blasphemy of Artemon splendidly, so it ought to have been the first thing objected, yet it is not even mentioned. Evidently that ancient writer did not know it. The author of the Vindiciae denies that this follows: "For it is established that Caius was ignorant of Ignatius because he did not name him; it is necessary that it also be established that he named all whom he knew to have written." He asserts that this cannot be established. But, with respect to the learned man, I would say that the most famous Dallaeus's argument is very strong. It is enough that Caius mentioned the chief and most celebrated writers before Zephyrinus who wrote that Christ is God and man. Now none was older or more celebrated than Ignatius. If, then, the Ignatian Epistles had been known to Caius, he would surely have named him along with the rest, indeed placed him before them all, and no fair judge of these matters will doubt it. Moreover, Caius, in listing his witnesses, stops at Justin and does not go any higher, evidently because he knew no one older than Justin who had plainly preached that Christ is at once God and man. He did know them, if we may believe the learned man, but passed them over because he thought their writings known to all. As if indeed no works of ecclesiastical writers produced before Zephyrinus were better known than those of Justin, Miltiades, Tatian, Clement, Irenaeus and Melito! Yet that ancient writer mentions these, and would have mentioned the Epistles of Ignatius too if they had been known at that time. Pearson, distrusting the earlier solutions, takes refuge in this third one: that Caius intended to produce only those writers who wrote against the Gentiles and, professedly, against heretics, which cannot be said of Ignatius. A wretched refuge for the learned man! That ancient writer, refuting the heresy of Artemon and striving to show that it is new, lists the chief writers who flourished before Zephyrinus and who asserted the divinity of Christ, whether professedly or otherwise. No one asserted it more clearly than Ignatius the Epistle-writer. Caius would therefore not have omitted him, had he been known to him, but would have set him at the head of the column.

units.la: XXI. Alterum Dallæi argumen[illegible, ~3 letters]a desumptum est ex quadam Ecclesiæ[illegible, ~3 letters]Alexandrinæ singulari traditione, Ignatianis legibus plane penitusque adversante. Est enim (inquit) hæc Ignatij Epistolici constans ac perpetua, in omnibus pœnè Epistolis constituta, & ad fastidium usque repetita & inculcata doctrina, non aliter, quam ab uno Episcopo Presbyteris praesidente regi posse ac debere singulas Christi Ecclesias, his subnectit Dallæus ipsa Epistolarum loca quae extant in Epistolis ad Ephesios, Magnesianos, Philadelphen-ses, Trallianos & Smyrnæos; Deinde ostendit alium fuisse usum Ecclesiæ Ale-xandrinæ, idque probat Hieronymi au-toritate, qui ita loquitur Epist. 85. quæ est ad Evagrium, Alexandriæ à Marco Evangelista usque ad Heraclam & Dionysium Episcopos, Presbyteris semper unum ex se electum, in excelsiori gradu collocatum, Episcopum nominabant: quomodo si exercitus imperatorem faciat; aut Diaconi eligant de se, quem industrium noverint, & Archidiaconum vocent. Hieronymo socium dat Eutychium Patriarcham Alexandrinum, qui sæculo nono præcipiti, & decimo ineunte floruit, ex cujus Annalibus Arabicè & Latinè Oxoniæ in Angliâ editis anno 1659. ista descripsit; Constituit Marcus Evangelista, unà cum Hanania (quem Marcus scilicet Patriarcham ordinaverat) duodecim Presbyteros, qui nempe cum Patriarcha manerent, adeò ut cum vacaret Patriarchatus, unum è duodecim Presbyteris eligerent, cujus capiti reliqui undecim manum imponentes ipsi benedicerent & Patriarcham crearent ; deinde virum aliquem insignem eligerent quem secum Presbyterum constituerent loco ejus qui factus est Patriarcha, ut ita semper extarent duodecim. Neque desiit Alexandriæ institutum hoc de Presbyteris, ut scilicet Patriarchas crearent ex Presbyteris duodecim, usque ad tempora Alexandri Patriarchæ Alexandrini, qui fuit ex numero illo trecentorum & octodecim (id est ex Patribus Nicænæ Synodi an. D. 325. sub Constantino celebratæ) post hæc observat præstantissimus Dallæus Eutychium de summâ rei cum Hieronymo consentire, de tempore leviter discrepare. Vindiciarum Auctor negat levem esse Hieronymum inter & Eutychium discrepantiam; Verùm quæcunque sit illa dissonantia, nec Viri docti causam juvare, nec Dallæi hypothesi nocere potest: in eo quippè conveniunt Hieronymus & Eutychius, quod utérque narret Alexandriæ Presbyteros per longum temporis spatium Episcopos sibi creare esse solitos, quod adversâ fronte pugnat cum Ignatianis placitis, juxta quæ nihil sine Episcopo fieri debet; nec mihi arridet Viri docti cavillatio, dicentis Hieronymum solam Presbyteris Episcopi nominationem concedere, non item electionem nec ordinationem, quasi ab aliis electo & or[?]
units.tr: XXI. The second argument of Dallaeus is drawn from a peculiar tradition of the Church of Alexandria, which plainly and utterly opposes the Ignatian rules. For this doctrine of the Ignatian Epistle, he says, is constant and perpetual, laid down in almost all the Epistles, and repeated and inculcated even to weariness: that the individual churches of Christ can and ought to be governed only by one bishop presiding over the presbyters. To this Dallaeus adds the very passages of the Epistles to the Ephesians, Magnesians, Philadelphians, Trallians and Smyrnaeans which contain it. Then he shows that the Church of Alexandria had a different practice, and proves this by the authority of Jerome, who speaks thus in Epistle 85, to Evagrius: At Alexandria, from Mark the Evangelist down to the bishops Heraclas and Dionysius, the presbyters always chose one from among themselves, placed him in a higher rank, and called him bishop, just as if an army should make its general emperor, or deacons should choose from among themselves one whom they knew to be diligent and call him archdeacon. To Jerome he adds as companion Eutychius, Patriarch of Alexandria, who flourished at the end of the ninth century and the beginning of the tenth, from whose Annals, published in Arabic and Latin at Oxford in England in 1659, he copied these things: Mark the Evangelist, together with Hananias (whom Mark had indeed ordained patriarch), appointed twelve presbyters, who were to remain with the patriarch, so that when the patriarchate was vacant, they would choose one of the twelve presbyters, and the other eleven would lay their hands on his head, bless him and make him patriarch. Then they would choose some outstanding man whom they would install as presbyter in place of him who had become patriarch, so that there would always be twelve. Nor did this practice at Alexandria concerning the presbyters cease, namely that they should make patriarchs from among the twelve presbyters, until the time of Alexander, Patriarch of Alexandria, who was one of that number of three hundred and eighteen (that is, of the Fathers of the Synod of Nicaea, held in the year of the Lord 325 under Constantine). After this, the most distinguished Dallaeus observes that Eutychius agrees with Jerome in substance and differs slightly in dating. The author of the Vindiciae denies that the discrepancy between Jerome and Eutychius is slight. But whatever that discrepancy is, it can neither help the learned man's cause nor harm Dallaeus's hypothesis. For Jerome and Eutychius agree in this, that both relate that the presbyters of Alexandria were accustomed, for a long span of time, to create bishops for themselves. This fights head-on with the Ignatian tenets, according to which nothing ought to be done without a bishop. Nor does the learned man's quibble please me, which says that Jerome grants to the presbyters only the naming of the bishop, not the election or the ordination, as if he had been elected and ordained by others, and the presbyters had merely given him the name of bishop; ... as if he had been elected by others and or-

units.la: Note: the left-margin references in the printed text read "Pearf. cap. 10. pag. 163. 164.165.", placed beside the lines "Hieronymum inter", "pantiam", "sonantia" and "nec Dallæi". dinato,solum Episcopi nomen indidissent Presbyteri; nam inquit, Hieronymus dicit quidem Episcopum ex Presbyteris electum, à Presbyteris non dicit; potuit autem ex Presbyteris ab aliis eligi, vel à populo, vel ab Episcopis aliis: Quid est argutari, si hoc non est? tamen reprehendere non veretur clarissimum Seldenum, qui ex Hieronymi verbis colligebat Episcopum Alexandrinum à Presbyteris electum & ordinatum fuisse; siquis hodie scriberet, Cardinales Romani unum ex se electum in excelsiori gradu seu in Altari collocatum, Papam nominant; & Vir doctus de solo Papæ nomine à Cardinalibus imposito id interpretaretur, electione aliis concessâ, profectò se deridendum propinaret; dicet forsan eruditus Pearsonius neminem late-re talem esse hodie Romæ consuetudinem; atqui regeram ego, non ignorabat etiam Hieronymus Alexandrini Episcopi electionem ac promotionem, plane ut narrat peragi solitam, per totum illud tempus quod designat: contrarium tamen probare nititur Vindiciarum Auctor pluribus veterum testimonijs, Epiphanij videlicet, Episcoporum Ægypti in Synodo congregatorum, Gregorij Nazianzeni & Sozomeni, quoniam suas in eligendo Alexandriæ Episcopo populo tribuunt partes,& præterea Liberati verbis qui pe-culiaris cujusdam in illius Episcopi ordi-natione cæremoniæ meminit; Hinc colli-git à Presbyteris Alexandrinis illius loci Episcopum initio electum non fuisse; sic ego quoque colligam Papam Romanum à solis Cardinalibus non eligi, quia populus suas habuit antiquitus in eo eligendo partes; nihil aliud respondere poterit Pearsonius, nisi res penitus mutatas suisse, nec in eodem statu perseverasse, quod sanè verum est: Nam Romæ populus qui in eligendo Pontifice suas olim partes habuit, jure suo dejectus est; Alexandriæ vero jus illud quod à Marco Evangelista usque ad Heraclam solis competebat Presbyteris, temporis lapsu populo etiam concessum fuit; Eutychius certè de electione & de ordinatione à Presbyteris factâ diserte loquitur; utramque autem in verbis Hieronymi comprehendi putavit doctissimus Holstenius qui Dissertatione primâ de Ministro confirmationis pag. 33. inde colligebat Presbyteros Alexandriæ Episcopis suis æquales fermè esse; nam post allata Hieronymi verba, quæ nos supra descripsimus, hæc habet. Unde constat Presbyteros Alexandriæ usque ad annum Christi 246. non tam Episcopos sibi constituisse; quàm Archipresbyteros: quibus exceptâ primæ Cathedræ dignitate, cæteri omnes compresbyteri in functionibus Ecclesiasticis esse quodammodo pares; sibi constituere Episcopos idem est, nisi me fallit animus, quod eos sibi eligere & præficere. Respondet secundò Pearsonius usum hunc Alexandrinum qualis qualis sit non esse disciplinæ Ignatianæ adeò contrarium, & ex diametro oppositum, ut inde ignoratio Ignatij Epistolici colligi possit, responsionis suæ hanc adfert rationem, usum illum videlicet obtinuisse in vacatione sedis, & ad electionem aut promotionem Episcopi tantùm spectare, Ignatium verò de electione aut promotione Episcopi nihil scripsisse. Sed hæc secunda Viri docti solutio priore non est so[?]lidior: si enim Presbyteris Alexandrinis licitum fuit sibi Episcopos constituere, quidni etiam alias absque Episcopo functiones obire? Et si quod est maximū jure facere potuerunt, in minoribus functionibus idem jus eis competivisse par est credere, ideóque Holstenius ex Hieronymi verbis ritè colligebat Presbyteros Episcopis exceptâ primæ Cathedræ dignitate, in functionibus Ecclesiasticis esse quodammodo pares: pares autem esse non poterant nisi illis aliquid facere sine Episcopo conce[illegible, ~3 letters]m fuisset, cùm Episcopo quædam sine Presbyteris facere verisimiliter liceret ; praeterea non solùm Sede vacante hic usus obtinuit, ut scribit Vindiciarum Auctor, sed etiam promotione factâ, docet enim nos Eutychius hanc fuisse Ecclesiæ Alexandrinæ consuetudinem, ut Presbyteri creato sibi Episcopo, Virum aliquem eligerent quem secum Presbyterum constituerent loco ejus qui factus est Patriarcha, ut ita semper extarent duodecim, quod quàm sit contrarium Ignatio Epistolico, qui negat sine Episcopo quicquam faciendum, nemo non videt ; Et certè non solent denegari minora, quibus majora competunt ; jam autem nihil majus in hoc rerum genere concipi potest, quàm Episcopum sibi eligendi ac ordinandi jus atque potestas ; & frustrà est Vir doctus dum scribit pag. 169. id tradi sine Eutychij autoritate, cùm totidem verbis id asserat celeberrimus ille Patriarcha Alexandrinus.
units.tr: dained, and the presbyters had merely given him the name of bishop. For, he says, Jerome indeed says that the bishop was elected from among the presbyters, but does not say by the presbyters; he could have been chosen from among the presbyters by others, either by the people or by other bishops. What is this but quibbling, if it is not that? Yet he does not hesitate to rebuke the most illustrious Selden, who gathered from Jerome's words that the bishop of Alexandria was elected and ordained by the presbyters. If anyone wrote today that the Roman cardinals, having chosen one from among themselves, place him in a higher rank or on the altar and call him Pope, and a learned man were to interpret this as referring only to the name of Pope conferred by the cardinals, with the election granted to others, he would surely expose himself to ridicule. Perhaps the learned Pearson will say that no such custom is known at Rome today. But I will retort that Jerome was not unaware of the election and promotion of the bishop of Alexandria, which were carried out, as he relates, throughout the whole period he designates. The author of the Vindiciae nonetheless strives to prove the contrary by several testimonies of the ancients: namely Epiphanius, the bishops of Egypt gathered in synod, Gregory Nazianzen and Sozomen, because they assign the people their own share in choosing the bishop of Alexandria; and besides, by the words of Liberatus, who mentions a peculiar ceremony in that bishop's ordination. From this he gathers that the bishop of that place was not at first elected by the presbyters of Alexandria. So I too will gather that the Roman Pope is not elected by the cardinals alone, since the people from of old had their own share in electing him. Pearson can reply nothing except that the circumstances were entirely changed and did not remain in the same state, which is certainly true: for at Rome the people, who once had a share in electing the Pontiff, has been deprived of that right; but at Alexandria the right which, from Mark the Evangelist down to Heraclas, belonged to the presbyters alone was in time also granted to the people. Eutychius certainly speaks plainly of an election and of an ordination performed by the presbyters, and the most learned Holstenius thought both were comprehended in Jerome's words. In his first Dissertation on the minister of confirmation, p. 33, he gathered from this that the presbyters of Alexandria were almost equal to their bishops. For after citing Jerome's words, which we have quoted above, he says: Hence it is clear that the presbyters of Alexandria, until the year of Christ 246, did not so much set up bishops for themselves as archpresbyters; for, the dignity of the first chair excepted, all the other co-presbyters were in some way equal in ecclesiastical functions. To set up bishops for oneself is the same thing, unless my mind deceives me, as to choose and to appoint them. Pearson replies secondly that this Alexandrian practice, whatever its character, is not so contrary to Ignatian discipline, nor so diametrically opposed to it, that from it the ignorance of the Ignatian Epistle could be inferred. For this reply he offers the reason that the practice prevailed during a vacancy of the see and concerned only the election or promotion of a bishop, whereas Ignatius wrote nothing about the election or promotion of a bishop. But this second solution of the learned man is no more solid than the first.
