For if it was lawful for the Alexandrian presbyters to set up bishops for themselves, why not also to perform other functions without a bishop? And if they could do the greatest thing by right, it is fitting to believe that the same right belonged to them in the lesser functions. So Holstenius rightly gathered from Jerome's words that the presbyters, the dignity of the first chair excepted, were in some way equal in ecclesiastical functions; but they could not be equal unless they were permitted to do something without the bishop, just as the bishop was probably permitted to do certain things without the presbyters. Moreover, this custom held sway not only during a vacant see, as the author of the Vindiciae writes, but also after a promotion had been made. For Eutychius teaches us that this was the custom of the Church of Alexandria: that once the presbyters had created a bishop for themselves, they would choose some man whom they would install as presbyter in place of him who had become patriarch, so that there would always be twelve. How contrary this is to the Ignatian Epistle, which denies that anything should be done without a bishop, no one fails to see. And surely lesser things are not usually denied to those to whom greater things belong. But nothing greater in this kind of matter can be conceived than the right and power to elect and ordain a bishop for oneself. And the learned man is wrong when he writes at p. 169 that this is handed down without the authority of Eutychius, since that most famous Patriarch of Alexandria asserts it in just so many words.

units.la: Aliud quiddam non minus mirabile ex eodem Eutychio observabat celeberrimus Dallæus, nullum videlicet totam Ægyptiam, numerosissimam ac amplissimam Ecclesiam à Marco ad Demetrium anno Domini circiter 190. ordinatum, Episcopum, præter unum Alexandrinum habuisse: cæteræ extra Alexandri[illegible, ~2 letters] parœciæ à Presbyteris absque Episcopis singulæ regebantur. En tibi ipsissima Eutychij verba ab Hanania quem constituit Marcus Evangelista Patriarcham Alexandriæ, usque in tempora Demetrij Patriarchæ ibidem (is Patriarcha fuit Alexandriæ undecimus) NVLLVS erat in Provinciis Ægypti Episcopus ; nec Patriarchæ ante eum crearunt Episcopos. Ille autem factus Patriarcha tres constituit Episcopos. Et primus hic fuit Patriarcha Alexandrinus qui Episcopos fecit. Mortuo Demetrio suffectus est Heraclas Patriarcha Alexandrinus, qui Episcopus constituit viginti. Vir doctus qui hac Eutychij narratione valdè urgebatur, varias excogitavit solutiones, ut telum illud ab Ignatij sui capite averteret, 1. dicit ex his Eutychij verbis minimè sequi totam Ægyptiam Ecclesiam Ignatij Epistolas ignorasse, quia omnes Ecclesiæ Ægyptiacæ sive aliquem Episcopum habuerint sive nullum, subjectæ erant Episcopo Alexandrino, Ignatium autem asserere illud demùm ministerium Ecclesiasticum rectè peragi, quod vel sub ipso Episcopo fit, vel quod ipse concesserit : quod fieri potuit in Ægyptiacis Ecclesijs Episcopo Alexandrino subjectis, quæ nullo alio Episcopo gauderent ; Hæc prima Vindiciarum Auctoris solutio ; sed parùm soliditatis habet ; nam si hoc non negat Eutychius, ut ait Pearsonius, non etiam asserit, ac proinde ex illius silentio nihil certi pro suâ sententiâ colligere potest ; Eutychij igitur verbis adhærendum est, & plures in Ægypto Ecclesias usque ad Demetrium absque Episcopis regi solitas ex illis concludendum; præterea quamvis vera essent quæ scribit Pearsonius de Ecclesiarū Ægyptiarum Episcopo Alexandrino subjectione, non ea propter cum istis Ignatij sui Decretis convenirent ; Quemadmodum Dominus sine Patre nihil facit, sic neque vos sine Episcopo & Presbyteris aliquid operemini; ita ad Magnesianos, & ad Ephesios, Iesus Christus Patris ipsius sententia est:ut & Episcopi per terræ fines constituti Iesu Christi sententia sunt; ad Philadelphienses, Spiritus prædicavit dicens hæc, sine Episcopo nihil faciatis; ad Trallesios, Necessarium est quemadmodum facitis, sine Episcopo nihil operari vos.
units.tr: Another point, no less remarkable, which the most celebrated Dallaeus observed from the same Eutychius, is that from Mark, who appointed Hananias as Patriarch of Alexandria, until the time of Demetrius, Patriarch there (he was the eleventh Patriarch of Alexandria), around the year of the Lord 190, the whole of Egypt, a very numerous and extensive Church, had no bishop except the one at Alexandria. The individual parishes outside Alexandria were each governed by presbyters without bishops. Here are Eutychius's own words: "From Hananias, whom Mark the Evangelist appointed Patriarch of Alexandria, down to the times of Demetrius, Patriarch there, there was NO bishop in the provinces of Egypt, nor did the Patriarchs before him appoint bishops. But when he was made Patriarch, he appointed three bishops. And he was the first Patriarch of Alexandria who made bishops. When Demetrius died, Heraclas became Patriarch of Alexandria, and he appointed twenty bishops." The learned author, who was hard pressed by this account of Eutychius, devised various solutions so as to turn that weapon away from the head of his Ignatius. (1) He says that it does not follow from these words of Eutychius that the whole Egyptian Church was ignorant of the Epistles of Ignatius, because all the Egyptian Churches, whether they had some bishop or none, were subject to the bishop of Alexandria; and Ignatius asserts that that ecclesiastical ministry is rightly carried out which is done either under the bishop himself or with his permission. This could happen in the Egyptian Churches subject to the bishop of Alexandria, which had no other bishop. This is the first solution of the defender of the Vindiciae. But it has little solidity. For if Eutychius does not deny this, as Pearson says, neither does he assert it, and so nothing certain can be gathered from his silence in support of that opinion. We must therefore adhere to the words of Eutychius and conclude that many churches in Egypt were customarily governed without bishops until the time of Demetrius. Moreover, even if what Pearson writes about the subjection of the Egyptian Churches to the bishop of Alexandria were true, it would not on that account agree with these decrees of his Ignatius: "As the Lord does nothing without the Father, so neither do you do anything without bishop and presbyters"; likewise to the Magnesians and to the Ephesians, "Jesus Christ is the mind of the Father, and the bishops appointed throughout the borders of the earth are in the mind of Jesus Christ"; to the Philadelphians, "The Spirit preached, saying these things: do nothing without the bishop"; to the Trallians, "It is necessary, as you do, to do nothing without the bishop."

units.la: Tum paulò post, cum Episcopum & Presbyteros, illum, ut Christum, hos, ut Concilium Dei & conjunctionem Apostolorum, revereri jussisset, sine his (inquit) Ecclesia non vocatur. Et paucis interjectis; qui sine Episcopo & Presbytero & Diacono, operatur aliquid, iste non mundus est in conscientia. Alia ejusdem commatis adducere possem: sed quæ hactenus descripsi satis superque demonstrant Ignatiana Ægyptiis ignota fuisse; alioqui singulos singulis Ecclesiis præfecissent Episcopos, cùm nihil in Ecclesiis sine Episcopo æquè ac sine Presbytero facere permittat Epistolicus Ignatius, nec majorem Episcopos habendi quàm Presbyteros necessitatem imponat; æquâ lege utrorúmque respectu, si istum audimus, tenentur Christiani, qui neque Dei Ecclesia censendi sunt aut vocandi, si Episcopis carent eorum coetus; liquet enim ex Epistolarum inscriptionibus de particularibus hîc agi Ecclesiis, quæ secundum istius scita, ita pendent ab Episcopis, ut eas Ecclesiarum nomine indignas judicet, quæ Episcopos non habent; quæ doctrina cùm Evangelica non sit, verum Ignatium nequaquam redolet. Pearsonius etiam hac primâ solutione non contentus, ad aliam transit, & historiolam illam, sic loqui amat, de tribus Episcopis à Demetrio primùm in Ægypto factis minimè fide dignam esse asserit; nempè Vir doctus plane militari ausu, nodum quem solvere nequit, ferro dissecat; ita nullus erit nodus insolubilis. Neque enim quicquam tam certum & perspicuum adduci poterit, quod non eadem arte eludatur. Ab Originibus Ecclesiæ Alexandrinæ nimis remotus fuit Eutychius, ut ejus narrationi adhibeatur fides; sed longè remotior Pearsonius, ac propterea minimè audiendus, dum narrationem illam septingentis quadraginta circiter annis post Eutychij mortem falsi insimulare non veretur; multa in Annalibus suis conscribendis peccata peccavit Eutychius, & à vero aliena narravit: Demus Viro docto hoc ita se habere; indene sequetur historiam de quâ lis est non esse fide dignam minimè gentium; rari sunt Historici in quibus plura reprehensione digna non reperias, & tamen si ob quaedam eorum peccata, caeteris narrationibus fidem detrahere velis, actum erit de historiâ temporum teste vetustatisque nuntiâ, & pessimè nobiscum agetur: Quid fiet de ipso Eusebio & de luculento quod Ignatianis perhibet testimonio, & quo tantopere delectatur Vir doctus, si illius omnia ad vivum resecantur: quoties enim in Historiâ suâ Ecclesiasticâ hallucinatus est, & quoties ob id à Viris doctis notatus.
units.tr: Then a little later, when he had bidden them to reverence the bishop as Christ, and the presbyters as the council of God and the bond of the Apostles, he says: "Without these the Church is not called [a Church]." And after a few words in between: "Whoever does anything without bishop, presbyter and deacon, he is not clean in conscience." I could adduce other sentences from the same passage, but what I have described so far sufficiently and more than sufficiently shows that the Ignatian writings were unknown to the Egyptians. Otherwise they would have placed a bishop over each single church, since the Epistolary Ignatius permits nothing to be done in the churches without a bishop any more than without a presbyter, and he does not impose a greater necessity of having bishops than of having presbyters. By the same law, with respect to both, if we heed him, Christians are bound; and those assemblies which lack bishops are not to be judged or called churches of God. For it is clear from the superscriptions of the Epistles that particular churches are meant, and according to his decrees these depend on bishops in such a way that he judges unworthy of the name of churches those which do not have bishops. Since this doctrine is not evangelical, it does not in the least smell of the true Ignatius. Pearson, not content even with this first solution, passes on to another, and he asserts, as he likes to put it, that the little story about the three bishops first made in Egypt by Demetrius is by no means worthy of belief. Indeed, this learned man, with a purely soldierly boldness, cuts with the sword the knot which he cannot loosen; so there will be no insoluble knot. For nothing so certain and clear can be brought forward that it cannot be evaded by the same device. Eutychius was too remote from the origins of the Alexandrian Church for his narrative to deserve belief; but Pearson was far more remote, and therefore is not to be heard at all, since he does not hesitate to brand that narrative as false some seven hundred and forty years after Eutychius's death. Eutychius committed many errors in writing his Annals and related things alien to the truth. Let us grant this to the learned man. Does it follow that a history of which this is the case is in no way worthy of belief? Historians are rare in whom you would not find many things worthy of reproof; and yet, if you wish to strip other narratives of credit on account of some of their errors, it will be all over with history, "the witness of the times and the messenger of antiquity," and we shall fare very badly. What will become of Eusebius himself, and of the splendid testimony he bears to the Ignatian writings, in which the learned man takes such delight, if all his statements are cut down to the quick? For how often did he go astray in his Ecclesiastical History, and how often has he been noted for this by learned men!

units.la: Verùm respondet tertiò eruditus Pearsonius, planè incredibile esse, ut nullus fuerit in totâ Ægypto Episcopus præter solum Alexandrinum, ante Demetrij Patriarchatum, & assertionem contrariam ex optimis historiae monumentis demonstrari posse. Optima illa historiae monu[?]menta nihil aliud sunt quàm Epistola ab Adriano Imperatore scripta ad Servianum Consulem circa A. D. 132. sexaginta fermè annis antequam factus est Patriarcha Demetrius, & quam ex Phlegonte Adriani liberto transcripsit Flavius Vopiscus in vita Saturnini. Hujus Epistolæ v r-ba sunt : Ægyptum quam mihi laudabeas[?], Serviane charissime , totam didici , levem , pendulam ,& ad omnia famæ momenta volitantem. Illi qui Serapin colunt , Christiani sunt: & devoti sunt Serapi , qui se Christi Episcopos dicunt. Nemo illic Archisynagogus Iudæorum, nemo Samarites, nemo Christianorum Presbyter, non mathematicus, non aruspex, non aliptes. Ipse ille Patriarcha quum Ægyptum venerit, ab alijs Serapidem adorare, ab alijs cogitur Christum. Ex istis Adriani verbis colligit Vir doctus falsam esse Eutychij narrationem, dum scribit nullum fuisse in tota Ægypto Episcopum, præter Alexandrinum usque ad Demetrij tempora: nam habemus hic ( inquit ) Patriarcham, Christi Episcopos, & Christianorum Presbyteros. Sed profectò non possum non mirari Vindiciarum Auctorem in istis levissimis præsidium quærentem,quasi falsi argui posset Eutychij historia de tribus Episcopis in Ægypto à Demetrio primùm creatis, quia Adriani Epistola longè ante Demetrij promotionem scripta, Episcoporum Christianorum in Ægy-pto meminit. Aliquem colorem, etsi forte evanidum haberet Viri docti argumentatio, si Adriano plane penitúsque compertæ fuissent res Christianorum; sed patet ex Epistolæ lectione falsa pleráque ei persuasisse homines Ægyptios infensissimos Iudæorum & Christianorum hostes; quis quæso unquam scripsit Adriani ætate eò usque deservuisse Episcoporum Christianorum pietatem, ut Serapidis cultu & adoratione vitam redimere, salutíque suæ consulere non dubitarent? contrà ne-mo nescit tanto Dei zelo per illa tempora flagrâsse Ecclesiarum Christianarum Pa-stores, ut mortem sponte & maximo cum gaudio pro Christi nomine oppeterent: Deinde quis vel fando audivit unum tunc temporis fuisse Deum Iudæis, Christianis, & Gentibus? Hoc tamen diserte profitetur Adrianus, quamvis in eadem scribat Epistolâ alios Christum, alios coluisse Serapin, ut taceam cæteram Deorum turbam, quos Ægyptij cum reliquis Paganis eâ tempestate vel superstitiosissimè venerabantur: Vnus (inquit) illis Deus est, hunc Christiani, hunc Iudæi, hunc omnes venerantur & gentes. Præterea quis concoquere potest quæ dicit de Patriarcha illo quem memorat , quod videlcet quum Ægyptum venerit, ab aliis Serapidem ado-rare , ab aliis cogitur Christum ; Nam si Christianorum Alexandrinorum fuit Patriarcha, ut nonnullis placet, ad Christum adorandum minimè cogebatur , in illius siquidem cultum ac venerationem libentissimè ferebatur , nihilque gratius atque jucundius ei contingere poterat, quàm Christum Dominum colendi ac adorandi jus atque potestas. Si verò Iu-dæorum fuit Patriarcha ut volunt Pearsonius, ejúsque popularis ac symmista Beveregius in Can. 6. Concilij Nicæni primi, quomodo à Christianis Christum adorare cogi potuit ? Tantáne fuit eâ tempestate Christianorum autoritas, ut homines à suâ religione alienos, ad Christum colendum vi ac minis impellere possent? cùm igitur tot sint in illâ Adriani Epistolâ cum veritate pugnantia, & quæ crassissimam rerum Christianarum ignorantiam produnt ; nil certi hinc excsulpi potest: sed ( inquit Pearsonius) habemus hic Christi Episcopos ,& Christianorum Presbyteros : quid tum inquiam ego ? Presbyteros nominat quos Episcopos nuncupaverat ; non solùm quia ijdem sunt Episcopi & Presbyteri juxta Scripturæ sacræ stylum, qui vigebat adhuc inter Christianos Adriani 'ætate ; sed etiam quoniam aliquid inaudiverat Adrianus de Presbyteris Alexandrinis qui unum ex se electum, Episcopum sibi constituebant, & ea propter Episcopi quodammodo erant ; His adde per Episcopos ac Presbyteros Adrianum intelligere forsan Patriarchæ Iudæorum Assessores, qui Apostoli dicebantur, & erant veluti Gentis seniores, & rerum judaicarum Episcopi seu Inspectores, de illis Patriarchæ rationem reddituri ; nec obstat quod eos Christianorum Episcopos ac Presbyteros indigetat. Scriptores enim Ethnici Iudæos cum Christianis non raro confundunt, quoniam Religio Christiana est Iudaïcæ veluti filia atque propago. Quicquid sit Vindiciarum Auctor nondum habens ubi sistat aliò confugit, scribitque certum esse neque Græcis neque Latinis notam fuisse traditio-nem illam de Episcopis in Ægypto à Demetrio primùm factis: ut id probet adfert Evaristi Epistolam ad omnes per Ægyptum fratres, hoc est, Episcopos; concedit quidem hanc Epistolam Evaristi non esse, sed ab Adversariis postulat ut largiantur Autorem Epistolæ plures Episcopos Evaristi ætate in Ægypto fuisse opinatum esse; sanè impostor qui hanc supposuit Epistolam antiqua tempora suis metiens , plures fuisse in Ægypto Evaristi ætate Episcopos credidit vel saltem credere simulavit, quoniam per ma-gno erant numero, sæculo quo Decreta-les suas crassissimo filo contextas primis Ecclesiæ Romanæ Episcopis supponebat; sed hæc Viri docti causam minimè ju-vant ; idem plane dico de verbis Suidæ & Chronographi Ioëlis , qui Leonidem Origenis patrem sub initio Demetrij Episcopum faciunt Ægyptiacum , cùm Epi-scopus nunquam fuerit ut fatetur ipse Pearsonius, quicquid opinati sint Scriptores illi qui eum Episcopi titulo insigniunt. Pergit eruditus Pearsonius , & in subsidium vocat Synodum quandam à Demetrio adversus Origenem congregatam ; illius Synodi meminit Photius in Bibliothecâ Cod. CXVIII. in hæc verba ex versione Schotti , Synodus Episcoporum coacta ,& Presbyterorum quorundam contra Origenem ; Vir doctus carpit versionem clarissimi Huetij qui Græca Photij sic Latinè reddidit , Synodus prior Episcopis ali-quot & Presbyteris conflata , nempè ægrè fert Pearsonius quod Huetius vocem aliquot de Episcopis ac Presbyteris æquè usurpaverit , quasi aliquot tantùm suissent & Episcopi & Presbyteri , cùm Episcopos fuisse plures , aliquos autem & Presbyteros afferat Vindiciarum Auctor. Quamvis doctissimi Huetij versio rite defendi queat, Viro docto tamen largiri volo, verba Photij, seu potius Pamphili Martyris à Photio descripta quemadmodum dicit, esse interpretanda; sed quid inde lucri habiturus sit non auguror: nihil enim vetat quin quatuor Episcoporum & quorundam Presbyterorum coetus, Episcoporum & aliquot Presbyterorum Synodus nuncupetur, cum Synodi audiant Dioecesanae quæ ex solo Episcopo & Dioecesis suæ Presbyteris constant, potiori igitur jure coetus quo de agimus Synodi Episcoporum & aliquot Presbyterorum nomen meretur: Nam si tres faciunt Collegium immò Ecclesiam ut scribit alicubi Tertullianus, quanto magis quatuor Episcopi cum aliquot Presbyteris Synodum sunt constituturi; quatuor autem illi Episcopi sunt Demetrius ipse unà cum tribus aliis quos primùm in Ægypto creârat Episcopis; plures erant, inquit, Episcopi quam Presbyteri esto, ergo major erat Ægypti Episcoporum numerus, quàm scribit Eutychius, negatur consequentia; Nam si quatuor huic Synodo interfuerunt Episcopi, Presbyteri verò tres tantùm, plures fuerunt Episcopi quàm Presbyteri, absque ullo Eutychianæ narrationis detrimento, cui donec validiora adferantur argumenta, constabit sua veritas. Verùm liberaliùs cum Viro docto est agendum, eíque concedendum plures quàm quatuor Synodo interfuisse Episcopos; Num propterea nutabit historiæ Eutychij fides, aut in falsi suspicionem veniet? Nequaquam; aliunde videlicet quam ex sola Ægypto evocari potuerunt Episcopi; & verisimile est Demetrium alios litteris suis præter Ægyptiacos invitasse, ut major[?]is esset momenti atque ponderis Decretum contra Origenem illâ in Synodo sanciendum:Sed quoniam voti sui compos non omninò fuit Demetrius, Synodi siquidem Patres Origenem Alexandriâ pellendum, neque in eâ versari aut docere permittendum decreverunt, Sacerdotij tamen dignitate nequaquaquam submovendum. Demetrius inquam qui molestè ferebat Origenem à Priori Synodo non exauctoratum fuisse, quosdam Ægypti Episcopos iterùm convocat, ij autem morè gerere Demetrio paratiores, Origenem, quem tunc temporis odio plus quàm Vatiniano prosequebatur, abjudicant, eúmque Sacerdotij dignitate submovent; Hæc ita gesta fuisse scribit Pamphilus apud Photium ubi suprà ; Nam post memoratam Prioris Synodi sanctionem , sic historiam Origenis prosequitur. Verùm Demetrius unâ cum quibusdam Episcopis Ægyptiis , Sacerdotio quoque illum abjudicat , subscribentibus etiam huic Decreto qui ei suffragati sunt. Iam nemo non videt Episcopos illos quos secundò congregavit Demetrius Ægyptios expressè nominari, oppositione facta ad alios qui in priori conventu Ægyptij non erant, non autem ad distinctionem cæterorum Ægypti Episcoporum, cùm in totâ Ægypto tres tantùm essent Episcopi à Demettrio ipso creati ; Et certè nulla alia idonea, ut mihi quidem videtur, adferri potest ratio ob quam Pamphilus observet Ægyptios fuisse Episcopos qui Origenis abjudicationi consenserunt, nisi ut implacabile Demetrij inOrigenem odium exaggeret, cæcámque notet subscribentium Episcoporum obedientiam ; cùm enim tale Decretum à priori Episcoporum & Presbyterorum conventu extorquere non potuerit Demetrius, fortè animo versans hanc vel similem Poëtæ sententiam, audaces fortuna juvat, Origènem Presbyteri gradu dejicere non dubitat, & ne solus hoc fecisse videretur, quosdam Ægypti Episcopos in suam sententiam traxit, suóque Decreto subscribere persuasit ; illi enim soli Decreto subscripserunt , qui Origenis exauctorationi consenserant, nempe pauci Ægyptij, non alij , ut fert Schotti versio , quihæc Græca verba , [?]τὴν συμφώνων αὐτῷ γεγενημένων[?], sic reddidit, quotquota ntea suffragati ei fuissent, cùm tamen ita vertenda essent, qui ei suffragati sunt; illos videlicet denotans qui unà cum Demetrio Origenem Sacerdotij dignitate submoverunt , quod ad prioris Synodi Patres referri non potest , sed ad eos qui hisce verbis designantur [?]ἄμα τισὶν ἐπισκόποις αἷς[?] [?]γυναικός[?], & forsan olim loco [?]τινῶν[?] quibusdam, legebatur [?]φυλῶν[?] tribus, quod Eutychij narrationi apprimè congruit, & præterea facilis est unius vocis in alteram permutatio. Vt ut est si Origenes ut scribit Vindiciarum Auctor , de abrogatâ veteri consuetudine, de autoritate paucorum novitiorúmque Episcoporum non disputavit, rationes apud se habuit, quibus permotus ista silentio præterivit; præterea conqueri potuit, sed ejus querelæ ad nos non pervenerunt ; His adde abrogationem veteris Ecclesiæ Alexandrinæ consuetudinis omnibus ita gratam fuisse , ut à nemine verisimiliter reprehenderetur : nam hoc pacto Ecclesia Alexandrina ad usum ac disciplinam reliquarum Ecclesiarum proximè accedebat ; nec mirum si Synodorum Demetrii Decretis consenserit si̇nlversus ferè orbis, sive Origenis ad Presbyteri gradum promotionem inconsulto suo Episcopo spectes, sive illius audax facinus inspicias, hoc est voluntariam sui abscissionem, prius illius temporis disciplinam sollicitabat, posterius naturæ leges violabat; neutrum igitur probari poterat, ideóque si Demetrius æquitatis ac justitiæ leges in Origenis causâ sequutus esset, nec iræ se permisisset, aut odium quo in eum flagrabat consuluisset, omnes orbis Christiani Provincias, ne unâ quidem exceptâ, Decretis suis consentientes dubio procul habuisset; sed quoniam pluribus compertum erat, Demetrium odio concitatum & iræ impotentem hæc Decreta contra Origenem condi curavisse quamvis eum antea multùm dilexisset, laudibúsque cumulasset, aliquot Provinciæ sanctionibus suis sunt refragatæ, ad id præterea industæ magno & excellenti Viri ingenio, qui multis admirationi erat. Vltra progredior, & aliquid amplius Viro doćto largiri non gravabor; per paucos illos videlicet Ægypti Episcopos qui Origenis abdicationi consenserunt Pamphilum intelligere partem modò eámque forte minorem Episcoporum Ægyptiorum, non ideò deterior erit Eutychij narratio, facilè in gratiam redibit cum Pamphilo Eutychius, & inter eos pacem ac amicitiam conciliare non erit arduum; ut id fiat. Ægyptus bifariam consideranda est, vel seorsùm à Lybiâ & Pentapoli & forsan etiam Thebaïde, qualis erat Demetrij ætate, vel una cum ijs junctim cujusmodi erat temporibus Pamphili; nemo enim horum studiorum notitiâ vel levissimè tinctus ignorat; Ægyptum, Thebaïdem, & utrámque Lybiam, Provinciam Episcopi Alexandrini Ecclesiasticam tunc temporis constituisse, ut liquidò constat ex Canone sexto Concilij Nicæni primi, necnon ex variis Operum sancti Athanasij locis, & quia Ægyptus sic proprie dicta omnium erat nobilissima, universa Dioecesis Ægypti nomine nuncupabatur; cùm igitur Eutychius scribit nullos fuisse in Provincijs Ægypti Episcopos præter Alexandrinum usque ad Demetrium qui tres primùm constituit, Ægyptum respicit priori modo, seorsùm videlicet à Thebaïde & Lybiâ utráque, in quibus regionibus non negat esse Episcopos Demetrij ætate, de solâ Ægypto loquitur ab illis Provincijs distinctâ: Pamphilus verò sub Ægypti nomine omnes illas complecti-tur Provincias, quæ eâ tempestate Provinciam Episcopi Alexandrini Ecclesiasticam constituebant ; mutuus ergo Pamphilum inter & Eutychium consensus, summa concordia. Hinc non parùm lùcis accedit duabus Synodis de quibus Pamphilus apud Photium ; plures priori Synodo interfuêre Episcopi præter Ægyptios proprie dictos , ex Thebaïde scilicet & utraque Lybiâ precibus & litteris Demetrij verisimiliter evocati ; sed quia Demetrio non parebant , nec ei subjecti erant ut Ægyptij ( nondum siquidem limites suos extra Ægyptum dilataverant Episcopi Alexandrini ) ab illis impetrare non potuit Demetrius Origenis abdicationem ; quâ re animadversâ ad suos iterùm se vertit Ægyptios Episcopos, & una cùm ijs Origenem Sacerdotij dignitate submovet. Hæc vera est ni fallor, & Eutychij narrationis & Synodorum Demetrij interpretatio, nullam enim vim verbis facit, Eutychium cum Pamphilo non committit, neque Pamphilum cum Eutychio, nodos solvit, tollit difficultates, & exiguis regiminis Ecclesiastici primordijs ac progressui est accommodatissima ; regimen quippe Ecclesiasticum sensim paulatímque , & veluti surdis quibusdam incrementis ad typum & exemplar regiminis civilis & politici formatum fuit , & tandem quæ usu ac consuetudine obtinuerant Præsules , Conciliorum Decretis firmata fuerunt & roborata ; non mirum igitur si Alexandri Alexandriæ Episcopi ætate paulò ante Concilium Nicænum penè centum Episcopi Ægypti consenserunt in condemnationem Arrij & aliquorum etiam Episcoporum,nam eâ tempestate Alexandro parebant,non solùm Ægyptus , sed etiam Thebaïs & Lybia utráque , fluxerant siquidem à Demetrij Synodis ad hoc usque tempus centum plus minus anni , intra quod temporis spatium Episcoporum numerus in illis Provincijs mirum in modum auctus est; quæ de Dionysio Demetrij post Heraclam successore subjungit Vir doctus , nihili plane sunt ; præterquam enim Heraclas Dionysij decessor & Demetrij immediadiatus successor viginti constituerat Episcopos, ut scribit Eutychius pag. 332. & ita plures erant ante Dionysium in Ægypto Episcopi , plaerique quos nominat Dionysius non ad Ægyptum proprie pertinebant, sed ad Thebaïdis & Lybiarum Provincias; nec à vero alienum putarim huic Dionysio Provincias illas Thebaïdem videlicet & utramque Lybiam, obedientiam primùm præstare coepisse , sive ad id sollicitatæ fuerint celeberrimâ sanctissimi[?] Viri famâ, sive urbis Alexandriæ magnitudine ac splendore, sive aliquâ aliâ ratione nobis incompertâ, & tunc primùm propriè jacta fuisse per omnes illas Provincias in gratiam Episcoporum Alexandrinorum jurium Metropoliticorum fundamenta, quæ postea Canone sexto Concilij Nicæni sunt confirmata. Græcis inquit Pearsonius atque Latinis ignota fuit traditio illa de tribus Episcopis à Demetrio primò in Ægypto factis, illud autem probat Scriptorum auctoritate, Eutychij vel æqualium vel supparium vel recentiorum, & qui in rebus Ecclesiæ Alexandrinæ Patriarchæ illius sedis sunt postponendi, ejusdem est commatis quod ultimò observat, Eutychium hanc historiolam tanquam traditionem à majoribus acceptam non referre, sed velut quæstionis Criticæ aut Philologicæ apud Arabas sui temporis agitatæ solutionem in honorem Ecclesiæ suæ factam.
units.tr: But the learned Pearson replies, thirdly, that it is quite incredible that there was no bishop in all of Egypt except the Alexandrian one before the patriarchate of Demetrius, and that the contrary assertion can be shown from the best historical monuments. Those best historical monuments are nothing other than a letter written by the Emperor Hadrian to the consul Servianus around the year 132, some sixty years before Demetrius became patriarch, which Flavius Vopiscus copied from Phlegon, Hadrian's freedman, in his Life of Saturninus. The words of this letter are: "I have learned all about Egypt, which you praised to me, dearest Servianus: it is light, fickle, and flitting about at every breath of rumour. Those who worship Serapis are Christians, and those who call themselves bishops of Christ are devoted to Serapis. There is no archisynagogue of the Jews there, no Samaritan, no Christian presbyter, who is not a mathematician, a soothsayer, or an anointer. The patriarch himself, when he comes to Egypt, is forced by some to worship Serapis and by others to worship Christ." From these words of Hadrian the learned man concludes that the account of Eutychius is false, where he writes that there was no bishop in all of Egypt except the Alexandrian one until the time of Demetrius; for, he says, "here we have a patriarch, bishops of Christ, and presbyters of the Christians." But I certainly cannot but wonder that the author of the Vindiciae, seeking support in such very slight evidence, should suppose that the story of Eutychius about three bishops first created in Egypt by Demetrius could be proved false because a letter of Hadrian, written long before Demetrius's promotion, mentions Christian bishops in Egypt. The learned man's argument might have some colour, though perhaps a faded one, if the affairs of the Christians had been completely and thoroughly known to Hadrian; but it is plain from reading the letter that he was persuaded of many false things by Egyptian men, bitter enemies of the Jews and Christians. Who, I ask, ever wrote that in Hadrian's day the piety of the Christian bishops had sunk so low that they did not hesitate to buy their lives and secure their own safety by the cult and worship of Serapis? On the contrary, no one doubts that in those times the pastors of the Christian churches burned with such zeal for God that they sought death willingly and with the greatest joy for the name of Christ. Next, who has ever heard, even by report, that at that time the Jews, the Christians and the Gentiles had one God? Yet Hadrian plainly professes this, although in the same letter he writes that some worshipped Christ and others Serapis, not to mention the rest of the crowd of gods whom the Egyptians, along with the other pagans of that age, venerated with the greatest superstition: "To them there is one God; him the Christians, him the Jews, him all nations worship." Moreover, who can make sense of what he says about that patriarch, namely that when he comes to Egypt "he is forced by some to worship Serapis and by others to worship Christ"? For if he was patriarch of the Alexandrian Christians, as some are pleased to think, he was not at all forced to worship Christ; he would have been most willing to be borne into the cult and veneration of Christ, and nothing could have happened to him more welcome and pleasing than the right and power of worshipping and adoring the Lord Christ. But if he was patriarch of the Jews, as Pearson and his fellow partisan Beveridge maintain on the sixth canon of the First Council of Nicaea, how could he have been forced to worship Christ by Christians? Was the authority of the Christians at that time so great that they could compel by force and threats men alien to their religion to worship Christ? Since, therefore, so many things in that letter of Hadrian conflict with the truth and betray the crudest ignorance of Christian affairs, nothing certain can be drawn from it. But (Pearson says) "here we have bishops of Christ and presbyters of the Christians." What then, I ask, do I say? He calls presbyters those whom he had called bishops; not only because bishops and presbyters are the same according to the style of Holy Scripture, which was still current among the Christians in Hadrian's day, but also because Hadrian had perhaps heard something about the Alexandrian presbyters who chose one of their own number and made him their bishop, and for that reason were in a sense bishops. To these add that by bishops and presbyters Hadrian perhaps understood the assessors of the Jewish patriarch, who were called apostles and were, as it were, the elders of the nation and the bishops or overseers of Jewish affairs, to render an account to the patriarch of them; nor does it stand in the way that he calls them bishops and presbyters of the Christians. For pagan writers not infrequently confuse the Jews with the Christians, since the Christian religion is, as it were, a daughter and offshoot of the Jewish. Whatever the case, the author of the Vindiciae, not yet having anywhere to stand, flees elsewhere, and writes that it is certain that the tradition about the bishops first made in Egypt by Demetrius was known neither to the Greeks nor to the Latins. To prove this he brings forward the letter of Evaristus to all the brothers throughout Egypt, that is, to the bishops. He does indeed concede that this letter is not Evaristus's, but he asks his opponents to grant that its author supposed there were several bishops in Egypt in the time of Evaristus. Certainly the impostor who put forward this letter, measuring ancient times by his own, believed, or at least pretended to believe, that there were many bishops in Egypt in the age of Evaristus, since they were numerous at that time, in the century in which he was putting forward his Decretals, crudely stitched together, as supposed works of the first bishops of the Roman Church. But these things do not help the cause of the learned man. I say exactly the same of the words of Suidas and of the Chronographer Joel, who make Leonides, the father of Origen, a bishop of Egypt at the beginning of Demetrius's time, although, as Pearson himself admits, he was never a bishop, whatever those writers who decorate him with the title of bishop may have thought. The learned Pearson goes on, and calls to his aid a certain synod gathered by Demetrius against Origen. Photius mentions this synod in the Bibliotheca, Codex 118, in these words, in the version of Schott: "A synod of bishops and certain presbyters gathered against Origen." The learned man carps at the version of the most illustrious Huet, who rendered Photius's Greek into Latin thus: "a first synod assembled of some bishops and presbyters." Pearson takes it badly that Huet used the word "some" equally of the bishops and the presbyters, as if there had been only a few bishops and a few presbyters, whereas the author of the Vindiciae maintains that there were more bishops and some presbyters. Although Huet's version can properly be defended, I am willing to grant the learned man that the words of Photius, or rather of the martyr Pamphilus whom Photius describes, as he says, must be interpreted in the way he suggests; but I do not foresee what gain he will reap from this. For nothing prevents a gathering of four bishops and certain presbyters from being called a synod of bishops and some presbyters; since diocesan synods, which consist of the bishop alone and the presbyters of his own diocese, are called synods, a gathering such as we are discussing deserves with still better right the name of a synod of bishops and some presbyters. For if Tertullian somewhere writes that three make a college, indeed a church, how much more will four bishops with some presbyters constitute a synod? Those four bishops were Demetrius himself together with the three others whom he had first created bishops in Egypt. "There were more bishops," he says, "than presbyters." Let it be so; then the number of bishops in Egypt was greater than Eutychius writes. The consequence is denied. For if four bishops were present at this synod, but only three presbyters, there were more bishops than presbyters, with no harm to the account of Eutychius, whose truth will stand until stronger arguments are brought against it. But let us deal more generously with the learned man and grant that more than four bishops were present at the synod. Will the credibility of Eutychius's history therefore waver, or fall under suspicion of falsehood? By no means; the bishops could have been summoned from elsewhere than from Egypt alone, and it is likely that Demetrius invited others besides the Egyptian bishops by his letters, so that the decree against Origen to be sanctioned in that synod might have greater weight and authority. But since Demetrius did not altogether get what he wanted, the fathers of the synod decided that Origen must be driven from Alexandria and must not be permitted to remain there or teach, yet he must not be removed from the dignity of the priesthood. Demetrius, I say, who was vexed that Origen had not been deposed by the former synod, again summoned certain bishops of Egypt; these, more ready to yield to Demetrius, condemned Origen, whom at that time he pursued with a hatred greater than that of Vatinius, and removed him from the dignity of the priesthood. Pamphilus, in Photius, where we have just cited him, writes that this happened in this way; for after the mentioned sanction of the former synod he continues the history of Origen thus: "But Demetrius, together with certain Egyptian bishops, also deprived him of the priesthood, and those who supported him also subscribed to this decree." Now everyone can see that those bishops whom Demetrius gathered a second time are expressly named as Egyptians, in contrast to others who in the former assembly were not Egyptians; not in order to distinguish them from the rest of the bishops of Egypt, since in all Egypt there were only three bishops created by Demetrius himself. And certainly, as it seems to me, no other suitable reason can be offered why Pamphilus should note that the bishops who agreed to Origen's deposition were Egyptians, except to heighten the implacable hatred of Demetrius against Origen, and to mark the blind obedience of the bishops who subscribed. For since Demetrius could not extort such a decree from the former assembly of bishops and presbyters, perhaps turning over in his mind that saying of the poet, "fortune favours the bold," he did not hesitate to degrade Origen from the rank of presbyter; and so that he should not seem to have done this alone, he drew certain Egyptian bishops into his opinion and persuaded them to subscribe his decree. For only those subscribed to the decree who had agreed to Origen's deposition, namely a few Egyptians, and no others, as Schott's version renders it, who rendered the Greek words "those who had agreed with him" [tēn symphōnōn autō gegenēmenōn] as "whoever had supported him up to then"; whereas they ought to have been rendered "who supported him." These words denote those who together with Demetrius removed Origen from the dignity of the priesthood, which cannot be referred to the fathers of the former synod, but to those who are designated in the words [ama tisin episkopois hais ...] "together with certain bishops," and perhaps "certain" [tinōn] was once read as "tribes" [phylōn], which fits Eutychius's account very well, and moreover an exchange of one word for another is easy. However that may be, if Origen, as the author of the Vindiciae writes, did not dispute about the abolition of the old custom or about the authority of a few newly made bishops, he had reasons of his own for passing over these things in silence. He may also have complained, but his complaints have not come down to us. Add to this that the abolition of the old custom of the Alexandrian Church was so pleasing to all that no one would probably have found fault with it; for in this way the Alexandrian Church drew closer to the practice and discipline of the other churches. Nor is it surprising that the decrees of Demetrius's synods were agreed to by almost the whole world. Whether you look at Origen's promotion to the rank of presbyter without the consent of his bishop, or consider his rash deed, that is his voluntary self-mutilation, the former violated the discipline of that time, the latter the laws of nature. Neither could therefore be approved; and so if Demetrius had followed the laws of equity and justice in Origen's case, and had not given way to anger, or had not consulted the hatred with which he burned against him, he would undoubtedly have had all the provinces of the Christian world, not one excepted, agreeing with his decrees. But since it was known to many that Demetrius, stirred by hatred and powerless against his anger, had caused these decrees against Origen to be framed, although he had formerly loved him greatly and heaped praises upon him, several provinces resisted his sanctions, the more so as they were supported by the great and excellent genius of that man, who was an object of admiration to many. I go further, and will not scruple to grant the learned man something more: let us suppose that by those few Egyptian bishops who agreed to Origen's deprivation Pamphilus means only a part, and perhaps a smaller part, of the Egyptian bishops; the account of Eutychius will not on that account be worse. Eutychius will easily come back into favour with Pamphilus, and it will not be difficult to bring about peace and friendship between them. To make this happen, Egypt must be considered in two ways: either apart from Libya and Pentapolis and perhaps also Thebais, as it was in Demetrius's time, or together with them, as it was in the time of Pamphilus; for no one even slightly versed in these studies is ignorant of this. It is clear from the sixth canon of the First Council of Nicaea, and also from various passages of the works of St Athanasius, that Egypt, Thebais and both Libyas constituted the ecclesiastical province of the bishop of Alexandria at that time; and since Egypt properly so called was the most noble of all, the whole diocese was called by the name of Egypt. Therefore, when Eutychius writes that there were no bishops in the provinces of Egypt except the Alexandrian one until Demetrius, who first created three, he regards Egypt in the first sense, that is, apart from Thebais and both Libyas, in which regions he does not deny that there were bishops in Demetrius's time; he speaks of Egypt alone, distinct from those provinces. Pamphilus, on the other hand, under the name of Egypt embraces all those provinces which at that time constituted the ecclesiastical province of the bishop of Alexandria. There is therefore a mutual agreement between Pamphilus and Eutychius, and complete harmony. Hence no small light falls on the two synods of which Pamphilus speaks in Photius: more bishops than the proper Egyptians were present at the former synod, from Thebais and both Libyas, most likely summoned by the prayers and letters of Demetrius; but because they did not obey Demetrius, nor were they subject to him as the Egyptians were (for the bishops of Alexandria had not yet extended their boundaries beyond Egypt), Demetrius could not obtain from them the deposition of Origen. Noticing this, he turned again to his own Egyptian bishops, and together with them removed Origen from the dignity of the priesthood. This, if I am not mistaken, is a true interpretation both of the account of Eutychius and of Demetrius's synods; for it does no violence to the words, does not set Eutychius against Pamphilus or Pamphilus against Eutychius, unties the knots, removes the difficulties, and is very well suited to the small beginnings and gradual progress of church government. For church government was formed gradually and step by step, with certain almost imperceptible increases, after the pattern and model of civil and political government; and at last what the bishops had obtained by use and custom was confirmed and strengthened by the decrees of councils. It is therefore no wonder that in the time of Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, shortly before the Council of Nicaea, nearly a hundred bishops of Egypt agreed to the condemnation of Arius and of certain other bishops too; for at that time not only Egypt but also Thebais and both Libyas obeyed Alexander, since a hundred years or so had passed from Demetrius's synods to this time, within which span of time the number of bishops in those provinces had increased wonderfully. What the learned man adds about Dionysius, Demetrius's successor after Heraclas, is of no account at all. For although Heraclas, Dionysius's predecessor and Demetrius's immediate successor, had created twenty bishops, as Eutychius writes on page 332, there were already more bishops in Egypt before Dionysius; and most of those whom Dionysius names did not belong properly to Egypt, but to the provinces of Thebais and the Libyas. Nor do I think it far from the truth that under this Dionysius those provinces, Thebais and both Libyas, first began to render obedience; whether they were moved to it by the very famous reputation of that most holy man, or by the greatness and splendour of the city of Alexandria, or by some other reason unknown to us, and that then for the first time the foundations of the metropolitan rights of the bishops of Alexandria were actually laid throughout all those provinces, to be afterwards confirmed by the sixth canon of the Council of Nicaea. Pearson says that the tradition about the three bishops first made in Egypt by Demetrius was unknown to the Greeks and the Latins; but he proves this by the authority of writers, Eutychius's contemporaries or near-contemporaries, or later ones, who must be placed below the patriarchs of that see in the affairs of the Alexandrian Church. The same kind of argument is found in his last observation, that Eutychius does not report this little story as a tradition received from his ancestors, but, as a solution made in honour of his own Church, to a critical or philological question debated among the Arabs of his time.

units.la: Nam occasionem quam habuit Eutychius hanc texendi narrationem, cum ipsâ narratione. confundit Pearsonius; quæcunque fuerit occasio, sufficit ut narratio sit meræ historica, historicam autem esse cuivis legenti patet: imò historiam repetit ab initio, ut propositæ quæstioni melius respondeat. At si erravit Eutychius in vocibus Abba & Papa, viderit ipse, errata ejus non praesto, quæ vera narrat am-plectòr.
units.tr: Pearson confuses the occasion that prompted Eutychius to weave this narrative with the narrative itself. Whatever the occasion was, it is enough that the narrative is purely historical, and anyone who reads it can see that it is historical. Indeed, he repeats the history from the beginning so that he answers the question put to him more fully. But if Eutychius erred in the words Abba and Papa, let him answer for it himself. I do not defend his errors; I accept what he narrates as true.

units.la: Sic vindicavimus ab exceptionibus Viri docti traditionem Ægyptiacam, ejusque originem ac durationem usque ad Demetrij tempora demonstravimus, eámque non fictam, ut vult Pearsonius, sed veram esse probavimus, quod confirmat Dallæus Ecclesiæ Æthiopicæ exemplo, Eutychianam traditionem, inquit, firmat idem institutum in antiquissimâ, ac nobilissimâ Ecclesiæ Ægyptiæ traduce, Æthiopicâ scilicet Christianitate, ad hæc usque tempora servatum. In omni enim Æthiopicâ Ecclesiâ, unus est jam ab antiquis temporibus Episcopus, Abuna, ut vocant, id est Patriarcha, qui etiam hodie ab Alexandrino Patriarcha consecratur, ac mittitur. Assertionis suæ testes quatuor adducit Dallæus, Alphonsum Mindesium, Nicolaum Godignum, Ioannem à Sanctis, Franciscum Alvarem; Hi omnes testantur Æthiopum Abunam ab Alexandrino Patriarcha mitti ac consecrari, neque alios conferre ordines, quàm Diaconatum & Presbyteratum, ut de more erat Episcopis Alexandrinis usque ad Demetrium, qui tres primùm constituit Episcopos; respondet Pearsonius ex eo quod hodie fit apud Christianos Æthiopas, minimè concludi posse idem. in Ægypto ad Demetrium usque observatum fuisse ; sed fallitur Vir doctus,nam valebit consequentia , donec probatum fuerit recentem esse hanc consuetudinem , nec ab initio apud Christianos il- los obtinuisse;ostendat istius usus originē, & antiquissimum non esse demonstret: quod certè difficillimum erit, præsertim si attendatur antiquorum rituum vulgò tenacissimas esse gentes quæ crassissimâ laborant ignorantiâ, nec eorum abrogationem facilè pati ; ut novos suscipiant, & à pristinis abducantur consuetudinibus, quibus mordicùs adhærent : Est igitur plus quàm verisimile hanc quâ de agimus consuetudinem in Ecclesiâ Æthiopicâ ab initio viguisse ,eandémque fuisse in hac Ecclesiæ Ægyptiæ traduce regiminis formam , quæ fuit in Ecclesiâ matrice Ægyptiâ videlicet ; nec diffitetur Pearsonius Æthiopas aliquando Christianam religionem ab Ægyptijs hausisse , de tempore tantùm quærit; cujus cognitio ( inquit ) erat ad hoc argumentum plane necessaria ; verùm illam necessitatem non capio; nam quocunque tempore id contigerit , nihil ad rem facit, dummodo regimen tale fuerit quale descripsimus ; regimen autem illud minimè toleratura erat Ecclesia Ægyptia Æthiopicæ mater , nisi suum plane similè initio fuisse exploratum habuisset: præterea de tempore adeò sollicitus esse non debet Vir doctus,cùm constet juxta popularis ejus Brerevvood videlicet observationem , Æthiopiam Episcopo Alexandrino à Patribus Concilij Nicæni primi contributam fuisse, quod ego potiùs de juris in Æthiopiam confirmatione interpretarer , & ita explicandus videtur Gelasius Cizicenus à quo sua mutuatus est Londinensis Professor: Liturgia verò Æthiopum Romæ impressa, quam memorat Pearsonius: & in quâ Archiepiscoporum & Episcoporum fit mentio, contra Historiæ veritatem, ad usum Latinorum dubio procul fuit accommodata; preces autem quæ extant in Missalibus Castelli quod attinet, ejusmodi sunt ut nihil certi hinc elici possit, Episcopos enim distinguunt à Sacerdotibus, & Sacerdotes à Presbyteris, quasi Sacerdotes medij cujusdam essent ordinis, Episcopos inter & Presbyteros, quod est omninò absurdum. Dallæus hisce exemplis non contentus, aliud adducit ex Germanicâ Bajoariorum gẽte desumptum: Nam ex Gregorij P. R. III. Epistolâ ad Bonifacium An. D. 739. datâ discimus, inquit, in illa gente & Christi fidem viguisse & Presbyteros fuisse, cum tamen nulli apud eos essent Epis-
units.tr: In this way I have defended the Egyptian tradition against the objections of this learned man. I have shown its origin and its duration up to the time of Demetrius, and I have proved that it is not fictitious, as Pearson claims, but true. Dallaeus confirms this with the example of the Ethiopian Church, saying: Eutychius's tradition is confirmed by the same practice, preserved to the present day in the most ancient and noble offshoot of the Egyptian Church, namely the Christianity of Ethiopia. For in every Ethiopian Church there has been, since ancient times, one bishop, called Abuna, that is, patriarch, who is even today consecrated and sent out by the Patriarch of Alexandria. Dallaeus brings four witnesses for his assertion: Alphonsus Mendes, Nicolaus Godignus, John of the Saints, and Francis Alvarez. All of them testify that the Ethiopian Abuna is sent out and consecrated by the Patriarch of Alexandria, and that he confers no orders other than the diaconate and the presbyterate, as was the custom of the bishops of Alexandria up to Demetrius, who first appointed three bishops. Pearson replies that from what happens today among the Ethiopian Christians nothing can be concluded about what was observed in Egypt up to Demetrius. But the learned man is mistaken. The inference would hold only if it were proved that this custom is recent and that it did not prevail among those Christians from the beginning. Let him show the origin of this practice and demonstrate that it is not most ancient. That will surely be very difficult, especially if one considers that peoples are generally most tenacious of ancient rites, that they live in the thickest ignorance, and that they do not easily suffer those rites to be abolished, so that they would take up new ones and be drawn away from the old customs to which they cling tenaciously. It is therefore more than probable that the custom we are discussing flourished in the Ethiopian Church from the beginning, and that the form of government in this offshoot of the Egyptian Church was the same as in the mother Egyptian Church. Pearson does not deny that the Ethiopians at some time received the Christian religion from the Egyptians; he only asks about the time, saying that knowledge of it was plainly necessary for this argument. But I do not see that necessity. Whenever that happened, it makes no difference to the matter, provided the government was such as we have described. Moreover, the Egyptian Church, the mother of the Ethiopian, would never have tolerated that government unless it had known for certain that the beginning was plainly similar. Besides, the learned man ought not to be so anxious about the time, since it is established, according to the observation of his fellow countryman Brerewood, that Ethiopia was assigned to the bishop of Alexandria by the Fathers of the first Council of Nicaea. I would rather interpret this as a confirmation of the right over Ethiopia, and Gelasius of Cyzicus seems to be the proper explanation of it. The London professor took his account from him. As for the Ethiopian liturgy printed at Rome, which Pearson mentions, and in which mention is made of archbishops and bishops, contrary to the truth of history, it was without doubt adapted to Latin use. As for the prayers that are found in the Missals of Castellus, they are of such a kind that nothing certain can be drawn from them, for they distinguish bishops from priests and priests from presbyters, as though priests formed an intermediate order between bishops and presbyters, which is utterly absurd. Dallaeus, not content with these examples, adduces another, taken from the German tribe of the Bavarians: For we learn from the letter of Pope Gregory III to Boniface, dated A.D. 739, that in that people both the faith of Christ flourished and presbyters existed, although there were no bishops among them at all, and that Vivilo, I know not who, was the first, whom Gregory himself consecrated to that order and sent to them.

units.la: Recherch de la diversité de langage et de religion, p. 272. (note text as printed above; marginal notes Pearf. pag. 187. 188. placed beside the text at "in quâ Ar-") scopi , & Vivilonem nescio quem primùm fuisse , quem ipse Gregorius à se in eum ordinem consecratum ad eos misit. Quid ad hæc Vir doctus, dicit primùm illud quod octavo sæculo factum est , non probare Epistolas Ignatianas sæculo secundo & tertio non extitisse; At id probat quod probare debet, scilicet Ignatiana Bajoarijs incognita fuisse, vel pro spurijs habita , dum religionem Christianam suscenperunt, alioqui Presbyteris solis Ecclesias suas non commisissent, contra quam diserte præcipit Epistolicus Ignatius. Secundo observat Pearsonius Vivilonem non fuisse primum illius gentis Episcopum , nec contrarium affirmare Gregorium, sed in locum Episcopi defuncti missum fuisse , hoc autem probat ex titulo præcedentis Gregorij Epistolæ quatuor Bajoarijs Episcopis inscriptæ , quasi negaret Dallæus plures tunc extitisse in Bajoariâ Episcopos, hoc tantum dicit nullum ante Vivilonem Bajoarios habuisse Episcopum , quod profecto ex Epistolâ clarè colligitur. Addit Dallæus neque septimo sæculo notam fuisse Epistolici Ignatij autoritatem Scotis Christianis, apud quos ex Beda didicimus[?] fuisse Insulæ Ionæ Abbatem Presbyterum , cujus juri & omnis Provincia, & ipsi etiam Episcopi subjecti essent; juxta exemplum primi Doctoris illius, qui non Episcopus, sed Presbyter extiterat, observat quidem Beda institutum istud ordine inusitato factum suisse, sed observatio ista causam non juvat Auctoris Vindiciarum, quoniam si nota fuissent Episcopis Scotis Ignatiana, vel institutum illud non toleras-sent, vel saltem ad id excusandum aliquid adduxissent: Canon Chalcedonensis quem adfert Vir doctus est plane dissimilis, nec quicquam commune habet cum Ionensium instituto; an autem Ionenses emunctae naris critici fuerint necne, nihil scire refert; hoc unum ex illorum extraordinario instituto colligimus, Ignatiana eis plane incognita, vel ab illis despecta fuisse.
units.tr: Recherche de la diversité de langage et de religion, p. 272. (The marginal notes of Pearson, pp. 187 and 188, are placed beside the text at "in quâ Ar-".) Bishop, and Vivilo, I know not who, was the first, whom Gregory himself consecrated to that order and sent to them. What does the learned man say to this? First, he says that what happened in the eighth century does not prove that the Ignatian epistles did not exist in the second and third centuries. But it does prove what it ought to prove: that the Ignatian writings were unknown to the Bavarians, or were regarded as spurious, when they embraced the Christian religion. Otherwise they would not have entrusted their churches to presbyters alone, contrary to what the Ignatius of the epistles expressly commands. Second, Pearson observes that Vivilo was not the first bishop of that nation, and that Gregory does not affirm the contrary, but that he was sent in place of a bishop who had died. He proves this from the title of the preceding letter of Gregory, which is addressed to four Bavarian bishops, as though Dallaeus denied that several bishops then existed in Bavaria. Dallaeus says only that before Vivilo the Bavarians had no bishop, and this is clearly gathered from the letter itself. Dallaeus adds that the authority of the Ignatian epistles was not known to the Scottish Christians even in the seventh century. From Bede we learn that among them the abbot of the island of Iona was a presbyter, and that the whole province, and the bishops themselves, were subject to his authority, following the example of the first teacher of that church, who was not a bishop but a presbyter. Bede indeed observes that this institution was established in an unusual order, but that observation does not help the author of the Vindiciae. For if the Ignatian writings had been known to the Scottish bishops, they would either not have tolerated that institution, or at least they would have offered something to excuse it. The canon of Chalcedon that the learned man cites is plainly unlike it and has nothing in common with the practice of the Iona men. Whether the men of Iona were shrewd critics or not, it matters nothing to us. From their extraordinary institution we gather only this: the Ignatian writings were plainly unknown to them, or were despised by them.

units.la: Omnibus Dallæi exemplis duo celeberrima subtexere non pigebit, quorum alterum à Scytharum Christianorum consuetudine petitum est, in universâ siquidem Scythiâ unus fuit Episcopus, qui sedem Tomis habebat, cæteræ Scytharum Ecclesiæ Presbyteris parebant, & ab eis regebantur, etsi multas haberent civitates, ut nos docet Sozomenus lib. 7. c. 19. Certè in Provinciâ Scythiâ, quamvis multæ urbes sint, unus est omnium Episcopus. Et lib. 6. c. 21. Hæc Provincia Scytharum multas urbes & vicos continet & castella. Metropolim autem habet Tomes, urbem magnam & opulentam. Vetus autem illic consuetudo etiamnum manet, ut totius Provinciæ Ecclesias unus tantum regat Episcopus. Hunc Scytharum morem non attigit Dallæus, non quia contempsit, sed quia non succurrit, ut amico monenti rescripsit; & sanè maximi erat momenti ad argumentum quod tractabat roborandū; ille quippe usus Ignatianis legibus planè penitusque adversatur; tamen eruditus Pearsonius ex isto Scytharum more colligit pag. 170. traditionem Ægyptiam de quâ fusè disseruimus Ignatianis minimè nocere, neque hinc sequi eorum ignorationem: & ut fœlicius procedat ejus Argumentatio, observat Scytharum Episcopum interfuisse Concilio Nicæno, cùm Ignatiana, inquit, essent notissima; Scytharum Episcopum Concilio interfuisse testatur Eusebius de vitâ Constantini lib. 3. c. 7. Sed Ignatiana tunc temporis notissima fuisse scribit nemo: contra affirmare non vereor Patribus Nicænis vel incognita fuisse, vel in nullo prætio habita: nam si pro germano Ignatij [?] cœtu ea habuissent, & ad illorum notitiam pervenissent, aliquem condidissent Canonem, ut impostorum singulis civitatibus ordinarentur Episcopi, nec solis Presbyteris administrandæ crederentur, & ad illud Decretum sanciendum eo magis impulsi fuiss-nc[?], quod plures alibi extra Scythiam essent urbes sine Episcopis Presbyterorum regimini permissæ; Hinc factum est ut trecenti & octodecim tantùm Episcop' Nicæam convenerint, ut discimus ex Niceta Choniate,qui præterea testatur in thesauro Orthodoxæ fidei, lib. 5. c. 5. Scytharum morem ad sua usque tempora perdurasse,id est ad duodecimum usque sæculum: Cùm enim (inquit) nondum civitatibus omnibus suis obtigisset Episcopus, eo[?] factum est, ut plures id temporis non convenerint. Provinciarum enim aliæ uni tantùm parebant, ut Scythia seu Russia in hodiernum usque diem. Aliæ duos, aut ad summum tres habebant, ut Dalmatia. Cùm hoc Nicænis Patribus cõpertum esset, nihilque disciplinæ Ignatianæ magis contrarium fingi posset; eos huic malo,decreto quodam obviam ituros esse par est credere, si illis cognitus atque probatus fuisset Epistolicus Ignatius. Alterum quod adfero exemplum ex usu penè similli desumptum est,obtinebat autem mos ille Iustini Imperatoris ætate in Taprobana insulâ,ubi nullus erat Episcopus, sed Presbyter in Persidę ordinatus Ecclesiam unà cum Diacono suo regebat; hoc ita esse narrat Cosmas Monachus apud Lucam Holstenium de Ministro confirmationis pag. 39. Legi, inquit, insignem relationem Cosmæ Monachi Indicopleustæ de Ta-probanâ Insulâ, quæ nunc Zeilan, olim Seiladiva dicebatur, ubi Iustini Imperatoris ætate Ecclesiam Christianorum Presbyter in Perside ordinatus unà cum Diacono suo regebat. Fragmentum Græcum de Topographia Christianâ illius Monachi videre contigit, in quo extat quod de Taprobana insulâ ex illo descripsit Holstenius, exceptâ temporis notâ, quæ in reliquo opere sine dubio est expressa; Græca autem sic sonant; habet hæc Insula Ecclesiam Persarum Christianorum ibi peregrè agentium, & Presbyterum in Perside ordinatum, & Diaconum & omnem Ecclesiasticam Liturgiam. His forte addi possent quæ observat reverendissimus Vsserius de Britannicarum Ecclesiarum primordiis pag. 668. non deesse qui unum tantùm in universo Pictorum regno Episcopum fuisse volunt; qui Abernethij in Strathernià consederit; sic enim in Scotichronico scriptum invenit his verbis: His temporibus fuit locus ille sedes principalis Regalis & Pontificalis totius regni Pictorum, quando non fuit nisi unus solus in regno Episcopus. Quicquid sit, quot sunt exempla ejusmodi, tot sunt contrà Epistolicum Ignatium Argumenta, sed de his hactenus.
units.tr: I will not hesitate to add two very famous examples to all of Dallaeus's instances. The first is taken from the custom of the Christian Scythians. In the whole of Scythia there was one bishop, who had his see at Tomis, and the other churches of the Scythians obeyed the presbyters and were governed by them, although they had many cities, as Sozomen tells us, book 7, chapter 19: Certainly in the province of Scythia, although there are many cities, there is one bishop for them all. And book 6, chapter 21: This province of the Scythians contains many cities and villages and fortresses. It has Tomis as its metropolis, a large and wealthy city. But the ancient custom still remains there, that one bishop alone governs the churches of the whole province. Dallaeus did not touch this Scythian custom, not because he despised it, but because it did not occur to him, as he wrote in reply to a friend who advised him. Certainly it would have been of the greatest importance for strengthening the argument he was handling. For that practice is wholly and utterly opposed to the Ignatian laws. Nevertheless the learned Pearson, from this Scythian custom, concludes on page 170 that the Egyptian tradition, which we have discussed at length, is in no way harmful to the Ignatian writings, and that it does not follow from it that they were unknown. And so that his argument may proceed more happily, he observes that a bishop of the Scythians was present at the Council of Nicaea, since the Ignatian writings, he says, were very well known. Eusebius, in his Life of Constantine, book 3, chapter 7, attests that a bishop of the Scythians was present at the council. But no one writes that the Ignatian writings were very well known at that time. On the contrary, I do not hesitate to affirm that they were either unknown to the Nicene Fathers or held in no esteem at all. For if they had held them as genuine works of Ignatius, and if they had come to their knowledge, they would have drawn up some canon ordering that bishops be appointed in each city, lest they be entrusted to presbyters alone. They would have been all the more moved to pass that decree because in many other places outside Scythia there were cities left to the government of presbyters alone. Hence it is that only three hundred and eighteen bishops gathered at Nicaea, as we learn from Nicetas Choniates. He further testifies, in the Thesaurus of Orthodox Faith, book 5, chapter 5, that the Scythian custom lasted down to his own times, that is, to the twelfth century: For since (he says) not all their cities had yet obtained a bishop at that time, it came about that not many bishops gathered. For some provinces obeyed only one, as Scythia or Russia does to this day. Others had two, or at most three, as Dalmatia did. Since this was known to the Nicene Fathers, and since nothing more contrary to Ignatian discipline could be imagined, it is right to believe that they would have moved to meet this evil with some decree, if the Ignatius of the epistles had been known and approved to them. The second example I cite is taken from a practice almost similar. That custom prevailed in the island of Taprobane in the time of the Emperor Justin, where there was no bishop, but a presbyter ordained in Persia governed the church together with his deacon. Cosmas the Monk, quoted by Lucas Holstenius in his work on the minister of confirmation, page 39, narrates that this was so: I have read, he says, a notable account by Cosmas the Indian-voyager Monk about the island of Taprobane, which is now called Ceylon and was formerly called Sieladiva, where in the time of the Emperor Justin the Christian church was governed by a presbyter ordained in Persia, together with his deacon. I have had the chance to see a Greek fragment of that monk's Christian Topography, in which is found what Holstenius took from him about the island of Taprobane, except for the note of time, which is certainly expressed in the rest of the work. The Greek words run thus: This island has a church of Persian Christians living there as strangers, and a presbyter ordained in Persia, and a deacon, and the whole ecclesiastical liturgy. To these might perhaps be added what the most reverend Ussher observes about the beginnings of the British churches, page 668: there are those who want only one bishop to have existed in the whole kingdom of the Picts, one who settled at Abernethy in Strathearn. For he found it written thus in the Scotichronicon: In those times that place was the principal royal and pontifical seat of the whole kingdom of the Picts, when there was only one bishop in the kingdom. Whatever the case, as many examples of this kind as there are, so many arguments are there against the Ignatian epistle. But enough of these matters for now.

units.la: IN VINDICIARVM
units.tr: On the Vindiciae

units.la: Partem posteriorem.
units.tr: The latter part.

units.la: EXCVSSIMVS Argumenta externa à testimonijs petita, quæ ex tribus primis Centurijs pro suis Ignatianis adduxerat Vir doctus, fuséque demonstravimus valere adhuc Dallæi objectiones ; etsi eas refellere pro virili, sed frustrà conatus sit eruditus Pearsonius; testibus in contrarium à Dallæo allatis auctoritatem suam vindicavimus, & præterea duo negativa Dallæi Argumenta expendimus , & Viri docti hypothesi non parum nocere ostendimus, idem de cæteris facilimè ostensuri , nisi brevitati studeremus , & observationes scribere tantùm statuissemus. Iam ventilanda nobis sunt Argumenta interna ex Epistolis ipsis ducta, quamvis non tàm Argumenta proponat ipse Pearsonius, ut in fronte seu in titulo promittebat , quàm Dallæi objectiones confutare nitatur. Ut ut est præcipua ex instituti ratione seligemus, eaque accuratè examinabimus, ut liquidò constet, uter causâ cadat, Dallæus nimirùm, an Pearsonius; scribit quidem Vindiciarum Auctor pag. 2. 3. 4. Opus Epistolicum de quo lis est, Apostolico Viro rectè competere, nihilque in eo esse quod imposturam prodat, sed quoniam contrarium ex sequentibus patebit, non est quod in istis refellendis immoremur. Observat primò Vir doctus de Episcopis quidem Asiæ multa loqui Ignatium, quos ibi tùm suisse constat, ídque probat quibusdam veterum testimonijs, imprimis Clementis Alexandrini qui ita loquitur apud Eusebium lib. 3. cap. 23. Cùm enim ex insulâ Patmo Ephesum redisset Ioannes, ad finitimas quoque Provincias rogatus se contulit, partim ut Episcopos constitueret, partim ut Ecclesias integras disponeret ac formaret, partim etiam ut homines sibi. à divino Spiritu inlicatos in clerum quendam seu sortem Domini seponeret. Hæc Clementis verba ex eo libro quem inscripsit, Quisnam dives salvandus sit, descripta sunt, Librum autem integrum anno proximè elapso edi curavit Franciscus Combefisius; Verùm animadvertere debebat Pearsonius; Veteres qui de Episcopis à Ioanne institutis loquuti sunt, ex usu sui temporis loquutos ,ut nihil dicam de ijs qui juxta Viri docti placita non loquuntur ,instar omnium erit unus Irenæus cujus hæc sunt verba apud eundem Eusebium , & in eodem capite mox laudato , Omnes ,inquit, Presbyteri qui cum Ioanne Domini discipulo in Asiâ familiariter versati sunt, ita sibi à Ioanne traditum testantur. Presbyteros nuncupat Irenæus , quos Clemens Episcopos dicit ; Hinc sequitur vel Irenæum ad Ioannis ætatem respexisse , Clementem verò ad suam , vel utrúmque Presbyteri & Episcopi vocibus indiscriminatim usum esse, quoniam Ioannis Apostoli temporibus, idem erat Presbyter qui Episcopus, unus idémque gradus,una eadémque dignitas , sed varijs insignita nominibus ; & sanè Clemens Alexandrinus in eadem narratione , nomen Episcopi & Presbyteri promiscuè usurpat: reliqui quos citat Pearsonius ex sui sæculi more sine dubio loquuti sunt. Secundò scribit eruditus Pearsonius Ignatium juxta Eusebij observationem munire potissimum Ecclesias adversus suâ ætate pullulantes & latè grassantes Hæreses ; si de suâ ætate pullulantibus & grassantibus Hæresibus solùm scripsisset Ignatius, verisimilior esset Viri docti ex Eusebio observatio; sed quia de Valentini hæresi agitur in Epistolico Ignatio, omni prorsus verisimilitudine caret ejusmodi observatio. Tertiò Eusebius, inquit, Ignatii Epistolas tantâ cum diligentiâ descripsit, quod ipsæ visæ sint Traditionem Apostolicam conservare, fateor plura esse in Epistolis quæ etiamnum extant, quæ doctrinam sapiunt Apostolicam, sed ideò non sequitur quin varias præ se ferant suppositionis notas. Instat Vir doctus & dicit Ignatium Charismatum meminisse tunc in Ecclesiâ maximè florentium, & Spiritus sancti ad se nonnunquam loquentis, quod posteriores facere non solent; Charismatum meminisse potuit Ignatius, cùm eorum meminerint Scriptores Ignatio posteriores; idem dico de allocutionibus & afflatibus Spiritus sancti qui Prophetiæ dono plures post Ignatii martyrium locupletavit variisque beavit visionibus, ut norunt qui hisce studis[?] aliquam operam navarunt, & Irenæi, Origenis, & Eusebii scripta non indiligenter versarunt. Tandem asserit Pearsonius nihil reperiri posse in Epistolis quibus de agimus, quod aliam seu posteriorem ætatem sapiat: Verùm hoc gratis affirmat Vir doctus, cùm de hæresibus post se natas loquitur Epistolicus Ignatius, ac proinde violationis temporum reum se manifestissimè prodat; nec verum est quod addit Pearsonius, pace illius dixerim, Dallæum Epistolas ipsas accuratissime inspicientem & diligentissime rimantem, nihil adhuc hujus generis offendisse; contrarium certe ex ijs quae scripturi sumus patebit, & ita dilucide ut in dubium vocari nequeat, quin Valentini hæresis post Ignatij mortem orta, Epistolarum confarcinatori cognita fuerit.
units.tr: We have run through the external arguments drawn from testimonies, which the learned man adduced for his Ignatian letters from the first three centuries. We have shown at length that Dallæus's objections still hold, though the learned Pearsonius tried, as far as he could, to refute them and failed. By the witnesses Dallæus cited against him, we have vindicated their authority. We have also weighed two negative arguments of Dallæus and shown that they do no small harm to the learned man's hypothesis. We could show the same easily for the rest, were we not aiming at brevity and had we not decided to write only observations. Now we must examine the internal arguments drawn from the Epistles themselves. Pearsonius does not so much propose arguments, as he promised on his title page, as strive to refute Dallæus's objections. Still, we will choose the principal ones, as our plan requires, and examine them accurately, so that it becomes clear which side falls, Dallæus or Pearsonius. The author of the Vindiciae writes on pp. 2, 3 and 4 that the epistolary work in dispute properly belongs to an apostolic man and that nothing in it betrays an imposture. But since the contrary will be clear from what follows, there is no need to linger on refuting these claims. First, the learned man observes that Ignatius speaks much of the bishops of Asia, who are known to have existed there at that time, and he proves this by certain testimonies of the ancients, above all Clement of Alexandria, who speaks thus in Eusebius, book 3, chapter 23: For when John had returned from the island of Patmos to Ephesus, he went also, at the request of the neighbouring provinces, partly to appoint bishops, partly to arrange and form whole churches, partly to set apart as clergy, or as the lot of the Lord, certain men marked out by the divine Spirit. These words of Clement are taken from the book he entitled Who is the rich man who will be saved? Franciscus Combefis had the whole book edited last year. But Pearsonius ought to have noticed that the ancients who spoke of bishops instituted by John spoke according to the usage of their own times. I say nothing of those who, by the learned man's own account, do not speak in this way. One, Irenaeus, will serve for all. His words, in the same Eusebius and the same chapter just cited, are: All the presbyters, he says, who were familiar with John the disciple of the Lord in Asia, testify that they were so handed down to them by John. Irenaeus calls presbyters those whom Clement calls bishops. From this it follows either that Irenaeus looked back to John's age and Clement to his own, or that both used the words presbyter and bishop interchangeably, since in the time of the apostle John the presbyter and the bishop were the same: one rank, one dignity, though marked by different names. Indeed, Clement of Alexandria himself, in the same narrative, uses the names bishop and presbyter interchangeably. The others whom Pearsonius cites no doubt spoke according to the custom of their own century. Second, the learned Pearsonius writes that Ignatius, according to Eusebius's observation, chiefly fortifies the churches against the heresies springing up and spreading widely in his own age. If Ignatius had written only about heresies springing up and spreading in his own age, the learned man's observation from Eusebius would be more probable. But since the heresy of Valentinus is discussed in the Ignatian Epistle, such an observation lacks all probability. Third, Eusebius, he says, copied out the letters of Ignatius with such care that they seem to preserve the apostolic tradition. I grant that many things in the Epistles which survive still savour of apostolic doctrine. But it does not follow that they do not bear various marks of spuriousness. The learned man insists that Ignatius mentioned charismata, which were then flourishing most in the Church, and the Holy Spirit speaking at times in his own person, which later writers do not usually do. Ignatius could have mentioned charismata, since writers later than Ignatius mention them. I say the same of the addresses and inspirations of the Holy Spirit, who enriched many after Ignatius's martyrdom with the gift of prophecy and blessed them with various visions, as those know who have taken some pains with these studies and have read the writings of Irenaeus, Origen and Eusebius with care. Finally, Pearsonius asserts that nothing can be found in the Epistles under discussion that savours of a later or different age. But the learned man affirms this without grounds, since Ignatius in the Epistles speaks of heresies that arose after his own time, and so he plainly reveals himself guilty of anachronism. Nor is it true, with respect be it said, that Dallæus, examining the Epistles most accurately and searching them most diligently, had found nothing of this kind so far, as Pearsonius adds. The contrary will certainly be clear from what we are about to write, and so clearly that it cannot be doubted that the heresy of Valentinus, which arose after Ignatius's death, was known to the compiler of the Epistles.

units.la: Hisce delibatis pergit Vir doctus, & ut ea quæ Dallæus adversus Epistolas Eusebio cognitas ex ipsis observavit, nullam omnino ad earum Autoritatem imminuendam vim habere ostendat, profitetur se eodem ordine quo Dallæus perscripsit singulatim omnia persequuturum esse. Incipit autem Dallæus ab argumento à tempore ducto, & cap.
