X. affirmat non pauca passim occurrere, quæ statam atque immotam temporum fidem, certissimum veritatis [?]ἐκεῖνον, graviter pulsant ac convellunt; plura ejusmodi adfert in illo capite, sed præter unum Hieronymi testimonium, cætera Vindiciarum Auctorem non feriunt, quoniam desumpta sunt vel ex Epistolis quas ipse rejicit, vel ex interpolationibus quibus contaminatæ fuerunt, quas pro germanis habet; Dallæus videlicet, hoc Ignatianarum Epistolarum negotium simul semelque totum tractare in se suscepit; ideoque ex omnibus Epistolis iuxta instituti rationem argumenta descripsit, ut opus integrum Ignatio abjudicaret; immerito igitur Dallæi propositum sugillat Vir doctus pag. 14. quasi lectorum oculis nebulam obtendere, & Theologorum Anglorum sententiae sæpè insidias struere voluisset; si candorem præstantissimi illius Theologi novisset Pearsonius, non adeò iniquum de eo judicium tulisset; sed missam faciamus præposteram Vindiciarum Auctoris reprehensionem, & Hieronymi testimonium expendamus, quod ita se habet, Nunquid non possumus tibi totam veterum Scriptorum seriem commovere, Ignatium, Polycarpum, Irenæum, Iustinum martyrem, multosque alios Apostolicos & eloquentes Viros, qui adversus Hebionem, & Theodotum Byzantinum, & Valentinum, hæc eadem sentientes plena sapientiæ volumina conscripserunt; quæ si legisses aliquando, plus sape[?]res. Hinc colligit Dallæus Ignatium scripsisse adversus Theodotum & Valentinum, quod cum vero Ignatio competere non possit, quia denatus erat ante natas istorum hæreses, de Epistolico interpretatur verba Hieronymi, cui solus Epistolicus Ignatius ex Eusebio notus erat: con[?]sequentiam probat Dallæus ex eo quod Polycarpus, Iustinus, aut Irenæus contra Theodotum non scripsit, neque scribere potuit si illum audimus, ut plane necesse sit ad Ignatium referri, quae de Theodoto dicit Hieronymus; verum Viri τῷ μακαρίτῃ[?] pace dixerim, haec partium enumeratio non usquequaque perfecta mihi videtur; Nam Hieronymus de multis aliis Apostolicis viris loquitur, qui quidem viri Apostolici, solos Apostolorum discipulos non complectuntur, sed eos etiam si Pearsonio fides, qui Apostolorum discipulis familiariter usi sunt, temporibusque Apostolicis vicini fuerunt: solis tamen Apostolorum discipulis cogruere Hieronymi verba putat Clarissimus Dallaeus, ac proinde ad Epistolicum Ignatium pertinere quae de Theodoto scripsit antiquus ille Ecclesiae doctor; sed quia angusta nimis est juxta Pearsonium ista viri Apostolici notio, consequentia Dallaeana ei non omnino necessaria videtur; quare illam istis exceptionibus pulsare non veritus est eruditus Pearsonius; sed propterea superior non extitit; Nam donec constet quis ex illis viris Apostolicis adversus Theodotum scripserit, Hieronymi verba non minus Ignatio congruent quam caeteris,non mirum igitur si Dallaeus ex illis argumentatus sit, nec mirum pariter si Pearsonius aliquid ex ijsdem adversus Dallaei argumentum exceperit; ambo enim ita agunt; ut in dubio maneat lectoris animus utriusque respectu; Dallæus siquidem semper affirmabit Ignatium scripsisse adversus Theodotum, quæ cùm de vero Ignatio dici nequeant, de Epistolico erunt intelligenda, seque hac ratione tuebitur, nullum alium Apostolicum virum adversus eum scribere potuisse; Pearsonius verò hanc Dallæi assertionem negabit, ob hanc præsertim rationem, quod Hieronymus loquitur de multis aliis Apostolicis Viris, per quos Vindiciarum Auctor non solos Apostolorum Discipulos intelligit, sed etiam discipulorum ipsorum auditores, & in genere scriptores omnes Catholicos qui temporibus Apostolicis vicini fuerunt. Negare non potest Dallæus hanc vocis Apostolici significationem usitatam esse; sed fateatur etiam Pearsonius necesse est, solis Apostolorum discipulis ac auditoribus non raro congruere, si posteriorem sequimur notionem vincit Dallæus, si priorem convellitur illius argumentatio; etsi forte non penitus refellatur; nihil certi igitur ex eruditorum virorum disputatione elicere poterit lector, nisi prius inter se conveniant de vera istius vocis in Hieronymi verbis significatione; intereà observo non plane Pearsonio cum Augustino convenire Nazareorum respectu ; Pearsonius siquidem existimare videtur Nazaraeos idem de Christo sentire cum Ebionaeis pag. 22. 32. 35. 57. Augustinus tamen utrosque ita distinguit, ut Ebionaeos Christum merum hominem dicere ; Nazaraeos autem eum Dei filium confiteri diserte affirmet ; & verisimile est Nazaraeos illius Ebionaeorum classis esse, qui Christum ex Virgine & Spiritu sancto natum dicebant, ut testantur Origenes, Eusebius & Theodoretus, cum caeteri eum ex Maria & Ioseph genitum docerent.
units.tr: Having touched on these points, the learned man proceeds. To show that the things Dallæus observed in the Epistles, which were known to Eusebius, have no force at all in diminishing their authority, he declares that he will go through everything one by one, in the same order in which Dallæus wrote. Dallæus begins with the argument from time, and in chapter X he asserts that not a few things occur everywhere which strike and overturn the fixed and unshaken faith of the dates, the most certain of truth. He brings forward many such things in that chapter. But apart from one testimony of Jerome, the rest do not touch the author of the Vindiciae, since they are drawn either from the Epistles he rejects, or from the interpolations with which they were corrupted, which he holds to be genuine. Dallæus, that is, undertook to treat this whole matter of the Ignatian letters at once and in a single sweep. Therefore he drew his arguments from all the Epistles, in keeping with his plan, so as to deny the whole work to Ignatius. The learned man, then, unjustly censures Dallæus's purpose on p. 14, as if he wanted to cast a fog before the readers' eyes and often to lay snares for the opinion of the English theologians. If Pearsonius had known the candour of that most distinguished theologian, he would not have passed so unfair a judgment on him. But let us set aside the Vindiciae author's premature reproof and weigh the testimony of Jerome, which reads thus: Can we not set before you the whole series of the ancient writers: Ignatius, Polycarp, Irenaeus, Justin Martyr, and many other apostolic and eloquent men, who wrote full volumes of wisdom against Hebion, Theodotus of Byzantium, and Valentinus, holding the same views? If you had ever read them, you would be wiser. From this Dallæus gathers that Ignatius wrote against Theodotus and Valentinus. Since this cannot be said of the true Ignatius, because he had died before those heresies arose, Dallæus interprets Jerome's words of the Epistolary Ignatius, the only Ignatius known to Eusebius. He proves the inference from the fact that Polycarp, Justin and Irenaeus did not write against Theodotus, and, if we listen to him, could not have written against him. So it is plainly necessary that what Jerome says about Theodotus be referred to Ignatius. But, with respect to the <τῷ μακαρίτῃ> [the late man] be it said, this enumeration of names does not seem to me altogether complete. For Jerome speaks of many other apostolic men, who are not confined to the disciples of the apostles alone, but include also those who, according to Pearsonius's view, were familiar with the apostles' disciples and lived close to apostolic times. Yet the most illustrious Dallæus thinks Jerome's words fit only the disciples of the apostles, and that therefore what that ancient Doctor of the Church wrote about Theodotus pertains to the Epistolary Ignatius. But because the notion of apostolic men is, according to Pearsonius, too narrow, Dallæus's inference does not seem entirely necessary to him. Therefore the learned Pearsonius did not hesitate to strike at it with these exceptions. But the inference does not for that reason fail. For until it is established who among those apostolic men wrote against Theodotus, Jerome's words fit Ignatius no less than others. It is no wonder, then, that Dallæus argued from them, nor equally no wonder that Pearsonius took something from the same words against Dallæus's argument. For both proceed in such a way that the reader's mind remains in doubt about each of them. Dallæus will always maintain that Ignatius wrote against Theodotus, and since this cannot be said of the true Ignatius, it must be understood of the Epistolary one. In this way he defends himself: no other apostolic man could have written against him. Pearsonius, however, will deny this assertion of Dallæus, chiefly on this ground, that Jerome speaks of many other apostolic men, by whom the Vindiciae author understands not only the disciples of the apostles but also the hearers of those disciples, and in general all the catholic writers who lived close to apostolic times. Dallæus cannot deny that this meaning of the word apostolic is in common use. But Pearsonius too must grant that the words of Jerome do not rarely fit the disciples and hearers of the apostles alone. If we follow the broader sense, Dallæus wins; if the narrower, his argument is overturned, though perhaps it is not wholly refuted. So the reader can draw nothing certain from the learned men's dispute, unless they first agree on the true meaning of that word in Jerome's sentence. Meanwhile I observe that Pearsonius does not wholly agree with Augustine about the Nazarenes. Pearsonius seems to think that the Nazarenes held the same views about Christ as the Ebionites, on pp. 22, 32, 35 and 57. Augustine, however, distinguishes the two so that he says the Ebionites called Christ a mere man, while the Nazarenes expressly confessed him to be the Son of God. It is likely that the Nazarenes were a class of those Ebionites who said that Christ was born of the Virgin and the Holy Spirit, as Origen, Eusebius and Theodoret testify, while the others taught that he was born of Mary and Joseph.

units.la: Caput undecimum Dallaei intactum relinquimus, ea enim quae in illo observantur, vel vindiciarum Auctorem non tangunt, vel tanti non sunt momenti ut nos detinere debeant, ideoque praetermisso isto capite ad duodecimum properamus, in quo extat palmerium ut ita dicam ex ipsis Epistolis adversus Ignatiana deductum Argumentum; scribit quippe Clarissimus Dallaeus Epistolas quas habemus, Valentini λόγον [?] ἀ Sige processisse fingentis, delirium diu post Ignatij mortem, editum & sparsum, disertis verbis memorare & refutare, unde colligit nothas esse ac spurias, cum nulla major aut illustrior suppositionis nota proferri queat quàm ejusmodi temporum violatio: Nam quomodo quaso verus Ignatius hæresim post suum Martyrium exortam notare & perstringere potuit? Hoc suum argumentum fusè persequitur Dallæus per totum caput sexdecim constans paginis, idque ab omnibus exceptionibus magnâ diligentiâ ut solet vindicare conatur; Pearsonius verò in eo argumento quo summopere urgetur refellendo, quinque insumit capita, 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. paginas videlicet circiter 63. Verba ex quibus argumentatur Dallæus, reperiuntur in Epistola ad Magnesianos; Unus Deus est, qui manifestavit seipsum per Iesum Christum Filium ipsius, qui est ipsius verbum æternum, non à silentio progrediens; ἐκ ἀπὸ Σιγῆς προελθὼν[?]. De verborum veritate nulla lis est Dallæum inter & Vindiciarum Auctororem[?], extant siquidem in Vsserij, & Vossij editionibus illius Latina, hujus Græca; quamvis nescio quo facto in vulgatis Ignatij Græcis Latinisque editionibus, quædam alia verba istorum loco habeantur; Conjiciebat Dallæus hanc mutationem consultò & ob aliquam rationem ab interpolatore factum suisse, veritas est nè ista si legerentur, Epistolas non Ignatij, sed alterius recentioris esse proderent, viditque istam Verbi scilicet à Sige emanationem Valentinum Ignatio recentiorem olere : eò delendam putavit, nè personati Ignatij drama proderet. Hanc Dallæi conjecturam ridet Pearsonius, etsi omni prorsùs verisimilitudine non careat : nec obstat quod scribit Vindiciarum Auctor, non ita sibi cavisse Interpolatorem, quin plura loquutus sit, quæ tria post Valentinum sæcula saperent ; fateor planos & impostores non semper sibi cavere, nec ita rebus suis prospicere, vt nihil eis planè excidat quod illorum adversetur proposito ; sed fateri debet etiam Vir doctus non malè aliquando rebus suis providere istiusmodi [illegible, ~2 letters]nfarcinatores, & ea sæpissimè expunge[illegible, ~2 letters] solere, quæ eorum judicio impostura prodere possent, fraudémque aperire, quæ sibi nocere putant isti homines eradunt, vel saltem ea ad suum propositum suffectis alijs verbis detorquere conantur ; quæ sibi adversari non animadvertunt, prætereunt, vel si aliquâ sollicitantur suspicione, ea aliquomodo incrustata & immutata propinant, sed quia deest illis in pluribus sagacitas atque solertia ingenij acumen, rerumque multarum notitia ; fieri non potest quin edant alicubi figmentorum suorum specimina, & seipsos fraudis & impostura reos agant ; sic se gessit Ignatianarum Epistolarum interpolator, qui Dallæi conjecturæ locum dedit; conjecturam autem suam suffultam volebat, primùm mirifico quodam Petavii effugio, quo illa de Sige verba à Valentini sensu abducere conatus est. Quid ad hæc Vir doctus; dicit Dallæum aliter atque aliter de Petavio sentire; quasi verò crimen sit de celeberrimo illo Iesuita ita sentire; dùm vera narrat ac sequitur, à Dallæo probatur, dum falsa scribit rejicitur: nihil aliud hoc in loco sibi vult Dallæus, nisi Petavium verba de quibus controvertitur, Valentinum notare vidisse, & ea propter plura ex[illegible, ~2 letters]gitasse, ut illa à Valentini sensu abduceret; secundò asserit ibidem Dallæus verba ista ad Valentini dogma adeò apta atque apposita esse, ut etiamsi mens auctoris aliò, dùm ea scriberet, respexisset: fieri tamen non potuerit, quin ea Irenæus si nosset, arriperet, & contra Valentini expositum à se somnium alicubi usurparet; cui scilicet adeò bellè congruunt, ut in id ipsum primò ab Auctore destinata non possint non videri, si totam orationem simpliciter, & absque ullo præjudicio legeris: constat tamen Irenæum nusquam in totâ contra Valentinianos disputatione, horum verborum meminisse. Respondet Pearsonius non ita disputasse Salmasium, non Albertinum, tinum , qui scriptas fuisse has Epistolas ante Irenæi libros ultro fatebantur , neque eas Irenæo incognitas fuisse vel somniabant ; de Dallæo agitur , non de Salmasio aut Albertino , ideóque recténe an malè senserit Dallæus investigandum ; pergit Vir doctus & hanc Dallæi conclusionem reprehendit. Ergo inquit Dallæus pag. 295. undecúnque hæc verba sumptasint, & quicúnque sit eorum de cætero sensus, illa tamen evidens nobis Argumentum ministrant, ad demonstrandam harum Epistolarum novitatem ac suppositionem. Itáne ait Pearsonius pag. 30. quicúnque sit horum verborum sensus: Ita profectò Vir doctissime, Dallæus enim ut quivis videt loquitur per concessionem, quasi diceret, ne diutiùs digladiemur de loco unde hæc verba descripta sunt, quia videlicet in vulgatis editionibus non extant, neque de sensu, quia nimirùm nullus affingi poteft, qui Valentini hæresim non pulsef: Hanc autem fuisse clarissimi Dallæi mentem ex sequentibus patet, sed Auctorem, inquit, hæc verba scribentem, illuc spectasse, quo ipsa feruntur, & in eum, quem feriunt, scopum rectà collineasse : quis dubitet? Ipsa autem in Valentinum ferri, eiusque delirium reapse ferire, non est, ut opinor, obscurius. Pænitcat [?] ergo Vindiciarum Auctorem[?] suae in Dallaeum reprehensionis, quando legitima est Dallaeana consequentia, ex Irenaei silentio ducta : Quae addit Pearsonius de Marcello nihili sunt, aliud enim fuit de Verbo Marcelli figmentum, aliud Valentini, & ingens inter utriusque silentium discrimen. Silentium quippe Marcelli praecessit Verbum, sed non produxit; Valentini vero silentium, Verbum antecess-sit[?] & genuit; verba autem Ignatiana Valentini Verbum feriunt, ea igitur verba adducturum fuisse Irenaeum contra Valentinum scribentem, si ei nota fuissent, par est credere, illa enim si suâ ætate extitissent non potuit ignorare Irenaeus, imprimis cùm auditor fuerit Polycarpi, Ignatianarum Epistolarum, si earum patronos audimus, Collectoris. Iam nemo non videt non adeò levem esse antecedentium conjecturarum velitationem, ut persuadere conatur eruditus Pearsonius, nec ab eo ut asserit difflatam esse; Quicquid sit ad Argumentum ipsum à Valentino ductum accedit: utque illud nullam vim ad elevandam Ignatij autoritatem, immò nè speciem quidem aut verisimilitudinem continere ostendat, quatuor propositionibus rem omnem se complexurum prositetur, quibus & veritatem luculenter exponet, & omnibus Adversariorum obje[?]ctionibus[?] manifestissimè occurret. Magna sunt quæ pollicetur Vir doctus, ideóque majorem laudem consequetur, si fidem liberare & promissis stare potest; Eum igitur sequamur, illiúsque rationes & argumenta expendamus, ut post accuratum examen veritas si fieri potest magis ac magis elucescat.
units.tr: We leave Dallaeus's eleventh chapter untouched, since the things noted there either do not touch the author of the Vindiciae or are not important enough to hold us back. So, passing over that chapter, we hurry on to the twelfth, where there is, so to speak, a palm-tree of argument drawn from the Epistles against the Ignatian writings. The most distinguished Dallaeus writes that the Epistles we have are the fabrication of someone who invented the Word [λόγον] from Silence [Σιγή] after the manner of Valentinus, a fiction published and spread long after Ignatius's death. He states this in plain words and refutes it, and from this he concludes that the letters are spurious and forged, since no clearer or more striking mark of forgery can be offered than such a violation of the times. For how, I ask, could the true Ignatius notice and attack a heresy that arose after his own martyrdom? Dallaeus pursues this argument at length through a whole chapter of sixteen pages, and, as is his habit, he labours with great care to defend it against every objection. Pearsonius, however, in refuting the argument by which he is so strongly pressed, spends five chapters on it, the 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th and 7th, that is, about sixty-three pages. The words on which Dallaeus argues are found in the Epistle to the Magnesians: There is one God, who manifested himself through Jesus Christ his Son, who is his eternal Word, not proceeding from silence [ἐκ ἀπὸ Σιγῆς προελθὼν]. There is no dispute between Dallaeus and the author of the Vindiciae about the truth of the words, for the Latin of them is found in the editions of Usher and Vossius, and the Greek in the other. Yet, I know not how, in the common Greek and Latin editions of Ignatius some other words stand in their place. Dallaeus conjectured that this change was made deliberately by an interpolator for some purpose: the truth is that if these words were read, they would show that the Epistles are not Ignatius's but those of some later writer. He saw that this emanation of the Word from Silence smelt of Valentinus, who was later than Ignatius, and so he thought it should be removed, lest the drama of the assumed Ignatius should be exposed. Pearsonius laughs at this conjecture of Dallaeus, although it is not wholly without likelihood. Nor does it matter that the author of the Vindiciae writes that the interpolator did not take such care that he did not say more things which savour of the three centuries after Valentinus. I grant that frauds and impostors do not always guard themselves, nor provide so well for their affairs that nothing at all slips out which runs counter to their purpose. But the learned man must also admit that such patchers do not always provide badly for their affairs, and that they very often are accustomed to strike out those things which, in their judgement, could betray the imposture. They erase whatever they think may harm them and expose their fraud, or at least they try to twist those things to their purpose by putting other words in place of them. Things which they do not notice are adverse to them they pass over; or if they are troubled by some suspicion, they serve them up somewhat plastered over and altered. But because in many cases they lack shrewdness, quickness of wit, and knowledge of many things, it cannot be that they fail to put out somewhere specimens of their fabrications and make themselves guilty of fraud and imposture. So the interpolator of the Ignatian Epistles behaved, and he gave occasion to Dallaeus's conjecture. He wished, however, to support his conjecture first by a remarkable evasion of Petavius, by which he tried to draw those words about Silence away from the sense of Valentinus. What does the learned man say to this? He says that Dallaeus thinks differently about Petavius at different times, as if it were a crime to think so about that most famous Jesuit. When he relates and follows the truth, he is approved by Dallaeus; when he writes falsehoods, he is rejected. Dallaeus means nothing else in this place than that Petavius saw that the words under dispute point to Valentinus, and that for this reason he laboured at many things in order to draw them away from the sense of Valentinus. Secondly, Dallaeus asserts in the same place that these words fit and suit the teaching of Valentinus so well that, even if the author's mind, in writing them, had regard to something else, it could not have failed that Irenaeus, if he knew them, would have seized upon them and somewhere used them against the dream of Valentinus, which he had set forth. They agree so well with that dream that, if you read the whole passage simply and without any prejudice, they cannot but seem to have been aimed by the author at that very thing first. It is nonetheless established that Irenaeus nowhere, in his whole disputation against the Valentinians, mentions these words. Pearsonius replies that Salmasius did not argue thus, nor Albertinus, who readily admitted that these Epistles were written before the books of Irenaeus, and did not even dream that they were unknown to Irenaeus. The question concerns Dallaeus, not Salmasius or Albertinus; so it must be investigated whether Dallaeus judged rightly or wrongly. The learned man goes on and finds fault with this conclusion of Dallaeus. Therefore, says Dallaeus on page 295, from wherever these words have been taken, and whatever their sense may be in other respects, they nevertheless supply us with a plain argument for demonstrating the newness and the forgery of these Epistles. Does Pearsonius, on page 30, say: whatever the sense of these words may be? Indeed so, most learned sir, for Dallaeus, as anyone can see, speaks by way of concession, as if he were saying: let us no longer wrangle about the place from which these words have been copied, because they are evidently not found in the printed editions, nor about their sense, since indeed no sense can be invented which does not strike at the heresy of Valentinus. That this was the mind of the most distinguished Dallaeus is clear from what follows: but the author, it says, who wrote these words, had regard to that to which they are directed, and aimed straight at the mark which they strike: who can doubt it? That they are aimed at Valentinus, and really strike at his folly, is not, I think, more obscure. Therefore the author of the Vindiciae should repent of his rebuke of Dallaeus, since Dallaeus's inference, drawn from the silence of Irenaeus, is a legitimate one. What Pearsonius adds about Marcellus is worth nothing, for the Word of Marcellus was one fiction and that of Valentinus another, and there is a vast difference between the silence of the one and the other. For the Silence of Marcellus came before the Word but did not produce it; but in Valentinus the Silence came before the Word and begot it. The Ignatian words, however, strike the Word of Valentinus, so it is right to believe that Irenaeus, when writing against Valentinus, would have brought forward those words had he known them, for if they had existed in his day he could not have been ignorant of them, especially since he was a hearer of Polycarp, the collector, if we listen to the defenders of the Ignatian Epistles. Now no one fails to see that the skirmish of the preceding conjectures is not so slight as the learned Pearsonius tries to persuade us, nor, as he asserts, has it been blown away. Whatever the case, he comes to the argument drawn from Valentinus itself. And so that he may show that it has no force for weakening the authority of Ignatius, nor even the appearance or likelihood of it, he professes that he will set out the whole matter in four propositions, by which he will both clearly expose the truth and most plainly meet all the objections of his opponents. The learned man promises great things, so he will win the greater praise if he can free the faith and keep his promises. Let us therefore follow him, and weigh his reasons and arguments, so that after a careful examination the truth may, if possible, shine forth more and more.

units.la: Quatuor propositionibus totidem assignavit capita, ita ut unaquæque suum habeat caput; prima Assertio caput quartum complectitur, & istis concipitur verbis, Autorem Epistolæ ad Magnesios verbis ex eâ prolatis hæresin Ebionitarum, neque ullam aliam respexisse. Assertionis probationem hanc adfert; Duæ, inquit, conjunctivæ particulæ, una initio huiusce sententiæ, altera principio sequentis inserta, satis manifestè ostendunt quo tota sententia referenda sit, & ad quid Autor Epistolæ, cùm eā scriberet, collineârit. Pertendit autem Vir doctus, Ebionem disertè ferire, & antecedentem sententiam quæ particulâ rationali enim sive nam indicatur, & sequentem quæ particulâ illativâ igitur designatur. Antecedens hæc est, si enim us-que nunc secundum Iudaismum vivimus, confitemur gratiam non recepisse. Sequens sic se habet, si igitur in veteribus rebus conversati, in novitatem spei convenerunt. Verba autem quæ ex eadem ad Magnesios Epistolâ adfert Dallæus, & quæ peculiarem Valentini hæresis characterem continere asserit, media sunt inter utrámque sententiam ab Auctore Vindiciarum descriptam ; ultrà progreditur eruditus Pearsonius, & quia Ebionæi Iudaïcis addicti erant consuetudinibus, affirmare non dubitat, Epistolæ scriptorem directè adversus Ebionem & sequaces militare, & cùm Christum dixit Verbum æternum, id breviter explicare ijs verbis, non à Sige procedens, seu ut vertit Pearsonius non à silentio proveniens, quemadmodum, inquit, verbum seu sermo omnis qui æternus non est : addit Vir doctus hanc adjectionem, non à Sige procedens, nihil aliud esse quàm exegesin sive explicationem æternitatis Verbi, eámque planè naturalem & obviam, & sine ullo respectu ad aliam aliquam peculiarem hæresin maximè propriam, reddentem veram notionem æterni verbi, & ab alio verbo non æterno rectè distinguentem ; quia hic est omnium hominum vulgaris de verbo conceptus, ut quod silentium respiciat, sitque præcedentis silentij solutio, quod probat pluribus testimonijs, ex sacris & profanis Scriptoribus desumptis. Hæ sunt primæ Viri docti ad Dallæi argumentum exceptiones, ingeniosissimæ sanè & acutissimum Vindiciarum Auctoris ingenium redolentes; sed vereor ne plus subtilitatis habeant quàm soliditatis, nam ut à novissima incipiam, quid opus erat explicatione istâ æternitatis Verbi, non à Sige procedens, ut ab alio verbo non æterno distingueret; Nonne æterni epitheto, à verbo humano quod silentium rumpit in tempore, satis superque distinguebatur? æternum enim & temporale, si ita l[illegible, ~2 letters]i fas est, contradictorie opponuntur, [illegible, ~2 letters] fieri potest ut quod ab omni parte æternum, sit temporale, neque tempora-le æternum, qui dicit æternum omnia quæ in tempore fiunt, æternitatis iure dejicit atque deturbat; si igitur Epistolæ ad Magnelios scriptor tantùm in animo habuit Christum Verbum æternum,à Verbo humano quod in tempore fit & citò transit distinguere, solâ æterni voce propositum finem est consecutus; nec aliâ ullâ ad rem per se claram & omnibus obviam enodandam explicatione egebat. Sed aliud est notatu dignissimum Christum videlicet non simpliciter dici Verbum æternum, at Verbum Dei æternum; En tibi Epistolæ Ignatianæ verba, unus Deus est, qui manifestavit seipsum per Iesum Christum filium ipsius, qui est ipsius Verbum æternum: Quoniam autem nota erat Auctori Epistolæ Valentinianorum hæresis, qui Verbum à silentio progredi docebant, hæc verba continenter subjecit, non à si-lentio progrediens, ut ita veram Christi Verbi æterni originem indicaret, & à salsâ secerneret, docendo nimirum Christum Verbum æternum à Deo Patre verâ in Divinis personâ provenire, ut fert Evangelium, non autem à Sige ut hario-l[illegible, ~1 letter]ntur Valentiniani, qui Verbum à si-[illegible, ~4 letters]io, tanquam à personâ divinâ, se-[illegible, ~2 letters]oris tamen sexus, gigni ac procreari falsò comminiscebantur. Cætera quæ in eadem Epistolâ ad hæreticum Valentini dogma spectant lubens prætermitto, quia de illis alius erit dicendi locus; Interim expendamus num directè Ebionem feriant Ignatij Epistolici verba, ut vult Vindiciarum Auctor; solos enim Ebionæos ea petere ac jugulare contendit pag. 33. 34. 35. & cap. 5. pag. 56. 57. neque id solum, sed præterea sibi gratulatur pag. 35. quod de Hæresi Ebionis ea dixerit, quæ nondum à quopiam dicta sunt.
units.tr: We have assigned four propositions, each with its own chapter. The first assertion occupies chapter four and is put in these words: The author of the Epistle to the Magnesians, in the words quoted from it, had in view only the heresy of the Ebionites and no other. He offers this proof of the assertion: Two conjunctive particles, one placed at the beginning of this sentence and the other inserted at the start of the following one, show quite plainly to what the whole sentence is to be referred, and at what the author of the Epistle was aiming when he wrote it. The learned man contends that he strikes Ebion directly, and he marks off the preceding sentence, introduced by the rational particle enim sive nam (for, or indeed), and the following sentence, designated by the illative particle igitur (therefore). The antecedent is this: For if we still live according to Judaism, we confess that we have not received grace. The following runs thus: If therefore they, having lived in ancient things, came to the newness of hope. The words which Dallaeus quotes from the same Epistle to the Magnesians, and which he asserts contain the peculiar mark of the heresy of Valentinus, lie between the two sentences described by the author of the Vindiciae. The learned Pearson goes further. Since the Ebionites were devoted to Jewish customs, he does not hesitate to affirm that the writer of the Epistle fights directly against Ebion and his followers. When he called Christ the eternal Word, he explains this briefly with the words not proceeding from Sige, or, as Pearson translates, not arising from silence, just as, he says, every word or speech which is not eternal does. The learned man adds that this addition, not proceeding from Sige, is nothing other than an exegesis or explanation of the eternity of the Word, and a quite natural and obvious one, made without any reference to some other peculiar heresy. It gives the true notion of the eternal Word and rightly distinguishes it from another, non-eternal word, because this is the common notion of the word among all men: that it refers to silence and is the solution of a preceding silence. He proves this by many testimonies drawn from sacred and profane writers. These are the learned man's first objections to Dallaeus' argument. They are certainly very ingenious and smack of the most acute intelligence of the author of the Vindiciae, but I fear they have more subtlety than solidity. To begin with the last point: what need was there for this explanation of the eternity of the Word, not proceeding from Sige, in order to distinguish it from another, non-eternal word? Was it not distinguished sufficiently, and more than sufficiently, from a human word, which breaks silence in time, by the epithet eternal? For eternal and temporal, if it is lawful so to speak, are contradictorily opposed. Nor can what is eternal in every respect be temporal, nor the temporal be eternal. Whoever says that everything which happens in time is eternal casts down and overturns the right of eternity. So if the writer of the Epistle to the Magnesians had in mind only to distinguish Christ, the eternal Word, from a human word which comes to be in time and quickly passes away, he attained his end by the single word eternal. He needed no other explanation to unfold a matter which is clear in itself and obvious to all. But there is one point most worthy of notice: Christ is not called simply the eternal Word, but the eternal Word of God. Here are the words of the Ignatian Epistle: There is one God, who manifested himself through Jesus Christ his Son, who is his eternal Word. Since the author of the Epistle knew the Valentinian heresy, which taught that the Word proceeded from silence, he at once added these words: not proceeding from silence. In this way he indicated the true origin of Christ's eternal Word and separated it from the false one, namely by teaching that Christ, the eternal Word, truly proceeds from God the Father in the divine person, as the Gospel says, and not from Sige, as the Valentinians babble. They falsely imagined that the Word was begotten and produced from silence as from a divine person of female sex. I gladly pass over the rest that in the same Epistle concerns the dogma of the heretic Valentinus, since there will be another place to speak of those matters. Meanwhile let us consider whether the words of the Ignatian Epistle strike Ebion directly, as the author of the Vindiciae wishes. For he contends that they seek out and slay only the Ebionites (pp. 33, 34, 35, and ch. 5, pp. 56, 57). Not only that, but he also congratulates himself (p. 35) that he has said about the heresy of Ebion things that no one has yet said.

units.la: Gratuletur sibi eruditus Pearsonius per me licet, gloriæ ejus non invideo, neque illi quicquam detractum volo; sed spero fore ut etiam mihi ignoscat si in ejus sententiam pedibus non concedo; plura siquidem sunt quibus moveor ut aliter sentiam; 1. Hæretici quos ferit Scriptor Epistolæ ad Magnesios Christi mortem negabant, quod de Ebionæis dici nequit, cùm de veritate mortis ac resurrectionis Domini nostri Iesu Christi minimè dubitarent, neque illi qui eum ex Viri cum Mariâ concubitu procreatum censebant, neque alij qui Christum ex Virgine & ex Spiritu sancto genitum fatebantur: utrique enim diebus Dominicis eadem quæ nos, inquit Eusebius Hist. l. 3. c. 27. in memoriam resurrectionis Domini peragebant: Theodoretus itidem Hæret. Fabul. lib. 2. Dominicam more nostro sanctificant. Diem verò Dominicam in memoriam resurrectionis Domini sanctificare non poterant; nisi de veritate mortis ejus planè penitúfque persuasi essent. Ebionæos igitur non notat Epistolæ Auctor, sed Hæreticos qui mortem Christi negabant ac proinde ejus resurrectionem ; neque alibi id disertius testatur Epistolicus scriptor, quam in illa pericope cujus primâ & ultima verba adduxit Pearsonius, relictis medijs quæ utrísque cohærent, & quæ diximus firmissimè probant: sic enim Vir doctissimus, si igitur illi divinissimi Prophetæ in veteribus rebus conversati, in novitatem spei venerunt, non amplius sabbatizantes, sed secundum Dominicam vitam viventes, &c. quomodo nos poterimus vivere sine illo, cujus & Prophetæ discipuli existentes, spiritu ipsum ut Doctorem spectabant. In istis verbis nulla prorsus fit mentio Hæreticorum Christi mortem negantium; at si verba interjecta describimus, nullus supererit dubitandi locus, ita enim Græca Latinè reddimus, si igitur in vetustis rebus versati, ad novitatem spei venerunt, non amplius Sabbatizantes, sed juxta Dominicam vitam viventes, in quâ & vita nostra exorta est per ipsum & mortem ipsius; quam quidam negant: per quod mysterium fidem accepimus, & propter hoc sustinemus, ut inveniamur discipuli Iesu Christi, solius Doctoris nostri. Non me latet veterem Vsserij Interpretem hæc Græca verba οἵ τινες ἀρνοῦνται [?] sic transtulisse, quod quidam negant; cùm tamen articulus Græcus qui pronominis relatiui vices agit, generis sit masculini, alij ad Christum ipsum referentes, sic reddiderunt, quem quidam negant. Ego verò contextui inhærendo, cum propinquiore substantivo, morte videlicet, construxi hoc pacto, quam quidam negant; Et ad hoc in primis inductus sum aliâ ejusdem Epistolæ pericope quæ paulò post sequitur his verbis; Hæc autem scribo dilecti mei, non quod cognoverim aliquos vestrûm sic esse affectos, sed sed ut minor vobis, cupio vobis prospectum, ne incidatis in hamos inanis gloriæ, sed ut plenè certiores redderemini eorum quæ in nativitate & passione, & resurrectione, quæ contigit tempore præfecturæ PONTII PILATI, verè & indubitanter gesta sunt à IesuChristo, spe nostrâ. Quis non videt cunćta Hæreticos illos petere qui veram Christi mortem ac resurrectionem oppugnabant, non verò Ebionem qui utrámque ultrò confitebatur: Valentiniani quidem aliquam Christo suo passionem ac resurrectionem tribuebant; sed quia omnia in illis ficta erant ac commentitia, neque de eis dici possit quòd verè & indubitanter factæ sint, plus quàm verisimile est Scriptorem Epistolæ ad Magnesios, ad eos feriendos rectà collineasse, eorúmque figmentum configere in animo habuisse. 2. Liquet Auctorem Epistolæ eos tangere Hæreticos qui Iesum à Christo separabant, & utrúmque à Verbo dividebant, quod in Ebionæos cadere non potest: Ebionæi siquidem Iesum & Christum pro uno eodémque habebant, neque illum, ut opinor, Verbi nomine unquam indigetabant, solum enim Evangelium secundum Hebræos recipiebant, id est Evangelium secundum Matthæum Hebraïcè scriptum, sed interpolatum & mutilatum, in illo autem Evangelio, nul-la prorsus Verbi mentio; sed in Evangelio secundum Ioannem; fateor equidem Epiphanium observare, ut scribit Pearsonius p. 57. quòd S. Ioannes refutat Ebionæos omnibus modis, dicens, quòd, in principio erat Verbum, & Verbum erat apud Deum, & Verbum erat Deus. Sed hisce verbis S. Ioanni tantum propositum fuit Domini nostri Iesu Christi æternitatem constituere, adversus impiam Ebionæorum opinionem, qui illum nudum hominem asserebant, non autem alicujus Ebionæorum Verbi nomenclaturam & naturam perstringere: Idem plane dico de verbis Eusebij à Viro docto allatis pag. 57. adversus Ebionæos qui Christum ex Virgine & Spiritu S. genitum esse non negabant, cùm tamen ante omnia illum extitisse non faterentur, utpote, ait Eusebius, Deum Verbum & sapientiam, nempe Eusebius hæc duo Epitheta Christo tribuit, non ipsi Ebionæi, qui Christum sub Verbi notione, meo sane judicio non agnoscebant; At Epistolæ ad Magnesios Scriptor Hæreticos ferit, qui non solum alium esse Iesum, alium Christum, alium denique Logum seu Verbum fabulabantur, neque illius æternitatem modo impugnabant, sed etiam à Patre, id est à veto[?] Deo exire negabant, à Sige enim illud progredi fingebant; ut igitur Epistolicus Ignatius veri Dei Verbum à fictitio Valentini Verbo semoveret, illud non à Sige procedere, diserte affirmat.
units.tr: Let the learned Pearson congratulate himself, so far as I am concerned. I do not begrudge his glory, nor do I wish anything to be taken from him. But I hope he will pardon me if I do not yield to his opinion, for there are several reasons that move me to think otherwise. (1) The heretics whom the writer of the Epistle to the Magnesians strikes denied the death of Christ. This cannot be said of the Ebionites, since they did not doubt the truth of the death and resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, nor did those who held that he was born of the intercourse of a man with Mary, nor the others who confessed that Christ was born of the Virgin and the Holy Spirit. For both, as Eusebius says (Hist. bk. 3, ch. 27), celebrated on the Lord's days the same things as we did, in memory of the resurrection of the Lord; and Theodoret likewise (Heret. Fab. bk. 2): they keep the Lord's day after our manner. But they could not sanctify the Lord's day in memory of the Lord's resurrection unless they had been thoroughly and completely persuaded of the truth of his death. So the author of the Epistle does not mean the Ebionites, but the heretics who denied the death of Christ and therefore his resurrection. The Epistle writer testifies to this no more clearly anywhere than in that passage whose first and last words Pearson quoted, leaving out the middle ones, which join the two ends together and which, as we have said, most firmly prove our point. For the most learned man writes thus: If therefore those most divine prophets, having lived in ancient things, came to the newness of hope, no longer keeping the Sabbath but living according to the Lord's life, etc., how shall we be able to live without him, whose disciples the prophets too were, and who looked to him as their teacher in the Spirit? In these words there is no mention at all of heretics who deny the death of Christ. But if we set out the words that were left out, no room for doubt remains. For we render the Greek into Latin thus: If therefore those who were versed in ancient things came to the newness of hope, no longer keeping the Sabbath, but living according to the Lord's life, in which our life also has risen through him and through his death, which some deny; through which mystery we have received faith, and on account of this we endure, so that we may be found disciples of Jesus Christ, our only teacher. I am not unaware that the older translator of Usher rendered the Greek words [οἵ τινες ἀρνοῦνται] as which some deny, although the Greek article, which takes the place of a relative pronoun, is masculine. Others, referring it to Christ himself, rendered it whom some deny. But I, holding to the context and to the nearer substantive, death namely, construed it thus: which some deny. I was led to this chiefly by another passage of the same Epistle, which follows shortly after, in these words: I write these things, my beloved, not because I have known any of you to be so affected, but so that, being less, I may care for you, lest you fall into the hooks of empty glory, but that you may be fully assured of the things that were truly and indubitably done by Jesus Christ, our hope, in his birth and passion and resurrection, which took place in the time of the governorship of Pontius Pilate. Who does not see that all these things are aimed at those heretics who attacked the true death and resurrection of Christ, and not at Ebion, who freely confessed both? The Valentinians indeed attributed some passion and resurrection to their Christ. But because everything in them was fictitious and made up, and it cannot be said of them that these things were truly and indubitably done, it is far more probable that the writer of the Epistle to the Magnesians aimed directly at striking them and had in mind to overthrow their fiction. (2) It is clear that the author of the Epistle is touching those heretics who separated Jesus from Christ and divided both from the Word, which cannot apply to the Ebionites. For the Ebionites regarded Jesus and Christ as one and the same, and, I think, never called him by the name of Word. They received only the Gospel according to the Hebrews, that is, the Gospel of Matthew written in Hebrew, but interpolated and mutilated, and in that Gospel there is no mention at all of the Word. It is true that Epiphanius, as Pearson writes (p. 57), observes that St. John refutes the Ebionites in every way, saying that in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. But St. John's purpose in these words was only to establish the eternity of our Lord Jesus Christ against the impious opinion of the Ebionites, who asserted that he was a mere man. He did not mean to attack any term or nature of a word peculiar to the Ebionites. I say the same plainly of the words of Eusebius quoted by the learned man (p. 57) against the Ebionites, who did not deny that Christ was born of the Virgin and the Holy Spirit, but did not confess that he existed before all things. Eusebius, he says, as being God the Word and wisdom, namely, Eusebius attributes these two epithets to Christ; the Ebionites themselves, in my judgment, did not acknowledge Christ under the notion of the Word. But the writer of the Epistle to the Magnesians strikes heretics who not only fabled that Jesus was one being and Christ another, and finally that the Logos or Word was a third, but who also not only attacked his eternity but denied that he came forth from the Father, that is, from the true God. For they imagined that he proceeded from Sige. So, in order to separate the true Word of God from the fictitious word of Valentinus, the Epistle writer Ignatius clearly affirms that it does not proceed from Sige.

units.la: Sed inquit Vindiciarum Auctor Ignatius hortatur ut à Iudaismo recedant qui Christianismum amplectuntur, scilicet Epistolae Auctor quisquis sit, occasione sumpta à veteribus Valentinianorum fabulis, quas initio pericopes tetigit, Magnesios monet ut à vetustis rebus ad spei ac vitæ novitatem transferantur; sed ita tamen ut in utráque pericope eos petat ac jugulet, qui Verbum à Sige non à vero Deo progredi comminiscebantur, & Christi mortem negabant, quorum illud in priori, hoc in posteriori notat pericope, nec obstant duæ conjunctivæ particulæ quibus innititur Viri docti argumentatio, cùm liquido constet Epistolæ verba Ebionitis competere non posse. Quæ sequuntur in reliquo capite facili negotio solvuntur, immò jam occupata fue-runt; cùm enim non alio tendant, quàm ad ostendendum verba de quibus lis est solos ferire Ebionitas, non est quòd ijs refellendis tempus frustrà insumamus, quando luce meridianâ clarius demonstravimus ea in Ebionæos cadere non posse: Multa dicit de discrimine verbi divini & humani, & quia Petavius eodem confugerat, ut ictum lethalem à suo Ignatio depelleret[?], multus est Pearsonius in celeberrimo illo Iesuita tuendo; plura urget exempla, quæ Ignatiano similia affirmat; ut suam verborum istorum, non à Sige progrediens interpretationem defendat, ea videlicet nihil aliud esse quàm exegesin & explicationem æternitatis Verbi divini, ut ab omni verbo sive sermone creato & humano distinguatur.Sed profectò nullum adferre potuit exemplum in quo verbum humanum à silentio progredi dicatur, est quidem sermo silentij solutio, at inde non sequitur silentium causam esse sermonis aut principium; hæc autem verba à Patre exire, ut loquitur Epistolicus Ignatius, verum generationis Christi principium indicant, non simpliciter terminum à quo coeperit generatio; Ergo & à Sige exire filium, quod negat Epistolæ scriptor, eodem quoque sensu intelligit, nimirum à Sige exire, ut à matre, ut à generationis, non simplici, unde coeperit termino, sed vero principio; adducat Vindiciarum Auctor, phrases Ignatianæ æquales, quæ simplicem generationis terminum significent non verum principium; nam donec talia protuIerit exempla, irriti erunt omnes illius conatus, etiamsi opem ei ferat Aristoteles, docens privativa esse principia, ex quibus, inquit Pearsonius, satis proprie aliquid fieri aut prodire dicitur; Præterquam enim principia ejusmodi non probantur hodie Viris eruditis, qui Physicæ arcana accuratiùs quàm Aristoles rimati sunt; certè Ignatianæ istius locutionis idonei interpretes non mihi videntur Philosophi, neque ad eam intelligendam eorum præceptis opus est, cùm nihil proclivius sit quàm illam de principio rei constitutivo interpretari, quod de silentio dici nequit; Ergo sermonem à silentio exire, locutio absurda est; si verò μετὰ[?] pro ἀπὸ cum Petavio quem tuetur Pearsonius, usurpas, absurdior erit,nam peregrina est & inusitata illa vocis ἀπὸ seu ab significatio, ad quam ideò non recurrendum, nisi urgente necessitate, quæ hic locum non habet;neque melius procedet Viri docti exceptio, si loco horum verborum à silentio, reponas ista ex silentio, & deinde ex cum post commutes, legáque post silentium nulla liquidem talis sit commutatio, nisi fortè de tempore agatur, & præterea non ex silentio dixit Epistolæ scriptor, sed à silentio; Quæ tandem observat Pearsonius de voce προελθεῖν[?], nihili plane sunt, nec Dallæi interpretationem ullo modo convellunt; Etiamsi Valentiniani aliâ voce quoque usi sint ad suorum Æonum emissiones significandas, ut scribit Vir doctus p. 39. nam varias ad id significandum voces eos usurpasse nihil vetat. Porrò hæ sunt meræ logomachiæ, & argutiæ Viro doctissimo indignæ; quia videlicet Dallæi argumentum refellere non potest, neque telum validâ manu in Ignatium suum contortum retorquere, mira quærit effugia eruditus Pearsonius, nescio quas vocum permutationes excogitat, & proprijs vocibus suâ sede depulsis, alias tanquam illarum vicarias sufficere satagit; Qui sic agit se victum fatetur, & ad incitas quodammodo redactum.
units.tr: But the author of the Vindiciae says that Ignatius urges Christians who embrace Christianity to turn away from Judaism. Whoever the author of the Epistle was, he took his occasion from the old fables of the Valentinians, which he touched on at the beginning of the passage, and he urges the Magnesians to pass from old things to the newness of hope and life. In both passages, however, he attacks and slays those who invented that the Word proceeds from Sige, not from the true God, and who denied Christ's death. The first passage marks the former error and the second the latter. The two conjunctive particles on which the learned man's argument rests do not stand in the way, since it is plain that the words of the Epistle cannot apply to the Ebionites. What follows in the rest of the chapter is resolved with little effort; indeed it has already been dealt with. For since its aim is nothing other than to show that the words under dispute strike only the Ebionites, there is no reason for us to waste time refuting them, when we have shown by clearer than noonday light that they cannot fall upon the Ebionites. He says much about the difference between the divine word and the human, and because Petavius had taken refuge in the same argument to ward off the deadly blow from his Ignatius, Pearsonius is busy defending that most famous Jesuit at length. He presses many examples that he asserts are similar to the Ignatian phrase, in order to defend his interpretation of the words not proceeding from Sige, namely that they are nothing other than an exegesis and explanation of the eternity of the divine Word, so that it is distinguished from every created and human word or speech. But he certainly could not bring forward a single example in which a human word is said to proceed from silence. Speech is indeed the breaking of silence, but it does not follow from this that silence is the cause or principle of speech. The words to come forth from the Father, as the Epistle of Ignatius speaks, indicate the true principle of the generation of Christ, not merely the terminus from which the generation began. Therefore the Epistle's writer also understands the Son to come forth from Sige in the same sense, namely to come forth from Sige as from a mother, as from a principle of generation, not as a bare terminus from which it began, but as a true origin. Let the author of the Vindiciae adduce Ignatian phrases equivalent to this which signify a mere terminus of generation and not a true principle. Until he produces such examples, all his efforts will be in vain, even if Aristotle comes to his aid, teaching that there are privative principles from which, says Pearsonius, something is said quite properly to be made or to proceed. For principles of this kind are not approved today by learned men, who have investigated the secrets of physics more carefully than Aristotle did. Certainly the suitable interpreters of this Ignatian expression do not seem to me to be philosophers, nor is their doctrine needed to understand it, since nothing is more obvious than to interpret it as a constitutive principle of a thing, which cannot be said of silence. Therefore a word to come forth from silence is an absurd expression. If, with Petavius whom Pearsonius defends, you use [μετὰ] for [ἀπὸ], it will be more absurd still, for that meaning of the word [ἀπὸ], or from, is foreign and unusual, and one should not have recourse to it unless under pressing necessity, which does not arise here. Nor will the learned man's exception proceed any better if, in place of these words from silence, you substitute out of silence, and then change out of into after, and read after silence; for there is clearly no such change, unless perhaps the question concerns time. Moreover, the author of the Epistle did not write out of silence but from silence. What Pearsonius observes about the word [προελθεῖν] is entirely worthless and does not in any way overturn Dallaeus's interpretation, even if the Valentinians used another word too to signify the emissions of their Aeons, as the learned man writes on p. 39. For there is nothing to prevent them from using various words for this purpose. Moreover, these are mere logomachies and quibbles unworthy of so learned a man. Because he cannot refute Dallaeus's argument, nor hurl back with a strong hand the weapon thrown against his Ignatius, the learned Pearsonius seeks wonderful escapes, invents I know not what exchanges of words, and, having driven the proper words from their place, busies himself in substituting others as their substitutes. One who acts thus confesses that he is defeated and has been driven, in a way, to the wall.

units.la: Sed forsan fœlicior erit Vindiciarum Auctor in stabiliendâ secundâ Assertione, quâ asserit cap. 5. verba illa non à silentio seu Sige progrediens, ut sunt ab Autore Epistolæ ad Magnesios prolata, ad Valentinum omninò non spectare, nec sine violentâ detorsione ad ejus hæresim exponendam & oppugnandam applicari posse. Verùm quando Dallæus contrarium plane affirmat; illum audire necesse est, antequam ad examen revocemus rationes quibus Pearsonius affirmationem Dallæanam pulsare, ac convellere conatur. Observat igitur Dallæus cap. 12. pag. 295.296. Irenæum duobus locis omnem Valentini Mataeologiam exponere; statim in libri limine, & Paulo post capite quinto. Primum enim caput, inquit, ad Valentinum pertinere ostendit, & præfixus ei titulus, & ipsa operis præfatio. Quod hoc pacto probat, Irenæus Valentinum fabulosam suam divinitatem sic disposuisse tradit, ut quemdam ante & supra omnia Æonem in sublimitatibus constitueret, quem Proarcham, & Propatora, & Bython vocaret, ( unde Tertuliani iocus, id nomen in sublimitatibus habitanti minimè congruere ) una cum Bytho extitisse Ennoeam quamdam, quam & ipsam quoque Charin, & Sigen nuncuparet: Ex Bytho in hanc Sigen immissione prodiisse Nun ( quem & Monogenem, & Patrem, & Principium rerum appellaret ) & cum eo Alethiam, id est veritatem: Nun porrò, & suam Alethiam emisisse λόγον καὶ Ζωὴν Verbum & Vitam. Capite inde quinto eadem apud Irenæum occurrunt, innominabilis primò Ἀνὼς[?], sive (ut habet vetus interpres) dualitas, Arrethum sive inenarrabilem (eum ipsum quem Bython priùs dixerat) & Sigen continens; tum altera ex hac prima prodiens Patris (qui idem cum Nun, & Alethiæ Ἀνὸς [?], & ex hac itidem emissa Λόγος [?] καὶ Ζωῆς Verbi & Vitæ Ἀνὸς [?], sive dualitas tertia, & ex hac item quarta Ἀνὸς homo & Ecclesia; sed & præter hanc Æonum Ogdoadem, alios insuper XXII. variè ab illis primis emissos induxisse Valentinum, ut essent universi XXX. quorum ultima Syzygia Theleti esset & Sophiæ. Præterea Christum & Iesum à Verbo divisisse; & Christum quidem finxisse extra aliorum Æonum pleroma à matre Sophia, ut puto, procreatum, excisâ à se umbrâ ad pleroma reversum esse; Iesum verò variè, modò à Theleto, modò à Christo, interdum ab homine & Ecclesiâ ortum dixisse, sed & eum cæteros Æonas ornasse, in hunc unum conferentes, quod optimum singuli atque pulcherrimum habebant. Eadem de Valentinianorum Theogoniâ Tertullianus, Epiphanius & alij, quorum nemo est, qui non ex Sige eductum à Valentino Logon, vel immediatè ut à matre Filium; vel certè mediatè; ut ab aviâ nepotem commemoret. Hactenus præstantissimus Dallæus.
units.tr: But perhaps the author of the Vindiciae will be more fortunate in establishing his second assertion, by which, in chapter 5, he asserts that those words not proceeding from silence or Sige, as they are put forward by the author of the Epistle to the Magnesians, do not refer at all to Valentinus, and cannot be applied without a violent distortion to expound and attack his heresy. But since Dallaeus affirms the contrary plainly, we must hear him before we call into question the arguments by which Pearsonius strives to shake and overturn Dallaeus's assertion. Dallaeus therefore observes, in chapter 12, p. 295-296, that Irenaeus twice expounds the whole mythology of Valentinus: at the very beginning of the book, and again a little later in chapter 5. For the first chapter, he says, shows that it pertains to Valentinus, both by its title and by the preface of the work itself. He proves this as follows. Irenaeus relates that Valentinus arranged his fabulous divinity in such a way that he placed in the heights a certain Aeon before and above all others, whom he called Proarche, Propator and Bythos (whence Tertullian's joke, that this name does not suit one who dwells in the heights). Together with Bythos there existed a certain Ennoea, whom he also called Charis and Sige. From the emission of Bythos into this Sige there came forth Nous (whom he also called Monogenes, Father and Principle of things), and with him Aletheia, that is, Truth. Nous, moreover, emitted his own Aletheia as Logos and Zoe, Word and Life [λόγον καὶ Ζωήν]. Then in chapter 5 the same things occur in Irenaeus: first the unnameable Anous [Ἀνοῦς], or, as the old translator has it, duality, containing Arrhetos, that is, the ineffable (the very one whom he had earlier called Bythos), and Sige. Then another, proceeding from this first, Father (who is the same as Nous, and Aletheia's [Anous], and from her in the same way emitted Logos and Zoe, Word and Life [Anous], or a third duality, and from this in turn a fourth Anous, man and Church). But besides this Ogdoad of Aeons, Valentinus also introduced twenty-two other Aeons, variously emitted by those first ones, so that there were thirty in all, of which the last syzygy was Thelete and Sophia. Moreover, he divided Christ and Jesus from the Word; he invented Christ as having been produced outside the pleroma of the other Aeons by his mother Sophia, I suppose, and, having cut off a shadow from himself, returned to the pleroma. Jesus he variously said to have arisen sometimes from Thelete, sometimes from Christ, and sometimes from man and the Church; and he adorned the other Aeons, bringing together into this one the best and most beautiful qualities that each possessed. Tertullian, Epiphanius and others relate the same things about the Valentinian theogony, and there is none of them who does not mention that Valentinus's Logos was educed from Sige, either immediately, as a son from his mother, or at least mediately, as a grandson from his grandmother. So far the most excellent Dallaeus.

units.la: Quid ad hæc respondeat doctissimus Vindiciarum Auctor, jam expendamus, primò diserte negat à Valentino unquam dictum & assertum esse, Verbum à Sige progredi, aut talem reperiri Genealogiam In iis Fragmentis Valentinianorum quæ etiamnūm extant, & in quibus quis Æon à Sige emis-sus sit, & ex quo Æone emissus sit Logus diserte docetur. Unum ex his apud Irenæum, alterum apud Epiphanium extare fateor, sed in neutro Logon ex Bytho & Sige emissum esse dici nagos;[?] si Dallæus Logon ex Sige immediatè ut à matre filium juxta Valentinum emissum esse scripsisset, aliquem forte colorem ha-beret. Viri docti argumentatio, at cùm Logi ex Bytho & Sige emissionem velim-mediatam vel mediatam proposuerit, & utrumvis admittendam esse asseruerit; incassum laborat Vir doctus ut hanc Dallæi opinionem sollicitet & labefactet; ipse enim diffiteri non audet, quin in Frag-mento Irenæano, Logus ex Bytho & Sige ut ab avo & avia nepos eductus comme-moretur, nempe mediantibus Nu & Alethia: Et sanè Irenæus Æonum Valentinianorum combinationes hoc disponie ordine, Bythus & Sige, Nus & Alethia seu veritas, Logus & Zoe seu vita; Logus igitur à Bytho & Sige educitur ut ab avo & avia nepos, à Nu verò & Alethiâ immediatè ut à parentibus filius nec aliter has fabulosas conjugationes percensent Tertullianus contra Valentinum cap. 7. & 8. Philastrius & Augustinus de Hæresibus, Theodoretus Haereticarum Fabularum lib. 1. cap. 7. nec ipse Epiphanius in Panario Hær. 31. sed inquit Pearsonius in Fragmento quod extat apud Epiphanium aliter se res habet ; Logus siquidem aut ex Nu & Alethia emittitur, mediantibus Anthropo & Ecclesiâ, aut ex Anthropo & Ecclesiâ ; largiamur Viro docto quod petit, ne hilum quidem proficiet ; Nam etiamsi eum quem vult sequamur ordinem in fictitijs Valentinianorum Æonibus numerandis ; Tamen nihilominus Logus ex Sige emittetur, si non ut ab aviâ nepos, saltem ut ab abaviâ abnepos, & in hoc solùm peccaverit Dallæus, quòd Logum Siges nepotem fecerit, non autem in eo quod illum ex Sige rectâ lineâ eductum affirmârit; stemma semper idem, gradus modò anticipatus, veluti Logus Sigen proximiore gradu contingeret. Præterea contra Clarissimum Blondellum contendit Vindiciarum Auctor, Fragmentum quod apud Epiphanium extat, non ex ipsius Valentini libro decerptum esse, sed ex quodam Valentinianorum scripto ; non ignorat autem eruditus Pearsonius Valentini discipulos varias constituisse sectas, & unamquámque sectam Haereticum magistri dogma ita interpolasse, ut sibi aliquid peculiare tribueret, quo ab aliis distingueretur; prudentiores vero ex Valentini discipulis, ut scribit Irenæus lib. i. cap. 6. asserebant Logum non ex Nu & Alethia emissum esse immediate, sed mediantibus Anthropo & Ecclesia seu potius ex Anthropo & Ecclesia procreatum, ecce Irenæi verba. qui prudentiores putantur illorum esse, non ex Logo & Zoe Anthropon & Ecclesiam, sed ex Anthropo & Ecclesia Logon & Zoen dicunt generatos; Ad hos igitur aut eorum similes respexisse Epiphanij Fragmentum non dubito; At Fragmentum quod apud Irenæum extat, proprium ipsius Valentini figmentum describit cap. 5. in illa autem descriptione Logus ex Sige emissus dicitur, non ut filius a matre, sed ut ab avia nepos, quod Dallaeo sufficit; Valentinus, inquit Irenæus, sic definivit, Dualitatem quandam innominabilem, cuius quidem aliquid vocari inenarrabile, aliud autem Sigen. Post deinde ex hac dualitate, secundam dualitatem emissam, cuius aliud quidem Patrem vocat, aliud autem Aletheiam. Ex hac autem quaternatione fructificari Logon & Zoen, Anthropon & Ecclesiam. Ergo juxta fabulosa Valentini placita, Logus ex Sige dicitur emissus, mediantibus Nu & Alethia, eodem plane modo hanc Logi prolationem referunt Philastrius, Epiphanius, Augustinus, Theodoretus. Nec est quod Vir doctus Dallæi distinctionem de emissione mediatâ vel immediatâ sugillet pag. 49. quasi verò nepotes ab avis non descendant, eorúmque non nominentur filij, & avi nepotum patres, ut Nabucadnetsar Belcat-saris pater, & Belcatsar Nabucadnetsaris filius cap. 5. Dan. Quemadmodum ergò nepotes ab avis & avijs descendere non absurdè dici potest, sic Valentini Logon ex Sige ut ab aviâ nepotem emitti pari ratione affirmare licet. Hæc, ait Vir doctus p. 49. distinguendi subtilitas & Valentini & Patrum ævo longè inferior esse cognoscitur, nec ibi adhiberi debuit ubi de nu-da eorum sententiâ quaeritur. Quid audio, nonne distinctione uti solemus, dum sese offert distinguendi occasio? Dallæo oblata fuit ab Ignatianorum patronis, quidni igitur eam adhibuisset? ut res alioquin involutas & veri specie à doctissimis Vi-ris coloratas explicaret, verúmque à sal-so secerneret; Nemo eorum (inquit iterum de Patribus agens) vel mediatè vel immediatè Logon vel ex Sige vel ex alia Æone eductum fuisse dixit. Fateor Patres verbis mediatè vel immediatè non esse abu-sos, quia ad ea usurpanda non eos coge-bat iniqua adversariorum importunitas, rem per se claram ac perspicuam negantium: Sed hinc non sequitur quin Logon ex aliquo Æone eductum asseruerint; Nus emittit ex semetipso Sermonem seu Logon, inquit Tertullianus contra Valentinum cap. 7. en immediatam Logi ex Nu emissionem, imò primam Æonum Tetradem, ut cæterorum principium ac causam ibidem repræsentat; Bythos & Sige, Nus & Veritas, prima quadriga defendit[?] Valentinianæ factionis, matrix & origo cunctorum. Ergo ex Sige educitur Logus,cùm ex primâ emittatur Tetrade, Irenæus pariter, mox enim dicebat, Valentinum definivisse ex prima dualitate Bythi & Siges, secundam emissam esse Nu videlicet & Aletheias; Ex hac autem quaternatione, fructificari Logon & Zoen Anthropon & Ecclesiam; si igitur ex primâ illâ quaternatione fructificatur Logus, ut loquitur vetus Irenæi interpres, id est si illo quaternario editus est, negari non potest quin ex Sige educatur, quando Sige ad primam illius tetradis conjugationem pertinet.
units.tr: Let us now weigh how the most learned author of the Vindiciae answers these points. First, he flatly denies that Valentinus ever said or asserted that the Word proceeds from Sige, or that any such genealogy is found in those fragments of the Valentinians that still survive, in which it is plainly taught which Aeon was sent forth from Sige and from which Aeon the Logos was sent forth. I grant that one fragment survives in Irenaeus and another in Epiphanius, but in neither is it said that the Logos was sent forth from Bythus and Sige. If Dallaeus had written that, according to Valentinus, the Logos was sent forth from Sige immediately, as a son from his mother, his statement might have some plausibility. But although the learned author set out the emission of the Logos from Bythus and Sige as either immediate or mediate, and asserted that either must be admitted, he labours in vain to disturb and overthrow Dallaeus's view. For he himself does not dare to deny that in the Irenaean fragment the Logos from Bythus and Sige is recorded as brought forth as a grandson from grandfather and grandmother, namely through the mediation of Nous and Aletheia. Indeed Irenaeus arranges the combinations of the Valentinian Aeons in this order: Bythus and Sige, Nous and Aletheia or Truth, Logos and Zoe or Life. The Logos is therefore led out from Bythus and Sige as a grandson from grandfather and grandmother, but from Nous and Aletheia immediately, as a son from parents. Tertullian against Valentinus (chapters 7 and 8), Philastrius and Augustine in their books on heresies, Theodoret in his Haereticarum Fabularum book 1, chapter 7, and Epiphanius himself in the Panarion, heresy 31, enumerate these fabulous couplings in no other way. But, says Pearson, in the fragment that survives in Epiphanius the matter stands differently: the Logos is either sent forth from Nous and Aletheia through the mediation of Anthropos and Ecclesia, or from Anthropos and Ecclesia. Let us grant the learned author what he asks, and it will not profit him a whit. For even if we follow the order he wishes in numbering the fictitious Valentinian Aeons, the Logos will still be sent forth from Sige, if not as a grandson from grandmother, at least as a great-grandson from great-grandmother. Dallaeus has erred only in making the Logos a grandson of Sige, not in asserting that he was led out from Sige in a direct line. The genealogy remains the same; only a degree has been brought forward, as if the Logos were related to Sige by a nearer step. Furthermore, against the most distinguished Blondel, the author of the Vindiciae contends that the fragment that survives in Epiphanius was not taken from the book of Valentinus himself but from some writing of the Valentinians. The learned Pearson does not ignore that the disciples of Valentinus formed various sects, and that each sect altered the heretical doctrine of its master so as to attribute to it something peculiar by which it might be distinguished from the others. But the more prudent of Valentinus's disciples, as Irenaeus writes in book 1, chapter 6, maintained that the Logos was not sent forth immediately from Nous and Aletheia, but through the mediation of Anthropos and Ecclesia, or rather was produced from Anthropos and Ecclesia. Here are Irenaeus's words: those who are thought the more prudent among them do not say that Anthropos and Ecclesia were generated from Logos and Zoe, but that Logos and Zoe were generated from Anthropos and Ecclesia. I do not doubt that Epiphanius's fragment looks to these men or others like them. But the fragment that survives in Irenaeus describes Valentinus's own invention (chapter 5). In that description the Logos is said to be sent forth from Sige, not as a son from his mother but as a grandson from his grandmother, and this is enough for Dallaeus. Valentinus, says Irenaeus, thus defined: a certain unnamable duality, of which one part is called inexpressible, and the other Sige. Afterwards, from this duality, a second duality was sent forth, of which one he calls the Father, the other Aletheia. From this quaternity, Logos and Zoe, Anthropos and Ecclesia are brought to fruition. Therefore, according to Valentinus's fabulous tenets, the Logos is said to be sent forth from Sige through the mediation of Nous and Aletheia. Philastrius, Epiphanius, Augustine and Theodoret describe this emission of the Logos in exactly the same way. Nor is there any reason for the learned author to disparage Dallaeus's distinction between mediate and immediate emission (p. 49), as if grandsons did not descend from grandfathers, or as if they were not called sons, and grandfathers were not called fathers of their grandsons, as Nebuchadnezzar was the father of Belshazzar, and Belshazzar the son of Nebuchadnezzar (Dan. 5). Just as it can fittingly be said that grandsons descend from grandfathers and grandmothers, so by the same reasoning we may affirm that, according to Valentinus, the Logos was sent forth from Sige as a grandson from his grandmother. This, says the learned author (p. 49), subtlety of distinction is known to be far later than the age of Valentinus and of the Fathers, and it ought not to have been applied here, where the question is about their bare opinion. What is this I hear? Do we not habitually use a distinction whenever an occasion to distinguish presents itself? The occasion was offered to Dallaeus by the defenders of the Ignatian letters, so why should he not have used it, in order to unfold matters otherwise entangled and coloured with the appearance of truth by the most learned men, and to separate the true from the false? None of them (he says again, speaking of the Fathers) said that the Logos was sent forth from Sige or from any other Aeon, either mediately or immediately. I grant that the Fathers did not misuse the words mediately or immediately, since the unfair importunity of their opponents, who denied what was clear and obvious in itself, did not compel them to use such terms. But it does not follow from this that they did not assert that the Logos was sent forth from some Aeon. Nous emits the Word, or Logos, from himself, says Tertullian against Valentinus, chapter 7. Here is the immediate emission of the Logos from Nous, and indeed the first tetrad of the Aeons, which he presents there as the principle and cause of the rest: Bythos and Sige, Nous and Truth, the first quaternity, the mother and origin of all, defends the Valentinian faction. Therefore the Logos is led out from Sige, since he is emitted from the first tetrad. Irenaeus likewise says, soon after, that Valentinus defined that from the first duality of Bythus and Sige a second was sent forth, namely Nous and Aletheia; and from this quaternity Logos and Zoe, Anthropos and Ecclesia are brought to fruition. If, then, the Logos is brought to fruition from that first quaternity, as the old translator of Irenaeus puts it, that is, if he was produced from that quaternary, it cannot be denied that he is led out from Sige, since Sige belongs to the first conjugation of that tetrad.

units.la: Quod observat Vindiciarum Auctor pag. 44. 45. Nun Monogenen sive unigenitum dictum esse, quòd ille solus ex Bytho & Sige natus est, cujuscúnque respectu id dicat Tertullianus, Dallæo non nocet; nam immediata Nu ex Sige emissio, mediatam Logi ex eadem Sige prolationem non impedit: Dallæus verò Logi ex Sige eductionem mediatam vel immediatam tuetur, alterutram, non utrámque; quamvis utráque aliquatenus defendi possit, mediata, si duas primas Æonum combinationes sejungis, immediata; si eas in primam conflas tetradem, ex qua totâ[?] emitti Logum asserere non veretur Valentinus apud Irenæum lib. 1. cap. 5. Ergo ex Sige quæ primam illius quaternarij cum Bytho conjugationem efficit; nec obstat quod dicit Pearsonius, Bythum videlicet soli Monogeni seu No, quod ab ipso natus esset, notum fuisse; non enim agitur de quorundam Æonum supra cæteros privilegijs, sed de eorum generatione ac procreatione, notus sit Bythus quantum Vir doctus voluerit soli Monogeni, hoc est No; Hinc minimè consequitur Logon ex Sige non emissum fuisse; familiarum primogeniti privilegijs quibusdam vulgò fruuntur præ minoribus natu; sed hæ prærogativæ non impediunt quominus natu minores ad eandem pertineant familiam, iisdemque sint fatiparentibus: At inquit Vindiciarum Auctor quod Bythus soli No notus fuit, non aliunde venit, quam ex eo quod ex ipso natus est; si valeret hæc Viri docti ratiocinatio,idem concludi posset de Aletheia quæ ex Bytho & Sige perinde ac Nus educta[?] fuit; & tamen non notus ei fuit Bythus, quærenda ergo alibi quàm in Monogenis nativitate istius quo gaudet privilegii ratio. Non diffitetur Pearsonius Aletheiam ex Bytho & Sige processisse, hoc solum dicit pag. 45. Aletheiam ex ijsdem quidem processisse Æonibus, sed post Monogenen seu Nun; Esto, hoc sibi peculiare habeat Nus, ex jure ut ita dicam primogenituræ suæ,ut solus Bythum noverit, illud non ægrè feret Alethia, dummodò sibi vicissim non invideatur ex ijsdem parentibus ortus ac nativitas; non igitur simplici ex Bytho & Sige procreatione hanc prærogativam consecutus fuerit Monogenes, sed potius procreationis seu nativitatis prioritate si sic loqui fas est. Præterea errat Vir doctus dum Aletheiam ex Bytho & Sige post Nun processisse scribit; cùm contrarium pateat ex Tertulliano & Irenæo, qui docent Aletheiam unà cum Monogene ex Bytho & Sige emissam esse; Irenæus siquidem observat lib. i. cap. i. Valentinum definivisse unà cum Nu emissam Veritatem; Tertullianus de eodem loquens hæc habet lib. contra Valent. cap. 7. Ita & ipse Padicam in gratiam Blondelli quædam esse in illo Fragmento, quæ illius causam optimè juvare videntur, quare Pearsonius verba illa quibus se tuetur Blondellus corrupta existimat, ut multa alia in eodem Fragmento, idem dicit de quibusdam Cyrilli Hierosolymitani verbis ab eodem Blondello allatis ex Catechesi 6.
units.tr: As to the Vindiciae author's observation (pp. 44–45) that Nous was called the Monogenes or only-begotten because he alone was born from Bythus and Sige, whatever respect Tertullian means by it, this does not harm Dallaeus. For the immediate emission of Nous from Sige does not exclude the mediate emission of the Logos from the same Sige. Dallaeus, however, defends the emission of the Logos from Sige as either mediate or immediate, one or the other, not both. Yet both can be defended to some extent: mediate, if you separate the first two combinations of the Aeons; immediate, if you merge them into the first tetrad, from which Valentinus, in Irenaeus book 1, chapter 5, does not hesitate to assert that the whole Logos was sent forth. So the Logos is from Sige, which forms the first conjugation with Bythus of that quaternary. Nor does it hinder that Pearson says Bythus was known only to the Monogenes or Nous, because he was born from him. The question is not about privileges of some Aeons above the others but about their generation and procreation. Let Bythus be known, as much as the learned man likes, only to the Monogenes, that is, Nous. From this it by no means follows that the Logos was not sent forth from Sige. Among families, the firstborn enjoys certain privileges over the younger sons, but these prerogatives do not prevent the younger sons from belonging to the same family and having the same parents. But the Vindiciae author says that Bythus was known only to Nous, and this arises from nothing else than the fact that Nous was born from him. If this reasoning of the learned man were valid, the same could be concluded about Aletheia, who was brought forth from Bythus and Sige just as Nous was, and yet Bythus was not known to her. So the reason for the privilege enjoyed by the Monogenes must be sought elsewhere than in his birth. Pearson does not deny that Aletheia proceeded from Bythus and Sige; he says only (p. 45) that Aletheia proceeded from the same Aeons, but after the Monogenes or Nous. Grant that Nous has this peculiar thing, by a right of, as it were, his firstborn status, that he alone knew Bythus; Aletheia will not be much aggrieved, provided that in turn her origin and birth from the same parents are not denied her. Therefore the Monogenes obtained this prerogative not by the mere procreation from Bythus and Sige, but rather by priority of procreation or birth, if I may speak so. Furthermore, the learned man is wrong when he writes that Aletheia proceeded from Bythus and Sige after Nous, since the opposite is evident from Tertullian and Irenaeus, who teach that Aletheia was sent forth from Bythus and Sige together with the Monogenes. Irenaeus observes in book 1, chapter 1, that Valentinus defined Truth as sent forth together with Nous, and Tertullian, speaking of the same, has this in book against Valentinus, chapter 7: So also the Father. I will say, for Blondel's sake, that there are certain things in that fragment which seem to support his case very well. For this reason Pearson thinks the words on which Blondel relies are corrupt, as many other things in the same fragment are. He says the same about certain words of Cyril of Jerusalem, quoted by the same Blondel, from the Catechesis 6.

units.la: Non omni igitur verisimilitudine caret Blondelli sententia, cùm rectè refelli nequeat, nisi loca unde deprompta est sollicitando, eáque mendosa atque corrupta dicendo. Cætera quæ cap. 5. comprehenduntur jam expendimus, dum ad Ebionæos haudquaquam respexisse Autorem Epistolæ ad Magnesios probavimus; quicunque enim fuerit Scriptoris illius scopus ac finis, sive ad unitatem Ecclesiasticam hortandi, sive ab hæresi Magnesios dehortandi, rem ita exsequitur, ut ad Valentinum feriendum eum rectè collineasse facilè dixeris, si utrámque pericopen à Dallæo laudatâ attento intuearis animo, præjudiciísque libero: Nam etsi forte omniaunum Valentinum singillatim non petant, cuncta tamen confertim & coglobatim Hæreticum illum jugulant: Imprimis quæ dicit de Iesu Christo, Dei filio, Verbo æterno, & non à Sige progrediente. Si de nudis ageretur nominibus, aliquem for[?]san colorem haberet Viri docti observatio pag. 51. scribentis Valentinianos eundem & Iesum, & Christum, & Logon nominare, quod probat Theodoreti auctoritate, Iesum (inquit lib. 1. c. 7.) inde produxerunt, quem & Servatorem appellant, & Christum Verbum, & Irenæi qui tradit nobis perfectum fructum, Iesum, quem & Salvatorem vocari, & Christum, & Logon, patronymicè, ac omnia, lib. 1. cap. 1. At Vindiciarum Auctorem non latet, Iesum Valentinianorum alium esse à Christo, alium à filio, alium à Verbo, alium denique ab omnibus; etiamsi eorum nuncupetur nominibus: Nam Christus patronymicè vocatur (inquit Epiphanius hær. 31.) propter supernum Christum, & Verbum propter supernum Verbum; immò omnia, ut ait Irenæus, quoniam ab omnibus esset: Ideóque ab omnibus divisus ut effectus à causâ.
