Iesus verò Christianorum idem est cum Christo, cum Filio, cum Verbo æterno ab uno vero Deo Patre exiens; Iam autem Dallæus Scriptoris Epistolæ ad Magnesios vestigia premens, non argumentatur ex nudis Iesu nostri nominibus seu attributis, sed ex eo quod est re vera, nempe Iesus Christus, filius Dei, Verbumque ejus æternum ab eo exiens, una eadémque divina persona; oppofitione factâ ad Iesum Valentinianorum qui divisus est à Christo, à Filio, & à Verbo, quod non ab uno Deo Patre emanat, ut nostrum, sed à Sige progreditur.
units.tr: Blondel's opinion therefore is not wholly lacking in plausibility, since it cannot be properly refuted except by casting doubt on the passages from which it is drawn and declaring them faulty and corrupt. We have already weighed the other matters contained in chapter 5, when we showed that the author of the Epistle to the Magnesians did not have the Ebionites in view at all. Whatever that writer's aim and purpose was, whether to exhort them to ecclesiastical unity or to dissuade the Magnesians from heresy, he so carries it out that you could easily say he rightly aimed at striking down Valentinus, if you look attentively and without prejudice at both passages cited by Dallaeus. For although perhaps not all of them attack Valentinus one by one, yet taken together and in a body they cut that heretic's throat. Especially so is what he says about Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the eternal Word, and not proceeding from Sige. If the matter concerned bare names, the learned man's observation at p. 51, that the Valentinians call the same one Jesus, and Christ, and Logos, would have some plausibility. He proves this by the authority of Theodoret: "They produced Jesus" (he says, book 1, ch. 7), "whom they also call Saviour, and Christ the Word", and by Irenaeus, who hands down to us the full list: "Jesus, whom they also call Saviour, and Christ, and Logos", by patronymic, and so on, book 1, ch. 1. But the author of the Vindiciae is not unaware that the Valentinians' Jesus is other than Christ, other than the Son, other than the Word, and finally other than all of them, even though he is called by their names. For "Christ is called patronymically", says Epiphanius (heresy 31), "on account of the supernal Christ, and Word on account of the supernal Word"; indeed "all things", as Irenaeus says, "since they came from all". Therefore he is divided from all as an effect is from its cause. But the Jesus of Christians is the same as Christ, the same as the Son, the same as the eternal Word going forth from the one true God the Father. Now Dallaeus, following closely the footsteps of the writer of the Epistle to the Magnesians, does not argue from the bare names or attributes of our Jesus, but from what he really is: namely Jesus Christ, Son of God, and his eternal Word going forth from him, one and the same divine person. The opposition is made to the Valentinians' Jesus, who is divided from Christ, from the Son, and from the Word, because he does not emanate from the one God the Father as ours does, but proceeds from Sige.

units.la: Frustrà igitur & immeritò gloriatur Vindiciarum Autor, velut Dallæi argumento satisfecisset, explicatâ & comprobatâ utráque Assertione, primâ videlicet & secundâ; argumentum siquidem Dallæi à Viri docti exceptionibus sic Vindicavimus, omnibúsque illius occurrimus objectionibus, ut deinceps ambigi nequeat, quin ad Valentinum illiúsque hæresin diserte respexerit Epistolarum Autor: contrarium sibi persuasum esse testatur Vir doctus; tamen nè quis in animis eorum, qui Salmasij, Blondelli & Dallæi rationibus hactenus assueti sunt, scrupulus hæreat, & ne suos etiam Usserium, Vossium & Hammondum deserere videatur, eorum responsiones quas firmissimas esse credit, resumere ac confirmare statuit; adeò ut, si quis adhuc sit qui exi-stimat Autorem ad hæresin quàm amplexus est Valentinus collineasse, nè hoc quidem quicquam valeat ad violationem temporum ostendendam, vel autoritatem Epistolarum ullo modo elevandam. Asserit enim tertiò, Hanc ipsam hæresin Valentino fuisse antiquiorem, & à vetustioribus
units.tr: Vainly and undeservedly, therefore, does the author of the Vindiciae boast as if he had satisfied Dallaeus's argument, by explaining and confirming both assertions, namely the first and the second. For we have so defended Dallaeus's argument against the learned man's objections, and met all his objections so fully, that it can no longer be doubted that the author of the Epistles clearly had Valentinus and his heresy in view. The learned man testifies that he is persuaded of the contrary. Nevertheless, lest any scruple remain in the minds of those who have hitherto been accustomed to the arguments of Salmasius, Blondel and Dallaeus, and lest he seem to desert his own men, Usher, Vossius and Hammond, he resolves to take up and confirm their answers, which he believes to be most firm. So that, even if there is anyone who still thinks that the author aimed at the heresy which Valentinus embraced, this too is of no value for showing a violation of the times, or for weakening the authority of the Epistles in any way. For he asserts thirdly that "this same heresy was older than Valentinus and derived from more ancient

units.la: Gnosticis derivatam, eamque præ ætate respicere potuisse S. Ignatium Martyrem, quatenus fuit ab antiquioribus Gnosticis prolata, & antequam in Valentini characterem fuit transformata: ut necesse non sit ad Valentinum hic recurrere. Ita eruditus Pearsonius cap. 6. pag. 59. hanc autem suam Assertionem per totum caput stabilire laborat, an faustis vel infaustis avibus videbimus, primò varia adfert in hanc rem Veterum testimonia, scribitque p.60. neminē eorum esse qui Valentinum veterem opinionem resuscitasse nō diserte tradat.
units.tr: Gnostics; and that St Ignatius the Martyr could have had regard to it in his own age, insofar as it was put forward by the more ancient Gnostics, and before it was transformed into the character of Valentinus; so that there is no need to have recourse to Valentinus here." Thus learned Pearson, in chapter 6, p. 59. He labours through the whole chapter to establish this assertion of his. We shall see whether it is with favourable or unfavourable omens. First he brings forward various testimonies of the Ancients on this matter, and at p. 60 he writes that there is none of them who does not expressly state that Valentinus revived an old opinion.

units.la: Doleo Virum doctum se gratis & inutiliter fatigâsse in describendis Veterum illorum testimonijs, cùm confitentem haberet adversarium: Dallæus quippe, ut ipse observat pag. 61. ingenuè fatetur cap. 12. pag 303. ipsam rerum sylvam atque materiam, ex quâ Valentinus sua composuit, jam apud vetustiores partim Gnosticos Hæreticos, partim etiam Poëtas, aut Philosophos Ethnicos fuisse; Veteres autem quorum citantur testimonia de materiâ ac semine hæresis Valentini loquuntur, necnon de ejus occasione; & nos docent hæresiarcham illum à veteribus Gnosticis occasionem sumpsisse suum impium dogma conflandi, ab ijsque semina & materiam matæolgiæ [?] suæ mutu[?]atum esse, nec hoc diffitetur præstantissimus Dallæus; De solâ formâ lis est,negat enim idem Dallæus ubi suprà eandem materiæ dispositionem ac compositionem, quam præ se fert Valentini hæresis, apud vetustiores fuisse Gnosticos; quoniam si hæc forma vetustiorum jam fuerat, nullus ergo proprius Valentinianæ doctrinæ character fuisset, quem fuisse Irenæus disertissimè docet. Viro docto igitur incumbit probare eandem fuisse vetustiorum Gnosticorum hæresis formam, eundémque characterem cum eo quem Valentinianæ hæresis proprium & peculiarem esse contendit Dallæus, & nisi hoc fœliciter exsequatur, actum erit de Epistolico suo Ignatio, cujus fronti ad sempiternam ignominiam inusta ac impressa manebit tanta suppositionis nota. Verus siquidem Ignatius neque Valentinum se posteriorem ferire, neque ejus hæresim pluribus post suum martyrium annis natam pulsare potuit; tamen si Logi ex Sige emissio, proprius fuit Valentinianæ hæresis character, negari non potest quin ad eam respexerit Autor Epistolæ ad Magnesios: Ostendat ergo necesse est doctissimus Vindiciarum Auctor, Valentinianæ doctrinæ proprium characterem, non talem esse qualem vult Dal-
units.tr: I regret that the learned man has wearied himself in vain and to no purpose in describing the testimonies of those ancient writers, since he had an opponent who concedes the point. Dallaeus, as he himself observes at p. 61, frankly admits in ch. 12, p. 303, that the very raw material from which Valentinus composed his system was already present among the older Gnostic heretics, and partly among the poets and pagan philosophers. The ancient writers whose testimonies are cited speak of the matter and seed of Valentinus' heresy, and also of its occasion; they teach us that this heresiarch took the occasion for forging his impious dogma from the ancient Gnostics, and that its seeds and material were borrowed from them. Nor does the most distinguished Dallaeus deny this. The dispute concerns only the form. For the same Dallaeus, in the passage above, denies that the arrangement and composition of matter which the Valentinian heresy displays were found among the older Gnostics. For if this form had already belonged to the older writers, there would be no distinctive character of Valentinian doctrine, and Irenaeus most clearly teaches that there was one. It is therefore incumbent on the learned man to prove that the form of the older Gnostic heresy was the same, and that it had the same character as that which Dallaeus contends is proper and peculiar to the Valentinian heresy. Unless he carries this out successfully, it will be all over for his Epistle of Ignatius, on whose brow such a mark of forgery will remain stamped and impressed to everlasting shame. For the true Ignatius could neither have attacked Valentinus as a later man, nor assailed a heresy born many years after his martyrdom. Yet if the emission of Logos from Sige was the proper character of the Valentinian heresy, it cannot be denied that the author of the Epistle to the Magnesians had it in view. The most learned author of the Vindiciae must therefore show that the proper character of Valentinian doctrine is not what Dal-

units.la: [?] The first word of the page is read as "tuatum"; it is probably "tantum" with a worn n, but the scan does not show it clearly. læus, Logique ex Sige generationem inter sua figmenta admisse Gnosticos Valentino antiquiores alioqui non stabit tertia Viri docti Assertio, quâ Hæresin hanc Valentino antiquiorem, & à veteribus Gnosticis acceptam, demonstrare in se recepit.
units.tr: Dallaeus, that the Gnostics, older than Valentinus, admitted among their fictions the generation of the Logos from Sige. Otherwise the learned author's third assertion will not stand, the one by which he undertook to show that this heresy is older than Valentinus and was received from the ancient Gnostics.

units.la: Vt hoc perfungatur labore,sententiam suam confirmare nititur, Blondello nimirum, & Dallæo occurrendo, deinde Dallæi argumenta refellere aggreditur; verba quæ Blondello adscribit Vir doctus pag. 61. reperire non potui, locum enim ex quo descripta sunt non indicat; quæ de Epistolis Ignatianis scripsit Præfat. in Apolog. Hieronymi, & in notis ad Epistolas clarissimi Viri Isaac Vossii de eodem argumento, legi & relegi, & tamen verba quibus de agitur non inveni; Verùm quia Blondellum in animo minimè habui, dum has observationes scribere decrevi, non est quod de eo anxiè solliciti simus: Aliquid nihilominus de eo dicam, ne videlicet de tanto Viro triumphasse putet Vindiciarum Autor. Observat siquidem Pearsonius Blondellum ex Irenæo, seu potius Irenæum ex Blondelli mente affirmare, proprium Valentini characterem combinationem Profundi & silentij protulisse. Contrarium verò existimat Vir doctus, hancque Bythi & Siges Syzygiam cœteris Gnosticis Valétino vetustioribus communem asserere non veretur, varijs Irenæi testimoniis in hanc rem adductis pag. 62. 63. Loca ex quibus deprompta sunt consului, testimonia ipsa expendi, nec quicquam omnino in iis animadverti, quod Blondello noceat, vel faveat Vindiciarum Autori, ex illis quidem discimus Gnosticos Valentino antiquiores de Bytho philosophatos esse, eúmque ut Deum agnovisse, at de Bythi & Siges conjugatione, altum apud Irenæum silentium, hanc autem combinationem, si Virum doctum audimus, urget Blondellus, de Bytho à Sige separato, nullámque cum eâ Syzygiam faciente non loquitur, fuit, inquit, Sige aut Bytho coæva, aut fortasse nomen ejus illo Bythi antiquius; non hoc quæritur, sed utrum Irenæus scripserit Gnosticos qui Valentinum præcesserunt, Bythi & Siges combinationem admisisse, non id scripsit in locis à Viro docto allatis, manet igitur firmissima Blondelli nostri argumentatio, eamque sollicitare incassum laboravit Pearsonius; instat iterùm, & Ennoean Simoni adfuisse observat. Ennoean verò illam ab initio Sigen appellatam ostendit ex quibusdam Eusebij verbis de Eccles. Theologiâ lib.2. cap.
units.tr: I have not been able to find the words that the learned man ascribes to Blondel at p. 61, since he does not indicate the place from which they were taken. What Blondel wrote about the Ignatian Epistles in the Preface to the Apology of Jerome, and in the notes of the most distinguished Isaac Vossius on the same subject, I have read and re-read, yet I have not found the words in question. But since I had no intention of dealing with Blondel when I decided to write these observations, there is no need for us to be anxious about him. Still, I will say something about him, lest the author of the Vindiciae think he has triumphed over so great a man. Pearsonius observes that Blondel, or rather Irenaeus as Blondel understood him, affirms that the proper character of Valentinus' heresy was the combination of the Profound and Silence. The learned man thinks the contrary, and does not hesitate to assert that this syzygy of Bythus and Sige was common to other Gnostics older than Valentinus, adducing various testimonies of Irenaeus to this effect at pp. 62 and 63. I consulted the passages from which they are taken and weighed the testimonies themselves, and I noticed nothing in them that harms Blondel or favours the author of the Vindiciae. From them we indeed learn that the Gnostics older than Valentinus philosophized about Bythus and acknowledged him as God; but about the conjugation of Bythus and Sige there is a deep silence in Irenaeus. Yet this combination, if we listen to the learned man, is what Blondel insists upon, and he does not speak of Bythus separated from Sige and forming no syzygy with her. Sige was, he says, coeval with Bythus, or perhaps her name was older than his. The question is not this, but whether Irenaeus wrote that the Gnostics who preceded Valentinus admitted the combination of Bythus and Sige. He did not write this in the passages the learned man has cited. Blondel's argument therefore remains most firm, and Pearsonius has laboured in vain to unsettle it. He presses again, and observes that Ennoea was present with Simon. That this Ennoea was called Sige from the beginning he shows from certain words of Eusebius in the Ecclesiastical Theology, book 2, ch. 9.

units.la: 9. quæ sic se habent ; Hæc supponere ausus est Marcellus ; quippe qui olim ait Deum extitisse,& quietem quamdam apud Deum imaginatur, secundùm illum impiorum hæreticorum Principem, qui impia dogmatizans, pronunciavit dicens, ERAT DEVS & SIGE. Verùm hæc tanti non sunt ut putat Pearsonius ; Nam de Deo loquitur Eusebius, non de Bytho ut Blondellus, non me latet Valentinianos & forte alios quosdam Hæreticos, fabulosum suum Bythum pro Deo habuisse , id est pro persona divinâ, & nobilioris sexus, sed Dei nomine infignitum eum non video ; præterea ponamus Deum apud Eusebium eundem esse cum Bytho Irenæi & aliorum qui de Gnosticis scripserunt, non inde sequetur conjugationem Bythi & Siges à Gnosticis Valentino antiquioribus inter sua figmenta numeratam esse ; ille siquidem impiorum Hæreticorum Princeps , ipse Valentinus erit, qui primus juxta Blondellum hanc Bythi & Siges Syzygiam somniavit ; pertendit tamen eruditus Pearsonius , de primâ Syzygiâ Bythi & Siges, tanquam ab omnibus Veteribus Gnosticis , non Valentinianis tantùm, agnitâ loqui Irenæum lib. 1. c. 5. Nam cùm novam quandam Archegonon ostonationem ab aliquibus Valentini discipulis excogitatam notasset , has volunt , inquit , virtutes suisse ante Bython & Sigen , ut perfectorum perfectiores appareant , & Gnosticorum magis Gnostici Viri. Et statim exclamat , O pepones , Sophistae vituperabiles,& non Viri. Prosecto miror Virum doctum ad haec Irenaei verba, velut ad sacram Anchoram confugere , cum in toto hoc capite de Valentino agat & ea in quibus ab illo differunt Discipuli tangat , ut fert titulus , quae sit Valentini sententia , in quibus discrepant adversus eum Discipuli ejus. A Gnosticis autem Valentinianis ad alios Gnosticos Valentino vetustiores non valet argumentatio ; non ignorat Pearsonius Valentinianos Gnosticorum nomen sibi imposuisse ut scribit Epiphanius haer.31.Et in plures sectas à se invicem discrepantes divisos esse , ex eorum numero erant qui ab Irenaeo designantur , nec ad alias sectas Valentini haeresi antiquiores pertinebant, ne illi quidem perfecti & Gnostici , quibus ipsi hoc suo invento perfectiores & magis Gnostici videri volebant , Valentino vetustiores dicendi sunt , nempe perfecti illi & Gnostici , quorum respectu isti de quibus loquitur Irenaeus perfectiores esse gloriabantur , non alii erant quàm Valentinus ipse , & primi ejus Discipuli , quibus novi isti ex eadem prosapiâ Magistri, Gnosticæ Sapientiæ palmam præripere, hoc eorum Theogoniæ addito figmento contendebant. Discipuli siquidem supra Magistrum sapere nitebantur, quod & in aliorum Magistrorum scholis plærúmque contingit, & in hujus præsertim Valentini impiissimâ sectâ accidisse, tum ex Irenæo, tum ex Tertulliano discimus, qui Valentini dogma primò simplicius, variè postmodum à Sectatoribus, ut fieri solet, auctum & interpolatum fuisse testatur: ita, inquit, nusquam jam Valentinus: & tamen Valentiniani, qui per Valentinum. Solus ad hodiernum Antiochiæ Axionicus memoriam Valentini integrâ custodiâ regularum ejus consolatur.
units.tr: 9. These are the words: Marcellus dared to put forward this same claim, for he once said that God came into being, and he imagines a certain rest in God, following that impious heretic leader who, teaching impious doctrines, declared: "THERE WAS GOD AND SIGE." But these things are not of the weight that Pearson thinks. For Eusebius speaks of God, not of Bythos as Blondel supposes. I am not unaware that the Valentinians, and perhaps certain other heretics, regarded their fabled Bythos as God, that is, as a divine person of the nobler sex, but I do not see that he was marked with the name of God. Moreover, let us suppose that the God in Eusebius is the same as the Bythos of Irenaeus and of the others who wrote about the Gnostics. It would still not follow that the pairing of Bythos and Sige was counted among their fictions by Gnostics older than Valentinus. For that impious leader of heretics would be Valentinus himself, who, according to Blondel, was the first to dream up this syzygy of Bythos and Sige. Nevertheless, the learned Pearson maintains that Irenaeus, in book 1, chapter 5, speaks of the first syzygy of Bythos and Sige as acknowledged by all the ancient Gnostics, not only by the Valentinians. For when he had noted a new invention of certain disciples of Valentinus, a sort of Archigonos emanation, he says: "They want these powers, he says, to have existed before Bythos and Sige, so that the more perfect may appear more perfect, and the Gnostic men more Gnostic." And at once he cries out: "Oh babblers, blameworthy sophists, and not men!" Truly I am surprised that the learned man should flee to these words of Irenaeus as to a sacred anchor, since in this whole chapter he treats of Valentinus and touches on the points in which his disciples differ from him, as the title says: "What is the opinion of Valentinus, and in what points his disciples disagree with him." But the argument does not hold, from the Valentinian Gnostics to other Gnostics older than Valentinus. Pearson is not unaware that the Valentinians gave themselves the name of Gnostics, as Epiphanius writes (Haer. 31), and that they were divided into many sects differing from one another. Those whom Irenaeus designates belonged to their number, and they did not belong to other sects older than the heresy of Valentinus. Nor should those "perfect and Gnostic" men, by whose standard these men of his own invention wished to appear "more perfect and more Gnostic," be called older than Valentinus. Those "perfect and Gnostic" men, in comparison with whom those whom Irenaeus speaks of boasted of being more perfect, were none other than Valentinus himself and his first disciples. These newer masters from the same stock were snatching the palm of Gnostic wisdom from them, contending for it by adding this fiction to their theogony. For the disciples strove to be wiser than the master, which also happens very often in the schools of other masters. We learn that this happened especially in the most impious sect of this Valentinus, both from Irenaeus and from Tertullian, who testifies that the doctrine of Valentinus was at first simpler, and afterwards, as usually happens, was enlarged and altered by his followers. "Thus," he says, "Valentinus is now nowhere; and yet the Valentinians, who are named after Valentinus. Only Axionicus of Antioch, down to the present day, preserves the memory of Valentinus by keeping his rules intact."

units.la: Pearsonius tamen se tuetur quibusdam Gregorij Nazianzeni verbis ex illius Orat. 23. descriptis, cum Simones, inquit, & Marciones, & Valentini quidam, & Basilidæ, & Cerdones, Cerinthi, etiam & Carpocrates, & omnes eorum nugæ & præstigiæ, posteaquam rerum omnium Deum perdiuturno tempore secuissent, bellúmque pro Bono adversus Creatorem gessi-sent [?], suomet deinde, ut æquum erat, Profundo absorptæ ac Silentio traditæ fuerunt. Sed nemo non videt Gregorium hoc solum velle, hæreses à se memoratas evanuisse tandem, nullámque prorsus Ecclesiæ molestiam[?] creare, ideóque scribit profundo ab- sorptas ac silentio traditas fuisse, allusione videlicet factâ ad Profundum & Silentium Valentini, cui illiúsque Sectatoribus competunt hæc ultima Nazianzeni verba, non autem cæteris quos nominat Hæreticis: At inquit Vindiciarum Auctor Elias Cretensis in orationem 23. Gregorij Nazianzeni, & Nicetas in Orat. XLIIII. Theologi verba de Simonianis explicant; Ex Elia quippe hæc describit; Ac Simoniani quidem octonarium numerum ob Æones eos quos colebat honore prosequebantur. Nugabantur enim Bythum cum suâ Sige congressum Mentem & Veritatem genuisse &c. Ista verò ex Niceta: Simoniani quidem octonarium propter csto[?] illos Magistri sui Æones honori habebant. Etenim ex Bythi cum Sige congressu Mentem ac Veritatem procreatas esse fabulatus est, atque ita primos parentes, ut jam distum est. Bythum & Sigen confixit. Ex duobus hisce testimoniis,hanc adversus Blondellum conclusionem elicit Vir doctus; Bythum igitur & Sigen inter Æones suos habuisse veteres illos ante Valentinum Gnosticos dixere quamplurimi, non habuisse ante Blondellum, opinor, nemo dixit. Quis non mirētur Vindiciarum auctorem de quamplurimis testibus gl[?]riantem; quamvis duos tantum laudet, eósque recentiores, ac ea propter minimè audiendos, nisi scriptorum se vetustiorum autoritate freti loquantur de rebus adeò vetustis, ab eorúmque ætate longè remotis, Nam ut est à Baronio rectè observatum Annal. Eccles.num. 12. Quod à recentiore Auctore de rebus adeò antiquis, sine alicujus vetustioris autoritate profertur, contemnitur. Cum igitur testes à Vindiciarum Auctore citati recentiores sint, & de rebus adeò antiquis sine alicujus vetustioris autoritate loquantur, juxta celeberrimi Annalistæ regulam contemnendi sunt; præsertim cùm ea narrent de Simonianis incognita planè veteribus qui varios Hæreticorum texuêre catalogos, Irenæo, inquam, Tertulliano, Philastrio, Epiphanio, Augustino, Theodoreto, qui sæculo quinto inclinato vivendi finem fecit, & tamen pluribus post Theodoretum sæculis floruerunt quos jam versamus Scriptores: Præterea si integras utriusque Scriptoris pericopes adduxisset Vir doctus, eorum inscitiam ac supinitatem hac in re prodidisset, & ijs quæ de Simonianis scribunt fidem penitùs detraxisset; Age ergo Eliæ Cretensis verba describamus; Simon, inquit, & Marcion Hæresiarchæ erant. Ac Simoniani quidem octonarium numerum ob Æones eos, quos colebant, honore prosequebantur. Nugabantur enim Bythum cum suâ Sigè congrefsum, Mentem & Veritatem genuisse. Ac generis principes Æones, ut diximus Bythum & Sigen fingebant: ab his autem secundos Mentem & Veritatem: ab his tertios Sermonem & Vitam, ab his denique quartos Hominem & Ecclesiam. Marcionitæ verò adaucto morbo tricenarium numerum venerabantur ob triginta Æones, quos ipsi colebant.
units.tr: Nevertheless, Pearson defends himself with certain words of Gregory Nazianzen, taken from his Oration 23: "When Simon and Marcion, and certain followers of Valentinus, and Basilides, and Cerdo, Cerinthus, and also Carpocrates, and all their trifles and deceits, had for a long time pursued the God of all things, and had waged war for the Good against the Creator, they were afterwards, as was right, swallowed up by the Deep and handed over to Silence." But everyone sees that Gregory means only this: that the heresies he has mentioned have at last vanished and create no trouble at all for the Church. For this reason he writes that they were swallowed up by the Deep and handed over to Silence, plainly alluding to the Deep and the Silence of Valentinus. These last words of Nazianzen fit Valentinus and his followers, but not the other heretics he names. But, says the author of the Vindiciae, Elias of Crete, on Gregory Nazianzen's Oration 23, and Nicetas, on Oration 44 of the Theologian, explain the words about the Simonians. Indeed, Elias describes these matters thus: "The Simonians honoured the number eight on account of those Aeons whom they worshipped. For they trifled that Bythos, having united with his Sige, begot Mind and Truth, etc." And Nicetas says this: "The Simonians held the number eight in honour because of those Aeons of their master. For he invented the story that Mind and Truth were produced from the union of Bythos with Sige, and so he made Bythos and Sige the first parents, as has been said." From these two testimonies the learned man draws this conclusion against Blondel: "That the ancient Gnostics before Valentinus said, very many of them, that Bythos and Sige were among their Aeons, I think no one has said that they were not among them before Blondel." Who would not wonder that the author of the Vindiciae boasts of very many witnesses, when he cites only two, and those more recent, and therefore not to be heard at all, unless they speak in reliance on the authority of older writers about matters so ancient and so remote from their own age? For, as Baronius correctly observed (Ann. Eccl., no. 12): "What is put forward by a more recent author about matters so ancient, without the authority of some older writer, is held in contempt." Since, then, the witnesses cited by the author of the Vindiciae are more recent, and speak of matters so ancient without the authority of any older writer, they are to be held in contempt by the rule of that most famous annalist. This is especially so since they relate things about the Simonians that were entirely unknown to the ancients, who drew up various catalogues of heretics: Irenaeus, I mean, Tertullian, Philastrius, Epiphanius, Augustine, and Theodoret, who ended his life in the declining fifth century. Yet the writers we are now examining flourished many centuries after Theodoret. Moreover, if the learned man had quoted the whole passages of each writer, he would have shown their ignorance and carelessness in this matter, and would have utterly destroyed the credit of what they write about the Simonians. Come, then, let us copy out the words of Elias of Crete: "Simon and Marcion were heresiarchs. The Simonians honoured the number eight on account of those Aeons whom they worshipped. For they trifled that Bythos, having united with his Sige, begot Mind and Truth. And they feigned that Bythos and Sige were the first Aeons, the princes of the race; from these came the second, Mind and Truth; from these the third, Word and Life; and from these at last the fourth, Man and Church. The Marcionites, however, with the disease grown worse, venerated the number thirty because of the thirty Aeons whom they worshipped."

units.la: Hoc enim delirii homines aiebant, quòd ex iis Æonibus qui apud Simonianos essent, Sermo quidem & Vita Æones decem rursum produxissent: Homo autem & Ecclesia duodecim alios Æones: qui quidem ad octo eos, quos modò recensuimus, adjuncti, tricenarium numerum efficiunt. Supervacaneum autem fuerit eorum quoque nomina scribere, ita anilia [?] sunt & aspernanda. Eadem prorsùs totidémque feré verbis narrat Nicetas, adeò ut alterum ab altero mutuatum esse opporteat. Quicquid sit liquidò constat utrúmque, Eliam videlicet & Nicetam, graviter hallucinatos esse, & plura in tantulo spatio peccasse peccata. Nam qui in Antiquitatis monumentis tantisper sunt versati facilè animadvertent,primò,quatuor Æonũ conjugationes quas Simonianis affingunt, ipsissimas esse. Valentini Syzygias, quæ primam Æonum Valentinianorum octonationem efficiunt, ut nos docent veteres qui de hærefibus ex professo tractarunt,cùm nihil tale de Simonianis scripserint.Secundò,ea quę de Marcionistis narrant mera esse vigilantium somnia,& à veritate alienissima;quis unquam vel fando audivit Marcionem ejúsque consectaneos triginta Æones coluisse ac veneratos esse? De Marcionistis scripserunt quamplurimi è vetustissimis Ecclesiæ scriptoribus, de eorum hæresi plura nobis tradiderunt ; At de triginta Æonibus ab illis cultis ne minimum quidem in Antiquorum Patrum scriptis extat vestigium : Quare non possum non mirari Vindiciarum Auctorem, ad istas aniles fabulas confugientem, & in ijs causæ suæ præsidium quærentem ; inanes voco fabulas quæ nullo antiquissimorum Scriptorũ nituntur testimonio,imò potiùs adversâ fronte pugnant cum ijs quæ de Simonianis & Marcionistis observarunt veteres Ecclesiæ Doctores, qui antiquas recensuerunt hæreses, eâsque de industriâ oppugnare ac confutare aggressi sunt: Nihil ergo boni augurari licet de causâ Viri docti, ad quam tuendam adhibentur non firmissima argumenta, neque validissima rationum momenta, sed frigidissima juniorum Scriptorum commenta, quibus crassissimam suam antiquarum hærefecon respectu produnt ignorantiam. Dicet forsan Clarissimus Pearsonius sua à Gregorio Nazianzeno hausisse Eliam & Nicetam: Equidem fateor quædam dicere Nazianzenum orat. XLIII. pag. 706. quæ Scholiastarum suorum opinioni viam sternere potuërunt; Nam de numeris agens, septenario videlicet Hebræis sacro , & quaternario , qui Pythagoreis in honore erat, Simonianis & Marcionistis octonarium & Tricenarium assignat quoniam parem quorundam Æonum numerum concelebrant ac venerantur. Verùm ex istis Theologi verbis nihil plane in gratiam suæ hypothesis exsculpere potest Vindiciarum Auctor; Æones enim nó nominat Gregorius , neque eorum recenset combinationes,ideóque nequaquâ sciri potest utrum Bythi & Siges Syzigiam Simonianis adscribat; Deinde vereor ne aliquid humani passus sit tantus Ecclesiæ doctor dùm Marcionistis Æones tribuit, præter vulgarem de illis hæreticis veterum Scriptorum sententiam ; præterea Nazianzeni verba obscura sunt nec intellectu facilia , & nisi commodam adhibeas interpretationem, vix excusari potest, benignior autem meo quidem judicio adhiberi nequit, quam ista, octonarium videlicet numerum , tribuendo Simonianis ob tres conjugationes quas excogitavit Simon Magus, radicésque nominavit, quæ quidem conjugationes cum Simone ipso & sua impurissima Helena, octonarium efficerunt numerum; Triginta vero Æones Valentinianis ( totidem quippe excogitabant ) non autem Marcion stis quibus id imprudenter affinxit Nazianzenus.
units.tr: For these deranged men said that from those Aeons which were among the Simonians, Word and Life produced ten further Aeons, and Man and Church twelve other Aeons. These, added to the eight we have just listed, make up the number thirty. It would be superfluous to write down their names as well, since they are so silly and to be despised. Nicetas relates the same things in almost the same words, so that one must have borrowed from the other. Whatever the case, it is clear that both of them, Elias and Nicetas, were badly mistaken, and erred in many points within a tiny space. For those who have been somewhat versed in the monuments of antiquity will readily notice, first, that the four pairings of Aeons which they attribute to the Simonians are exactly the syzygies of Valentinus, which make up the first ogdoad of the Valentinian Aeons, as the early writers who treated heresies professedly teach us. Yet they wrote nothing of this kind about the Simonians. Second, what they relate about the Marcionites is the pure dream of men who are awake, and utterly alien to the truth. Who ever heard, even by hearsay, that Marcion and his followers worshipped and venerated thirty Aeons? Very many of the most ancient writers of the Church have written about the Marcionites, and have handed down many things to us about their heresy. But of thirty Aeons worshipped by them not even the smallest trace survives in the writings of the ancient Fathers. Therefore I cannot but wonder at the author of the Vindiciae, who flees to these old wives' fables and seeks in them a defence for his cause. I call these fables empty, since they rest on no testimony of the most ancient writers. Indeed, they fight with a face set against what the ancient teachers of the Church observed about the Simonians and Marcionites, men who recorded the ancient heresies and took pains to refute and confute them. Therefore nothing good can be hoped for the cause of the learned man, for which no very firm arguments or very strong considerations are brought forward to defend it, but only the coldest inventions of later writers, by which they betray their very gross ignorance of the ancient heresies. Perhaps the most famous Pearson will say that Elias and Nicetas drew their material from Gregory Nazianzen. I admit that Nazianzen, in Oration 43 (p. 706), says some things which may have paved the way for the opinion of their commentators. For when he speaks of numbers, he assigns the number seven, sacred to the Hebrews, and the number four, which was held in honour by the Pythagoreans, and to the Simonians and Marcionites he assigns the numbers eight and thirty, since they celebrate and venerate an equal number of certain Aeons. Yet from these words of the Theologian the author of the Vindiciae can extract absolutely nothing in favour of his hypothesis. For Gregory does not name the Aeons, nor does he list their combinations; therefore it can by no means be known whether he ascribes the syzygy of Bythos and Sige to the Simonians. Further, I fear that so great a teacher of the Church may have suffered some human error when he attributed Aeons to the Marcionites, apart from the common opinion of the older writers about those heretics. Moreover, Nazianzen's words are obscure and not easy to understand, and unless you apply a suitable interpretation they can hardly be excused. In my judgment, however, no more fitting interpretation can be applied than this: that he attributed the number eight to the Simonians because of the three pairings which Simon Magus devised and called roots, which pairings, together with Simon himself and his most impure Helena, made up the number eight. And the thirty Aeons he assigned to the Valentinians (for they devised exactly that many), not to the Marcionites, to whom Nazianzen inadvertently attached them.

units.la: Vindicata celeberrimi Blondelli opinione, videamus quid adversus Dallæi sententiam objiciat doctissimus Vindiciarum Auctor; Dallæus siquidem asserebat Logon ex Sige, tanquam à matre filium, vel tanquam ab avia nepotem, procreatum esse, neminem ante Valentinum docuisse, hancque Logi ex Sige emanationem proprium esse ac peculiarem hæresis Valentini characterem: Pearsonius vero contra affirmat Basilidem inter Gnosticos Valentino vetustiores fuisse, & de Logo pariter ac Valentinum sensisse, quod probat pag. 65. quibusdam Theodoreti verbis Fab. Hæret. lib.5. cap. xi, cum inquit, Valentini de Verbo sententiam recitasset, hæc addit, Basilides quoque si[?]liter alium Unigenitum, aliud Verbum, & aliam dixit esse Sapientiam; hinc colligit Basilidem Monogenem & Verbum similiter distinxisse, quia Verbum ex Monogene similiter eduxit; hæc consequentia est Viri docti, non autem Theodoreti; Theodoretus siquidem hoc tantum observat Valentinum Vnigenitum distinxisse à Verbo, Verbum à Christo, Christum à Iesu, idémque fecisse Basilidem, sed de Verbi à Monogene educatione penitus tacet. At Irenæus, inquit, de Basilide ita loquitur lib. 1 cap. 23. ostendit Nun primò ab Innato natum Patre, ab hoc autem natum Logon; fateor hæc de Basilide scripsisse Irenæum, hisque similia de eodem tradere Epiphanium & Theodoretum, sed ista Viri docti causam minimè iuvant, nulla siquidem Siges fit mentio inter Basilidis figmenta, docebat quidem Basilides à Nu natum Logon, sed à Nu & Sige emissum esse nusquam docuit; primus ex Gnosticis hoc afferuit Valentinus, nullusque ante eum Logi ex Sige emanationem commentus est; Basilides, ait Pearsonius p. 65. & illi Gnostici inter quos ipse fuit, neque Bython neque Nun sine συζύγοις suis Æonem ullum procreâsse docuerunt[?]. Cùm hæc lego, vix oculis meis credo, contraria prorsus à vetustioribus Ecclesiæ Scriptoribus edoctus; Nam Irenæus, Tertullianus, Philastrius, Epiphanius, Theodoretus, fabulosam Basilidis Theogoniam sic repræsentant; Nus ab Innato natus Patre, à Nu Logos, à Logo Phronesis, à Phronesi autem Sophia & Dynamis, à Dynami & Sophiâ, virtutes, &c[?] principes & Angeli &c. Ubinam sunt quaesò fictitia illa numina deterioris sexus, id est fœminæ sine quibus Æones ullos in Basilidis schola procreari audacter negat Pearsonius[?] quorsum antiqui illi Doctores aliter se gerunt, dum Valentini mataeologiam commemorant, Bython videlicet cum Sige conjungentes, Nun cum Veritate, Logon cum Vita &c. Nisi quia juxta Valentini figmenta, ex primâ Syzigiâ, educitur secunda, ex secundâ tertia, & ita de cæteris; quod de Basilidis Æonibus dici nequit, si forte Æonum voce usus est; à solo quippe Innato Patre emissum esse Nun, & à solo Nu eductum Logon fabulabatur; de Basilidianis οὐσίους[?] apud veteres altissimum silentium. Instat Vir doctus & Syzigias quasdam fuisse apud Basilidianos contendit, quoniam Basilides Menandri discipulus fuit, qui Syzygiam, inquit, Patris Incogniti & Ennoeæ tradidit eiusque Sententiam Basilides non concidit, sed in immensum extendit. De Menandri Virtute incognita seu Patre & de Ennoea loquuti sunt Ecclesiastici Scriptores, sed an Patris Incogniti & Ennoeæ Syzygiam tradiderit, non diserte dicunt, sed in gratiam Viri docti Syzygiam illam Menandro largiamur, quid inde consequetur, Basilidem, inquiet, Menandri discipulum eandem admisse Syzygiam, esto eam adm serit[?] Basilides, nihil propterea efficies adversus Dallæum, donec probaveris illam Menandri Syzygiam, eandem plane esse cū Valentiniana Bythi & Siges conjugatione, & hoc opus, hic labor est: Verùm ne aliquis adhuc supersit tergiversandi locus,nego Basilidem Menandri Sy-zygiam admisisse, & inter figmenta sua numerasse, & mecum negab ꝛ[?] Theodoretus Hæret. Faf. lib. i.[?] cap. 2. nam de Menandro loquens, Hunc, inquit, habuere magistrum Saturnilus & Basilides, quo um ille Antiochiam ad Oorntem[?] fluvium sitã Patriam sibi esse prædicabat, Basilides vero Ale-xandriam, qui & magistro & sibi invicem contrarias fabulas confixere. Eat nunc Vir doctus, & Basilidi quantum volet affingat quam Menandri dicit esse Syzygiam; ego Theodoretum sequar, & Basilidem Menandro cōtraria excogitasse firmissimè credam. Basilides, pergit eruditus Pearsonius, Menandri sententiam non concidit, non concidit sanè, neque id concedere molé-stum erit; sed, inquit in immensum exténdit, pace tuâ Vir doctissime in immensum non extendit, neque de Menandri doctrinâ id dicit Irenæus, à quo hæc verba accepit Pearsonius, sed de ipsissimo Basilidis impio dogmate, ecce Irenæi verba lib. 1. cap. 23. initio; Basilides ut altius aliquid & verisimilius adinvenisse videatur, in immensum extendit sententiam doctrinæ suæ. De doctrinâ suâ agitur, non de Menandri sententiâ, cui contrarium erat Basilidis figmentum, ut nos docuit Theodoretus, & diversum præterea à Saturnili condiscipuli hæresi, ut testatur cum Theodoreto Irenæus lib. 1. cap. 22. In immensum autem doctrinam suam extendisse dicitur Basilides, quoniam plura confixit quàm Menander & Saturnilus, quorum ille amborum fuit magister, Saturnili videlicet & Basilidis, iste verò, Saturnilus nempe, ejusdem magistri unà cum Basilide discipulus; qui quidem Basilides dogma suum in immensum præ illis extendisse ob multa censendus est, imprimis propter cœlos CCCLXV. quos ab Angelis fabricatos delirabat.
units.tr: Having vindicated the opinion of the most celebrated Blondel, let us see what the most learned author of the Vindiciae objects against Daillé's view. Daillé asserted that Logos was produced from Sigē, as a son from his mother or a grandson from his grandmother, that no one before Valentinus had taught this, and that this emanation of Logos from Sigē is the proper and peculiar mark of Valentinus's heresy. Pearson, on the other hand, maintains that Basilides was older than Valentinus among the Gnostics and thought about the Logos in the same way as Valentinus. He proves this on p. 65 from some words of Theodoret, Fab. Haeret. bk. 5, ch. 11, where, after reporting Valentinus's view of the Word, Theodoret adds: Basilides too said in a similar way that the Only-begotten is one thing, the Word another, and Wisdom another. From this Pearson infers that Basilides distinguished the Monogenes and the Word in the same way, because he likewise derived the Word from the Monogenes. This is the learned man's inference, not Theodoret's. Theodoret only observes that Valentinus distinguished the Only-begotten from the Word, the Word from Christ, and Christ from Jesus, and that Basilides did the same; but about the derivation of the Word from the Monogenes he is wholly silent. But Irenaeus, Pearson says, speaks of Basilides thus in bk. 1, ch. 23: He shows that Nous was first born from the Unbegotten Father, and from him Logos was born. I admit that Irenaeus wrote this about Basilides, and that Epiphanius and Theodoret hand down similar things about him; but these passages do not help the learned man's cause at all. There is no mention of Sigē among the fictions of Basilides. Basilides did teach that Logos was born from Nous, but he nowhere taught that it was sent forth from Nous and Sigē. Valentinus was the first of the Gnostics to assert this, and no one before him invented the emanation of Logos from Sigē. Basilides, says Pearson on p. 65, and those Gnostics among whom he himself lived, taught that neither Bython nor Nous produced any Aeon without their syzygies. When I read this I can hardly believe my eyes, since the older writers of the Church have taught me the opposite. For Irenaeus, Tertullian, Philastrius, Epiphanius and Theodoret all present Basilides's mythical theogony in this way: Nous was born from the Unbegotten Father, from Nous Logos, from Logos Phronesis, from Phronesis Sophia and Dynamis, from Dynamis and Sophia virtues, etc., principalities and angels, etc. Where, I ask, are those fictitious deities of the inferior sex, that is, the females, without whom Pearson boldly denies that any Aeons were produced in Basilides's school? Why do those ancient teachers speak otherwise when they recall Valentinus's mataeology, joining Bython with Sigē, Nous with Alētheia, Logos with Zōē, and so on? Unless it is because, according to Valentinus's fictions, the second is produced from the first syzygy, the third from the second, and so on in the same way; and this cannot be said of Basilides's Aeons, if indeed he used the word Aeon at all. For he fabled that Nous was sent forth from the Unbegotten Father alone, and that Logos was brought forth from Nous alone. As for the Basilidians' ousious [οὐσίους] among the ancients, there is the deepest silence. The learned man presses further and contends that there were certain syzygies among the Basilidians, since Basilides was a disciple of Menander, who, he says, handed down the syzygy of the Unknown Father and Ennoia, and Basilides did not overturn his doctrine but extended it immensely. The ecclesiastical writers speak of the Unknown Power or Father and of Ennoia in relation to Menander, but they do not expressly say that he handed down a syzygy of the Unknown Father and Ennoia. Still, let us grant the learned man that syzygy for Menander. What will follow from it? You will say, he argues, that Basilides, as Menander's disciple, admitted the same syzygy, even if Basilides did admit it. But you will gain nothing against Daillé by this, unless you prove that Menander's syzygy is exactly the same as the Valentinian conjunction of Bython and Sigē, and that is the real work and labour here. Yet, so that no place for evasion may remain, I deny that Basilides admitted Menander's syzygy and counted it among his fictions; and Theodoret, Haeret. Fab. bk. 1, ch. 2, denies it with me. For speaking of Menander, he says: Saturninus and Basilides had this man as their teacher. Menander used to proclaim that Antioch, situated by the river Orontes, was his homeland, while Basilides was from Alexandria; and both of them, though they had the same teacher, devised fables contrary to him and to each other. Let the learned man now go on and attribute to Basilides as much as he likes of what he calls Menander's syzygy. I will follow Theodoret, and I firmly believe that Basilides devised doctrines contrary to Menander's. Basilides, the learned Pearson goes on, did not overturn Menander's doctrine. Certainly he did not overturn it, and it will not be troublesome to concede this. But, he says, he extended it immensely. With respect, most learned sir, he did not extend it immensely; nor does Irenaeus, from whom Pearson took these words, say this about Menander's teaching. He says it about Basilides's own impious dogma. Here are Irenaeus's words at the beginning of bk. 1, ch. 23: Basilides, so that he might seem to have discovered something more profound and plausible, extended the teaching of his doctrine immensely. The subject is his own doctrine, not Menander's opinion. Basilides's fiction was contrary to Menander's, as Theodoret taught us, and it was also different from the heresy of Saturninus, a fellow disciple, as Irenaeus, together with Theodoret, testifies in bk. 1, ch. 22. Basilides is said to have extended his doctrine immensely because he devised more than Menander and Saturninus did. Menander was the teacher of both of them, while Saturninus was a disciple of the same teacher together with Basilides. Basilides is to be considered to have extended his dogma immensely beyond those others for many reasons, above all because of the three hundred and sixty-five heavens which he raved were fashioned by angels.

units.la: Verùm aliud habet Vindiciarum Auctor quo probet Basilidem idem cum Valentino de Logo sensisse; observat siquidem Irenæum lib. 2. cap. 16. disputare aggressum esse adversus Valentiniaporum[?] primum ordinem emissionis, quo emissum aiunt de Bytho & hujus Ennoea Nun & Alethian. Et cap. 18. disputationem ita concludere. Hæc autem quæ dicta sunt de Sensus (id est Nus) emissione, similiter & adversus eos qui à Basilide sunt, aptata sunt, & adversus reliquos Gnosticos, à quibus & himitia emissionum accipientes, convicti sunt in primo libro. Postquam hæc Irenæi verba adduxit Vir doctus, de suo adijcit, Illa autem initia emissionum, quæ à primis Gnosticis derivarunt Valentiniani quæ fuerint porró quærendum est. Non diu quærendum erit nec longâ opus erit inquisitione, facili enim negotio deprehendemus unde hæc emissionum initia acceperint Valentiniani; Emissionum initia dixi cum Irenæo, qui de emissionum initijs tantùm loquitur, non autem de integris emissionibus, alioqui dixisset Valentinum à Basilide & reliquis Gnosticis, suas Æonum emissiones partim accepisse, vel saltem quasdam emissiones ab ijs derivasse; cùm autem de solis emissionum initijs agat, facile reperientur quædam ejusmodi initia, & in hæresi Simonis Magi Gnosticorum omnium parentis, nam in primâ conjugatione Nun reponit, Nus verò est Deus masculus secundæ Valentinianorum Syzygias; præterea Simon ille Magus dicebat se esse super omnia Patrem, & infinitam quandam potentiam, quam & universorum radicem appellavit; quod non malè congruit Valentinianorū Bytho seu Propatori, quem velut perfectum Æonem, invisibilem, incomprehensibilem, ingenitum, exhibent, & in invisibilibus ac innarrabilibus agentem. Deinde Basilides ipse quoque Gnosticus tria trium primarum Valentini emissionum initia subministrat, Ingenitum, Nun, & Logon, dixit enim ut tradunt antiqui Ecclesiae Doctores, Ingenitum primam omnium Mentem genuisse ( hoc est Nun ) ex Nu processisse Logon; vides igitur Valentinum a Gnosticis derivasse, non Syzygias integras, sed initia primae quae ex Bitho seu Ingenito & Sige constat, secundae quae ex Nu & Alethia, conflata est, & tertiae quam ex Logo & vita fabricarunt. Sed Vindiciarum Auctor scribit pag. 65. 66. Eliam Cretensem & Nicetam quorum verba mox descripsimus, asserere primam Valentini octonationem a Gnosticis deductam esse, decada autem & duodecada de suo addidisse Valentinum, Eliae Cretensis & Nicetae hallucinationes iam supra dispunximus, ideoque eas iterum excutere non est necesse: unum addam Eliam videlicet & Nicetam, nequaquam tradere, ut scribit Vir doctus, Valentinum decada & duodecada de suo addidisse; Hoc enim de Marcionistis diserte profitentur, non autem de Valentinianis : Sed quoniam eruditus Pearsonius optime novit ista Valentino, non Marcioni competere, Valentinum pro Marcionistis substituit, & quæ Elias & Nicetas scribere debebant expressit: Et hoc pacto eorum hallucinationem & inscitiam tacitè reprehendit, necnon Gregorij Nazianzeni incogitantiam qui commentatoribus suis errandi ansam præbuit, cùm Orat. 44. Simonianis & Marcionistis tribuit, quæ uni congruunt Valentino. Nihilominus tamen primam Ogdoada à Simonianis accepisse Valentinum ex Irenæo confirmare nititur, Irenæus enim cùm emissionem Logi ordine refutasset, & ad emissionem Hominis & Ecclesiæ qui primæ Ogdoadis postremi Æones fuere, pervenisset, lib. 2. cap. 18. inquit, notat Valentinianorum Parentes, vetustiores Gnosticos furti malè facti eos accusâ[?]e. De eâ autem quæ est ex his secundâ emissione Hominis & Ecclesiæ, ipsi patres eorum falsò cognominati Gnostici impugnant adversus invicem sua propria indicantes; & malos fures semetipsos convincentes: aptabiles esse magis emissiones dicentes uti verisimile ex Homine Verbum, sed non ex Verbo Hominem emissum, & esse Hominem Verbo anteriorem, & hunc esse qui est super omnia Deus. Ex his Irenæi verbis colligit Vir doctus pag. 66. Gnosticos fuisse Valentinianorum parentes, nec hoc negat Dallæus, imò ultrò fatetur Valentinum Theogoniæ suæ materiam à vetustioribus Gnosticis aliquomodo accepise : ab illis, ait Pearsonius tres primas Syzygias aperte sumpserunt, sive furati sunt Valentiniani: Vnde hæc habet Vindiciarum Auctor ? Quorumnam Veterum testimonijs sua nitatur assertio, ostendat ? Et in quibus Antiquitatis monumentis hæc legerit,indicet? Alioquin eadem facilitate contemnentur ; quâ proferuntur: Irenæus de mutuis Gnosticorum & Valentinianorum furtis loquitur , solámque Hominis ex Verbo emissionem in Valentinianis à Gnosticis argui observat, de integrâ Hominis & & Ecclesiæ Syzygiâ nihil aliud dicit, nisi in medium adduci à Gnosticis, ut notetur præpostera Hominis ex Verbo emissio, cùm Verbum ab Homine educi potiùs existimarent. Hæc Vindiciarum Auctori reponi possent, & nisi me fallit animus illius ex Irenæo argumentationi refellendæ abundè sufficerent: Verùm ut liberaliùs cum eo agamus, & Irenæi mens omninò percipiatur, sciendum est 1. Valentinianos omnes Gnosticorum nomen sibi imposuisse: 2. plures fuisse Valentinianorum sectas inter se discrepantes quarum alia vetustiores erant, aliæ recentiores: 3. in Irenæi verbis à Viro doĉto alatis latis agi tantùm de varijs Valentini Discipulis, quorum alij aliorum Parentes dici poterant, priores videlicet posteriorum, & juniorum vetustiores; Rem autem ita se habere liquet primò ex eo quod Gnostici Valentino ipso vetustiores, Æonum Valentinianorum emissiones nondum natas perstringere non poterant; nam quæ non sunt argui nequeunt; secundò ex ipso Irenæo qui de mutuis rixis ac furtis agit; quomodo autem inter se rixari poterant, & sibi invicem furta objicere Gnostici Valentino vetustiores, & Valentini ipsius Discipuli à quibus antiqui Gnostici aliquid derivasse non est verisimile. Dicet fortè eruditus Pearsonius superesse adhuc tunc temporis Gnosticos à quibus sua figmenta sumpserunt Valentiniani, quorum Gnostici eapropter Patres dici meruerunt; verùm nihil planè proderit Viro docto hæc exceptio, nisi eam confirmet veterum Scriptorum testimonijs, & præterea ostendat Gnosticos illos à Valentinianis accepisse, æquè ac Valentinianos à Gnosticis; nam Irenæus diserte profitetur utrósque inter se contendisse, furtáque sibi mutuò exprobrasse, vel ut illius verba usurpem, adversus invicem (id est sibi invicem) sua propria indicantes. His adde à nullo Gnosticorum Valentino vetuftiore , primam Ogdoada derivare potuisse Valentinianos , cùm nullibi comparet , præterquàm in fabulosis Valentini illiúsque Discipulorum Theogonijs ; Excutiantur omnia Simonis Magi Gnosticorum omnium Parentis figmenta , expendantur & exagitentur Menandri , Saturnii , Basilidis , & aliorum qui Gnosticorum ante Valentinum fuêre Antesignani, commentitia Numina, nusquam inter ea Ogdoada de quâ lis est reperies, & quid dico Ogdoada, ne quidem ultimam Ogdoadis Syzygiam , Hominis videlicet & Ecclesiæ , de quâ præcipuè agit Irenæus. Sed ne diutiùs[?] istis immoremur, consulendus est ipse Irenæus, qui nobis facem præferet, & veram istius loci explicationem ministrabit , eam ipsam videlicet quam nos tuemur; Libro siquidem primo cap. 6. varias Valentinianorum profert opiniones, ideóque hic titulus capiti est præfixus ; Quæ sunt in quibus non consonant adversus invicem hi , qui sunt à Valentino omnes ; Ex illis autem opinionibus hæc una est, quæ ad rem quam tractamus maxime facit; Qui , inquit , prudentiores putantur illorum esse , non ex Logo & Zoe, Ἀνθρώπο[?] & Ecclesiam , sed ex Ἀνθρώπο[?] & Ecclesia , Logon & Zoen dicunt generatos. Quivis videt Gnosticos quorum fit mentio in Irenæi testimonio à Vindiciarum Auctore adducto , non alios esse quàm ipsius Valentini Discipulos, qui secus ac ille & inverso ordine , ex Anthropo & Ecclesia, Logon & Zoen emissos esse contendebant ; Et quia in loco à Pearsonio laudato , hæc leguntur , & esse Hominem Verbo anteriorem , & hunc esse qui est super omnia Deus : Ne quis putet verba ista Valentinianorum nugis adversari , audiendus est idem ipse Irenæus , qui de iisdem Valentinianis agens , sic loquitur lib. 1. cap. 7. Alij sunt qui ipsum Propatorem omnium & Proarchen , & Proanennoeton , Anthropon dicunt vocari, & hoc esse magnum & absconditum mysterium , quoniam quæ est super omnia virtus , & continet omnia , Anthropos vocatur, & ideò Filium Hominis se dicere Salvatorem. Hinc consequitur[?] Hiriolari Vindiciarum Auctorem , dum ex præconceptâ opinione ad Gnosticos Valentino vetustiores refert , quæ ipsius Valentini Discipulos respiciunt ; negari siquidem non potest, post ea omnia quæ ex Irenæo descripsimus , de Valentinianis agi, qui & ipsi Gnostici fuêre, & alij aliorum Patres, sed ita tamen ut sibi invicem furta objicerent , & malos fures semetipsos convincerent. Quæ autem scribo contra Vindiciarum Auctorem , eadem scripta volo adversus Virum alium eruditum qui nihil plane novi dicit, nec quicquam notatu dignum observat; nisi quod se commendabilem reddere voluit: Virum doctissimum Ioannem Dallæum, iniquè deprimedo,& Dionysium Petavium suprà illum adulatoriè nimis extollendo; nempe Petavij vestigia premens, Valentinianorum sigen, de nudo silentio interpretatur, ideóque tanti Viri autoritate, à quo sua accepit, infrunitam de Sige sententiam se posse tueri gaudet. Verùm proptereà Dallæum traducere non debebat; nec quicquam causæ erat cur illi injuriosè insultaret, eúmque elato supercilio despiceret; Nam Vir iste in hisce studijs, Dallæo longè est inferior nec in scriptis Patrum æquè ac ille versatus; cum Dallæus in Antiquitatis monumentis exercitatissimus illa penitùs combiberit, & in succum quodammodò verterit.
units.tr: The Author of the Vindiciae has another argument, by which he tries to prove that Basilides held the same view as Valentinus about the Logos. He observes that Irenaeus, in book 2, chapter 16, set out to dispute against the Valentinians' first order of emission, by which they say that from Bythos and his Ennoea there were emitted Nun and Aletheia. And in chapter 18 he concludes the discussion thus: But what has been said about the emission of Sensus (that is, Nus) applies similarly to those who come from Basilides, and to the other Gnostics, from whom they also took the beginnings of the emissions, and they were refuted in the first book. After quoting these words of Irenaeus, the learned man adds on his own account: But what the origins of the emissions were, which the Valentinians derived from the first Gnostics, must be further investigated. There will be no need for a long search or lengthy inquiry, for we shall easily discover where the Valentinians got these beginnings of the emissions. I say "beginnings of the emissions" with Irenaeus, who speaks only of the beginnings of the emissions and not of the complete emissions. Otherwise he would have said that Valentinus took his emissions of the Aeons, wholly or in part, from Basilides and the other Gnostics, or at least derived certain emissions from them. But since he treats only of the beginnings of the emissions, certain such beginnings are easily found also in the heresy of Simon Magus, the parent of all the Gnostics. For in the first conjugation he places Nun, and Nus is the male God of the second syzygy of the Valentinians. Moreover, that Simon the Magician said that he was the Father above all things and a certain infinite power, which he also called the root of all things. This agrees well with the Bythos or Propator of the Valentinians, whom they present as a perfect, invisible, incomprehensible, unbegotten Aeon, acting in things invisible and unutterable. Next, Basilides, also a Gnostic, supplies the beginnings of the first three emissions of Valentinus: the Unbegotten, Nun, and Logos. For he said, as the ancient Doctors of the Church relate, that the Unbegotten begot the first of all minds (that is, Nun), and from Nus the Logos proceeded. You see, then, that Valentinus derived from the Gnostics not the complete syzygies, but the beginnings of the first, which consists of Bythos or the Unbegotten and Sige; of the second, which was compounded of Nus and Aletheia; and of the third, which they fashioned from Logos and Zoe. But the Author of the Vindiciae writes on pages 65 and 66 that Elias of Crete and Nicetas, whose words we have just transcribed, assert that Valentinus' first Ogdoad was derived from the Gnostics, while Valentinus added the Decad and Dodecad on his own account. The delusions of Elias of Crete and Nicetas we have already refuted above, so there is no need to examine them again. I will add only this: Elias and Nicetas nowhere teach, as the learned man writes, that Valentinus added the Decad and Dodecad on his own account. For they expressly state this of the Marcionites, not of the Valentinians. But since the learned Pearson knew very well that these things belong to Valentinus and not to Marcion, he substituted Valentinus for the Marcionites and expressed what Elias and Nicetas ought to have written. In this way he tacitly rebukes their delusion and ignorance, and also the carelessness of Gregory Nazianzen, who gave his commentators occasion for error when, in Oration 44, he attributed to the Simonians and Marcionites things that apply only to Valentinus. Nevertheless, he strives to confirm from Irenaeus that Valentinus took his first Ogdoad from the Simonians. For when Irenaeus, in book 2, chapter 18, had refuted in order the emission of the Logos, and had come to the emission of Anthropos and Ecclesia, who were the last Aeons of the first Ogdoad, he says: he notes that the parents of the Valentinians, the more ancient Gnostics, accuse them of having done ill-gotten theft. Concerning the second emission of Anthropos and Ecclesia, which comes from these, their so-called fathers, the Gnostics falsely named, attack one another, showing their own things and convicting themselves as wicked thieves, saying that the emissions are more fitting: that the Word is likely to be emitted from Anthropos, but not Anthropos from the Word, and that Anthropos is earlier than the Word, and that he is the God who is above all things. From these words of Irenaeus the learned man gathers, on page 66, that the Gnostics were the parents of the Valentinians. Dallaeus does not deny this; indeed he freely admits that Valentinus in some measure received the material of his theogony from the more ancient Gnostics. Pearson says: from them the Valentinians openly took, or rather stole, the first three syzygies. Where does the Author of the Vindiciae get this? Let him show the testimonies of the ancients on which his assertion rests, and let him indicate in which monuments of antiquity he read this. Otherwise it will be dismissed as easily as it is put forward. Irenaeus speaks of the mutual thefts of the Gnostics and the Valentinians, and observes that only the emission of Anthropos from the Word is charged against the Valentinians by the Gnostics. Concerning the whole syzygy of Anthropos and Ecclesia he says nothing except that the Gnostics bring it forward to show the absurd emission of Anthropos from the Word, since they thought rather that the Word should be drawn out from Anthropos. These things could be replied to the Author of the Vindiciae, and, unless I am mistaken, they would be quite sufficient in Irenaeus to refute his argument. But so that we may deal with him more generously, and so that the mind of Irenaeus may be fully grasped, it must be noted: first, that all the Valentinians took to themselves the name of Gnostics; second, that there were several sects of the Valentinians differing among themselves, some older and others more recent; third, that in the words of Irenaeus, which the learned man has cited, the discussion concerns only the various disciples of Valentinus, of whom some could be called the parents of others, namely the older of the younger and the earlier of the later. That this is so is clear, first, from the fact that Gnostics older than Valentinus himself could not attack the emissions of the Valentinian Aeons, which did not yet exist, for things that do not exist cannot be charged; second, from Irenaeus himself, who speaks of mutual quarrels and thefts. But how could the Gnostics older than Valentinus quarrel among themselves and charge each other with thefts, and how could Valentinus' own disciples, from whom the ancient Gnostics had derived anything, be likely? Perhaps the learned Pearson will say that Gnostics still existed at that time, from whom the Valentinians took their fictions, and that for this reason the Gnostics deserved to be called Fathers. But this exception will be of no use at all to the learned man unless he confirms it by the testimonies of ancient writers, and further shows that those Gnostics took from the Valentinians just as the Valentinians took from the Gnostics. For Irenaeus expressly states that both contended among themselves and reproached each other with thefts; or, to use his own words, attacking one another (that is, each other), showing their own things. Add to this that the Valentinians could not have derived the first Ogdoad from any Gnostic older than Valentinus, since it appears nowhere except in the fabulous theogonies of Valentinus and his disciples. Let all the fictions of Simon Magus, the parent of all the Gnostics, be examined; let the inventions of Menander, Saturninus, Basilides, and others who were the forerunners of the Gnostics before Valentinus, be weighed and sifted. Nowhere among them will you find that Ogdoad of which we are speaking, and why do I say the Ogdoad? Not even the last syzygy of the Ogdoad, namely Anthropos and Ecclesia, of which Irenaeus chiefly treats. But that we may not linger longer over these matters, let Irenaeus himself be consulted, who will hold up a torch for us and supply the true explanation of this passage, namely the very one we maintain. In book 1, chapter 6, he sets out the various opinions of the Valentinians, and therefore this title is prefixed to the chapter: What are the points on which those who are all from Valentinus disagree among themselves? Among these opinions, this one is most relevant to the matter we are treating: Those who are thought to be more prudent among them, he says, do not say that Logos and Zoe were generated from Anthropos and Ecclesia, but that Anthropos and Ecclesia were generated from Logos and Zoe. Anyone can see that the Gnostics mentioned in the testimony of Irenaeus cited by the Author of the Vindiciae are none other than the disciples of Valentinus himself, who, contrary to him and in the reverse order, contended that Logos and Zoe were emitted from Anthropos and Ecclesia. And because in the passage praised by Pearson these words are read, that Anthropos is earlier than the Word, and that he is the God who is above all things, let no one think these words of the Valentinians conflict with their trifles. Let Irenaeus himself be heard, who, speaking of the same Valentinians, says in book 1, chapter 7: There are others who say that the Propator of all, the Proarche, and the Proanennoetos himself is called Anthropos; and this, they say, is the great and hidden mystery, since the power that is above all things and contains all things is called Anthropos, and therefore he calls himself the Son of Man, the Saviour. From this it follows that the Author of the Vindiciae is trifling when, from a preconceived opinion, he refers to the older Gnostics things that concern the disciples of Valentinus himself. For it cannot be denied, after all that we have described from Irenaeus, that the Valentinians are meant, who were themselves Gnostics, and some of them the fathers of others, yet in such a way that they charged each other with theft and convicted themselves as wicked thieves. What I write against the Author of the Vindiciae, I wish to be written equally against another learned man, who says nothing new at all and observes nothing worth noting, except that he wanted to make himself conspicuous: the most learned Jean Daillé, whom he unfairly depresses, while he excessively and flatteringly exalts Denis Petau above him. Indeed, treading in the footsteps of Petavius, he interprets the Valentinian Sige as a bare silence, and therefore rejoices that he can defend his unfounded opinion about Sige by the authority of so great a man, from whom he received it. But he ought not to have belittled Daillé for this, and there was no reason why he should insult him so rudely and despise him with a haughty brow. For this man is far inferior to Daillé in these studies, and is not as versed in the writings of the Fathers as Daillé was, since Daillé, most practised in the monuments of antiquity, had thoroughly absorbed them and, in a sense, turned them into his own substance.

units.la: XV. Explosis Vindiciarum auctoris rationibus, quibus probare nitebatur, suorum Æonum primas Syzygias accepisse Valentinianos à Gnosticis Valentino vetustioribus, expendendæ supersunt quas ad Dallæi argumenta adfert exceptiones; primum cui occurrit argumentum ex variis Tertulliani locis depromptum est: Tertullianus siquidem de Præscript. cap. 34. & lib. 1. contr. Marc. cap. 21. docet temporibus Apostolorum nullos surrexis-se hæreticos, qui Creatorem universorum summum & unum esse Deum negarent, vel de eo controversiam moverent: Marcionem cum suo Apelle & Valentinum SOLOS PRIMOSQVE fuisse, qui id genus litis moverint. Hinc colligebat Dallæus pag. 298. apud nullos ante Valentinum hæreticos Logon ex Sige prodeuntem extitisse; quoniam qui ex Sige Logon educunt, ij de creatore Deo controversiam movent, & alterum Deum suspicari audent, quod ante Marcionem & Valentinum nemo suspicari ausus est; Dallæi argumentum in hanc formam compegit Pearsonius pag. 66.
units.tr: Having dismissed the arguments of the author of the Vindiciae, by which he strove to prove that the Valentinians received the first syzygies of their Aeons from the Gnostics who were older than Valentinus, there remain to be weighed the objections he raises against Dallaeus's arguments. The first argument that meets us is drawn from various passages of Tertullian. Tertullian, in the De Praescriptione, chapter 34, and in the first book Against Marcion, chapter 21, teaches that in the times of the Apostles no heretics arose who denied that the Creator of all things is the highest and only God, or who raised controversy about him; and that Marcion with his Apelles and Valentinus were ALONE AND FIRST to raise this kind of dispute. From this Dallaeus inferred, at page 298, that no heretics before Valentinus had produced Logos emerging from Sige, since those who derive Logos from Sige raise controversy about the Creator God and dare to suspect another God, which no one dared to suspect before Marcion and Valentinus. Pearson, at page 66, put Dallaeus's argument into this form:

units.la: Nemo ante Valentinum docuit alium esse Deum præter Creatorem
units.tr: No one before Valentinus taught that there is another God besides the Creator.

units.la: Omnes qui Bythum & Sigen induxe-runt, docuerunt alium esse Deum præter Creatorem. Ergo.
units.tr: All those who introduced Bythos and Sige taught that there is another God besides the Creator. Therefore:

units.la: Qui Bython & Sigen inducerent ante Valentinum nulli fuerunt.
units.tr: Those who introduced Bythos and Sige before Valentinus did not exist.

units.la: Hujus Syllogismi Minorem admittit propositionem; Majorem autem negat, & aperte falsam esse pronunciat; Negatæ propositionis rationem hanc profert, ex variis videlicet Veterum, imprimis Irenæi, testimonijs quæ describit, liquidò constare multos ante Valentinum negasse Deum summum creâsse mundum, adeóque præter Creatorem alium Deum esse docuisse. Idem ferè dicit in genere Cotelerius in Epist. ad Magnef. pag. 449. nullis ad hoc probandum Antiquorum Patrum adductis testimonijs: fatetur tamen neminem ante Marcionem (cum quo involvit Magistrum ejus Cerdonem) Apellem atque Valentinum aperte ac ipsis verbis plures Deos dixisse; & id solùm à Tertulliano doceri putat in locis à Dallæo citatis. Ego verò respondeo Dallæum non suo marte ita argumentatum esse, sed ex Tertulliani verbis ex quibus suam elicuit conclusionem, ac proinde Dallæi non est proprie istud argumentum, sed ipsius Tertulliani, qui Dallæo illud ministravit, ideoque cum hac limitatione illud propositi Dallæus, si Tertullianum audimus, ut est à Vindiciarum Auctore observatum pag. 68. cùm igitur majorem syllogismi propositionem negat Vir doctus, Tertullianum ferit potiùs quàm Dallæum, qui Tertulliani verbis penitùs adhæsit: Quamvis forte in eo peccaverit præstantissimus [?] Dallæus: Tertulliani quippe verba contra Veterum consensum non erant urgenda, sed meâ quidem sententiâ satius erat illius mentem benignè interpretari, quàm eum nudè ac simpliciter sic argumentantem inducere. Secundum Dallæi argumentum est (inquit Pearsonius pag. 68. ) Hæretici Valentino vetustiores omnes se ipsi negabunt Logon Siges vel filium vel nepotem induxisse. Dallæus sanè hoc dicit pag. 298. Respondet Vindiciarum Auctor, neque Gnosticorum Veterum, neque Valentinianorum quemquam Logon Siges filium induxisse, neque de nepotibus Siges aut Gnosticos illos aut Valentinianos quicquam philosophatos esse : Cùm autem, ait, addit Dallæus, eam lauream Valentini esse, qui ex omnibus Hæresiarchis illam Æonum ogdoadem princeps instituerit, in quâ ex Bytho & Sige per Nun & Alethian Logos cum Zoe prodit ; id omnino dicit quod nemo ante eum affirmavit, cujúsque contrarium multi asseruerunt : Nos verò suprà fusè demonstravimus id merito à Dallæo affirmatum esse, omnibúsque Viri dócti occurrimus objectionibus, & primam Æonum Ogdoadem à principe Valentino confictam esse validissimis probavimus argumentis, pergit eruditus Pearsonius, & ita de Dallæo loquitur ; ad sua confirmanda nihil aliud adducit Vir doctissimus, quàm quòd in omnibus ab Irenæo recitatis Hæreticorum vetustiorum Theogonis, non appareat Logi è Sige emissio: Quasi verò hoc non abundè sufficiat ad Dallæi assertionem confirmandam; Ex Irenæo & alijs vetustissimis Scriptoribus discimus quæ fuerint Hæreticorum Valentino vetustiorum figmenta, & quæ ipsius Valentini ejúsque Discipulorum fabulosæDivinitates,apud nullos autem Valentino vetustiores Logon è Sige emissum comperimus: Veteres illi Scriptores de hæresibus datâ operâ scripserunt; Hæreticorum omnium catalogos non indiligenter contexuerunt, impias eorum doctrinas, commenta, fabulas ac deliramenta accuratè expenderunt,& tamen si Vindiciarum Auctorem audimus, vix quicquam certi hac de re ex Antiquorum Patrum monumentis depromere possumus, cùm integras omnium Hæreticorum Genealogias non repræsentaverint. Ergo perfunctoriè hoc argumentum tractarunt antiquissimi Scriptores, & labore sponte suscepto maximâ cum negligentiâ perfuncti sunt? Quomodo igitur exploratas habebimus hæresèon omnium differentias? Et quomodo alias ab aliis secernere poterimus? Si adeò negligentes fuêre Ecclesiastici Scriptores, ut ex illis minimè nosse valeamus quid unaquæque docuerit hæresis, etiamsi id assequi pro virili conemur. Sed ut propius ad rem quâ de agitur accedamus, dicat Vir doctus, Num putet Simonem Magum, Menandrum, Saturnilum, Basilidem, Carpocratem, Epiphanem, & Prodicum, Gnosticorum omnium Valentino vetustiorum famosissimos, Num, inquam, putet eos omnes eandem planè cum Valentino hæresim confinxisse; si affirmat, contradicit Irenæo, Tertulliano & quotquot de hæresibus scripserunt; si negat discrimen aliquod inter istas hæreses agnoscit, ostendat igitur quâ in re differat Valentini hæresis, à cæterorum Gnosticorum hæresibus Valentinianâ antiquioribus: pertendit Dallæus & merito, Logi è Sige emissionem, peculiarem esse Valentiniana-næ hæresis characterem; donec igitur Vindiciarum Auctor probaverit hanc Logi è Sige eductionem, communem esse Valentino cum aliis Gnostici generis hæreticis, valebit præstantissimi Dallæi assertio: Nam quæ de Simonianis suprà observavit eruditissimus Pearsonius, à nobis excussa sunt, & luce meridianâ clarius demonstratum, falsos esse Eliam & Nicetam, necnon ipsum Gregorium Nazianzenum, dùm Simonianis & Marcionistis tribuunt, quæ solis congruunt Valentin a nis[?]. Nec est quod Vir doctissimus caussetur Irenæi silentium, veluti integras hæreticorum istorum Genealogias non repræsentaverit; nam quæ ab Irenæo & aliis de fictitiis istis Genealogiis nobis tradita sunt; abundè sufficiunt ad singulas istorum hæreses discernendas, aliasque ab aliis separandas. Sed inquit Pearsonius pag. 69. ratio scribendi ab Irenæo observata, à Dallæo minimè est perpensa, si causam rogas, hanc habebis, observo, ait, Dallæi verba; Primum caput ad Valentinum pertinere ostendit, & præfixus ei titulus, & ipsa Operis præfatio. Agnosco Dallæi verba quæ extant cap. 12. p. 295. Quid ad hæc Vindiciarum Auctor, imò verò, inquit, & præfatio & titulus, & Capitis ipsius tota series ostendit ad ipsius Discipulos il-lud pertinere, quos ab illo in quamplurimis descivisse omnes notârunt. Mera profecto cavillatio; Dallæus siquidem de Valentino loquitur, non ut illius Discipulos hac ejiciat, ut ita dicam, categoriâ, sed ad exclusionem tantùm aliorum hæreticorum Valentino vetustiorum; liquet autem ex Præfationis & Capitis primi lectione, agere Irenæum non de solis Valentiniani Discipulis, ut ait Vir doctus, sed etiam de ipso Valentino, quicquid sit de titulo Capiti præfixo, apud veterem Irenæi interpretem. Verum ut probet Pearsonius Irenæum integras Gnosticorum Genealogias non repræsentasse, observat inter Æonas Basilidis Valentino seniores numerari Ennoean, eam autem Sigen non nominasse Basilidem, inquit pag. 70. quis inde colligat, quod Irenæus hoc non affirmat. Si locum in quo Ennoea inter Æonas Basilidis numeratur, indicâsset eruditissimus Vindiciarum Auctor, non minimam à nobis gratiam iniisset; Ennoea enim inter Æonas Basilidis nusquam comparet, apud eos qui de hæresibus ex professo tractarunt, Irenæum dico, Tertullianum, Philastrium, Epiphanium, Augustinum, Theodoretum ;. Unde igitur hanc Ennoean tanquam è Basilidis Æonibus unum hauserit Pearsonius indicare debebat. Verùm enimverò animadvertisse mihi videor hariolationis causam, in errorem scilicet inductus est à Cornario Epiphanii interprete, qui Basilidis Phronesim, reddidit per Intelligentiam, Pearsonius verò Ennoean maluit dicere, Phronesis tamen Prudentiam propriè sonat, vel ut loquitur Tertullianus in recensendis Basilidis Æonibus Providentiam. Sic enim Basilidis Æones duobus in locis disponit Epiphanius. Hær. 24. Ingenitum, ab hoc procreata Mens, à Mente Verbum, à Verbo Prudentia, à Prudentiâ Potentia & Sapientia, à Potentiâ & Sapientiâ Principatus, Potestates & Angeli; Eodem plane ordine fabulosos istos Æonas numerant Irenæus, Tertullianus & alij; De Ennoea Pearsoniana ne γῆ[?] quidem.
units.tr: He admits the minor premise of this syllogism, but denies the major and declares it plainly false. He gives the reason for his denial: from the various testimonies of the Ancients, above all Irenaeus, which he describes, it is clear that many before Valentinus had denied that the highest God created the world, and so had taught that there is another God besides the Creator. Cotelerius says much the same in general, in his note on the Epistle to the Magnesians, page 449, without citing any testimonies of the ancient Fathers to prove it. He nevertheless admits that no one before Marcion (with whom he includes his teacher Cerdo) and Apelles and Valentinus openly and in so many words spoke of several Gods; and he thinks this is taught only by Tertullian in the passages cited by Dallaeus. I, however, answer that Dallaeus did not reason in this way on his own strength, but from the words of Tertullian, from which he drew his conclusion. Therefore this is not properly Dallaeus's argument but Tertullian's own, which Tertullian supplied to Dallaeus. Hence Dallaeus put it forward with this limitation, if we listen to Tertullian, as the author of the Vindiciae has noted at page 68. So when this learned man denies the major premise of the syllogism, he strikes at Tertullian rather than at Dallaeus, who clung closely to Tertullian's words. Yet perhaps the most excellent Dallaeus erred in this: Tertullian's words were not to be pressed against the consensus of the Ancients. In my opinion, however, it was better to interpret his meaning kindly than to present him as arguing so bare and simple a case.
