The second argument of Dallaeus, says Pearson at page 68, is this: All the heretics older than Valentinus will themselves deny that Logos was introduced as the son or grandson of Sige. Dallaeus certainly says this at page 298. The author of the Vindiciae replies that neither any of the ancient Gnostics nor any of the Valentinians introduced Logos as the son of Sige, nor did those Gnostics or Valentinians philosophize about grandsons of Sige. But when Dallaeus adds, he says, that this is the glory of Valentinus, who among all the heresiarchs first set up that ogdoad of Aeons in which from Bythos and Sige, through Nous and Aletheia, Logos comes forth with Zoe, he says what no one before him had affirmed, and what many have asserted to be the contrary. We, however, have above demonstrated at length that Dallaeus was right to affirm this, and we have met all the objections of the learned man and proved by very strong arguments that the first ogdoad of Aeons was devised by the leader Valentinus. So the learned Pearson goes on, and speaks of Dallaeus thus: the most learned man adduces nothing else to confirm his position except that in all the theogonies of the older heretics recited by Irenaeus there does not appear the emission of Logos from Sige. As if this did not amply suffice to confirm Dallaeus's assertion! From Irenaeus and other very ancient writers we learn what fictions of the heretics older than Valentinus were, and what the fabulous divinities of Valentinus himself and his disciples were; but among any who are older than Valentinus we find no Logos emitted from Sige. The ancient writers wrote about heresies on purpose; they compiled catalogues of all heretics with no little diligence; they weighed carefully their impious doctrines, inventions, fables and ravings. Yet if we listen to the author of the Vindiciae, we can hardly draw anything certain on this matter from the monuments of the ancient Fathers, since they did not set forth the complete genealogies of all the heretics. Did the most ancient writers, then, treat this argument carelessly and perform a task they had undertaken of their own accord with the greatest negligence? How then shall we have a sure knowledge of the differences among all the heresies? And how shall we be able to separate one from another? If the ecclesiastical writers were so negligent that we can hardly know from them what each heresy taught, even though we try our utmost to attain this. But to come closer to the matter in question, let the learned man say whether he thinks that Simon Magus, Menander, Saturninus, Basilides, Carpocrates, Epiphanes and Prodicus, the most famous Gnostics older than Valentinus, all devised exactly the same heresy as Valentinus. If he affirms this, he contradicts Irenaeus, Tertullian and all who wrote about heresies. If he denies it, and acknowledges some difference between those heresies, let him show then in what respect the heresy of Valentinus, which was later than the other Gnostic heresies, differs from them. Dallaeus insists, and rightly, that the emission of Logos from Sige is the peculiar mark of the Valentinian heresy. Therefore, until the author of the Vindiciae has proved that this emission of Logos from Sige was common to Valentinus and to other heretics of the Gnostic kind, the most excellent Dallaeus's assertion will stand. For what the most learned Pearson observed above about the Simonians has been examined by us, and it has been shown clearer than the noonday light that Elias and Nicetas, and Gregory Nazianzen himself, are wrong in attributing to the Simonians and Marcionites what agrees only with the Valentinians. Nor is there reason for the most learned man to complain of Irenaeus's silence, as if he had not set forth the complete genealogies of those heretics. For what Irenaeus and others have handed down to us about those fictitious genealogies is quite enough to distinguish each of those heresies and to separate them from one another. But, says Pearson at page 69, the method of writing observed by Irenaeus has been very little weighed by Dallaeus. If you ask the reason, you will have it thus. I observe, he says, Dallaeus's words: He shows that the first chapter pertains to Valentinus, both the title prefixed to it and the preface of the Work itself. I acknowledge Dallaeus's words, which stand in chapter 12, page 295. What does the author of the Vindiciae reply to this? On the contrary, he says, both the preface and the title, and the whole sequence of the chapter itself, show that this pertains to his disciples, whom everyone has noted to have departed from him in very many points. This is pure quibbling. For Dallaeus speaks of Valentinus, not so as to expel his disciples from this, so to speak, category, but only to exclude the other heretics older than Valentinus. It is clear from reading the preface and the first chapter that Irenaeus deals not only with the disciples of Valentinus alone, as the learned man says, but also with Valentinus himself, whatever may be the case with the title prefixed to the chapter in the old translator of Irenaeus. But to prove that Irenaeus did not set forth the complete genealogies of the Gnostics, Pearson observes that among the Aeons of Basilides the older ones, before Valentinus, are counted as Ennoea, but that Basilides did not name her Sige, he says at page 70, what does anyone infer from this, since Irenaeus does not affirm it? If the most learned author of the Vindiciae had pointed out the place in which Ennoea is counted among the Aeons of Basilides, he would have earned no small thanks from us. For Ennoea nowhere appears among the Aeons of Basilides in those who treated heresies professedly: I mean Irenaeus, Tertullian, Philaster, Epiphanius, Augustine and Theodoret. Whence then Pearson should have indicated that he drew this Ennoea as one of Basilides's Aeons. But I seem to perceive the cause of his conjecture: he was led into error by Cornarius, the translator of Epiphanius, who rendered Basilides's Phronesis as Intelligence, while Pearson preferred to say Ennoea. Yet Phronesis properly means Prudence, or, as Tertullian says when listing Basilides's Aeons, Providence. For Epiphanius lays out Basilides's Aeons in this way in two places. Heresy 24: Unbegotten; from him was produced Mind; from Mind, Word; from Word, Prudence; from Prudence, Power and Sapience; from Power and Wisdom, Principality, Powers and Angels. Irenaeus, Tertullian and others count these fabulous Aeons in exactly the same order. Of Pearson's Ennoea there is not a trace.

units.la: Ventum est tandem ad tertium Dallæi argumentum ex hisce Irenæi verbis depromptum lib. 1. cap. 5. Qui est primus ab eâ quæ dicitur Gnostica hæresis, antiquas in suum characterem doctrinas transferens Valentinus, sic definivit; Ita græca Irenæi verba convertit vetustissimus illius Interpres, nec male Scriptoris Græci mentem expressit; Dallæus postquam Irenæi verba Græca adduxit, observat Petavium frustrà verba ista ab eâ quæ dicitur Gnostica hæresis, cum verbo transferens conjungere, & sic interpretari, ut velit Valentinum intelligi illas doctrinas ex Gnosticorum hæresi deprompsisse. Alia (inquit Dallæus pag.302.) est Irenæi mens, Valentinum ex illa Gnosticorum hæresi primum fuisse, qui ex veteribus doctrinis ad suam formam translatis & aptatis, quod subjicit, dogma tradiderit; Hanc autem veram esse Irenæi mentem probat, 1. ex eo quòd nullus ante Valentinum hæreticus ex Sige Logon ortum esse definiverit: 2. quia verbum Græcum μεταρμοζὶν[?] quo usus est Irenæus, proprie est μεταδιδέναι τὴν ἁρμονίαν[?], indéque [illegible, ~9 letters] corrigere, emendare; unde concludit veteres illas doctrinas, quaecunque sint, non totas & integras, & sic ut erant, apud vetustiores, immutatas, sed à se mutatas, & pro suo arbitrio castigatas, & correctas in proprium Valentinum characterem transtulisse. Characterem autem Valentini proprium, nihil aliud esse Irenæo putat Dallæus, quàm propriam doctrinæ ejus formam. Firmissimum hoc Dallæi argumentum, objectiunculam vocat quidam Societatis Sorbonicæ Theo* logus; Non enim, inquit, Irenæus de Sige peculiariter agit; verum de toto Valentini diagrammate. Vbi qui Græcè sciunt voces ὁ μὲν γὰρ πρῶτος [?] nequaquam referent ad ἔτως [illegible, ~3 letters] ἐξηγορήσαν [?]. Ideò ponitur ὁ μὲν γὰρ πρῶτος quia præcesserat ἀνὸ τῶν καὶ τεῖων ὄντων [?], & quia sequitur, ἕκαστος ἀλλ' ἀλλος ἀλλ' ἄλλοι [?]. Quis non miretur Scriptorem istum cui validissima argumenta objectiunculæ sunt vel solo halitu diffandæ, & tamen objectiunculam illam solvere non potest, imò eam attingere aliquomodó reformidat, forte hoc jus sibi arrogat ex Doctoratus prærogativâ, ut solidissima argumenta in objectiunculas, & objectiunculas in argumenta firmissima convertere pro arbitrio sibi licere putet; Irenæus, inquit, non de Sige peculiariter agit, verum de toto Valentini diagrammate; Quid tum ? Nonne in illo diagrammate reperitur Logi è Sige emissio ? Satisfaciat Dallæo petenti ut alius Valentini doctrinæ proprius sibi indicetur character, ostendatúrque in cæterorum Gnosticorum Valentino antiquiorum Theogoniis Logi ex Sige emissio ? Cùm hoc ostendere deberet, aliò confugit, & nescio quas comminiscitur ratiunculas, seu potiùs subterfugia, ut ictum declinet, & litem reddat interminabilem; negari non potest quin Valentinus novam sectam condiderit, æquè ac Saturnilus, aut Basilides, aut quivis de isto grege alius: Ergo aliquid peculiare habuit, & ab alijs diversum, alioqui non nova fuisset illius hæresis, cùm id tamen diserte profiteantur Veteres qui de hæresibus scripserunt. Affirmat Dallæus Valentini sectam in Logi ex Sige eductione à cæteris differre : Duo igitur illius adversarijs demonstranda incumbunt; 1. Logi ex Sige emissionem reperiri in fabulosis aliorum Hæreticorum Valentino seniorum Theogonijs: 2. quâ in re consistat proprius Valentinianæ doctrinæ character: Neutrum facit Societatis Sorbonicæ Theologus, quia scilicet nodum quem solvere non potest, Criticæ suæ gladio audacter secare non veretur hoc pacto, qui Græcè sciunt voces ὁ [illegible, ~4 letters] πρῶτ[?]ῳ nequaquam referent ad οὕτως ἐξηνοφόρησεν[?] imò eò omninò referent, neque aliò proprie sunt referendæ; nec est quod dicat ideò poni hic enim primus, vel qui enim est primus, quia præcesserat cùm sint duo vel tres, & quia sequitur, Secundus verò, alius autem, alij vero: Irenæus siquidem hoc solum significare voluit, ex omnibus Gnosticis primum fuisse Valentinum qui sic definivit. Doctissimus Vindiciarum Auctor aliâ insistere viâ mihi videtur; nam primùm pag. 71. Petavij interpretationem tuetur, etsi meo quidem judicio jure defendi nequeat, ecce Irenæi verba, ὁ μὲν γὰρ πρῶτῳ[?] ἀπὸ τῆς λεγομένης γνωσικῆς αἱρέσεως τὰς ἀρχαίας εἰς ἴδιον κακακτῆς[?] διδασκαλίας μεθαρμόσας Οὐαλεντῖνος, ὅτως[?] ἐξηνοφόρησεν. Petavius sic Latinè reddidit apud Epiphanium Hær. 31. num. 32. Etenim qui à Gnosticorum Hæresi deprompta quædam initia primus peculiaris ad Sectæ formam transtulit. Nemo est qui Græca Irenæi Paulò accuratius cum Latinâ Petavij versione contenderit, qui celeberrimi illius Iesuitæ interpretationem non exsufflet; Certè vetus Irenæi Interpres Autoris mentem non malè assecutus est, nec ab illius verbis longè recessit ita vertendo, qui enim est primus ab eâ quæ Gnostica dicitur hæresis, antiquas in suum characterem doctrinas transferens Valentinus, sic definivit. Quivis videt antiquissimum hunc interpretem Graeca Irenaei fidelissime reddidisse, & ad eum propius accedere recentiorem, qui sic transtulit. Siquidem Valentinus qui primus ex eâ sectâ, quae Gnostica nuncupatur, veteres doctrinas ad characterem suum & institutum accommodavit, ad hunc modum docet. Vt ut est firmissimum est, quicquid dicat Pearsonius pag. 72. Dallaei argumentum ex voce πξῶτ@ deductum hoc pacto, pag. 301. Si haec Valentinus ex Gnostica primus definivit, certè nullus ante eum Gnosticus sic definiverat, Logon adeò ex Sige fructificatum (quod unum est ex illis sic à Valentino definitis) nemo ante eum Gnosticus deliraverat. Vindiciarum Auctor respondet Dallaeum niti interpretatione, quae sententiam Irenaei mirè confundit, & ab ejus mente prorsus aliena est, & statuere Logon ex Sige fructificatum esse unum ex illis à Valentino definitis, cùm Valentinus non dicat Logon ex Sige, sed ex primâ tetrade fructificatum, idque non quòd à Sige sed quod ab Alethiâ emissus esset, quae in eadem tetrade post Sigen fuit. Quid est argutari, si hoc non est, Logon ex primâ tetrade fructificatum esse fatetur Pearsonius, Sige est in primâ illius tetradis Syzygiâ, ergo ex Sige ortum esse Logon oportet, si non immediatè , saltem mediantibus Nu & Alethia; Verùm ut indicet quisnam fuerit peculiaris Valentini hæresis character, dicit pag. 72. Fabulam Triginta Æonum illi propriam fuisse, decada & duodecada adjecisse opinatur Pearsonius; primam verò Ogdoada à Veteribus accepisse, & ordinem tantùm secundæ tetradis mutâse; sed jam suprà explosimus commentum illud de primâ Ogdoade à Vetustioribus Gnosticis acceptâ; ideóque concidit Viri docti ratiocinatio, quæ prætereà Irenæi narrationi omninò adversatur; quæ dicit de voce μεταχαρακτηρίζειν[?], quòd sæpe simpliciter transferre, aut adaptare significat, non semper, mutare, multò minùs in melius, corrigere scilicet, aut emendare, nihili planè sunt, nec Dallæo quicquam nocent; fatetur enim plerásque Valentini hæresis materias eàsdem esse, quæ vetustiorum Hæreticorum, materiarû verò inter se compositionem ab ijs diversissimam, & hanc harmoniæ & compositionis in aliam formam, seu in alium characterem, mutationem ac translationem, designat apud Irenæum vox μεταχαρακτηρισμὸς[?]. Cùm ergo ex ijs quæ disputata sunt constet, ex omnibus vetustissimis hæreticis, primum extitisse Valentinum, qui Logon à Sige progredi, aut exire docuerit. Illud postremò concludendum superest, omninò ad Valentinum respexisse Auctorem Epistolæ ad Magnesios, adeóque Ignatio juniorem necessario fuisse.
units.tr: We have come at last to Dallaeus's third argument, drawn from these words of Irenaeus, Book 1, chapter 5: "Valentinus, who is the first from the so-called Gnostic heresy, transferring ancient doctrines into his own character, defined it thus;" That most ancient translator rendered the Greek words of Irenaeus this way, and he expressed the mind of the Greek writer not badly. After quoting Irenaeus's Greek words, Dallaeus observes that Petavius has tried in vain to join the words "from the so-called Gnostic heresy" with the word "transferring," and to interpret them so as to make Valentinus be understood to have drawn those doctrines from the Gnostic heresy. "Irenaeus's mind is otherwise," says Dallaeus (p. 302), "that Valentinus was first from that Gnostic heresy, who, taking old doctrines and fitting them to his own form, handed down the dogma that follows." He proves that this is the true mind of Irenaeus: first, because no heretic before Valentinus defined that the Logos arose from Sige; second, because the Greek verb metarmozein [μεταρμοζὶν], which Irenaeus used, properly means to pass on a harmony, and hence to correct or amend. From this he concludes that those old doctrines, whatever they were, were not transferred whole and entire, nor as they stood among the older writers, but were altered by Valentinus himself, corrected at his own discretion, and carried over into Valentinus's own character. Dallaeus thinks that the "character proper to Valentinus" is nothing else in Irenaeus than the proper form of his teaching. This very firm argument of Dallaeus a certain theologian of the Sorbonne calls a little objection; "For," he says, "Irenaeus is not speaking particularly of Sige, but of the whole diagram of Valentinus." Here, those who know Greek will not at all refer the words ho men gar prōtos [ὁ μὲν γὰρ πρῶτος] to houtōs exēgorēsen [οὕτως ἐξηγορήσεν]. "The phrase ho men gar prōtos is used because he had gone before," and "because there follows" hekastos allos alli [ἕκαστος ἄλλος ἄλλη]... Who would not marvel at this writer, for whom the strongest arguments are little objections to be blown away with a breath, and yet who cannot solve that little objection, nor even dares to touch it in any way? Perhaps he claims for himself, from the privilege of his doctorate, the right to turn the most solid arguments into little objections, and little objections into the firmest arguments, as he thinks he may at his pleasure. "Irenaeus," he says, "is not speaking particularly of Sige, but of the whole diagram of Valentinus." So what? Is it not in that diagram that the emission of the Logos from Sige is found? Let him satisfy Dallaeus, who asks that some other character proper to the teaching of Valentinus be pointed out, and let him show that the emission of the Logos from Sige is found in the theogonies of the other Gnostics who were older than Valentinus. Since he ought to have shown this, he flees elsewhere and invents I know not what petty reasonings, or rather evasions, so as to dodge the blow and make the dispute endless. It cannot be denied that Valentinus founded a new sect, just as Saturninus, or Basilides, or anyone else of that crowd did. Therefore he had something peculiar of his own, different from the others; otherwise his heresy would not have been new, though the ancient writers who wrote about heresies openly profess that it was. Dallaeus asserts that Valentinus's sect differs from the others in the emission of the Logos from Sige. Two things therefore lie upon his opponents to demonstrate: (1) that the emission of the Logos from Sige is found in the fabulous theogonies of other heretics older than Valentinus; (2) in what the proper character of the Valentinian doctrine consists. The theologian of the Sorbonne does neither, because, namely, the knot he cannot untie he does not hesitate to cut boldly with the sword of his criticism, in this way: "those who know Greek will not at all refer the words ho prōtos [ὁ πρῶτος] to houtōs exēgorēsen [οὕτως ἐξηγορήσεν]. Rather, they will refer them altogether there, and properly there alone. Nor is there reason for him to say that 'hic enim primus' or 'qui enim est primus' is used because he had gone before, since there are two or three, and because there follows 'secundus vero,' 'alius autem,' 'alii vero.'" Irenaeus, indeed, wished to signify only this, that among all the Gnostics Valentinus was the first who defined it thus. The most learned author of the Vindiciae seems to me to pursue another path; for first, on p. 71, he defends Petavius's interpretation, though in my judgement it cannot rightly be defended. Behold the words of Irenaeus: ho men gar prōtos apo tēs legomenēs gnōstikēs hairesēs tas archaias eis idion charaktēra metharmosas Oualentinos, houtōs exēgorēsen [ὁ μὲν γὰρ πρῶτος ἀπὸ τῆς λεγομένης γνωστικῆς αἱρέσεως τὰς ἀρχαίας εἰς ἴδιον χαρακτῆρα μεταρμόσας Οὐαλεντῖνος, οὕτως ἐξηγορήσεν]. Petavius rendered this into Latin thus, in Epiphanius, Heresy 31, no. 32: "For he who first transferred certain beginnings drawn from the heresy of the Gnostics into the form of a peculiar sect." No one has compared the Greek of Irenaeus more carefully with the Latin version of Petavius without blowing away the interpretation of that most famous Jesuit. Certainly the old translator of Irenaeus has caught the author's mind not badly, and by rendering it thus he has not strayed far from its words: "For Valentinus, who is the first from the heresy called Gnostic, transferring ancient doctrines into his own character, defined it thus." Anyone can see that this most ancient interpreter rendered the Greek of Irenaeus most faithfully, and that the more recent translator, who rendered it thus, comes closer to him: "For Valentinus, who first from that sect which is called Gnostic, adapted the old doctrines to his own character and plan, teaches in this manner." However it is, the argument of Dallaeus drawn from the word prōtos [πρῶτος] is most firm, whatever Pearson says on p. 72. Dallaeus argues in this way, on p. 301: "If Valentinus was the first to define these things from the Gnostics, certainly no Gnostic had defined them thus before him; the Logos, indeed, brought forth from Sige (which is one of those things defined thus by Valentinus), no Gnostic before him had dreamed of." The author of the Vindiciae answers that Dallaeus relies on an interpretation which wonderfully confuses the sense of Irenaeus and is wholly alien to his mind, and that he asserts that the Logos brought forth from Sige is one of those things defined by Valentinus, whereas Valentinus does not say that the Logos was from Sige, but "brought forth from the first tetrad," and that not because he was sent from Sige but because he was sent from Aletheia, who in the same tetrad came after Sige. What is this quibbling? If it is not the case that Pearson admits the Logos was brought forth from the first tetrad, and Sige is in the first syzygy of that tetrad, then the Logos must have arisen from Sige, if not immediately, at least through the mediation of Nous and Aletheia. But to indicate what was the peculiar character of Valentinus's heresy, Pearson says on p. 72 that the fable of the Thirty Aeons was peculiar to him, and he thinks Valentinus added the decad and the dodecad, while he received the first ogdoad from the ancients and only changed the order of the second tetrad. But we have already above exploded that fiction that the first ogdoad was received from the older Gnostics; therefore the reasoning of this learned man collapses, which moreover is wholly contrary to the narrative of Irenaeus. What he says about the word metacharakterizein, that it often means simply to transfer or to adapt, and not always to change, much less to change for the better, that is, to correct or amend, is absolutely nothing and does no harm to Dallaeus. For he admits that the materials of the Valentinian heresy are for the most part the same as those of the older heretics, but that the arrangement of the materials among themselves is most different from theirs; and this change and translation of the harmony and composition into another form, or another character, Irenaeus designates by the word metacharakterismos [μεταχαρακτηρισμός]. Since therefore it is established from what has been argued that among all the most ancient heretics Valentinus was the first who taught that the Logos proceeds, or comes forth, from Sige, it remains only to conclude at last that the author of the Epistle to the Magnesians certainly looked to Valentinus, and therefore must necessarily have been younger than Ignatius.

units.la: XVIII. Excussimus tres doctissimi Vindiciarum Auctoris assertiones, nulliusque planè ponderis esse ad suum Ignatium tuendum fusè demonstravimus, superest quarta quam ita proponit cap. 7. probari certò non posse ipsos Valentini errores Ignatio fuisse penitùs incognitos. Doctor ille Sorbonicus cujus aliquoties mentionem fecimus, observat huic sententiæ patrocinari Victorinum & Autpertum in Apocalypsim, cùm dicunt Valentinum Hæresim suam disseminâsse vivente Ioanne Apostolo si Vir ille eruditus loca ex quibus hæc desumpsit indicasset, à quærendi labore nos liberasset; Quicquid sit neque Victorinus neque Autpertus audiendi sunt, cùm de re adeò antiquâ loquantur sine alicujus vetustioris auctoritate, imò contra omnium veterum testimonia scribant Valentinum hæresim suam disseminâsse vivente Ioanne Apostolo; nam Victorinus anno 303. ut vulgò fertur Martyr pro Christi fide occubuit, Autpertus verò octavo sæculo inclinato vivendi finem fecit; fatetur quidem idem qui suprà Scriptor, nonnullos ex Antiquis Valentinianæ luis exortum ad tempora Antonini Pij retulisse; sed huic objectioni se facturum satis putat, si dicit Hæreticis de more esse, diu clam docere, ita ut tunc à quibusdam cognoscantur, ab aliis ignorentur; At Victorino & Autperto minus comperta fuisse Valentinianæ hæresis initia par est credere, quàm vetustioribus Scriptoribus qui diserte testantur Valentinum seriùs quàm isti volunt impium suum dogma disseminâsse; & quia iterùm objici poterat ex Tertulliano De Præscript. cap. 30. Valentinum sub Eleuthero Papa vixisse adhuc, ac proinde juxta Victorini & Autperti supputationem, ad centesimum circiter annum produxisse, respondet nihil vetare quominùs ad hanc provectam ætatem pervenerit ille Hæresiarcha, cùm tamen rarissimum sit homines denasci centenario majores, qualis fuerit Valentinus oportet, si vivente Ioanne Apostolo hæresim suam disseminare cœpit; Verba autem Tertulliani quod spectat, ea errorem vel mendum continere audacter pronunciat; & tamen nullam prorsùs istius assertionis adfert rationem, ideóque mihi contemnenda videtur, & eadem facilitate neganda, quâ proponitur. Doctissimus Vindiciarum Auctor aliâ viâ procedit, ut probet Ignatium Valentini sententiam cognoscere potuisse; sic autem argumentatur pag. 75. Si Polycarpi doctrina & Ignatio & S. Ioanni & aliis etiam Apostolis cognita fuerit, Valentini etiam doctrina saltem ab Ignatio cognosci potuit. Ego vero consequentiam istius propositionis nego, & concedo antecedens; Vir tamen doctus in antecedente probando totus est, de consequente parum aut nihil sollicitus; ut haec omnia clariora evadant, Pearsonij argumentum in hanc formam compingendum est.
units.tr: XVIII. We have examined the three most learned assertions of the author of the Vindiciae and have fully shown that they carry no weight at all in defending his Ignatius. There remains a fourth, which he proposes in chapter 7: the very errors of Valentinus cannot with certainty be shown to have been wholly unknown to Ignatius. That Sorbonne doctor, whom we have mentioned several times, notes that Victorinus and Autpert in their commentary on the Apocalypse support this view, when they say that Valentinus spread his heresy while the apostle John was still living. If that learned man had indicated the passages from which he drew this, he would have spared us the labour of searching. Whatever the case, neither Victorinus nor Autpert deserves a hearing, since they speak of so ancient a matter without the authority of any older writer, and indeed they write against the testimony of all the ancients that Valentinus spread his heresy while the apostle John was living. For Victorinus, as is commonly reported, died as a martyr for the Christian faith in 303, and Autpert ended his life when the eighth century was already declining. The same writer as above admits that some of the ancients placed the rise of the Valentinian mischief in the time of Antoninus Pius, but he thinks he will sufficiently answer this objection by saying that it is customary for heretics to teach secretly for a long time, so that at one time they are known to some and unknown to others. Yet it is fair to believe that the beginnings of the Valentinian heresy were less well known to Victorinus and Autpert than to the older writers, who clearly testify that Valentinus spread his impious doctrine later than these men would have it. And since it could again be objected, from Tertullian, On Prescription, chapter 30, that Valentinus was still alive under Pope Eleutherius, and so, by the reckoning of Victorinus and Autpert, lived on to about the hundredth year, he replies that nothing prevents that heresiarch from reaching such an advanced age, although it is very rare for men to live beyond a hundred years, as Valentinus must have done if he began to spread his heresy while the apostle John was living. As for Tertullian's words, he boldly declares that they contain an error or a corruption, yet he brings no reason at all for this assertion, and so it seems to me that it may be dismissed as easily as it is proposed. The most learned author of the Vindiciae proceeds by another route, to prove that Ignatius could have known the opinion of Valentinus, and argues thus on p. 75: If the teaching of Polycarp was known to Ignatius, and to John the apostle and the other apostles as well, the teaching of Valentinus could at least have been known to Ignatius. I, however, deny the consequence of this proposition and grant the antecedent. The learned man, however, is wholly taken up with proving the antecedent and is little or not at all concerned with the consequent. To make all this clearer, Pearson's argument must be drawn up in this form:

units.la: Quisquis doctrinam Polycarpi cognovit, Valentini etiam doctrinam cognoscere potuit
units.tr: Whoever knew the teaching of Polycarp could also have known the teaching of Valentinus.

units.la: Atqui Ignatius Polycarpi doctrinam cognovit
units.tr: But Ignatius knew the teaching of Polycarp.

units.la: Ergo Ignatius Valentini etiam doctrinam cognoscere potuit.
units.tr: Therefore Ignatius could also have known the teaching of Valentinus.

units.la: Hujus Syllogysmi Minorem concedo, Majorem nego; nam ex cognitione doctrinae Polycarpi, non recté colligitur haeresis Valentinianae cognitio[?]: Quippè Ignatius doctrinam Polycarpi cognoscere potuit, & Valentini sententiam ignorare, ut revera ignoravit. Ad eam quam nego propo-sitionem confirmandam, hoc solùm adfert Vir doctus, Valentinum videlicet vivente adhuc Polycarpo mortuum esse; esto, mortuus sit Valentinus vivente adhuc Polycarpo : Hinc minimè consequitur Valentini sententiam ab Ignatio cognitam fuisse , scilicet Valentinus mori potuit vivente adhuc Polycarpo , & virus suum spargere pluribus post Ignatij martyrium annis , nulla siquidem inter hæc duo contrarietas , simile Vindiciarum Auctori proponam argumentum, ut nobis respondendo, sibi pariter respondeat; sed ante omnia duo mihi supponenda sunt ; 1. Ordinatores Ioannis Pearsonij Presbyteri ejus doctrinam penitùs cognovisse, alioqui eum Presbyterum nunquam ordinassent ; 2. Ordinatores illos aliquot post annis mortuos esse, ante natam Dallæi de Ignatianis opinionem, his ita positis sic argumentum meum confi-cio.
units.tr: I grant the minor premise of this syllogism and deny the major. For from knowledge of Polycarp's teaching it is not rightly concluded that knowledge of the Valentinian heresy follows. Ignatius could have known the doctrine of Polycarp and been ignorant of the opinion of Valentinus, as in fact he was. To confirm the proposition I deny, the learned man brings forward only this: that Valentinus died while Polycarp was still alive. Granted, let Valentinus have died while Polycarp was still alive. From this it by no means follows that the opinion of Valentinus was known to Ignatius. For Valentinus could have died while Polycarp still lived, and spread his poison for many years after Ignatius' martyrdom; there is no contradiction between these two things. I will set out a similar argument against the author of the Vindiciae, so that by answering us he may answer himself as well. But first two things must be supposed by me: (1) that the ordainers of John Pearson as presbyter had thoroughly known his teaching, since otherwise they would never have ordained him presbyter; (2) that those ordainers died some years later, before Dallaeus' opinion about the Ignatian letters arose. With these things so laid down, I construct my argument thus:

units.la: Quisquis doctrinam Ioannis Pearsonij cognovit, Dallæi etiam de Ignatianis sententiam cognoscere potuit.
units.tr: Whoever knew the teaching of John Pearson could also have known the opinion of Dallaeus about the Ignatian letters.

units.la: Atqui ordinatores Ioannis Pearsonij illius doctrinam cognoverunt.
units.tr: But the ordainers of John Pearson knew his teaching.

units.la: Ergo ordinatores Ioannis Pearsonij Dallæi de Ignatianis sententiam cognoscere potuerunt.
units.tr: Therefore the ordainers of John Pearson could have known the opinion of Dallaeus about the Ignatian letters.

units.la: Qvum non est ovo similius, ideò argumentum nostrum refellere non poterit Pearsonius, quin suum æquè refellat; unum forte excipiet Vir doctissimus, nempe ex suppositione nostra constare mortuos esse Ioannis Pearsonij Ordinatores ante natam Dallæi de Ignatianis opinionem, cum non constet de Ignatij morte ante exortam Valentini hæresim. Ego vero contendo non minus constare de Ignatij Martyrio ante exortam hæresim Valentinianam, quàm de morte Ordinatorum Ioannis Pearsonij ante natam ex suppositione Dallæi de Ignatianis sententiam.
units.tr: As one egg is like another, Pearson will not be able to refute our argument without equally refuting his own. Perhaps the most learned man will make one exception, namely that on our supposition it is established that the ordainers of John Pearson died before Dallaeus' opinion about the Ignatian letters arose, whereas it is not established that Ignatius died before the Valentinian heresy arose. But I contend that it is no less established that Ignatius' martyrdom came before the rise of the Valentinian heresy than that the ordainers of John Pearson died before Dallaeus' opinion about the Ignatian letters arose, on our supposition.

units.la: XIX. Dallæus ut id probet observat p. 308. vel ipso Hammondo judice satis esse ταχυλῶς [?] observâsse Valentinum Romam sub Hygino illius Ecclesiæ Episcopo circa A.D.140. venisse. A. D.144. nosci cœpisse: permansisse usque ad Anicetum, qui A. D. 167. Episcopus est ordinatus. Post hæc ita pergit; Tertullianus etiam ultrà Anicetum summovet. Ita enim de Marcione & Valentino; Constat illos (inquit) neque adeò olim fuisse, Antonini ferè principatu, & in Catholicæ primo doctrinam credidisse apud Ecclesiam Romanensem, sub Episcopatu Eleutherij benedicti. Eleutherium autem, ait Dallæus, qui maturrimè, A. D. 171. Episcopum ordinatum volunt, Soteris successorem, qui Anicetum exceperat. Cùm ergo constet Ignatium A.D. 107. vel ( ut alij volunt ) 109. martyrium Romæ fecisse : clarum certumque est tam multis post ejus obitum annis vulgatam Valentini mataeologiam Martyri notam esse non potuisse: ut plane necesse sit Epistolæ ad Magnesianos scriptorem, qui Valentini Theogoniam scivisse deprehenditur, alium ab Ignatio fuisse. Hactenus præstantissimus Dallæus : Doctissimus Vindiciarum Auctor negat pag. 76. 77. Valentinum vitam usque ad Eleutherium produxisse, quia Irenæus lib. 3. cap. 4. de illo sic scribit, Valentinus ve-nit Romam sub Hygino, increvit vero sub Pio, & prorogavit tempus usque ad Anicetum. Ex his colligit Pearsonius ad tempora Aniceti pervenisse Valentinum, neque diutius vixisse ; verba Irenæi Græca sic transtulit Henricus Valesius Vir doctissimus apud Eufeb. Hist. Eccl. lib. 4. cap. xi. Valentinus Romam venit Pontificatu Hygini. Viguit autem temporibus Pij, & ad Anicetum usque permansit παρέμεινεν[?] ; sed qui dicit Irenæus Valentinum ad Anicetum usque Romæ permansisse, non statim negat illum diutius vixisse, & ad Eleutheri tempora pervenisse. Instat Vir doctus atque Valentino competere non posse, quod scribit Tertullianus loco mox laudato, eum videlicet in Catholicæ doctrinam credidisse, & semel ac iterum ejectum fuisse; si rogas quare non competat? Quoniam, inquit, quae de iterata ejectione & perpetuo discidio a Tertulliano commemorantur, non Valentino, sed Cerdoni ab Irenaeo tribuuntur lib. 3. cap. 4. At nihil vetat quin idem Valentino contingere potuerit; Irenaei aequalis prope erat Tertullianus, & quodammodo par, non est igitur verisimile eum, dum ista de Valentino scribebat, ad Irenaei de Cerdone narrationem respexisse, & Valentinum Cerdonis loco animi incogitantia substituisse, imo Valentini historiam adeo exacte noverat Tertullianus, ut absque eo foret, circunstantiam notatu dignissimam ignoraremus, cum de ea nullam prorsus mentionem fecerit Irenaeus, Valentinum scilicet Episcopatus spe se aliquando lactâsse, & quia repulsam tulit, bellum veritati indixisse; sperauerat (inquit Tertullianus adverf. Valentin. cap. 4.) Episcopatum Valentinus quia & ingenio poterat & eloquio. Sed alium ex martyrij praerogativa loci potitum indignatus, de Ecclesia authentica regulae abrupit, ad expugnandam conversus veritatem. Si Irenaeum latuit adeo memorabilis circunstantia, nequaquam mirari debemus si eum pariter latuerit, iterata Valentini de Ecclesia ejectio. Quasi vero pietatem semel & iterum simulare nesciverit vafer ille Hæresiarcha, ut voti compos fieret, & ad Episcopatum promoveretur; donec tandem detectâ illius fraude ac impostura de Ecclesiâ penitus ejectus est. Objicit Vir doctus quæ dicit Tertullianus advers. Valent. cap. 5. nempe Iustinum Philosophum & Martyrem scripsisse adversus Valentinum, Iustinus autem mortuus erat ante Eleutheri Pontificatum; fateor Tertullianum id de Iustino scripsisse, sed fieri potest ut idem Valentinus contra quem stilum exercuit Iustinus, orthodoxam postea fidem semel & iterum mentitus de Ecclesiâ sub Eleuthero Papa bis ejectus sit: Si hoc dicis sibi constabit Septimius, nec hic diruet, quod alibi ædificavit.
units.tr: XIX. Dallaeus, to prove this, observes on p. 308 that, by the judgement of Hammond himself, it is enough to have roughly [παχυλῶς] observed that Valentinus came to Rome under Hyginus, bishop of that church, about A.D. 140; that he became known in A.D. 144; that he remained until Anicetus, who was ordained bishop in A.D. 167. After this he continues: Tertullian also places him beyond Anicetus. For thus he writes of Marcion and Valentinus: It is established that they (he says) were not so very long ago, in the reign of Antoninus, and first believed the Catholic doctrine in the Roman church, under the episcopate of the blessed Eleutherius. Eleutherius, says Dallaeus, whom they wish to have been ordained bishop very early, in A.D. 171, was the successor of Soter, who had succeeded Anicetus. Since it is therefore certain that Ignatius suffered martyrdom at Rome in A.D. 107, or (as others wish) 109, it is clear and certain that the Valentinian theogony, spread so many years after his death, could not have been known to the martyr. So it is plainly necessary that the writer of the Epistle to the Magnesians, who is shown to have known the theogony of Valentinus, was someone other than Ignatius. So far the most distinguished Dallaeus. The most learned author of the Vindiciae denies, on pp. 76-77, that Valentinus lived on until Eleutherius, because Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 4, writes of him thus: Valentinus came to Rome under Hyginus, indeed flourished under Pius, and prolonged his time up to Anicetus. From this Pearson concludes that Valentinus reached the time of Anicetus and lived no longer. Henricus Valesius, a most learned man, translated Irenaeus' Greek thus, in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 4, chapter 11: Valentinus came to Rome in the pontificate of Hyginus. He flourished indeed in the times of Pius, and remained up to Anicetus [παρέμεινεν]. But one who says that Irenaeus states Valentinus remained at Rome until Anicetus does not at once deny that he lived longer and reached the times of Eleutherius. The learned man insists that what Tertullian says in the passage just cited cannot apply to Valentinus, namely that he believed in Catholic doctrine and was cast out of the Church once and again. If you ask why it cannot apply? "Because," he says, what is recorded by Tertullian about repeated expulsion and perpetual schism is attributed by Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 4, not to Valentinus but to Cerdo. But nothing prevents the same thing from having happened to Valentinus too. Tertullian was almost a contemporary of Irenaeus and in some measure his equal. It is therefore not likely that, in writing these things about Valentinus, he had in mind Irenaeus' account of Cerdo and, through carelessness, put Valentinus in Cerdo's place. Indeed Tertullian knew the history of Valentinus so exactly that without him we would not know a circumstance most worthy of note, of which Irenaeus makes no mention at all: that Valentinus once flattered himself with hope of the episcopate, and because he was rebuffed declared war on the truth. Valentinus had hoped (says Tertullian, Against Valentinus, chapter 4) for the episcopate, since he had both talent and eloquence. But indignant that another had obtained it by the prerogative of martyrdom, he broke away from the authentic Church of the rule, and turned to assail the truth. If Irenaeus was unaware of so memorable a circumstance, we ought not to wonder if he was likewise unaware of Valentinus' repeated expulsion from the Church. As if that cunning heresiarch had not known how to feign piety once and again, so as to gain his wish and be promoted to the episcopate, until at last his fraud and imposture were detected and he was utterly cast out of the Church. The learned man objects what Tertullian says against Valentinus, chapter 5, namely that Justin the philosopher and martyr wrote against Valentinus; but Justin died before the pontificate of Eleutherius. I admit that Tertullian wrote this of Justin, but it can happen that the same Valentinus against whom Justin wrote, having feigned the orthodox faith once and again, was cast out of the Church twice under Pope Eleutherius. If you say this, Septimius will be consistent, and he will not here pull down what he built elsewhere.

units.la: Sed largiamur Eruditissimo Vindiciarum Auctori, ad tempora Aniceti pervenisse Valentinum, neque diutius vixisse, nihil propterea proficiet, nec minus frustranei erunt illius adversus Blondellum conatus; Blondellus siquidem Præfat. in Apolog. pro Sentent. Hieron. pag. 45. 46. observat Valentinum non ante annum à martyrio Ignatij vel XL. vel XXXVI. Hæreticum agnitum esse, unde colligit ante eum annum refutari à quoquam non potuisse; propositionem suam probat Clarissimus Blondellus Eusebij testimonio qui hæc habet in Chronico ad An. Dom. CXLIV. Valentinus Hæreticus agnoscitur, & permanet usque ad Anicetum; Ignatius vero ut scribit pro fide passus est, vel An. Dom. 104. juxta Adonem, vel secundum alios A. 109. Eusebij verba agnoscit Pearsonius, sed ( inquit pag. 77. ) idem non dicit quod Blondellus, ante hunc annum eum Hæreticum agnitum non fuisse; imò Blondellum ab Eusebio clarè refelli affirmat; quia in Græcis ad annum Antonini Pij tertium habet, sub Hygino Romæ Episcopo Valentinus propriæ hæresεos Conditor Romæ agnitus est, unde hanc elicit conclusionem Vir doctus, agnitum esse Valentinum tanquam Hæresiarcham sub Hygino anno CXLI. secundum Eusebium; annus siquidem Antonini tertius incidit in Annum Christi CXLI. Vult igitur eo anno Romæ agnitum esse secundum calculum Eusebianum; alibi antè, respondeo primò non extare Eusebij Chronicorum Canonum Græca omnia, sed tantùm reliquias quas magno labore nec minori industriâ collegit Vir summus Iosephus Scaliger; quorsùm ergo reliquias illas præferemus integro Temporum Thesauro quem Latinum habemus ex Hieronymi versione? Si ex alijs ipsius Eusebij scriptis hæ reliquiæ Collectæ fuissent, profectò major fides Græcis adhibenda esset quàm Latinis: At cùm ex Scriptoribus Hieronymo longè junioribus, præsertim ex Georgio Syncello qui opus suum adornavit anno DCCXCII. excerpserit Scaliger quæ Eusebij nomine in Thesauro Temporum edidit Græcè, nihil causæ est cur Latina Hieronymi Græcis reliquijs postponamus, imò potiùs Anno 144. Romæ in-notuisse Valentinum, cum Hieronymo, meâ quidem sententiâ, dicendum est, quàm anno 141. juxta Scaligeri excerpta, etsi parùm aut nihil planè referat utroli-bet anno agnitus fuerit: sed (inquit Pearsonius) Romæ tunc agnitus est, alibi ante, imò ante annum CXLIV. ita agnitus est ut etiam refutatus sit, quod fieri non potuisse asserit Blondellus; Ut id probet Vir doctissimus, adfert primò hæc Eusebij verba in Chronico, ad annum CXLII. Iustinus Philosophus librum pro nostrâ religione conscriptum Antonino reddidit. Observat secundò Iustinum in eo ipso libro mentionem facere alterius libri contra hæreses & Sectas omnes à se compositi, fateor Iustinum in Apologiâ primâ quæ in Editionibus malè pro secundâ habetur, hæc scribere; Est autem nobis liber contra hæreses & sectas omnes compositus; Eum tamen librum Scriptum fuisse sub fine imperij Adriani ut asserit Pearsonius pag. 78. aperte nego; nec ut aliter sentiam moveor istis Cedreni verbis, qui de eo Imperatore loquens ait, juxta Viri docti observationem; sub hoc Iustinus Philosophus contra omnes hæreses viriliter se gesit. Ex his omnibus tamen colligit Vindiciarum Auctor, Iustinum in eo libro scripsisse contra Valentinianos, ut testatur Tertullianus; ac proinde ante annum CXLIV. non tantùm refutari potuisse, contrà quàm volebat Blondellus, sed reapse refutatum esse, & discipulos ejus: Et ante eum annum Hæreticum agnitum esse, & diu quidem ante;cùm Iustinus Martyr in Dialogo cum Tryphone Iudæo, sub initio Antonini Pij scripto, discipulorum Valentini tanquam Hæreticorum meminerit, quos vocat atheos & impios, & quibuscum Catholicos communionem nullam habuisse testatur: Hactenus eruditissimus Pearsonius. Verùm strustrà se torquet ut Valentinum antiquiorem faciat; argumenta quibus id demonstrare conatur infirma sunt, & perquam exigui momenti; A Cedreno tantùm habet Iustinum librum suum contra hæreses sub fine imperij Adriani elaborasse; quasi verò audiendus sit Cedrenus de re adcò antiquâ sine vetustioris autoritate scribens; Cedrenus inquam Scriptor undecimi seculi, qui id affirmat, quod à vetustiorum nemine observatum est; Deinde si proprie loqui velimus, id non affirmat Cedrenus, significat modò Iustinum contra omnes hæreses viriliter se gessisse; illud quidem observat, ut ait Pearsonius, de Imperatore Adriano scribens: At Amanuensium incuriâ, vel Scriptorum juniorum ignorantiâ, hoc Iustini volumen sub Antonino Pio elaboratum, ad finem imperij Adriani referri potuit. Nec id mirabitur quisquam, si hæc Gerardi Ioannis Vossij de Cedreno verba legit, ut ipse mutilárat priores, ita ejus quoque volumen mutilárunt juniores, idque judicio nullo, sine ordine temporum, sine delectu rerum. Vindiciarum Auctor qui illud optimè novit, Cedreni verbis non planè nititur, illa quidem profert ut opinionem suam de tempore quo Iustini liber scriptus est confirmet, sed dubitanter profert: Nam postquàm dixit; Eum autem librum scriptum sub fine imperij Adriani vix dubitandum est, addit continenter, præsertim si Cedreno credamus; aliter sanè loquuturus erat si Cedrenum putasset testem omni ex-ceptione majorem: sed quoniam vacillantem hic[?] de re Scriptoris fidem non igno-
units.tr: But let us grant to the most learned author of the Vindiciae that Valentinus came down to the time of Anicetus and did not live any longer. Even so, this will gain him nothing, and his attempt against Blondel will be no less pointless. Blondel, in the Preface to his Apology for the Sentences of Jerome, pp. 45. 46., observes that Valentinus was recognised as a heretic not earlier than about forty or thirty-six years after the martyrdom of Ignatius, and from this he infers that before that time no one could have refuted him. The most distinguished Blondel supports his proposition by the testimony of Eusebius, who in his Chronicle, under the year of the Lord 144, has this: Valentinus is recognised as a heretic, and he remains until Anicetus. Ignatius, as he writes, suffered for the faith either in the year of the Lord 104, according to Ado, or, according to others, in 109. Pearsonius acknowledges Eusebius's words, but (he says, p. 77) it does not say what Blondel says, that he had not been recognised as a heretic before this year. Indeed, he asserts that Blondel is clearly refuted by Eusebius, because in the Greek text, under the third year of Antoninus Pius, Eusebius has: under Hyginus, bishop of Rome, Valentinus, the founder of his own heresy, was recognised at Rome. From this the learned man draws the conclusion that Valentinus was recognised as a heresiarch under Hyginus in the year 141 according to Eusebius, since the third year of Antoninus falls in the year of Christ 141. He wishes, therefore, that he was recognised at Rome in that year according to Eusebius's reckoning, but elsewhere earlier. My reply is, first, that not all of Eusebius's Chronicle Canons survive in Greek, but only the fragments which the great Joseph Scaliger gathered with no less diligence than labour. Why then should we prefer those fragments to the complete Thesaurus of Times, which we have in Latin in Jerome's translation? If these fragments had been collected from Eusebius's other writings, certainly more trust ought to be given to the Greek than to the Latin. But since Scaliger excerpted what he published in Greek under Eusebius's name in the Thesaurus of Times from writers much later than Jerome, especially from George Syncellus, who finished his work in the year 792, there is no reason why we should set Jerome's Latin behind the Greek fragments. Indeed, in my opinion it must rather be said that Valentinus became known at Rome in the year 144, with Jerome, than in the year 141, according to Scaliger's excerpts, although it matters little or nothing in which year he was recognised. But (says Pearsonius) he was then recognised at Rome, and earlier elsewhere, indeed before the year 144, and in such a way that he was also refuted, which Blondel asserts could not have happened. To prove this, that most learned man first cites these words of Eusebius in the Chronicle, under the year 142: Justin the Philosopher presented to Antoninus a book written for our religion. Secondly, he observes that Justin, in that same book, makes mention of another book, composed by himself against all heresies and sects. I grant that Justin writes this in his First Apology, which in the editions is wrongly held to be the second: Moreover, we have composed a book against all heresies and sects. Yet I flatly deny that this book was written at the end of Hadrian's reign, as Pearsonius asserts, p. 78. Nor am I moved to think otherwise by those words of Cedrenus, who, speaking of that emperor, says, according to the learned man's observation: under this man Justin the Philosopher bore himself manfully against all heresies. From all these things, however, the author of the Vindiciae concludes that Justin wrote in that book against the Valentinians, as Tertullian testifies; and therefore that before the year 144 they could not only have been refuted, contrary to what Blondel wanted, but had actually been refuted, and also their followers; and that before that year he had been recognised as a heretic, and indeed long before, since Justin Martyr, in his Dialogue with the Jew Trypho, written at the beginning of the reign of Antoninus Pius, mentions the followers of Valentinus as heretics, whom he calls godless and impious, and testifies that Catholics had no fellowship with them. So far the most learned Pearsonius. But he twists himself in vain to make Valentinus the older; the arguments by which he tries to show this are weak and of very little weight. He has only Cedrenus for the claim that Justin worked on his book against heresies at the end of Hadrian's reign. As if Cedrenus, a writer of the eleventh century, who asserts what no earlier writer has observed, ought to be heard on so ancient a matter without the authority of an older witness! Moreover, if we wish to speak strictly, Cedrenus does not even assert this; he only signifies that Justin bore himself manfully against all heresies. He does indeed note this, as Pearsonius says, while writing about the emperor Hadrian. But through the carelessness of copyists, or the ignorance of later writers, this volume of Justin, composed under Antoninus Pius, could have been referred to the end of Hadrian's reign. No one will be surprised at this if he reads these words of Gerardus Joannes Vossius about Cedrenus: as he himself mutilated the earlier writers, so later writers have mutilated his volume too, and that without any judgement, without order of times, without selection of matters. The author of the Vindiciae, who knows this very well, does not rest plainly on Cedrenus's words. He brings them forward to confirm his opinion about the time when Justin's book was written, but he brings them forward hesitantly. For after saying, that book was written at the end of Hadrian's reign, and there is hardly any doubt of it, he immediately adds, especially if we believe Cedrenus. He would certainly have spoken differently if he had thought Cedrenus a witness beyond all exception. But since he did not ignore that the writer's trustworthiness on this matter was wavering, he does not press that testimony at all, being content to bring it forward in the way we usually bring forward those authorities to which we do not give very ready assent nor full trust. The learned man's argument rests above all on the testimony of Eusebius, who places Justin's First Apology in the year of the Lord 142. And…

units.la: rabat, illius testimonium nequaquam urget, illud adducere contentus, nempe ut ea solemus adferre, quibus non adeo facilem praebemus assensum, nec omnimodam adhibemus fidem. Argumentum Viri docti nititur imprimis Eusebij testimonio, qui primam Iustini Apologiam confert in annum Domini CXLII. Et quia in illâ Apologiâ libri contra omnes haereses à se compositi meminit Iustinus, colligit Pearsonius hanc Iustini Scriptionem sub fine Imperij Adriani exaratam esse. Sed nego iterum opus illud à Iustino adeò maturè compositum esse, vel saltem in eo ullam Valentinianorum mentionem tunc temporis esse factam, quia nondum nati erant, testatur quidem Tertullianus scripsisse Iustinum contra Valentinianos, sed an in eodem libro hoc praestiterit Iustinus nequaquam dicit, alium fortè librum contra eos scripsit, nisi malis dicere eum post exortam Valentini haeresim, quae contra Valentinianos scripsit, operi suo adjecisse, & ut ita contigisse credam, faciunt ipsius Iustini verba, ex quibus colligere fas est, Iustinum librum suum contra haereses nondum vulgasse, cùm Apologiam suam Antonino Pio reddidit, sic enim loquitur pag. 70. Est autem nobis liber contra haereses & sectas omnes composititius, quem si legere volueritis, dabimus. Nempe penes se habebat librum, nec illum publici iuris adhuc fecerat, ut pullulantes subinde hæreses configere posset. Verum enimvero ut omnis cavillandi ansa Vindiciarum Auctori præcidatur, affirmare non vereor vel graviter hallucinatum esse Eusebium decem circiter annorum prochronismo vel à Librariis interpolatos efse annorum numeros, & annum Domini CLII. in annum CXLII. magna animi incogitantiâ mutatum esse, cum Iustinus ipse cui plus credendum est quàm Eusebio, diserté testetur se Apologiam suam scribere post annum à Christi nativitate CL. Ante annos (inquit pag. 83.) centum quinquaginta nos asseveramus Christum sub Cyrenio natum esse, docuisse autem quæ docuit, posterius sub Pontio Pilato. Ergo vel hallucinatus est Eusebius, vel annorum numeri in illius Chronico ab imperitis Librariis conturbati sunt, cum à Christi nativitate ad id usque tempus quo Iustinus Apologiam suam scribebat, fluxerint anni plus quàm centum quinquaginta; Ergo quivis videt exaratam fuisse illam Apologiam anno CLII. vel saltem anno CLI. Valentinus autem Romæ agnitus fuit anno CXLIV. ut vult Llondellus, vel anno CXLI. ii Vindiciarum Auctori credimus: Ergo contra Valentinianos scribere potuit Justinus vel post annum CXLI. juxta Viri docti supputationem, vel juxta Blondelli calculum post annum CXLIV. & scriptionis illius mentionem facere in Apologiâ post annum Domini CL. vel CLI. exaratâ. Frustrà igitur ad finem Imperij Adriani refert libri Justini contra hæreses compositionem, cùm tardiùs scriptum fuisse constet; Nec obstat quod Valentinianorum meminit in Dialogo cum Tryphone[?]: Nam Dialogus ille sub initio Imperij Antonini Pij minimè scriptus est, cùm sit Apologiâ posterior; Apologia autem non exarata fuit ante annum Imperij Antonini decimum-quartum vel decimum-tertium, id est ante annum Christi CLII. vel CLI. qui quidem anni respondent annis XIII. & XIV. Antonini qui regnavit annos XXII. Non me latet Scaligerum Litteratorum sui seculi facilè principem, cujus auctoritate se quodammodo tuetur Pearsonius pag. 8o. aliter sentire de tempore quo Justinus scripsit Apologiam suam & Dialogum cum Tryphone, putat enim Vir ille summus Apologeticum scriptum esse circa initium Antonini Pij; Dialogum verò sub fine Adriani: sed pace tanti Viri dixerim, falsus est suâ opinione, cùm contrarium pateat ex Iustino, Apologetici sal-tem respectu, ut ipse fatetur Scaliger in Animadversionibus Eusebianis, sic enim ad num. MMCLVII. pag. 219. ultimae editionis; Iustinus à Christo, ad id tempus quo scribebat Apologeticum hunc, quum de Marcione loquitur, putat annos CL; quod tempus congruit medio imperio Antonini. Sed constat eum circa initium Antonini Pij librum Apologeticum Imperatori obtulisse. Vnde id constet si rogas, hoc responsum feres. Nam, ut suprà monuimus, (pag.216.) de bello Iudaico sub extremum Hadriani imperium gesto loquens, vocat τὸν τῶν γεγενμένων πόλεμον[?], nuperum bellum. Profectò seriò nobis dolet quòd Viro tanto exciderit ratio adeò infirma: Quasi verò de bello ante annos circiter quindecim confecto, ita loqui non potuerit Iustinus; Nam bellum illud Iudaicum, de quo loquitur, finem accepit anno Christi CXXXV. Iustinus autem Apologeticum scribebat anno CLI. vel CLII. certè bellum ante aliquot annos gestum merito dici potest bellum nuperum ut vertit ipse Scaliger. Nec melioris esset commatis quam adfert probatio ut ostendat Dialogum cum Tryphone sub fine Adriani elaboratum esse, nisi Iustini verba interpolata essent, & vox γινόμενον in locum γενόμενον suffecta fuisset; illa siquidem tempus signat præsens , ista vero præteritum, Scaliger Dialogi verba quæ extnat ferè initio sic legit ;Trypho,inquit vocur , sum autem ex circumcisione Hebræus , φύγων τὸν τὴν γινόμενον πόλεμον· Iustinus vero τὸν τὴν γενόμενον πόλεμον, quia bellum anteà gestum designat , non autem bellum quod gereretur adhuc cum hæc scribebat: Vindiciarum Auctor in eo dissentit à magno Scaligero , quod ad initia Antonini refert Dialogum cum Tryphone, quem ego compositum puto eodem ferè tempore quo liber Apologeticus, sed post eum; Præterea Græca Iustini verba proferens, omisit nescio quo consilio vocem γινόμενον, cùm Scaliger γινόμενον substituisset, Pearsonius verò sic, φύγων τὸν τὴν πόλεμον[?], vertit tamen ex nupero bello profugus: Græca proprie sonant , qui fugi ex bello quod nuper, vel quod non ita pridem gestum est, id est nostrâ ætate. Postquam hæc scripseram meminini me aliquando legisse in Annotationibus Eusebianis Clarissimi Viri Henrici Valesii aliquid explicationi meæ favens; ideóque eas consului in cap. 8. lib. 4. pag. 64. ubi reperi Virum illum Linguæ Græcæ callentissimum, notare Ruffinum, & Christophorsonum qui Græca Iustini verterunt apud Eusebium, in hoc quod nunc geritur bello Iudaico, necnon Scaligerum qui in eodem errore versatus est, in loco videlicet à nobis supra indicato & expenso ; Putavit enim, inquit, τὸ νῦν dici non posse nisi de re admodum recenti, ne dicam præsenti ; probat tamen Valesius varijs exemplis τῶν dici posse de re quæ nostrâ ætate facta est ; idémque valere τὸ μετ' ἡμᾶς, quod Eusebius usurpare solet de rebus multò antè gestis; Imò Iustinus ipse Apolog. 1. vulgò 2. pag. 72. de Antinoo qui obierat anno Domini CXXX. ita loquitur. ἀντίνοος νῦν γεγενομένος, Interpres vertit Antinoi qui non ita pridem inter homines fuit; apud Eusebium lib. 4. cap. 8. ἀντίνοος τῆς νῦν γενομένης, Valesius Latinè reddidit. Antinoi qui nuperrimè vixit, quamvis mortuus sit quinquennio integro ante belli Iudaici finem.
units.tr: Our learned author of the Vindiciae relies on the testimony of Eusebius, who dates Justin's First Apology to the year of the Lord 142. And because Justin mentions in that Apology a book he had written against all heresies, Pearsonius concludes that this writing of Justin's was composed toward the end of Hadrian's reign. But I deny again that this work was written so early by Justin, or that any mention of the Valentinians was made in it at that time, since they had not yet been born. Tertullian does indeed testify that Justin wrote against the Valentinians, but he does not say that Justin did this in the same book. Perhaps Justin wrote another book against them. Or, if you prefer to say that he added to his work what he wrote against the Valentinians after Valentinus' heresy arose, then I would believe it happened so. The words of Justin himself support this, from which it is right to conclude that Justin had not yet published his book against the heresies when he gave his Apology to Antoninus Pius. For he speaks thus on p. 70: We have a book against all heresies and sects composed, which we will give you if you wish to read it. Clearly he still had the book in his own possession and had not yet made it public, so that he could confront the heresies that kept springing up. But so that every pretext for cavilling may be cut off from the author of the Vindiciae, I do not hesitate to affirm that either Eusebius was gravely mistaken by about ten years' anachronism, or the numbers of the years were altered by copyists, and in great carelessness the year of the Lord 152 was changed to 142. For Justin himself, whom we should believe more than Eusebius, plainly testifies that he wrote his Apology after the year 150 from Christ's birth. A hundred and fifty years ago (he says, p. 83) we affirm that Christ was born under Cyrenius, but that he taught what he taught later, under Pontius Pilate. So either Eusebius was mistaken, or the numbers of the years in his Chronicle were thrown into confusion by ignorant copyists. For from Christ's nativity to the time when Justin was writing his Apology more than 150 years had passed. Therefore anyone can see that the Apology was written in the year 152, or at least in 151. Valentinus, however, was recognized at Rome in the year 144, as Blondel holds, or in 141, as we believe with the author of the Vindiciae. So Justin could have written against the Valentinians either after the year 141, by the reckoning of our learned author, or, by Blondel's calculation, after the year 144, and could have mentioned that writing in an Apology written after the year of the Lord 150 or 151. It is therefore in vain that the composition of Justin's book against the heresies is put back to the end of Hadrian's reign, since it is clear that it was written later. Nor does it stand in the way that he mentions the Valentinians in the Dialogue with Trypho. For that Dialogue was not written at the beginning of Antoninus Pius' reign at all, since it is later than the Apology. The Apology, moreover, was not written before the fourteenth or thirteenth year of Antoninus, that is, before the year of Christ 152 or 151, which years correspond to the thirteenth and fourteenth years of Antoninus, who reigned twenty-two years. I am not unaware that Scaliger, the easily foremost scholar of his century, on whose authority Pearsonius to some extent relies (p. 80), thinks differently about the time when Justin wrote his Apology and his Dialogue with Trypho. For that great man thinks the Apologeticum was written around the beginning of Antoninus Pius, and the Dialogue toward the end of Hadrian. But with due respect to so great a man, I must say he is mistaken in his opinion, since the contrary is evident from Justin, at least with regard to the Apologeticum, as Scaliger himself admits in his Animadversions on Eusebius. For at number MMCLVII, p. 219 of the last edition, he says: Justin, when he speaks of Marcion, reckons 150 years from Christ to the time when he was writing this Apologeticum; this time agrees with the middle of Antoninus' reign. But it is established that about the beginning of Antoninus Pius he offered the Apologeticum to the emperor. If you ask how this is established, you will get this answer: For, as we noted above, (p. 216) speaking of the Jewish war waged toward the end of Hadrian's reign, he calls it [τὸν τῶν γεγενμένων πόλεμον], the recent war. Truly it grieves us seriously that so great a man should have fallen into reasoning so weak. As if Justin could not have spoken thus about a war finished some fifteen years earlier! For that Jewish war, of which he speaks, came to an end in the year of Christ 135, while Justin was writing the Apologeticum in 151 or 152. Certainly a war waged some years before can rightly be called the recent war, as Scaliger himself translates it. Nor would the proof be any better of the passage he adduces to show that the Dialogue with Trypho was elaborated toward the end of Hadrian's reign, unless Justin's words had been altered and the word γινόμενον had been substituted in place of γενόμενον. For the one signifies the present time, the other the past. Scaliger reads the words of the Dialogue, which occur almost at the beginning, thus: Trypho, he says, is named, but I am a Hebrew by circumcision, fleeing the war that is taking place [φύγων τὸν τὴν γινόμενον πόλεμον]. But Justin has [τὸν τὴν γενόμενον πόλεμον], because it designates a war waged earlier, not a war still being waged when he was writing these things. The author of the Vindiciae differs from the great Scaliger in this: he refers the Dialogue with Trypho to the beginning of Antoninus' reign, whereas I think it was composed at about the same time as the Apologetic book, but after it. Moreover, quoting the Greek words of Justin, he has omitted for some reason the word γινόμενον, whereas Scaliger had substituted γινόμενον; Pearsonius, however, renders it thus: φύγων τὸν τὴν πόλεμον, and translates it fleeing from the recent war. But the Greek properly sounds like who fled from a war which was waged recently, or not very long ago, that is, in our own age. After I had written these things, I remember having once read in the Eusebian Annotations of the most distinguished Henri de Valois something favouring my explanation. So I consulted them on chapter 8 of book 4, p. 64, where I found that that most learned man in Greek, noting that Rufinus and Christophorson, who translated Justin's Greek words in Eusebius, rendered them in this war which is now waged against the Jews, and also Scaliger, who was in the same error in the very passage we indicated and examined above, says: For he thought, he says, τὸ νῦν could be said only of a very recent, not to say present, matter. Yet Valesius proves by various examples that τῶν can be used of a matter that happened in our own age, and that τὸ μετ' ἡμᾶς, which Eusebius is accustomed to use of things done long before, has the same force. Indeed Justin himself, in Apology 1 (commonly 2), p. 72, speaking of Antinous, who had died in the year of the Lord 130, says thus: [ἀντίνοος νῦν γεγενμένος]. The translator renders it Antinous, who not long ago lived among men; in Eusebius, book 4, chapter 8, it is [ἀντίνοος τῆς νῦν γενομένης], which Valesius rendered into Latin as Antinous who lived most recently, although he had died a full five years before the end of the Jewish war.

units.la: Pergit eruditissimus Vindiciarum Auctor, atque pag. 78. Epiphanium observare originem Valentini obscuram suisse, quod non minimum vetustatis indicium putat Pearsonius ; Epiphanius quidem Hær. XXXI. quæ est Valentini pag. 164. Editionis Petavianæ, scribit plerósque Valentini patriam ignorasse, & unde ortus sit nescivisse, quia solum illius natale Scriptorum nullus expressit ; famâ timen incertâ & ambiguâ didiscerat Epiphanius Valentinum Phrebonitem esse ex Ægypti quadam orâ, & inde Alexandriam profectum, Græcorum artibus institutum esse. Verùm hoc non diserte affirmat Epiphanius, sed in ambiguo positam esse veritatem testatur: Nec quicquam causæ est cur Vir doctus ex obscurâ Valentini origine Magnum colligat vetustatis indicium: Præterquam enim ex obscurissimis forte satus erat parentibus, Hæresim aliquandiu occultasse videtur, pietatémque simulasse donec Episcopatus spe dejectus, ad expugnandam conversus est veritatem, ut scribit Tertullianus: Num autem in Ægypto vel alibi id contigerit, aut quando contigerit non narrat: Hoc igitur in Ægypto factum non par est credere, cùm alibi fieri potuerit; Vir doctissimus qui ejusmodi argumenta infirma esse probè noverat, aliâ viâ rem aggreditur, & Valentinum admodum antiquum fuisse, ex ipsorum Valentinianorum gloriatione, & ex Veterum monumentis persuadere conatur. Valentiniani siquidem gloriabantur Valentinum auditorem fuisse Theodadis; Theodadem verò Pauli familiarem. Verùm ut liberè dicam quod sentio, nollem Eruditissimum Vindiciarum Auctorem ad vanissimam Hæreticorum jactantiam confugere, ut Valentino Hæresiarchæ Antiquitatem æquo majorem tribuat ; Ignoratne Pearsonius solitos esse Hæreticos maximam affectare antiquitatem, ut sub venerandæ antiquitatis specie incautos decipiant, ac simplicioribus imponant. Fatetur quidem Vir doctus Valentinianos eâ in re fallere potuisse ; tamen quia à nobis ( inquit pag. 79. ) refelli non possunt, videamus an quod illi tradidêre, cum iis cohæreat quæ à Catholicis prodita sunt. Cohærere autem nititur demonstrare his Irenæi verbis Præfatione lib. 4. Hi qui ante nos fuerunt, & quidem multò nobis meliores, non tamen satis potuerunt contradicere his qui sunt à Valentino, quia ignorabant regulam ipsorum, ut aliquid hinc eliciat in gratiam causæ suæ, observat Irenæum loqui de ijs qui ante ætatem suam vixerunt, ipsum verò Irenæum non longè à temporibus Apostolorum fuisse, ut ait Augustinus, cui succinit Basilius, unde colligit Valentinianos fuisse propè Apostolica tempora, & cum Apostolicis Viris conversatum esse ipsum Valentinum. Mira profectò ratiocinatio, quæ Viri docti causam nequaquam juvat ; Etsi fateamur Valentinianos propè Apostolica tempora fuisse Irenæi respectu, Irenæum verò non longè à temporibus Apostolorum respectu juniorum, imò Valentinum ipsum cum Apoftolicis Viris per ætatem conversari potuisse, cum Polycarpo videlicet & Justino eorumque æqualibus; sed hinc non sequitur Hæreticum agnitum fuisse ante annum Domini CXLIV. vel ante annum CXLI. ut mox putabat ipse Pearsonius. Instat iterùm Vir doctus, & ex Marcionis ætate, de Valentini ævo decerni posse putat pag. 79.80.81. ætatem verò Marcionis ex Irenæo & Tertulliano eruere nequaquam valens, ad Origenis libros contrà Celsum se convertit; quoniam Celsus Marcionistarum in iis meminit lib. 5. pag.272. ultimæ editionis GraecoLat.Celsum autem sub Adriano vixisse, & post Adriani mortem sub imperio Antonini Pij scripsisse (nempe sub initio Antonini, non diu post mortem Adriani) colligit Pearsonius ex istis Origenis verbis lib. 1. pag. 8. Duos autem fuisse Celsos Epicureos accepimus, priorem quidem sub Nerone, hunc autem sub Adriano, & posterioribus temporibus. Hinc concludit Valentinum longè vetustiorem esse quàm existimabat Blondellus,quia Veteres omnes docent eum fuisse Marcione antiquiorem. Hæc summa argumentationis doctissimi Vindiciarum Auctoris. Ut huic objectioni fiat satis, concedo Valentinum hæresim suam disseminasse prius quàm Marcionem, quamvis ambo eadem circiter ætate vixerint; Celsum verò adeò antiquum esse, ut putat Pearsonius, apertè nego; fateor scripsisse Origenem eum sub Adriano & posteà vixisse; sed nihil affirmat Origenes, se ita accepisse solùm dicit, adeò ut tota illius narratio incerto nitatur rumore, potiùs quàm certâ veri notitiâ: & fanè si rem attentè consideramus, non adeò antiquum esse reperiemus: Nam cùm Origenes dicit Celsum sub Adriano fuisse & posteà, significat eum per illud temporis spatium floruisse, sic enim loqui solent scriptores; florere autem non potuit ante annum circiter tricesimum; ponamus igitur medio Adriani imperio floruisse, Trajani initio natum esse oportebit, id est anno Christi XCVIII. vel XCIX. Si ultimis Adriani annis illum floruisse dixeris, ad annum Trajani circiter septimum, Christi CV. ejus nativitatem referre necesse erit, adjice annis Celsi plus minus triginta, septem vel octo Adriani annos, quibus floruisse dicendus est, si Origenis narrationi credimus; quadraginta circiter annos natus erit, dùm Adrianus naturæ cessit; si autem quadragesimum attigerat annum, cùm Adrianus vivere desijt, ultra Octuagesimum vitam prorogâsse dicendum erit; quod non est verisimile. Ut ut est constat Celsum sub Adriano non floruisse, neque forte sub Antonino Pio, nisi sub fine illius imperij floruerit; vixit potius circa tempora Marci Antonini Philosophi, & sub Commodo Marci filio; quod ita probo, Lucianus Samosatensis librum suum qui Alexander seu falsus Vates inscribitur, Celso nuncupavit, cùm ab eo rogatus esset ut vitam impostoris illius literis mandaret; in eo autem libro meminit Lucianus Marci Cæsaris, ac belli Marcomanici ab eo gesti, neque meminit tantùm, sed Marcum vocat θεὸν[?], hoc est Divum, quod arguit naturæ cessisse, ac jam locatum fuisse cœlo, eíque successisse Commodum filium, succedere autem non potuit ante annum Domini CLXXX.quo Marcus Imperator in Pannoniâ morbo perijt. Celsus igitur sub Marco & Commodo floruit, & eapropter Marcionistarum mentionem facere potuit, quando Marcion hæreses suas circa annum Domini 145. disseminare cæpit; Et quoniam discipulos suos docebat adhuc, cùm Iustinus Apologeticum primum scribebat, nempe circa annum Christi CLII. ut demonstravimus, de eo sic loqui potuit. Marcio vero Ponticus etiamnum discipulos suos docet; non ut indicet Marcionem diu hæresim suam sparsisse antequam hæc scriberet, ut ait Pearsonius, sed tantum ut moneat superesse adhuc Hæresiarcham illum, ejúsque discipulos nondum sectam separatim constituisse; sed inquit Marcionistarum meminit Dialogo cum Tryphone pag. 253. Quid tum? inquam ego, Dialogum quippe post Apologeticum exaratum arbitramur, & tunc forsan in varias abierant sectas Marcionis discipuli: Præterea de Marcionis discipulis non magis mihi loqui videtur Iustinus, quàm de Marci præstigiatoris sectatoribus, qui quidem Marcus è Valentini discipulis fuit unus: sunt eorum (inquit pag. 253.) quidam qui vocantur Μαρκιωνισταὶ[?]. Quicquid sit parùm refert Iustinum Marcionistarum meminisse, cùm de ijs loqui potuerit, ut fusè suprà ostendimus: Nam Cerdon Marcionis Magister Romam profectus est eodem quo Valentinus anno, si Eusebium audimus, cujus hæc sunt verba in Chronico ad annum Domini CXLI. Sub Hygino Romanæ Vrbis Episcopo Valentinus Hæresiarches, & Cerdo Magister Marcionis Romam venerunt. In Excerptis Græcis Scaligeri ad eundem annum, notatur utrumque Romæ sub Hygino agnitum esse; idem planè docet Irenæus lib. 1. cap. 28. & lib. 3. cap. 4. cujus verba refert Eusebius Hist. Eccles. lib. 4. cap. ii. Ergo Marcion Cerdoni succedere potuit circa annum CXLV. & Marcionis meminisse Iustinum anno CLII. Rem autem ita se habere liquet ex Epiphanio Hær. 42. ubi narrat Marcionem ob vitiatam Virginem Ecclesiâ ab ipso Parente Sinopes Episcopo pulsum, Romam se contulisse, & cùm à Presbyteris qui Ecclesiam Romanam vacante Sede post Hygini mortem administrabant, in communionem non admitteretur, Hæresim architectatus est, Cerdonis vestigiis insistens, quod circa annum Christi CXLV. ut mox dicebamus contigit. Hæc adeò clara sunt ut satis mirari nequeam, doctissimum Vindiciarum Auctorem affirmare esse ausum pag. 81. vel saltem ut rem maximè probabilem statuere; Cerdonem si non antè, ipso tamen statim initio Hadriani sua deliria disseminâsse, ut hinc concluderet Valentinum, quem Cerdone antiquiorem supponit, sua spargere potuisse ante undecimum annum Traiani, eáque ab Ignatio ante martyrium potuisse cognosci. Nam contrarium planè constat ex ijs omnibus quæ hactenus scripsimus, necnon ex Veterum omnium testimonijs, qui Cerdonem viginti quinque annis plus minus juniorem faciunt, Valentinum vero circiter triginta quatuor, vel triginta quinque: Præterea nihil causæ est cur Pearsonius Valentini antiquitatem supra Cerdonem jactet, ut instituto patrocinetur: cùm ijdem Scriptores æquales esse Valentinum & Cerdonem testentur, & Romam sub Hygino venisse asserant: Imprimis Irenæus qui aliquot post annis contra eos scribebat, illorúmque hæreses refutabat. Frustrà autem Vir doctus nescio quam Hæreticorum istorum successionem comminiscitur, ut Valentinum plus æquo vetustiorem reddat, lectorique persuadeat Hæreticos quibus de agitur, successisse alijs alios per varia temporis intervalla, & à se invicem pluribus annis dissitos esse: Commentitiam vocavi quam repræsentat successionem Eruditus Pearsonius, ratione videlicet ætatis, non autem ratione doctrinæ, alij siquidem ab alijs acceperunt ac furati sunt; Et sic intelligenda sunt hæc quæ de-scribit Epiphanij verba Hær. XLI. initio, Cerdo quidam his & Heracleoni successit, ex eorum schola existens. Epiphanij verbis de suo adjicit Vir doctus, Heracleon Colarba-so, Colarbasus Ptolomaeo, Ptolomaeus Epiphani, Epiphanes Secundo, Secundus Valentino successit. Si de doctrinæ successione loquitur Pearsonius ferri possunt quæ dicit, si de ætate, veluti multùm temporis inter illos intercessisset, fallitur; Nam parùm aut nihil feré interceßit. Alij quidem post alios dogmata sua spergebant, sed adeò exiguâ temporis intercapedine, ut sibi invicem succeßisse ratione ætatis vix dici possint. Verbi gratiâ Secundus Valentino successisse dicitur; Epiphanius tamen Hær. XXXII. quæ est Secundianorum diserte testatur pag. 208. Secundum eodem tempore quo Valentinus extitisse. Idem planè dicit Hær. XXXI. pag. 163. neque id observat de Secundo solùm, sed etiam de Colarbaso & Ptolomæo, omnes hi, inquit, eodem tempore emerserunt; nempe nullâ feré interposità morâ sibi proximè succedebant, & hæreses suas alij post alios intra exiguum temporis spatium disseminabant: Præterea non convenit inter veteres scriptores, nùm Heracleon Colarbaso successerit, an Colarbasus Heracleoni, & Ptolomæus Secundo, aut Secundus Ptolomæo: Nam apud Tertullianum Heracleon præcedit Colarbasum, imò Ptolomæum apud Theodoretum; apud Philastrium verò Secundus Ptolomæo postponitur; Epiphanes autem Secundo non succeßit, sed ei se adjunxit ut nos docet Epiphanius. Insuper diversa illa Veterum in istis Hæreticis recensendis ratio atque methodus, non aliundè venit quàm ex eo quod eodem tempore prodierunt, & exiguo admodum intervallo alij ab alijs dissiti fuerunt; Vnde colligimus hos Valentini discipulos Magistri fuisse æquales, Valentinum verò Cerdonis, ambo quippe Romam sub Hygino profecti sunt, & primis Antonini Pij annis agniti.
units.tr: The most learned author of the Vindiciae goes on, at p. 78, to observe that Valentinus's origin was obscure, which Pearsonius thinks is no small sign of antiquity. Epiphanius, in Haer. 31, which is on Valentinus (p. 164 of the Petavian edition), writes that most people did not know Valentinus's homeland and did not know where he came from, because no writer had recorded his birthplace. Yet Epiphanius had learned by uncertain and doubtful report that Valentinus was a Phrebonite from a certain coast of Egypt, and that he went from there to Alexandria and was trained in Greek learning. But Epiphanius does not state this plainly; he testifies that the truth is left in doubt. Nor is there any reason why the learned man should infer from Valentinus's obscure origin a great sign of antiquity. For apart from the possibility that he was born of very obscure parents, he seems to have concealed his heresy for a while and to have feigned piety, until, disappointed in his hope of a bishopric, he turned to attack the truth, as Tertullian writes. But whether this happened in Egypt or elsewhere, and when it happened, he does not relate. It is therefore not right to believe that this happened in Egypt, since it could have happened anywhere. The most learned man, who knew well that arguments of this kind are weak, approaches the matter another way, and tries to persuade us that Valentinus was very ancient, from the boasting of the Valentinians themselves and from the records of the ancients. The Valentinians indeed boasted that Valentinus had been a hearer of Theodas, and Theodas a familiar of Paul. But, to speak frankly as I think, I would not wish the most learned author of the Vindiciae to take refuge in the most empty boasting of heretics, so as to give the heresiarch Valentinus more antiquity than is fair.
