Does Pearsonius not know that heretics were accustomed to claim the greatest antiquity, so that under the appearance of venerable age they might deceive the unwary and impose on the simpler sort? The learned man admits indeed that the Valentinians could have deceived in this matter; yet because they cannot be refuted by us (he says, at p. 79), let us see whether what they handed down agrees with what has been published by the Catholics. He tries to show this agreement from these words of Irenaeus in the preface to book 4: Those who were before us, and indeed much better than us, nevertheless could not sufficiently contradict those who are from Valentinus, because they did not know their rule. From this he draws something in favour of his cause: he observes that Irenaeus is speaking of those who lived before his own age, and that Irenaeus himself was not far from the times of the Apostles, as Augustine says, and Basil agrees, whence he infers that the Valentinians were close to Apostolic times and that Valentinus himself associated with Apostolic men. A marvellous line of reasoning, which in no way helps the cause of the learned man! Even if we grant that the Valentinians were close to Apostolic times in relation to Irenaeus, and that Irenaeus was not far from the times of the Apostles in relation to later writers, and even that Valentinus himself could by his age have associated with Apostolic men, namely with Polycarp and Justin and their contemporaries, yet it does not follow from this that the heretic was known before the year of the Lord 144, or before the year 141, as Pearsonius himself soon supposed. The learned man presses again, and thinks that from the age of Marcion the date of Valentinus can be decided, at pp. 79, 80, 81. But since he cannot draw Marcion's date from Irenaeus and Tertullian, he turns to the books of Origen against Celsus; because Celsus mentions the Marcionites in them, book 5, p. 272 of the latest Greek-Latin edition. Pearsonius gathers from these words of Origen in book 1, p. 8, that Celsus lived under Hadrian and wrote after Hadrian's death under the rule of Antoninus Pius (namely early in Antoninus's reign, not long after Hadrian's death): We have heard that there were two Epicurean Celsi, the earlier indeed under Nero, and this one under Hadrian and in later times. From this he concludes that Valentinus is much older than Blondellus thought, because all the ancients teach that he was older than Marcion. This is the sum of the argument of the most learned author of the Vindiciae. To answer this objection, I grant that Valentinus spread his heresy before Marcion, although both lived at about the same time. But that Celsus is so ancient as Pearsonius thinks, I plainly deny. I grant that Origen wrote that he lived under Hadrian and afterwards; but Origen affirms nothing more than that he had heard this, so that his whole account rests on uncertain rumour rather than on certain knowledge of the truth. And indeed, if we consider the matter carefully, we shall find that he was not so ancient. For when Origen says that Celsus was under Hadrian and afterwards, he means that he flourished through that span of time, for writers usually speak so; but a man cannot flourish before about the thirtieth year of his age. If we suppose, then, that he flourished in the middle of Hadrian's reign, he must have been born at the beginning of Trajan's reign, that is, in the year of Christ 98 or 99. If you say he flourished in the last years of Hadrian, we must date his birth to about the seventh year of Trajan, the year of Christ 105; add to his years some thirty, and the seven or eight years of Hadrian during which he is said to have flourished, if we believe Origen's account; he will have been about forty years old when Hadrian departed from nature. But if he had reached his fortieth year when Hadrian ceased to live, it must be said that he prolonged his life beyond his eightieth year, which is not probable. However it is, it is established that Celsus did not flourish under Hadrian, nor perhaps under Antoninus Pius, unless he flourished toward the end of that rule. He lived rather about the time of Marcus Antoninus the philosopher, and under Commodus, son of Marcus. I prove it thus: Lucian of Samosata dedicated to Celsus his book which is entitled Alexander or the False Prophet, when he was asked by him to commit the life of that impostor to writing. In that book Lucian mentions the Emperor Marcus and the Marcomannic war waged by him; and he not only mentions him but calls Marcus [theon], that is, divine, which shows that he had passed from nature and was already placed in heaven, and that his son Commodus had succeeded him. But Commodus could not have succeeded before the year of the Lord 180, in which the Emperor Marcus died of disease in Pannonia. Celsus therefore flourished under Marcus and Commodus, and for that reason could mention the Marcionites, since Marcion began to spread his heresies about the year of the Lord 145. And since he was still teaching his disciples when Justin was writing his first Apology, namely about the year of Christ 152, as we have shown, Justin could speak of him thus: Marcion of Pontus still teaches his disciples. He did not thereby indicate, as Pearsonius says, that Marcion had long spread his heresy before Justin wrote this, but only to warn that this heresiarch was still alive and that his disciples had not yet formed a separate sect. But, says Pearsonius, Justin mentions the Marcionites in the Dialogue with Trypho, p. 253. What of it? I reply: we think the Dialogue was written after the Apology, and perhaps by then the disciples of Marcion had gone off into various sects. Moreover, Justin does not seem to me to speak of the disciples of Marcion any more than of the followers of Marcus the sorcerer, who was indeed one of the disciples of Valentinus: There are some of them (he says, p. 253) who are called [Marcionitai]. Whatever the case, it matters little that Justin mentioned the Marcionites, since he could speak of them, as I have shown at length above. For Cerdo, the master of Marcion, went to Rome in the same year as Valentinus, if we listen to Eusebius, whose words in the Chronicle for the year of the Lord 141 are: Under Hyginus, bishop of the city of Rome, Valentinus the heresiarch and Cerdo, the master of Marcion, came to Rome. In the Greek Excerpts of Scaliger for the same year it is noted that both were recognised at Rome under Hyginus. Irenaeus plainly teaches the same thing, in book 1, chapter 28, and book 3, chapter 4, whose words Eusebius reports in Ecclesiastical History, book 4, chapter 11. Therefore Marcion could have succeeded Cerdo about the year 145, and Justin could have mentioned Marcion in the year 152. That this is so is clear from Epiphanius, Haer. 42, where he relates that Marcion, having been expelled from the Church by his own father, the bishop of Sinope, because of his violation of a virgin, went to Rome; and when he was not admitted to communion by the elders who administered the Roman Church while the see was vacant after the death of Hyginus, he devised a heresy, following in the footsteps of Cerdo; which happened about the year of Christ 145, as we were just saying. These things are so clear that I cannot sufficiently wonder that the most learned author of the Vindiciae dared to affirm, at p. 81, or at least to set down as a very probable thing, that Cerdo, if not before, yet at the very beginning of Hadrian's reign, had spread his follies, in order to conclude from this that Valentinus, whom he supposes to be older than Cerdo, could have spread his own teaching before the eleventh year of Trajan, and so could have been recognised by Ignatius before his martyrdom. For the opposite is plainly established by all that we have written so far, and by the testimonies of all the ancients, who make Cerdo about twenty-five years younger, and Valentinus about thirty-four or thirty-five. Moreover, there is no reason why Pearsonius should boast of Valentinus's antiquity above Cerdo's, so as to support his undertaking, since the same writers attest that Valentinus and Cerdo were contemporaries, and assert that both came to Rome under Hyginus; above all Irenaeus, who wrote against them some years later and refuted their heresies. The learned man vainly invents I know not what succession of these heretics, so as to make Valentinus more ancient than is fair and to persuade the reader that the heretics in question succeeded one another over various intervals of time, and were separated from one another by many years. I have called the succession which Pearsonius presents fictitious, in respect of age, but not in respect of doctrine; for some took from others and plagiarised them. And so the words of Epiphanius in Haer. 41, at the beginning, must be understood thus: Cerdo, a certain man, succeeded these and Heracleon, being one of their school. To Epiphanius's words the learned man adds on his own: Heracleon to Colarbasus, Colarbasus to Ptolemy, Ptolemy to Epiphanes, Epiphanes to Secundus, Secundus succeeded Valentinus. If Pearsonius speaks of succession of doctrine, what he says may be tolerated; if of age, as if a great deal of time had elapsed between them, he is mistaken, for little or almost nothing elapsed. Some indeed spread their doctrines after others, but in so small an interval of time that they can scarcely be said to have succeeded one another in terms of age. For example, Secundus is said to have succeeded Valentinus; yet Epiphanius, in Haer. 32, which is on the Secundians, expressly testifies at p. 208 that Secundus appeared at the same time as Valentinus. He says plainly the same thing in Haer. 31, p. 163, and observes this not only of Secundus but also of Colarbasus and Ptolemy: all these, he says, emerged at the same time; that is, with hardly any delay they followed hard upon one another, and one after another spread their heresies within a small span of time. Moreover, the ancient writers do not agree whether Heracleon succeeded Colarbasus or Colarbasus Heracleon, and whether Ptolemy succeeded Secundus or Secundus Ptolemy. For in Tertullian Heracleon comes before Colarbasus, and in Theodoret Ptolemy comes before him; but in Philastrius Secundus is placed after Ptolemy; and Epiphanes did not succeed Secundus, but joined himself to him, as Epiphanius teaches us. Furthermore, that varied practice and method of the ancients in listing these heretics arises from nothing else than that they appeared at the same time, and were separated from one another by a very small interval. Hence we gather that these disciples of Valentinus were contemporaries of their master, and Valentinus of Cerdo; for both went to Rome under Hyginus and were recognised in the first years of Antoninus Pius.

units.la: His ita expositis & Valentini ætate firmissimè constitutâ, nihil amplius hac de re dicendum esset, nisi Vindiciarum Auctor Dallæum de novo adoriretur, & nos eapropter, ne illum deseramus, ad Saturnili & Basilidis ætatem examinandam & explorandam cogeret. Præstantissimus Dallæus ex Saturnili & Basilidis ætate sic argumentatus erat cap. 12. pag. 308. Saturnilus & Basilides annis post Ignatij martyrium pluribus, quàm viginti sua deliria apud homines spargere coeperunt. Valentinus autem post hos duos erupit; fatetur Eruditissimus Pearsonius Valentinum post eos duos erupisse, sed non magno intervallo; at interim aperte negat ullo modo probari posse Basilidem tot annis post Ignatij mortem sua deliria spargere coepisse: Deinde Dallæum reprehendit quod plures quàm viginti annos hoc loco nominat, capite autem X. ad quod lectorem remittit, Epocham Hæreseos Basilidianæ figit, & annos XXVII. post Ignatij martyrium numerat. Verùm reprehendendi cachoete laborare oportet, qui ea arguit quæ minimè arguenda videntur. Dallæus enim cap. 10. pag. 286. non simpliciter numerat annos XXVII. post Ignatij mortem, sed circiter XXVII. Ignatij martyrium in annum Christi CVII. cum Vsferio conferendo; cap. verò XII. plures quàm viginti annos nominat, plures autem quam viginti anni, ad annos circiter XXVII. extendi possunt, vel ad annos circiter XXV. si Ignatij mortem conseras, non jam cum Vsferio, sed cum alijs in annum CIX. nulla igitur in Dallæi verbis ἀντιλογία, nulláque ideò Vindiciarum Auctori justa carpendi occasio. Verba Eusebij in Chronico, inquit, ad annum Hadriani XVII. Domini verò CXXXIV. quasi fundum sententiæ laudat Dallæus. Plura Veterum testimonia citat Clarissimus Dallæus ut probet Basilidem principatu Hadriani hæresim suam disseminare coepisse; Initium facit à Clemente Alexandrino, qui Stromateon libros scribebat seculo secundo præcipiti annos circiter quinquaginta post Basilidis mortem, eadem in urbe in quâ Hæresiarcha ille pestiferum suum venenum sparserat; Hæc autem ex lib. 7. pag. 764. describit; Infrà (id est post Pauli mortem) circa tempora Hadriani Imperatoris fuerunt qui hæreses excogitarunt, & pervenerunt usque ad ætatem Antonini natu majoris, sicut Basilides. Huic Clementis traditioni adamussim congruere, observat idem Dallæus, Firmiliani Cyprianeo ævo Cæsareæ in Cappadocia Episcopi, testimonium quod sic se habet, sed & Valentini & Basilidis tempus manifestum est, quod & ipsi post Apostolos, & post longam ætatem, adversus Ecclesiam Dei scelerati mendacijs suis rebellaverint. Huc etiam refert quæ dicit Irenæus lib. 3. cap. 3. de Clementis ad Corinthios Epistolâ (quam non multis ante Ignatij martyrium annis scriptam opinatur Dallæus) nempe vetustiorem esse Hæreticis alterum Deum super Demiurgum, factorem horum omnium quæ sunt, comminiscentibus. Et lib. 5. cap. 20. Omnes isti hæretici valde posteriores sunt, quàm Episcopi, quibus Apostoli tradiderunt Ecclesias, adeóque & Ignatio qui horum Episcoporum unus fuit. Nec his contentus Dallæus Eusebium in medium profert qui Hist. lib.4.cap.7. narrat Saturninum Antiochenum & Basilidem Alexandrinum principatu Hadriani hæreses suas disseminare coepisse, & quidem rectè Clarissimo atque Eruditissimo Valesio judice; Et in Chronico ad annum Hadriani XVII. Domini verò CXXXIV. Basilidem Hæresiarcham exhibet, à quo, inquit, Gnostici. Eusebio subjungit Theodoretum qui testatur lib. 1. Hæret. Fab. cap. 2. Saturnilum & Basilidem, ambos sub Hadriano fuisse; Et Isidorum Hispalensem qui Hadriani principatum exhibens, per idem tempus, inquit, Aquila Ponticus, interpres secundus post LXX. Oritur; Et Basilides hæresiarcha agnoscitur. Unum adjiciam testimonium ex Græca Historiarum Synagoge, quam cum Chronico Eusebiano edi curavit Scaliger, depromptum; ibi enim auctor quisquis sit principatum Hadriani percurrens, postquam observavit Marcum primum ex gentibus Jerosolymitanum Episcopum constitutum esse, addit Tunc Saturninus Antiochenus & Basilides Alexandrinus, & Carpocrates variarum hæreseon patres & architecti agniti sunt; Marci autem Ordinationem refert Eusebius in Chronico ad annum Hadriani XIX. Domini vero CXXXVI. Duobus ante Hadriani mortem annis.
units.tr: Having set out these matters, and with Valentinus's date firmly established, nothing further would need to be said on this subject, except that the author of the Vindiciae attacks Dallaeus afresh. For that reason, so as not to leave him unanswered, we must examine and test the dates of Saturninus and Basilides. The most distinguished Dallaeus argued about the dates of Saturninus and Basilides as follows (ch. 12, p. 308): Saturninus and Basilides began to spread their follies among men more than twenty years after the martyrdom of Ignatius. Valentinus burst forth after these two. The most learned Pearson concedes that Valentinus appeared after those two, but not by a large interval. Yet he flatly denies that it can be shown in any way that Basilides began to spread his follies so many years after the death of Ignatius. He then rebukes Dallaeus for speaking of more than twenty years in this place, while in chapter 10, to which he sends the reader, Dallaeus fixes the epoch of the Basilidian heresy and counts twenty-seven years after the martyrdom of Ignatius. But those who argue against things that do not seem open to argument must themselves be suffering from a kind of perversity. For Dallaeus, in chapter 10 (p. 286), does not simply count twenty-seven years after the death of Ignatius, but about twenty-seven, placing Ignatius's martyrdom in the year of Christ 107 in agreement with Usher. In chapter 12, however, he speaks of more than twenty years, and "more than twenty years" can be stretched to about twenty-seven years, or to about twenty-five if you compare the death of Ignatius not with Usher but with others, placing it in the year 109. There is therefore no [ἀντιλογία] contradiction in Dallaeus's words, and so the author of the Vindiciae has no just occasion for censure. "The words of Eusebius in the Chronicle," he says, "for the seventeenth year of Hadrian, which is the year 134 of the Lord, Dallaeus praises as the foundation of his opinion." The most distinguished Dallaeus cites further testimonies of the ancients to prove that Basilides began to spread his heresy in the reign of Hadrian. He begins with Clement of Alexandria, who was writing his Stromata in the second century, about fifty years after the death of Basilides, in the same city in which that heresiarch had spread his deadly poison. He describes this in book 7, p. 764: Later (that is, after the death of Paul) around the times of the emperor Hadrian there were those who devised heresies, and they came down to the age of Antoninus the Elder, like Basilides. The same Dallaeus observes that the testimony of Firmilian, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia in the age of Cyprian, agrees exactly with this tradition of Clement: but the time of Valentinus and Basilides is evident, since they too, after the Apostles and after a long age, have rebelled against the Church of God with their wicked lies. To this he also refers what Irenaeus says in book 3, chapter 3, about Clement's Epistle to the Corinthians (which Dallaeus thinks was written not many years before the martyrdom of Ignatius): namely, that the heretics who invented another God above the Demiurge, the maker of all these things, are of later date. And in book 5, chapter 20: All these heretics are much later than the bishops to whom the Apostles handed over the Churches, and so later than Ignatius too, who was one of these bishops. Not content with these, Dallaeus brings forward Eusebius, who in his History, book 4, chapter 7, relates that Saturninus of Antioch and Basilides of Alexandria began to spread their heresies under Hadrian, and rightly so, in the judgment of the most distinguished and learned Valesius. And in the Chronicle, for the seventeenth year of Hadrian, which is the year 134 of the Lord, he presents Basilides as the heresiarch from whom, he says, the Gnostics. To Eusebius he adds Theodoret, who testifies in book 1 of the Heretical Fables, chapter 2, that Saturninus and Basilides both lived under Hadrian. He also adds Isidore of Seville, who, giving the reign of Hadrian, says: At the same time, he says, Aquila of Pontus, the second translator after the Seventy, arose; and Basilides is recognised as heresiarch. I will add one more testimony, taken from the Greek Synagogue of Histories, which Scaliger had published along with Eusebius's Chronicle. There the author, whoever he is, running through the reign of Hadrian, after noting that Mark was first appointed bishop of Jerusalem from among the Gentiles, adds: Then Saturninus of Antioch and Basilides of Alexandria, and Carpocrates, were recognised as the fathers and architects of various heresies. Eusebius's Chronicle records Mark's ordination for the nineteenth year of Hadrian, which is the year 136 of the Lord, two years before Hadrian's death.

units.la: Videamus jam quid Dallæanis argumentis repositurus sit Eruditissimus Vindiciarum Auctor; Observat primò pag. 82. Hieronymum in Catalogo, voce Agrippa, hæc habere. Mortuus est autem Basilides à quo Gnostici in Alexandria temporibus Hadriani. Putátque eum respexisse ad illa Chronici Eusebii verba ad annum Domini CXXXIV. Basilides Hæresiarches in Alexandriâ commoratur, à quo Gnostici. Conjectura est Viri docti nullâ solidâ ratione subnixa; sed etsi daremus ad illa verba respexisse Hieronymum, non ideò sequetur idem esse in Alexandriâ commorari, & mori in Alexandriâ, Basilides quippe Alexandriæ per aliquot annos sub Hadriano commorari potuit, ab anno videlicet Hadriani XVII. & posteà naturæ cedere: post eum annum nusquam comparuit, inquit Pearsonius, Unde hoc hausit? aliquem Veterum indicet qui id testetur? Si ex Eusebii silentio illud infert, frustrà est; Nam Eusebius Hæreticorum ætatem designare solet, nullámque deinceps aut admodùm raram eorum mentionem facere, nisi forte dùm Scriptores Ecclesiasticos stilum adversus illos exercentes exhibet, quod cùm non animadverterit Hieronymus, verisimile est eum in animum induxisse suum Basilidem temporibus Hadriani mortuum esse; quoniam Eusebius observatâ semel Basilidis in Urbe Alexandriâ commoratione, de illo penitùs tacet in reliquo Chronico. Huic ex Hieronymo desumptæ exceptioni occurrit Dallæus pag. 287. Baronii rationes refellendo; sic autem occurrit: Id nescio quàm verum sit, certè non videtur cohærere cum iis, quæ Clementem suprà audiebamus tradentem, scilicet Basilidem pervenisse ad Antonini Pij ævum: Apposita sanè responsio, fieri enim non potest ut Basilides Hadriani temporibus denatus, si Hieronymum audimus, ad Antonini Pij ætatem pervenerit, ut tradit Clemens, nisi Hieronymum cum Clemente ita conciliemus, dicendo nimirum Clementem hoc tantùm velle, Basilidem pervenisse ad ætatem Antonini exclusivè: Hieronymum verò Basilidis mortem conferre in ultimum Imperij Hadriani annum: Nam eodem anno Hadriano successit Antoninus: Alioquin si inter se contendantur hi duo testes, quin præferendus sit Hieronymo Clemens, nemo opinor inficias ibit: Clemens scribebat annos circiter quinquaginta post Basilidis ætatem: Hieronymus autem pluribus quàm ducentis annis ab illis temporibus fuit remotus: His adde in quinque codicibus manu exaratis libri S. Hieronymi de Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis legi moratus est, pro mortuus est ut tradit Vir Eruditus Ioannes Cotelerius in lib. 6. Constit. Apostolicarum pag. 265. hancque tuetur lectionem, utpote Eusebiano Chronico ab Hieronymo converso apprime congruentem, necnon cum Clementis testimonio amicè conspirantem. Sed quibusdam aliis Hieronymi verbis adversus Luciferianos cap. 8. abutitur Pearsonius pag. 83. quæ si ad vivum recesentur, & à sequentibus sejungantur, aperte falsa sunt: Nam innuere videntur Basilidem Apostolorum temporibus fuisse. Apostolis adhuc (inquit) in sæculo superstitibus, &c. Tunc Simon Magus & Menander, discipulus ejus, Dei se asseruere virtutes: Tunc Basilides summum Deum Abraxas, cum trecentis sexaginta quinque editionibus commentatus est. Pearsonius Æonibus legit pro editionibus: Ego potiùs sinerem, cum trecentis sexaginta quinque editionibus, totidem enim cælos ab Angelis fabricatos somniabat, ac proinde trecentas sexaginta quinque editiones seu probolas. Dico igitur Hieronymi verba falsa esse & Vetustiorum adversari testimonijs, si quæ de Basilide narrat ad Apostolorum tempora referantur: Verùm ne ad illud tempus referamus, faciunt sequentia à Viro docto præterita, quamvis aliam sibi fuisse mentem in illis declaret: Nam post enumeratos aliquot Hæreticos, Simonem, Menandrum, Nicolaum, Saturninum, Basilidem, Ophitas, Carpocratem, Cerinthum, Ebionem, & cæteras pestes, continenter adjicit, quorum plurimi, vivente adhuc Ioanne Apostolo, eruperunt, hoc est paulò ante ejus mortem, quæ contigit ut vulgò creditur, anno Domini centesimo vel centesimo primo : Hieronymus non de omnibus quos recensuit Hæreticis id asserit, sed de plurimis, è quorum numero non fuêre Saturninus, neque Basilides Saturnino posterior, nec, meo judicio, Menander ipse amborum Magister, gister.; nisi ultimis S. Ioannis vitæ annis eum vixisse dixeris, testatur enim Theodoretus Hæret. Fab. lib. 2. in Præf. Menandrum superstitibus Apostolis extitisse, hoc est paulò ante D. Ioannis obitum, prætereà benignâ interpretatione egent Theodoreti verba, aliter non sibi constabit celeberrimus Scriptor. Instat tamen Vindiciarum Auctor, aitque Basilidem, si Basilidianis ipsis credamus, habuisse Magistrum Glauciam, suisseque illum Glauciam S. Petri interpretem. Ita quidem Basilidiani apud Clementem Alexandrinum,qui eorum gloriationem contemnit, ridétque commentum lib. 7. Strom. pag. 764. Tamen si Virum doctum audimus non hoc statim repudiandum quòd à Basilidianis dictum sit, quòd ei ætati minimè repugnat quam nostri etiam agnoscunt. Attonitus certè hæreo, dùm ejusmodi audio paradoxa, seu potiùs[?] suavia vigilantium somnia, nostrorum siquidem nullus hanc Basilidis ætatem agnovit, sed eâ longè inferiorem: Si Glaucias, pergit Pearsonius, erat interpres S. Petri, Synchronus fuit Menandru, quem omnes fatentur discipulum fuisse Simonis Magi. Siccine [illegible, ~8 letters] est VindiciaAuctor ut commentitio Basilidianorum Glauciæ à Clemente reprobato, favorabilis ex solo causæ studio esse velit: Menandrum autem Simonis discipulum fuisse ambiguè dicitur: Discipulus enim vel auditorem designat, & hoc sensu Menandrum Simonis discipulum fuisse non est verisimile; aliter vix est credibile Basilidem qui Menandrum Magistrum habuit, ad ætatem pervenisse Antonini Pij, juxta Traditionem Clementis Alexandrini: nam mortuus est Simon sub Nerone; vel potius sub Claudio cui successit Nero A. D. LV. Nero autem ipse obijt anno Domini LXIX. Ergo tunc temporis Menander XXXV. vel XXXX annos natus erat, cùm pluribus ante Neronis mortem immò ante ejus Imperium annis Simoni eum operam dedisse opportuerit, secundum Viri docti supputationem; Ergo medio Trajani Imperio erat annorum LXXX. plus minus; ætate autem adeò provecta illum docuisse par non est credere: docuisse autem tùm necesse est, immò etiam tardiùs, si illo Magistro usus est Basilides, qui Hadriani temporibus agnitus est, ut unâ voce testantur Veteres, nisi Magistrum eum dicas Scriptorum respectu, non autem vivæ vocis. At si per discipulum sectatorem intelligis, Simonis discipulus fuit Menander, nam illius fuit sectaror ac successor, ut loquuntur Irenæus, Eusebius & Theodoretus; Hinc liquet non floruisse Menandrum sub Vespasiano, ut dicit Pearsonius, neque sub Domitiano, sed sub Trajano, sub quo illius meminit Eusebius Hist. lib. 3. cap. 26.
units.tr: Let us now see what the most learned author of the Vindiciae will reply to Dallaeus's arguments. First, he observes (p. 82) that Jerome in the Catalogue, under the word Agrippa, has these words: Basilides died, from whom the Gnostics in Alexandria, in the times of Hadrian. He thinks Jerome had in mind those words of Eusebius's Chronicle for the year of the Lord 134: Basilides the heresiarch lived in Alexandria, from whom the Gnostics. This is a conjecture of a learned man, supported by no solid reasoning. But even if we grant that Jerome had those words in mind, it does not follow that "to live in Alexandria" and "to die in Alexandria" are the same thing. Basilides could have remained in Alexandria for some years under Hadrian, namely from the seventeenth year of Hadrian, and afterwards have departed this life. "After that year he appears nowhere," says Pearson. Where did he draw this from? Let him point out some ancient writer who bears witness to it. If he infers it from Eusebius's silence, the inference is worthless. For Eusebius is accustomed to mark the age of heretics and afterwards to make little or no mention of them, except perhaps when he presents ecclesiastical writers who are directing their pen against them. Jerome did not notice this, and it is likely that he came to think that his Basilides died in the times of Hadrian, since Eusebius, once he had noted Basilides's residence in the city of Alexandria, is entirely silent about him in the rest of the Chronicle. Dallaeus meets this objection, taken from Jerome, in p. 287, when refuting the arguments of Baronius. His answer is this: I do not know how true this is, but it certainly does not seem to cohere with what we heard Clement teaching above, namely that Basilides reached the age of Antoninus Pius. The reply is certainly apt. For it cannot be that Basilides died in the times of Hadrian, if we listen to Jerome, and yet reached the age of Antoninus Pius, as Clement hands down, unless we reconcile Jerome with Clement by saying that Clement means only this, that Basilides reached the age of Antoninus exclusively, while Jerome places Basilides's death in the last year of Hadrian's reign, for in that very year Antoninus succeeded Hadrian. Otherwise, if these two witnesses are set against each other, I suppose no one will deny that Clement is to be preferred to Jerome. Clement was writing about fifty years after Basilides's time, while Jerome was removed from those times by more than two hundred years. Add to this that in five manuscript codices of Jerome's book on Ecclesiastical Writers the reading moratus est ("lived") is found instead of mortuus est ("died"), as the learned John Cotelier reports in book 6 of the Apostolic Constitutions, p. 265. He defends this reading, since it fits very well with Eusebius's Chronicle as translated by Jerome, and agrees harmoniously with Clement's testimony. But Pearson, at p. 83, abuses certain other words of Jerome against the Luciferians, chapter 8, which, if they are examined closely and separated from what follows, are plainly false. For they seem to suggest that Basilides belonged to the times of the Apostles: While the Apostles were still living in the world, he says, etc. Then Simon Magus and Menander, his disciple, claimed to be the powers of God. Then Basilides, commenting on the highest God Abraxas, with three hundred and sixty-five emanations. Pearson reads Aeons for emanations. I would rather let it stand as with three hundred and sixty-five emanations, for he dreamed that there were as many heavens fabricated by angels, and therefore three hundred and sixty-five emanations or probolae. I say, then, that Jerome's words are false and contrary to the testimonies of earlier writers, if what he relates about Basilides is referred to the times of the Apostles. But let us not refer it to that time. The sentences that the learned man passes over support this, although he declares that he had a different intention in them. For after listing several heretics, Simon, Menander, Nicolaus, Saturninus, Basilides, the Ophites, Carpocrates, Cerinthus, Ebion, and the other pests, he goes on immediately: most of whom broke out while the Apostle John was still living, that is, shortly before his death, which, as is commonly believed, took place in the year of the Lord 100 or 101. Jerome does not assert this of all the heretics he has listed, but of most of them, and of these Saturninus was not one, nor Basilides, who was later than Saturninus, nor, in my judgment, Menander himself, the teacher of both. Unless you say that he lived in the last years of St John's life. For Theodoret testifies, in the preface to book 2 of the Heretical Fables, that Menander appeared while the Apostles were still alive, that is, shortly before the death of St John. Moreover, Theodoret's words need a charitable interpretation, otherwise the celebrated writer will not be consistent with himself. Yet the author of the Vindiciae insists, and says that Basilides, if we believe the Basilidians themselves, had Glaucias as his teacher, and that this Glaucias was an interpreter of St Peter. Indeed the Basilidians say this, according to Clement of Alexandria, who scorns their boast and laughs at the invention, book 7 of the Stromata, p. 764. Nevertheless, if we listen to the learned man, this should not be rejected at once merely because it was said by the Basilidians, since it does not in the least conflict with that age, which even our own writers acknowledge. I am certainly astonished and hesitate when I hear such paradoxes, or rather pleasant dreams of wakeful men, for indeed none of our writers recognised this age for Basilides, but a much later one. If Glaucias, Pearson goes on, was an interpreter of St Peter, he was a contemporary of Menander, whom everyone admits was a disciple of Simon Magus. Is the author of the Vindiciae so [illegible, ~8 letters] that he wishes the invented story of the Basilidians about Glaucias, which Clement rejected, to be accepted as credible, simply from zeal for his cause? It is said ambiguously that Menander was a disciple of Simon. For disciple designates a pupil, and in this sense it is not likely that Menander was a disciple of Simon. Otherwise it is scarcely credible that Basilides, who had Menander as his teacher, reached the age of Antoninus Pius, according to the tradition of Clement of Alexandria. For Simon died under Nero, or rather under Claudius, whom Nero succeeded in the year 55. Nero himself died in the year of the Lord 69. Therefore at that time Menander was thirty-five or forty years old, since, according to the learned man's calculation, he must have been given to Simon many years before Nero's death, indeed before Nero's reign. So in the middle of Trajan's reign he was about eighty years old. It is not right to believe that he taught at so advanced an age. Yet he must have taught then, or even later, if Basilides used him as his teacher, and Basilides was recognised in the times of Hadrian, as the ancients testify with one voice, unless you call Menander his teacher in respect of his writings rather than of the living voice. But if by disciple you mean follower, Menander was Simon's disciple, for he was his follower and successor, as Irenaeus, Eusebius and Theodoret put it. Hence it is clear that Menander did not flourish under Vespasian, as Pearson says, nor under Domitian, but under Trajan, under whom Eusebius mentions him in his History, book 3, chapter 26.

units.la: Eruditissimus Pearsonius aliquod quaerit praesidium in hisce Epiphanii verbis Hær. 31. num. 2. quæ describit juxta Petavii versionem, postquam Græca exhibuit. Valentinus iste prioribus illis à me autea commemoratis tempore est posterior, Basilide nimirum ac Saturnilo, Ebione, Cerintho ac Merintho eorúmque socíis. Siquidem omnes uno tempore ad humani generis exitium profusi sunt: Quanquam Cerintbus ac Merinthus & Ebion paululum antegressi sunt. Hinc colligit Vir doctus non multum temporis intercessisse inter Cerinthum Hæreticum in Asiâ agnitum antequam S.Ioannes Evangelium scripserat, & Basilidem, teste Epiphanio[?]. Si tempus illud Vindiciarum Auctori limitare libuisset, illius mentem facilius percipéremus [?]: sed quoniam id facere neglexit, respondemus Epiphanium de tempore loqui in genere, ut ostendat Valentinum cæteris quos nominat Hæreticis posteriorem esse, quantum autem temporis intercesserit inter eos & Valentinum non dicit, nec quantum à Cerintho remotus fuerit Basilides decernit; hoc solùm vult Epiphanius, hæreticos illos eadem ætate exortos esse, nempe intra spatium annorum circiter quadraginta plus minus quod verissimum est; non me latet has voces eodem tempore brevius aliquando tempus designare: At ne ita hoc in loco eas explicemus vetat quod tractamus argumentum; quia aliunde constat Basilidem à Cerintho remotiorem esse quàm putat Pearsonius. Instat Vir doctus & ista Epiphanij verba urget quanquam Cerinthus, ac Merinthus & Ebion paululum antegressi sunt. Esto, non ideò sequetur Basilidem Cerintho tam vicinum fuisse, quàm arbitratur Vindiciarum Auctor; Iustinus suprà bellum nuperum vocabat, bellum ante quindecim annos gestum; quidni etiam Epiphanius de spatio annorum circiter quadraginta, tanquam de modico tempore loqui potuerit? Prætereà Petavij versio quam sequutus est Pearsonius, Græco textui non respondet adamussim; versio quippe Latina de Cerintho ipso loquitur; Græcus verò contextus de illius sectatoribus; ὀλίγῳ δὲ[?] πρόσθεν μᾶλλον οἱ περὶ Κηρίνθον[?], καὶ Μενάνδρον καὶ Ἐβίωνας; Quivis videt non de ipsis agi Hæresiarchis, sed de eorum sectatoribus, qui Magistris posteriores fuêre, & quos Epiphanius eodem in loco sub his vocibus complexus est, καὶ τὰς ἀμφ᾽ αὐτ[?]ὰς, Petavius reddit eorúmque socis, vertendum erat eorúmque sectatoribus: verbi gratia οἱ ἀμφὶ seu περὶ τὸν Ἐπίκουρον[?], sunt Epicurei Epicuri discipuli ac sectatores; Illi autem Cerinthi sectatores Valentinum modico tempore antegressi sunt; nam cum Saturnino & Basilide prodire cœperunt ut testatur ibidem Epiphanius; Saturninus & Basiiides Valentinum non magno intervallo præcesserunt, si Virum doctum audimus; Valentinum ante annum Domini CXLI.vel CXLIV. nequaquam agnitum esse fusè demonstravimus; Ergo non longè ante illud tempus exorti sunt si Epiphanio credimus, quibus de agitur Cerinthi sectatores. Aliud habet Pearsonius quo se tueatur pag. 82. illud scilicet quod tradit Eusebius Hist. lib. 4. cap. 7. de Agrippa Castore, quòd sub imperio Hadriani Basilidis luculentam confutationem scripsit, in quâ & mentionem fecit XXIV. librorum ab eo in Evangelium scriptorum, neque tantùm adversus Basilidem, sed & filium ejus Isidorum scripsit teste Theodoreto ; Unde concludit Pearsonius Basilidem qui sub Hadriano tot libros ediderat, filiúmque ac discipulum notum etiam scriptorem tunc habuit, sub Trajano sua docuisse par esse credere : mera conjectura nulla solidâ ratione fulta. Agrippa Castor sub fine imperij Hadriani Basilidem confutavit ; potuit ergo tot libros antea scribere, & forte etiam antequam haeresim suam spargere coepisset ; Isidorus verò filius ejus eodem tempore figmenta sua disseminabat, & eapropter ab eodem Agrippa refutatus fuit ; Recentiorum testimonia, Ioelis videlicet Chronographi, & Albufaraij non moror, quoniam de rebus adeò antiquis sine vetustiorum auctoritate loquuntur, immò ijs plane contraria docent.
units.tr: The most learned Pearson seeks some support in these words of Epiphanius, Heresy 31, sec. 2, which he gives following Petavius' version after quoting the Greek: "This Valentinus is later in time than those earlier heretics I mentioned before, namely Basilides and Saturninus, Ebion, Cerinthus and Merinthus and their companions. For all of them were launched at one time for the destruction of the human race, although Cerinthus, Merinthus and Ebion went a little before." From this the learned man infers that not much time passed between Cerinthus, recognised as a heretic in Asia before St John wrote his Gospel, and Basilides, as Epiphanius attests. If the author of the Vindiciae had wished to fix that interval, we would more easily grasp his meaning; but since he neglected to do so, we reply that Epiphanius speaks of time in general, to show that Valentinus is later than the other heretics he names. How much time lay between them and Valentinus he does not say, nor does he determine how far Basilides was removed from Cerinthus. Epiphanius only means that those heretics arose in the same age, that is, within a span of about forty years more or less, which is quite true. I am not unaware that the words "at the same time" sometimes denote a shorter period, but the subject we are treating forbids us to explain them that way here, because it is established from other sources that Basilides was more remote from Cerinthus than Pearson thinks. The learned man presses on and urges these words of Epiphanius: "although Cerinthus, Merinthus and Ebion went a little before." Granted; yet it does not follow that Basilides was as close to Cerinthus as the author of the Vindiciae supposes. Justin, above, calls the recent war a war waged fifteen years earlier; why should Epiphanius not likewise speak of a span of about forty years as a modest time? Moreover, the version of Petavius which Pearson followed does not correspond exactly to the Greek text. The Latin speaks of Cerinthus himself, whereas the Greek context speaks of his followers: "a little before, rather, those about Cerinthus, and Menander and Ebion." Anyone can see that the subject is not the heresiarchs themselves but their followers, who came after their masters. Epiphanius sums up these followers in the same passage with the phrase "and their companions" [καὶ τὰς ἀμφ᾽ αὐτάς], which Petavius renders "their companions"; it should have been rendered "their followers." For example, "those about Epicurus" [οἱ ἀμφὶ or περὶ τὸν Ἐπίκουρον] are the Epicureans, the disciples and followers of Epicurus. Those followers of Cerinthus went a little before Valentinus, for they began to appear together with Saturninus and Basilides, as Epiphanius himself testifies in the same place. Saturninus and Basilides preceded Valentinus by no great interval, if we listen to the learned man. We have demonstrated at length that Valentinus was not recognised before the year of the Lord 141 or 144. Therefore, if we believe Epiphanius, the followers of Cerinthus of whom we speak arose not long before that time. Pearson has another argument to defend himself, at p. 82, namely what Eusebius relates in Hist. book 4, ch. 7, about Agrippa Castor: that under Hadrian he wrote a brilliant refutation of Basilides, in which he also mentioned the twenty-four books Basilides had written on the Gospel, and that he wrote against not only Basilides but also his son Isidore, as Theodoret witnesses. From this Pearson concludes that we should believe Basilides, who had published so many books under Hadrian and had a son and disciple who was also a known writer, taught his doctrines under Trajan. This is a mere conjecture, supported by no solid reasoning. Agrippa Castor refuted Basilides near the end of Hadrian's reign; he could therefore have written so many books earlier, perhaps even before Basilides began to spread his heresy. Isidore, his son, meanwhile was disseminating his fictions at the same time, and for that reason was refuted by the same Agrippa. I shall not dwell on the testimonies of more recent writers, Joel the chronographer and Albufaraius, since they speak of such ancient matters without the authority of older writers, and indeed teach things plainly contrary to them.

units.la: Explosâ igitur falsâ Eruditissimi Vindiciarum Auctoris Chronologiâ, examinandae supersunt, quas opponit ad Veterum à Dallaeo allata testimonia exceptiones: Inchoat à Clemente Alexandrino, cujus locum mirè corruptum arbitratur pag. 84. 85. Verùm de totâ pericope non agitur, nollem enim diffiteri [?] quin aliquam experta sit interpolationem, in fine praesertim & forte etiam in principio: Sed affirmare non vereor sana esse & integra, omnisque prorsus corruptionis expertia quae descripsit Dallaeus ad aetatem Basilidis constituendam, & affirmabit mecum quisquis locum ipsum consulere non dedignabitur: Adeo clara sunt omnia ac perspicua, ut illum sponte caecutire oporteat, aut nimio φιλονικίας[?] amore corripi, qui de illis litem sit moturus; Sed si corrupta non sunt, male intellecta esse contendit Pearsonius; Cur ita? Quia Clemens, inquit, non dicit eos de quibus loquitur sub Hadriano primùm sua deliria docuisse. Hoc tantùm dicit, eos qui haereses excogitârunt circa tempora Hadriani extitisse. Egregium subterfugium; Unde quaeso Haereticorum aetatem novimus, nisi ex Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis, qui eam nos ignorare non patiuntur? Clemens Alexandrinus vetustissimus Scriptor & Irenaei aequalis diserte testatur Basilidem circa tempora Hadriani haeresim suam excogitasse, & usque ad aetatem Antonini Pii pervenisse; tamen ecce paraphrasim istorum verborum quam exhibet Vir doctus pag. 83. Menander floruit sub Vespasiano, Basilides eum audivit sub Domitiano, sub Trajano haeresim suam efformavit atque prodidit. Scholam sub Hadriano condidit; Hanc Pearsonij explicationem, verborum Clementis paraphrasim vocare non dubitavi, quia ad ea illum respexisse par est credere, ut videlicet Clementem in suam sententiam obtorto collo traheret; quamvis Clemens nihil omnino dicat de Domitiano neque de Trajano, non prætermissurus certè si sub Domitiano Menandrum audivisset Basilides, hæresímque suam sub Trajano efformassèt atque prodidisset. Si valet Viri docti ratiocinatio, ejusque Veteres interpretandi methodus, nihil certi remanebit in totâ antiquitate Ecclesiasticâ, cujus studio nuncium mittere oportebit, nisi oleum & operam perdere velimus: Scriptores Ecclesiastici ob nihil aliud tempora quibus floruere Hæretici signant, quàm ut eorum exploratam ætatem habeamus, neque eos suas hæreses priùs disseminasse putemus, eorum ergo testimonijs standum est, nec ea pro arbitrio sollicitare cuiquam licitum esse debet. Cùm igitur præter Clementem Alexandrinum plures alij Scriptores à Dallæo laudati idem prorsus de Basilidis ætate tradiderint, frustra se torsit Vir doctus ut eum antiquiorem esse ostenderet, Veterumque testimonia contra illorum verba ac mentem interpretaretur, histo-rias [?] & Chronologias nobis non ex rerum veritate, sed ex suo commoda contexendo. Verba autem Henrici Valesij quæ sugillat Pearsonius pag. 86.87. commodè explicari possunt, si dicimus hanc esse Valesij mentem, sub Hadriano videlicet Hæreticos primùm ex latebris prodijsse, hoc est magno cum impetu & velut agmine facto erupisse, impiáque sua dogmata tunc certatim spargere cœpisse, quod verissimum est. Accedo jam ad Firmiliani Cæsareæ in Cappadociâ Episcopi testimonium; Sed & Valentini (inquit) & Basilidis tempus manifestum est, quod & ipsi post Apostolos, & post longam ætatem adversus Ecclesiam Dei sceleratis mendacijs suis rebellaverint.
units.tr: Having therefore dismissed the false chronology of the most learned author of the Vindiciae, we must examine the objections he raises against the testimonies of the Ancients which Daillé adduced. He begins with Clement of Alexandria, whose passage he thinks is wonderfully corrupt (pp. 84–85). But the whole paragraph is not in question. I would not deny that it has suffered some interpolation, especially at the end and perhaps also at the beginning. But I do not hesitate to affirm that the parts Daillé cited to fix Basilides' date are sound and intact and free from any corruption. Whoever will not disdain to consult the passage itself will agree with me, for everything in it is so clear and plain that one would have to be wilfully blind, or seized by excessive love of contention, to raise a dispute about it. But if the text is not corrupt, Pearson contends that it has been misunderstood. Why so? Because, he says, Clement "does not say that those of whom he speaks first taught their delusions under Hadrian; he only says that those who devised the heresies existed about the time of Hadrian." An excellent escape! For where, I ask, do we learn the age of the heretics, except from ecclesiastical writers, who do not allow us to be ignorant of it? Clement of Alexandria, a very ancient writer and contemporary of Irenaeus, expressly testifies that Basilides devised his heresy about the time of Hadrian, and lived on until the age of Antoninus Pius. Yet look at the paraphrase of these words which the learned man gives at p. 83: "Menander flourished under Vespasian; Basilides heard him under Domitian; under Trajan he formed and published his heresy; he founded his school under Hadrian." I have not hesitated to call this explanation of Pearson's a paraphrase of Clement's words, because it is right to believe he looked to them, so that he might twist Clement by force to his own opinion. Yet Clement says nothing at all about Domitian or Trajan. He would certainly not have passed over these matters if Basilides had heard Menander under Domitian and formed and published his heresy under Trajan. If the learned man's reasoning and his method of interpreting the Ancients were valid, nothing certain would remain in the whole of Church antiquity, and we would have to labour in vain, wasting our oil and effort. Ecclesiastical writers mark the times when heretics flourished for no other reason than that we may have their age established, and not suppose that they spread their heresies earlier. We must therefore abide by their testimonies, and it should not be permitted to anyone to twist them at will. Since, then, besides Clement of Alexandria, several other writers cited by Daillé have handed down exactly the same account of Basilides' age, the learned man has wasted his effort in trying to show that he is earlier, and in interpreting the testimonies of the Ancients against the sense and meaning of those writers, weaving histories and chronologies for us not from the truth of the facts but to suit himself. As for the words of Henri de Valois which Pearson disparages at pp. 86–87, they can be explained fairly if we say that this was Valois' meaning: that under Hadrian heretics first came out of their hiding places, that is, burst forth with great violence and as an army, and then began eagerly to spread their impious doctrines. This is very true. I now come to the testimony of Firmilian, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia: "But the time of Valentinus and Basilides (he says) is clear, that after the Apostles, and after a long age, they rebelled against the Church of God with their wicked lies."

units.la: Respondet Pearsonius pag. 87. Firmilianum loqui non de initio hæreseos Basilidianæ, sed de Basilidis rebellione contra Ecclesiam. Faceta sanè distinctio, quasi Hæretici adversus Ecclesiam non rebellent, ubi primùm hæreses suas disseminant: Respondet secundò per Apostolos intelligi debere Petrum & Paulum; sed hæc responsio non est priore solidior: Firmilianus de Apostolis loquitur in genere & indefinitè; Vir doctus tamen ad Petrum & Paulum, ut causæ inserviat, Firmiliani verba restringit. Verùm enimverò ut appareat istius responsionis vanitas, consulenda sunt quæ immediatè præcedunt apud Firmilianum ; cùm & Marcion Cerdonis discipulus inveniatur serò post Apostolos & post longa ab eis tempora , sacrilegam adversus Deum traditionem induxisse. Negari non potest quin per Apostolos hoc in loco intelligendi sint omnes Apostoli ; Marcion enim pestiferum suum venenum Apostolis omnibus jam extinctis spargere cœpit,satente ipso Vindiciarum Auctore , qui Cerdonem Marcionis Magistrum ipso statim initio Hadriani sua deliria disseminâsse putat , quamvis id seriùs præstiterit. Quorsum igitur per eosdem Apostolos , cum de Basilide agitur , non omnes intelligemus Apostolos?Utróque enim loco eadem mens Firmiliano , eadémque ferè locutio:Firmilianus,inquit Pearsonius, ita seipsum explicat , dum Stephanus vapulat ; ita Viro doćto videtur,sed egregiè fallitur ; hanc tamen Firmiliani explicationem se reperisse opinatur in istis verbis , adhuc etiam infamans Petrum & Paulum beatos Apostolos , quasi hoc ipsi tradiderint. Hinc colligit Firmilianum hos duos solùm designasse Apostolos, dum dixit Basilidem post Apostolos adversus Ecclesiam Dei rebellâsse. Sed animadvertere debebat Vir doctus , Firmilianum ultimo in loco Petri & Pauli tantùm meminisse, quoniam ex omnibus Apostolis hos solos in Epistolis suis haereticos execratos esse existimabat, nosque ut eos evitemus monuisse; nam post haec verba, quasi hoc ipsi tradiderint, continenter subjicit, qui in Epistolis suis Haereticos execrati sunt, & ut eos evitemus monuerunt. Praeterea quomodo manifestum erit Basilidis tempus, si cum Viro docto dicas eum sub Trajano floruisse, cùm caeteri Scriptores Ecclesiastici temporibus Hadriani agnitum esse rotundè pronuncient. Nihil dico de argumento ex Epistolae Clementis antiquitate deprompto, quia de illius Epistolae aetate non planè convenit inter Doctos; Irenaei verò testimonium quod spectat haud exigui mihi videtur esse momenti, Omnes isti Haeretici (inquit lib. 5. c. 20.) valdè posteriores sunt, quàm Episcopi, quibus Apostoli tradiderunt Ecclesias, queritur statim Vir doctus Dallaeum omisisse verba quae sequuntur, & hoc in tertio libro cum omni diligentia manifestavimus; sed parum referebat ea describere, cùm distertius testari non posset omnes illos Haereticos de quibus hactenus egerat, Ignatio valdè esse posteriores, Ignatius siquidem horum Episcoporum quibus Apostoli Ecclesias tradiderunt unus fuit. Sed (inquit Pearsonius pag. 88.) nihil hoc loco dicit, quod non antea dixerat (hoc est in libro tertio) At cum omni diligentia uteretur, nihil de aetate Basilidis dixit, de qua nunc disputatur.
units.tr: Pearson replies at p. 87 that Firmilian is speaking not of the beginning of the Basilidian heresy but of Basilides' rebellion against the Church. A witty distinction indeed, as if heretics did not rebel against the Church when they first spread their heresies! Secondly, he replies that "the Apostles" must be understood as Peter and Paul. But this answer is no more solid than the first. Firmilian speaks of the Apostles in general and indefinitely, whereas the learned man restricts Firmilian's words to Peter and Paul to serve his cause. But to make the emptiness of this reply plain, we must consult what immediately precedes in Firmilian, since Marcion, the disciple of Cerdo, is found to have introduced his sacrilegious tradition against God late, "after the Apostles and after long ages from them." It cannot be denied that "the Apostles" here must mean all the Apostles, for Marcion began to spread his pestilent poison when all the Apostles were already dead. The author of the Vindiciae himself concedes this, since he thinks Cerdo, Marcion's teacher, spread his delusions at the very beginning of Hadrian's reign, although Marcion did so later. Why then, when the subject is Basilides, should we not understand by the same Apostles all the Apostles? The meaning of Firmilian is the same in both places, and nearly the same wording. "Firmilian," says Pearson, "explains himself in this way when he attacks Stephen." This seems so to the learned man, but he is gravely mistaken. He thinks he has found this explanation of Firmilian in those words, "still further slandering Peter and Paul, the blessed Apostles, as if they had handed this down themselves." From this he infers that Firmilian designated only these two Apostles when he said that Basilides "rebelled against the Church of God after the Apostles." But the learned man ought to have noticed that Firmilian mentions only Peter and Paul in the last place because he thought they alone of all the Apostles had cursed heretics in their Epistles and warned us to avoid them. For after these words, "as if they had handed this down themselves," he immediately adds, "who in their Epistles cursed heretics" and "warned us to avoid them." Moreover, how will the time of Basilides be "manifest" if, with the learned man, you say he flourished under Trajan, when other ecclesiastical writers flatly declare that he was known in the times of Hadrian? I say nothing of the argument drawn from the antiquity of Clement's Epistle, since learned men do not fully agree about the date of that Epistle. But the testimony of Irenaeus, as far as it concerns us, seems to me of no small weight: "All these heretics" (he says in book 5, ch. 20) "are far later than the bishops to whom the Apostles handed over the Churches." Straightaway the learned man complains that Daillé omitted the words that follow, "and this we have shown with all diligence in the third book." But it mattered little to copy them, since Irenaeus could not have testified more clearly that all those heretics of whom he had so far treated were far later than Ignatius, for Ignatius was one of those bishops to whom the Apostles handed over the Churches. "But" (Pearson says, p. 88) "he says nothing here that he had not said before," that is, in the third book. "But he had used all diligence there, and he said nothing about the age of Basilides, which is now in dispute." Even if we grant this to the learned man, the very express testimony of Irenaeus does not lose any of its weight on that account. Irenaeus speaks without any evasion about whatever else was done in the third book. And if in the third book he said nothing precisely about the age of Basilides, yet he...

units.la: Si id largiamur Viro docto, non propterea minoris erit ponderis expressissimum Irenaei testimonium, qui sine ulla ambage loquitur, quicquid de caetero in tertio libro praestitum sit : Deinde si in tertio libro nihil de aetate Basilidis praecise dixit, illam tamen satis superque indicavit, imprimis dum Valentinum venisse Romam sub Hygino tradidit, increvisse sub Pio, & prorogasse tempus usque ad Anicetum ; Nam Basilides Valentinum quidem praecessit, sed non magno intervallo, ut fatetur Vir doctus ; Tandem, uti spero, omnibus Vindiciarum Auctoris ad argumentum a Valentini Sige deductum exceptionibus abunde responsum est, quatuor ejus Assertiones quae totidem continentur capitibus accurate expendimus, rationes quibus Assertiones suas stabilire nisus est refellimus, objectiones omnes solvimus, & argumentis haud infirmis demonstravimus, pulsari ab Auctore Epistolae ad Magnesio Valentini haeresim, pluribus post Ignatij martyrium annis exortam. Unde nobis oritur certissima suppositionis nota, quae si sola esset abunde sufficeret, ut Ignatio abjudicentur quæ illius nomine circumferuntur Epistolæ cum sint spuriæ ac nothæ, à plano quodam seu impostore diu post sanctissimi Martyris mortem confictæ & consarcinatæ.
units.tr: Even if we grant this to the learned man, the most explicit testimony of Irenaeus is no less weighty. He speaks without any hedging about whatever was established in the third book. Moreover, although in the third book he did not state the date of Basilides exactly, he indicated it more than sufficiently. In particular, he reports that Valentinus came to Rome under Hyginus, flourished under Pius, and extended the period to Anicetus. For Basilides preceded Valentinus, but not by a long interval, as the learned man himself admits. Finally, as I hope, a full answer has been given to all the objections of the author of the Vindiciae to the argument drawn from the Sige of Valentinus. We have carefully examined his four assertions, which are contained in four chapters. We have refuted the reasons by which he tried to establish his assertions, solved all his objections, and shown by no weak arguments that the author of the Epistle to the Magnesians attacks the heresy of Valentinus, which arose many years after the martyrdom of Ignatius. From this arises a most certain mark of forgery, which would by itself be quite sufficient to deny to Ignatius the letters that circulate under his name. Since they are spurious and bastard, they were fabricated and patched together long after the death of the most holy martyr by some ordinary forger or impostor.

units.la: Quæ cum ita sint à pluribus Dallæi argumentis examinandis ac vindicandis abstinere possem: Nihilominus tamen quædam alia breviter percurrere non gravabor. Eruditissimus Vindiciarum Auctor cap. 8. quatuor illius expendit argumenta cap. 13. comprehensa, primum ductum est ex quibusdam Epistolæ ad Smyrnæos verbis; Sed hunc locum obiter tangit Dallæus, ut observat ipse Pearsonius, & illum proferre contentus, nequaquam urget pag. 313. Secundum, quædam Dallæi conjectura nititur, nempe opinatus est Vir doctissimus fuisse Ignatij ævo in militiâ Romanâ, certum quendam militum ordinem Leopardorum appellatione nuncupatum, quoniam ad Romanos scribit Epistolicus Ignatius, vinctus sum decem Leopardis, quod est militaris ordo: Sed quando his solis verbis nititur Dallæi argumentum, nulliusque veteris Scriptoris fultum est testimonio, non usquequaque solidum mihi videtur. Tertium quo Ignatianas impugnat Epistolas argumentum, ex eo ducitur quod Scriptor publicè pœnitentes admittat, & post satisfactionem reconciliet Ecclesiæ, quod tempore Martyris nondum obtinere arbitrabatur. Verùm falsus est suâ opinione præstantissimus Dallæus, eámque propterea emendaturus erat si vixisset, ut amico rescripsit, qui hac de re illum monuerat, eíque loca pro receptione pœnitentium apud vetustissimos Ecclesiæ Scriptores indicaverat. Quartum Dallæi argumentum majoris est momenti, & Onesimum spectat, de quo Scriptor Epistolæ ad Ephesios ita loquitur; Plurimum enim multitudinem vestram in nomine Dei suscepi in Onesimo, qui in charitate inenarrabili est, vester autem in carne Episcopus: Pertendit Dallæus hanc de Onesimo narrationem, temporum seriem turbare, & Epistolæ auctorem loqui de homine velut vivente qui jampridem erat mortuus; Ut id probet observat ex Vsserio pag. 316. Græcorum Menæa & Symeonem Metaphrastem non agnoscere Onesimum Martyrem fuisse Ephesi Episcopum, Constitutionum Apostolicarum Scriptorem affirmare eum Berææ Episcopum fuisse, Dorotheum & Hippolytum asserere Gaium Timothei in Ephesino Episcopatu successorem fuisse. Nicephorum denique tradere Onesimum sub Domitiano obijsse. Eruditissimus Vindiciarum Auctor pag.97. negat hinc sequi, Onesimum quendam Gaij successorem Epheso minimè praefuisse, cùm Ignatius ad martyrium tractus est: Nempe fieri posse putat Vir doctus duos fuisse Onesimos, quorum alter sub Domitiano Martyr obierit, alter verò Gaio Episcopo Ephesino successerit, eíque Ecclesiae praefuerit, dum Ignatius vinctus Romam ducebatur ; Reverendissimus Vsserius hunc nodum paulò aliter solvit , suspicatur videlicet duos fuisse Onesimos, utrúmque Ephesi Episcopum, unum Seniorem, Pauli discipulum, sub Domitiano passum: alterum Gaij successorem, Ignatio superstitem. Dallæus huic distinctioni sic occurrit pag. 316. Sed hæc ne admittantur, prohibet primò Bedæ, Adonis, Notkeri, & aliorum fides, qui istum ab Ignatio Epistolico memoratum Onesimum magno omnes consensu Pauli discipulum fuisse affirmant. Pearsonius ait se talem consensum non reperire; quia solus Ado de Ignatij Onesimo mentionem facit in libello de festivitatibus Apostolorum ad XIIII. Kalend. Mart. Reliqui eundem Onesimum Philemonis servum à B. Paulo Ephesinae Ecclesiae post Timotheum constitutum fuisse Episcopum tradunt, nullâ Ignatij mentione factâ; observat praeterea idem Pearsonius Adonem qui Onesimum S. Pauli Ignatianum facit, non narrare eum sub Domitiano obiisse. Narrat Nicephorus, nuperus est scriptor, ait Vir doctus, & quia solus refert eâ tempestate martyrium subijsse Onesimum, non immeritò illi fidem denegare Baronium asserit, præsertim si de Episcopo Ephesino intelligatur. Nam si ille Episcopus (inquit pag.97) Beræ fuit, non autem Ephesi, ut alij Nicephoro antiquiores volvere, ad nos non pertinet. Quis enim non videt Onesimo S. Pauli, Episcopo Beraæ, temporibus Domitiani defuncto, Onesimum alium post Timotheum & Gaium Epheso præesse potuisse sub imperio Trajani. Si rem ipsam consideres fieri potuit quod dicit Vir doctus, sed si Traditionem spectes nequaquam; Nam Beda, Vsuârdus, Notkerus & Ado testantur Onesimum Pauli Ephesinæ Ecclesiæ Episcopum Ordinatum esse; immò eundem esse cum Ignatiano diserte tradit Ado. Hinc forte nata Clarissimi Vsserij suspicio, qui, si Dallæum audimus, suspicatus est duos fuisse Onesimos, utrúmque Ephesi Episcopum, ita Vsserij mentem interpretatus est præstantissimus Dallæus, etsi forte aliam explicationem ferre possint verba à Reverendissimo Vsserio usurpata,Not. in Epist. Ignatij ad Ephes. pag. 5.
units.tr: Since this is so, I could abstain from examining and defending the many arguments of Daillé. Nevertheless, I will not hesitate to run briefly through some others. The most learned author of the Vindiciae, in chapter 8, weighed four of his arguments, gathered in chapter 13. The first is drawn from some words of the Epistle to the Smyrnaeans. Daillé touches on this passage only in passing, as Pearson himself observes, and, being content to cite it, does not press it at all (p. 313). The second rests on a conjecture of Daillé's. He thought, as a most learned man, that in the age of Ignatius there was in the Roman army a certain order of soldiers called "Leopards," because Ignatius writes to the Romans: I am bound to ten leopards, which is a military order. But since Daillé's argument rests on these words alone and is supported by no testimony of any ancient writer, it does not seem to me entirely solid. The third argument by which Daillé attacks the Ignatian letters is that the writer admits publicly penitents and, after satisfaction, reconciles them to the Church, which he thought was not yet the practice in the time of the martyr. But that most distinguished man was mistaken in his opinion, and he would have corrected it had he lived, as he wrote in reply to a friend who had warned him about this matter and had pointed out passages on the reception of penitents among the most ancient writers of the Church. The fourth argument of Daillé is of greater weight, and concerns Onesimus, of whom the writer of the Epistle to the Ephesians speaks thus: For I have received your whole congregation in the name of God in Onesimus, who is of inexpressible love, and your bishop in the flesh. Daillé contends that this account of Onesimus disturbs the order of the times, and that the author of the Epistle speaks of a man as if he were still living, though he had long been dead. To prove this he observes, from Ussher (p. 316), that the Greek Menaea and Symeon Metaphrastes do not acknowledge that Onesimus the martyr was bishop of Ephesus; that the author of the Apostolic Constitutions affirms he was bishop of Berea; that Dorotheus and Hippolytus assert that Gaius was the successor of Timothy in the see of Ephesus; and finally that Nicephorus relates that Onesimus died under Domitian. The most learned author of the Vindiciae (p. 97) denies that it follows from this that some Onesimus, successor of Gaius, did not preside over Ephesus when Ignatius was led away to martyrdom. Indeed, the learned man thinks it possible that there were two Onesimi, one of whom died a martyr under Domitian, while the other succeeded Gaius as bishop of Ephesus and presided over the Church while Ignatius was being led bound to Rome. The Most Reverend Ussher solves this knot a little differently: he suspects, namely, that there were two Onesimi, each bishop of Ephesus, one the elder, the disciple of Paul, who suffered under Domitian, and the other the successor of Gaius, who survived Ignatius. Daillé meets this distinction thus (p. 316): But these views must not be admitted, since first the trustworthy testimony of Bede, Ado, Notker and others prohibits them, who all with one accord affirm that the Onesimus mentioned by Ignatius in his letter was a disciple of Paul. Pearson says that he does not find such unanimity, since only Ado mentions the Onesimus of Ignatius, in his little book on the feasts of the Apostles on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March. The others say that Onesimus, the slave of Philemon, was made bishop of the Church of Ephesus after Timothy by the blessed Paul, without any mention of Ignatius. Pearson further observes that Ado, who makes the Onesimus of Ignatius the Onesimus of St. Paul, does not relate that he died under Domitian. Nicephorus, the learned man says, is a recent writer, and because he alone reports that Onesimus suffered martyrdom at that time, Baronius rightly says that his authority may be refused, especially if he is understood to speak of the bishop of Ephesus. For if that bishop (he says, p. 97) was bishop of Berea and not of Ephesus, as other writers older than Nicephorus record, it does not concern us. For who does not see that Onesimus, bishop of Berea and disciple of St. Paul, could have died in the times of Domitian, and that another Onesimus could have presided over Ephesus after Timothy and Gaius under the reign of Trajan? If you consider the matter in itself, what the learned man says could have happened; but if you consider tradition, by no means. For Bede, Usuardus, Notker and Ado testify that Onesimus was ordained bishop of Paul's Church at Ephesus; indeed Ado plainly states that he is the same as the Ignatian Onesimus. Perhaps from this arose the suspicion of the most illustrious Ussher, who, if we listen to Daillé, suspected that there were two Onesimi, each bishop of Ephesus. Daillé, most distinguished, interpreted Ussher's meaning in this way, although the words used by the Most Reverend Ussher may perhaps bear another explanation (Notes on the Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, p. 5).

units.la: Quidquid sit Vir doctus primæ diffidens solutioni, alteram profert, ut ostendat Onesimum Philemonis servum & Ephesi Episcopum sub Domitiano martyrium non subiisse, sic autem ratiocinatur, Onesimus vel Gaio vel Timotheo successit (expungatur Gaius, nam post Timotheum sedisse tradunt, qui de illius Episcopatu Ephesino loquuntur) Timotheus primus Ephesinæ Ecclesiæ Episcopus, sub Vespasiano martyrio conatus fuit, ut tradit Nicephorus, testatúrque ejusdem Martyrium in Bibliotheca Photij Cod. CCLIV. Persecutio secunda sub Domitiano extremis illius Imperatoris temporibus excitata est. Sub hac persecutione obdormivisse Timotheum credendum est, brevis autem ea fuit. Iam quis credet Onesimum, qui si forte in Ephesinâ Ecclesiâ Timotheo, Episcopus suffectus est, sub eadem persecutione passum fuisse, & non potiùs ad undecimum Trajani annum perdurasse? Hactenus Eruditissimus Pearsonius. Ego vero illi concedendo Timotheum primum fuisse Ephesinæ Ecclesiæ Episcopum, quamvis proprie Episcopus nusquam fuerit, sed Evangelista & veluti secundus Apostolus, nulli privatæ Ecclesiæ alligatus. Ego inquam aliter ratiocinabor, Timotheus ut tradit Nicephorus, cui succinit ejusdem Martyrium apud Photium, sub Vespasiano martyrio coronatus fuit (ita Vir doctus pag. 98.) Ergo sub Domitiani persecutione eum obdormivisse non credendum est, cùm sub Vespasiano obiisse tradant testes à Viro docto laudati; si igitur Onesimus Timotheo successit sub Vespasiano, creditu facilimum est, eum sub Domitiani persecutione passum fuisse.Pergit Vindiciarum Auctor ut probet Dallæum ex ordine temporum evincere frustra conatū esse, Onesimum C. aut XC.annorum futurum fuisse, si ad annum Domini CIX. aut CXI. perdurassẹt, quam Martyris ætatem, aiebat Dallæus, æquè ac aliorum similium observaturi erant Scriptores, si eâ verè passus esset. Dallæi argumentum hoc nitebatur fundamento, Onesimum videlicet ævi maturum fuisse dùm Paulus ad Philomenem scripsit, id est anno Domini LVI. ut putant Eruditi. Pearsonius ut probet frustraneos esse Dallæi conatus, negat Epistolam ad Philemonem scriptam esse anno Domini LVI. quia Româ scripta est, dum in Vinculis erat Paulus, esto, nec hoc nos dissitemur, at, inquit, Romam ante A. D. vulgarem LXIV. vidisse S. Paulum nemo probabit. Cur id affirmet Vir doctus divinare non possum; Annon liquet ex Actis Apostolorum [?]cap.
units.tr: Whatever the case, the learned man, distrusting his first solution, offers another, to show that Onesimus, the slave of Philemon and bishop of Ephesus, did not suffer martyrdom under Domitian. He reasons thus: Onesimus succeeded either Gaius or Timothy (strike out Gaius, for those who speak of his episcopate at Ephesus say that he sat after Timothy). Timothy, the first bishop of the Church of Ephesus, was martyred under Vespasian, as Nicephorus relates, and the martyrdom of the same man is attested in Photius's Bibliotheca, codex 254. A second persecution was stirred up under Domitian in the last years of that emperor. Timothy must be believed to have fallen asleep during this persecution, but it was a short one. Now who will believe that Onesimus, if he was perhaps appointed bishop in the Church of Ephesus in place of Timothy, suffered under this same persecution, and did not rather endure to the eleventh year of Trajan? Thus far the most learned Pearson. But I, granting to him that Timothy was the first bishop of the Church of Ephesus, although strictly speaking he was never a bishop, but an evangelist and as it were a second apostle, bound to no single local church, I, I say, will reason otherwise. Timothy, as Nicephorus relates, and Photius's account of his martyrdom agrees with him, was crowned with martyrdom under Vespasian (so the learned man, p. 98). Therefore it is not to be believed that he fell asleep during the persecution of Domitian, since the witnesses cited by the learned man report that he died under Vespasian. If, then, Onesimus succeeded Timothy under Vespasian, it is very easy to believe that he suffered in the persecution of Domitian. The author of the Vindiciae goes on to prove that Daillé tried in vain to show, from the order of the times, that Onesimus would have been ninety or a hundred years old had he lived until the year of the Lord 109 or 111, which age, Daillé said, the writers would have noted, as they do for other similar cases, if he had really suffered at that age. Daillé's argument rested on this foundation: that Onesimus was of mature age when Paul wrote to Philemon, that is, in the year of the Lord 56, as the learned think. Pearson, to prove that Daillé's attempts are futile, denies that the Epistle to Philemon was written in the year of the Lord 56, because it was written at Rome while Paul was in chains. Granted, we do not deny this either, but, he says, no one will prove that St. Paul had been seen at Rome before the common year of the Lord 64. Why the learned man affirms this I cannot divine. Is it not clear from the Acts of the Apostles, in chapter

units.la: XXIV. XXV. XXVI. XXVII. Felicem in Iudæâ Præfecturâ accepisse Portium Festum successorem ; Festum verò Paulum mox , paulò postquam venerat in Provinciam, misisse captivum Romam ad Cæsarem ; quem Paulus appelleverat, Felici autem successor datus est Festus anno secundo Neronis juxta supputationem Eusebij in Chronico , qui quidem annus; incidit in annum Domini LVII. ineuntem ; Ergo initio illius anni Paulus Romam Vinctus missus est , ibíque biennium egit in propriâ æde conductâ , & tunc Epistolam ad Philemonem scripsit, primo ut videtur illius biennij anno, adhuc enim Vinctus erat, cùm exacto biennio Vinculis sit solutus ; Romam ergo idit Paulus ante A. D. vulgarem LXIV. quod negabat doctissimus Pearsonius.
units.tr: XXIV, XXV, XXVI, XXVII. Felix was succeeded in the province of Judaea by Porcius Festus. Soon after Festus arrived in the province, he sent Paul to Rome as a prisoner to Caesar, since Paul had appealed to him. According to Eusebius's reckoning in the Chronicle, Festus succeeded Felix in the second year of Nero, and that year falls in the beginning of the year of the Lord 57. So at the start of that year Paul was sent to Rome in chains, and there he spent two years in a house he had rented for himself. It was then that he wrote the Epistle to Philemon, probably in the first year of those two, since he was still in chains; at the end of the two years he was released from his bonds. Paul therefore went to Rome before the year 64 of the common era, which the most learned Pearson denied.

units.la: Verùm enimverò ut ad Onesimum redeat Oratio, admodùm suspecta videntur quæ de illius martyrio & Episcopatu Ephesino narrant ætatis mediæ Scriptores, sine alicujus vetustioris autoritate : Author quidem constitutionum Apostolicarum illius meminit Episcopatus, non Ephesini sed Beræensis , quâ in re ab alijs dissentit ; sed quam mereatur fidem planus ille, cujus ætas non minus incerta est, quàm Beræensis Onesimi Episcopatus, norunt Eruditi: Certè si genuina Veterum Scriptorum consulimus monumenta, nullam planè de Onesimi martyrio & Episcopatu mentionem fieri in illis reperiemus, in ijs præsertim locis in quibus ea commemorari oportebat, si ab illis cognita fuissent. Chrysostomus, Hilarius Diaconus, Pelagius, Hieronymus, Theodoretus, Primasius, Epistolam ad Philemonem in unius Onesimi gratiam scriptam, commentati sunt, eorum nullus tamen illius Martyrium aut Episcopatum memorat, etsi opportunissima esset memorandi occasio; Chrysostomo imprimis qui eos reprehendens qui hanc Epistolam superfluò adjectam dicebant, quandoquidem pro re adeò parva, pro Viro uno scilicet conscripta est, innumeris illos criminibus dignos pronuntiat, multis de causis quas in medium profert, quibus Viri Martyrium & Dignitatem Episcopalem adjungere non piguisset, si ei comperta fuissent, ut Epistolæ utilitatem ac præstantiam magis ac magis commendaret. Prætereà habemus vetustissimum Martyrologium, quod licet falsò nomen Hieronymi præferat, paulò post obitum ejus evulgatum est, ut putant Eruditi; in illo autem Martyrologio nulla prorsus mentio Onesimi, quamvis hotata sint multa Martyrum nomina ad eundem diem quo passum esse Onesimum arbitrantur, nempe XIV. Kalend. Mart. Non immerito igitur Dallæus turbari temporum seriem ab Ignatio Epistolico scripsit.
units.tr: But to return to Onesimus: the stories told by medieval writers about his martyrdom and his episcopate at Ephesus seem very doubtful, since no older authority supports them. The author of the Apostolic Constitutions does mention an episcopate of Onesimus, but not at Ephesus; he places it at Beroea, and in this he differs from the others. Yet learned men know how much trust deserves that anonymous writer, whose date is no less uncertain than the episcopate of Onesimus at Beroea. Certainly, if we consult the genuine monuments of the early writers, we find no mention at all of Onesimus's martyrdom or episcopate, especially in those passages where it ought to have been recorded, had they known of it. Chrysostom, Hilary the Deacon, Pelagius, Jerome, Theodoret and Primasius all wrote commentaries on the Epistle to Philemon, which they said was written for the sake of Onesimus alone. Yet none of them mentions his martyrdom or his episcopate, although the occasion for mentioning them was most suitable. Chrysostom above all, rebuking those who said that this Epistle was added superfluously, since it was written about so small a matter and for one man alone, declares that they deserve countless condemnations; he gives many reasons, and he would not have been reluctant to add the martyrdom and episcopal dignity of Onesimus to them, had he known of them, in order to commend the usefulness and excellence of the Epistle more and more. Moreover, we have a very old Martyrology which, although it falsely bears the name of Jerome, was published, as learned men think, shortly after his death. In that Martyrology there is no mention whatever of Onesimus, although many martyrs' names are listed for the day on which they think Onesimus suffered, namely the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March. Dallaeus was therefore not wrong to write that the order of the times was disturbed by the Epistle of Ignatius.

units.la: Dallæus cap. 17. p. 338. observat Epistolicum Ignatium Dominicæ carnis veritatem adversus Hæreticos confirmantem, verba quædam, veluti Christi, sic recitare Epist. ad Smyrn. Et quando ad eos qui circa Petrum, venit, ait ipsis: Apprehendite, palpate me, & videte, quoniam non sum dæmonium incorporeum. Sibi autem persuadere non potest clarissimus Dallæus, verum Ignatium Christi verba, ex impuris apocryphorum lacunis ficta, quàm vera ex certis ac divinitus inspiratis libris apud Smyrnæos promere maluisse: Quid ad hæc Vindiciarum Auctor?
