Plures insumit paginas ( pag. 101. 102. 103. 104. ) ut probet apocryphis uti licere, eáque aliquando laudare, quasi hoc negaret Dallæus, quem latere non poterat apocrypha à vetustissimis Ecclesiæ Scriptoribus citari, immò ab ipsis Iesu Christi Apostolis, ut à Iuda Prophetia Enoch; Sed aliud est apocrypha aliquando laudare, aliud verò apocryphorum verba disertis Christi verbis sufficere, quod facit Scriptor Epistolæ ad Smyrnæos ; si quam tangit historia in Evangelio nostro non extaret, minoris culpæ reus esset, & forte nulli reprehensioni obnoxius, sive eam descripserit ex Evangelio Hebraico, quo utebantur Nazareni, ut opinantur plures Viri Eruditi, sive eam hauserit ex traditione non scripta, ut post Casaubonum arbitratur Pearsonius ; Sed quoniam eadem extat Historia in Evangelio nostro, gravius atque luculentius exposita, credibile non est Apostolorum discipulum, veritatis fontes fastidiendo, & ipsissima Christi verba quodammodo contemnendo, alia illorum loco usurpare voluisse, præsertim cum quæ ad id locorum in libris nostris habentur, non minus essent ad carnis Dominicæ veritatem confirmandam, apposita, quàm illud ab Epistolico Ignatio allatum: Quis, quæso sanæ mentis homo præstantiora non putet ; & ad demonstrandam carnis Dominicæ veritatem validiora, hæc Evangelica, Spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, sicut me videtis habere, & ea quæ de Thoma ejusdem argumenti scripta sunt, quàm plebeia illa & auribus Christianis insueta, non sum daemonium incorporeum. Tamen Vir alius Eruditus qui nullam Dallæi perstringendi elabi finit occasionem, Dallæano argumento se satisfecisse putat notis suis in Epist. ad Smyrn. pag. 460. hisce verbis, citationem Apocryphorum non caussabitur contra Ignatium, quicunque meminerit a Clemente idem committi in Epistolâ ad Corinthios teste etiam Photio. Vim argumenti Dallæi dissimulat, citationem Apocryphorum contra Ignatium minimè caussatur Dallæus, Apocryphorum tantum verba in locum Christi verborum substitutionem damnat, utpote à reverentiâ divinis libris debitâ alienam. Ex stellæ descriptione quæ Magis præivit argumentatus est Dallæus pag. 365. extat illa descriptio in Epistolâ ad Ephesios; Ut illam tueatur descriptionem Pearsonius, plura adfert Veterum testimonia pag. 126. 127. qui de Stellâ Magis prælucente magnificè locuti sunt; Verum quæ adducit Pearsonius ex Veteribus nequaquam paria sunt cum Ignatianis, idem dico de Societatis Sorbonicæ Theologo accerrimo Dallæanorum Censore; Nullibi enim reperias illius stellæ descriptionem istius Ignatianæ parem. Stella in Cœlo fulsit, splendore superans omnes stellas, & lux illius ineffabilis erat, & stuporem incussit ipsius novitas. Omnia autem reliqua astra, unâ cum Sole & Lunâ chorus fuere stellæ illius, ipsa verò lumen suum extendebat super omnia vel supra omnia, &c. unde soluta est omnis Magia. Proferant Viri docti ex Veterum scriptis stellae Magis praeeuntis descriptiones Ignatianae prorsus similes, & istud Dallaei argumentum, caeteris contenti, deseremus, sed donec id praestiterint,non aegre ferent si illud non adeo parvi facimus. Aliud argumentum adversus Ignatiana deprompsit Dallaeus cap. XXII. pag. 366. &c. ex eo quod Epistolae ad Smyrnaeos Scriptor quosdam sui aevi Haereticos Eucharistiâ abstinuisse affirmat, quòd cùm à Veteribus qui haereseon contexuêre catalogos, non sit traditum, ab alio quàm ab Ignatio scriptam esse hanc Epistolam existimat Dallaeus. Doctor Sorbonicus in eandem Epistolam pag. 460. Dallaeum arguit quasi perperam acceperit vocem προσευχῆς[?] pro omni prorsus oratione, cùm Ignatius aut loquatur de prece mysticâ, aut potiùs intelligat preces Liturgicas. Verùm quando mentem suam non explicat Epistolae Scriptor, iniqua est Dalleanae observationis censura ; Etsi concedere non verear intelligi posse precem mysticam, id est Orationem Dominicam, quâ solâ fertur olim consecrâsse Apostolos. Secundò Dallaei responsionem temerariam vocat. Quotus quisque est, inquit, qui nihil novi & alibi indicti dicat; Dum de rebus facti agitur, juniores à senioribus accipere debent, & posteriores à prioribus, nihilque novi & alibi indicti dicere, quod secus fit, dum est quæstio juris; tunc enim fieri potest ut quisque aliquid novi & alibi indicti dicat. Hæc igitur Viri Eruditi observatio nihili plane est: Sed ne gratis & temerè Dallæi responsionem temerariam appellasse videatur, ita pergit. Debuit consulere Vir non indoctus Epiphanium, Tertullianum, Hieronymi Indiculum, Augustinum, Theodoritum, &c. Didiscisset rejectam fuisse à Phantasticis Hæreticis vetustissimis, Gnosticis & Ophitis, veram Eucharistiam, substitutâ in illius locum falsâ, infandâ nimirum turpitudine, consuetudine impiâ & βλασφήμῳ[?]. Consuluerat dubio procul hos Scriptores Dallæus, & quoniam nullos deprehenderat in eorum Scriptis Hæreticos qui Ignatij ætate Eucharistia abstinuerint, suppositititiam[?] credidit Epistolam ad Smyrnæos, in quâ Hæreticorum quorundam Eucharistiâ abstinentium fit mentio; Nec quicquam causæ est cur Gnosticos & Ophitas opponit Vir doctus, quasi Eucharistiâ abstinuerint; suam enim habuerunt Eucharistiam, execrandam illam quidem, sed tamen Eucharistiam infandis illorum mysterijs dignissimam; Iam autem non quæritur proprie qualis fuerit eorum Eucharistia, sed utrum illa penitus caruerint, de re agitur, non de rei modo seu qualitate: Præterea Gnostici illi & Ophitæ quos profert posteriores fuerunt Ignatio, ideóque Viri Eruditi causam minimè juvant; Quæ habet de Priscillianistis, Messalianis, Manichæis, Archonticis, nihil ad rem faciunt. Meliora sunt quæ sequuntur, non omnes videlicet Docetas Eucharistiam repudiasse, quod est verissimum. Sed inquit Vir doctus, Dallæus innuit Simonianos non effe Christiani nominis Hæreticos, hæc ambiguè dicuntur, nam si intelligit Dallæum innuere Simonem Hæresim suam ante Christi adventum disseminasse, neque ad illas pertinere hæreses quæ post illius in cœlum ascensionem exortæ sunt, fallitur; At si hoc tantùm vult; Dallæum significare Simonianos Christum nequaquam pro Auctore suo professos esse, verum dicit; id enim disertis verbis tradit, illius igitur erat hanc Dallæi observatio-nem, si sibi non arridebat, refellere, & tunc nostrum fuisset illam refutationem expendere: Ultra progreditur Vir Clarissimus, & Dallæum iterùm arguit, quod Simonem & Simonianos brevi ipsis Claudij, quibus exorti erant temporibus, defecisse scribit. Verùm Dallæus de suo id non scribit, Eusebium habet testem, cujus ipsissima profert verba pag. 367.
units.tr: Dallaeus, chapter 17, page 338, observes that the Epistle of Ignatius, which defends the truth of the Lord's flesh against the heretics, relates certain words of Christ as follows, in the Epistle to the Smyrnaeans: And when he came to those who were about Peter, he said to them: Take hold of me, touch me, and see that I am not an incorporeal demon. The most illustrious Dallaeus cannot persuade himself that Ignatius preferred to bring forth the words of Christ, invented from the impure pools of the apocryphal books, rather than the true words from the certain and divinely inspired books that the Smyrnaeans possessed. What does the author of the Vindiciae reply to this? He spends many pages (101, 102, 103, 104) to prove that it is lawful to use the apocryphal books and sometimes to praise them, as if Dallaeus denied this, though he could not be unaware that the apocryphal books were cited by the most ancient writers of the Church, and indeed by the Apostles of Jesus Christ themselves, as Jude cites the prophecy of Enoch. But it is one thing to praise the apocryphal books at times, and another to let the words of the apocryphal books stand in place of the plain words of Christ, which the writer of the Epistle to the Smyrnaeans does. If the story he touches upon did not exist in our Gospel, he would be guilty of a lesser fault, and perhaps liable to no reproach at all, whether he drew it from the Hebrew Gospel used by the Nazarenes, as many learned men suppose, or drew it from unwritten tradition, as Pearson thinks after Casaubon. But since the same story exists in our Gospel, set out more weightily and more clearly, it is not credible that a disciple of the Apostles, scorning the fountains of truth and in a way despising the very words of Christ, would have wished to use other words in their place, especially when the passages in our books on this matter were no less suited to confirming the truth of the Lord's flesh than what Ignatius cites. Who, I ask, of sound mind would not think these Gospel words more excellent, and more forceful for demonstrating the truth of the Lord's flesh: A spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me having, and what is written about Thomas on the same point? Compare them with that plebeian phrase, unfamiliar to Christian ears, I am not an incorporeal demon. Yet another learned man, who lets no opportunity of attacking Dallaeus escape him, thinks he has answered Dallaeus's argument in his notes on the Epistle to the Smyrnaeans, page 460, in these words: "No one who remembers that Clement committed the same fault in his Epistle to the Corinthians, as Photius also testifies, will accuse Ignatius of citing the Apocrypha." He disguises the force of Dallaeus's argument. Dallaeus does not accuse Ignatius merely of citing the Apocrypha; he condemns only the substitution of the words of the Apocrypha for the words of Christ, as foreign to the reverence owed to the divine books. From the description of the star which went before the Magi, Dallaeus argued on page 365. That description is found in the Epistle to the Ephesians. To defend this description, Pearson adduces many testimonies of the ancients on page 126 and 127, who spoke magnificently of the star shining before the Magi. But the passages Pearson adduces from the ancients are by no means like the Ignatian one. I say the same of the most keen censor of the Dallaeans, the theologian of the Sorbonne. For nowhere will you find a description of that star like this Ignatian one: A star shone in heaven, surpassing all the stars in its brightness, and its light was ineffable, and its novelty struck wonder. And all the other stars, together with the sun and moon, formed a choir around that star; but it itself extended its light over all things, or above all things, etc., whence all magic was dissolved. Let learned men produce from the writings of the ancients descriptions of the star going before the Magi that are wholly like the Ignatian ones. We shall abandon this argument of Dallaeus, content with the rest; but until they do so, they should not take it amiss if we do not think it of very little weight. Dallaeus drew another argument against the Ignatian writings, chapter 22, page 366 and following, from the fact that the writer of the Epistle to the Smyrnaeans affirms that certain heretics of his time abstained from the Eucharist. Since the ancient writers who compiled catalogues of heresies have not handed this down, Dallaeus thinks that this Epistle was written by someone other than Ignatius. The Sorbonne doctor, on the same Epistle, page 460, accuses Dallaeus of having wrongly taken the word προσευχῆς [prosevchēs] to mean every kind of prayer, whereas Ignatius either speaks of mystical prayer or rather means liturgical prayers. But since the writer does not explain his meaning, the censure of Dallaeus's observation is unfair. Yet I would not hesitate to concede that mystical prayer may be understood, that is, the Lord's Prayer, by which alone the Apostles are said to have once consecrated. Secondly, he calls Dallaeus's answer rash. "How few are there," he says, "who do not say something new and not stated elsewhere?" When matters of fact are in question, the younger should learn from the older and the later from the earlier, and should say nothing new and unstated elsewhere; but it is otherwise when a question of right is at issue, for then anyone may say something new and unstated elsewhere. This observation of the learned man is therefore altogether worthless. But lest it seem that he rashly called Dallaeus's answer rash without cause, he goes on: "This man, not unlearned, ought to have consulted Epiphanius, Tertullian, Jerome's Index, Augustine, Theodoret," etc. "He would have learned that the true Eucharist was rejected by the most ancient phantastic heretics, the Gnostics and the Ophites, and in its place was substituted a false one, of unspeakable filth, an impious and blasphemous [βλασφήμῳ] custom." Dallaeus had doubtless consulted these writers, and since he found in their writings no heretics in Ignatius's time who abstained from the Eucharist, he believed that the Epistle to the Smyrnaeans, which mentions certain heretics abstaining from the Eucharist, was spurious. Nor is there any reason why the learned man should set the Gnostics and Ophites against him, as if they had abstained from the Eucharist. For they had their own Eucharist, detestable indeed, but still a Eucharist, most worthy of their unspeakable mysteries. Now the question is not properly what kind of Eucharist they had, but whether they lacked it altogether; the matter concerns the thing itself, not merely its kind or quality. Besides, those Gnostics and Ophites whom he cites were later than Ignatius, so the learned man does not help his cause at all. What he says about the Priscillianists, Messalians, Manichaeans and Archontics has nothing to do with the matter. Better are the points that follow: namely, that not all the Docetists rejected the Eucharist, which is most true. But the learned man says that Dallaeus hints that the Simonians were not heretics of the Christian name. These words are ambiguous. If he understands that Dallaeus hints that Simon spread his heresy before Christ's coming, and that these were not the heresies that arose after Christ's ascension into heaven, he is mistaken. But if he means only that Dallaeus signifies that the Simonians did not profess Christ as their author, he speaks the truth; for Dallaeus says this in plain words. It was therefore for him, if this observation of Dallaeus did not please him, to refute it, and then it would have been our task to weigh that refutation. The most illustrious author of the Vindiciae goes further and again accuses Dallaeus of writing that Simon and the Simonians fell away shortly after the times of Claudius, in which they had arisen. But Dallaeus does not write this on his own authority; he has Eusebius as witness, whose very words he quotes on page 367.

units.la: Doctissimus Vindiciarum Autor huic Dallæi argumento occurrens cap. XI. p.131. 132. 133. fatetur neminem præter Ignatium de istius temporis Hæreticis diserte affirmasse, quod Eucharistiâ abstinuerint; Hæc ingenua Viri docti confessio, illius causæ non parum nocet; Verisimile enim non est Hæreticorum istorum notitiam fugisse Irenæum, Tertullianum, & cæteros qui amplissimos & accuratissimos Hæreticorum contexuêre Catalogos; Siccine officii sui tam negligentes fuêre Veteres illi Scriptores ut rem adeò memorabilem, & quam scire intererat, silentio præterierint, cùm tot alias res multò minoris momenti litteris tradere non sint dedignati? Profectò vix est credibile; Verùm enimverò ne solo Epistolici[?] Ignatij testimonio nitatur de istis Hæreticis traditio; scribit Vir doctus Polycarpum eosdem Hæreticos ferire, fundamentum hujus abstinentiæ indicare, & reliqua cum Ignatio perstringere. Tamen Polycarpi verba quæ adseri si inspicias, reperies nullam prorsùs Hæreticorum fieri mentionem, nihilque plane dici de Eucharistiâ, nec de illius abstinentiâ. Quæ sequuntur apud Virum Eruditissimum non sunt melioris commatis: Nam etsi concedamus ex Menandri Scholâ prodijsse qui asserebant, non esse credendum in eum qui crucifixus est, non propterea sequitur eos Eucharistiam reprobasse eáque abstinuisse, nec jam quæritur, num Eucharistiâ abstinere debuerint, quandoquidem Christum mortuum non putabant; sed utrum reapse abstinuerint, quod Veterum nemo tradidit præter Epistolicum Ignatium. Nonne multos quotidie cernimus res tametsi inter se pugnantes, unà tamen tueri ac defendere ? Nonne ipse Marcion Christum verè mortuum esse negabat, Eucharistiam tamen non repudiabat ? Nec Virum doctum juvat dicere Marcionem Sacramenta propria habuisse : Ignatium autem de Ecclesiæ Sacramento sine dubio intelligendum esse, à quo & Marcion abstinuit. Quoniam ad rem quam tractamus confirmandam abundè sufficit Marcionem Eucharistiam celebrâsse ; utrum autem eadem fuerit cum Catholicorum Eucharistiâ, aut diversa non refert ? Author siquidem Epistolæ ad Smyrnæos à quâ abstinuerint Hæretici quorum meminit Eucharistiâ, non dicit, eos Sacramento illo abstinuisse nudè ac simpliciter tradit. Cæterùm ostendebamus mox Dallæum ab Eusebio accepisse quæ de Simonianis habet, nec hoc diffiteri possunt Viri docti; quamvis Eusebii verba de primis tantum Simonis discipulis ac cultoribus intelligenda putem, non autem de omnibus qui ex ejus Schola prodierunt, & qui diu post ejus mortem perdurârunt. De Interpolatoris autem verbis & consilio non est quod anxiè solliciti simus; coniecturis hac in re agit Dallæus, coniecturis etiam agunt illius adversarij: Ex coniecturis autem quibus plus æquo forsan indulgent, nihil certi elici potest.
units.tr: The most learned author of the Vindiciae, meeting this argument of Daillé in chapter 11 (pp. 131–133), concedes that no one except Ignatius clearly stated that the heretics of that time abstained from the Eucharist. This candid admission does the learned man's cause no small harm. For it is unlikely that Irenaeus, Tertullian and the others who compiled full and careful catalogues of heretics were unaware of these people. Were those ancient writers so negligent of their duty that they passed over in silence a matter so noteworthy and so important to know, when they did not disdain to record many other things of far lesser importance? Surely this is hardly credible. But lest the tradition about these heretics rest on the testimony of the Ignatius of the Epistles alone, the learned man writes that Polycarp too attacks the same heretics, indicates the basis of this abstention, and touches on the rest together with Ignatius. Yet if you look at the words of Polycarp that he cites, you will find no mention of heretics at all, and nothing said about the Eucharist or about abstaining from it. What the learned man adds next is no better. For even if we grant that those who asserted that one should not believe in him who was crucified came from the school of Menander, it does not follow that they rejected the Eucharist and abstained from it. Nor is the question now whether they ought to have abstained from the Eucharist, since they did not think Christ had died, but whether they in fact abstained, which none of the ancients reported except the Ignatius of the Epistles. Do we not every day see many people defend and uphold together things that clash with one another? Did not Marcion himself deny that Christ had truly died, and yet not reject the Eucharist? Nor does the learned man help his case by saying that Marcion had his own sacraments, and that Ignatius must undoubtedly be understood of the sacrament of the Church, from which Marcion too abstained. For to confirm the point we are discussing, it is quite enough that Marcion celebrated the Eucharist; whether it was the same as the Catholics' Eucharist or a different one makes no difference. The author of the Epistle to the Smyrnaeans does not say that the heretics he mentions abstained from the Eucharist; he simply records that they abstained from that sacrament, without qualification. But I have just shown that Daillé took from Eusebius what he says about the Simonians, and the learned men cannot deny this; although I think Eusebius' words are to be understood only of Simon's first disciples and followers, and not of all who came out of his school and who lasted long after his death. As for the words and purpose of the Interpolator, we need not be anxiously concerned. Daillé argues by conjecture in this matter, and his opponents also argue by conjecture. But from conjectures, which they perhaps indulge more than is fair, nothing certain can be drawn.

units.la: Cap. XXIV. Dallæus scribit plura occurrere in Ignatianis Epistolis, non satis ut videtur cum Martyris modestiâ, quam summam fuisse perhibent, consentanea; Exemplum profert ex Epistolâ ad Trallianos in quâ supercœlestium scientiam sibi vindicat; Multa, inquit, sapio in Deo: sed meipsum mensuro, ut non in gloriatione perdar. Tum paulò post; Nonne possum vobis supercœlestia scribere? Sed timeo ne parvulis existentibus vobis damnum apponam. Et condonate mihi: ne forte non potentes capere, strangulemini. Etenim ego, non secundum quodcunque ligatus sum, sed potens scire cœlestia, & loci positiones Angelorum, & constitutiones, principiationes, visibiliaque & invisibilia: præter hoc jam & discipulus sum. Doctissimus Pearsonius huic obiectioni plura reponit ut Ignatij sui modestiam sartam tectam tueatur ; Quædam etiam regerit Societatis Sorbonicæ Theologus suprà nominatus, qui asserere non veretur pag. 452. non potuisse majori cum demissione loqui Martyrem de cognitione Cælestium sibi divinitus concessâ, quàm negando se esse discipulum, ac profitendo multa sibi deesse. Verùm vix cordatis persuasuri sunt Viri Eruditi, à modestiâ non discessisse Epistolicum Ignatium ; certè non modesti hominis est, sed vani & gloriosi, si quid habet excellens & eximium, id efferre apud alios, atque ostentare: Epistolæ autem ad Trallianos Scriptor ita de se loquitur, ut ea dicat quæ difficille sit cum modestiæ præsertim Christianæ, ingenio ac moribus conciliare. Et ut liquidò constet rem ita se habere ut dicimus, comparandi sunt inter se D. Paulus & Ignatius Epistolicus: Apostolus quidem adversariorum & æmulorum suorum iniquitate coactus, quò Apostolatus sui gloriam defenderet, suámque apud Corinthios existimationem tueretur, de suis revelationibus aliquid, sed obscurè ac veluti non de se, sed de alio quodam loquens, innuit potiùs, quàm significat: Ignatius verò nulla justa & necessaria causa compulsus de cælestium cognitione gloriatur, & ad suæ illius singularis, planéque angelicæ de Angelis & invisibilibus, scientiæ arcana & mysteria ante Trallianorum oculos jactanda intempestivè festinat. Prætereà B. Paulus non semel hujus suæ ut appellat insipientiæ, veniam poscit ac deprecatur: Epistolico Ignatio alia planè mens, quia scilicet alio agebatur spiritu ; Quod de vero Ignatio ne suspicari quidem debemus, cùm enim Apostolorum auditor.fuerit ac discipulus, maximam eorum modestiam illum semper imitatum esse; nec ab illius legibus tantillum deflectere voluisse sanctissimum Martyrem, par est credere, contra quam fecit Author Epistolæ ad Trallianos. Ex ijs autem quæ scripsit Polycarpo idem Epistolicus Ignatius, & adfert Dallæus ubi supra, non æquè facilè forsan colligi potest modestiæ ac verecundiæ leges eum violasse, etsi eas quodammodo prætergressum esse videatur, quicquid dicat Eruditissimus Pearsonius, primò in eo quod Martyris nomen assumit, præter usum ac consuetudinem quæ in Ecclesiâ suâ ætate obtinebat, ut liquet ex Lugdunensium nostrorum exemplo à Dallæo allato, & à Vindiciarum Auctore in responsione prætermisso, non secus ac Martyris nomenclaturâ quam etiam inta[?]tam reliquit pag.142. nec mirum, cùm Martyrem nunquam se appellasse Ignatium affirmet pag.146. ita tamen se appellat in Epistolæ ad Polycarpum inscriptione Græcâ quæ interpolata non est. Secundò quia Polycarpo suo condiscipulo, & admirabili Smyrnensis Ecclesiæ Episcopo, tanquam Tyroni Magister scribit. Et frustrà est Vir doctus dum dicit, monet eum ut juniorem senior, ut charum amicus, ut liberum vinctus, ut Episcopum Confessor, &c. Nam præterquam quòd incertum est num Polycarpo longè senior fuerit Ignatius, verisimile insuper est verum Ignatium cum eo honorificentius acturum esse, nempe ut fratrem cum fratre, & Episcopum cum Episcopo, sed tanti nominis Episcopo cui Ecclesiam suam Antiochenam Pastore viduatam commendatam voluit.
units.tr: Chapter 24. Daillé writes that many things occur in the Ignatian Epistles which, as it seems, do not agree well with the modesty of the martyr, which was said to be very great. He gives an example from the Epistle to the Trallians, in which the writer claims for himself knowledge of things above heaven: I have much wisdom in God, but I measure myself, so that I may not be lost in boasting. And a little later: Can I not write to you of heavenly things? But I fear that, since you are still infants, I may do you harm. Pardon me, lest perhaps, being unable to grasp them, you be choked. For I am not bound by any ordinary rule, but am able to know heavenly things, and the positions of the angels, and their orders and principalities, both visible and invisible. Besides this, I am also already a disciple. The most learned Pearson replies to this objection at length, in order to keep the modesty of his Ignatius intact. The theologian of the Sorbonne mentioned above also offers some replies, and does not hesitate to assert (p. 452) that the martyr could not have spoken of the knowledge of heavenly things granted him by God with greater humility than by denying that he is a disciple and professing that many things are lacking to him. But learned men will hardly be persuaded that the Ignatius of the Epistles did not depart from modesty. Certainly it is not the mark of a modest man, but of a vain and boastful one, if he has something excellent and remarkable, to vaunt it before others and show it off. The writer of the Epistle to the Trallians speaks of himself in a way that is hard to reconcile with modesty, especially with Christian modesty, in disposition and conduct. To make it quite clear that the matter stands as we say, St Paul and the Ignatius of the Epistles must be compared with each other. The Apostle, compelled by the injustice of his adversaries and rivals, so as to defend the glory of his apostleship and maintain his standing among the Corinthians, does refer to his revelations, but obscurely, speaking as though not of himself but of some other man; he hints rather than states. Ignatius, however, compelled by no just and necessary cause, boasts of his knowledge of heavenly things, and hastens unseasonably to display before the eyes of the Trallians the secrets and mysteries of his singular and almost angelic knowledge of angels and invisible things. Moreover, St Paul more than once asks pardon for, and disowns, what he calls his folly; the Ignatius of the Epistles has an entirely different attitude, since clearly he was driven by another spirit. We ought not even to suspect this of the true Ignatius. For since he was a hearer and disciple of the Apostles, it is right to believe that he always imitated their great modesty, and that the most holy martyr was unwilling to deviate even slightly from their rules; contrary to what the author of the Epistle to the Trallians did. From what the same Ignatius wrote to Polycarp, which Daillé also cites above, it may perhaps not be so easy to conclude that he violated the rules of modesty and humility, although it seems he went beyond them in some way, whatever the most learned Pearson says. First, in that he assumes the name of martyr, contrary to the usage and custom that prevailed in his Church at that time, as is clear from the example of our Lyons church cited by Daillé and passed over by the author of the Vindiciae in his reply; no less so in his use of the title of martyr, which he also retains (p. 142). And this is no wonder, since he is said never to have called himself a martyr (p. 146), yet in the Greek inscription of the Epistle to Polycarp, which is not interpolated, he so names himself. Second, because he writes to Polycarp, his fellow disciple and the admirable bishop of the Smyrnaean Church, as a master to a novice. And the learned man is wrong when he says that the elder admonishes the younger as a dear friend, the free man admonishes the bound, the confessor admonishes the bishop, and so on. For, apart from the fact that it is uncertain whether Ignatius was far older than Polycarp, it is also likely that the true Ignatius would have behaved towards him with more honour, namely as brother with brother and bishop with bishop, and especially towards a bishop of such standing, to whom he wished his own Church of Antioch, widowed of its pastor, to be committed.

units.la: A rebus ipsis, quæ Epistolas Ignatio Martyri aliena manu subditas fuisse arguunt; transit Dallæus ad orationem & verba ex quibus contexta est oratio; & postquàm observavit orationem ipsam multiplicem, neque unius generis aut coloris, ostendere Epistolas non esse unius ejusdémque Auctoris, sexque primas, quas Vsserius ex Veteribus Anglicanis libris protulit, tristes esse, salebrosas, rudes & incultas, scribit cap. XXV. pag. 378. primum illud in his occurrere, quod in omnibus duodecim Epistolis Ignatij nomini adjectum legitur Theophori cognomentum, illiúsque cognomenti fabulosam aperit originem pag. 379. Vindiciarum Auctor totum fere caput duodecimum insumit in explicatione vocis Theophori, pluráque dicit quæ reconditam sapiunt eruditionem, lectionémque multijugam; Vir alius Eruditus cujus aliquoties mentionem fecimus, aliquid etiam de usu ac significatione hujus vocis adnotat in Epist. ad Ephes. pag. 447. sed quæ dicunt Viri docti Dallæum non feriunt, neque Dallæani argumenti vim elevant; Quare gratis se fatigavit Eruditissimus Pearsonius in coacervandis Veterum testimonijs, quibus probaret vocem hanc Θεοφόρος[?] antiquis Ecclesiæ Scriptoribus esse maximè familiarem: Quasi vocis istius usum simpliciter negaret Dallæus: Hoc solùm affirmat Dallæus neminem præter Epistolicum Ignatium se Theophorum identidem indigetasse, neque hoc Epitheton tanquam cognomen sibi arrogasse; Unde illi oritur nova adversus Epistolas Ignatianas suppositionis nota. Multis Veterum testimonijs istiùs vocis usum ac familiaritatem demonstravit Pearsonius; nullum tamen exemplum adferre potuit Sancti alicujus qui instar Ignatij Theophori cognomen sibi tribuerit. Nec quicquam causæ est cur fictitiæ quidem & fabulosæ iftiius nominis notioni, prout à Græcis posterioribus traditur, Acta Ignatiana ab Vsserio edita opponat; cùm enim à nemine Veterum, ac ne recentiorum quidem, laudata sint nec memorata, nullam prorsùs fidem merentur; frustrà igitur Vir doctus ex illis probare nititur Ignatium Theophorum appellatum à nostris ideò fuisse, quod Deum fide & sanctimoniâ in corde habitantem portasset; Nam certò certiùs est Ignatium, quandiu vixit Theophori cognomentum non habuisse, & quo tempore id cognomen diu post mortem habere cœpit, non ob aliam rationem Theophorus appellatus est, quam quod hunc Domini Christi manibus puerum olim susceptum fuisse crederent, prout à præstantissimo Dallæo est demonstratum.
units.tr: From the facts themselves, which show that the Epistles were attached to the martyr Ignatius by another hand, Daillé passes on to the style and the words of which the style is made up. After observing that the style itself is manifold, neither of one kind nor of one colour, and that the Epistles are not by one and the same author, and that the first six, which Ussher brought forward from the old English books, are dry, rough, uncouth and unpolished, he writes in chapter 25 (p. 378) that the first thing to occur in these is that the epithet Theophorus is added to the name of Ignatius in all twelve Epistles, and he reveals the fabulous origin of this epithet (p. 379). The author of the Vindiciae spends almost all of chapter 12 explaining the word Theophorus, and says many things that taste of recondite learning and wide reading. Another learned man, whom we have mentioned several times, also notes something about the use and meaning of this word in the Epistle to the Ephesians (p. 447). But what the learned men say does not touch Daillé, nor does it weaken the force of Daillé's argument. So the most learned Pearson wore himself out for nothing in piling up testimonies of the ancients, to prove that this word [Θεοφόρος] was very familiar to the early Church writers. It is as if Daillé simply denied that the word was used at all! Daillé affirms only this: no one except the Ignatius of the Epistles repeatedly called himself Theophorus, nor did anyone claim this epithet for himself as a surname. From this arises a new mark of suspicion against the Ignatian Epistles. Pearson has shown the use and familiarity of this word by many testimonies of the ancients; yet he could bring forward no example of any saint who, like Ignatius, attributed to himself the surname Theophorus. Nor is there any reason why the Ignatian Acts published by Ussher should be set against the notion of this name as fictitious and fabulous, as Greek writers of later times hand it down. For since no one among the ancients, nor even among the more recent, has praised or mentioned them, they deserve no credit at all. So the learned man tries in vain to prove from them that Ignatius was called Theophorus by our people because he had carried God, who dwells in the heart through faith and holiness. For it is most certain that while Ignatius lived he did not have the surname Theophorus, and at the time when he began to have that surname, long after his death, he was called Theophorus for no other reason than that they believed he had once been taken up as a child in the arms of the Lord Christ himself, as has been demonstrated by the most distinguished Daillé.

units.la: Quod sequitur argumentum apud Dallæum, multò majoris est momenti, ideóque palmarium vocat illúdque toto capite XXVI. latè persequitur: Vim autem argumenti ita proponit pag. 386. Epistololarum Scriptor Presbyteri & Episcopi nomina, non semel aut iterùm, sed perpetuò, & in omnibus ubique Epistolis, alitet[?] usurpat, quàm Apostoli & Apostolici Viri, eorúmque etiam discipuli. Hic enim duo illa nomina plané eodem sensu accipit, quo à tertij sæculi, & sequentium Christianis ad hæc usque tempora accepta fuisse & scimus, & libenter concedimus: sic nimirum, ut duas dignitates à se invicem distinctas significent: Episcopusque is intelligatur, qui Presbyter quidem ipse quoque est; sed & Presbyterio præest, & in eorum Collegio caput est; Presbyter verò is sit qui Episcopo subest. Unde necessario exsurgunt tres in Ecclesiâ ministrorum ordines; Episcopus, primus & summus: Presbyter, secundus & medius; Diaconus denique tertius & infimus: Argumentum duabus constat propositionibus, quarum prior usum ac consuetudinem spectat Epistolici Ignatij in Episcopi & Presbyteri nominibus usurpandis; posterior usum ac consuetudinem Apostolorum, & Apostolicorum Virorum, eorúmque etiam discipulorum planè diversam; Utrámque propositionem fusè pro-bat Dallæus, illam pag. 386. 387. 388. Hanc verò in sequentibus. Videamus jam quibus exceptionibus hoc Dallæi argumētum refellere nituntur Viri Eruditi: Inchoabo à Societatis Sorbonicæ Theologo, qui in Epistolam ad Magnesianos[?] pag. 448. argumentum istud quod Dallæo palmarium est, adeò contemnit ac despicit, ut ne quidem argumentum, illius judicio, dici mereatur, adeò infirmum est ac invalidum. Ita contemptim de hoc argumento loquitur Vir iste Eruditus, ut vel solo habitu illud difflatum iri non dubites: Nulla laus igitur erit, nullum operæ prætium, argumentum confutare, quod ne quidem argumentum dici meretur, adeò infirmum est ac invalidum. Illud tamen refellere non aggreditur, nisi rem salsissimam tanquam verissimam supponendo, Apostolico videlicet sæculo duos extitisse Sacerdotij gradus, superiorem & inferiorem, re diversos, quanquam nomine communi. Constat enim ex Scripturis sacris duos tantùm extitisse Apostolorum ætate sacrorum ministrorum ordines & gradus, alterum Episcoporum qui ijdem erant cum Presbyteris, Diaconorum alterum. Evolvat Scripturas Sacras Vir doctus, eásque diurnâ nocturnâque versset manu, nullum alium repertus est præter duos istos ministrorum sacrorum ordines, duorum autem Sacerdotij graduum, re diversorum, quanquam nomine communi, nullum prorsus in libris divinitùs inspiratis deprehensurus est vestigium: Nullum certè deprehenderunt ex Veterum Scriptorum numero plures, ne ipse quidem Urbanus II. Papa ex Cathedrâ loquens, cujus Decretum infra allaturi sumus, ex quo liquebit Pontificem illum, cujus autoritati se subjicere debet quivis Doctor Sorbonicus, credidisse duos tantùm extitisse in primitivâ Ecclesiâ sacros ordines, Diaconorum scilicet & Presbyterorum; Episcoporum non meminit, quia ijdem erant Presbyteri qui Episcopi: Subruto igitur pessimo Viri Eruditi fundamento, corruat necesse est tota ædificij moles. Ergo non tale est Dallæi argumentum, quale dicebat Societatis Sorbonicæ haud contemnendus Theologus, cùm illi refellendo sit impar, eíque hæreat aqua dùm illud refutare conatur.
units.tr: The next argument in Dallaeus is of much greater weight. He therefore calls it the chief argument and pursues it at length throughout chapter 26. He states its force as follows, on page 386: the writer of the Epistles uses the names Presbyter and Bishop not once or twice but constantly, and in all his Epistles everywhere, in a way that differs from the Apostles, the apostolic men, and their disciples as well. For he takes those two names in exactly the sense in which we know, and gladly concede, that Christians from the third century and later have understood them down to our own times: so that they signify two dignities distinct from one another. By Bishop is understood the one who is indeed himself also a presbyter, but who also presides over the presbytery and is the head of their college. A Presbyter, however, is one who is subordinate to the bishop. From this there necessarily arise three orders of ministers in the Church: the Bishop, the first and highest; the Presbyter, the second and middle; and finally the Deacon, the third and lowest. The argument consists of two premises. The first concerns the usage and custom of Ignatius' Epistles in employing the names Bishop and Presbyter. The second concerns the usage and custom of the Apostles, the apostolic men, and their disciples, which is quite different. Dallaeus proves each premise at length: the first on pages 386, 387 and 388, the second in what follows. Let us now see by what exceptions learned men try to refute this argument of Dallaeus. I shall begin with a theologian of the Sorbonne Society, who, on page 448 of his work on the Epistle to the Magnesians, so despises and scorns this argument, which he calls the chief one for Dallaeus, that in his judgement it does not even deserve to be called an argument, so weak and feeble is it. This learned man speaks so contemptuously of the argument that you would not doubt it would be blown away by that tone alone. "There will therefore be no credit, no profit in refuting an argument which does not even deserve to be called an argument, so weak and feeble is it." Yet he does not undertake to refute it, except by supposing as true a thing that is utterly false, namely that in the apostolic age there were two grades of priesthood, one higher and one lower, differing in reality though having a common name. For it is established from the holy Scriptures that in the age of the Apostles there were only two orders and grades of sacred ministers: one of Bishops, who were the same as Presbyters, and the other of Deacons. Let the learned man unroll the holy Scriptures and turn them over with his hand by day and by night: he will find no other order besides these two orders of sacred ministers, and he will find no trace whatever, in the divinely inspired books, of two grades of priesthood differing in reality though sharing a common name. Certainly none has been found by many of the ancient writers, not even Pope Urban II, speaking from the chair, whose decree we shall quote below. From it will be clear that this Pontiff, to whose authority any Sorbonne doctor ought to submit, believed that only two sacred orders existed in the primitive Church, those of Deacons and Presbyters. He makes no mention of Bishops, because the Presbyters were the same as the Bishops. Once the worst foundation of the learned man is overturned, the whole structure of the edifice must necessarily fall. So the argument of Dallaeus is not of the kind that the not-to-be-despised theologian of the Sorbonne Society said it was, since he is unequal to refuting it and sticks fast in the water while he tries to refute it.

units.la: Vindiciarum Auctor de Dallæi argumento non multò modestiùs loquitur, levissimum enim illi videtur, & præterea hoc laborare incommodo putat, quod omnis vis ejus à Dallæo in suarum partium ruinis posita est; Et ne gratis & sine causâ hæc à Viro docto dici arbitreris, hanc primò istiùs effati adfert rationem pag. 155. Dum Autorem Epistolarum (inquit) fecundo sæculo non scripsisse vult Dallæus, quòd eo toto aliter Christiani omnes loquuti sint, Salmasii & Albertini sententiam iam convellit, qui eum medio secundi saeculi tempore Epistolas edidisse docuerunt. Salmasij & Albertini sententia haec fuit, Epistolas de quibus lis est Ignatio à plano quodam subditas esse, idem plane sentit Dallaeus; Ergo Salmasij & Albertini opinionem non convellit, cum summa sit inter eos hac de re concordia; Salmasius quidem & Albertinus eas citius editas esse putarunt, Dallaeus vero serius: sed haec temporis differentia, ipsum rei fundum, ut ita dicam, non spectat, cujus respectu Dallaeo cum aliis optimè convenit; Adde quod Salmasius & Albertinus aliter quàm dicit Dallaeus secundi saeculi Christianos loquutos esse non asserunt, etsi maturiorem opinati sint Epistolarum Ignatianarum editionem; Et forte si superstites essent, re melius perpensa in Dallaei sententiam concederent. Secundò observat Vir doctus largiri Dallaeum Hammondo tres ordines seu gradus in Ecclesiâ extitisse, sub Apostolorum tempore, qui nomina Episcopi & Presbyteri promiscuè usurpasse dicuntur. Dum Dallaei locum à Vindiciarum Auctore designatum consulo, rem aliter se habere reperio; Dallaeus enim hoc non largitur Hammondo, velut illi persuasum fuisset tres in Ecclesiâ extitisse ordines seu gradus sub tempore Apostolorum, immò disertis verbis significat se de re ipsâ nunc non disputare, interea dilatâ in alium locum & in aliud tempus de numero Ecclesiasticorum ordinum disputatione, per concessionem agit cum Hammondo, ut scilicet ex nominum quibus Ordines sacri nuncupantur confasione adversus Ignatiana argumentari possit: Sed ipsum Dallæum audire satius erit. Nunc (inquit pag. 386.) de re ipsa non disputo. Donemus doctissimo Hammondo, quod ille tam vehementer cupit, hos tres ordines jam ipsis Apostolorum temporibus, ita ut diximus, in Ecclesiâ stetisse. Ordinum certè nomina, de quibus nunc solis disputo, nondum ipsis Apostolorum & Apostolicorum temporibus ita à se invicem distincta fuisse videntur, ut non aliquando, immò sæpissimè nomen Presbyteri, quod secundi ordinis ministros nunc significat, de iis diceretur, quos nunc volunt esse primi; & vicissim Episcopi, quod est primi ordinis nomen, de secundi ordinis ministris acciperetur, &c. Jam quivis videt Dallæi verba à Viro docto male accepta fuisse, & in sensum Auctoris menti plane contrarium detorta.
units.tr: The author of the Vindiciae speaks of Dallaeus' argument with no more modesty. He thinks it very slight, and he also holds that it labours under this disadvantage, that all its force rests on Dallaeus in the ruins of his own side. Lest you think these things are said by this learned man without reason or cause, I first cite the reason he gives for this statement, on page 155: "Since Dallaeus wants the author of the Epistles not to have written in the second century, because all Christians then spoke differently throughout that whole period, he now overturns the opinion of Salmasius and Albertinus, who taught that he published the Epistles about the middle of the second century." The opinion of Salmasius and Albertinus was that the Epistles which are disputed as Ignatius' were put out by some forger. Dallaeus holds exactly the same view. Therefore he does not overturn the opinion of Salmasius and Albertinus, since there is complete agreement between them on this matter. Salmasius and Albertinus thought the Epistles were published earlier, and Dallaeus later; but this difference of time does not touch the very ground of the matter, so to speak, and in respect of that Dallaeus agrees well enough with the others. Add that Salmasius and Albertinus do not assert that Christians of the second century spoke otherwise than Dallaeus says, although they thought the Ignatian Epistles were published at a later date. Perhaps, had they been still alive, they would on fuller consideration have agreed with Dallaeus' opinion. Second, the learned man observes that Dallaeus grants to Hammond that three orders or grades existed in the Church under the time of the Apostles, which are said to have used the names Bishop and Presbyter indiscriminately. When I consult the passage of Dallaeus that the author of the Vindiciae cites, I find the matter stands otherwise. Dallaeus does not grant this to Hammond as if he had been persuaded that three orders or grades existed in the Church in the time of the Apostles. On the contrary, he states in plain words that he is not now disputing the matter itself, but has postponed the discussion of the number of ecclesiastical orders to another place and another time. For the present he proceeds by concession with Hammond, so that from the confusion in the names by which the sacred orders are called he may argue against the Ignatian writings. But it will be better to hear Dallaeus himself. "Now," he says, on page 386, "I do not dispute the matter itself. Let us grant to the most learned Hammond what he so eagerly desires, that these three orders stood in the Church already in the times of the Apostles, as we have said. But the names of the orders, which alone I now discuss, do not seem to have been so distinct from one another even in the times of the Apostles and apostolic men, that the name Presbyter, which now signifies ministers of the second order, was never, indeed very often, applied to those whom they now want to be of the first; and conversely that Bishop, which is the name of the first order, was not applied to ministers of the second order, and so on." Now anyone can see that Dallaeus' words have been badly understood by the learned man and twisted into a sense plainly contrary to the author's mind.

units.la: XXX. His præmissis Vindiciarum Auctor ad objectionem Dallæanam confutandam propiùs accedit, illiqué confutandæ totum caput decimum-tertium, Dallæano nec minus prolixum, nec minus laboriosum impendit, nequaquam opinor facturus, si omnium levissima esset, quod tamen lectori persuasum esse cupit; Et quoniam quatuor Assertionibus id late persequitur, eas sigillatim expendere decrevimus, ne aliquid a nobis sine responsione praetermissum queratur. Prima Assertio haec est pag. 156. Quamplurimi Secundi Saeculi Scriptores idem discrimen inter vocabula Episcopatus & Presbyteri observarunt, quod observat Ignatius; Ergo falsum est quod asserit Dallaeus & tanquam Argumenti fundamentum ponit; Omnes Secundi Saeculi Scriptores promiscue eas voces usurpasse. Ut id probet, falsoque niti fundamento Dallaei objectionem demonstret, varia adducit Veterum testimonia pag. 157. & sequent. in quibus Episcopi & Presbyteri nomina ita a se invicem distincta esse contendit, ut Episcopi nomen solis primi ordinis Sacerdotibus tribuatur; Presbyteri vero iis qui sunt ordine in secundo, & quos hodie vocant minores Sacerdotes. Sed plura Viro Eruditissimo regeri possunt, 1. e numero testium expungendi sunt Author Actorum Passionis S. Ignatii, qui nullam aut certe perexiguam fidem meretur, & Hadrianus Imperator cujus Epistolam ad Servianum Consulem jam suprà excussimus. 2. ex plerisque testimonijs à Viro docto allatis, hoc solum colligitur Episcopi nomen videlicet Ecclesiarum Rectoribus à vetustissimis Scriptoribus sæpè tribui solitum esse, quod non diffitetur Dallæus. 3. Si integra extarent opera, quorum fragmenta quædam tantùm refert Eusebius, ex quibus sua descripsit testimonia Vindiciarum Auctor, pateret sine dubio Scriptores illos quos laudat, discrimen inter vocabula Episcopatus & Presbyterij non semper observasse, sed multoties ea promiscuè usurpasse. 4. malâ fide Dallæi sententiam repræsentat, quasi negaret discrimen illud inter Episcopi & Presbyteri nomina à Veteribus usquam observatum esse ; Tamen alia mens fuit Dallæo, qui dumtaxat asserit Ignatium ingens semper discrimen statuere inter hæc duo nomina, præter usum & consuetudinem secundi sæculi Scriptorum, qui istis vocabulis indiscrimitim utuntur. 5. Denique pluribus testimonijs ex scriptis Apostolorum & Apostolicorum Virorum depromptis, promiscuum istorum nominum usum confirmavit Clarissimus Dallæus, quibus quid responsurus sit doctissimus ejus adversarius, videbimus infra ubi ea examinare libebit. Porrò quæstio Chronologica quam adversus Blondellum nostrum exagitat Vir doctus non adeò magni est momenti, ut in utriusque partis rationibus examinandis diutius immorari sit necesse: Nam sive citiùs sive seriùs Photino successerit Irenæus in regiminæ Ecclesiæ Lugdunensis, parùm aut nihil refert, cùm aliunde suppetant testimonia apud Secundi Sæculi Scriptores, in quibus cernere est Episcopos Presbyterorum nomine insignitos: Ergo absque ullo Causæ Dalliæanæ detrimento, testimonio à Blondello in eum finem adducto carcere possumus; præsertim cùm ipse Irenæus de quo hoc in loco agitur, plura subministret testimonia quæ Dallæi hypothesi non parùm patrocinantur. Vt igitur paucis rem expediam, observo Blondelli sententiam Eusebiani Chronici autoritate niti: Eusebius siquidem & in Excerptis Græcis Scaligeri, & in versione Latinâ Hieronymi quartam Persecutionem confert in annum Marci Aurelij septimum, Domini verò CLXVII. Eandem Epocham sequuti sunt recentiorum pleríque sive Chronographi sive Historicij. Fateor non sibi constare Eufebium; nam in Historiâ post Chronicum Canonem scriptâ, Persecutionem Gallicanam ad decimum septimum ejusdem
units.tr: XXX. With these things premised, the author of the Vindiciae comes closer to refuting Dallaeus' objection, and he devotes to refuting it the whole of his thirteenth chapter, which is no less long and laborious than Dallaeus' own. I do not think he would have done so if it were the slightest of all objections, though he wants the reader to be persuaded of this. Since he pursues the matter at length through four assertions, I have decided to weigh each of them separately, so that no one can complain that something has been passed over by us without reply. The first assertion is this, on page 156: "Very many writers of the second century observed the same distinction between the terms Episcopate and Presbyter that Ignatius observes. Therefore what Dallaeus asserts, and puts forward as the foundation of his argument, is false: that all writers of the second century used these words indiscriminately." To prove this, and to show that Dallaeus' objection rests on a false foundation, he cites various testimonies of the ancients on pages 157 and following, in which he contends that the names Bishop and Presbyter are so distinct from one another that the name Bishop is given only to priests of the first order, and Presbyter to those who are in the second order, whom today they call lesser priests. But many things can be said against this most learned man. (1) From the number of witnesses must be struck out the author of the Acts of the Passion of St Ignatius, who deserves little or no credit; and the Emperor Hadrian, whose letter to the consul Servianus we have already examined above. (2) From most of the testimonies brought forward by the learned man, only this is gathered: that the name Bishop was often given by the most ancient writers to the rulers of churches, which Dallaeus does not deny. (3) If the works whose fragments Eusebius merely reports, from which the author of the Vindiciae drew his testimonies, were still extant in full, it would no doubt be clear that those writers whom he praises did not always observe the distinction between the terms Episcopate and Presbyterate, but very often used them indiscriminately. (4) He misrepresents Dallaeus' opinion, as if he denied that the ancients had ever observed the distinction between the names Bishop and Presbyter. Yet Dallaeus meant something else: he only asserts that Ignatius always drew a sharp distinction between these two names, contrary to the usage and custom of the writers of the second century, who used these words indiscriminately. (5) Finally, by many testimonies taken from the writings of the Apostles and apostolic men, the most distinguished Dallaeus confirmed the promiscuous use of these names. How his most learned adversary will reply to these we shall see below, when it pleases us to examine them. Moreover, the chronological question which the learned man pursues against our Blondel is not of such great moment that it is necessary to linger long in examining the arguments of either side. For whether Irenaeus succeeded Pothinus in the governance of the Church of Lyons sooner or later matters little or nothing, since there are other testimonies among the writers of the second century in which one may see bishops marked with the name of presbyters. So without any harm to the Dallaean cause we may set aside the testimony that Blondel brought forward for this purpose, especially since Irenaeus himself, of whom we are speaking here, supplies many testimonies that do not a little support Dallaeus' hypothesis. To explain the matter briefly, I observe that Blondel's opinion rests on the authority of Eusebius' Chronicle. For Eusebius, both in the Greek excerpts of Scaliger and in Jerome's Latin version, places the fourth persecution in the seventh year of Marcus Aurelius, that is, in the year 167 of the Lord. Most recent writers, both chroniclers and historians, have followed this same date. I admit that Eusebius is not consistent with himself; for in his History, written after the Canon of the Chronicle, he refers the Gallican persecution to the seventeenth year of the same

units.la: Marci Antonini annum refert; Sed inde non sequitur, si Blondellum audimus (in Apologiâ de sententiâ Hieronymi cap. 8. pag. 23.) præferenda esse quæ scribit Eusebius in Historiâ ijs quæ in Chronico tradidit, & de quorum veritate dubitare nefas putat Blondellus, ut pote certis circumstantiarum characteribus diversimodè munitâ. Vt ut est cum utrīque suppetant rationum momenta, Blondello scilicet & eximio Ignatianorum Vindici, utrumvis sequi liberum erit. Vnum moneo, gravissimè errare doctissimum Vindiciarum Auctorem, dum scribit pag. 160. Marcum Aurelium Melitonis Sardiensis Apologiâ pro Christianis permotum, de sedandâ persecutione ad Commune Asiæ scripsisse, quod XV. Imperij sui anno factum arbitratur. Melito enim Apologiam suam Marco obtulit sub finem Imperij ejus, ut fatetur Vir doctus, nempe postquam Commodum filium consortem Imperij fecerat, ut nos docet Eusebius Hist. lib. 4. cap. 26. & ut merito existimat Vir doctissimus Henricus Valesius in Præm. lib. 5. pag. 85. Quamvis paulò aliter sentire videatur in lib. 4. cap. 26. pag. 82. At Epistola Marci Imperatoris ad Commune Asiæ scripta fuit primo Imperij ejus anno: immerito igitur Vir doctus Valesium notat pag. 161. quod Marci Epistolam ad hunc annum refert Annot. in lib. 4. cap. 13. Eusebi pag. 66. & in cap. 26. pag. 83. Valesius enim non argumentatur ex tertio tantum Marci consulatu, sed imprimis ex anno XV. Tribunitiae potestatis in eadem Epistola praenotato, licet[?] eo anno tertium Consul esset ( inquit Vir doctus ) is tamen XV. Tribunitiae potestatis esse non potuit. Quare esse non potuit? Quia ( inquit ) tertium Consul dicebatur non tantum eo anno quo Consulatum gessit, sed omnibus sequentibus, nisi alium Consulatum iniret. Marcus autem postea Consul non fuit, ideoque per omnes Imperij annos tertium Consul dictus est. Quae de tertio Marci Consulatu tradit Vindiciarum Auctor vera sunt; At inde perperam colligit, primum Marci Imperij annum, in XV. Tribunitiae potestatis minime incidere posse; Marcus Aurelius XIX. annos Imperavit, primus Imperij annus coincidit cum XV. Tribunitiae potestatis; ultimus vero cum ejusdem potestatis XXXIV. ut liquet ex Onuphrii Fastis ad annum urbis 914. & ex illius Commentario in lib. 2. Fast. pag 229. cum 236. ubi ex variis nummorum inscriptionibus eundem eruit annorum numerum, eodem ordine ac serie dispositorum sed de primâ Assertione plus satis.
units.tr: He reports it as the year of Marcus Antoninus. But it does not follow from this, if we listen to Blondel (in his Apology on Jerome's opinion, ch. 8, p. 23), that what Eusebius writes in the History should be preferred to what he handed down in the Chronicle. Blondel thinks it wrong to doubt the Chronicle, since its dates are supported in various ways by the marks of circumstances. However that may be, since arguments are available on both sides, namely those of Blondel and of the distinguished defender of the Ignatians, it will be open to follow whichever one likes. I give one warning. The most learned author of the Vindiciae errs very gravely when he writes on p. 160 that Marcus Aurelius, moved by the Apology of Melito of Sardis for the Christians, wrote about calming the persecution to the Commune of Asia, and that this was done in the fifteenth year of his reign. For Melito offered his Apology to Marcus toward the end of his reign, as the learned man admits, namely after Marcus had made his son Commodus a partner in the empire. Eusebius teaches us this in Hist. book 4, ch. 26, and the most learned Henri Valois rightly thinks so in the Preface to book 5, p. 85, although he seems to think otherwise in book 4, ch. 26, p. 82. But the letter of the Emperor Marcus to the Commune of Asia was written in the first year of his reign. So the learned man rightly notes that Valois, on p. 161, wrongly refers Marcus's letter to this year, in his notes on Eusebius book 4 ch. 13, p. 66, and ch. 26, p. 83. For Valois does not argue only from Marcus's third consulship, but chiefly from the fifteenth year of tribunician power noted in the same letter: although he was consul for the third time in that year (says the learned man), he nevertheless could not be in the fifteenth year of tribunician power. Why could he not? Because (he says) he was called consul for the third time not only in the year in which he held the consulship, but in all the following years, unless he entered upon another consulship. Marcus was not consul afterwards, and so through all the years of his reign he was called consul for the third time. What the author of the Vindiciae hands down about Marcus's third consulship is true. But from it he wrongly concludes that the first year of Marcus's reign cannot fall in the fifteenth year of tribunician power. Marcus Aurelius reigned nineteen years. The first year of his reign coincides with the fifteenth year of tribunician power, and the last with the thirty-fourth year of the same power, as is clear from Onuphrius's Fasti at the year of the city 914, and from his commentary on Fasti book 2, p. 229 with 236, where from various coin inscriptions he draws the same number of years, arranged in the same order and sequence. But that is enough about the first assertion.

units.la: Ad Secundam igitur venio, quæ sic se habet pag. 165. Asserimus nullum Secundi Sæculi Scriptorem adeò promiscuè vocabulis Episcopi & Presbyteri usum esse, ut simplici Presbytero in secundo ministerij gradu constituto unquam Episcopi nomen tribueret. Ut istius Assertionis vanitas appareat, & quàm captiosè hæc dicantur quivis deprehendere possit, age Dallæi objectionem recolamus: argumentatur Dallæus adversus Ignatiana, ex eo quod Epistolarum Scriptor præter Apostolorum, & Ecclesiasticorum ad A. D. CC. Scriptorum consuetudinem Episcopum & Presbyterum, illum de primi, hunc de secundi gradus Sacerdote semper ac constanter, nunquam aliter dicat. Non diffitetur doctissimus Vindiciarum Auctor, quæ de Ignatio dicuntur Epistolico, hoc solum igitur negare debet, ita loquutum esse Ignatium præter Apostolorum, & Ecclesiasticorum secundi sæculi Scriptorum consuetudinem; Et quia de re facti agitur, illius erat negationis suæ rationes reddere, eámque variis Veterum testimoniis confirmare; & præterea quæ à Dallæo contrà allata sunt refellere; respondentis vices agit Vir doctus, ideóque adversarij objectioni inhærere debet, eámque rectà confutare, immoto stante quæstionis statu, quem tamen sollicitare & mutare non veretur. Non enim quæritur num verum an falsum sit nullum secundi sæculi Scriptorem simplici Presbytero in secundo ministerij gradu constituto unquam Episcopi nomen tribuisse : Hoc tantùm quæritur utrum secundi sæculi Scriptores Episcopi & Presbyteri vocabula promiscuè usurpaverint ; affirmativam tuetur Dallæus. Ergo vel neganda est vel concedenda Propositio illa affirmativa ; Negari non potest, utpote pluribus Veterum Scriptorum testimonijs firmata & stabilita, si concedatur, prout eam concedi necesse est, in magno versatur periculo Epistolarum Scriptor, qui præter secundi sæculi Scriptorum consuetudinem Episcopum de primi, Presbyterum de secundi gradus Sacerdote semper ac constanter, nunquam aliter dicit. Estne credibile Apostolorum discipulum eorum exemplum adeò parvi fecisse, & Ecclesiasticorum secundi sæcnli Scriptorum usum ac consuetudinem tam elatè ac superciliosè contempsisse , ut vocabulis Episcopi & Presbyteri promiscuè uti noluerit. Quas autem comminiscitur rationes Vir doctus, ob quas ab Apostolorum, & Apostolicorum Virorum consuetudine Ignatium suum discessisse putat, adeò leves sunt ac frivolae, ut eas à tanto Viro litteris traditas esse satis mirari non possim. Et quod admirationem auget, tanquam verum supponit quod in quastione est, tres nimirum fuisse temporibus Ignatij sacros ordines; Quamvis id à Dallaeo nequaquam concessum optimè nosset.
units.tr: I come, then, to the second, which stands thus on p. 165: We assert that no writer of the second century used the words bishop and presbyter so promiscuously that he ever gave the name of bishop to a simple presbyter placed in the second grade of ministry. To see the emptiness of this assertion, and how craftily these things are said, anyone can perceive it if we recall Dallaeus's objection. Dallaeus argues against the Ignatian letters from the fact that the author of the Epistles, contrary to the custom of the Apostles and of the ecclesiastical writers up to about AD 200, always and consistently, and never otherwise, calls Episcopum the priest of the first grade and Presbyterum the priest of the second. The most learned author of the Vindiciae does not deny what is said of Ignatius in the epistles. So he ought to deny only this: that Ignatius spoke thus contrary to the custom of the Apostles and of the ecclesiastical writers of the second century. And since the matter is one of fact, it was his task to give the grounds for his denial and to confirm it by various testimonies of the Ancients, and besides to refute what Dallaeus has brought against it. The learned man takes the place of one who answers, and so he ought to cling to the adversary's objection and refute it directly, the state of the question standing unchanged. Yet he does not hesitate to disturb and change that state. For the question is not whether it is true or false that no writer of the second century ever gave the name Episcopi to a simple Presbyteri placed in the second grade of ministry. The only question is whether the writers of the second century used the words Episcopi and Presbyteri promiscuously; Dallaeus maintains the affirmative. Therefore that affirmative proposition must either be denied or conceded. It cannot be denied, since it is supported and established by the testimonies of many Ancient writers. If it is conceded, as it must be, the author of the Epistles is in great danger, since he, contrary to the custom of the second-century writers, always and consistently, and never otherwise, calls Episcopum the priest of the first grade and Presbyterum the priest of the second. Is it credible that a disciple of the Apostles held their example in such low esteem, and so haughtily and disdainfully despised the custom and usage of the ecclesiastical writers of the second century, that he was unwilling to use the words bishop and presbyter promiscuously? As for the reasons the learned man invents, for which he thinks his Ignatius departed from the custom of the Apostles and of the apostolic men, they are so slight and frivolous that I cannot sufficiently wonder that they were set down in writing by so great a man. And what increases the wonder is that he takes as true what is in question, namely that there were three sacred orders in Ignatius's time, although he could have known very well that Dallaeus by no means conceded this.

units.la: Ejusdem prosùs farinæ est tertia doctissimi Viri Assertio, quæ istis continetur verbis. Nullum omninò secundi sæculi Scriptorem, cùm gradus enumerat, aut cùm de singularibus sui temporis ministris loquitur, nomen Presbyteri ei qui Episcopus esset tribuisse. Dallæi argumentum tale est; Ecclesiastici secundi sæculi Scriptores Episcopi & Presbyteri vocabulis indifferenter usi sunt, Ignatius Epistolicus ea nunquam promiscuè usurpavit, unde colligit supposititias esse quæ Ignatij nomine circumferuntur Epistolas; Minor in confesso est; Major est indefinita & illimitata; Vir tamen doctus qui eam concedere vel negare debebat, neutrum facit, indefinitam definit, & limitat illimitatam; Nullus secundi sæculi Scriptor, cùm gradus enumerat, aut cùm de singularibus sui temporis ministris loquitur, nomen Presbyteri ei qui Episcopus esset tribuit; At hæc solutio Dallæi argumentum propriè non respicit: Dallæus enim non diserte negat quosdam sæculi Scriptores, post natam graduum distinctionem, & postquam ex uno duo facti sunt (quod secundo sæculo inclinato & ad finem vergente contigisse est verisimile) non negat inquam aliquod quandoque discrimen observasse inter Episcopatus & Presbyteratus vocabula, quod imprimis factum crediderim, dum enumerabantur gradus, quoniam tunc aliis alios opponere erat necesse, ut ab invicem secernerentur; At hoc non impedit quominus Presbyteros nuncupent quos Episcopos constanter nominat Epistolicus Ignatius, vocibusque Episcopatus & Presbyteratus frequentissimè utantur; Quod Dallæo abundè sufficit ut verò abjudicet Ignatio quæ illius nomen præferunt Epistolas, in quibus cernitur stilus ab Apostolorum sermone planè diversus, & dicendi charactere à sæculi Scriptorum charactere omninò alienus; Ignatius castè & religiosè hoc nominum discrimen servat, neque unum cum altero uspiam confundit, quia, si Virum doctum audimus, confluebant ad eum in itinere ab Ecclesiis Asiæ, & Episcopi, & Presbyteri, & Diaconi complures ordine & munere & nomine & dignitate distincti: Et quod ei maximè necessarium videbatur præcipuè inculcabat, ut ab Hæreticis & Schismaticis caverent, remediúmque hoc malo maximè opportunum indicabat, ut Clero suo omnes adhærerent, & Christianam unitatem colerent, omnésque Cleri ordines sui loci dignitatem obtinerent. Hæc levissima ratio Viri doɛti causam minimè juvat, quoniam ut mox dicebamus falsâ nititur suppositione nimirùm tres fuisse tempore Ignatij sacros ordines: Secundò quale est admirandum istud remedium adversus, hæreses & Schismata, ut omnes scilicet Cleri ordines sui loci dignitatem obtineant: Profectò Christianorum saluti contra Hæreticos & Schismaticos malè olim prospectum est, si defuerunt remedia Ignatiano isto magis opportuna magisque efficacia: Quorsùm efficacissimi istius remedij non meminit Irenæus in suis adversus Hæreses libris, neque Augustinus contra Donatistas omnium Schismaticorum deterrimos acerrimè disputans; nec denique Augustino vetustiores qui Novatianorum Schisma insectati sunt. Tertio falsum est quod affirmat Vir doctus pag. 166. Nullum omnino secundi saeculi Scriptorem, cum gradus enumerat, nomen Presbyteri ei qui Episcopus esset tribuisse; contrarium patet ex Epistola Polycarpi ad Philippenses; Subjecti estote Presbyteri[?] & Diaconis sicut Deo & Christo ; si Episcopum habuissent Philippenses Presbyteris superiorem, eum non oblituru erat Polycarpus : Quis dabit ( inquit Vir doctus ) Episcopum Philippensium tunc in vivis fuisse ? Respondeo neque superstitem neque mortuum fuisse Philippensium Episcopum Presbyteris superiorem, nullum quippe ejusmodi Episcopum noverant Philippenses ; nam si habuissent, & nuper mortuus esset, eos sine dubio de illius morte erat consolaturus, & ut alium in ejus locum substituerent moniturus atque hortaturus. Quod addit, aut cùm de singularibus sui temporis ministris loquitur, frivolum est nec Dallæo nocet, & præterea eadem falsâ nititur suppositione de tribus in Ecclesiâ Ignatij ætate ordinibus sacris ; frivolum autem esse nec Dallæani argumenti vim elevare constat ; 1. quia Dallæi propositio non est universalis affirmans quæ negativâ particulari everti possit ; non enim affirmat Dallæus omnes secundi sæculi Scriptores, Episcopi & Presbyteri vocabulis promiscuè semper usos esse, hoc si affirmaret, appositæ essent Viri doćti exceptiones, sed cùm nihil ejusmodi asserat præstantissimus Dallæus, frustrà est Vindiciarum Auctor dum tales adhibet exceptiones. 2. falsa est Viri doćti negativa ut liquet ex verbis Polycarpi mox descriptis, Polycarpus siquidem supremos Ecclesiæ Philippensium rectores nuncupat Presbyteros, qui etiam Episcopi appellabantur, immò seipsum in Epistolæ inscriptione Presbyteri nomine insignit, saltem nihil aliud sonare videntur hæc inscriptionis verba, Polycarpus, & qui cum eo sunt Presbyteri: Nam si gradum Presbyteratu superiorem obtinuisset, à Presbyteris suis Episcopi nomenclaturâ se distinxisset, præterea Irenæus qui Polycarpi auditor fuerat, quique libros suos adversus hæreses XV. circiter post illius mortem annis scribebat, eum Beatum & & Apostolicum Presbyterum vocat apud Eustreb. lib.5. cap. 20. 3. non plane constat Epistolicum Ignatium gradus semper enumerare, vel de singularibus sui temporis ministris loqui, quoties Episcopos à Presbyteris adeo caste ac religiose secernit; nec quicquam causæ est cur celeberrimus Ignatianorum vindex Episcopos demortuos & antiquiores, superstitibus & præsentibus opponat pag. 167. 178. Quasi Irenæo licitum fuerit illos Presbyteros appellare, hos verò nequaquam; Irenæus enim de Episcopis se antiquioribus non solùm ita loquitur, sed etiam de præsentibus ac superstitibus: Franciscus Combefisius in novissimo Auctario Bibliothecæ Græcorum Patrum, Symbolas quasdam S. Irenæi ex variis Catenis collectas exhibet, in quarum unâ hæc legas velim. Ejus generis Presbyteros alit Ecclesia, de quibus & Petrus ait, DABO PRINCIPES TVOS IN PACE, ET EPISCOPOS TVOS IN IVSTITIA.
units.tr: The third assertion of the most learned man belongs to the same kind, and it is contained in these words: No writer of the second century at all, when he enumerates the grades, or when he speaks of the particular ministers of his own time, ever gave the name of presbyter to one who was a bishop. Dallaeus's argument runs as follows. The ecclesiastical writers of the second century used the words bishop and presbyter interchangeably; Ignatius, the writer of the Epistles, never used them promiscuously; from this he infers that the Epistles circulating under Ignatius's name are spurious. The minor premise is admitted; the major is indefinite and unlimited. The learned man, who ought either to concede or to deny it, does neither: he defines what is indefinite and limits what is unlimited. "No writer of the second century, when he enumerates the grades or speaks of the particular ministers of his own time, gave the name of presbyter to one who was a bishop." But this solution does not properly meet Dallaeus's argument. Dallaeus does not expressly deny that some writers of that age, after the distinction of grades had arisen and after the one office had become two (which probably happened as the second century declined and drew to its close), sometimes observed a distinction between the words bishopric and presbyterate. I believe this was done chiefly when the grades were being enumerated, since then one had to set one grade against another so that they could be told apart. But this does not prevent Ignatius, the writer of the Epistles, from calling presbyters those whom he constantly names bishops, and from using the words episcopate and presbyterate very frequently. This is quite enough for Dallaeus to deny outright that the Epistles bearing Ignatius's name are genuinely his, since in them is seen a style quite different from the language of the Apostles and entirely foreign to the manner of writing of the writers of that age. Ignatius keeps this distinction of names purely and religiously, and nowhere confuses one with the other. For, if we listen to the learned man, bishops, presbyters and deacons, distinguished in order, office, name and dignity, flocked to him on his journey from the churches of Asia. And what seemed to him most necessary he especially urged: that they should beware of heretics and schismatics, and he pointed out as the most suitable remedy for this evil that all should cling to their clergy, cultivate Christian unity, and that every order of clergy should keep the dignity of its place. This very slight reason does nothing to help the learned man's cause, because, as we said just now, it rests on the false supposition that there were three sacred orders in the time of Ignatius. Secondly, what a wonderful remedy this is against heresies and schisms, namely that all orders of clergy should keep the dignity of their place! Certainly the salvation of Christians against heretics and schismatics was poorly provided for in former times, if such a remedy, more suitable and more effective than this Ignatian one, was lacking. Why does Irenaeus, in his books against heresies, make no mention of this most effective remedy? Nor does Augustine, who argues most sharply against the Donatists, the worst of all schismatics; nor, finally, do those who came before Augustine and attacked the schism of the Novatians. Thirdly, it is false what the learned man asserts on page 166: No writer of the second century at all, when he enumerates the grades, ever gave the name of presbyter to one who was a bishop. The contrary is clear from Polycarp's Epistle to the Philippians: Be subject to the presbyters and deacons as to God and Christ. If the Philippians had had a bishop set over the presbyters, Polycarp would not have overlooked him. "Who will grant," says the learned man, "that the bishop of the Philippians was alive at that time?" I reply that the bishop of the Philippians, set over the presbyters, was neither living nor dead, for the Philippians knew of no such bishop. For if they had had one, and he had recently died, Polycarp would certainly have consoled them over his death, and would have advised and urged them to put another in his place. As for his addition, or when he speaks of the particular ministers of his own time, it is trifling and does no harm to Dallaeus; moreover it rests on the same false supposition about three sacred orders in the Church of Ignatius's age. That this is trifling, and does not weaken the force of Dallaeus's argument, is clear for the following reasons. 1. Dallaeus's proposition is not a universal affirmative, which could be overturned by a particular negative. For Dallaeus does not affirm that all the writers of the second century always used the words bishop and presbyter promiscuously. If he had affirmed this, the learned man's exceptions would have been apposite. But since the most distinguished Dallaeus asserts nothing of the kind, the author of the Vindiciae is wasting his time in bringing forward such exceptions. 2. The learned man's negative is false, as is clear from the words of Polycarp just quoted. For Polycarp calls the supreme rulers of the Church of the Philippians presbyters, who were also called bishops. Indeed he himself marks himself with the title of presbyter in the inscription of the Epistle; at least these words of the inscription seem to mean nothing else: Polycarp, and the presbyters who are with him. For if he had held a grade higher than the presbyterate, he would have distinguished himself from his fellow presbyters by the title of bishop. Moreover Irenaeus, who had been a hearer of Polycarp, and who was writing his books against heresies about fifteen years after Polycarp's death, calls him the blessed and apostolic presbyter, in Eusebius, book 5, chapter 20. 3. It is not at all clear that the Epistle-writer Ignatius always enumerates the grades, or speaks of the particular ministers of his own time, whenever he so purely and religiously separates bishops from presbyters. Nor is there any reason why the most renowned defender of the Ignatians sets dead and earlier bishops against living and present ones on pages 167 and 178, as if it were lawful for Irenaeus to call the former presbyters and not the latter. For Irenaeus speaks thus not only of earlier bishops, but also of present and living ones. Francis Combefis, in the recent Appendix to the Library of the Greek Fathers, gives some symbolic passages of St. Irenaeus collected from various catenae, and I would have you read this in one of them: The Church nourishes presbyters of this kind, of whom Peter also says: I WILL MAKE YOUR PRINCES PEACE, AND YOUR BISHOPS RIGHTEOUSNESS.

units.la: Restat quarta doctissimi Vindiciarum Auctoris Assertio, quæ non magis quàm cæteræ Dallæo incommodat; Nam à nominibus ex quorum confusione petitum est Dallæi argumentum, ad ipsos transit ordines quorum numerum non sollicitavit adversarius, neque an duo aut tres Ignatii ætate in Ecclesiâ fuerint anxiè quæsivit; si duos tantùm fuisse affirmasset Dallæus, tunc quartæ Viri docti Assertioni locus fuisset, quâ asserit pag. 172. tres sacros ordines seu gradus distinctos in Ecclesiâ fuisse eâ ætate quâ S. Ignatius Epistolas scripsisse dicitur. At cùm nihil tale affirmaverit, nec quæstionem de ordinum sacrorum numero attigerit, frustrà est Vir doctus dum quartam suam Assertionem quæ de ipsis agit Ordinibus, Dallæi argumento ex promiscuo vocabulorum usu deprompto opponit: Quid est certamen fugere, vimque argumenti adversarii declinare, si hoc non est ? Quid non dicturus erat Vir doctus, si Vfferij & Hammondi argumentis respondisset Dallæus, ut ipse nunc Dallæo respondet?
units.tr: There remains the fourth assertion of the most learned author of the Vindiciae, which troubles Dallaeus no more than the others do. For from the names, whose confusion gave rise to Dallaeus's argument, it passes on to the orders themselves, the number of which the opponent did not trouble about, nor did he anxiously inquire whether there were two or three in the Church in Ignatius's time. If Dallaeus had affirmed that there were only two, then the learned man's fourth assertion would have had a place, in which he asserts on page 172 that there were three distinct sacred orders, or grades, in the Church at the age in which St. Ignatius is said to have written the Epistles. But since Dallaeus affirmed nothing of the kind, and did not touch on the question of the number of sacred orders, the learned man is wasting his time when he opposes his fourth assertion, which deals with the orders themselves, to Dallaeus's argument drawn from the promiscuous use of words. What is it to flee the contest and to dodge the force of the opponent's argument, if this is not? What would the learned man not have said, if Dallaeus had replied to the arguments of Usher and Hammond as he now replies to Dallaeus himself?
