units.la: Qui respondentis partes agit adversarij argumento inhærere debet, quæ illi objiciuntur solvere, nec à quæstione proposita tantillùm deflectere. Tamen contrarium plane fecit Eruditissimus Vindiciarum Auctor,in eo magis culpandus quod hæc scripsit pag. 155. Dallæus dat Hammusondo [?] tres sub Apostolorum tempore, qui nomina Episcopi & Presbyteri promiscuè usurpasse dicuntur, tres Ordines seu gradus in Ecclesiâ extitisse. Quo sensu id Hammondo dederit Dallæus explicavi supra. Iam hoc solùm volo, constare scilicet ex istis Viri docti verbis, Dallæo hanc de Ordinum Sacrorum numero quæstionem tractare minimè propositum fuisse; De re ipsâ non disputat Ignatianorum impugnator, de solis agitur nominibus, dilatâ forte in aliud tempus de sacrorum ordinum numero quæstione; percurratur caput XXVI. quod prolixum esse & laboriosum tradit Vir doctus, & quo toto Dallæus suum persequitur Palmarium argumentum, nullibi reperietur illum ex Ordinum sacrorum numero argumentatum esse, nec ad hanc quæstionem elucidandam animum applicuisse; Illius verba quæ extant pag. 386. iterum describere non pigebit. Nunc de re ipsa non disputo. Ordinum nomina, de quibus nunc solis disputo, nondum istis Apostolorum & Apostolicorum temporum ita à se invicem distincta fuisse videntur, ut non aliquando, immo saepissime nomen PRESBYTERI, quod secundi ordinis ministros nunc significat, de iis dicetur, quos nunc volunt esse primi; & vicissim EPISCOPI, quod est primi ordinis nomen, de secundi ordinis Ministris acciperetur.
units.tr: One who plays the part of the respondent ought to stick to the opponent's argument, to solve the objections raised against him, and not to swerve a whit from the question proposed. Yet the most learned author of the Vindiciae has done quite the opposite, and he is the more to be blamed because he wrote these words on page 155: Dallaeus grants to Hammond that under the times of the Apostles three orders or grades existed in the Church, of whom the names bishop and presbyter are said to have been used promiscuously. I have explained above in what sense Dallaeus granted this to Hammond. Now I want only this to be established: it is clear from the learned man's own words that Dallaeus had no intention of treating this question about the number of sacred orders. The impugner of the Ignatians does not dispute the matter itself; he deals only with the names, perhaps postponing to another time the question of the number of sacred orders. Let anyone run through chapter 26, which the learned man says is long and laborious, and in which Dallaeus pursues his chief argument throughout. Nowhere will he find that Dallaeus argued from the number of sacred orders, or applied his mind to clearing up that question. I will not be troubled to write out again his words, which stand on page 386: Now I do not dispute about the thing itself. The names of the orders, about which alone I now dispute, do not seem to have been so distinguished from one another in the times of the Apostles and the Apostolic age, that the name PRESBYTER, which now denotes the ministers of the second order, was never, indeed very often, applied to those whom they now wish to be of the first, and conversely the name BISHOP, which is the name of the first order, was applied to ministers of the second order.

units.la: Non potuit difertius testari præstantissimus Dallæus de solis se ordinum nominibus disputaturum esse, nec ad rem ipsam examinandam ullo modo accessurum. Argumento igitur ex solâ nominum confusione desumpto inhærere debebat Ignatianorum vindex, nec in aliud excurrere, ut scilicet conflictum vitaret, nec ad lineam à Dallæo descriptam decertaret. Sed Virum doctum audiamus suam disputandi methodum sic defendentem p. 172. ne Salmasii sententiam intactam relinquere, aut concessioni Dallæanæ nimis fidere videar, de hac re ulterius differendum esse putavit. Sit igitur quarta Assertio, Eâ ætate quâ S. Ignatius Epistolas scripsisse dicitur tres sacros ordines seu gradus distinctos in Ecclesiâ fuisse. Si de Salmasio ageretur, qui, ut dicitur, duos tantum ordines sacros in Ecclesiâ fuisse ævo Ignatiano docebat ; aliquem colorem haberet quarta Viri docti Assertio, quæ Dallæi respectu est prorsus ἀπροσηλύτως[?]. Dallæus ob nihil aliud Hammondo largitus est tres ordines jam ipsis Apostolorum temporibus in Ecclesiâ extitisse, nisi quoniam de ipsis agere non decreverat, aliter certè rem tractaturus erat, si quæstionem de sacrorum ordinum numero ad examen revocare statuisset ; At quia ad argumentum quod toto capite XXVI. fusè persequitur, non pertinet altera de sacrorum ordinum numero disputatio, eam intactam reliquit ; Dallæi ergo exemplo cujus rationes expendit Vindiciarum Auctor, eam præterire debebat, solis adversarij argumentis refellendis intentus ; Verùm enimverò neglectis disputationis præceptis, suíque immemor ossicij Vir doctus, monstrum sibi fingit quod debellet, extra oleas divagatur, & in vastissimum excurrit campum, novum proponendo argumentum, ad pompam magis & ostentationem, quàm ad nodos solvendos enodandásque difficultates comparatum, ne Virum doctum in his sequamur erroribus vetant disputandi leges ; à quibus discedere religio est ; cùm enim Dallæi argumenta ab adversarij exceptionibus Vindicare tantummodo statuerimus : Nemo opinor nobis vitio vertet,si alia quæ illum non feriunt infoluta prætermittimus. Et ut palàm fit quartam Viri docti assertionem Dallæum nequaquam spectare , considerandum est illius argumentum hoc niti fundamento, quod Epistolarum scriptor semper & ubique Episcopatum à Presbyteratu distinguit, Episcopi nomen majoribus , ut hodie loquuntur, Sacerdotibus constantissimè tribuendo , Presbyteri verò minoribus qui sunt ordine in secundo, idque præter Apostolorum & Ecclesiasticorum ad An. D. CC. Scriptorum consuetudinem , qui vocabulis istis promiscuè & indifferenter usi sunt, tam ij qui ante institutos tres ordines scripserunt quàm alij qui post eorum floruerunt institutionem ,non enim diffiteretur Dallæus tres fuisse in Ecclesiâ ante finem secundi sæculi sacros ordines distinctos, & ex uno duos esse factos sæculo illo inclinato & ferè præcipiti : potuit ergo absque ullo causæ detrimento Hammondo largiri quod mox observabat Vir doctus , nempe ex solâ nominum confusione disputare in animo habebat adversus Epistolarum Scriptorem qui ab Apostolici sermonis ideâ & Apostolicorum secundi sæcundi Scriptorum usu ac consuetudine planè penitúsque discessit, quod de vero Ignatio suspicari non debemus, absit enim ut concedamus aliquid ejusmodi sanctissimo contigisse Martyri, quem doctrinæ & sermonis Apostolorum necnon Virorum Apostolicorum tenacissimum fuisse par est credere: vel si ab usu recepto discedere voluisset, ut Epistolarum Scriptor qui ab eo omninò descivit, verisimile est illum Christianos quibus scribebat, quique Apostolico assueti erant sermoni hac de re moniturum esse, animíque sui sensa explicaturum, ne forte ob insolentem ac inusitatum sermonem, neque mentem ejus capere, neque illius verba intelligere possent. Cùm ultra nominum confusionem non progressus sit Dallæus, nec de re ipsâ disputârit, ultra nos etiam progredi vetat instituti ratio, extra quam excurrere non licet: Tamen quia Vindiciarum Auctor sub finem capitis levissimis quibusdam rationibus confusionem illam nominum ex quâ argumentatus est Dallæus, pulsare nititur, age eas breviter expendamus.
units.tr: The most distinguished Dallaeus could not have declared more clearly that he would dispute only about the names of the orders, and that he would in no way come to the matter itself. The defender of the Ignatian letters should therefore have kept to the argument drawn solely from the confusion of names. He ought not to have run off elsewhere, either to avoid the contest or to fight outside the line Dallaeus had drawn. But let us hear the learned man defending his method of disputing, on p. 172: lest I appear to leave Salmasius's opinion untouched, or to rely too much on Dallaeus's concession, he thought the matter needed to be pursued further. Let the fourth assertion therefore stand: that in the age in which St Ignatius is said to have written his letters, there were three distinct sacred orders or grades in the Church. If the discussion concerned Salmasius, who, as is said, taught that there were only two sacred orders in the Church in the age of Ignatius, the learned man's fourth assertion would have some colour. As regards Dallaeus, however, it is utterly unprovoked [ἀπροσηλύτως?]. Dallaeus granted Hammond that there were already three orders in the Church in the very times of the Apostles for no other reason than that he had not decided to deal with that question. Had he resolved to bring the question of the number of sacred orders under examination, he would certainly have treated the matter differently. But since the second dispute, about the number of sacred orders, does not belong to the argument which he pursues at length in the whole of chapter XXVI, he left it untouched. Following Dallaeus's example, whose reasoning the author of the Vindiciae has weighed, he ought to have passed it over, intent only on refuting the arguments of his opponent. But the learned man, neglecting the rules of disputation and forgetful of his own duty, invents a monster for himself to overcome. He wanders beyond the olive groves and runs out onto a vast plain, proposing a new argument designed more for show and display than for untying knots and resolving difficulties. The rules of disputation forbid us to follow the learned man in these errors, and it is a matter of conscience not to depart from them. Since we have resolved only to defend Dallaeus's arguments against the objections of his opponent, I think no one will blame us if we leave unanswered the other points which do not touch him. And so that it may be plain that the learned man's fourth assertion in no way concerns Dallaeus, we must consider that his argument rests on this foundation: the writer of the letters always and everywhere distinguishes episcopate from presbyterate, consistently applying the name bishop to the greater priests, as they now say, and the name presbyter to the lesser, who hold the second order. This is contrary to the custom of the Apostles and of the ecclesiastical writers up to the year 200, who used these words promiscuously and without distinction, both those who wrote before the three orders were instituted and those who flourished after their institution. For Dallaeus did not deny that there were three distinct sacred orders in the Church before the end of the second century, and that two were made from one in that century, which was declining and almost headlong. He could therefore grant Hammond, without any damage to his cause, what the learned man goes on to observe, namely that he intended to dispute only about the confusion of names against the writer of the letters, who departed altogether from the idea of Apostolic speech and from the usage and custom of the Apostolic writers of the second century. We should not suspect this of the true Ignatius. Far be it from us to concede that anything of this kind happened to that most holy martyr, who, it is right to believe, was most tenacious of the teaching and language of the Apostles and of the Apostolic men. Or if he had wished to depart from the accepted usage, as the writer of the letters, who utterly abandoned it, did, it is likely that he would have warned the Christians to whom he wrote, who were accustomed to Apostolic speech, about this matter, and would have explained his meaning, lest they should be unable to grasp his mind or understand his words because of his unusual and strange language. Since Dallaeus did not proceed beyond the confusion of names and did not dispute the matter itself, the plan of my work forbids me to go further than he did, beyond which it is not permitted to run. Nevertheless, because the author of the Vindiciae, near the end of the chapter, tries to shake that confusion of names on which Dallaeus based his argument by means of some very slight reasons, let us briefly weigh them.

units.la: Primò scribit pag. 180. Nullum secundi, vel etiam tertij sæculi Scriptorem in scriptis Apostolicis confusa esse nomina Episcopi & Presbyteri observâsse. Frivola certè observatio, non negavit Vir doctus plures secundi sæculi Scriptores his vocibus promiscuè usos esse : Unde igitur promiscuum vocabulorum istorum usum expiscati sunt, nisi ex Scriptis Apostolicis, in quibus confusa esse nomina Episcopi & Presbyteri eos observâsse opportet? Quamvis enim id disertis verbis non testati sint, rebus ipsis plus satis significarunt; neque ab Apostolici sermonis ideâ eos discessisse par est credere. Secundò observat pag. 181. Dallæum neminem Chrysostomo, Theodoreto, Hieronymo vetustiorem nominare, ut probet Ephesi, unius urbis, plures non primi sed secundi gradus præpositos Episcoporum nomine significari, Act. XX. 27.28. Nominavit Dallæus qui commentaria in hunc Scripturæ locum conscripserunt; sed hoc non impedit quominus secundi sæculi Scriptores Episcopi & Presbyteri vocabula, juxta scripturæ sacræ usum ac consuetudinem, eodem planè sensu usurpaverint.
units.tr: First, he writes on p. 180 that no writer of the second or even the third century is found to have confused the names bishop and presbyter in Apostolic writings. This is certainly a frivolous observation. The learned man did not deny that several writers of the second century used these words promiscuously. Where, then, did they learn this promiscuous use of the words, if not from the Apostolic writings, in which the names bishop and presbyter must have been confused? For although they did not testify to this in express words, they signified it quite sufficiently by the facts themselves. Nor is it right to believe that they departed from the idea of Apostolic speech. Second, he observes on p. 181 that Dallaeus names no one older than Chrysostom, Theodoret and Jerome, to prove that at Ephesus, a single city, several men of the second, not the first, grade were designated by the name of bishops (Acts 20:27-28). Dallaeus did name those who wrote commentaries on this passage of Scripture. But this does not prevent the writers of the second century from using the words bishop and presbyter, in accordance with the usage and custom of Holy Scripture, in exactly the same sense.

units.la: At Irenæus, inquit, non putavit eosdem Viros eo loci & Episcopos fuisse dictos & Presbyteros, & ad unius urbis Ecclesiam pertinuisse ; Ecce Irenæi verba quibus sententiam suam tuetur lib. 3. cap. 14. In Mileto enim convocatis Episcopis & Presbyteris, qui erant ab Epheso, & à reliquis proximis civitatibus. Hinc colligit Vir doctus Paulum neque unius urbis, neque solos secundi ordinis præpositos convocâsse, neque illos Episcopos appellâsse. Sed turpiter errat : Irenæus enim Pauli vestigia calcans unius ejusdémque gradus præpositos, Episcopos & Presbyteros appellat; & si de solis Ecclesiæ Ephesinæ præpositis non loquitur Irenæus, à D. Lucæ narratione seorsùm abit, in quâ soli memorantur Ephesini præpositi: Verum hoc nihil ad rem facit, cùm constet ex sequentibus quæ Viro docto describere non libuit, Irenæum quos Episcopos & Presbyteros vocaverat, eos posteà Episcopos tantùm appellare : hæc enim Apostoli verba ad omnes quos alloquebatur præpositos adjicit. Attendite igitur & vobis, & omni gregi, in quo vos Spiritus proposuit Episcopos regere Ecclesiam Domini, &c. Ergo consusa esse in Scriptura sacrâ nomina Episcopi & Presbyteri animadvertit Irenæus, aliter de Presbyteris minimè dicturus erat, quod Spiritus Sanctus eos proposuit Episcopos. Tertiò dixerat Dallæus p.392. Apostolum cap. 1. Epistolæ ad Titum Episcoporum nomine donare, quos à Tito constitui præcipit per Cretæ civitates Presbyteros. Respondet Vindiciarum Auctor pag. 181.182. Clementem Alexandrinum, Tertullianum, & Origenem aliter planè sensisse; Quamobrem? Quia multa, inquit, eáque distinctè Episcopo & Presbytero data praecepta in scripturâ observarunt, non minùs quàm Diaconis & Viduis. Sed frustrà est celeberrimus Ignatianorum propugnator; Nam Scriptores quos laudat ad verba quibus de agitur nequaquam respexerunt, cùm in illis nulla prorsus mentio fiat Diaconorum nec Viduarum, sed tantùm Presbyterorum, quos Episcopos appellat: Praeterea Origenem non moror, quoniam floruit post tempus à Dallaeo constitutum; Clemens verò & Tertullianus quorum aetate tres in Ecclesiâ fuisse sacros ordines inter se distinctos non negamus, praecepta unicuíque generi propria in scriptura sacrâ se deprehendisse putarunt, ut solent Veteres qui non raro scripturae sacræ verba sui temporis moribus ac institutis accommodare non verentur; sed ita tamen ut ipsi Episcopi & Presbyteri nomina indiscrimatim us[?]rpaverint, sicut à Dallaeo demonstratum est.
units.tr: But Irenaeus, he says, did not think that the same men in that place were called both bishops and presbyters, and that they belonged to the church of a single city. Here are Irenaeus's own words, by which he supports his opinion, in book 3, chapter 14: For at Miletus, having summoned the bishops and presbyters who were from Ephesus and from the other neighbouring cities. From this the learned man infers that Paul did not summon the leaders of a single city, nor only those of the second order, and did not call them bishops. But he errs shamefully. For Irenaeus, treading in Paul's footsteps, calls the leaders of one and the same grade both bishops and presbyters. And if Irenaeus does not speak only of the leaders of the church of Ephesus, he departs from the narrative of St Luke, in which only the Ephesian leaders are mentioned. But this has nothing to do with the matter, since it is clear from what follows (which it did not please the learned man to describe) that Irenaeus, after calling them bishops and presbyters, then calls them only bishops. For the Apostle adds these words to all the leaders he addressed: Take heed therefore to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Spirit has placed you as bishops to rule the Church of the Lord, etc. Therefore Irenaeus observed that the names bishop and presbyter are confused in Holy Scripture. He would never have spoken of the presbyters at all in this way, saying that the Holy Spirit placed them as bishops, had he thought otherwise. Third, Dallaeus had said on p. 392 that the Apostle, in chapter 1 of the Epistle to Titus, gives the name of bishops to those whom he orders Titus to appoint presbyters in the cities of Crete. The author of the Vindiciae replies on pp. 181-182 that Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian and Origen thought quite differently. Why so? he says, because they observed that many precepts were given in Scripture distinctly to the bishop and the presbyter, no less than to the deacons and widows. But the most celebrated champion of the Ignatians is mistaken. For the writers he cites did not in the least have in view the words under discussion, since in them there is no mention at all of deacons or widows, but only of presbyters, whom he calls bishops. Moreover, I do not dwell on Origen, since he flourished after the time fixed by Dallaeus. Clement and Tertullian, in whose age we do not deny that there were three distinct sacred orders in the Church, thought they had found in Holy Scripture precepts proper to each kind. This is what the Ancients often do, who do not hesitate to adapt the words of Scripture to the customs and institutions of their own time. But they did so in such a way that they used the names bishop and presbyter indiscriminately, as Dallaeus has shown.

units.la: Pergit hoc pacto Vir doctus pag. 183.
units.tr: The learned man proceeds in this way, p. 183.

units.la: Nemo eorum omnium qui communia Episcopi & Presbyteri nomina in SS. Scripturis fuisse putabant, in eo sermonis genere Apostolos sequutus est, aut alium quenquam sequutum esse dixit. Haec observatio falsa nititur suppositione quam supra explosimus, neminem scilicet ante quartum saeculum communionem horum nominum in libris Apostolicis deprehendisse, quod quàm falsum sit ex ijs quæ hactenus scripsimus quivis facilè judicare potest; Nec minus falsum quod addit p. 185. Aërium, quem tanquam Hæreticum odiosissimè insectatus est Epiphanius, primum omnium harum vocum communionem ad suam sententiam confirmandam protulisse: Plures enim longè ante Aërium extiterunt laudatissimi Scriptores, qui Episcopi & Presbyteri nominibus promiscuè usi sunt. Quæ sequuntur ad finem usque capitis Dallæum non feriunt; constat enim de facto, plures scilicet ex Veteribus hanc nominum communionem asseruisse: Num autem veris an falsis ad illam afferendam impulsi sint rationibus, & an in suâ sententiâ explicandâ consenserint vel dissenserint, nostra non refert; quandoquidem facti non juris quæstionem excutimus. Cæterùm miror Virum doctum nihil plane respondere huic ex 1. Tim. 4. 14. à Dallæo descripto testimonio p. 389. Noli negligere gratiam quæ in te est (Ministerij Evangelici gratiam intelligit) quæ data est tibi per prophetiam, cum impositione manuum Presbyterij. Observat clarissimus Dallæus hunc unicum esse in divinis libris locum, in quo Christiani Presbyterij mentio fiat ; sed ita ut id nomen ministrorum primi gradus Collegium necessario significet, non autem secundi, quibus scilicet ordinandi & imponendi manus facultas, huic Collegio à Paulo attributa, nulla, inquit, ex eorum dogmate est, qui hunc secundum gradum à primo diversum statuunt. Palmarium sanè argumentum & aliquâ Vindiciarum Auctoris responsione dignissimum.
units.tr: No one of all those who thought that the common names Bishop and Presbyter occur in the Holy Scriptures has followed the Apostles in that manner of speaking, or said that anyone else has followed them. This observation rests on a supposition which we have already overturned above, namely that no one before the fourth century found the common use of these names in the Apostolic books. How false this is anyone can easily judge from what we have written so far. Equally false is what he adds on p. 185, that Aërius, whom Epiphanius attacked most bitterly as a heretic, was the first of all to bring forward the common use of these names in support of his opinion. For many very celebrated writers existed long before Aërius who used the names Bishop and Presbyter interchangeably. What follows up to the end of the chapter does not touch Dallaeus. It is established as a matter of fact that several of the ancients asserted this common use of the names. Whether they were moved to assert it by true or false reasons, and whether they agreed or disagreed in explaining their opinion, does not concern us here, since we are examining a question of fact, not of right. Moreover, I wonder that the learned man says absolutely nothing in reply to this testimony from 1 Tim. 4:14, cited by Dallaeus on p. 389: Do not neglect the grace that is in you (he understands by grace the grace of the evangelical ministry) which was given to you through prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. The most distinguished Dallaeus observes that this is the only place in the divine books where the Christian presbytery is mentioned; but that this name necessarily signifies the college of ministers of the first rank, and not of the second, to whom the power of ordaining and laying on hands, which Paul attributes to this college, belongs, according to him, by the doctrine of none who hold that this second rank is distinct from the first. This is certainly a strong argument and one most worthy of some answer from the Author of the Vindiciae.

units.la: Excussis rationibus quibus Dallæani argumenti ex nominum confusione deducti, vim atque pondus elevare nisus est doctissimus Ignatianorum patronus ; ad ea refellenda quæ pro tribus sacris ordinibus scripsit, libenter nos accingeremus, ni vetaret ut diximus instituti ratio : Tamen quamvis quæstionem illam indiscufsam relinquere decreverim, duo aut tria testimonia contra trium sacrorum ordinum numerum, à nemine quod sciam adhuc adducta, describere non pigebit, ut appareat quæ fuerit Veterum de Ordinum sacrorum institutione sententia ; Primum desumptum est ex Libello de pressuris Ecclesiasticis Attonis Episcopi Vercellensis & decimi sæculi Scriptoris ; Is enim tom. 8. Spicilegij Dacherij pag. 6 3. postquam hæc B. Apostoli ad Timotheum verba citaverat, adversus Presbyterum accusationem ne recipias, & illa ejusdem Apostoli ex eadem Epistolâ & eodem capite quinto ; Delinquentes autem coram omnibus argue, ut caeteri metum habeant, de suo addit, Non enim facile credi debet de Episcopo vel Presbytero, quorum ordo adhuc divisus non erat. Secundum ministrat Vrbanus Papa II. qui primus omnium Pontificum Rom. Subdiaconos ad Episcopatum admisit, opportunitate exigente, si tamen Pontifex Romanus vel Metropolitanus ita fieri consenserit; has autem conditiones Decreto suo apponi curavit, quia Subdiaconatus ad sacros Ordines qui duo tantùm initio fuêre non pertinebat; Vrbani autem Decretum anno Domini M. XCI. conditum est in Concilio Beneventano, extatque apud Marcam de concord. lib. 8. ad calcem cap. XIII. pag. 332. Nullus deinceps, inquit, in Episcopum eligatur, nisi in sacris ordinibus religiosè vivens inventus est. Sacros autem Ordines dicimus, Diaconatus, atque Presbyteratus. Hos siquidem solos primitiva lege Ecclesia habuerit, super his solum praeceptum habemus Apostoli. Subdiaconis verò, qui & ipsi altaribus administrant, opportunitate exigente concedimus, sed rarissimè; si tamen spectatae sint religionis & scientiae. Quod ipsum non sine Romani Pontificis vel Metropolitani licentiâ fieri permittimus. Tertium quod profero testimonium depromptum est ex Canonum Collectione propediem edendâ quæ Anselmo tribuitur, & ex quâ observat Vir doctissimus Antonius Augustinus de Emendatione Gratiani Dial. XV. lib. 1. ultimæ editionis pag. 172. Anselmum hoc referre ex Hieronymo in Epist. ad Titum cap. 1.
units.tr: Having examined the arguments by which he tried to weaken the force and weight of Dallaeus's argument drawn from the confusion of names, the most learned defender of the Ignatians set himself to refute what he wrote in favour of three holy orders. We would gladly take up that task, were it not that the plan of this work, as I have said, forbids it. Still, although I have decided to leave that question undiscussed, I will not hesitate to set out two or three testimonies against the number of three sacred orders, which, so far as I know, no one has yet adduced, so that it may appear what the opinion of the ancients was about the institution of the sacred orders. The first is taken from the little book On the Ecclesiastical Oppressions by Atto, Bishop of Vercelli and a writer of the tenth century. For in volume 8 of Dacherius's Spicilegium, p. 63, after quoting these words of the blessed Apostle to Timothy, Do not receive an accusation against a presbyter, and that other saying of the same Apostle from the same epistle and the same fifth chapter, Those who sin, rebuke in the presence of all, so that the others may fear, he adds on his own: For it ought not to be readily believed about a bishop or a presbyter, whose order was not yet divided. The second is supplied by Pope Urban II, who was the first of all the Roman Pontiffs to admit subdeacons to the episcopate, when circumstances required it, provided that the Roman Pontiff or the metropolitan agreed to it. He took care to attach these conditions to his decree because the subdiaconate did not belong to the sacred orders, which at the beginning were only two. Urban's decree was issued in the year of the Lord 1091, in the Council of Benevento, and it is found in Marca, On the Concord, book 8, at the end of chapter 13, p. 332: No one, it says, shall henceforth be elected bishop unless he is found living a religious life in the sacred orders. We call the sacred orders the diaconate and the presbyterate. For the Church under the primitive law had only these, and concerning these alone we have the precept of the Apostle. But to subdeacons, who also minister at the altars, we grant, when circumstances require it, but very rarely, provided they are esteemed for piety and learning. And this too we permit to be done only with the licence of the Roman Pontiff or the metropolitan. The third testimony I offer is taken from the collection of canons soon to be published, which is attributed to Anselm, and from which the very learned Antonio Agustín observes, in his On the Emendation of Gratian, dialogue 15, book 1, in the last edition, p. 172, that Anselm reports this from Jerome's commentary on the Epistle to Titus, chapter 1.

units.la: Olim idem erat Presbyter qui & Episcopus, & quæ sequuntur; sed illiserio dolet quòd ista scripserit Hieronymus, prout testatur observatione quam subjicit; Totus, inquit, ille Hieronymi locus, nisi plenius scribatur, & cùm aliis Hieronymi scriptis conferatur, nocere magis quàm prodesse potest. Nempe Vir ille perspicax Augustinus hunc Hieronymi locum Hierarchiæ Romanæ adversari animadvertebat; sed magis adhuc memorabile est quod scribit in additionibus in hunc Dialogum XV. pag. 178. An-selmus lib. 7. cap. 127. Polycarpus lib. 2. tit. 39. Rubrica scriptum est: Presbyter idem est qui Episcopus, ac solâ consuetudine præsunt Episcopi. Polycarpus quem laudat, non est (inquit pag. 361.) Scriptoris nomen, sed libri à Gregorio Presbytero collectore Canonum conscripti. Qua ætate vixerit Gregorius ille Presbyter non dicit. Quicquid sit ex his quæ descripsimus testimonijs facilè colligitur, istos mediæ seu saltem, inclinatæ ætatis Scriptores vetustioribus omninò concinere: testantur enim temporibus Apostolorum Episcoporum & Presbyterorum ordinem nondum divisum esse, ex uno siquidem gradu duo nondum fuerant facti, nullo alios primitivâ lege habuisse Ecclesiam ordines sacros præter Presbyteratum & Diaconatum, soláque consuetudine præesse Episcopos, hoc est Presbyteris esse superiores: Quod quàm sit alienum à doctissimi Vindiciarum Auctoris sententiâ nemo non videt.
units.tr: Formerly the same man was presbyter and bishop, and what follows. But Agustín grieves at this passage, which Jerome wrote, as he bears witness in the observation he adds: The whole of that passage of Jerome, unless it is written out more fully and compared with his other writings, can do more harm than good. That sharp-sighted man, Agustín, clearly saw that this passage of Jerome was adverse to the Roman hierarchy. Yet what he writes in the additions to this dialogue 15, p. 178, is even more worth noting: Anselm, book 7, chapter 127; Polycarp, book 2, title 39. The rubric reads: The presbyter is the same as the bishop, and the bishops preside only by custom. As for Polycarp, whom he praises, it is not (he says, p. 361) the name of a writer, but of a book written by Gregory the Presbyter, the collector of canons. He does not say in what age that Gregory the Presbyter lived. Whatever may be the case with the testimonies we have set out, it is easily gathered from them that these writers of the middle or at least of a leaning age agree entirely with the more ancient ones. For they testify that in the times of the Apostles the order of bishops and presbyters was not yet divided, since two had not yet been made out of one rank; that the Church under the primitive law had no sacred orders other than the presbyterate and the diaconate; and that bishops presided only by custom, that is, that they were superior to presbyters. How far this is from the opinion of the most learned Author of the Vindiciae, no one fails to see.

units.la: Ultimum Dallæi argumentum quod examinandum suscipio, & à Viri docti exceptionibus Vindicandum, ex Epistolarum inscriptionibus depromptum est: Dallæus cap. XXX. pag. 415. 416. 417. Contendit inscriptiones illas mirificas esse, laciniosas, inconditas, prodigiosæ longitudinis, præter omnium antiquissimorum Sanctorum usum, ut Clementis, Polycarpi, Smyrnensium, Lugdunésium, Cypriani, Cornelij, Firmiliani, &c. qui Epistolis suis inscriptiones ab Ignatianis longè diversas præfixerunt; utrúmque probavit præstantissimus Dallhus adductis in medium descriptísque tùm Epistolici Ignatij, tùm aliorum inscriptionibus; ut ex utrarúmque collatione liqueret Ignatianás, unâ ad Polycarpum exceptâ, tales esse quales asserit; Respondet Vindiciarum Auctor cap.16. pag. 211.212. tres ex earum numero excipiendas esse, nempe Inscriptiones ad Smyrnæos , ad Ephesios, & ad Trallesios, neque enim, inquit, contra has vel una exceptione utitur Vir doctissimus: Miror profecto hæc scripsisse Eruditissimum Pearsonium,cùm diserte testetur Dallæus , præter eas quæ sunt ad Mariam Castabalitam, & ad Polycarpum, & ad Antiochenos, & ad Philippenses , cæterarum octo longissimas esse, & laciniosas & impeditissimas inscriptiones, quasdam etiam plane prodigiosas, vel hyperbatis, & hiulcis ac pendentibus , necdum absolutis membris, deformes,vel inanibus & streperis epithetis luxuriantes , vel aliquo denique vitio insignes.Iam autem inter illas octoEpistolas quarum à Dallæo perstringuntur inscriptiones , numerantur sex Vindiciarum Auctori probatæ & pro genuinis habitæ ; aliquâ ergo exceptione utitur Dal-læus contra Inscriptiones Epistolis ad Smyrnæos,ad Ephesios, & ad Trallesios præfixas: Præterea idem Dallæus p. 417. illam ad Smyrnæos , & ipsam pariter ad Ephesios particulatim exagitat ac reprehendit; Verum equidem est Dallæum Inscriptionem quæ Epistolæ ad Romanos præscribitur integram descripsisse, & in illâ expendendâ, illiúsque vitijs notandis paulò diutiùs immoratum esse; nec immeritò, nam ejusmodi est, ut eam totam patienter legere, vix aliquem reperias, qui sustineat: Illam tamen qualis extat apud Vetustissimum Vsserij Interpretem, exhibere non gravabor : Ignatius qui & Theophorus,habenti propitiationem in magnitudine Patris altissimi, & Iesu Christi solius Filij ipsius, Ecclesiæ dilectæ & illuminatæ in voluntate volentis omnia quæ sunt secundum dilectionem Iesu Christi Dei nostri, quæ & præsidet in loco chori Romanorum, digna Deo, digna decentiâ, digna beatitudine, digna laude, digne ordinata, digne casta, & præsidens in charitate, Christi habens legem, Patris nomen, quam & saluto in nomine Iesu Christi Filij Patris, secundum carnem & spiritum unitis in omni mandato ipsius, impletis gratiâ Dei indivisim, & abstractis ab omni alieno colore, plurimùm in Domino Iesu Christo Deo nostro immaculatè gaudere. Quis ferat Inscriptionem adeò prolixam, involutam & impeditam, necnon coacervatis & malè congestis laudis epithetis scatentem ? longitudinem tuetur Vindiciarum Auctor exemplo S. Pauli qui longiusculam Epistolæ ad Romanos præfixit inscriptionem; fatetur Dallæus, non brevem & expeditam esse, ut vulgò mos erat, Paulinam inscriptionem, sed longiusculam, & nonnihil involutam, ob res gravissimas quibus plena est. At Deus bone! quantum est discriminis Paulinas inter & Ignatianas Epistolarum inscriptiones, sive res ipsas spectes, sive Oratiotionem attendas: Præterea quòd Apostololus semel atque iterùm fecerat, in omnibus paenè Epistolis fecisse Epistolicum Ignatium affirmat Dallæus; Coacervata (inquit Pearsonius) & spumosa Epitheta damnat: Quidni damnaret? cùm ea usurpet Epistolarum Scriptor præter consuetudinem Ecclesiasticorum Scriptorum Ignatij vel æqualium vel supparium, vel denique eo longè juniorum, ut liquet ex varijs à Dallæo allatis Inscriptionibus: Excusat, si Virum doctum audimus, gentis Syrorum in scribendo mos, & familiaris consuetudo: Quamobrem? Quia, inquit, Asiaticum loquendi genus reprehendebant Critici Veteres; sed nihil aliud expectabant ab ijs qui in Asiâ semper vixerunt, quod probat Ciceronis testimonio qui Asiaticos Oratores nimis redundantes esse scribit; unde colligit neminem miraturum esse, si redundantes & tumidæ videantur Inscriptiones Ignatianæ; quoniam ex Asiâ vel Syriâ Autor profectus est: Addit Vir doctus alium characterem Epistolis convenire familiaribus, alium vero quodammodo elatiorem dum ad civitates scribitur, & hoc ultimo usum esse Ignatium in Epistolâ ad Romanos: Sed pace doctissimi Viri dictum sit; hæc sunt vanissima subterfugia; Nam 1. etsi nimis redundantes sint Asiatici Oratores in Orationibus suis, hinc non sequitur redundantes & tumidas fuisse quas Epistolis suis præscribebant Inscriptiones; dum ad civitates scribitur, paulò quodammodo elatiores debent esse Epistolæ, esto; At ex eo quod paulò elatiores sunt quæ ad civitates scribuntur Epistolæ, colligi non potest redundantes & tumidas fuisse æquè ac Ignatianas illarum Inscriptiones. 2. Proferat Vir doctus Syrorum & Asiaticorum Inscriptiones Epistolarum Ignatianis similes, ut excusatum habeamus Epistolicum Ignatium; donec enim protulerit, vix ferri poterunt illius laciniosæ & impeditissimæ Inscriptiones: 3. Asiaticus erat Polycarpus, extátque illius ad Philippenses Epistola, cujus hæc Inscriptio est; Polycarpus, & qui cum eo sunt Presbyteri, Ecclesiæ Dei, quæ est Phi-lippis, misericordia vobis, & pax à Deo omnipotente, & Iesu Christo salvatore nostro abundet. Asiatici erant Smyrnæi, Inscriptio tamen Epistolæ Ecclesiæ Smyrnensis, Ecclesiæ Dei apud Philomelium, & omnibus ubicunque terrarum sanctæ & Catholicæ Ecclesiæ populis inscriptæ, simplicissima est, nihilque prorsus commune habet cum Ignatianis. Ecclesia Dei quæ est Smyrnæ, Ecclesiæ Dei apud Philomelium, & omnibus ubicunque terrarum sanctæ & Catholicæ Ecclesiæ populis, misericordia, pax & caritas Dei Patris, & Domini nostri Iesu Christi multiplicetur. Syri & Asiatici erant plerique eorum qui Paulum Samosatensem Sacerdotio abdicarunt, nihil ideò redundans aut tumidum reperies in Epistolæ illorum Synodicæ Inscriptione apud Eusebium lib. 7. cap. 30. Dionysio & Maximo, & omnibus per universum orbem comministris nostris, Episcopis, Presbyteris & Diaconis, & universæ Ecclesiæ Catholicæ quæ sub cælo est, Helenus & Hymenæus, Theophilus, &c. Carissimis fratribus in Domino salutem. Nec quicquam causæ est cur Vir doctus excipiat, Ignatium solum & vinculis innexum Florentissimas salutare Ecclesias, quasi tunc Inscriptiones longissimas, inconditas & impeditissimas, præter omnium an-tiquissimorum Sanctorum usum, Epistolis præfigere liberum esset, Hæc enim Pearsonij observatio plus subtilitatis habet quàm soliditatis : immò si verum ama-mus, frigidum est commentum in eum tantùm finem excogitatum, ut scilicet Epistolicus Ignatius indemnis evadat; & ut istius commenti vanitas magis inno-tescat, & omnia quæ inter Ignatii & aliorum Epistolas profert discrimina penitus explodantur, unico contentus ero exemplo quod extat apud Eusebii lib. 6. cap. XI. ibi enim talem habemus Ale-xandri in cappadociâ primùm, deinde Hierosolymis Episcopi ad Antiochensem Ecclesiam Epistolæ Inscriptionem. Alexander servus Dei, & vinctus Iesu Christi, beatissimæ Antiochensium Ecclesiæ in Domino salutem: Alexander ipse unicus & vinculis innexus perinde ac Ignatius, Florentissimam, ut quivis videt, salutat Ecclesiam totius Orientis Metropolim, cujus Pastor fuerat verus Ignatius : nec propterea coacervatis & congestis Epi-thetis eam variis ornat encomiis aut summis effert laudibus : Charismata autem quæ tempore Ignatii in Ecclesiis apparebant, Epistolarum Scriptorem non excusant; apparebant etiam tempore Narcissi cujus adjutor fuit Alexander prout liquet ex cap. 9. ejusdem libri Eusebii; quæ sequuntur apud Pearsonium pag. 216.217. alibi excussimus. Et ita tandem suscepto labore perfuncti sumus, præcipuè Dallæi argumenta adversus omnes doctissimi Vindiciarum Auctoris objectiones defendimus, & ab ejus Vindicavimus exceptionibus, idem de cæteris facili negotio facturi, nisi abundè sufficerent quæ ex-pendimus, ut Ignatio Apostolorum discipulo, sanctissimoque Christi martyri abjudicentur, quæ illius nomen falsò præferunt Epistolæ.
units.tr: The last of Dallæus's arguments that I undertake to examine, and to defend against the objections of the learned man, is drawn from the inscriptions of the Epistles. Dallæus (chap. 30, pp. 415–417) contends that these inscriptions are strange, rambling, disordered and of prodigious length, contrary to the practice of all the most ancient saints, such as Clement, Polycarp, the Smyrnaeans, the Lugdunenses, Cyprian, Cornelius, Firmilian and others, who prefixed to their Epistles inscriptions quite unlike the Ignatian ones. The most distinguished Dallæus proved both points by bringing forward and setting out the inscriptions of the Epistles of Ignatius and of the others, so that from comparing the two it would be plain that the Ignatian inscriptions, with the single exception of the one to Polycarp, are what he says they are. The author of the Vindiciae answers (chap. 16, pp. 211–212) that three of their number must be excepted, namely the inscriptions to the Smyrnaeans, to the Ephesians and to the Trallians, for, he says, the most learned man uses not one exception against these. I am truly surprised that the most learned Pearson wrote this, since Dallæus clearly testifies that, apart from those to Mary of Castabala, to Polycarp, to the Antiochenes and to the Philippians, the other eight are very long, rambling and most entangled inscriptions, some even utterly prodigious, deformed by hyperbata, gaping and dangling clauses, members not yet finished, or swollen with empty and noisy epithets, or in short notable for some fault or other. Now among those eight Epistles whose inscriptions Dallæus criticises are six which the author of the Vindiciae approves and holds to be genuine. Dallæus therefore does use some exception against the inscriptions prefixed to the Epistles to the Smyrnaeans, to the Ephesians and to the Trallians. Moreover, the same Dallæus (p. 417) assails and censures the inscription to the Smyrnaeans, and likewise that to the Ephesians, item by item. It is true that Dallæus transcribed the whole inscription prefixed to the Epistle to the Romans, and lingered somewhat longer over examining it and noting its faults, and not undeservedly, for it is of such a kind that you would hardly find anyone who could patiently read it through. Nevertheless I will not hesitate to set it out as it stands in the most ancient translation of Ussher: Ignatius, who is also Theophorus, to the church which has obtained mercy in the magnificence of the Father Most High and of Jesus Christ His only Son, beloved and enlightened by the will of Him who wills all things that are according to the love of Jesus Christ our God, which also presides in the place of the region of the Romans, worthy of God, worthy of honour, worthy of felicity, worthy of praise, worthily ordered, worthily pure, and presiding in love, bearing the law of Christ, bearing the name of the Father, which I also salute in the name of Jesus Christ the Son of the Father, to those united in the flesh and spirit in every commandment of His, filled indivisibly with the grace of God and cleansed from every alien colour, to rejoice most abundantly in the Lord Jesus Christ our God without blemish. Who could endure an inscription so prolix, tangled and entangled, and teeming with heaped-up and ill-assorted epithets of praise? The author of the Vindiciae defends its length by the example of St Paul, who prefixed a rather lengthy inscription to his Epistle to the Romans. Dallæus admits that the Pauline inscription is not brief and quick, as was the common custom, but somewhat long and a little involved, because of the very weighty matters with which it is full. But good God! How great is the difference between the inscriptions of the Pauline Epistles and the Ignatian ones, whether you look at the matters themselves or attend to the style! Moreover, Dallæus affirms that what the Apostle did once and again, the Epistolary Ignatius did in almost all his Epistles. Pearson says that Dallæus condemns coacervated and frothy epithets. Why would he not condemn them, since the writer of these Epistles uses them contrary to the custom of the ecclesiastical writers, whether contemporaries or near-contemporaries of Ignatius, or indeed much later than he, as is clear from the various inscriptions Dallæus brings forward? He is excused, if we listen to the learned man, by the custom and familiar habit of the Syrian people in writing. Why? Because, he says, the ancient critics found fault with the Asiatic style of speaking, but expected nothing else from those who always lived in Asia, which he proves by the testimony of Cicero, who writes that the Asiatic orators were too exuberant. From this he concludes that no one will be surprised if the Ignatian inscriptions seem exuberant and swollen, since the author came from Asia or Syria. The learned man adds that one style suits familiar letters, and another, somewhat more elevated, when writing to cities, and that Ignatius used this latter in his Epistle to the Romans. But with all due respect to the most learned man, these are the emptiest of evasions. For, first, even if the Asiatic orators are too exuberant in their speeches, it does not follow that the inscriptions they prefixed to their Epistles were exuberant and swollen. Granted, letters written to cities ought to be somewhat more elevated; but from the fact that letters written to cities are somewhat more elevated, it cannot be inferred that their inscriptions were exuberant and swollen in the same way as the Ignatian ones. Second, let the learned man produce inscriptions of Epistles by Syrians and Asiatics similar to the Ignatian ones, so that we may hold Epistolary Ignatius excused; until he does, his rambling and most entangled inscriptions can hardly be borne. Third, Polycarp was an Asiatic, and his Epistle to the Philippians survives, with this inscription: Polycarp, and the elders who are with him, to the church of God which is at Philippi: mercy to you, and peace from God Almighty and from Jesus Christ our Saviour, be multiplied. The Smyrnaeans were Asiatics, yet the inscription of the Epistle of the church of Smyrna, to the church of God at Philomelium, and to all the congregations of the holy and Catholic Church everywhere in the world, is most simple and has nothing at all in common with the Ignatian ones. The church of God which is at Smyrna, to the church of God at Philomelium, and to all the congregations of the holy and Catholic Church everywhere in the world: mercy, peace and love be multiplied from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ. Many of those who deposed Paul of Samosata from the priesthood were Syrians and Asiatics, yet you will find nothing swollen or exuberant in the inscription of their synodal Epistle, in Eusebius book 7, chap. 30: To Dionysius and Maximus, and to all our fellow-ministers throughout the whole world, bishops, elders and deacons, and to the whole Catholic Church under heaven, Helenus and Hymenaeus, Theophilus, etc., to our dearest brethren in the Lord, greeting. Nor is there any reason why the learned man should except Ignatius alone, bound in chains, who greets the flourishing churches, as though it were then lawful, contrary to the custom of all the most ancient saints, to prefix to Epistles inscriptions very long, disordered and most entangled. For this observation of Pearson has more subtlety than soundness. Indeed, if we love the truth, it is a cold contrivance, devised for the sole purpose that Epistolary Ignatius may escape unharmed; and so that the vanity of this contrivance may become more evident, and all the differences which he brings forward between the Epistles of Ignatius and those of others may be utterly exploded, I shall be content with one example, found in Eusebius book 6, chap. 11. There we have the inscription of an Epistle from Alexander, first bishop in Cappadocia and then at Jerusalem, to the church of Antioch: Alexander, servant of God and prisoner of Jesus Christ, to the most blessed church of the Antiochenes, greeting in the Lord. Alexander himself, alone and bound in chains just as Ignatius was, greets the most flourishing church, as anyone can see, the metropolis of all the East, whose minister Ignatius had truly been; yet he does not adorn it with heaped-up and piled-up epithets, nor extol it with the highest praises. As for the charismata which appeared in the churches in the time of Ignatius, they do not excuse the writer of the Epistles; they appeared also in the time of Narcissus, whose helper Alexander was, as is clear from chap. 9 of the same book of Eusebius. What follows in Pearson, pp. 216–217, we have examined elsewhere. And so at last, having undertaken the labour, we have finished, having defended Dallæus's principal arguments against all the objections of the most learned author of the Vindiciae, and having vindicated them from his exceptions. We would do the same with ease for the rest, were it not that what we have examined is quite enough to deprive of the name of Ignatius, the disciple of the Apostles and most holy martyr of Christ, those Epistles which falsely bear his name.

units.la: OBSERVATIONES IN ANNOTATIONES GUILLELMI BEVEREGII IN CANONES APOSTOLICOS.
units.tr: Observations on the Annotations of William Beveridge on the Apostolic Canons.

units.la: GUILLELMUS BEVEREGIUS qui Pandectas Canonum SS. Apostolorum & Conciliorum ab Ecclesiâ Græcâ receptorum, necnon Canonicarum SS. Patrum Epistolarum, magno reipublicæ litterariæ bono, nuper edidit, Canones illos, imprimis Apostolicos eruditissimis illustrare dignatus est observationibus, in quibus haud vulgarem viri docti & in hoc litterarum genere non sine laude versati, cernere est eruditionem. Etsi meo quidem judicio plura scripserit quæ omnium forsan eruditorum palato non sunt sapitura; Ab illis tamen examinandis ac refellendis lubens abstinuissem, ni Beveregius iisdem cum Pearsonio permotus rationibus, Dallæum nostrum fœlicis recordationis virum, etde Ecclesiâ Dei optimè meritum adortus efset, & velut Pseudapostolicorum Canonum antiquitatis inimicum quodammodo exagitâsset. Ut justa igitur tanti Viri nomini & famæ soluam parentalia, eum adversus posteriorem istum non mediocri eruditione adversarium etiam defendere decrevi. Si veritatis minus amans fuisset Dallæus, celeberrimos istos impugnatores non expertus esset: At quoniam amica magis illi fuit veritas, quàm Plato nec Socrates, stylum in eum strinxerunt doctissimi Viri, veriti scilicet ne prostrata jaceret, quam divinam putant divinitusque institutam, Episcoporum supra Presbyteros eminentia & autoritas, si epistolis Ignatianis & Apostolicis Canonibus [?]arua penitus detraheretur. Nempe Ignatius epistolicus Episcopatum, Presbyteratum & Diaconatum identidem occinit, ut persuadeat tres ab initio extitisse in Ecclesiâ Sacrorum ministrorum ordines inter se distinctos, nec aliter ferè reprobæ monetæ, hoc est Pseudapostolicorum canonum cusor ac malleator: Quamobrem Viri eruditi magnique Hierarchiæ Ecclesiasticæ tibicines, Scriptorum ejusmodi, quibus præcipuè innititur omnis Episcoporum ὑπεροχὴ[?] patroci-nium ultrò suscipiunt; quanto cum succes-su id præstiterit vindiciarum Auctor osten-dimus, num autem ex sententiâ Beyeregio successerit labor ab eo susceptus, jam disquirendum est. Beveregius equidem canones, dequibus lis est Apostolis non adscribit, de illorum tantum antiquitate certat, eosque longè vetustiores esse contendit, quàm arbitratus est Dallæus. Verum antequàm regularum istarum vetustatem expendat, duas agitat quæstiones, alteram de canonum numero, de eorum autoritate alteram. Priorem quæstionē quod spectat, eam sic definit Vir doctus, nihil certi de canonum numero ante Dionysium. Exiguum haberi posse; At postquam Monachus ille Scytha & deinde Abbas Romanus, Codicem Canonum Ecclesiæ Orientalis è Græca in Latinam Linguam transtulerat, cui etiam Latinam suam Canonum quinquaginta sub Apostolorum nomine versionem præfixerat; solos illos quinquaginta Canones per totum propemodùm Occidentem, Apostolorum titulo dignatos esse opinatur Beveregius, & inter reliquos Conciliorū Canones à Dionysio versos observari cœpisse non [?]eretur affirmare, quod quàm falsum sit, fusè adversus Pearsonium demonstravimus: Apud Græcos verò obtinuisse LXXXV non dissitemur, ab eo usque tempore quo Joannes Scholasticus, Primò Antiochiæ presbyter, posteà verò ad thronum Constantinopolitantum à Justiniano imperatore promotus, suam Canonum collectionem edidit in L. titulos distributam, quibus Canones hos-ce Apost. LXXXV. inter alios Concilio-rum commiscet. Ut de numero sic & de authoritate horum Canonum, quæ altera est quæstio, in varias, inquit Vir doctus, abitur partes, alijs ab Apostolis vel compositos, vel saltem Clementi dictatos asserentibus, alijs vero dubios & suppositicios esse, & Apostolis falsò adscriptos contendentibus; Damasceni siquidem opinio, qui falsos & nuperos istos Canones divinis libris per intolerabilem, Planéque Sacrilegam audaciam exæquavit, jam olim explosa est, & ab ipso Beveregio merito damnatur. Quicquid sit Vir eruditus ut inter duas latitantem opiniones ipsam inuestiget veritatem, & summam quoad ejus fieri potest, Canonum horum antiquitatem, ijsque debitam exinde pendentem autoritatem inueniat, antiquiora SS. Patrum qui annum quingentesimum præcesserunt, vo-lumina consulere statuit; Quæ pro suorum Canonum antiquitate allaturus est fingillatim discutiemus, si prius monuero duos Isidoros à Beveregio in unum conflari videri pag. 2.3. Nempe Isidorum Hispalésem Archiepiscopum magni nominis virum & anno septimi sæculi sexto & tricesimo de[?]hatum, consulto confundere videtur, cum Isidoro Mercatore noni saeculi tenebrione, qui stramineas primorum Pontificum Romanorum Decretales epistolas pessimo consilio consarcinavit; quoniam quos hic Mercator Canones probat Apostolicos, ille reijcit, & à sede Apostolicâ mimimè receptos diserte testatur: prout à nobis contra Ignatianorum Patronum ostensum est, ubi etiam quae describit Hincmari verba Beveregius pag. 3. explicavimus, & locum quodammodo luxatum appositè ni fallor restituimus,
units.tr: William Beveridge, who lately published his Pandects of the Canons of the Holy Apostles and of the Councils received by the Greek Church, together with the canonical Epistles of the Holy Fathers, to the great benefit of the literary republic, has deigned to illustrate those canons, chiefly the Apostolic ones, with learned observations. In them one can discern no ordinary erudition in a learned man who is practised in this kind of literature and deserving of praise. Although in my judgment he has written a good deal that will perhaps not please the taste of every scholar, I would gladly have refrained from examining and refuting those points, had Beveridge not been moved by the same reasons as Pearson and attacked our Daillé, a man of happy memory who deserved very well of the Church of God, and had he not, as it were, harried him as an enemy of the antiquity of the pseudo-Apostolic Canons. So, to pay the due funeral rites to the name and reputation of so great a man, I have resolved to defend him also against this later opponent, who is no mean scholar. If Daillé had been less a lover of truth, he would not have had to face those most famous assailants. But since truth was dearer to him than Plato, or even Socrates, those most learned men have drawn their pens against him, fearing, of course, that the eminence and authority of bishops over presbyters, which they believe divine and divinely instituted, would lie prostrate and be stripped away entirely if the Ignatian letters and the Apostolic Canons were taken from them. Indeed Ignatius, in the letters, repeatedly sings of bishop, presbyter and deacon, so as to persuade us that from the beginning there were three orders of sacred ministers in the Church, distinct from one another. Hardly otherwise acts the coiner and hammerer of the base pseudo-Apostolic canons. Therefore learned men and the champions of the great ecclesiastical hierarchy readily take up the defence of those writings on which the whole primacy [ὑπεροχὴ] of bishops especially rests. We have shown with what success the author of the Vindiciae accomplished this; now it must be inquired whether the labour Beveridge undertook succeeded according to his own opinion. Beveridge indeed does not ascribe the canons in dispute to the Apostles; he contends only about their antiquity, and maintains that they are far older than Daillé thought. But before he weighs the antiquity of these rules, he raises two questions, one about the number of the canons and the other about their authority. As to the first question, the learned man settles it thus: nothing certain can be held about the number of the canons before Dionysius. But after that Scythian monk, and then Roman abbot, had translated the code of canons of the Eastern Church from Greek into Latin, and had prefixed to it his own Latin version of fifty canons under the name of the Apostles, Beveridge thinks that those fifty canons alone were honoured with the title of Apostolic throughout almost the whole West, and that the other canons of the councils, as translated by Dionysius, began to be observed; he does not hesitate to affirm this, though how false it is I have demonstrated at length against Pearson. Among the Greeks, however, we do not deny that the eighty-five obtained, from the time when John Scholasticus, first presbyter of Antioch and afterwards promoted by the emperor Justinian to the throne of Constantinople, published his collection of canons, distributed into fifty titles, in which he mingles these eighty-five Apostolic canons among the other canons of the councils. As to the number, so also as to the authority of these canons, which is the second question, the learned man says, the opinions go in different directions: some assert that they were composed by the Apostles, or at least dictated by Clement; others hold them doubtful and spurious, and contend that they were falsely ascribed to the Apostles. The opinion of Damascene, who put these false and recent canons on a level with the divine books through intolerable and frankly sacrilegious audacity, has long since been exploded, and Beveridge himself rightly condemns it. Whatever the case, the learned man, that he may find the truth lurking between the two opinions, and as far as possible the highest antiquity of these canons and the authority due to them, has resolved to consult the older volumes of the Holy Fathers, which preceded the year five hundred. We shall discuss individually what he will bring forward for the antiquity of his canons, if I first point out that Beveridge seems to have run two Isidores together, on pages 2 and 3. Namely, he seems deliberately to confuse Isidore, archbishop of Seville, a man of great name who died in the year 636 of the seventh century, with Isidore Mercator, the forger of the ninth century, who with the worst design patched together the straw-like decretal letters of the first Roman pontiffs. For what this Mercator approves as Apostolic, the other rejects, and expressly testifies that they were by no means received by the Apostolic See. As we have shown against the patron of the Ignatians, where we also explained the words of Hincmar that Beveridge describes on page 3, and, unless I am mistaken, appositely restored a passage somewhat dislocated.

units.la: His praemissis expendenda sunt quae profert Vir doctus testimonia, ut Canonibus suis summam comparet antiquitatem; Telam à Chalcedonensi synodo exorsus, usque ad ipsa tempora quibus hi Canones illi constituti videntur, hoc est, ad prima propemodum Ecclesiae recens natae incunabula eam gradatim ascendendo protrahere molitur, ut ait num. 8. pag. 3. 4. Utrum Viri docti tela bilix sit an triplix ignoratur. Vereor tamen ne staminis male subtexta trama pessimam conficiat carbasum.Ex Synodo Chalcedonensi haec Can. xxii. verba describit, non licere clericis post mortem sui Episcopi, res ad eum pertinentes diripere, sicut antiquis quoque Canonibus prohibitum est. Per hos antiquos Canones nullum alium designari putarvir doctus praeter Canonem XL. Apost. quo cautum est ne mortuo Episcopo rerum Ecclesiasticarum occasione, quæ propria fuerant Episcopi interciderent, sive diriperentur: Interpretationis suæ istam adfert rationem Beveregius, quòd nullos alios Synodo Chalcedonensi vetustiores Canones invenire est hoc prohibentes, præter Apostolicos. Profecto satis mirari non possum hæc à Beveregio scripta esse, quem scilicet latere non poterat, paria præcipere Synodi Antiochenæ Can. XXIV. centum & decem annos ante Chalcedonensem; Ad Canonem igitur Antiochenum eò magis referenda sunt Patrum chalcedonensium verba, quòd Antiochenæ regulæ omnibus notissimæ erant, & ab ipsis Chalcedonensibus Patribus dissertissimè, neque semel ex codice Ecclesiæ universalis citatæ; cùm Canonum Apostolicorum codicis, neque in Chalcedonensi Synodo, neque in superioribus retrò monumentis ulla extet mentio. Dallæus contra Turrianum disputans eandem adhibuerat solutionem ad objectionem ex Synodo Chalcedonensi depromptam, Dallæi solutionem impugnare debebat Beveregius, & Turrianum à quo pleraque sua accepit argumenta adversus ipsum Dallæum fortiter tueri: Canoni Antiocheno non intempestivè forte adijcias Canonem xxxii. Codicis Canonum Ecclesiae Africanae ex Concilio Carthaginensi anno Domini cccccxix. habiti. Ut ut est quoniam clarissimus Dallæus pleraque Beveregij argumenta refellit Turrianicis occurrendo objectionibus, ne actum agere videamur, ea solùm deinceps examinaturi sumus quae de novo proponit, & Dallæi responsiones ab ejus exceptioni-bus, si aliquibus forte utitur, vindicaturi.
units.tr: With these things premised, we must weigh the testimonies the learned man brings forward, so as to give his canons the highest antiquity. Beginning from the Council of Chalcedon, he labours to bring the web gradually up, step by step, to the very times in which these canons seem to have been established, that is, to the nearly first beginnings of the newly born Church, as he says in section 8, pages 3 and 4. Whether the learned man's weapon is two-edged or three-edged is not known. I fear, however, that a warp badly woven into the threads will make a very bad cloth. From the Synod of Chalcedon he describes these words of canon 22: it is not lawful for clergy, after the death of their bishop, to plunder the property belonging to him, as has also been forbidden by the ancient canons. The learned man thinks that by these ancient canons no others are meant except canon 40 of the Apostolic canons, which provides that, when a bishop dies, the property of the Church should not be lost or plundered on the pretext of what had been the bishop's own. Beveridge gives this reason for his interpretation: that no older canons prohibiting this can be found before the Council of Chalcedon except the Apostolic ones. Truly I cannot sufficiently wonder that Beveridge wrote this, since he could not fail to know that the Synod of Antioch, canon 24, enjoins the same things, a hundred and ten years before Chalcedon. Therefore the words of the Chalcedonian Fathers must be referred all the more to the Antiochene canon, because the Antiochene rules were known to everyone and were cited by the Chalcedonian Fathers themselves very clearly, and not only once, from the code of the universal Church. But of a code of the Apostolic canons there is no mention, either at Chalcedon or in any earlier record. Daillé, disputing against Turrian, had used the same answer to the objection taken from the Council of Chalcedon. Beveridge ought to have refuted Daillé's answer, and to have defended vigorously Turrian, from whom he took most of his arguments against Daillé himself. Perhaps it would not be out of place to add to the Antiochene canon canon 32 of the code of canons of the African Church, from the Council of Carthage held in the year of the Lord 419. However that may be, since the most illustrious Daillé refutes most of Beveridge's arguments by meeting the objections of Turrian, lest we seem to be going over old ground, we shall henceforth examine only those points which he now proposes, and defend Daillé's replies against his objections, if he perhaps uses any.

units.la: In totâ Præfatione ubi agit de numero & autoritate necnon de antiquitate istorum Canonum, paucissima adfert pag. 3. 4. quibus à Dallæo abundè satisfactum non fuerit; adeò ut etiamnum valeant illius responsiones, quando nullis adversus eas usus est exceptionibus Vir doctus. Nouum adfert pro antiquitate Canonum Apostolicorum testimonium, ex quodam Concilio provinciali desumptum; celebratum est anno ccclxxxxiv[?] Constantinopoli, de Agapio & Bagadio, utroque Episcopatum Bostræ sibi vendicante, in quo Nectarius Constantinopolitanus & reliqui Patres decernebant, Episcopum accusatum non nisi Synodi & provinciæ Episcoporum sententiâ deponendum esse, sicut etiam Apostolici definière Canones. His ultimis verbis ad Can. Apost. lxxiv. respexisse Concilij Pa-tres contendit Beveregius; Turrianus maxiinus [?] antiquitatis helluo, & acerrimus Canonum istorum propugnator, testimonium istud vel non viderat vel contempserat; nulla enim Dallaei ad hoc testimonium extet responsio. At propterea non est quod sibi gratuletur Beveregius, quasi multum conferrent ad suorum Canonum antiquitatem stabiliendam, huius Synodi verba; Plura siquidem reponi possunt; 1. Canon LXXIV. ad quem respexisse Concilij Patres hariolatur, Graecis tunc temporis vix notus erat; Nemo enim Graecorum Canones L x x x v. in lucem protulit ante Joannem Antiochenum qui sub Justiniano florebat fatente ipso Beveregio: 2. Canon ille synodicae definitioni qua de agitur nequaquam congruit, nihilque fere cum ea commune habet. 3. Balsamon, Zonaras & Aristenus qui hanc synodicam definitionem interpretati sunt, nihil plane dicunt de Canone Apostolico, neque ad eum respexisse Synodum innuunt; observant dumtaxat Canonem duodecimum Synodi Carthaginensis ista Constantinopolitana posterioris rem aliter definiisse, & constitutionis ex qua argumentatur Vir doctus vim atque pondus elevasse, quod minime facturi erant Carthaginenses Patres, si eam Apostolico Canone inniti arbitrati essent.
units.tr: In the whole preface, where he treats of the number and authority, and also of the antiquity of these canons, he brings forward very few things on pages 3 and 4 which have not been amply answered by Daillé, so that his replies still hold, since the learned man has used no objections against them. He brings forward a new testimony for the antiquity of the Apostolic canons, taken from a certain provincial council, which was held at Constantinople in the year 394, concerning Agapius and Bagadius, both of whom claimed the bishopric of Bostra. In it Nectarius of Constantinople and the other Fathers decreed that a bishop accused could be deposed only by the sentence of the synod and of the bishops of the province, just as the Apostolic canons also decreed. Beveridge contends that the Fathers of the council had these last words in view when referring to Apostolic canon 74. Turrian, the greatest glutton of antiquity and the keenest champion of these canons, either had not seen this testimony or had despised it; for no answer of Daillé to this testimony exists. But Beveridge has no reason to congratulate himself on this account, as if the words of this synod contributed much to establishing the antiquity of his canons. Many things can indeed be replied. 1. Canon 74, to which he guesses the Fathers of the council referred, was then scarcely known to the Greeks. For no Greek brought out a collection of eighty-five canons before John of Antioch, who flourished under Justinian, as Beveridge himself admits. 2. That canon does not at all agree with the synodal decision in question, and has almost nothing in common with it. 3. Balsamon, Zonaras and Aristenus, who interpreted this synodal decision, say nothing at all about an Apostolic canon, nor do they hint that the synod had it in view. They only observe that the Constantinopolitan Fathers of the later synod settled the matter differently from canon 12 of the Synod of Carthage, and weakened the force and weight of the enactment from which the learned man argues. The Carthaginian Fathers would certainly not have done this if they had thought it rested on an Apostolic canon.

units.la: 4. Nullum praecise Canonem indicant Constantinopolitani Patres, nullamque cujusdam Canonum Apostolicorum sylloges mentionem faciunt, sed de Canonibus Apostolicis generaliter loquuntur; 5. Dallæus certis atque evidentibus argumentis demonstravit, illam Apostolicorum, Canonum farraginem falsam ac fictitiam esse ab ignoto tenebrione multis post Apostolorum & Clementis mortem temporibus confarcinatâ, quod imprimis de triginta quinq; postremis inter quos numeratur Canon. IXXIV.[?] intelligendum est, si Dallæi argumenta refellisset Vir doctus, nostrum esset illius responsiones expendere & confutare, sed quoniam pleraque intacta reliquit, exceptis quibusdam Dallæi conjecturis quæ ad Canonum istorum antiquitatem spectant, Dallæanis argumentis inhærere nos opportet, donec ab Adversario refellantur. 6. Fatetur ipse Beveregius Canones istos neque ab Apostolis neque à Clemente illorum discipulo conditos esse; Ergo per Canones Apostolicos Constantinopolitani Patres Ecclesiasticos significant Canones ante illud tempus constitutos, quales sunt Canones IV. XII. XIII. XIV. XV. Concilii Anthiocheni ante quadraginta tres annos sanciti &ad quos respectum habuisse Synodi Constantinopolitanæ Episcopos nullus dubito; immo forte etiam ad Canonem quartum magni Concilii Nicæni, ubi Episcopum ab omnibus provinciæ Episcopis constituendum esse decernitur : ab iis enim eum deponi opportet à quibus est constitutus , nempe non minor debet esse abdicantium quàm constituentium numerus. Ideóque Arabianus Ancyræ Episcopus & Constantinopolitanorum Patrum unus hunc Nicænum Canonem ante annos circiter LXX. conditum laudat , ut ostendat iniquam esse Bagadii Episcopi à duobus solis Episcopis factam depositionem. Cæterum Canones istos Ecclesiasticos Apostolicorum nomine nuncupant Patres , non solùm quia doctrinæ Apostolorum consonos eos esse putabant , sed etiam quoniam præcepta majorum leges Apostolicas arbitra-bantur, ut loquitur Hieronymus Epist. 28. ad Lucinium.
units.tr: 4. The Constantinopolitan Fathers name no single canon precisely, nor do they mention any collection of certain Apostolic Canons. They speak of the Apostolic Canons only in general terms. 5. Dallaeus has demonstrated, by certain and evident arguments, that this jumble of Apostolic Canons is false and fictitious, patched together by some unknown scribbler many centuries after the deaths of the Apostles and Clement. This applies above all to the last thirty-five, among which is numbered Canon LXXIV.[?] If the learned man had refuted Dallaeus's arguments, it would be our task to weigh his answers and refute them. But since he has left most of them untouched, apart from certain conjectures of Dallaeus about the antiquity of those canons, we must hold to Dallaeus's arguments until the Adversary refutes them. 6. Beveregius himself admits that these canons were composed neither by the Apostles nor by Clement, their disciple. Therefore by "Apostolic Canons" the Constantinopolitan Fathers mean the ecclesiastical canons enacted before that time, such as canons IV, XII, XIII, XIV and XV of the Council of Antioch, enacted forty-three years earlier. I do not doubt that the bishops of the Synod of Constantinople had regard to these, and perhaps even to the fourth canon of the great Council of Nicaea, where it is decreed that a bishop must be appointed by all the bishops of the province. For he ought to be deposed by those by whom he was appointed, since the number of those removing him must not be smaller than the number of those who appointed him. Hence Arabianus, bishop of Ancyra and one of the Constantinopolitan Fathers, cites this Nicene canon, enacted about seventy years earlier, to show that the deposition of Bagadius, bishop, carried out by only two bishops, was unjust. Moreover, the Fathers called these ecclesiastical canons by the name of Apostolic not only because they thought them consonant with the teaching of the Apostles, but also because they judged the precepts of their elders to be Apostolic laws, as Jerome says in Epistle 28 to Lucinius. Epist. 28.

units.la: III. Secundùm testimonium ad quod Dallæus nihil reposuit , quia à nemine ante Beveregium objectum fuit descriptum est non ex Epistolâ secundi Concilii universalis Constantinopoli habitæ anno Domini CCCLXXXI. ut hariolatur Vir doctus, sed ex alterius Synodi anno sequenti ea-dem in urbe congregatæ , ad Damasum, Ambrosium, aliosque tunc temporis Ro-mæ congregatos Epistolâ , quâ inter alia dicunt , antiqua , ut probè [?]nostra obtinuit
units.tr: III. The testimony to which Dallaeus made no reply, because no one before Beveregius had objected to it, is taken not from the letter of the second universal Council, held at Constantinople in the year of the Lord 381, as the learned man conjectures, but from a letter of another Synod gathered in the same city the following year, addressed to Damasus, Ambrose and the others then assembled at Rome. In it, among other things, they say: the ancient sanction, as has rightly prevailed among us

units.la: lib.c.9. sanctio, & sanctorum Patrum qui Nicææ congregati sunt, regula : nimirum ut Antistites una cum finitimis (modo ipsis visum fuerit) Episcopis, prout utile judicaverint, ordinationes faciantin suis ipsorū provinciis;Per antiquam illam sanctionem designari opinatur Beveregius Can. Apost. xiv. & xv. quod nulla Synodo Nicænâ, si illum audimus, antiquior lex extitit quæ hoc constituit, præter Canones illos Apostolicos. At quam vana sit ac frivola eruditi Viri ratiocinatio, pluribus demonstratum imus, 1. Designati Canones nihil plane dicunt de Episcoporum ordinationibus, de quibus expresse agitur in testimonio allato, ut cuivis legenti patet; unde liquet, ut id obiter notem, ad fictitios istos Canones minime confugiendum esse, quoties apud Veteres fit mentio alicujus sanctionis antiquæ quæ in genuinis quos habemus Conciliorum Canonibus hodie non extat, plures siquidem ejusmodi sanctiones usu & consuetudine obtinuêre, quæ tamen litteris statim traditæ non fuêre. 2. Si tunc temporis extitissent prædicti Canones, & ad eos respexissent Synodi Constantinopolitanæ Patres, plusquam verisimile est eos hanc Canonum collectionem memoraturos esse æquè ac Nicænorum Patrum regulam, vel saltem Canones ipsos suis numeris indicaturos, 3. Fieri potest ut duabus locutionibus seu phrasibus unam & eandem rem significaverint Patres, nempe regulam Nicænam quæ eorum respectu antiqua erat, ut pote ante annos LVII, promulgata. 4. Si antiquam illam sanctionem à Nicænorum Patrum regulâ diversam esse contendit Vir doctus; respondeo sanctionem illam antiquam usu ac consuetudine tacitè, ut alia plura, introductam esse, & continuâ praxi roboratam, donec tandem à Concilio Nicæno primo in Canonem redacta & scripto mandata fuit: rem autem ita se habere facilè demonstrari potest; Eusebius enim de Narcisso Episcopo Hierosolymitano verba faciens, tradit Hist. li. 6.cap.10.alium ejus loco Episcopum à vicinis Episcopis constitutum esse; Cœterum, inquit, post Narcissi fugam, ignaris omnibus ubinam gentium ageret, visum est finitimarum Ecclesiarum Episcopis alium ejus loco Episcopum ordinare, Dium nomine. Narcisso verò ut ita dicam redivivo, & ad ejusdem Ecclesiæ clavum sedenti, Alexander Hierosolymarum Episcopus ordinatur & velut adjutor datur, ob admodùm provectam Narcissi ætatem, annos quippe natus erat sexdecim supra centum; quomodo ei adjutor datus sit Alexander, & ad Episcopatum promotus Hierosolymitanum, si rogas, respondebit Eusebius cap. xi. Hoc factum esse consentientibus Vicinarum Ecclesiarum Episcopis ; nulla prorsus mentione facta legis aut sanctionis scriptae quae hoc praeciperet, non obliturus certe si aliquam tunc temporis extitisse scivisset ; nempe juxta confuetudinem jam receptam egerunt Palaestini Episcopi , non autem secundum aliquem scriptum Canonem ; Haec autem contigerunt annos circiter cxx. ante Concilium Nicaenum ; a quo primum ista consuetudo scripto ut opinor , mandata est. Verum enimuero , ne vulgari suo paralogismo in quo tantopere se jactat Beveregius , imposterum abutatur Turriani vestigia calcans, consulat quaeso quae adfert Clarissimus Dallaeus cap. 8. pag, 513. 514. ut paralogismi illius vanitatem ostendat ? ejus expendat interrogationes , illisque appositè. respondeat ? & ni argumenti sui vitium deprehendit,eum talpa caeciorem esse opportet; Quoties offendit Beveregius loca quaedam apud Veteres , in quibus fit mentio Ecclesiasticorum & Apostolicorum Canonum , vel antiquae legis , sanctionis aut definitionis , statim ea avidus arripit , & ad Canonum suorum antiquitatem commendandam & confirmandam etiam obtorto collo trahit : praesertim dum nullum in caeteris quae supersunt antiquitatis monumentis istiusmodi sanctionum extat vestigium. Tamen ut ex his locis rite argumentari possit Vir doctus, duo mihi neceffaria videntur : alterum ut quibus de agimus sanctiones in vetustis Conciliorum Canonibus non reperiantur : nam si reperiuntur:quin ad vera illa ac genuina monumenta referendæ sint, potiùs quàm ad notha & spuria, quales sunt Apostolici Canones, dubitabit nemo : Alterum verò ut in ApostolicisCanonibus habeantur quotquot Veteribus memoratæ sunt plurimis in locis, antiquæ definitiones seu regulæ, vetustæque ac canonicæ Ecclesiæ leges : Alioquin si quædam memoratæ sunt quarum ne minimum quidem in totâ lxxxv. Can, Apost. sylloge cernere est vestigium ; eas ab antiquo usu & prisca consuetudine arcessamus & evocemus opportet. Tales autem sunt illi Canones, illæque leges, sanctiones ac regulæ quarumm eminerunt Nicæni Patres Can. xviii. & forte etiam xiii, Ancyrani Can.21. & Neocæsarienses Can, x i v. prout est à Dallæo nostro observatum : Ergo Beveregiani argumenti vim penitus elevabo, quoties vetustas illas leges,ex quibus pro Canonum suorum æquo majore antiquitate argumentari solet, vel ad genuina quæ superstunt Veterum monumenta referam, vel ad antiquum usum & priscam aliquam consuetudinem quæ in Ecclesiâ obtinebat, antequam ullus hac de re Canon ab aliquâ Synodo conditus esset.
units.tr: lib.c.9. ...and the rule of the holy Fathers who met at Nicaea: namely, that the bishops, together with the neighbouring bishops (if it seemed good to them), should make appointments in their own provinces as they judged expedient. Beveregius thinks that this ancient sanction is designated by Canons 14 and 15 of the Apostolic Canons, since, if we listen to him, no law older than the Nicene Synod laid this down, apart from those Apostolic Canons. But how vain and frivolous the learned man's reasoning is, we shall demonstrate at length. 1. The Canons cited say nothing at all about the appointment of bishops, which is expressly the subject of the testimony quoted, as is plain to anyone who reads it. From this it is clear, to note it in passing, that one must by no means have recourse to those fictitious canons whenever among the ancients mention is made of some ancient sanction which does not today appear in the genuine canons of the Councils that we have. For many such sanctions had force through use and custom, yet were not committed to writing at once. 2. If the aforementioned canons had existed at that time, and the Fathers of the Synod of Constantinople had had regard to them, it is more than likely that they would have mentioned this collection just as they mentioned the rule of the Nicene Fathers, or at least would have indicated the canons themselves by their numbers. 3. It is possible that the Fathers signified one and the same thing by two different expressions, namely the Nicene rule, which in their view was ancient, being promulgated fifty-seven years earlier. 4.
