If the learned man contends that that ancient sanction differs from the rule of the Nicene Fathers, I reply that this sanction was introduced tacitly through use and custom, like many others, and was strengthened by continuous practice until at last it was reduced to a canon by the first Council of Nicaea and committed to writing. That this is so can easily be shown. Eusebius, speaking of Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem, relates in Hist. book 6, chapter 10, that another bishop was appointed in his place by the neighbouring bishops: However, he says, after Narcissus fled, when everyone was ignorant where in the world he was living, it seemed good to the bishops of the neighbouring Churches to ordain another bishop in his place, Dius by name. But when Narcissus, so to speak, came back to life and sat again at the helm of the same Church, Alexander was ordained bishop of Jerusalem and given as a kind of assistant, because Narcissus was very far advanced in age, indeed sixteen years over a hundred. If you ask how Alexander was given as his assistant and promoted to the bishopric of Jerusalem, Eusebius in chapter 11 will answer: This was done with the agreement of the bishops of the neighbouring Churches. There is no mention at all of any written law or sanction which prescribed this. Certainly Eusebius would not have passed over it if he had known that any such existed at that time. Clearly the Palestinian bishops acted according to a custom already accepted, not according to some written canon. These events occurred about 120 years before the Council of Nicaea, by which, as I think, this custom was first committed to writing. But indeed, lest Beveregius again abuse his familiar paralogism, in which he so greatly boasts, and, treading in the footsteps of Turrianus, let him please consult what the most distinguished Dallaeus adduces in chapter 8, pages 513–514, in order to show the vanity of that paralogism. Let him weigh Dallaeus's questions and answer them to the point; and if he does not perceive the flaw in his own argument, he must be blinder than a mole. Whenever Beveregius comes upon certain passages among the ancients which mention ecclesiastical and Apostolic Canons, or an ancient law, sanction or definition, he eagerly seizes them at once and drags them, even by force, to commend and confirm the antiquity of his canons, especially since no trace of such sanctions is found in the other surviving monuments of antiquity. Yet if the learned man is to argue soundly from these passages, two things seem necessary to me. The first is that the sanctions in question should not be found in the ancient canons of the Councils. For if they are found there, no one will doubt that they must be referred to those true and genuine monuments rather than to spurious and forged ones, such as the Apostolic Canons. The second is that whatever the ancients mention in many places as ancient definitions or rules, and as the venerable and canonical laws of the Church, should be found in the Apostolic Canons. Otherwise, if some things are mentioned of which not even the least trace can be discerned in the whole collection of eighty-five Apostolic Canons, we must derive and summon them from ancient usage and primitive custom. Such are those canons, laws, sanctions and rules which the Nicene Fathers (Can. 18, and perhaps also Can. 13), the Ancyrene (Can. 21) and the Neocaesarean (Can. 14) brought to light, as our Dallaeus has observed. Therefore I will utterly overthrow the force of Beveregius's argument whenever I refer those ancient laws, from which he is wont to argue for the greater antiquity of his canons, either to the genuine monuments of the ancients that survive, or to ancient usage and some primitive custom which prevailed in the Church before any canon on this matter had been enacted by any Synod.

units.la: Hoc pacto facilè occurram verbi gratia Objectioni ex Theodoreto ductæ: Theodoretus enim Hist. lib. 5. cap.xxiii.Euagrij in Episcopum Antiochenum ordinationem damnat, ut pote à Paulino solo decessore, & jam decedente factam, contra Ecclesiasticam regulam & multos Canones, qui neque morienti Episcopo permittunt ut suo loco quemquam constituat, & omnes provinciæ Episcopos convocari jubent. Præterea absque tribus Episcopis ordinationem cujusquam Episcopi fieri vetant. Mirari subit hoc Theodoreti testimonium à Turriano prætermissum esse, tamen etsi nihil intactum reliquerit ut Canonibus Apostolicis quos deperibat fidem compararet; illud saltem inter Turrianica argumenta apud Dallæum non comparet: At Turriano multò nasutior Beveregius per Canones quos transgressum esse Paulinum tradit Theodoretus, significari Can. Apost. 1. & lxxvi. affirmare non veretur: Ego verò contra rejectis spuriis Can. Nicæn. iv. & Antiochen. xix & xxiii. Designari acriter contendo, nec aliter hunc Theodoreti locum interpretatur in Annotationibus suis Doctissimus Henricus Valesius. Hisce Canonibus adcijci potest xx. Concilii Arelatensis primi an.cccxiv. Præterea absurdam plane esse Viri doɖti[?] ratiocinationem liquet, ex eo quod Canon primus Pseudapostolicus Episcopi ordinationem à duobus Episcopis factam probat, Theodoretus autem Evagrii ordinationem vitiosam esse tradit & minimè Canonicam, quod absque tribus Episcopis ordinationem cujusquam Episcopi Canones fieri vetant : Canon vero LXXVI. Episcoporum tantum cognatos speĉtat, qualis non erat Evagrius Paulini respeĉtu, addo quod adeò obscurus erat tunc temporis Canon ille ut nondum in lucem prolatum esse par sit credere.
units.tr: In this way I shall easily meet, for example, the objection drawn from Theodoret. For Theodoret, in his Church History book 5, chapter 23, condemns the ordination of Evagrius to the see of Antioch, as made by Paulinus alone, and when he was already dying, "contrary to the ecclesiastical rule and many canons, which neither permit a dying bishop to appoint anyone in his place, nor order all the bishops of the province to be convoked. Moreover, they forbid the ordination of any bishop without three bishops." It is surprising that this testimony of Theodoret was passed over by Turrianus; yet although he left nothing untouched in order to bring his faith into line with the Apostolic Canons, which he was losing, at least this one does not appear among the Turrianic arguments in Dallaeus. But Beveregius, much keener-scented than Turrianus, does not hesitate to affirm that by the canons which Theodoret says Paulinus transgressed, the first and seventy-sixth Apostolic Canons are meant. I, on the contrary, vigorously maintain that the spurious canons iv, and xix and xxiii of Antioch are designated, and the learned Henricus Valesius interprets this passage of Theodoret in his notes in no other way. To these canons may be added canon xx of the First Council of Arles, of the year 314. Moreover, it is plainly clear that the reasoning of the learned man is absurd, since the first pseudo-apostolic canon proves that an ordination of a bishop made by two bishops is valid, whereas Theodoret says that the ordination of Evagrius was faulty and not at all canonical, because the canons forbid the ordination of any bishop without three bishops. The seventy-sixth canon concerns only the kinsmen of bishops, and Evagrius was not such in relation to Paulinus. I add that that canon was so obscure at the time that it is fitting to believe it had not yet been brought to light.

units.la: Objeĉtionem à Georgii Cappadocis in Sedem Alexandrinam, expulso Athanasio, intrusione violentâ petitam occupavit Dallæus cap. ix. pag.522[?]. cujus responsioni addi potest Concilii Ancyrani Canon xviii. anno cccxiv. conditus.
units.tr: The objection drawn from the violent intrusion of George of Cappadocia into the see of Alexandria, after the expulsion of Athanasius, was dealt with by Dallaeus in chapter 9, page 522[?]. To his response may be added canon xviii of the Council of Ancyra, enacted in the year 314.

units.la: Quæ adfert ex lib. 3. cap. lxi. & lxii. de vitâ Constantini Imperatoris facilè diluuntur, si per Canonem Apostolicum, Apostolorum intelligis traditionem, & per Ecclesiasticam Sanctionem Canonem Nicænum xv. vel consuetudinem seu usum antiquum qui ante illud Concilium in Ecclesiâ vigebat, & tacito Christianorum consensu pro lege habebatur, donec tanidem à Nicœnis Patribus in Canonem fuit redactus & litteris traditus ; Præterea Constantinus de Canonum Apostolicorum collectione penitus tacuit, nullumque præcise Canonem designavit.
units.tr: The things he adduces from book 3, chapters 61 and 62, of the Life of the Emperor Constantine are easily refuted, if by "Apostolic canon" you understand the tradition of the Apostles, and by "ecclesiastical sanction" canon xv of Nicaea, or the ancient custom and usage which prevailed in the Church before that council and was held as law by the tacit consent of Christians, until at length it was drawn up as a canon by the Nicene Fathers and committed to writing. Moreover, Constantine kept entirely silent about any collection of the Apostolic Canons, and designated no canon precisely.

units.la: Pergit Vir Doctus, Alexander, inquit; Episcopus Alexandrinus ad Alexandrum Episcopum CP. scribens, Episcopos aliquos, qui eos, quos ipse excommunicaverat, in Communionem recepissent, criminatur, eo quod nec Apostolica regula id permittit, apud Theodoretum Hist. Eccles. lib. 1. cap. 4. Hæc Alexandri verba de Can. Apost. xii. xiii, & xvi. explicat Beveregius. Simili argumento ex aliis Veterum scriptis deprompto occurrit Dallæus cap. 8. Nos ad istud reponimus 1. nullum ab Alexandro indicari peculiarem Canonem, nullamque ab eo memorari Canonum Apostolicorum Syllogen, 2. Apostolicam illam regulam Alexandro nihil aliud esse quàm Canones ante Concilium Nicænum sancitos velut Can. liii. Concilii Eliberitani anno cccv. celebrati, vel xvi. Concilii Arelatensis primi anno cccxiv. habiti, vel denique ut remalitius repetam Canonem illum non scriptum, publicoque tametsi tacito, omnium usu ac consensu receptum, secundum quem Clerus Romanus vacante sede post Hygini mortem, nempe circa annum Domini cL. Marcionem ob vitiatam virgi-nem à proprio Parente excommunicatum, in Communionem admittere recusavit, ab Apostolorum Discipulis,ut ait Epiphanius, edoctus, Cur me, inquit Marcion Seniores illos alloquens, recipere noluistis? Responderunt illi. Nobis injussu venerandi Patris tui facere istud non licet. Una siquidem fides est, & animorum una consensio: neque contra spectatissimum Comministrum Patrem tuum moliri quippiam possumus. Apud Epiphan. Hær. xlii. pag. 302. 303. Ecce Apostoli-cum Canonem, non fictitium illum quidem aut spurium, sed verum ac genuinum, ab Apostolis Discipulis suis traditum, & ab Apostolorum Discipulis, non scripto, sed usu ac praxi ad successores transmissum; Nam ab Apostolorum Discipulis edocti Ecclesiæ Romanæ Seniores seu Presbyteri, Marcionem à Patre excommunicatum recipere noluerunt; quia scilicet, hæc erat Ecclesiæ Disciplina ut ab aliis excommunicati, ab aliis sine excommunicantium con-sensu non admitterentur: Quid ad hæc repositurus sit Beveregius non video, nul-lus siquidem ei superest tergiversandi lo-cus, cum ipse fateatur secundo labente & ineunte tertio à Christi nativitate seculo constitutos esse, quos cæco prosequitur amore, Canones Apostolicos; Epiphanii autem narratio tempus à Viro doćto præstitutum antecessit. Hinc sequitur levissimam esse nulliusque omnino momenti quam ex verbis Alexandri Alexandrini Episcopi elicit conclusionem Beveregius pag.3. totam videlicet Nicænam Synodum non latuisse Canones istos Apost. quoniam huic Synodo interfuit postea Alexander: Nam ex iis quæ hactenus scripsimus luce meridianâ clarius patet. Alexandrum ipsum ad istos Canones nequaquam respexisse, nondum quippe ab impostore conflati erant: pertendit tamen acerrimus Canonum propugnator, eos Synodum non latuisse, idque ex ipsis Canonibus ab eâ constitutis demonstrari posse. Verùm nihil causæ est cur in istis refellendis immoremur, donec Dallæi ad hæc argumenta responsiones confutaverit Vir doctus.
units.tr: The learned man goes on: "Alexander," he says, "bishop of Alexandria, writing to Alexander, bishop of Constantinople, accuses some bishops who had received into communion those whom he himself had excommunicated, on the ground that not even the Apostolic rule permits this," in Theodoret, Church History book 1, chapter 4. Beveregius explains these words of Alexander as referring to Apostolic canons xii, xiii and xvi. Dallaeus, chapter 8, meets a similar argument drawn from other writings of the Fathers. To this we reply: 1. Alexander indicates no particular canon, nor does he mention any collection of Apostolic Canons. 2. That Apostolic rule was for Alexander nothing other than canons enacted before the Council of Nicaea, such as canon liii of the Council of Elvira, celebrated in the year 305, or canon xvi of the First Council of Arles, held in the year 314; or finally, to repeat more briefly, that unwritten canon, received by the common, though tacit, public use and consent of all, according to which the Roman clergy, when the see was vacant after the death of Hyginus, about the year of the Lord 150, refused to admit to communion Marcion, excommunicated by his own father for having violated a virgin. As Epiphanius says, they had been taught this by the disciples of the Apostles. "Why," said Marcion, addressing those elders, "did you not wish to receive me?" They replied: "It is not lawful for us to do this without the command of your venerable father. There is indeed one faith and one agreement of minds; nor can we undertake anything against your most distinguished fellow minister, your father." In Epiphanius, Heresy 42, pages 302, 303. Behold an Apostolic canon, not fictitious or spurious indeed, but true and genuine, handed down by the disciples of the Apostles, and transmitted to successors by the disciples of the Apostles not in writing but by usage and practice. For the elders or presbyters of the Roman Church, taught by the disciples of the Apostles, refused to receive Marcion, excommunicated by his father; because, clearly, this was the discipline of the Church, that those excommunicated by some were not admitted by others without the consent of those who had excommunicated them. What Beveregius will reply to this I do not see, for he has no room left for evasion, since he himself admits that the Apostolic Canons, whom he pursues with a blind love, were constituted in the second century as it ends and the third begins after the birth of Christ; yet Epiphanius's narrative precedes the time fixed by the learned man. It follows that the conclusion Beveregius draws on page 3 from the words of Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, is most slight and of no weight at all, namely that the whole Nicene Synod was not unaware of those Apostolic Canons, since Alexander later attended this synod. For it is clearer than noonday light from what we have written so far that Alexander himself did not have those canons in view at all, since they had not yet been fabricated by the impostor. Yet this most zealous champion of the canons insists that the Synod was not unaware of them, and that this can be shown from the canons enacted by it. But there is no reason for us to linger over refuting these points until the learned man has refuted Dallaeus's responses to these arguments.

units.la: Quæ sequuntur initio pag.4. ejusmodi sunt ut vix responsionem mereantur argumentatur enim ex tractatu de ablutione pedum qui sub Cypriani nomine circumfertur, quamvis probè novit Cypriani non esse tractatum illum, sed Arnoldi Abbatis Bonævallensis duodecimi seculi Scriptoris; (si modo inquit, Cypriano rectè adscribatur) dubitanter loquitur, cùm tamen Arnoldi esse ignorare Beveregium non pateretur Oxoniensis istius libri Codex manu exaratus, præter alia multa quæ Cypriano illum abjudicant, & Arnoldo Bernardi æqua-li & amico adscribunt.
units.tr: What follows at the beginning of page 4 is of such a kind that it hardly deserves a reply. For he argues from the treatise on the washing of feet, which circulates under the name of Cyprian, although he knows well that this treatise is not Cyprian's but that of Arnold, abbot of Bonneval, a writer of the twelfth century; (he speaks doubtfully, he says, "if indeed it is rightly ascribed to Cyprian"), yet Beveregius could not be ignorant that it is Arnold's, since the manuscript of this Oxford book, written by hand, besides many other things which deny it to Cyprian, ascribes it to Arnold, the contemporary and friend of Bernard.

units.la: Memorat Tertullianus lib. de Jeiuniis cap. XIII. quæ præcepta agebantur per Græcias Concilia; Ut autem talia Concilia haberentur, nusquam tunc temporis præceptum legimus; ait Vir doctus, præterquam Canone Apost. XXXVII. Mira certè Beveregii argumentatio, quasi ab ipsis Ecclesiis præcipi non potuerint illa Concilia aliquot menses vel etiam annum integrum, antequam celebrarentur, ut hodie fit apud Protestantes in Gallia & alibi: Secundo in omnibus codicibus manu exaratis non legitur præcepta, sed præter ea, prout legerunt ultimi Tertulliani editores. Urget tandem Vir doctus hæc ejusdem Tertulliani verba, ad hæreticos vetamur accedere lib. de præscript cap. XII. velut Can. Apost. XLV. vel LXV. indigetare voluisset, tamen nihil ejusmodi cernere est apud Tertullianum, qui si aliquò respexit, ad istud Divi Pauli præceptum eum spectasse omninò est verisimile. Hæreticum hominem, post unam & alteram admonitionem reijce: Ut qui noris eversum esse cum qui sit ejusmodi, & peccare, & qui suopte judicio sit condemnatus. Tit. 3. 10. 11.
units.tr: Tertullian, in his book On Fasting, chapter 13, mentions the things that were enjoined by the councils held throughout Greece. But, says the learned man, we nowhere read at that time of any precept that such councils should be held, except in Apostolic Canon xxxvii. Certainly a strange argument of Beveregius, as if those councils could not have been enjoined by the churches themselves some months or even a whole year before they were held, as today happens among the Protestants in France and elsewhere. Second, in all the manuscripts written by hand one reads not praecepta but praeter ea, as the latest editors of Tertullian have read it. The learned man finally presses these words of the same Tertullian, "we are forbidden to approach heretics," from the book On Prescription, chapter 12, as if they were drawn from Apostolic Canon xlv or lxv; yet nothing of the kind can be discerned in Tertullian, who, if he looked to any passage, very probably had in view that precept of the Apostle Paul: "Reject a heretical man after one or two warnings, knowing that such a man is perverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgement." Titus 3:10-11.

units.la: V. Priusquam ulterius progrediatur Vir doctus duo observati; 1. Hosce Canones sub variis nominibus antiquitus cognitos suisse; Sed perperam se torquet in inuestigandis Canonum qui nondum conflati erant nominibus, non entium non sunt qualitates nec nomina. 2. non 1. solos sed plures antiquis hisce Patribus innotuisse, adeo ut xxxv. posteriores ejusdem ætatis ac 1. priores non immeritò censeantur. Verum salsissimam esse hanc propositionem demonstravimus, dum argumenta ad eam confirmandam allata, & quæ jam tantùm indicat pag. 4. discussimus ac refellimus.
units.tr: Before the learned man proceeds further, I observe two things: 1. That these canons were known in antiquity under various names. But he wrongly torments himself in searching for names of canons which had not yet been collected; non-existent things have no qualities or names. 2. That not only the first ones but many more were known to these ancient Fathers, so that the thirty-five later ones are not unjustly reckoned of the same age as the first. But we have shown this proposition to be most absurd, while we discussed and refuted the arguments adduced to confirm it, which he merely indicates on page 4.

units.la: Ut ut est arbitratur Beveregius istos Canones à Viris Apostolicis, hoc est, secundo labente & ineunte tertio à Christi nativitate seculo constitutos passim deinceps innotuisse, quod sic probat pag. 4. Hoc, inquit, non ex eo tantùm liquet, quod quarto demum currente seculo pro antiquis habiti fue-rint; sed exinde præcipuè quod secundâ tertiaque fluente à Verbo incarnato centuriâ, om-nes vel plerosque saltem (à quibus & de cæteris facile est conjecturam facere) in Ecclesiâ Christianâ obtinuisse, ex Clemente Alexandrino, Origene, Tertulliano, aliisque ejusdem ætatis Scriptoribus & Ecclesiasticis historiis abundè constet. Verùmen imuerò utramque Viri docti propositionem negamus, nempe Canones à viris Apostolicis constitutos esse. Et secundo labente & ineunte tertio à Christi nativitate seculo conditos: Nec minus falsæ sunt quibus id adstruere nituntur rationes; Neque enim quarto demum currente seculo pro antiquis habiti fuerunt, ut perperam asserit Beveregius, neque secundâ tertiaque fluente à Verbo incarnato centuriâ in Ecclesiâ Christianâ obtinuerunt; affirmat quidem id abunde constare ex Veteribus quibusdam quos designat Scri-ptoribus, at cùm nihil planè ad id probანdum ex illis describat, respondendi onere ac necessitate nos levat, quid autem in explicandis Canonibus sit præstiturus suo loco expendemus. Interim observat Vir do-ctus nonnullos ex hisce Canonibus à Conciliis tunc dierum celebratis editos esse; sed hæc observatio illius causam minimè juvat, non negabat Dallæus à variis Conciliis pleraque sua accepisse planum & impostorem qui Canonum Pseudapostolicorum syllogen consarcinavit: at inde non sequitur Canonum istorum farraginem quarto demum currente seculo pro antiquâ ha-bitam esse, nec in Ecclesiâ Christianâ secundo tertioque obtinuisse: Non diffiteor quasdam in Ecclesiâ Christianâ secundo & tertio seculo obtinuisse consuetudines quæ pro legibus habebantur, immò quosdam scriptos Canones, sed aliquem extitisse Canonum Ecclesiasticorum Codicem secundo labente & ineunte tertio à Christi nativitate seculo collectum diserte nego, tantùm abest ut tunc dierum obtinuerit Canonum Apostolicorum Syllogè ; Hinc liquet intempestivè à Beveregio scribi Canonem septimum de Paschalis celebritatis tempore à Conciliis Romano, Palæstino, Pontico, Gallico, Osroeno, aliisque constitutum esse anno circiter CIXXXXVIII[?]. Eusebius quidem Hist. Eccl. lib. 3. cap. 23. horum Conciliorum meminit, sed nihil planè refert utrum ex istis vel ex aliis posterioribus Conciliis desumptus fuerit Canon Apostolorum septimus ; quamuis probare nequeat Vir doctus Canonem quo de agimus ab hisce Conciliis accepisse regularum istarum confarcinatorem : immò verisimilius est à Nicænis Patribus sua de paschalis celebritatis tempore mutuatum esse impostorem ; Nam ab eo tantùm tempore convenerunt inter se Christiani de celeberrimi istius Festi die, cùm antea diversis illud celebrarent diebus, alij videlicet eodem cum Judæis die, alij verò Resurrectionis Dominicæ die : Hæc autem diversitas nequaquam erat futura, si Canones Apostolici Codex Canonum Ecclesiæ primitivæ (hoc est Ecclesiæ fecundi labentis aut ineuntis vel saltem currentis tertii seculi ) meritissimo jure nuncupari debent, utáit Beveregius pag. 5. Idem plane dico de Canonibus xxxxvi. & xxxxvii. à viro doćto indicatis pag. 4. quorum ille hæreticorum baptismum non approbat, iste verò rebaptizari præcipit ab hæreticis baptizatos : si enim tertio seculo iam adulto extitisset Codex iste Canonū Ecclesiæ primitivæ, non est credibile Stephanum Pontificem Romanum hæreticos omnes sine baptismo admissurum esse, & contrariam Cypriani praxim damnaturum, nec Cyprianum hûc Codicem silentio fuisse prætériturum, ut suam de omnibus rebaptizandis hæreticis tueretur sententiam : Præterea Patres Concilii Arelatensis 1. anno Dom. cccxiv. habiti Canonem viii. nunquam condidissent, eo siquidem decernunt ut omnes hæretici in nomine Trinitatis baptisati sine baptismo recipiantur, nullâ prorsus Codicis alicuius Canonum Ecclesiæ primitivæ[?] mentione facta ; Instat Vir doctus, & Canones Apostolicos in unum corpus tertio demum currente seculo collectos esse contendit, isti que Hinemari Rhemensis verbis demonstrare nititur, Canones qui vocantur Apostolorum, antequam Episcopi Concilia liberè inciperent celebrare, à devotis quibusque collecti; Verùm cùm Hincmarus noni seculi Scriptor de re adeò antiquâ absque alicujus vetustioris autoritate id proferat, illius hac de re testimonium contemni debet, his adde Hincmarum eodem in loco scribere hosce Canones Episcopalium Conciliorum autoritate minimè constitutos esse, contra quàm sentit Beveregius pag. 4. neque id solum, sed ita de illis loquitur ut ab eo ferè contemptos non dubites.
units.tr: Be that as it may, Beveregius thinks these canons were drawn up by the apostolic men, that is, at the end of the second century and the beginning of the third after Christ's birth, and that they became known everywhere in succession. He proves this on p. 4: This is clear not only from the fact that they were held to be ancient only in the fourth century, but chiefly because in the second and third centuries after the Word was made flesh they were in use, or at least most of them (and from these one can easily conjecture about the rest), throughout the Christian Church; this is abundantly evident from Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Tertullian and other writers and church historians of the same age. But we deny both propositions of this learned man: that the canons were drawn up by apostolic men, and that they were composed at the end of the second and the beginning of the third century after Christ's birth. The reasons by which he tries to establish these are just as false. For they were not held to be ancient only in the fourth century, as Beveregius wrongly asserts, nor were they in use in the Christian Church during the second and third centuries after the Word was made flesh. He does indeed claim that this is abundantly evident from certain ancient writers whom he names, but since he describes nothing from them that proves it, he relieves us of the burden and necessity of answering. What he will accomplish in explaining the canons we shall weigh in its proper place. Meanwhile the learned man observes that some of these canons were issued by councils held in those days. But this observation does not help his cause at all. Dallaeus did not deny that most of their content came from various councils; but the man who is a fraud, who stitched together the collection of Pseudo-Apostolic canons, does not follow from this. It does not follow that this heap of canons was held to be ancient in the fourth century, or that it was in use in the Christian Church in the second and third centuries. I do not deny that certain customs were in use in the Christian Church in the second and third centuries, which were regarded as laws, and even some written canons. But I flatly deny that any collection of ecclesiastical canons existed at the end of the second and the beginning of the third century after Christ's birth. So far was the collection of Apostolic canons from being in use in those days. Hence it is plain that Beveregius wrongly writes that the seventh canon, on the time of the Paschal celebration, was established at about the year 198 by the councils of Rome, Palestine, Pontus, Gaul, Osrhoene and others. Eusebius, in Hist. Eccl. bk. 3, ch. 23, does mention these councils, but he says nothing at all about whether the seventh Apostolic canon was taken from these or from some other later councils. Although the learned man cannot prove that the compiler of those rules took the canon in question from these councils, it is more probable that the impostor borrowed it from the Nicene Fathers on the time of the Paschal celebration. For only from that time did Christians agree with one another about the day of this most celebrated feast. Before that they celebrated it on different days: some on the same day as the Jews, others on the day of the Lord's Resurrection. This difference would by no means have existed if the Apostolic Canons ought rightly to be called the Code of the Canons of the Primitive Church (that is, of the Church of the second century, either at its close or its beginning, or at least of the running third century), as Beveregius says on p. 5. I say exactly the same about canons 46 and 47, which the learned man cites on p. 4. The one does not approve the baptism of heretics, and the other orders that those baptized by heretics be rebaptized. For if this Code of the Canons of the Primitive Church had existed already in the adult third century, it is not credible that Stephen, the Roman Pontiff, would have admitted all heretics without baptism and condemned the practice of Cyprian. Nor would Cyprian have passed over this Code in silence, in order to defend his opinion that all heretics must be rebaptized. Moreover, the Fathers of the First Council of Arles, held in the year of the Lord 314, would never have framed their eighth canon. For by it they decree that all heretics baptized in the name of the Trinity are to be received without baptism, and they make no mention at all of any Code of canons of the Primitive Church. The learned man insists, and contends that the Apostolic Canons were collected into one body only at the end of the third century. He tries to prove this from the words of Hincmar of Reims: the canons which are called Apostolic were collected by various devout men before the bishops began to hold councils freely. But since Hincmar, a writer of the ninth century, offers this about so ancient a matter without any authority older than himself, his testimony on the point ought to be disregarded. Add to this that Hincmar, in the same place, writes that these canons were by no means established by the authority of episcopal councils, contrary to what Beveregius thinks on p. 4. And not only that: he speaks of them in such a way that you cannot doubt he almost despised them.

units.la: Vir tamen doctus non parum sibi gratulatur, quod ad suam de Canonibus Apostolicis vulgò dictis sententiam quam proximè accedere opinatur Albaspinæum Episcopum Aurelianensem observ.li. 1.cap. 13. ubi vetustam hanc Canonum collectionem nihil aliud esse contendit, quàm Breviarium & Epitomen privatorum Conciliorum, & rerum ab Episcopis privatis sanctitarum, qui Ecclesias Græcas ante Concilium Nicænum administrarunt. Clarissimus Dallæus hanc Doctissimi Albaspinæi opinionem expendit & refellit lib. 3. cap. xxi. At quoniam nonnulla ex iis quæ contra Albaspinæum profert argumentis, Beveregianæ sententiæ repugnare videntur, ea paucis, ut loci inquit, ratio postulat, discutiemus, nihil scilicet intactum relinquet eruditissimus Canonum Apostolicorum Patronus, ut Dallæi argumenta confutet, hancque Canonum Syllogen, Codicem Canonum Ecclesiæ primitivæ fuisse euincat; Sed priufquam Beveregii rationes accuratius excutiantur, quædam adnotanda mihi videntur, 1. Dallæus fatetur pag. 670. Albaspinæi sententiam proximè ad verum accedere, si ipsam Canonum Apostolicorum materiam, seorsim ab eâ formâ, quam in hac Sylloge habet, sumptam nudè, sim-pliciterque spectemus: quia apparet plurima ac ferè omnia, ex quibus hæc Sylloge constat, decreta, si per se singula consi-derentur, variis temporibus, aliis alia sæculis & locis, toto quatuor primorum sæculorum decursu in Orientali Ecclesiâ facta fuisse, ut optimè demonstrant argumenta ab Albaspinæo allata. 2. Albaspinæi observationi illud quoque adjecit Dallæus, videri & ex Antiocheno Concilio desumptos non paucos hujus Apostolicæ[?] farraginis Canones, ut alteros cum alteris conferenti liquebit. 3. Et-si Dallæo cum Albaspinæo eo usque non malè conveniat, non autem cum Beveregio, qui hosce Canones quotquot sunt tertio demum currente sæculo in unum corpus collectos perperam affirmat; in eo tamen ab Albaspinæo dissentit Dallæus, quod cum eo fateri non potest omnia quæ in his Canonibus habentur, ex privatis Græcorum, sive Conciliorum, sive Episcopo-rum actis decretisque sumpta fuisse. Opinionis suæ istam adfert rationem, quædam videlicet in his legi, quæ ab omnis Græcanicæ Ecclesiæ, præsertim ante Nicænam Synodum Doctrinâ sic abhorrent, ut non sit verisimile, ea unquam ab ullo Græcorum Catholicorum sive Concilio, sive Episcopo, fuisse tradita; Exemplum profert ex Can. ixxxv[?]. Ideo decernitur tres Maccabaicos, & oc[illegible, ~2 letters] Constitutionum Apostolicarum libros inter Canonicos esse recensendos, Dallæus autem de hoc Decreto verba faciens sic loquitur, Quis enim quæso Vetustiorum, non dico Latinorum, Sed & Græcorum Patrum, tertium librum Maccabaicum in sacrum Veteris Testamenti, vel Clementinarum Constitutionum octo volumina in Novi Canonem ante hujus Syllogess patrem retulerat.
units.tr: Yet the learned man congratulates himself not a little that he thinks his opinion about the so-called Apostolic Canons comes very close to that of Albaspinus, bishop of Orléans, in Observations bk. 1, ch. 13. There Albaspinus contends that this ancient collection of canons is nothing other than an abridgment and epitome of private councils, and of the matters decided by private bishops who governed the Greek churches before the Council of Nicaea. The most distinguished Dallaeus examined and refuted this opinion of the most learned Albaspinus in bk. 3, ch. 21. But since some of the arguments that he brings against Albaspinus seem to oppose the opinion of Beveregius, the matter requires us, as the place demands, to discuss them briefly. The most learned defender of the Apostolic Canons will leave nothing untouched, so that he may refute Dallaeus's arguments and prove that this collection of canons was the Code of the Canons of the Primitive Church. But before Beveregius's arguments are examined more closely, some points seem to me worth noting. (1) Dallaeus admits on p. 670 that Albaspinus's opinion comes very near the truth if we consider the very matter of the Apostolic Canons, taken apart from the form that it has in this collection, simply and plainly. For it is evident that most of the decrees of which this collection consists, if each is considered by itself, were made in the Eastern Church at various times, some in one age and place, others in another, throughout the whole course of the first four centuries. The arguments that Albaspinus brings forward demonstrate this very well. (2) Dallaeus added to Albaspinus's observation that not a few of these Apostolic canons appear to have been taken from the Council of Antioch, as will be plain to anyone who compares them with one another. (3) And although Dallaeus agrees well enough with Albaspinus so far, though not with Beveregius, who wrongly asserts that all these canons, however many there are, were collected into one body only at the end of the third century, Dallaeus does differ from Albaspinus in this: he cannot agree with him that everything contained in these canons was taken from the private acts and decrees of the Greeks, whether of councils or of bishops. He gives this reason for his opinion: some things are read in them which so greatly conflict with the teaching of the whole Greek Church, especially before the Synod of Nicaea, that it is not likely they were ever handed down by any Catholic Greek, whether council or bishop. He offers an example from canon 85: it is decreed that the three books of the Maccabees and the Constitutions of the Apostles, in eight books, are to be counted among the canonical books. Dallaeus, speaking of this decree, says: For who, I ask, of the older writers, I do not say of the Latins, but even of the Greek Fathers, had reckoned the third book of the Maccabees among the sacred books of the Old Testament, or the eight volumes of the Clementine Constitutions in the New Testament canon before the compiler of this Synopsis?

units.la: Respondet Beveregius pag. 5. primò quod ad libros Maccabaicos spectat, in antiquissimâ Græcâ Canonum collectione à Joanne Antiocheno elaborată tit. 1. ubi hic Canon extat, nullam omnino librorum Maccabaicorum mentionem occurrere, unde colligit libros istos in recentioribus horum Canonum editionibus, aliâ quàm priorum conditorum manu insertos videri; Ego verò Beveregii conclusionem nego, eo magis quod in versione Latinâ Collectionis Joa. Anthiocheni numerantur tres libri Maccabaici : nec est quod editorum incuriam arguat Vir doctus in Canonem LXXXV. pag. 39. quasi eorum negligentia ac supinitate in Latinam versionem irrepserint : Verisimilius enim est in Graeco quodam Codice manu exarato ita legisse editores & interpretes, alioquin hac de re lectorem erant mo[?]ituri ; nisi malis dicere Joh. Antiochenum libros Maccabaicos in suâ collectione de industriâ omisisse, quoniam in Ecclesiæ Græcæ scripturarum Canone illius ætate non extabant, ut liquet ex Canone quem exhibet Leontius Joh. Antiocheni ut quibusdam placet æqualis vel suppar de Sectis act. 2. tom. XI. Bibl. Pat. pag. 496. Quid autem, ait Vir doctus, si concedamus tres Maccabaicos libros dicto Canoni ab initio insertos fuisse? Hoccine probando esset, hos Canones nec ante Concilium Nicaenum constitutos esse? nihil minus. Immo optimè probatur ; Nam si tertio currente seculo in unum corpus collecti sunt omnes isti Canones ut tradit Beveregius, quomodo factum est ut libri Maccabaici omissi sint in Canonicorum Veteris Testamenti librorum catalogis ante & post Concilium Nicaenum contextis, ut fatetur ipse Canonum propugnator? Certè vix est credibile eos in suis catalogis omissuros esse Gregorium Nazianzenum, Amphilochium , Athanasium , Epiphanium , qui post Concilium Nicænum Scripserunt , necnon Synodum Laodicenam Nicænâ pluribus annis posteriorem,si tunc dierum extitisset Canonum Apostolicorum farrago , quam Codicem Canonum Ecclesiæ primitivæ indigetare non veretur Beveregius. Hisce diffidens solutionibus Vir doctus alió confugit , observatque in duobus antiquissimis versionis τ̃ῶν ȝ.[?] MSS.tres Maccabaicos, inter reliquos Veteris Testamenti libros recenseri, saltem in Vaticano Codice ante mille ducentos annos , ut putat , exarato , in altero verò qui in Angliâ asservatur,quiqueVaticanum annis æquat saltem si non superat , tertius Maccabaicorum reliquis Veteris Testamenti libris subnectitur , quibus, inquit, suffragantur, non tantùm editionesVeneta & Complutensis , sed & antiqua Syriaca versio, quâ sic inscribitur , item liber tertius Maccabæorum. Verùm ista Beveregii causam minimè juvant , cùm enim proximo alterove post concessum Nicænum seculo exarati sint illi Codices , fatente ipso Dallæi adversario , Dallæani argumenti vim nequaquam elevant Beveregianæ observationes , quando hoc solum ostendere aggres-sus est Dallæus , Canones scilicet Aposto-licos non ante Synodum Nicænam sancitos esse : Tamen veri prorsus dissimillimum arbitratur Beveregius, tres Maccabaicos inter Canonicos V. T. libros in illis Codicibus recenseri, nisi ante illam Synodum in eorum censum alicubi relati suissent ; Ego contrarium plane colligo ex eo quod ab Ecclesiasticis Scriptoribus Synodo Nicæna vetustioribus Maccabaici inter Canonicos V. T. libros nusquam numerati sunt : Præterea frustra antiquos illos versionis τῶν ό[?]. Manu exaratos Codices urget Vir doctus, cum liquido constet Maccabæorum libros ab Ecclesia Judaica pro Canonicis nunquam habitos, sed ad Scripta Apocrypha amandatos, ut tradunt Veteres. Præsertim Hieronymus cujus ætate extra Canonicorum censum rejiciebantur Maccabaici libri, tertius imprimis, neque id solum, sed ipse Gregorius Papa primus li. 19. in Job. cap. 13. initio diserte testatur libros illos non esse Canonicos. Origines pergit Beveregius, tres Maccabæorum reliquis sacræ Scripturæ libris non obscure subjungere videtur, quod probat quibusdam illius verbis apud Euseb. Hist. Eccles. lib. 6. cap. 25. ubi Origines post enumeratos Canonicos omnes V. T. libros, addit juxta Valesii versionem ; Extra horum censum sunt libri Maccabæorum qui inscribuntur Sarbet Sarbane el. Hinc[?] sequi putat Vir doctus tres Maccabæorum libros ab Origene designari ; Tamen si accuratè perpendantur Origenis verba, non magis de tribus quam de duobus eum loquutum esse apparebit, τὰ μακχαβαϊκὰ[?] enim de duobus æquè ac de tribus explicari possunt. Præterea perinde est si tres aut duos numeras, quando Maccabaici omnes libri extra Canonicorum classem & ordinem ab Origene recensentur, laudant Maccabæorum libros, si Beveregium audimus, Tertullianus, Clemens Alexandrinus, & alii ejusdem ætatis Scriptores ; Verum eos laudant ut alia Scripta Apocrypha, ex quibus plura subinde describunt testimonia ; salsum est igitur Maccabæorum libros viginti duobus Hebraicis tunc temporis tanquam Canonicos fuisse subjunctos, nonnullis quidem in locis duos, in aliis tres : nec obstat quod Scripturæ Canon nondum exactè determinatus erat. Quamvis enim ab his plures, ab illis pauciores libri Canonici numerentur, in eo tamen convenerunt omnes antiqui Scriptores ante & post Concilium Nicænum, quod Maccabæorum libros, tertium præsertim à Canonicorum censu eliminarunt.
units.tr: Beveridge responds, p. 5, first as to the Maccabean books. In the very ancient Greek collection of canons compiled by John of Antioch, title 1, where this canon stands, no mention of the Maccabean books occurs at all. From this he infers that those books were inserted into the more recent editions of these canons by a hand other than that of the original compilers. I, however, deny Beveridge's conclusion, the more so because the Latin version of John of Antioch's collection lists three Maccabean books. The learned man need not charge the editors with carelessness regarding canon 85, p. 39, as if their negligence and inattention had crept into the Latin version. It is more likely that the editors and translators read this in some Greek manuscript, otherwise they would have been bound to tell the reader about it. Unless you would rather say that John of Antioch deliberately omitted the Maccabean books from his collection, because they were not in the Greek Church's canon of Scripture in his age. This is clear from the canon that Leontius, said by some to be a contemporary or near equal of John of Antioch, sets out in On the Sects, act. 2, in volume 11 of the Bibliotheca Patrum, p. 496. The learned man says: But what if we grant that three Maccabean books were inserted into the said canon from the beginning? Would that prove that these canons were not established before the Council of Nicaea? By no means. Indeed it proves this very well. For if all those canons were gathered into one body in the third century, as Beveridge teaches, how is it that the Maccabean books were omitted from the catalogues of the canonical books of the Old Testament, which were compiled before and after the Council of Nicaea, as the defender of the canons himself admits? It is hardly credible that Gregory Nazianzen, Amphilochius, Athanasius and Epiphanius, who wrote after the Council of Nicaea, would have omitted them from their catalogues, and likewise the Synod of Laodicea, several years later than Nicaea, if at that time there had existed that medley of the Apostolic Canons which Beveridge does not hesitate to call the Code of the Canons of the Primitive Church. Distrusting these solutions, the learned man takes refuge elsewhere. He observes that in two very ancient manuscripts of the version of the [Seventy], the three Maccabean books are listed among the other books of the Old Testament: at least in the Vatican Codex, written, as he thinks, about twelve hundred years ago, and in the other, which is kept in England and which equals the Vatican in age, if it does not surpass it, the third book of the Maccabees is appended to the other books of the Old Testament. In support of this, he says, stand not only the Venetian and Complutensian editions, but also the ancient Syriac version, which is inscribed thus: likewise the third book of the Maccabees. But these things do not help Beveridge's cause at all. For since those codices were written in the century following the Council of Nicaea, or one century after it, as Daillé's own opponent admits, Beveridge's observations do not in any way weaken the force of Daillé's argument, since Daillé has undertaken to show only this: that the Apostolic Canons were not established before the Synod of Nicaea. Yet Beveridge thinks it entirely unlikely that the three Maccabean books were listed among the canonical books of the Old Testament in those codices, unless they had been reckoned among them somewhere before that Synod. I conclude the very opposite from the fact that the Maccabean books are nowhere numbered among the canonical books of the Old Testament by ecclesiastical writers earlier than the Synod of Nicaea. Moreover, the learned man presses those ancient manuscripts of the version of the [Seventy] in vain, since it is clear that the Jewish Church never regarded the books of the Maccabees as canonical, but relegated them to the apocryphal writings, as the ancients testify. Above all, Jerome, in whose age the Maccabean books, especially the third, were rejected from the canonical list, testifies to this. Nor is this all: Pope Gregory the First, in the beginning of chapter 13 of book 19 on Job, expressly declares that those books are not canonical. Beveridge goes on: he seems to append the third book of the Maccabees to the other books of Holy Scripture, not obscurely; this he thinks is proved by some words of Origen in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 6, chapter 25, where Origen, after enumerating all the canonical books of the Old Testament, adds, according to Valesius' version: Outside the number of these are the books of the Maccabees, which are entitled Sarbet Sarbane el. From this the learned man thinks it follows that Origen designates three books of the Maccabees. Yet if Origen's words are weighed carefully, it will appear that he speaks no more of three than of two, since [τὰ μακχαβαϊκὰ] can be explained equally of two or of three. Moreover, it makes no difference whether you count three or two, since Origen lists all the Maccabean books outside the class and order of the canonical books. Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, and other writers of the same age, if we listen to Beveridge, praise the books of the Maccabees. But they praise them as they praise other apocryphal writings, from which they frequently quote many testimonies. It is therefore false that the books of the Maccabees were added to the twenty-two Hebrew books of that time as canonical, some in some places two, in others three. Nor does it stand in the way that the canon of Scripture was not yet exactly fixed. For although more or fewer canonical books are counted by different writers, all the ancient writers, before and after the Council of Nicaea, agreed on this: that they excluded the books of the Maccabees, especially the third, from the number of the canonical books.

units.la: Accedo ad octo Clementinarum Constitutionum volumina, ex quibus contra antiquitatem horum Canonum disputat Dallæus; Dallæum arguit Beveregius, ac si quæ hodie sub Apostolicarum Constitutionum nomine circum feruntur, cum iis confunderet quæ Epiphanii temporibus extabant: Sed Dallæi mentem non percepit non ita disputat Dallæus, ut pote qui fuissime probavit lib. 1. de Pseudepig. Apostol. cap. 2. longè diversas esse hodiernas Constitutiones, ab iis quæ Epiphanii ævo legeban- tur.
units.tr: I come now to the eight volumes of the Clementine Constitutions, against the antiquity of which Daillé argues. Beveridge charges Daillé with confusing the Constitutions which are circulated today under the name of the Apostolic Constitutions with those which existed in Epiphanius' time. But he has not grasped Daillé's meaning. Daillé does not argue in this way; indeed he most clearly proved, in book 1 of On the Pseudepigrapha of the Apostles, chapter 2, that the present Constitutions are very different from those which were read in Epiphanius' day.

units.la: Hoc solum vult Clarissimus Dallæus, Cõstitutiones illas sive hodiernas sive Epiphanianas à nemine ante Concilium Nicænum in Canonem Scripturæ relatas esse, unde colligit post illa tempora vixisse Ca- nonum Apostolicorum Consarcinatorem. Unus Epiphanius circa annum Domini CCCLXXV. Clementinas Constitutiones aliquâ cum laude nominavit, ante eum nemo; His adde Epiphanium ipsum disertè testari in verbis à Viro docto allatis, opus illud dubiæ apud multos esse fidei, etsi illud non improbandum putet; At neque Epiphanius qui post Synodum Nicænam claruit, neque alius quisquam Synodo vetustior octo Constitutionum libros inter Canonicos recensuit, frustra igitur ex Epiphanii verbis, liquere opinatur Beveregius, Constitutiones illas ab Epiphanio laudatas Summæ tunc temporis in Ecclesiâ autoritatis fuisse: Siccine libri dubiæ, incertæ ac controversiæ fidei apud quarti seculi Christianos summæ fuerint autoritatis? Cōstitutionum opus negat Epiphanius esse ἀδόκιμον, reprobum, sive reprobatum, sed inde non sequitur summæ fuisse autoritatis, non ignorat acerrimus Canonum Vindex libros ἀντιλεγομένας[?] & quibus contradicitur extra Canonicorum censum à Veteribus recensitos esse : Laudat quidem Epiphanius quod in eo opere continueretur omnis ordo Canonicus, nihil in esset vel à fide vel à Disciplinâ Ecclesiæ alienum. At non ideò fit ( aiebat Dallæus lib. 1. cap. 2. pag. 37. ) ut libros à Clemente veré scriptos, veréque ab Apostolis instituta dictataque, quæcunque in illis narrantur, fuisse crediderit. Multis enim libris nihil in est vel à fide vel àDisciplinâ Ecclesiæ alienum,quos non id circo dixeris vel Clementinos, vel Apostolicos : Sed concedamus eruditò Beveregio, vel certè donemus fuisse in eâ sententiâ Epiphanium, ut exististimaverit suarum illarum Diataxeon veré authores, scriptoresque fuisse Apostolos, quorum nomen præferebant, non ideò conseceris, vel id verum esse, vel saltem idem sensisse Græcam illius temporis Ecclesiam. Immò contrarium tradit ipse, multos videlicet de illo Constitutionum opere dubitasse : jam autem iniquum esset unum multis præferri : Præterea hoc probandum sufceepit [?] Dallæus, hos Canones non ante Synodum Nicænam sancitos esse, ut contrarium adstruat Beveregius Epiphanium qui 1. post Synodum annis scribebat in medium profert, nullumque Scriptorem Epiphanio antiquiorem laudare potuit, qui Maccabaicos libros & Clementinas Constitutiones in Scripturæ Canonem referret,quod Dallæo firmo fuit argumento ab impostore post Synodum Nicænam conflatum esse, qui aliter decernit, LXXXV. Apostolicum Canonem. Nec caute egit Dallæus, ut Be- veregius, quia duarum Clementis Episto- larum ad Corinthios non meminit, ta- menetsi in Canonem N. T. eodem in loco referantur, æque ac Constitutiones Apostolicæ : ita agendum esse arbitratus est Dallæus, quoniam abunde sufficiebant quæ annotavit ad demonstrandum Synodo Nicænâ recentiorem esse Apostolicum de quo lis est Canonem; Nec quicquam causæ est cur scribat primam Clementis Epistolam ad Corinthios in plerisque Ecclesiis publicè lectam fuisse : Hinc enim non sequitur in Canonicorum librorum censu fuisse; aliter eadem plane ratione idem concluderes de Polycarpi Epistola, de libro Hermæ, de quadam Soteris Episcopi Rom. Epistola, & de Ephraemi Edessenæ Ecclesiæ scriptis quæ publicè etiam legebantur in quibusdam Ecclesiis. Denique tandem altera Clementis Epistola à Veteribus ut spuria semper reprobata fuit, contra quam decernit Apostolicus Canon.
units.tr: The most distinguished Daillé wishes only this: that those Constitutions, whether present-day or those known to Epiphanius, were admitted into the canon of Scripture by no one before the Council of Nicaea. From this he concludes that the compiler of the Apostolic Canons lived after that time. Only Epiphanius, around the year of the Lord 375, mentioned the Clementine Constitutions with some praise; before him no one did. To this add that Epiphanius himself plainly testifies, in the words the learned man quotes, that this work is of doubtful faith to many, although he thinks it is not to be rejected. Yet neither Epiphanius, who flourished after the Synod of Nicaea, nor anyone else older than that Synod numbered the eight books of the Constitutions among the canonical books. Beveridge therefore thinks in vain that it is clear from Epiphanius' words that the Constitutions which he praised then had the highest authority in the Church. Could books of doubtful, uncertain and disputed faith have had the highest authority among Christians of the fourth century? Epiphanius denies that the work of the Constitutions is ἀδόκιμον, reprobate, or rejected; but it does not follow that it had the highest authority. The keen champion of the canons is not unaware that books which are spoken against [ἀντιλεγομένας] and which are contradicted were listed by the ancients outside the number of the canonical books. Epiphanius indeed praises the work because in it the whole canonical order is kept, and nothing in it is alien either to faith or to the discipline of the Church. But, as Daillé said in book 1, chapter 2, page 37, it does not follow from this that he believed the books were truly written by Clement, and that whatever is narrated in them was truly instituted and dictated by the Apostles. For many books contain nothing alien either to faith or to the discipline of the Church, yet you would not for that reason call them Clementine or Apostolic. But let us grant to the learned Beveridge, or at least let us allow, that Epiphanius was of the opinion that the authors of those Ordinances were truly the Apostles whose names they bore. You will not for that reason conclude either that this is true, or at least that the Greek Church of that time thought the same. Indeed Epiphanius himself reports the contrary, that many doubted that work of the Constitutions; and it would be unfair to prefer one man to many. Moreover, Daillé undertook to prove that these canons were not established before the Synod of Nicaea, in order to refute Beveridge's contrary assertion, and he brings forward Epiphanius, who wrote one year after the Synod, and no writer earlier than Epiphanius could be cited who listed the Maccabean books and the Clementine Constitutions in the canon of Scripture. This was a firm argument for Daillé that the Apostolic Canon 85, which decrees otherwise, was put together by an impostor after the Synod of Nicaea. Nor did Daillé act carelessly, as Beveridge says, in not mentioning the two Epistles of Clement to the Corinthians, even though they are listed in the same place in the canon of the New Testament, just like the Apostolic Constitutions. Daillé judged that he should proceed this way, since what he had noted was quite enough to show that the Apostolic Canon in question is more recent than the Synod of Nicaea. Nor is there any reason why he should write that the first Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians was read publicly in most churches. For it does not follow from this that it was in the number of the canonical books. Otherwise, by the very same reasoning, you would conclude the same about the Epistle of Polycarp, the Shepherd of Hermas, a certain Epistle of Soter, bishop of Rome, and the writings of Ephraim of the church of Edessa, which were also read publicly in some churches. Finally, the second Epistle of Clement was always rejected by the ancients as spurious, while the Apostolic Canon decrees otherwise.

units.la: Transit Beveregius à Dallæanis ex ipsâ horum Canonum materiâ contra ipsorum antiquitatem ductis argumētis, ad ea quæ ex eorum formâ objiciuntur. Verùm pace Viri docti dictum sit, non omnia Dallęi argumenta ex Canonum materia desumpta expendit, sed ea tantùm quæ cap. 21. contra ipsorum antiquitate adduxit: Tamen quàdo Dallæi sententiam de istorum Canonum antiquitate confutare sibi proposuit Eruditus Beveregius, omnia adversarij argumenta quæ plura sunt numero, & quibus ex ipsis Canonibus ipsorum arguere ac demonstrare suscepit novitatem, examinare ac refellere debebat; At quoniam veritus est ne incassum laboraret, neve oleum perderet ac operam, unicum Dallæi argumetum ex Canonum materia depromptum, infaustis licet avibus, refutasse contentus, cætera labori parcens intacta reliquit, ut scilicet victoriam quam facilem falsò putabat sibi compararet. sed à quâ eum longè abesse, causàque hactenus cecidisse non dubito. Verùm felicius fortè procedet Beveregij ratiocinatio in discutiendis quæ ex Canonum formâ petuntur objectionibus, & ut rem facilius exsequatur,Albaspinæi primò, deinde suam de his Canonibus sententiam profert,Dallæumque contra illam sic disputantem exhibet. Si res itase haberet, omnino hanc syllogen Codici Canonum Ecclesiæ universalis ejus authores inservissent; immò primo Codicis loco posuissent, velut & à Viris Apostolicis exortum, & ipsâ antiquissimi temporis vetustate venerabile monumentum. Hanc Dallæi objectionem ridet Beveregius, asseritque æquè facile esse eam refellere ac recitare; magno tamē circuitu illius aggreditur refutationem; statim observat Codicem Canonum Ecclesiæ universæ à Canonibus Nicænis incipere, nec quoslibet antea constitutos Canones complecti, præter Ancyranos & Neocæsarienses,quos etiam à Cōcilio Nicæno confirmatos fuisse tradit, idque Synodi Florentinæ authoritate; Unde colligit mirum videri non debere si Canones quibus de agimus, illi Codici minimè inferti fuerint, quoniam auctori dicti Codicis propositum fuit eos solos Canones col-ligere, qui vel à Nicænâ Synodo confirmati sunt, vel post eam constituti,non autem vetustiores istos Apostolicos multis annis antea sancitos. Quæ dicebat Vir doctus de Dallæi objectione,illius solutioni apprimè congruunt;in quâ scilicet omnia levissima sunt,nulliusque ponderis: Vnde quaeso habet Beveregius auctori Codicis propositum fuisse eos solos Canones colligere,qui vel à Nicaenâ Synodo confirmati sunt, vel post eam constituti ? Edat vel unum vetustum Scriptorem qui hoc testetur,& cujus testimonium omni sit exceptione maius? Cum autem nullum planè proferat, & de suo tantū hoc affirmet, non ægrè laturum illum puto, si à nobis eadem quâ profertur facilitate contemnatur ; nec meliora sunt quae tradit de Canonum Ancyranorum & Neocaesariensium à Nicaenâ Synodo confirmatione; nulla siquidem hujusce confirmationis extat mentio in Synodi Florentinae sessione septimâ quam citat; En Synodi verba, Ante primam Synodum multae aliae celebratae sunt: Antiochiae adversus Paulum Samosatenum: Ancyrae contra eos, qui non suscipiebant accedentes ad fidem, quod prius Christum abnegassent propter tormenta: & Neocaesareae tertia: quas omnes Synodos recepit Synodus Nicaena. Synodos illas admisit Concilium Nicaenum, ab eo confirmatas esse non dicitur,& si ob id tantùm Codici Canonum Ecclesiae universae inserti sunt Canones Ancyrani & Neocaesarienses, quia à Synodo Nicaena recepti sunt, eadem planè ratione inserendi erant Sardicenses à secundâ Synodo Oecumenicâ,si iisdē Florentinis Patribus credimus,suscepti,quamvis hallucinatos esse Florentinos Patres non dubitem, non enim de Sardicensi Synodo loquuntur Constantinopolitani Patres Can. V. ut opinabantur Florentini, sed de Antiochenâ anno Domini CCCLXXXVIII.habitâ,in quâ lectus est Tomus Occidentalium, Epistola scilicet Synodica Damasi Papæ ante paucos annos scripta,cui subscripserunt Episcopi Orientales num. 146. sed donemus Beveregio Canones Ancyranos & Neocæsarienses à Synodo Nicænâ secundum Florentinos Patres fuisse confirmatos, nihil propterea proficiet: Synodus quippe Florentina nimis recens est ut de re adeò antiquâ sine vetustioris authoritate testari queat, censit & tredecim annos supra mille post confessum Nicænū, præsertim cùm nihil ejusmodi occurrat in antiquis Ecclesiæ Scriptoribus, nec in ipso Canonum Ecclesiæ universæ Codice;immò còtrarium ex ipso Codice colligitur, hic enim titulus Ancyranis præfixus est Canonibus, CONCILII ANCYRANI CANONES XXV. Qui quidem priores sunt Nicænis, sed ideò postpositi sunt propter authoritatem Synodi Oecumenicæ. Si à Synodo Nicænâ confirmati fuissent, lectorem hac de re moniturum esse colléctorem par est credere; idem dico de Canonibus Neocaesariensibus hoc titulo praenotatis.
units.tr: Beveregius now moves from the arguments Dallaeus drew from the content of these Canons against their antiquity to the objections raised from their form. With respect to the learned man, it must be said that he did not weigh all of Dallaeus's arguments drawn from the content of the Canons, but only those which Dallaeus adduced against their antiquity in chapter 21. Yet when Beveregius set himself to refute Dallaeus's view of the antiquity of these Canons, he ought to have examined and refuted all of his opponent's arguments, which are many, and by which Dallaeus undertook to prove their novelty from the Canons themselves. But fearing that he would labour in vain and waste his oil and effort, he was content to refute the single argument Dallaeus drew from the content of the Canons, though with unlucky omens, and left the rest untouched, sparing himself the trouble, so that he might win the victory he falsely thought would be easy. I do not doubt, however, that he is far from it and that his cause has so far fallen. Perhaps, though, Beveregius's reasoning will proceed more happily in dealing with the objections drawn from the form of the Canons. To carry this out more easily, he first sets out Albaspinaeus's view and then his own view of these Canons, and presents Dallaeus disputing against it as follows: If the matter stood so, the authors of the Code of the universal Church would certainly have included this collection; indeed they would have put it first in the Code, as a work that came from the Apostolic men and a monument venerable for the very antiquity of its age. Beveregius laughs at this objection of Dallaeus and says it is as easy to refute as to recite; yet he approaches the refutation by a long detour. He first observes that the Code of the Canons of the universal Church begins with the Canons of Nicaea and does not include any Canons enacted earlier, except those of Ancyra and Neocaesarea, which he says were also confirmed by the Council of Nicaea, on the authority of the Synod of Florence. From this he concludes that it should not seem surprising if the Canons we are discussing were not inserted in that Code, since the compiler of the Code intended to gather only those Canons which were either confirmed by the Synod of Nicaea or enacted after it, and not those more ancient Apostolic Canons decreed many years before. What the learned man says about Dallaeus's objection fits very well with its solution, in which, of course, everything is very slight and of no weight. Hence I ask, on what grounds does Beveregius claim that the compiler of the Code intended to gather only those Canons which were either confirmed by the Synod of Nicaea or enacted after it? Let him produce even one ancient writer who attests this, and whose testimony is beyond all exception. But since he produces none at all and merely asserts this on his own account, I think he will not take it badly if it is dismissed by us with the same ease with which it is put forward. Nor is what he offers about the confirmation of the Canons of Ancyra and Neocaesarea by the Synod of Nicaea any better. For no mention of such a confirmation is found in the seventh session of the Synod of Florence which he cites. Here are the words of the Synod: Before the first Synod many others were held: at Antioch against Paul of Samosata; at Ancyra against those who would not receive those coming to the faith, who had first denied Christ because of torments; and the third at Neocaesarea; all which Synods the Synod of Nicaea received. The Council of Nicaea admitted those Synods; it is not said that it confirmed them. And if the Canons of Ancyra and Neocaesarea were inserted in the Code of the Canons of the universal Church for this reason only, that they were received by the Synod of Nicaea, then by exactly the same reasoning the Sardican Canons, if we believe the same Florentine Fathers, ought to have been inserted, since they were accepted by the second Ecumenical Synod. Although I do not doubt that the Florentine Fathers were mistaken here, for the Constantinopolitan Fathers in Canon V did not speak of the Synod of Sardica, as the Florentines supposed, but of the Synod of Antioch held in the year of the Lord 388, in which was read the Tome of the Westerners, namely the synodal letter of Pope Damasus written a few years before, which the Eastern bishops subscribed, number 146. But let us grant Beveregius that the Canons of Ancyra and Neocaesarea were confirmed by the Synod of Nicaea according to the Florentine Fathers; nothing will be gained for him by this. For the Synod of Florence is far too recent to bear witness to so ancient a matter without the authority of an earlier witness. It thought also thirteen years beyond a thousand after the Nicene Creed was confessed; especially since nothing of the kind occurs in the ancient writers of the Church, nor in the Code of the Canons of the universal Church itself. Indeed the opposite is gathered from that very Code, for this title is prefixed to the Ancyran Canons: THE CANONS OF THE COUNCIL OF ANCYRA, XXV. These indeed are earlier than the Nicene, but they were placed after them on account of the authority of the Ecumenical Synod. If they had been confirmed by the Synod of Nicaea, it is right to believe that the compiler would have warned the reader of this; I say the same of the Neocaesarean Canons, which are prefaced by this title.

units.la: CONCILII NEOCÆSARIENSIS CANONES XIV.
units.tr: THE FOURTEEN CANONS OF THE COUNCIL OF NEOCAESAREA.

units.la: Qui quidem sunt Ancyrani posteriores, Nicaeni vero antiquiores. Pergit eruditissimus Beveregius aitque Codicem suum Canonum Ecclesiæ primitivæ (hoc est Canonum Apostolicorum Syllogen) diu in Ecclesiâ seorsim jam obtinuisse, ac proinde non opus esse, ut Canones in eo comprehensi de novo colligerentur, multo minus ut antiquus iste Codex novo conjungeretur, qui non eo nomine compositus fuit ut antiquam, sed tantùm ut præsentem Ecclesiæ disciplinam exhiberet, eam nimirum quæ à Conciliis nuper celebratis constituta est. At quàm sit frivola hæc secunda Viri docti ratiocinatio, ex sequentibus patebit observationibus: 1. Pro concesso & pro vero sibi sumit, quod nos negamus, nempe antiquissimam esse Canonum Apostolicorum collectionem, quam Codicem Canonum Ecclesiæ primitivæ nuncupare amat; etiam si tantam illius vetustatem nondum probaverit: 2. Æquè falsum est quod innuit, Canones videlicet Apostolicos ad Ecclesiæ disciplinam Synodo Nicænâ antiquiorem spectare tantùm; plures tamen ex illis Canonibus ad disciplinam quæ longè post Concilium Nicænum in Ecclesiâ obtinebat pertinere non dubitâbit, qui eos accuratè legerit: 3. Nulla igitur adferri potest idonea causa ob quam Codici Canonum Ecclesiæ universæ inserti sunt Canones Ancyrani & Neocæsariensēs, Apostolici nequaquam, præter istam quod scilicet nundum confi&i erant Canones Pseudapostolici & in unum corpus colle&i. 4. Denique si colle&tores Canonum Ecclesiæ universæ, colle&tioni suæ inserere noluissent, hunc Canonum Ecclesiæ primitivæ Codicem, ut illum indigetat Beveregius, vel ut loquitur Albaspinæus hoc Breviarium ac Epitomen Ecclesiasti-corum ante Nicænam Synodum apud Græcos Decretorum: Alicubi saltem honorificam illius mentionem erant facturi, ne adeo venerandum antiquitatis Ecclesiasticæ monumentum ab illis contemptum videretur; quod cùm nullibi fecerint, certò certius est eis prorsus incognitam fuisse hanc Canonum Apostolicorum Syllogen: In Codice Canonum Ecclesiæ Africanæ, inquit, nullum è decretis, quæ sub Cypriano aliisque veteustioribus [?] Africæ Conciliis divulgata fuerant, continetur, forte, immò contrarium plane liquet ex Epistolis Cypriani in quibus cernere est eadem adversus Transmarinas appellationes decreta quæ in Codice leguntur Africano præte-rea eà[?] verisimile est plura istiusmodi decreta suo Codici inserturos esse Patres Africanos, si in Prædecessorum scriptis frequentiora occurrissent, vel si exstitisset in Ecclesiis Africanis Codex alius vetustior, eum commemorare dubio procul illos non piguisset.
units.tr: These are the Ancyran canons, which are later; the Nicene canons are earlier. The most learned Beveregius goes on and says that his codex of the canons of the primitive Church (that is, the collection of the Apostolic Canons) had long been in use in the Church by itself, and therefore there was no need for the canons it contains to be collected afresh, much less for this ancient codex to be joined to a new one. It was not compiled to exhibit the ancient discipline, but only the present discipline of the Church, namely that established by the councils lately held. But how frivolous this second reasoning of the learned man is will be clear from the following observations. 1. He takes for granted and as true what we deny, namely that the collection of the Apostolic Canons, which he likes to call the Codex of the Canons of the Primitive Church, is the most ancient, although he has not yet proved such great antiquity. 2. It is equally false what he suggests, that the Apostolic Canons concern only the discipline of the Church prior to the Synod of Nicaea. Yet anyone who reads them carefully will not doubt that many of those canons pertain to the discipline that prevailed in the Church long after the Council of Nicaea. 3. No suitable reason can therefore be given why the Ancyran and Neocaesarean canons, which are by no means Apostolic, were inserted into the Codex of the Canons of the Universal Church, except that the Pseudapostolic canons had not yet been fabricated and gathered into one body. 4. Finally, if the compilers of the Canons of the Universal Church had not wished to include this codex in their collection, they would at least have made some honourable mention of it somewhere, so that so venerable a monument of ecclesiastical antiquity should not seem to have been despised by them. Since they never did so, it is more than certain that this collection of Apostolic Canons was entirely unknown to them. He says that in the Codex of the Canons of the African Church nothing is contained of the decrees that had been published under Cyprian and other more ancient councils of Africa; perhaps so, but indeed the contrary is quite clear from the letters of Cyprian, in which one can see the same decrees against appeals overseas as are read in the African Codex. Moreover, it is likely that the African Fathers would have inserted more decrees of this kind into their codex, had they occurred more often in the writings of their predecessors, or had there existed in the African Churches another, older codex; undoubtedly they would not have been reluctant to mention it.

units.la: Ad aliud Dallæi argumentum properat Beveregius, quod istis exhibet verbis: Tum siquis extitisset hujusmodi Codex, cur nunquam eum diserte ac nominatim memorant Ancyrani, Nicæni, Neocæsarienses, Antiocheni, aliique Patres? Huic argumento respondet Vir Doctus, primum Codicem Canonum Ecclesiæ universæ collectum fuisse ante Concilium Ephesinum, à quo tamen, nusquam memoratur; negat tamen inde sequi dictum Codicem tunc temporis non extitisse: Esto, non hinc sequatur tunc dierum non extitisse, sequitur saltem vel adhuc incognitum esse, vel nullam illius memorandi se obtulisse occasionem; quæ addit ut ostendat memoratos esse à Veteribus Apostolicos Canones alibi excussimus, ideoque non est quod diutius immoremur in istis refellendis quæ adduxit Beveregius pag. 6. num. xx.
units.tr: Beveregius hurries on to another argument of Dallaeus, which he presents in these words: Then, if such a codex had existed, why do the Ancyrans, the Nicenes, the Neocaesareans, the Antiochenes and other Fathers never mention it expressly and by name? To this argument the learned man replies, first, that the Codex of the Canons of the Universal Church was compiled before the Council of Ephesus, which nevertheless nowhere mentions it. He denies, however, that it follows from this that the said codex did not exist at that time. Granted that it does not follow that it did not exist in those days; it follows at least that it was either still unknown or that no occasion of mentioning it presented itself. He adds this to show that the Apostolic canons cited by the ancients have been examined by us elsewhere, and therefore there is no reason to linger long over refuting what Beveregius adduced at p. 6, no. xx.

units.la: Dallæus, inquit, interrogativum hoc argumentum ulterius sic prosequitur. Cur non interdum aliquem ex istius Codicis Canonibus indicato ac nominato numero, sub quo in eo positus extat, citarunt ac laudarunt? Verbi gratia hoc modo; Decernit Canon Apostolorum primus, vel tricesimus, vel quinquagesimus, &c. Sicuti à Patribus Chalcedonensibus in Codice Ecclesiae universalis usurpatum est; quo scilicet Codicis Canonem quartum, octogesimum tertium, quartumque, & nonagesimum quintum, sextumque his diserte numeris expressis, laudasse ac descripsisse nuper demonstravimus. Hactenus Dallæus cujus agnosco verba; Jam Beveregii responsum expendamus; quæ dicit de Concilio Ephesino mox diluimus, nec firmiora sunt quæ addit de Concilio Chalcedonensi hoc pacto, Si Patres Chalcedonenses dictum Codicem nusquam ita laudassent, hocce argumento esset, eum tunc temporis non extitisse? Quid etiam si Acta Concilii Chalcedonensis periissent, istum quoque Codicem una periisse necesse est? Sane nec Concilium Chalcedonense supradictum Codicem Canonum Ecclesiae universae, in Canonibus suis, sed tantum in Actis citat. Haec ambigue dicuntur, quandoquidem enim ex concessione Codex Canonum Ecclesiae universae ante Concilium Chalcedonense compositus est, ex Concilii silentio non sequeretur quidem tunc temporis non extitisse Codicem illum, at saltem sequeretur vel Patribus incognitum[?] fuisse, vel nullam illis datam fuisse eum memorandi occasionem: Canonum autem Apostolicorum Syllogen quod spectat, à Nicænis, Ancyranis, Neocæsariensibus, Gangrensibus, Antiochenis, Laodicenis, Constantinopolitanis, Ephesinis, & Chalcedonensibus, nunquam diserte ac nominatim memoratur, etiamsi pluries eam memorandi occurrerit occasio, unde sequitur necessario vel nondum conflatam esse, vel saltem in latebris delituisse, adeo ut penitus incognita fuerit: Si autem ex Actorum Concilii Chalcedonensis jactura, non sequitur una periisse Codicem Canonum Ecclesiæ universæ, ex eo tamen quod in illis Actis memoratur iste Codex, sequitur tunc temporis extitisse, quod de Canonum Apostolicorum Sylloge dici nequit; In Canonibus Ancyranis, Neocæsariensibus, Anthiochenis, &c. Si Virum doctum audimus, Canones Ecclesiæ primitivæ, æquè diserte citantur, ac Ecclesiæ universæ, in Chalcedonensibus; At contrarium evicimus, vel evicerat ante nos Dallæus cujus argumentis nihil prorsus repositit Beveregius. Si Acta dictorum Conciliorum (pergit Vir Doctus) non minus quàm Chalcedonensis etiamnum extarent, in iis forsitan antiquissimum hunc Codicem indicato ac nominato Canonum numero laudatum inveniremus, non secus ac Canones Ecclesiæ universæ in Actis Chalcedonensibus. Profecto si sic argumentari liceat, nihil certi remanebit in antiquitatis Ecclesiasticæ monumentis: Omnia siquidem voce forsitan incerta reddes; nec ubi consistas habebis; Scilicet disertiùs se victum fateri non poterat eruditus Beveregius, quàm ita argumentando.
units.tr: Dallaeus, he says, pursues this interrogative argument further in this way: Why did they not at some time cite and praise some canon of this codex by its indicated and named number, under which it stands in that codex? For example, in this manner: The first, or thirtieth, or fiftieth canon of the Apostles decrees, etc. As the Chalcedonian Fathers did in the Codex of the Universal Church, in which they expressly cited and transcribed the fourth, eighty-third, ninety-fifth and sixth canons by their numbers; as we recently demonstrated. So far Dallaeus, whose words I acknowledge. Now let us weigh Beveregius's reply. What he says about the Council of Ephesus we have just refuted, and what he adds about the Council of Chalcedon is no firmer, in this way: If the Chalcedonian Fathers had nowhere cited the said codex in this manner, would this be an argument that it did not exist at that time? And if the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon had perished, must that codex also have perished together with them? Indeed the Council of Chalcedon does not cite the aforesaid Codex of the Canons of the Universal Church in its own canons, but only in the Acts. These things are said ambiguously. For since, by concession, the Codex of the Canons of the Universal Church was compiled before the Council of Chalcedon, it would not follow from the silence of the Council that the codex did not exist at that time; but it would at least follow that it was either unknown to the Fathers or that no occasion of mentioning it was given to them. As for the collection of Apostolic Canons, however, it is never expressly and by name mentioned by the Nicene, Ancyran, Neocaesarean, Gangrene, Antiochene, Laodicean, Constantinopolitan, Ephesine and Chalcedonian councils, even though the occasion for mentioning it arose many times. From this it necessarily follows that it had either not yet been put together or at least lay hidden in obscurity, so that it was altogether unknown. If, however, from the loss of the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon it does not follow that the Codex of the Canons of the Universal Church perished too, yet from the fact that this codex is mentioned in those Acts it does follow that it existed at that time. This cannot be said of the collection of Apostolic Canons. In the Ancyran, Neocaesarean, Antiochene, etc. canons... If we listen to the learned man, the canons of the Primitive Church are cited just as expressly as those of the Universal Church in the Chalcedonian Acts. But we have shown the contrary, or Dallaeus had shown it before us, and Beveregius has replied nothing at all to his arguments. If the Acts of the said Councils (the learned man goes on) were still extant no less than that of Chalcedon, we would perhaps find this most ancient codex cited in them by its indicated and named number, just as the canons of the Universal Church are in the Acts of Chalcedon. Indeed, if one may argue in this way, nothing certain will remain in the monuments of ecclesiastical antiquity. For you make everything uncertain with the word perhaps, and you will have no firm footing. Surely the learned Beveregius could not have confessed more plainly that he was beaten than by arguing in this way.

units.la: Eum tamen ultimum Dallæi Argumentum sic proponentem audiamus, Denique hunc Apostolicum Codicem (si is vere tum fuisset habitus pro Breviario) quis Gelasium sapientissimum, ut ferunt, Antistitem, quis Episcopos Romani Concilii septuaginta, inter Apocrypha procul ab Ecclesiasticis libris rejecturos fuisse crediderit. Respondet Beveregius primo incertum esse, utrum haec verba, Liber Canonum Apostolorum Apocryphus, in Gelasii decreto, ut ab ipso & 70. Episcopis edito, lecta fuerint necne. Secundò nihil aliud confici ex illis Decreti verbis, præterquam eundem à Romanâ Ecclesiâ tunc temporis non receptum fuisse, & Apostolorum nomen ei falsò impositum. Utramque objectionem diluimus adversus doctissimum Pearsonium disputando, ideoque eas missas hic facimus, ne actum agere videamur: Insuper mirari desinat Beveregius, quo tandem fato talia Dallæo exciderint; Dei enim providentia factum est, ut Vir tantus hoc argumentum tractandum suscipéret, ne scilicet deinceps aliquod in hisce fictitiis Canonibus præsidium quærerent acerrimi Ecclesiasticæ Hierarchiæ propugnatores, nec quicquam hactenus adduxit Beveregius, quo Dallæi de Canonum istorum antiquitate senten-tia, vel minimum convulsa nedum labefactata fuerit.
