units.tr: Let us hear, however, Dallaeus's last argument as he puts it: Finally, who would have believed that the wisest prelate Gelasius, as they say, and the seventy bishops of the Roman council, would have rejected this Apostolic codex, if it had truly been regarded as a breviary at that time, far away among the apocryphal books, far from the ecclesiastical books? Beveregius replies, first, that it is uncertain whether the words The Book of the Apostolic Canons is apocryphal were read in the decree of Gelasius, as published by him and the seventy bishops, or not. Second, nothing else can be gathered from those words of the decree except that the same book was not received by the Roman Church at that time, and that the name of the Apostles was falsely attached to it. We have refuted both objections in disputing against the most learned Pearson, and therefore we pass over them here, lest we seem to be doing the same thing twice. Furthermore, let Beveregius cease to wonder by what fate such things have escaped Dallaeus. It was by the providence of God that so great a man undertook to treat this argument, so that the most zealous defenders of the ecclesiastical hierarchy might not seek any further protection in these fictitious canons. And Beveregius has so far adduced nothing by which Dallaeus's opinion about the antiquity of those canons might be shaken even in the least, let alone overthrown.

units.la: Unum adhuc illi superesse videtur, ut ipsius videlicet Dallæi de tempore quo collecti sunt hi Canones, sententiam paucis expendat; hanc, inquit, ipse profert eodem capite, pag. 685. his verbis conceptam. Denique si de tempore quæratur, quo pseud-apostolica illa, & apocrypha Canonum collectio facta & edita primum fuerit, apparet ex iis quæ hactenus disputata sunt, eam neque ante quintum seculum adultum innotuisse, & quinto exeunte jam extitisse publicarique captam esse. Postea observat idem Beveregius Dallæum priorem hujus sententiæ suæ partem, quâ hanc collectionem non ante quintum seculum adultum innotuisse statuit, non probare tantùm, sed & demonstrare posse sibi videri; nempe verbis quæ mox descripsimus, ista continenter subjicit Dallæus; Prius demonstrat universale omnium qui ante A. D. CCCCLI. vixerunt de[?] ea silentium, quod abundè supra demonstra-tum est. Neque enim credibile est, nullam ejus mentionem, si extitisset, facturos fuisse Eusebium, Hieronymum, & alios illorum temporum eruditissimos scriptores, qui etiam ea, quae Apocrypha judicabant, praecipuè quae Apostolis assi[?]cta erant, diligenter persequi, & refellere solent. Videamus jam quid hisce reponat doctissimus Beveregius, dicit primò, falsum esse quod hîc pro concessō assumit Dallæus, omnes nimirum qui ante A. D. CCCCLI. vixerunt, de hac collectione siluisse, multo magis eum hoc abunde demonstrasse, ut ex iis, inquit, quae superius disputavimus, apparet. Nos argumenta Beveregii excussimus ac refellimus, nihilque ex variis quae descripsit testimoniis, ad confirmandam suorum Canonum antiquitatem, colligi posse fusè probavimus, vel à Dallæo ipso probatum indicavimus. Ratiocinationem suam sic prosequitur Vir doctus, si illud verum esset, minime probaret, nedum demonstraret hos Canones ante annum CCCCLI. non extitisse. Neque enim Eusebius nec Hieronymus nec alii, quos scimus, ejusdem aetatis cum utrovis scriptores, Canones Ancyranos aut Neocaesarienses commemorarunt, quos tamen ante dictum annum constitutos esse ac divulgatos, inter omnes convenit. Si res ut parest perpendisset eru[?]diditus Beveregius , non ita argumentatus effet ; Ingens siquidem est discrimen ; non enim paria sūtquæ de Canonibus Ancyranis & Neocæsariensibus observat , cum iis quæ observat Dallæus de Apostolicis ; si Ancyrani & Neocæsarienses Canones , Eusebii vel Hieronymi aliorumque illorum temporum Scriptorum ætate , publico cuidam Canonum Ecclesiæ Codici inserti fuissent, non dubitandum quin ab illis essent commemorandi , saltem Codicis cui inserti fuissent, aliquam fecissent mentionem ; At nondum in Codicem Canonum Ecclesiæ universæ relati erant ; non mirum igitur si Canonum istorum qui in localibus ac particularibus Synodis sanciti erant , & qui ad paucorum adhuc notitiam pervenerant, non meminerunt. Verùm alia fuit Canonum Apostolicorum sors atque fortuna; Nam si Viro docto credimus ante Synodum Nicænam in unum corpus ab Apostolicis v ris[?] collecti sunt , & Codicem Canonum Ecclesiæ primitivæ constituerunt ; Quomodo ergo fieri potuit ut Eusebium, Hieronymum , aliosque ejusdem ætatis eruditissimos scriptores latuerit adeò venerandum suâ vetustate monumentum; Nam si cognitus illis fuisset istiusmodi Codex,illos allicubi eum memoraturos esse est plusquam verisimile ; Ex eo autem quod nullibi id præstiterint, legitimè colliges[?] nullum tunc dierum extitisse talem Codicem: in desuetudinem abjisse istos Canones, & alios eorum loco generalium Synodorum authoritate substitutos hariolatur Beveregius: At unde hæc habet, edat Auctorem à quo accepit, & quando nullum profert neque proferre potest adeò temerariæ assertionis idoneum testem, exsufflandæ sunt vanissimæ Viri docti conjecturæ, quæ à præconceptâ opinione, & immoderato causæ studio proficiscuntur. Siccine in desuetudinem abjerant hi Canones Eusebij ætate, ut eorum memoria penitus interciderit[?] ? Eusebij inquam, qui Synodo interfuit Niceniæ cujus tempore obtinebat adhuc juxta Beveregij supputationem, Codex iste Canonum Ecclesiæ primitivæ: Profecto hæc sunt suavia vigilantium somnia. Neque forte meliora sunt quæ sequuntur; Vltimò, inquit, etiamsi Eusebius, Hieronymus, aliique eruditissimi Scriptores ea quæ Apocrypha judicabant; præcipuè quæ Apostolis affecta[?] erant, diligenter persequi ac refellere consueti sunt, non tamen necesse est, ut de his etiam Canonibus meminerint: nam nullus Turrianus, nullus Bovius adhuc exortus erat, qui eos ipsis Apostolis affingebat. Et quid illis opus erat opinionem oppugnare, quæ nullos adhuc propugnatores habebat? Vel probare[?] hos Canones Apostolis falsò adscriptos esse, cùm nemo illud assereret.
units.tr: One thing still seems to remain for him: to weigh briefly Dallæus's own view of the time when these Canons were collected. He states it in the same chapter, p. 685, in these words: Finally, if one asks the time when this pseudo-apostolic and apocryphal collection of Canons was first made and published, it appears from what has been argued so far that it was not known in its full form before the fifth century, and that at the close of the fifth century it was already in existence and was beginning to be published. Afterwards the same Beveregius notes that Dallæus does not merely think he proves the first part of this view, namely that this collection was not known in full before the fifth century, but that he can also demonstrate it. Dallæus goes on immediately, in the words just quoted: First he shows that there is a universal silence on the part of all who lived before A.D. 451 about it, which has been amply demonstrated above. For it is not credible that Eusebius, Jerome, and the other most learned writers of those times would have made no mention of it, had it existed. They were accustomed to examine carefully, and to refute, the things they judged apocryphal, especially those ascribed to the Apostles. Let us now see how the most learned Beveregius replies. He says first that it is false that Dallæus assumes as granted, namely that all who lived before A.D. 451 were silent about this collection; and that Dallæus has proved this much more than abundantly, as, he says, appears from what we argued above. We have examined and refuted Beveregius's arguments, and we have shown at length that nothing can be drawn from the various testimonies he cites to confirm the antiquity of his Canons; or else we have pointed out that Dallæus himself has already proved this. The learned man continues his reasoning thus: If that were true, it would by no means prove, let alone demonstrate, that these Canons did not exist before the year 451. For neither Eusebius nor Jerome nor the others, writers of whatever age we know of, mention the Canons of Ancyra or Neocaesarea, which yet, all agree, were established and published before that year. If the learned Beveregius had weighed the matter as it deserves, he would not have argued so. The difference is great. The case of the Canons of Ancyra and Neocaesarea is not the same as the case of the Apostolic Canons with which Dallæus deals. If the Canons of Ancyra and Neocaesarea had been inserted in some public code of the Church's Canons in the age of Eusebius, or Jerome, or the other writers of that time, there is no doubt they would have had to be mentioned by them, or at least the code into which they had been inserted would have been mentioned. But they had not yet been entered into a code of the Canons of the whole Church. It is no wonder, then, that they did not mention those Canons, which had been enacted in local and particular synods and had come to the notice of only a few. But the lot and fortune of the Apostolic Canons was different. For if we believe the learned man, they were collected into one body by Apostolic men before the Synod of Nicaea and constituted a code of the Canons of the primitive Church. How, then, could it have happened that Eusebius, Jerome, and the other most learned writers of that age overlooked a monument so venerable for its antiquity? For if such a code had been known to them, it is more than likely that they would have mentioned it somewhere. From the fact that they nowhere did so, you will rightly conclude that no such code existed at that time. Beveregius guesses that these Canons fell into disuse, and that others were substituted for them by the authority of the general synods. But whence he has this, let him name the author from whom he received it. Since he produces no witness fit to support so rash an assertion, his most empty conjectures, which spring from a preconceived opinion and an immoderate zeal for his cause, must be blown away. Did these Canons really fall so completely into disuse in Eusebius's time that all memory of them perished? Of Eusebius, I say, who attended the Synod of Nicaea, at whose time, by Beveregius's own reckoning, that code of the Canons of the primitive Church was still in existence! Surely these are the pleasant dreams of men who keep watch. Nor perhaps are the things that follow any better: Lastly, he says, even if Eusebius, Jerome, and the other most learned writers were accustomed to examine carefully and refute the things they judged apocryphal, especially those ascribed to the Apostles, it is not necessary that they should have mentioned these Canons also. For there was as yet no Turrianus, no Bovius, who ascribed them to the Apostles themselves. And why did they need to attack an opinion which as yet had no defenders? Or to prove that these Canons were falsely ascribed to the Apostles, when no one was asserting it?

units.la: Non possum satis mirari hæc tanto Viro excidisse ; Omnem enim culpam in Turrianum & Bovium rejicit , quasi primi hosce Canones Apostolis affinxissent, fateor graviter peccasse Bovium & Turrianum, dum Canones istos[?] ab ipsis Apostolis con- ditos esse acerrimè contenderunt ; At in eo primi non peccarunt , quod eorum nomine præno tatos esse voluerunt , non enim ex seipsis hanc Canonibus nomenclaturam præfixerunt , nec eam proprio marte excogitarunt , sed ab ipsis Canonum collectoribus eam mutuo acceperunt; Nam quicunque sint , qui hos Canones college- runt , eorum certè mens fuit, ut verè ab Apostolis omnes conditi atque editi crederentur, & hic, qui eos continet Codex, ab ipsis Apostolis factus , digestus , conscriptusque & promulgatus censeretur ; Et ne putes hæc à nobis gratis fingi , ipsos consulamus Canones ex quibus liquido constabit , verissima esse quæ asserimus; Canon verbi gratia xxix. editionis Beve- regianæ contra Simoniacos , Petrum ex authorum suorum numero unum fuisse di- serté testatur , adeoque Petri Collegas, unaque cum iis ipsum Petrum , hoc est omnes Apostolos authores se habere docet.
units.tr: I cannot sufficiently wonder that such a great man let these things slip. He lays all the blame on Turrianus and Bovius, as if they were the first to ascribe these Canons to the Apostles. I grant that Bovius and Turrianus erred gravely in insisting so fiercely that these Canons were founded by the Apostles themselves. But the first collectors did not go wrong in wishing them to be labelled with the Apostles' names. For they did not themselves attach this title to the Canons, nor did they invent it by their own effort; they took it over from the collectors of the Canons. Whoever these collectors were, their intention was certainly that all the Canons should be believed to have been truly founded and published by the Apostles, and that this code which contains them should be regarded as made, arranged, written up, and promulgated by the Apostles themselves. Lest you think we make up these things without grounds, let us consult the Canons themselves, from which it will clearly be established that what we assert is most true. Canon 29 in Beveregius's edition, for example, against the Simoniacs, expressly declares that Peter was one of its authors. Thus it teaches that Peter's colleagues, and Peter together with them, that is, all the Apostles, are its authors.

units.la: Si quis Episcopus, per pecunias hanc sit dignitatem assecutus, vel Presbiter, vel Diaconus, deponatur, & ipse, & qui eum ordinavit, & à communione etiam omnino exscindatur, ut SIMON MAGUS à ME PETRO. idipsum profitetur Canon L. in Dionysii versione: Non enim dixit NOBIS Dominus, in morte meâ baptizate, sed euntes, docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomine Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus Sancti. Idem plane colligitur ex Canone LXXXII. ubi de sermo est ad ministerij Ecclesiastici gradum idoneo qualis, inquiunt, noster quoque Onesimus visus est, non alium intelligunt Onesimum, quàm Philemonis fugitivum, Pauli discipulum. Denique nequis superfit dubitandi locus, Apostolos se diserte vocant Canone ultimo, dum Actus Apostolorum quos in divinum post Clementinas Constitutiones referunt Canonem, sic describunt, κ’[?] αἱ πράξεις ἡμῶν τῶν Ἀποστόλων, & Actus nostri Apostolorum. Perperam autem queritur Vir doctus p. 20. 39. adjectum esse ab interpolatore quodam pronomen ἐμῶν in Can. XXII. ubi de Petro agitur, non secus ac ἡμέτερος in LXXXII. ubi de Onesimo, cum hæc sit constans Codicum fere omnium lectio. Jam quivis videt non parùm hallucinatum esse Beveregium dum Turriano & Bovio imputavit, quod mortasiu[illegible, ~1 letter]primi Canones istos Apostolis adscripserunt, cùm tamen hac in re collectorum vestigia sint secuti, nec ab illis vel minimum discesserint, nisi forte in eo quod Clementem Canonum Scriptorem arbitrati sunt. Hinc consequitur 1. vanissimam esse Beveregii ad Dallæi argumentum responsionem, quando nunc constat ipsos Canonum collectores eos Apostolis tribuisse; 2. seculo tertio non extitisse horum Canonum Codicem, aliter eum commemoraturi erant Eusebius, Hieronymus, aliique ejusdem ætatis cum utrovis Scriptores, cùm illum præsertin Sanctis Domini Apostolis affictum viderent; 3. Non Ecclesiasticos vocatos fuisse olim hos Canones, ut tradit pluribus in locis Vir doctus, sed Apostolicos; Nam ab Apostolis conditos esse, omnibus persuasum voluerunt eorum primi collectores; 4. ab Apostolicis Viris in unum corpus minimè collectos fuisse, quicquid dicat Beveregius; Nam Apostolici Viri Apostolis Canones non erât adscripturi, quos ab illis haudquaquam sancitos probè noverant; Restat igitur ut ab impostore quodam conflati sint ac consarcinati, & in hanc quam videmus speciem compositi.
units.tr: If any bishop has obtained this dignity through money, or any presbyter or deacon, let him be deposed, and he himself, and whoever ordained him, and let him be wholly cut off from communion, as SIMON MAGUS was by ME, PETER. The same thing is declared by Canon 50 in Dionysius's version: For the Lord did not say to US, "Baptize in my death," but "Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." The very same is gathered from Canon 82, where there is talk of a man fit for the grade of ecclesiastical ministry: such, they say, as our own Onesimus appeared to be. They understand no other Onesimus than the fugitive slave of Philemon, Paul's disciple. Finally, lest any room for doubt remain, the Canons call themselves Apostles plainly in the last canon, where they describe the Acts of the Apostles, which after the Clementine Constitutions they reckon as the divine canon, thus: [αἱ πράξεις ἡμῶν τῶν Ἀποστόλων], the Acts of us the Apostles. The learned man complains wrongly, on pp. 20 and 39, that a certain interpolator added the pronoun [ἐμῶν] in Canon 22, where Peter is spoken of, just as [ἡμέτερος] in Canon 82, where Onesimus is spoken of, since this is the reading of nearly all the manuscripts without exception. Now anyone can see that Beveregius was greatly mistaken when he charged Turrianus and Bovius with ascribing these Canons to the Apostles, since in this matter they followed the footsteps of the collectors and departed from them in nothing at all, except perhaps in thinking that Clement was the author of the Canons. From this it follows: first, that Beveregius's answer to Dallæus's argument is worthless, since it is now established that the collectors of the Canons themselves ascribed them to the Apostles; second, that no code of these Canons existed in the third century, for Eusebius, Jerome, and the other writers of that age, whichever of them we mean, would have mentioned it otherwise, since they saw it ascribed to the holy Apostles of the Lord; third, that these Canons were not called ecclesiastical in former times, as the learned man teaches in many places, but Apostolic; for the first collectors wanted everyone to be persuaded that they had been founded by the Apostles; fourth, that they were by no means collected into one body by Apostolic men, whatever Beveregius may say; for Apostolic men would not have ascribed to the Apostles Canons which they knew well had never been sanctioned by them. It remains, therefore, that they were put together and patched up by some impostor, and composed into the form we now see.

units.la: Cætera Viri docti prosequamur, & quid posterioris Dallæani argumenti partis con-
units.tr: Let us go on with the rest of the learned man's remarks, and examine what he offers in reply to the con-

units.la: firmatione reponat examinemus, Daneus quinto exeunte seculo extitisse publicarique cœptam esse Canonum Apostolicorum Syllogen, sic probat. Posterius vero ex Gelasii decreto an. D. CCCCLXXXXIV. facto patet; in quo scilicet ea collectio damnata est; Ergo paucis ante illud tempus annis ab homine hæretico, Græci generis, consarcinatam fuisse probabile est. Hanc Dallæi consequentiam parvi facit Beveregius, quoniam eadem ratione, ut illi quidem videtur, colligi posset, Arnobii, Africani, Lactantii, & ipsius quoque Tertulliani opuscula in eodem decreto damnata, etiam paucis ante illud tempus annis consarcinata fuisse. Sed pace Viri eruditissimi dictum sit; Dallæi mentem, quem immeritò astutiæ insimulat, non est omnino assecutus: Hæc ultima Dallæi verba cum præcedentibus cohærent, in præcedentibus hanc de quâ lis est syllogen ante an. D. CCCCLI. non innotuisse affirmavit, nec contrarium demonstrare potuit Beveregius, eandem tamen collectionem exeunte seculo quinto Gelasii decreto damnatam cernit; hinc jure merito concludit, paucis ante illud tempus annis consarcinatam esse: quod de Arnobii, Africani, Lactantii & Tertulliani opusculis dici nequit, quæ scilicet longè ante Gelasii ætatem exarata esse non ignoramus; si ingenuè, inquit, & omni, ut par est amoto præjudicio hos Canones tractassset Dallæus, eos potiùs ex hoc Gelasii decreto multis ante illud tempus annis collectos fuisse asseruisset, ut pote qui istis etiam diebus adeò vetusti erant, ut Canones Apostolorum appellati essent. Neque enim credibile est, ut quingentis propemodum post Apostolos annis ipsum eorum nomen libro alicui inscriberetur, qui non multis saltem ante illud tempus annis conscriptus fuerat. Beveregii ratiocinatio falsâ nititur suppositione, istos videlicet Canones temporis lapsu Apostolorum Canones nuncupatos esse, cùm olim Ecclesiastici audirent; nam mox demonstravimus ab eo quo collecti sunt tempore, collecto-ribus propositum fuisse eos Apostolis adscribere ac proinde Canones Apostolorum indigetare; nec ob aliud quicquam ab Apostolis ipsis sancitos esse persuasum voluerunt, quàm ut eorum nomen illis inscriberetur; vera ergo horum Canonum nomenclatura, non aliunde quam ab ipso collectorum consilio ac proposito petenda est, qui plus satis significarunt, non aliter quàm Canones Apostolorum appellandos esse, nempe planiisti & impostores Apostolorum nomen impudentissimè mentiti sunt, ut decretorum suorum farragini pondus darent. Perperam ergo scribit Beveregius ex hac Canonum appellatione concludere debuisse Dallæum, eos multis ante Gelasianum decretum annis collectos suisse, nec obstat quod Gelasij ætate Canones Apostolorum appellati sunt, quasi majorem illis compararet ejusmodi nomenclatura vetustatem: quando ita nuncupati sunt, ubi primum in hanc quam videmus formam fuerunt conflati: Præterea parum sibi constare videtur Vir doctus, hic ut qui-vis videt ex hac appellatione eorum colligit antiquitatem, tamen paulo supra ex eadem Canonum denominatione eos ad scripta Apocrypha amandandi occasionem arripuisse Gelasium affirmare non veretur: Ipse quidem, inquit, [?]nullus dubito, nec cuiuis, ut opinor, dubium esse potest, quin si Apostolorum nomen hisce Canonibus numquam inscriptum fuisset, sed Ecclesiastici tantum Canones, ut olim sic perpetuo appellati essent, nec Gelasius eos inter Apocryphos recensuisset, nec Dallaeus eorum antiquitatem tot verbis unquam oppugnasset. Hæc adeo [?]ἀσύγκατα videntur, ut difficile conciliari queant: Vix enim concipi potest, unum eundemque libri cuiusdam titulum ad illius honorem simul & ignominiam præfixum fuisse, tamen dum ex Apostolorum nomine Canonibus inscripto eorum in[?]fers antiquitatem, ad honorem inscri[?]ptum profiteris; at dum in eodem quo prænotati sunt nomine, damnationis eorum materiam quæris & argumentum ad ignominiam impositum non diffiteris; quæ duo, meo quidem judicio una consistere non possunt. Frustra est igitur Vir doctus dum Scribit Dallæi argumenta quæ infirma illi videntur, firmissimis refelli; Nondum enim firmissima illa Beveregii argumenta offendi, nec Dallæanorum infirmitatem deprehendi, fateor Scripsisse Dallæum hos Canones non ante quintum seculum idque adultum confistos fuisse, nempe in hanc quam videmus speciem; sed hactenus nihil adduxit Beveregius quo hæc Dallæi conjectura confutata sit: Eos, inquit, à Patribus qui ante illud tempus, sive ante A.D. CCCCL. claruerunt, sæpius commemoratos esse superius ostendimus. Nos verò vana esse & futilia quæ in hanc rem attulit eruditus Beveregius plus satis demonstravimus: Quæ addit de Dionysio Exiguo jam supra excussimus, dum Pearsonianas Vindicias expendebamus: Observatio enim Viri docti de tempore quo Dionysius suam Canonum collectionem elaboravit, hypothesi quam tuemur nequaquam nocet, cùm post tempus à Dallæo designatum facta fuerit.
units.tr: firmation of the latter part of Dallaeus's argument. Dallaeus proves that the collection of Apostolic Canons began to be published toward the end of the fifth century, as follows: But the later date is clear from the decree of Gelasius, made in the year of our Lord 494, in which this collection was condemned. Therefore it is probable that it was pieced together by a heretic of Greek origin a few years before that time. Beveregius thinks little of this inference of Dallaeus, since, by the same reasoning (as he seems to think), it could be concluded that the little works of Arnobius, Africanus, Lactantius, and Tertullian himself, which are condemned in the same decree, were also pieced together a few years before that time. But with all respect to so learned a man, it must be said that he has not fully grasped Dallaeus's meaning, which he unjustly accuses of cunning. Dallaeus's last words cohere with what precedes. In the earlier part he asserted that this collection was unknown before the year 451, and Beveregius could not show the contrary; yet he sees that the same collection was condemned by the decree of Gelasius at the end of the fifth century. From this he rightly concludes that it was pieced together a few years before that time. This cannot be said of the works of Arnobius, Africanus, Lactantius, and Tertullian, which, as we know, were written long before the age of Gelasius. If, he says, Dallaeus had handled these Canons honestly and, as is fitting, with all prejudice set aside, he would rather have asserted that they were collected many years before that time, on the basis of this decree of Gelasius, since even in those days they were so ancient that they were called the Canons of the Apostles. For it is not credible that about five hundred years after the Apostles their very name would be inscribed on a book that had been written only a few years before that time. Beveregius's reasoning rests on a false supposition, namely that these Canons came to be called the Canons of the Apostles through the lapse of time, since the Ecclesiastical writers heard them so named long ago. For we have just shown that at the time they were collected, the collectors intended to ascribe them to the Apostles, and therefore to call them the Canons of the Apostles. They wished it to be believed that they had been sanctioned by the Apostles themselves for no other reason than that the Apostles' name be written over them. The true name of these Canons, therefore, must be sought from nothing other than the design and purpose of their collectors, who made it abundantly plain that they were to be called nothing but the Canons of the Apostles; clearly these were deceivers and impostors who most shamelessly lied about the Apostles' name in order to lend weight to their heap of decrees. Beveregius is therefore wrong to write that Dallaeus ought to have concluded from this name of the Canons that they were collected many years before the decree of Gelasius. Nor does it stand in the way that in the age of Gelasius they were called Canons of the Apostles, as if such a name gave them greater antiquity: they were so named from the moment they were first fashioned into the form we see. Moreover, the learned man seems not to be consistent with himself. He sees, as anyone does, that from this title he infers their antiquity, yet a little earlier he does not hesitate to say that Gelasius seized upon this same name of the Canons as an occasion for relegating them to the apocryphal writings. Indeed, he says, I doubt not, nor, I think, can it be doubtful to anyone, that if the name of the Apostles had never been inscribed on these Canons, but only the Ecclesiastical Canons, as they had been called from of old and always, then neither would Gelasius have listed them among the Apocrypha, nor would Dallaeus ever have assailed their antiquity with so many words. These things seem so incongruous [ἀσύγκατα] that they can hardly be reconciled. For it can scarcely be conceived that one and the same title of a book was prefixed to it both for its honour and for its disgrace. Yet while you infer its antiquity from the name of the Apostles inscribed on the Canons, you profess that it is an honour; while, under the same name by which they were previously marked, you seek the ground of their condemnation and do not deny that the name was imposed as a stigma. These two things, in my judgement, cannot stand together. It is therefore in vain that the learned man, while writing, refutes with the firmest arguments the arguments of Dallaeus, which seem weak to him. For I confess I have not yet met with those firmest arguments of Beveregius, nor have I detected the weakness of the Dallaean position. I grant that Dallaeus wrote that these Canons were not formed before the fifth century, and then in the form we see; but so far Beveregius has brought nothing by which this conjecture of Dallaeus is refuted. Eos, he says, have been often cited by the Fathers who flourished before that time, or before A.D. 450; we have shown above. But we have shown abundantly enough that what the learned Beveregius has brought forward on this point is empty and trifling. What he adds about Dionysius Exiguus we have already examined above, when we weighed the Pearsonian Vindiciae. For the learned man's observation about the time when Dionysius worked out his collection of Canons does no harm at all to the hypothesis we defend, since it was made after the date assigned by Dallaeus.

units.la: Pergit Beveregius & Justiniani Imperatoris testimonio, Dallæi de Canonum antiquitate sententiam refellere suamque confirmare nititur; quia hos Canones Novella vi. laudare videtur hisce verbis quæ ex illâ constitutione describit Vir doctus, Quod quidem certè futurum credimus, si sacri illi Canones diligenter observentur, quos nunquam satis laudati, adorationeque digni, & qui ipsum Filium Dei conspexerunt, illi-que ministrarunt Apostoli nobis reliquerunt, ac Sancti Patres custodierunt, & interpreta-ti sunt. Hæc de LXXXV. Canonibus Apostolicis interpretatur Vir doctus, nec ab eo hac in re dissentit Dallæus, sed propterea Dallæi sententiam non confutat Beveregius, quandoquidem Justinianus quinquaginta plusminus annos post tempus à Dallæo denotatum Imperator renunciatus est: At inquit Vir doctus, si hi Canones præcedente tantum seculo eoque adulto ab hæretico aliquo confecti fuissent, miror nullum tunc temporis Dallæum extitisse, qui Imperatori aurem velleret, eumque certiorem faceret, Canones abipso laudatos, non inter antiqua nedum Apostolica decreta, sed inter nuperrimè consarcinata recentiorum hæreticorum figmenta recensendos esse. Si valeret hæc Beveregij ratiocinatio, eadem planè ratione librorum Sibyllinorum causam tueri possem: Nemo enim nescit à Justino Martyre, à Theophilo Antiocheno, à Clemente Alexandrino, à Tertulliano & aliis laudatos fuisse istos libros; quamvis Justinus iisdem scripserit diebus quibus conflata sunt Oracula Sibyllina, Theophilus verò, Clemens, Tertullianus post Justinum quidem, sed eodem seculo: fiigitur[?] Viri docéti[?] verba hoc pacto usurpem, miror nullum tunc temporis Blondellum extitisse, qui Scriptoribus istis aurem velleret, eosque certiores faceret, Oracula ab ipsis laudata, non inter antiqua nedum Noachi Nurus seu Berosi filiæ Oracula, sed inter nuperrimè confarcinata recentiorum Impostorum figmenta recensenda esse: si inquam hæc illius verba usurpem, quid responsurus sit non video; objectionem enim nostram diluere non potest, quin suam pariter diluat, neque nobis respondere quin sibi ipsi respondeat: idem dico de Constantino Imperatore qui de Sibyllinis Oraculis magnificentiùs loquutus est, quàm de Canonibus Apostolicis Justinianus. Sed ut ad ipsos Canones propius accedamus, quos ab Apostolis sancitos opinabatur Justinianus, miror nullum tunc temporis extitisse Beveregium, qui Imperatori aurem velleret, eumque certiorem faceret, ab Apostolis minimè conditos esse, sed secundo exeunte tertiove nondum adulto seculo à primitivis Synodis constitutos, & mox etiam in corpus istud quod etiamnum habemus collectos fuisse: Nam hæc est de horum Canonum antiquitate Viri doćti sententia. Tamen quemadmodum ex eo quod nullus Beveregius Imperatorem hac de re monuit, non sequitur Canones ab Apostolis reapse sanctitos esse, sic etiam ex eo quod nullus tunc temporis Dallæus extitit qui Justinianum certiorem redderet istorum Canonum Syllogen à recentioribus impostoribus, in eam quam videmus formam conflatam esse, non sequitur adeò vetustam esse ut existimat Vir doctus; Ultra progreditur doctissimus Beveregius, & quoniam Joannes Presbyter Antiochenus qui circa suprema Justiniani Augusti tempora ad thronum CP. promotus est, Canones Apostolicos in suo Nomocanone reliquis Synodalibus interseruit, hinc colligit partem Nomocanonis prius constitutos esse: Verùm quando nullam dicti sui rationem adfert, nulloque Veterum Scriptorum testimonio suam confirmat assertionem, non est quod in istis refellendis immoremur, unum tamen est quod satis mirari nequeo, Beveregium scilicet hoc gratis proferre, nulla prorsus mentione factâ alterius Nomocanonis Joannis Antiocheni Nomocanone vetustioris; si ostenderet Vir doctus extitisse ante Joannem Antiochenum Nomocanonem cui inserti erant Apostolici Canones, concederemus eos à Joanne Antiocheno aliorum exemplo suo insertos esse ; At quia nihil ejusmodi demonstrare potest, perperam asserit Joannem Antiochenum Apostolorum Canones suo Nomocanoni inseruisse, eo nomine quod pars Nomocanonis prius constituti essent; Certè satius erit dicere Joannem Antiochenum sua sponte nulloque provocatum exemplo hoc fecisse, post suam Canonum collectionem ante Nomocanonem elaboratam, & in quâ primi occurrunt Apostolici, saltem dum exhibetur Canonum ordo seu dispositio, necnon in totius Operis Præfatione. Nec quicquam causæ est cur Justiniani Imperatoris Dignitatem, atque doctissimorum Virorum quos ille ad Ecclesiasticas pariter ac civiles colligendas leges undique convocaverat, urgeat eruditionem, perinde ac Joannis Constantinopolitani Episcopi, reliquorumque Græcarum Ecclesiarum Antistitum, ut inde concludat Canones Apostolicos quos ab omnibus observari præcipiunt, adeò vetustos esse, ut si non ab ipsis Apostolis, à Viris saltem Apostolicis secundo tertiove post Christum incarnatum seculo constitutos esse ; Plus enim ei largimur quàm postulat , fatémur siquidem Justinianum & Viros illos doctissimos quorum meminit , existimasse Canones de quibus lis est ab ipsis Apostolis veré conditos esse , ac proinde antiquissimos utpote primis Christianismi annis constitutos ; & nisi hoc eis persuasum fuisset , eos dubio procul tanquam fictos & spurios rejecissent : Beveregius autem disertè negat ab Apostolis fuisse sancitos , nihil ergo in gratiam hypothesis suæ exsculpere potest, vel à Justiniano , vel à Joanne Antiocheno, vel à cæteris quos designat Viris doctissimis ; Antiquitas enim quam Canonibus adscribunt Apostolicis , ab eâ plane diversa est quam illis tribuit Vir doctus ; illi siquidem nullam aliam eis assingunt antiquitatem, præter Apostolicam ab ipsis manantem Apostolis, quos velut legitimos Canonum parentes venerantur , alia mens Beveregio qui eos secundo tertiove ineunte post Verbi incarnationem seculo conditos arbitratur : Hæ duæ opiniones ut quivis videt sibi invicem adversantur , nec amicè conciliari queunt ; Nam si obtinet Justiniani de Canonum antiquitate sententia , ruit Beveregiana ; At si stat Beveregiana, pessum ibit Justinianea : Quomodo quæso una consistere possunt duæ opiniones , quarnm altera Canones ab ipsis Apostolis sancitos affirmat, altera vero tertio ineunte seculo longè post mortem Apostolorum constitutos esse contendit? Et quamvis minus absurdam putem Beveregii quàm Justiniani de Canonum vetustate sententiam, non ideo probabilis mihi videtur, cùm nullo solido nitatur fundamento, nullisque rationum momentis hactenus confirmari potuerit.
units.tr: Beveregius goes on to use the testimony of the Emperor Justinian, trying to refute Dallaeus's opinion about the antiquity of the Canons and to confirm his own. He thinks Justinian praises these Canons in Novella 6, in these words, which the learned man quotes from that constitution: "This will certainly come to pass, we believe, if those holy Canons are carefully observed, which the Apostles, who saw the Son of God himself and ministered to him, have left to us, and which the holy Fathers have guarded and interpreted. They are never sufficiently praised and deserve reverence." The learned man takes this as referring to the eighty-five Apostolic Canons, and Dallaeus does not disagree with him on this point. Beveregius, however, does not on that account refute Dallaeus's view, since Justinian became emperor some fifty years or so after the date Dallaeus assigned. But, the learned man says, if these Canons had been compiled by some heretic in the preceding century, and that century already well advanced, I wonder that no Dallaeus arose at that time to pull the emperor's ear and warn him that the Canons quoted by him should not be counted among ancient, let alone Apostolic, decrees, but among the fabrications of recent heretics, stitched together not long ago. If Beveregius's reasoning held good, I could defend the cause of the Sibylline books by exactly the same argument. No one doubts that these books were quoted by Justin Martyr, Theophilus of Antioch, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian and others. Justin, it is true, wrote in the same days in which the Sibylline Oracles were put together, while Theophilus, Clement and Tertullian wrote after Justin but in the same century. If I were to use the learned man's words in this way, I would wonder that no Blondel arose at that time to pull these writers' ears and warn them that the oracles they quoted should not be counted among ancient oracles, let alone those of Noah's daughters-in-law or the daughters of Berosus, but among the recently stitched-together fabrications of recent impostors. If I were to use his words in this way, I do not see what he would reply. He cannot dissolve our objection without dissolving his own too, nor answer us without answering himself. I say the same of the Emperor Constantine, who spoke more grandly of the Sibylline Oracles than Justinian did of the Apostolic Canons. But to come closer to the Canons themselves, which Justinian believed were sanctioned by the Apostles: I wonder that no Beveregius arose at that time to pull the emperor's ear and warn him that they were by no means founded by the Apostles, but were set up by the early synods at the end of the second or in the third century, not yet well advanced, and were soon also gathered into the body of canons we still have. For this is the learned man's opinion about the antiquity of these Canons. Yet just as the fact that no Beveregius warned the emperor about this does not mean that the Canons were really sanctioned by the Apostles, so the fact that no Dallaeus arose at that time to inform Justinian that the collection of these Canons was put together in the form we see by recent impostors does not mean that it is as old as the learned man thinks. Beveregius goes further still. Because John the Presbyter of Antioch, who was promoted to the throne of Constantinople near the last years of the Emperor Justinian, inserted the Apostolic Canons among the other synodal canons in his Nomocanon, Beveregius infers that the part of the Nomocanon was constituted earlier. But since he offers no reason for his claim and confirms his assertion by no testimony of the ancient writers, there is no need for us to linger on refuting it. One thing, however, I cannot sufficiently wonder at: that Beveregius puts this forward without any mention of another Nomocanon, older than the Nomocanon of John of Antioch. If the learned man showed that there existed, before John of Antioch, a Nomocanon into which the Apostolic Canons had been inserted, we would grant that John of Antioch inserted them following the example of others. But since he can demonstrate nothing of the kind, he wrongly asserts that John of Antioch inserted the Apostles' Canons into his Nomocanon on the ground that a part of the Nomocanon had been constituted earlier. It would certainly be better to say that John of Antioch did this of his own accord, without being prompted by any example, after making his own collection of canons, and before the Nomocanon was worked out, a collection in which the Apostolic Canons appear first, at least where the order or arrangement of the canons is set out, and also in the preface to the whole work. Nor is there any reason why Beveregius should press the dignity of the Emperor Justinian, and the learning of the most learned men whom he summoned from every quarter to collect the ecclesiastical and civil laws, or that of John, Bishop of Constantinople, and the other leaders of the Greek churches, in order to conclude from them that the Apostolic Canons, which they order to be observed by all, are so ancient that, if they were not made by the Apostles themselves, they were at least made by men of apostolic times, in the second or third century after Christ was made flesh. For I grant him more than he asks. I concede that Justinian and those most learned men whom he mentions thought that the Canons in question were truly made by the Apostles themselves, and therefore very ancient, having been set up in the first years of Christianity. And if they had not been persuaded of this, they would undoubtedly have rejected them as fictitious and spurious. But Beveregius expressly denies that they were sanctioned by the Apostles. So he cannot extract anything in favour of his hypothesis, whether from Justinian, from John of Antioch, or from the other most learned men he names. The antiquity which they ascribe to the Apostolic Canons is quite different from that which the learned man assigns to them. They attribute to them no other antiquity than the apostolic, flowing from the Apostles themselves, whom they revere as the lawful parents of the Canons. Beveregius has a different view, since he thinks they were made in the early part of the second or third century after the Word was made flesh. As anyone can see, these two opinions are opposed to each other and cannot be reconciled in friendship. For if Justinian's opinion about the antiquity of the Canons holds, Beveregius's falls, and if Beveregius's stands, Justinian's will perish. How, I ask, can two opinions stand together, one of which affirms that the Canons were sanctioned by the Apostles themselves, while the other contends that they were constituted in the early third century, long after the death of the Apostles? And although I think Beveregius's view of the Canons' antiquity is less absurd than Justinian's, it does not seem probable to me, since it rests on no solid foundation and has so far been unable to be confirmed by any weighty arguments.

units.la: Porrò Vir doctus conjecturam suam profert de primo Canonum collectore, quem Clementem Alexandrinum arbitratur, & hujusce conjecturæ rationes adducit in Canonem ultimum pag. 40. ubi observat primò eundem fuisse, qui Canones hosce, ac qui Constitutiones Apostolicas collegit, & quidem eum Clementem nuncupatum fuisse, quem tamen alium esse ab Episcopo Romano, qui ad Corinthios scripsit, exinde liquere opinatur, quod Clemens iste ab Epistolarum scriptore distinguitur, saltem ita videtur Beveregio, quoniam dum in ipso Canone Clementis Epistolæ commemorantur, non dicitur ἐμὲ Κλήμεντος, sed in genere, sine adjecto pronomine, Clementis Epistolæ duæ; at ubi de Constitutionibus agitur pronomen etiam præficitur, Constitutiones vobis Episcopis per me Clementem δὲ[?] ἐμοῦ Κλήμεντος. Hæc Viri docti observatio adeò levis est, ut satis mirari nequam[?] cur eam scripto mandare voluerit; Ex ipsis siquidem Constitutionibus liquet, impostorem qui eas in illam quam videmus speciem consarcinavit, omnibus persuasum voluisse illas ab ipsis Apostolis scriptas & per Clementem Romanum fuisse perlatas, prout à Dallæo fusè ac solidè demonstratum est de Pseudepigraphis lib. 1. Cap. XIX. Verùm missis istis Constitutionibus quæ non sunt instituti nostri, ad Canones redeo quos ab eodem Clemente, non Romano illo quidem, sed Alexandrino, æquè ac Constitutiones, collectos suspicatur; sed quantum à vero aberret hæc Beveregii conjectura, omnique prorsus careat verisimilitudine, jam supra demonstravimus, dum eam fuisse Collectorum mentem probavimus, ut verè ab Apostolis omnes conditi, atque editi crederentur, & hic, qui eos continet Codex ab ipsis Apostolis factus promulgatusque censeretur quod certè ex Canonibus XXIX. L. LXXXII. & LXXXV. colligitur. Vir tamen doctus apud Eusebium se reperisse putat, quo conjecturam suam tueatur, quia scilicet Eusebius Hist. lib. 6. cap. XIII. testatur Clementem Alexandrinum librum scripsisse cui titulus fuit Κανὼν ἐκκλησιαστικὸς ἢ περὶ τοὺς ἰουδαΐζοντας[?], quæ verba sic latinè reddidit Clarissimus Valesius, Liber ille qui Ecclesiastica regula inscribitur, seu adversus eos qui errores Judæorum sequuntur. Nec quicquam in illa verba ut pote intellectu facillima annotavit Vir ille eruditissimus, liquido enim constat regulam illam cujus [illegible, ~8 letters] Eusebius eos solum spectare qui Judæorum sequebantur errores : Ex illis tamen infert Beveregius Clementem Alexandrinum primum fuisse Canonum Apostolicorum Collectorem ; sed nullius planè momenti erit ista Beveregii inductio, quandiu non probabit omnes quibus de agimus Canones, adversus eos qui errores Judæorum sequuntur, constitutos esse; hoc siquidem Canonis Ecclesiastici à Clemente conscripti & ab Eusebio commemorati unicum fuit argumentum, nec alios quam judaizantes feriebat : Eusebii verbis adjicit D. Hieronymi testimonium qui in Catalogo Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum eundem Clementem Scripsisse refert, De Canonibus Ecclesiasticis, & adversum eos, qui Judæorum sequuntur errorem ; idem observat Photius à Viro docto etiam laudatus Cod. cxi. sed ipsissima Sophronii Hieronymiani Catalogi Interpretis Græci verba non describit, nec etiam Eusebii, quamvis istius menti sese accommodet, ejusque verborum sensum non male exhibeat hoc pacto, Scripsit de Canonibus Ecclesiasticis, adversum eos qui Judæorum sequuntur errorem; Photius ergo æque ac Eusebius testatur librum Clementis de Canonibus Ecclesiasticis, adversum judaizantes tantum conscriptum fuisse; Hieronymus vero qui opus adversus judaizantes à Canonum[?] Ecclesiasticorum libro distinguere videtur, ipsius Eusebii verbis à quo sua accepit emendandus est, & in rectam à quâ deviavit viam revocandus: Præterea liber Canonum Ecclesiasticorum non idem est cum libro Canonum Apostolicorum: At Canones hosce (inquit Beveregius pag. 40.) qui jam APOSTOLICI vocantur, ECCLESIASTICOS olim dictos fuisse, in Præfatione ex Veterum Scriptorum monumentis palam fecimus. Nos verò contrà luce meridianâ clarius demonstravimus, Canones illos Ecclesiasticos, quorum in Præfatione meminit Vir doctus, alios plane fuisse ab Apostolicis, qui ubi primum in unum corpus collecti sunt, Apostolorum nomen juxta Collectorum mentem præferunt, & Apostolici appellati sunt; Quamplurima in iis, ait pag. 40. contra Judæos decernuntur, esto, decernantur in hisce Canonibus quamplurima contra Judæos, dummodo plerique, quod diffiteri non potest Beveregius, alio respiciant, & in alium collineent scopum; Liber autem Clementis cui titulus fuit Canon [?]on Ecclesiasticus adversus solos Judaizantes compositus est, nec alios perstringebat praeter eos qui Judaeorum sequebantur errores, sive in Paschatis celebratione, sive in caeterorum Synagogae Judaicae ritum observatione. Ergo tantum abest ut credibilis sit Beveregii conjectura, in dicto scilicet Clementis libro Apostolicos hosce Canones primo collectos fuisse & divulgatos, quod nihil magis absonum magisque absurdum ab eo usquam dici potuerit.
units.tr: Moreover, the learned man puts forward his conjecture about the first collector of the Canons, whom he thinks was Clement of Alexandria, and he gives the reasons for this conjecture in his note on the last Canon, page 40. There he observes, first, that the same man collected these Canons and the Apostolic Constitutions, and that this Clement was named as the one who is distinct from the Roman bishop who wrote to the Corinthians. He thinks this is clear because the Clement of the Canons is distinguished from the writer of the Epistles, at least as it seems to Beveregius: when the Epistles of Clement are mentioned in the Canon itself, the author does not say "by me Clement" but speaks in general terms without a pronoun, Clementis Epistolæ duæ ("the two Epistles of Clement"). But where the Constitutions are discussed, the pronoun is added: Constitutiones vobis Episcopis per me Clementem ("the Constitutions to you bishops by me Clement") [ἐμοῦ Κλήμεντος]. This observation of the learned man is so trivial that I can hardly wonder why he wanted to put it in writing. For it is clear from the Constitutions themselves that the impostor who stitched them together into the form we see wished everyone to believe that they were written by the Apostles themselves and carried to us by Clement of Rome, as Dallaeus has demonstrated fully and soundly in his book on the Pseudepigrapha, book 1, chapter 19. But, setting aside these Constitutions, which are not the subject of my study, I return to the Canons, which he suspects were collected by the same Clement, not indeed the Roman but the Alexandrian, just as the Constitutions were. How far from the truth this conjecture of Beveregius is, and how utterly lacking in any likelihood, I have already shown above, when I proved that the intention of the collectors was that all the Canons should be believed to have been truly composed and issued by the Apostles, and that this code, which contains them, should be considered to have been made and promulgated by the Apostles themselves. This is certainly gathered from Canons 29, 82 and 85. Yet the learned man thinks he has found in Eusebius something to support his conjecture, namely that Eusebius, in Church History book 6, chapter 13, testifies that Clement of Alexandria wrote a book entitled Κανὼν ἐκκλησιαστικὸς ἢ περὶ τοὺς ἰουδαΐζοντας ("Ecclesiastical Rule, or concerning those who Judaize"). The most illustrious Valesius rendered these words into Latin thus: Liber ille qui Ecclesiastica regula inscribitur, seu adversus eos qui errores Judæorum sequuntur ("that book which is entitled The Ecclesiastical Rule, or against those who follow the errors of the Jews"). That most learned man made no note on these words, as they are very easy to understand. For it is clearly established that the rule (of which the title is illegible) was aimed by Eusebius only at those who followed the errors of the Jews. Yet Beveregius infers from these words that Clement of Alexandria was the first collector of the Apostolic Canons. But this inference of Beveregius will have no weight at all, unless he proves that all the Canons we are discussing were directed against those who follow the errors of the Jews. For this was the sole subject of the Ecclesiastical Canon written by Clement and mentioned by Eusebius, and it struck none but the Judaizers. To Eusebius's words Jerome adds his testimony, who in the Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers reports that the same Clement wrote De Canonibus Ecclesiasticis, & adversum eos, qui Judæorum sequuntur errorem ("On the Ecclesiastical Canons, and against those who follow the error of the Jews"). Photius, whom the learned man also cites (Codex 111), makes the same observation, but he does not give the exact words of Sophronius, the Greek translator of Jerome's Catalogue, nor those of Eusebius, although he conforms to Eusebius's meaning and expresses the sense of his words not badly in this way: "He wrote de Canonibus Ecclesiasticis, against those who follow the error of the Jews." Photius, therefore, like Eusebius, testifies that Clement's book on the Ecclesiastical Canons was written only against the Judaizers. Jerome, who seems to distinguish the work against the Judaizers from the book of Ecclesiastical Canons, must be corrected by the words of Eusebius, from whom he took his account, and brought back to the right path he has strayed from. Moreover, the book of the Ecclesiastical Canons is not the same as the book of the Apostolic Canons. Beveregius says on page 40: At Canones hosce ("But these Canons") qui jam ("which now") vocantur APOSTOLICI ("are called Apostolic"), ECCLESIASTICOS olim dictos fuisse, in Præfatione ex Veterum Scriptorum monumentis palam fecimus ("that they were formerly called Ecclesiastical, as we made clear in the Preface from the records of the ancient writers"). But we, on the contrary, have demonstrated more clearly than the noonday light that those Ecclesiastical Canons, which the learned man mentions in his Preface, were quite different from the Apostolic ones. Once these were gathered into one body, they bear the name of the Apostles, in accordance with the intention of the collectors, and they were called Apostolic. He says on page 40 that very many decrees in them are directed against the Jews. Granted, very many decrees in these Canons are against the Jews, provided that, as Beveregius cannot deny, most of them look to another object and aim at another goal. But the book of Clement entitled Ecclesiastical Canon was composed against the Judaizers alone and attacked none but those who followed the errors of the Jews, whether in the celebration of Easter or in the observance of the other rites of the Jewish synagogue. Therefore, Beveregius's conjecture, that Clement's book in question first collected and published these Apostolic Canons, is so far from credible that nothing more absurd or unlikely could ever have been said by him.

units.la: Posteaquam ea omnia discussimus quae pro suorum Canonum antiquitate in Praesatione adduxit eruditissimus Beveregius, quae in singulis explicandis Canonibus observat, superest ut percurramus, quae inquā ad rem quam tractamus spectant: Sed quoniam pleraque à nobis hactenus confutata sunt, vel à Dallaeo occupata fuerant ac explosa pensum susceptum facile absolvemus, verbi gratia ad Can. 1. & LXXVI. minime respexisse Theodoretum Hist. lib. 5. cap. XXIII. ostendimus, nec ad XVI. cum XII.XIII. Alexandrum Alexandrinum Episcopum apud Theodoretum Hist. Eccles. lib. 1. cap. IV. nec denique probari posse septimum à Conciliis quorum meminit Eusebius Hist. Eccles. lib. 3. cap. XXIII. secundo seculo exeunte constitutum esse. Canones autem XXI. XXII. XXIII. XXIV. de iis qui se abscindunt, expenderat Dallæus, eorumque novitatem ex iis quæ de-cernunt appositè collegerat, varia prose-rens voluntariæ abscissionis exempla, Ori-genis imprimis qui corpus suum evitare ausus est, ejusmodi facinus minimè aggressurus egregius adolescens, tantæque jam in illa ætate eruditionis, ut Scholæ Alexandrinæ Ecclesiæ præesset, si in publicâ Ecclesiæ luce extitissent tunc temporis Canones sub excommunicationis vel depositionis poena id prohibentes; Veri tamen haud dissimile videtur, si Beveregium audimus, aliquos saltem eorum, si non omnes, ad quos Demetrius scripserat, Episcopos, in unum congregatos, hac de re deliberationem injisse, & quatuor hos de Eu-nuchis Canones vel primò constituisse, vel ante constitutos renovasse, quod ultimum illi magis arridet; Mihi verò summopere displicet, non solum quia omni prorsus veri specie caret Origenem adeò audax facinus fuisse aggressurum, si extitisset aliquis ejusmodi Canon, sed etiam quoniam Demetrius de violato ab Origene Canone nusquam conquestus est, istjusmodi Canonis, inquit Vir doctus, expressè non meminit, eum tamen obscurè indigetare videtur, cùm de spontaneâ Origenis exectione certior factus, eum bono animo esse jubet, Eufeb. Hift. lib. 6. cap. viii. Quis præter Beveregium ex istis Demetrii verbis concluderet aliquem adversus eos qui se abscindunt Canonem ab Origene violatum esse ? Nonne abunde sufficiebat Demetrio, quod Origenes rem adeò absurdam, & à naturæ, civitatumque, ac Dei denique ipsius legibus alienam ausus esset, ut illum bono animo esse juberet ? Nollem equidem negare, neque negabat Dallæus, quin ex Origenici facinoris occasione, aliquis forasse ab Alexandrinis ante Concilium Nicænum hac de re constitutus fuerit Canon ; At inde non sequitur ad eandem ætatem pertinere quam habemus Canonum Apostolicorum Syllogen; Impostor qui eam consarcinavit sua de iis qui se abscindunt decreta, vel ab hoc Canone si quandoque extitit, vel potius à Nicæno primo mutuo accepit. Demetrius, inquit Vir eruditus, Cæsariensem & Hierosolymitanum Episcopos criminatus est, quod Origenem in Presbyterii gradum promovissent, videlicet contra Can. xxii. quo constituitur, ut qui se mutilavit, ne sit Clericus. Nisi enim, pergit Beveregius, hujusmodi decretum antea editum fuisset, non video quare Demetrius hoc iis vitio verteret. Ego verò aliam istius criminationis causam reperio, in eo scilicet quod commemorati Episcopi Origenem ditionis non suae ad Presbyterii gradum, inconsulto Demetrio promoverunt; hanc autem suisse veram ac legitimam criminationis causam innuit Eusebius Hist. lib. 6. cap. viii. postquam enim observavit Demetrium erga Origenem mutatum, illius facinus literis ad omnes ubique terrarum Episcopos Scriptis, proscindere tanquam absurdissimum caepisse, continenter addit, quia, vel ut vertit Clarissimus Valesius, quippe probatissimi & maximè insignes apud Palaestinam Antistites, Caesariensis scilicet & Hierosolymitanus, cùm Origenem prærogativâ & supremi honoris apice dignum judicassent, manus ei imponentes Presbyterum ordinaverant. Hoc certè Demetrio doluit, idcircò eos accusationibus suis conatus est involvere, nec aliter hunc Eusebii locum interpretatur idem Valesius in annotationibus suis, ut fatetur ipse Beveregius: Eusebius (inquit p.114.) causam aperit, cur Demetrius qui antea Origenem tantopere dilexerat subitò mutatus, eum ubique litteris suis laceraverit; eo quod scilicet Caesariensis & Hierosolymitanus Episcopi eum ad Presbyterii gradum promoviserunt. In quo non mediocris injuria Demetrio illata esse videbatur, tum ab Episcopis illis, tum ab Origene. Ab Origene quidem, quod ab externis Episcopis manus sibi imponi passus fuisset, nec ab Episcopo civitatis suæ honorem illum Presbyterii expectasset : ab Episcopis vero , quod Alexandrinæ schole Magistrum hoc facto ad Ecclesiam suam transtulissent. Nec obstat Epistola Ecclesiastica, quam secum attulisse Origenem Athenas per Palæstinam , ubi ordinatus est , proficiscentem testatur Hieronymus in Catalogo , in Origene & in Alexandro Hierosolymitano Episcopo : Nam si vera sunt quæ narrat Hieronymus, Epistola illa commendatitia tantùm fuit, ut debitum scilicet inculpatis ejus moribus testimonium perhibendo , a fratribus perhumanè exciperetur , illud testimonium signat Alexander apud Hieronymum dum ait Origenem juxta Demetrii testimonium Presbyterum a se constitutum esse. Verùm testimonium Origeni a Demetrio perhibitum , nullum jus Alexandro Palæstinisque Episcopis in eum concedebat , ideoque eum sine Episcopi Alexandrini consensu Presbyterum ordinare non poterant. Præterea de veritate Epistolæ quam secum attulisse Origenem refert Hieronymus non satis constat, illius saltem non meminit Eusebius ; Photius verò vel potius Pamphilus Martyr & Eusebius apud illum Cod. 118. contrarium planè testantur , Origenemque absque Demetrii venià Athenas profectum esse tradunt, hincque in eum excitatam omnem tempestatem commemorant hoc pacto : Demetrius Alexandriæ Præsul, Origenem multum laudans, in paucis carissimum habebat. At cum hic absque bonâ suî Episcopi veniâ Athenas profecturus esset, Theotecnus Cæsareæ Palæstinæ tum Episcopus, secus eum quàm opporteret, Presbyterum ordinavit, non improbante factum hoc Alexandro Hierosolymorum Episcopo. Hinc Demetrio amor in odium vertit, laudesque mox cum vituperatione commutatæ. Nec quicquam causæ est cur ista Ægypti & Alexandriæ Episcoporum in Epistolâ Synodicâ adversus Origenis do-ctrinam, verba laudet Vir doctus, Presbyter Ordinatus à Canonicâ & ab unâ verâ manu. Nam primo nimis recentes sunt hi testes, ut de re adeò antiquâ & ante ccc. annos gestâ certò testari possint, deficien-te præsertim vetustiorum autoritate ; Secundò crassissimam rerum Origenis produnt ignorantiam, dùm scribunt eum ab Heracla Alexandriâ pulsum esse quod tamen à Demetrio Heraclæ decessore factum esse nemo nescit ; Tertiò etiamsi demus Viro docto Episcopos Ægypti & Alexandriæ agnoscere Origenem à Canonica manu ordinatum esse, ne hilum quidem proficiet, cùm hoc solum significare voluerint, Origenem ab Episcopo rite & Canonicè ordinato ad Presbyterii gradum fuisse promotum, & forte ab ipso Demetrio promotum falso putarunt, & deinde ab Heracla ejus successore Alexandria pulsum adeo istarum rerum fuerunt ignari. Ex his omnibus liquet Demetrium Episcopos Cæsariensem & Hierosolymitanum criminatum esse, quod suæ ditionis hominem se inconsulto Presbyterum constituerunt, in Origenem vero exarsisse quod ab externis Episcopis manus sibi imponi passus est, cum ab Episcopo civitatis suæ honorem illum Presbyterii expectare debuisset.
units.tr: Having now examined all the points that the most learned Beveregius brought forward in his Preface for the antiquity of his canons, and the observations he makes in explaining the individual canons, it remains to go through what concerns the matter we are treating. Since most of these have already been refuted by us, or were previously taken up and dismissed by Dallaeus, I shall easily finish the task I have undertaken. For example, we have shown that Can. 1 and LXXVI do not refer at all to Theodoret, Hist. lib. 5, cap. XXIII; nor do XVI and XII-XIII refer to Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, in Theodoret, Hist. Eccles. lib. 1, cap. IV; nor can it be proved that the seventh canon was established at the end of the second century by the councils that Eusebius mentions, Hist. Eccles. lib. 3, cap. XXIII. Dallaeus had examined canons XXI, XXII, XXIII and XXIV, concerning those who mutilate themselves, and had fittingly gathered their novelty from what they decree, setting out various examples of voluntary self-mutilation, above all that of Origen, who dared to do this deed, though he was an outstanding young man who would never have undertaken such a crime, and who was already at that age so learned that he presided over the school of the Church at Alexandria. If canons forbidding this under penalty of excommunication or deposition had then existed in the open light of the Church, he would not have done it. Yet it seems not unlike the truth, if we listen to Beveregius, that at least some, if not all, of the bishops to whom Demetrius had written gathered together, took counsel on this matter, and either first established these four canons on eunuchs or renewed them after they had been established earlier; this latter view pleases him more. But I strongly disapprove, not only because there is no appearance of truth at all in the idea that Origen would have dared such a bold deed if any such canon had existed, but also because Demetrius never complained that a canon had been violated by Origen. The learned man says that Demetrius does not expressly mention any such canon, though he seems to hint at it obscurely, when, having been informed of Origen's voluntary castration, he bids him be of good cheer, Eusebius, Hist. lib. 6, cap. viii. Who, apart from Beveregius, would conclude from these words of Demetrius that Origen had violated a canon against those who mutilate themselves? Was it not enough for Demetrius that Origen had dared a deed so absurd, and so alien to nature, to civil societies, and indeed to the laws of God himself, that he bade him be of good cheer? I would indeed not wish to deny, and Dallaeus did not deny, that some canon on this matter may perhaps have been established by the Alexandrians before the Council of Nicaea, on the occasion of Origen's deed. But it does not follow from this that it belongs to the same age as the collection of Apostolic Canons that we have. The impostor who patched it together either took his decrees concerning those who mutilate themselves from this canon, if it ever existed, or, more probably, took them from the First Council of Nicaea. Demetrius, says the learned man, accused the bishops of Caesarea and Jerusalem because they had promoted Origen to the rank of presbyter, plainly contrary to Can. xxii, by which it is decreed that he who has mutilated himself shall not be a cleric. For unless, Beveregius goes on, such a decree had been issued earlier, I do not see why Demetrius would have found fault with this. I, however, find another cause for this accusation: namely, that the bishops mentioned had promoted Origen to the rank of presbyter within a jurisdiction not their own, without consulting Demetrius. That this was the true and legitimate cause of the accusation is indicated by Eusebius, Hist. lib. 6, cap. viii. For after observing that Demetrius had changed towards Origen, and had begun to tear apart his deed in letters written to bishops everywhere as most absurd, he adds at once: because, as the most distinguished Valesius translates it, the most approved and most eminent prelates in Palestine, namely those of Caesarea and Jerusalem, had judged Origen worthy of the privilege and the highest honour, and laying hands upon him had ordained him a presbyter. This certainly grieved Demetrius, and therefore he tried to entangle them in his accusations. Valesius himself, in his notes, interprets this passage of Eusebius no differently, as Beveregius himself admits: Eusebius (he says, p. 114) explains the cause why Demetrius, who had previously loved Origen so much, was suddenly changed and tore him apart everywhere in his letters, namely because the bishops of Caesarea and Jerusalem had promoted him to the rank of presbyter. In this, a considerable wrong seemed to have been done to Demetrius, both by those bishops and by Origen. By Origen indeed, because he had allowed himself to be ordained by bishops from outside, and had not waited for that honour of the presbyterate from the bishop of his own city; by the bishops, because by this act they had transferred the master of the Alexandrian school to their own church. Nor does the ecclesiastical letter, which Jerome, in his Catalogue, under Origen and under Alexander, Bishop of Jerusalem, says Origen carried with him as he set out through Palestine to Athens, where he was ordained, stand in the way. For if what Jerome relates is true, that letter was only a letter of recommendation, so that by bearing the testimony due to his blameless character he might be received very kindly by the brethren. Alexander, in Jerome, signifies this testimony when he says that Origen had been appointed a presbyter by himself according to the testimony of Demetrius. But the testimony that Demetrius gave to Origen conceded no right to Alexander or to the Palestinian bishops over him, and therefore they could not ordain him a presbyter without the consent of the Bishop of Alexandria. Moreover, it is not sufficiently certain whether the letter that Jerome says Origen carried with him was genuine; at least Eusebius does not mention it. Photius, or rather Pamphilus the Martyr and Eusebius as cited by him, Cod. 118, plainly testify the contrary, and report that Origen set out for Athens without Demetrius's permission. They then recount the whole storm that broke out against him, in this way: Demetrius, Bishop of Alexandria, praising Origen greatly, held him very dear in a few respects. But when he was about to set out for Athens without the good permission of his bishop, Theotecnus, then Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, ordained him a presbyter, contrary to what was proper, and Alexander, Bishop of Jerusalem, did not disapprove of this deed. Hence love turned into hatred for Demetrius, and praises were soon exchanged for reproach. Nor is there any reason why the learned man should praise these words of the bishops of Egypt and Alexandria in their Synodal Letter against the doctrine of Origen, a presbyter ordained by a canonical and by one true hand. For, first, these witnesses are too recent to be able to testify with certainty about a matter so ancient and transacted more than three hundred years before, especially since the authority of earlier writers is lacking. Second, they betray the grossest ignorance of Origen's affairs, since they write that he was expelled from Alexandria by Heraclas, which yet no one is unaware was done by Demetrius, Heraclas's predecessor. Third, even if we grant the learned man that the bishops of Egypt and Alexandria acknowledge that Origen was ordained by a canonical hand, it will not help him in the least, since they could have meant only this: that Origen had been promoted to the rank of presbyter by a bishop duly and canonically ordained, and perhaps they falsely thought he had been promoted by Demetrius himself; and then, being so ignorant of these matters, they had him expelled from Alexandria by Heraclas, his successor. From all this it is clear that Demetrius accused the bishops of Caesarea and Jerusalem because they had made a man from his jurisdiction a presbyter without consulting him, and that he burst out against Origen because he had allowed himself to be ordained by bishops from outside, when he ought to have awaited that honour of the presbyterate from the bishop of his own city.

units.la: Argumento ex Canone xxv. ducto quasi à Basilio sub antiqui Canonis nomine laudatus esset abunde satisfecit Dallæus, quæ de Prætextato Rhotomagensi Episcopo ibidem scribit Beveregius, Dallæi de Canonum antiquitate sententiam nimimè pulsant: Hanc enim Canonum syllogen seculo quinto adulto conflatam ac consarcinatam esse arbitratur Dallæus, quæ autem in Can. xxv. ex Gregorio Turonensi narrat Vir doctus seculo sexto inclinato & ferè præcipiti contigerunt, hoc est centum circiter annos post tempus à Dallæo denotatum: Nemini igitur mirum videri deberet, si intra tantum temporis intervallum, hisce Canonibus consensum tandem præbuissent Gallicani Præsules: Verum rem ita narrat Gregorius Turonensis ut Beveregii causæ non parùm noceat; ex illa, siquidem narratione liquet Canones quibus de agimus Gallicanis Episcopis hactenus incognitos fuisse, nec Canonum Codici quo utebantur insertos: Nam Gregorius de quaternione qui Apostolicos continebat Canones, tanquam de novo quaternione loquitur, & Gallicano Canonum Codici novissimè adnexo: Beveregius cautè egit, & quaternionis novitate ossensus, hæc Gregorij verba quaternio novus in ista commutavit, quaternio unus; Gregorius tamen quaternionem illum novum nuncupat, & de Rege Chilperico qui eum transmiserat verba faciens, sic rem narrat. Ipse vero ad Metatum discessit, transmittens librum Canonum in quo erat quaternio novus adnexus, habens Canones quasi Apostolicos continentes hæc: Episcopus in homicidio, adulterio, & perjurio deprehensus à Sacerdotio divellatur. In Canonem xxvi. innuit Concilium Chalcedonense Can. 14. ad hunc Apostolicum Canonem respexisse his verbis, Quoniam in nonnullis Provinciis concessum est Lectoribus & Cantoribus uxores ducere: Sed fallitur Vir doctus, Canon siquidem Chalcedonensis nonnullas tantùm memorat Provincias in quibus Lectoribus & Cantoribus concessum erat uxores duce-re: [?]se : Apostolicus vero illis solis ubique gen-tium hoc permittit, illis inquam solis ut habent Canonis verba; Ex iis qui non du-ctâ[?] uxore ad clerum promoti sunt, jubemus, si velint, uxorem ducere, Lectores & Cantores solos: At Chalcedonenses Patres voce exclusivâ solos non utuntur, nempe ad nonnullarum Provinciarum consuetudinem respiciebant, in quibus Lectoribus & Cantoribus hoc jus concedebatur, verbi gratia in Africanis ubi non soli Lectores & Cantores, ut sciscunt Apostolici Canones, hoc jure gaudebant, sed quotquot ad Clerum promoti erant, exceptis Episcopis, Presbyteris & Diaconis, prout liquet ex Codice Canonum Ecclesiæ Africanæ Can. iii. iv. xvi. lxx. quorum tres primi anno Domini cccccxix. conditi sunt, ultimus anno cccci. sancitus fuit, & ad varias Ecclesiarum consuetudines perinde ac Chalcedonensis accommodatus, ecce Canonis verba, Præterea, cùm de quorumdam Clericorum, quamvis erga uxores proprias, incontinentia referretur: placuit, Episcopos, & Presbyteros, & Diaconos secundùm priora statuta etiam ab uxoribus continere: quod nisi fecerint, ab Ecclesiastico removeantur officio. CÆTEROS AUTEM CLERICOS ad hoc nō cogi, sed secundum uniuscuiusque Ecclesiæ consuetudinem observari debere. Profectò non est verifimile Carthaginenfes Patres hoc Decretum fancituroc esse, nec Ecclesiarum confuetudinem memoraturos, fi extitisset tunc temporis Apostolicus Canon qui solis Lectoribus & cantoribus uxores ducendi potestatem concedit. Canonem XXIX. contra Simoniacos expendimus & adversus Pearsonium demonstravimus nihil pro istius Syllogesantiquitatehinc[?] exsculpi posse; Tamen si Beveregio credimus hic Canon ipsis Tertulliani diebus observatus est, quoniam Tertulianus hæc scribit Apolog. cap. XXXIX. Præsident probati quique seniores honorem istum non pretio, sed testimonio adepti, neque enim pretio ulla res Dei constat: Fateor obtinuisse ipsis Tertuliani diebus sanctissimam hanc disciplinam, ut nemo per pecunias ad Ecclesiasticas promoveretur Dignitates; At inde sequi nego observatum fuisse tunc temporis Apostolicum Canonem: Immò ex hac Tertullianei ævi disciplinâ, & ex Canonibus S. Basilii & Concilii Chalcedonensis, & forsan aliis suum conflavit Planus ille qui istam Canonum farraginem consarcinavit. Argumentis ex Canonibus. XXXIV. XXXV. XLIX. L. desumptis occurrit Clarissimus Dallæus: Nos verò ea refellimus quæ ex XXXVII. XL. XLV. XLVII, descripta sunt. Cæteris quæ à triginta quinque postremis Canonibus sibi ministrari putat Beveregius abunde etiam vel à Dallæo vel à nobis satisfactum est, necnon iis omnibus quæ à vetustioribus Scriptoribus & ab antiquis deprompsit Synodis ad eandem Canonum antiquitatem stabiliendam ac confirmandam. Quamobrem hîc sisto gradum, etsi plures adhuc in annotationes Beveregianas fieri possent observationes, cum in eas quibus Canones illustravit Apostolicos, tum in alias quibus cæteris Canonibus aliquam lucem afferre conatus est: sed ne scribendi cacoëthe me laborare putet eruditissimus Beveregius, hoc labore haud invitus supersedeo: Eo magis quod præstantissimum Dallæum Virum nunquam satis laudatum adversus duos celeberrimos adversarios tueri ac defendere tantùm mihi propositum fuit: an id recte præstiterim necne, aliorum esto judicium.
units.tr: Having argued from Canon 25, which Beveregius cites as if from Basil under the name of an "ancient canon," Dallaeus has amply answered him. What Beveregius writes there about Prætextatus, bishop of Rouen, does not overturn Dallaeus's view of the antiquity of the canons. Dallaeus holds that this collection of canons was pieced together in the mature fifth century. The events Canon 25 narrates from Gregory of Tours, however, happened in the sixth century, when it was already declining and nearly headlong, about a hundred years after the date Dallaeus assigns. No one should therefore find it strange that within so short an interval the Gallican bishops at last gave their assent to these canons. Yet Gregory tells the story in a way that does real harm to Beveregius's cause. His narrative makes clear that the canons in question were unknown to the Gallican bishops until then and were not inserted in the canon-book they used. Gregory speaks of the quire that contained the Apostolic canons as a new quire, newly attached to the Gallican canon-book. Beveregius, cautious and offended by the novelty of the quire, changed Gregory's words quaternio novus ("new quire") into quaternio unus ("one quire"). Gregory nonetheless calls it a new quire, and in speaking of King Chilperic, who had sent it, he relates the matter thus: "He himself departed to Metatus, sending a book of canons in which a new quire was attached, containing canons as if Apostolic, namely: a bishop caught in murder, adultery, or perjury is to be torn from the priesthood." On Canon 26, Beveregius claims that the Council of Chalcedon, Canon 14, had this Apostolic canon in view when it said, "Since in some provinces readers and singers have been permitted to take wives." But the learned man is mistaken. The Chalcedonian canon mentions only some provinces in which readers and singers were allowed to marry. The Apostolic canon, by contrast, grants this permission everywhere and to these alone, I say to these alone, as the words of the canon have it: "Of those who have been promoted to the clergy without having taken a wife, we order that, if they wish, they may take a wife: readers and singers only." The Chalcedonian Fathers, however, do not use the exclusive word "only." They had in mind the custom of certain provinces, where this right was granted to readers and singers. In Africa, for example, the right was enjoyed not only by readers and singers, as the Apostolic canons decree, but by all who had been promoted to the clergy, except bishops, presbyters and deacons. This is clear from the Code of Canons of the African Church, canons 3, 4, 16 and 70. Of these, the first three were enacted in the year of the Lord 419 and the last in 400-something, and it was adapted to the various customs of the churches just as the Chalcedonian canon was. Behold the words of the canon: "Moreover, since it was reported that some clerics were incontinent even towards their own wives, it has been decided that bishops, presbyters and deacons, according to the earlier statutes, are to abstain even from their wives; and if they do not, let them be removed from ecclesiastical office. The other clerics are not to be compelled to this, but are to be observed according to the custom of each church." It is certainly not likely that the Carthaginian Fathers would have enacted this decree, or mentioned the custom of the churches, if at that time there had existed an Apostolic canon granting the power to marry to readers and singers alone. We examined Canon 29, against the Simoniacs, and showed against Pearson that nothing supporting the antiquity of that collection can be carved out of it. Yet if we believe Beveregius, this canon was observed in the very days of Tertullian, since Tertullian writes in the Apology, chapter 39: "Approved elders preside, having obtained that honour not by money but by testimony; for nothing of God's is obtained by money." I grant that this most holy discipline prevailed in Tertullian's own day, so that no one was promoted to ecclesiastical dignities through money. But I deny that it follows that the Apostolic canon was observed at that time. Indeed, from this discipline of Tertullian's age, and from the canons of St Basil and the Council of Chalcedon, and perhaps from others, that Planus conflated and patched together his hodgepodge of canons. The most distinguished Dallaeus has met the arguments drawn from Canons 34, 35, 49 and 50, and we have refuted those described from Canons 37, 40, 45 and 47. As for the rest, which Beveregius thinks are supplied to him by the last thirty-five canons, satisfaction has been amply given either by Dallaeus or by us, and likewise for everything he has drawn from older writers and ancient synods to establish and confirm the same antiquity of the canons. Therefore I halt here, although more observations could still be made on the Beveregian annotations, both on those with which he illustrated the Apostolic canons and on those with which he tried to shed light on the other canons. But lest the most learned Beveregius think that I am suffering from an itch to write, I gladly give up this labour. All the more so, since my only purpose has been to defend and uphold the most excellent Dallaeus, a man never praised enough, against two very famous adversaries. Whether I have done this rightly, let others judge.
